The record's first single, an inexplicable remake of 25 or 6 to 4, bombed and threatened to take the album with it.  Will You Still Love Me?  That one saved the day but pretty much locked the band into its seemingly permanent power ballad phase.  Producer David Foster plays down the group's vaunted horn section and utilizes a lot of outside-the-band songwriters for material.  Like I said, it ain't pretty.  Two-and-one-half horns.  Recommended to diehards and Chicago completists, like yours truly.  This review is centered on the Rhino Flashback reissue.

title: CSN:  Live "Allies" by default
text: The inevitable in-concert follow-up to the out of left field success of CSN's Daylight Again, which had begun as a low priority Stills - Nash duo LP.  Atlantic Records execs refused the duo concept and demanded a trio LP (for boosted sales purposes) and so, allies on vinyl if not in arms.  The live album is very nice, but hardly essential, except for the pair of solid studio tracks that open the set, War Games and Raise a Voice.  Leftovers from the Atlantic-refused Stills - Nash project, I believe.  Concert wise, Stills kicks it up a few notches on both Turn Your Back on Love and Dark Star, the trio delivers a lovely cover of the Beatles' Blackbird, Crosby's best moment is also a cover (Joni Mitchell's For Free) but from an earlier tour, and Nash contributes a solid version of his own then-recent hit Wasted on the Way.  All in all, Allies is a curious amalgam of studio, live, and past tour recordings.  I replaced my lost LP with a Japanese CD version several years ago, and I'm very happy with it -- great sound.  Three-and-one-half stars.

title: Failed CSNY reunion project
text: Had high hopes when I bought this one all those many years ago.  CSNY reunion, yeah!  American Dream, the title song, is the only keeper.  And it's a good one. One of Neil Young's best political rockers, based on the trials and travails of JFK wannabe Gary Hart (remember him?).  Otherwise, it's all pretty forgettable filler material, and filled to the brim with an obnoxious air of self-import at that.  Self-righteous rockers from the day desperately trying -- and failing -- to appear current and meaningful in a very changed 1988 musical landscape, a million miles from their early '70s salad days.  For completists only.

title: Dragging out the '60s / '70s anti-war movement as a career move ... eech!
text: Listened to this one for the first time in a very long time recently and now I'm wondering why.  Maybe with everything that's going on in Ukraine and in our own radically politically divided nation my thoughts just drifted in that direction.  Whatever.  Neil Young's Living with War was pure mind cheese, musically, lyrically and politically.  Deja Vu Live simply adds CSN's political dross and musical gloss to those proceedings and has nothing whatever to do with Deja Vu, the group's legendary 1970 LP.  I wish I'd given this one a pass.  My oh my, how the mighty have fallen.  One-and-one-half peace symbols, and I'm being generous.

title: Chicago 16, the band's 1982 comeback album
text: The band's surprise '80s comeback, and it's a good one.  Hard to Say I'm Sorry.  Love Me Tomorrow.  What You're Missing.  Oh, yeah, it's all good, if something of a shift away from their much-celebrated horn-driven '70s sound.  And even bigger things -- and bigger ballads and changes -- were coming a bit farther on down the line in the form of the Peter Cetera-dominated Chicago 17.

title: Yet another Chicago live retrospective
text: The remains of what was once a proud and incredibly inventive '70s horn band (and an '80s power ballad hit machine), along with a revolving door cast of replacement musicians, delivers the big hits live and in-concert one more time.  This band has never really gotten over the untimely death of Terry Kath (the heart and soul of the group), nor the defection of hitmaking singer/songwriter/bassist Peter Cetera for a solo career.  Not to mention the firing of founding member/drummer Danny Seraphine and the fact that Robert Lamm tends to save his most interesting compositions for his own solo efforts.  So, here we go, one more time, into the way-back machine to a better Chicago time of hit singles, huge radio support, and fans who are hungry for more of the same.  But it just ain't the same, is it?  Three-and-one-half stars from a nostalgic, long-time, completist fan.  Recommended to same.

title: The legendary Chicago II, live in-concert, except it's not
text: Chicago II is the one that made me a fan, back when the band and I were young.  It was so impressive that it sent me back to purchase CTA, their first double-album and original band name (Chicago Transit Authority).  All these decades later, here comes this full live in-concert version of Chicago's 1970 breakthrough double-album, except it's not, really.  Band membership makes the difference in this type of 'remembering a classic' situation, doesn't it?  This is through-the-turnstile, new millennium Chicago, the band of a thousand members and ex-members.  So, the music is there and so are Robert Lamm, James Pankow, and Lee Loughnane, along with a cast of hired-gun players.  But where's the heart and soul and deep musical connection?  MIA, sadly.  Maybe it's time to put the legend to rest.  Maybe it's time for the Lamm, Pankow, Loughnane Band.  Two-and-one-half horns from me.  For Chicago cultists / completists only.

title: Chicago at their '80s commercial peak
text: A big record in the day, Chicago 19 marked the end of their second platinum era.  With the exception of Chicago Greatest Hits, 1982-1989, their Warner / Reprise hit years had hit the skids.  The hits were still coming on this collection, but they were mostly power ballads delivered by outside writers.  And the production was very '80s and non-horns.  I Don't Wanna Live Without Your Love.  Look Away.  You're Not Alone.  We Can Last Forever.  What Kind of Man Would I Be?  Big sellers.  Big radio hits.  Big ballads.  But they all had a sense of 'haven't we all been here before?' about them.  And that downbeat sense would bring along the oncoming downturn in record sales and airplay for the studio follow-up, Chicago Twenty-one (a must to avoid).  Three-and-one-half stars from me, mostly for nostalgic reasons.  Recommended for fans of post-Peter Cetera '80s Chicago.

title: Quite possibly the legendary Chicago's worst record
text: A truly boring snoozer of an album, and quite possibly their worst album to that point.  Chasin' the Wind is the only worthwhile track, imho.  I owned the CD back in the day and gave it away to my then-next-door neighbor, a big time Chicago fan.  Being the completist I am, I eventually felt compelled to get a copy back in my collection.  Mission accomplished.  Can't recommend it, unless you're a completist too.

title: Chicago, born for this moment, or living off past glories?
text: You've got to tip your hat to them just for their sheer perseverance if nothing else.  Chicago's Born for This Moment (Chicago XXXVIII) lives as much in the past as it does the present, and while it's not a bad album, it certainly pales in the shadow of the original band's mighty '70s work.  What has become a revolving door membership is led by three original members -- Robert Lamm, James Pankow, Lee Loughnane -- who appear to have basically turned over the reins to producer Joe Thomas and new lead (read Peter Cetera-like) singer, Neil Donell, both of whom are all over the record.  The trademark horns are dominant again, as are the group vocals, while the solid songcraft is mostly a throwback to the band's self-contained days.  The title song references (I've Been) Searchin' So Long, Our New York Time opens with Beginnings acoustic guitar riffing, She's Right features Robert Lamm doing his best vocal tribute to the late Terry Kath, and on and on.  Everything old is new again.  You get the picture.  Well played and sung and pleasant enough, but this set will not make you forget past glories from their golden years.  Three-and-one-half stars for their sheer tenacity and for continuing to fight the good fight.

title: CSN's Live It Up, yeah okay, but first they've got to live down that cover
text: The follow-up to the weak CSNY reunion album, American Dream, Live It Up features the worst LP cover art by a major rock act, ever.  Totally killed the idea of taking the LP seriously (which was actually fairly good despite being mired in '80s-style production cliches).  It also served to damage the trio's artistic reputation in a big way -- with critics and fans.  There are strong moments (Haven't We Lost Enough, Got to Keep Open), middling moments (Live It Up, After the Dolphin), and head-scratching weak moments (Tomboy, If Anybody Had a Heart).  It all adds up to three-and-one-half stars from me.  The carry-over effect was that their next release, After the Storm, while a stronger collection of songs, was an even bigger sales failure bomb.  Atlantic lost interest and good ol' Uncle Neil bailed them out by joining them for Looking Forward, released on Reprise.  The quartet album didn't exactly set sales records either, but it did restore a certain air of respectability to CSN.

title: Stephen Stills:  Wrong by You?
text: No Hiding Place is Manassas-worthy.  The rest is basically the dregs of a once wonderful career.  Think I've played it about a half-dozen times throughout the years, always hoping maybe, just maybe he was ahead of the curve, and I'd missed it.  I mean, look at all those great guests (Jimmy Page, Bernie Leadon, Graham Nash, Chris Hillman, Herb Pedersen).  Nope.  With the lone exception of No Hiding Place, it's strictly bombs away for Right by You, wrong for you if you paid your hard-earned cash for it.  Two stars and recommended strictly to Stills completists.

title: Post-Manassas, Stills is struggling to find his groove
text: Post-Manassas, Stephen Stills appears to have been struggling to find, or redefine, himself.  These three '70s Columbia LPs, Stills (1975), Illegal Stills (1976), Thoroughfare Gap (1978), are generally written off by critics, but they're really the work of an artist desperate to reclaim his reputation.  Disc One pairs-off both Stills and Illegal Stills, and to good effect.  Stills has always been my favorite of the three, as it contains several of his strongest songwriting efforts (Turn Back the Pages, My Favorite Changes, First Things First, As I Come of Age).  Illegal Stills fares less well, but still has plenty of highlights to recommend it (Buyin' Time, Midnight in Paris, Stateline Blues, and a smokin' cover of Neil Young's The Loner).  And then there's Disc Two, Thoroughfare Gap alone and all by itself, quite possibly the weakest Stills solo album up to this time.  The title track is truly great and belongs somewhere else.  The best of the rest are covers (Gregg Allman's Midnight Rider, Buddy Holly's Not Fade Away).  The sound is very good throughout; the packaging is up to BGO's usual high-quality standard; the liner notes are well-written and informative.  Highly recommended to fans of solo Stills, CSN, CSNY, and '70s FM-Rock in general.

title: Five limes and coconuts for Harry's Gold
text: The late, great Harry Nilsson.  Fantastic songwriter, incredible singer, true music biz outsider, master wit and humorist.  This is a great three-disc set, mostly chronologically arranged, and an excellent vehicle to celebrate the great man's career or to introduce a newbie to the Nilsson oeuvre.  Oddly enough, his biggest singles hits were covers -- of Freddie Neil's Everybody's Talkin' and Badfinger's Without You.  And some of his best-known compositions were hits for others -- Three Dog Night's One, Blood, Sweat & Tears' Without Her, the Monkees' Cuddly Toy.  Strange career moves, I suppose.  That's as may be, but they were Harry's moves, and his fans still love him for them.  The big ones are here (Coconut, Spaceman, Me & My Arrow, Best Friend, I Guess the Lord Must Be in New York City, Jump into the Fire, Remember (Christmas), As Time Goes By, in addition to those mentioned above), as well as many very good to great album deep cuts.  A nice booklet of photos and liner notes would've made it all the better, but at this bargain price, well, that's merely quibbling.  Hats off to Harry, five limes & coconuts and very highly recommended.

title: One of the founding fathers of country-rock, covering familiar country titles
text: Richie Furay, founder of Poco and thus one of the original fathers of the country-rock genre, delivers a very enjoyable covers album with "In the Country."  That clear-eyed voice that soared on such memorable tracks as A Good Feelin' to Know, Let's Dance Tonight, Crazy Eyes, Fallin' in Love, and so many other country-rock classics, hasn't lost a step.  While it would certainly have been nice to hear some newly written Furay compositions, this covers collection stands as a heartfelt testament to the sense of fun, power, and joy that continues to emanate from the genre he helped to create and maintain.  For me, a lifelong Poco and country-rock fan, the highlights include Richie's takes on John Denver's Take Me Home, Country Roads, Lonesome Town (the classic Ricky Nelson hit), and Marc Cohn's Walking in Memphis.  Very enjoyable and definitely recommended to other Poco, country-rock fans.

title: Rita Wilson's Christmas, short and sweet
text: Lovely.  Very nice, indeed.  As Christmas-like a mood as you could possibly wish for.  But be aware, this is an extended player, a mini album, not a full-length disc.  Maybe that's why it's titled The Christmas Sessions rather than The Christmas Album.  Very enjoyable, nonetheless, and certainly recommended.

title: The Stills-Young Band?  Not really.
text: Listened to Crosby-Nash's classic Wind on the Water all the way through recently, then decided to give its mirror duo's mid '70s effort a spin.  It was an effort to get through it all (nine tracks), but I did.  The only truly memorable song included here is Young's Long May You Run, a genuine '70s classic.  The rest is a very musically schizophrenic affair that veers back and forth between Young's country-rock stoner jams and Stills' white guy BLOOZE misadventures.  The parts never jell into a solid whole, so you never quite get the feeling of a Stills-Young Band -- no such entity in evidence here, really.  Two-and-one-half stars, as opposed to the five stars I gave to the "lesser two CSNY talents" effort, released at almost the same time.  Can't recommend this one, unless you're a completist.

title: Crosby-Nash playing back when the music mattered
text: Replayed this one all the way through for the first time in a very long time the other day.  Wow!  What a live in-concert recording it was -- and is, as it stands up incredibly well.  Absolutely killer band, interesting set-list (although it could've used a couple of Nash's familiar hits to balance things out a bit), and Crosby & Nash at the top of their vocal duo game.  For anyone who still thinks that it was strictly the Stills - Young artistic fireworks that consistently drove the CSNY mothership, I'd suggest taking a serious listen to this concert album.  Believe me when I say that David and Graham were definitely NOT missing Stephen and Neil on this tour!  Highly recommended to C-N, CSN, CSNY fans, as well as to fans of '70s live rock album recordings in general.  It's a good 'un!

title: Back when Graham and David were still the best of friends ...  magic sometimes happened!
text: The best and most (commercially) successful of all the Crosby-Nash duo releases.  Crosby absolutely shines here (Carry Me alone is an absolute wonder and worth the price of admission), and Nash is right in the pocket throughout (his Fieldworker seems more relevant than ever, some 46 years down the line).  The title track joint effort (no pun intended) is as good as anything CSNY has ever attempted to put down on tape.  Wind on the Water (the album), incidentally, outpaced and outsold the Stills-Young Band's Long May You Run LP, released almost concurrently.  For this lifelong fan of the band, it's their only five-star duo album.  Very highly recommended.

title: Single disc version of John Denver's Wildlife Concert
text: Half-of his double-disc Wildlife Concert release, The Best of John Denver Live is a bit of a misnomer.  There are a lot of hits in the 16-song track list, yes.  But a lot of well-known Denver favorites are missing and replaced with less essential deep cuts.  Docked one star for that slight.  Quibbling, I know.  Regardless, it's a nicely packaged representation of the late singer / songwriter's concert program, played by an exceptional band and sung by a late-career John Denver in very good voice, indeed.  Produced for disc by Bob Irwin, who does his usual masterful job.  Not exactly essential, but definitely recommended.

title: JT and Carole, it's a live love fest
text: Nostalgia of the best kind.  Hadn't listened to this one in a while, but I'm glad for whatever it was that made me slip it into my disc player recently.  Two old friends, and singer / songwriter masters, getting together again, just to revisit some music with past compadres and make some new memories.  For themselves and their combined audiences.  As comfortable as a well broken-in pair of sandles and jeans, the set just washes over you like summer rain.  It's such a cozy groove that you barely notice the occasional musical spanner in the works.  Recommended for James Taylor, Carole King, '70s singer / songwriter fans.

title: Carole King's Vault release from her career peak years
text: Carole King at the peak of her Tapestry era success.  Recorded live in 1971, a truly magical year for King and the Laurel Canyon pop scene, the Carnegie Hall concert was a kind of homecoming for the artist formerly best known as a pop songwriter.  And what a homecoming it was!  Some 51 years down the line, it stands as the best of her live albums, even if it languished in the vaults for 25 of those years before finally seeing the light of day.  From the I Feel the Earth Move opener, to the (You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman closer, it's one highlight after another for both the artist and her enraptured hometown audience.  Excellent packaging, notes, and sound make this one a no-brainer.  Very highly recommended.

title: The Stones, alive & well, one more time ...
text: Have had this one in my collection for years and years, and recently played it front-to-back for the first time in some time.  The Stones' umpteenth live collection, but a very interesting one.  From the Unplugged era, and far more plugged in than any of the Unplugged releases ever were, including Springsteen's Plugged.  As stripped down as the Stones are ever likely to get, and as intense and entertaining as ever.  The set list is interestingly all over the map of their career, yet it all jells into one solid live in-concert program.  Over the years, it's become one of my favorites.  Highly recommended to Stones' fans, as well as fans of off-the-beaten-path in-concert LPs.

title: Remember Brewer & Shipley?  They were more than One Toke Over the Line ...
text: One of the great folk-rock duos of the early '70s, Brewer & Shipley are remembered today as a kind of one hit wonder act.  One Toke Over the Line is a song worth being remembered for, but the guys deserved a much better fate. The four LPs that make up these two discs are solid and of a piece.  If you remember and liked their big hit single from the '70s, you'll find a whole lot more of their acoustic-based, harmony drenched folk-rock to enjoy in this double-disc set.  Very good songs.  Very good sound.  Very good liner notes.  A lot to like here; definitely recommended.

title: Elvis ballads for St. Valentine's Day, or any time
text: Career-spanning, single-disc, ballad-heavy compilation.  Makes a perfect Valentine's Day gift for the Elvis fan in your life.  Non-Valentine, casual Elvis fans will find a lot to love here as well.  The collection is heavily slanted toward the '60s (ten of the 22 cuts included), when Elvis could sing just about anything and do it wonderfully well.  Great performances of very good to excellent material (well-known hits, b-sides, and deep cuts).  Recommended to both hardcore and casual Elvis fans, as well as fans of classic '60s pop balladry in general.

title: Once upon a time, The Don ruled the airwaves
text: People forget what a big deal Donovan was back in the day.  For a little over a half-decade (1966-71), he delivered hit after hit, album after album, concert after concert.  He was happening, everywhere.  The cream of his legacy is contained on this 15-track collection, and it's simply amazing.  Colours and Catch the Wind are the original Hickory Records folk versions.  I still prefer the remakes made for the original release of this LP.  Then there's the string of hit singles, including Sunshine Superman, Mellow Yellow, There Is a Mountain, Wear Your Love Like Heaven, and the often covered, never matched Season of the Witch.  This reissue expands the track-list to 15 with four later singles: Atlantis, To Susan on the West Coast Waiting, Barabajagal (with the Jeff Beck Group), and Riki Tiki Tavi.  As good as you may recall, and actually better than you might remember.  Highly recommended, especially to fans of '60s / '70s AM / early FM rock.

title: Stones in '81 - Still Life, Still Live
text: American Tour, 1981, hyping the band's then-current Tattoo You LP.  Oldies, covers, new tracks, and a sense of ... confusion?  Confusion of the "Where do we stand in this new 'I want my MTV' world?"  Well, that question was rendered moot by the runaway success of their patchwork Tattoo album, as well as its chart-topping single, Start Me Up and the turnout for this tour.  The Stones continued to rule, justifiably so.  A too brief single disc release that should have added some bonus tracks from the tour as a remastered reissue.  Still, four stars and definitely recommended.

title: Love The Rolling Stones Live, oh yeah!
text: The Stones in concert back in '77, the double-disc Love You Live is likely my favorite of their many live releases.  They're dug in deep in the groove, playing like it really means something, and never for a moment simply going through rote rock 'n' roll motions.  The set list is killer.  The performances have an impact and immediacy unmatched on other live sets.  The band is in its prime and in street fighting form.  Love You Live?  Right back to you boys!  Very highly recommended.

title: Sebastian's early post-Spoonful career celebrated
text: John Sebastian's Reprise releases, minus Real Live.  John B. Sebastian was the biggest success of his five Reprise LPs, but The Four of Us, Tarzana Kid, and Welcome Back all deliver plenty of highlights.  The third disc included here is a DVD of a BBC in-concert broadcast from 1970, never seen in America.  This post-Lovin' Spoonful period should have been huge (commercially) for Sebastian and Reprise, especially in the wake of his high-profile association with the Woodstock event and film.  That only his JBS solo debut proved to be a solid commercial success (in spite of a label battle between MGM and Reprise) remains a bit of a head-scratcher.  Artistically, all four studio releases stand tall a half-century plus down the line.  Highly recommended, especially to fans of great '60s / '70s pop songwriting.

title: The Stones kickin' it in Texas back in '78
text: The Rolling Stones touring behind the Some Girls album back in 1978, and absolutely kickin' it in Texas, on this long overdue live in-concert release.  If you love the Stones, you'll definitely love this one.  Even if you're just a casual fan, you'll find plenty to like in here.  Excellent setlist, Mick in fine vocal form, and the band absolutely ferocious.  Definitely recommended to Stones, '70s Rock, and live album fans.  It won't disappoint.

title: Steve Forbert simply keeps on doing
text: Another year, another Steve Forbert pearl.  Regardless of the latest marketplace flashes in the pan, he simply keeps on doing.  Following his muse, delivering the goods to fans and friends, creating works of uncompromised artistry.  2015's "Compromised," in which the idea of compromise means meeting on common ground, served to continue Forbert's series of high-end, lo-fi missives from the rock 'n' roll side of life.  And it's a good 'un that has only seemed to get better with the passage of time.  Three-and-a-half stars from me, and definitely recommended.

title: Forbert's Magic:  Weaving a musical future from the past
text: Released as a kind of ride-along to his Big City Cat autobiography, The Magic Tree emerges from the mists of Steve Forbert's past as one of his best records in years.  It's made up of musically fleshed out versions of leftover demos from previous projects.  Like a kind of a folk-rock take on the Who's Odds & Sods, or the Stones' Tattoo You (in a much lower spotlight, mind you), The Magic Tree develops new pictures from previously discarded negatives.  And yes, a new musical whole is developed from the parts, one that ebbs and flows with the natural feel of a newly conceived recorded statement.  Highly recommended.  Read the book, then groove on this; I don't think you'll be disappointed.

title: Good Times in Monkeeville
text: Something the Monkees would've never expected during the group's '60s heyday: excellent reviews to match the solid sales.  Things have changed, for sure.  In the day, the boys couldn't have bought the kind of reviews being lavished on this album.  And good on them!  "Good Times!" stands as a charming and affectionate coda to the one-time Prefab Four's legacy.  With Michael Nesmith's recent passing, following the deaths of Peter Tork and Davy Jones, it's down to Micky Dolenz to "carry that weight," to borrow a song title from their towering Beatles role models.  Based on his excellent work here, I'm sure Mick's up to the task.  Highly recommended to fans of '60s pop.

title: 'Rita Wilson' stands in the shadow of her AM / FM covers collection
text: Follow-up to her superior AM / FM collection of covers.  This album of originals isn't in the same league as that mostly great cover song record, but vocally, musically and production-wise it stands on its own quite nicely.  While it's unlikely she'll ever make her living as a songwriter, Rita Wilson has a seductive vocal style and is a fine lyrical interpreter.  Unfortunately, she hasn't delivered herself a lot to work with (lyrically) in these rather trite tunes.  Three-and-a-half stars from me, but I'd welcome another covers disc in a heartbeat.  Recommended to fans of '70s Laurel Canyon-style pop.

title: Harry's ahead of the curve, as usual
text: Long before it became fashionable, the late Harry Nilsson took a pop star's left turn by delivering this album of covers of the classic American songbook.  And it still stands up as one of the best, maybe THE BEST of a now very large genre.  If you're a Nilsson fan and somehow missed it, give it a chance -- I think you'll love it.  If you're a Nilsson newbie, pick up the Schmilsson trio (Nilsson Schmilsson, Son of Schmilsson, and this one) and prepare to be blown away.  He may be long gone, but his legacy remains as strong as ever.  Very highly recommended.

title: Experience Jimi all over again
text: Along with Smash Hits, the best Jimi Hendrix compilation.  It actually supplants the older collection, as it contains all that disc's main titles while expanding the track list to 20 titles.  Nicely packaged with a booklet containing terrific liner notes and rare photos.  And the disc itself boasts excellent sound improvements.  The Experience Hendrix version of The Best of Jimi Hendrix is the best single-disc Jimi retrospective.  Very highly recommended.

title: Honkin' but hardly essential
text: Not bad, but not especially memorable.  Aerosmith's Honkin' on Bobo is a mildly diverting album, but non-essential and lightweight, nonetheless.  For hardcore fans only, definitely not the place for newbies to start.  Three honks on bobo.

title: Chicago, 40 years down the line
text: Listening to this two-disc set front to back, beginning to end, it becomes painfully obvious that their best years were behind them when they left Columbia.  That band had been musically adventurous, exciting and a bit unpredictable.  The Warner years, on the other hand, saw them delivering less and less interesting power ballads (usually by outside songwriters).  As their creativity dried up, there also appeared to be a revolving door of band membership, making Chicago less and less distinct and more faceless than ever.  The Columbia tracks still deliver the goods and are available elsewhere in better collections.  The Warners material remains as cheesy as ever and is also available separately.  Three stars.

title: Chicago's looking back
text: A throwback to the band's horn-driven, group vocals sound.  So, yes, it sounds good.  Unfortunately, there's little in the way of the old day's great songwriting in evidence here.  As a result, things get old real fast.  At least they're not slogging their way through more Diane Warren power ballads on this one; and that's a plus from me.  Three and one-half stars.

title: Finding his way to greatness
text: Rodney Crowell, the early years.  He's finding his way to greatness.  Great singer.  Great songwriter.  Great performer.  Great bandleader.  He would eventually attain them all, and you can see (hear?) the beginnings of his legendary career in these grooves.  Very impressive, a definite recommendation to Americana fans, as well as singer / songwriter and country-rock fans in general.

title: Linda's Greatest Hits sets combined
text: Hits and nothing but the hits.  By combining Linda Ronstadt's two Asylum Greatest Hits sets on one disc, Rhino has created the only one you'll need if you're looking for Ronstadt retrospective.  Radio hits, hit country and pop singles, Adult Contemporary chart hits, they're all here and sounding better than ever.  This disc delivers the goods for both the diehard and casual fan.  Five stars and highly recommended.

title: The mother of all motherships
text: Led Zeppelin lent inspiration to hundreds of bands, not to mention millions of listeners.  Mothership is the motherlode collection of the band's incredible legacy.  Beautifully packaged and sounding fantastic, this two-disc set includes pretty much all the highlights, touching upon every one of the band's original albums.  A favorite or two might be missing, of course, but that's true of any (all?) "Best of" collections, yes?  Five blimps flying high and strong from me.

title: Essential Janis?  Absolutely!
text: As advertised: 18 essential tracks culled from the Janis box set.  The perfect starting point to introduce someone to her music and career.  Highly recommended to both long-time and casual fans, as well as Joplin newbies.

title: The Street Was Always There ... and so was Eric Andersen
text: One of the great unsung heroes of the American folk, folk-rock, singer/songwriter scenes of the '60s and '70s.  Eric Andersen never reached the level of popular success he so truly deserved, but he's just kept on plugging along, year after year, decade after decade, album after album, label after label.  The Street Was Always There is a fine example of his later recorded work.  His voice is deeper, and a bit worn around the edges, yet as soulful and beautiful as ever.  This covers collection may not be classic Andersen, but it is a solid journeyman's effort.  Much like Andersen himself.  Three-and-one-half stars from this longtime fan.

title: Everly Bros during the lost years
text: A solid two-fer release of a pair of Everly Bros LPs from their lost years.  Both albums were deserving of a better fate than "lost in the wilderness."  Country-rock ahead of the curve, Pass the Chicken & Listen and Stories We Could Tell are musically miles away from the boys' golden years material.  Still, the harmonies are as tight and beautiful as ever, and the song selections are actually more adventurous than the reliable hits years of the '50s and '60s.  These records won't appeal to everyone, but if you loved the Everlys back in the day and have a jones for real down-home country-rock, I think you'll find a lot to like here.

title: Led Zeppelin's magnificent remasters
text: The band resisted the idea of a Greatest Hits collection throughout its legendary career.  So, when this two-disc set (culled from the Led Zeppelin Remasters box set) was issued it was welcomed with wide-open arms by fans and critics alike.  Hits just about all the highlights in a career positively packed with them, and the remastering is magnificently done.  Very highly recommended.

title: An artistic peak for Led Zeppelin
text: Black Dog, Rock and Roll, Stairway to Heaven ... What more needs to be said?  The classiest of all classic rock.  Remastered and sounding better than ever.  Five stars and very highly recommended to anyone who loves Rock at its absolute best and most adventurous.

title: Miles of memorable Mitchell aisles
text: One of my all-time favorite Joni Mitchell albums.  Alive & kickin'!  Jazz, R&B, pop, folk, and rock influences merge into an amazing and thoroughly intoxicating whole.  A breakthrough LP at the time of release, it has held up incredibly well.  And with the remastering upgrades, it sounds better and more alive than ever.  Very highly recommended.

title: Sunday has never been the same since
text: Not the best Spanky compilation, but a pretty good one.  You can't argue with what's included, I mean hits are hits are hits.  But there's a certain lack of depth to a 40-minute collection attempting to adequately cover a multi-album career like Spanky & Our Gang's.  Still, if it's a brief musical overview for the casual fan you're looking for, 20th Century Masters is sure to fill the bill.  Three and a half stars.

title: Girl From the North Country, London calling
text: This is the original London cast, not the current Broadway version.  Very moving, very well-done.  Haven't seen the New York production yet, but I'm hopeful of doing that soon.  In the meanwhile, I'll continue to revel in the Old Vic version.  Highly recommended.

title: A straight-up reissue of Barry McGuire's career high-water mark
text: As much a P.F. Sloan album (he wrote 7 of the 12 tracks) as a Barry McGuire LP, Eve of Destruction gave McGuire a high-water mark that he'd never again achieve.  It's pretty much strictly an exercise in nostalgia.  His take on the ultimate looking back song of the era, Try to Remember (from The Fantasticks), pretty much sums it all up -- talking to listeners from all the way back in 1965!  And Sloan's Eve of Destruction, sadly, seems to remain relevant and current from generation to generation to generation.  Other highlights include Dylan's She Belongs to Me and It's All Over Now, Baby Blue and Ian & Sylvia's You Were on My Mind.

title: Surprising solid sidebar story from the Steppenwolf leader
text: A pair of decidedly left field detours from Steppenwolf's founder, lead singer, and main driving force.  Forgotten Songs & Unsung Heroes and My Sportin' Life are cast in the early '70s singer / songwriter mode, and they both work surprising well, considering John Kay's "heavy metal thunder" reputation with the Wolf.  Presented as a two-fer here, the 18 tracks that make up these two originally separately released LPs flow well and play like a solid '70s double LP.  Kay's songwriting manages to stand proudly alongside his covers of such classics as Hank Williams' You Win Again, Robert Johnson's Walkin' Blues, Hank Snow's I'm Movin' On, and even Steel Dan's Walter Becker / Donald Fagen's Giles of the River.  A very pleasant surprise and highly recommended to fans of early '70s rock.

title: Plays like a great Dylan "Best Of" collection
text: Original Bob Dylan recordings that form the basis for the stage musical.  Absolutely fabulous!  Plays like a fan-selected Dylan "Best of," and it's a great one.  The obvious hits, off-the-beaten-path tracks, and stunning deep album cuts.  You don't have to see the show to enjoy this one.  Highly recommended.

title: Tom Petty's first "Best of" is still a winner
text: TP's MCA years celebrated.  His first "Best of" stands up incredibly well.  Timeless rock 'n' roll in the best sense.  Great songs, great playing, great singing.  Great retrospective.  An album that honors the past while living in the present moment, just like the late, great Mr. Petty did himself.  Very highly recommended.

title: Nothing but the Best of Bowie
text: Truth in advertising here, a rarity in the music business.  This compilation really is The Best of Bowie.  The hits and nothing but the hits.  All killer, not a bit of filler.  I've given this disc away to numerous friends as a gift for various occasions, and they've always been thrilled to get it -- without exception.  Very highly recommended.

title: Bruce's Greatest hits?  I just don't know about that
text: The first Springsteen compilation.  Put together to provide a home for -- and to celebrate -- his Streets of Philadelphia soundtrack single success.  To my ears, it has never held together as an album.  It ignores his first two LPs (on which his early reputation was built) completely and glosses over his third (the star-making Born to Run).  At the expense of more important recordings, this "hits" set is padded out with previously unreleased bonus tracks.  Greatest Hits?  Well, I'm not so sure.  Recommended to novices and completists.

title: Winning, if hardly defining Bob Seger retrospective
text: Incomplete, but solid.  Bob Seger's first Greatest Hits set is a winning, if hardly defining, mid-career retrospective.  There are more complete variations available, but this one is pretty well chosen -- and bargain priced -- for the casual fan.  A good place to start for someone interested strictly in his early radio hits.

title: Celebrating the Stones' second and third decades
text: From Classic to Glitter to Grunge, 20 years of Rolling Stones rock 'n' roll magic.  Jump Back celebrates The Stones' second and third decades of churning out massive hit singles and memorable albums.  Every track included carries special memories -- musical, personal, nostalgic, or whatever.  You can't listen to this collection without falling into the Stones groove over and over again.  A total winner, and (IMHO) one of the very best of the band's many compilation releases.  Highly recommended.

title: Best of the savage young Stones, the Allen B. Klein years
text: All the great Stones' hits from the early years.  From the 1964 London Records era through to the birth of the Atlantic-distributed Rolling Stones Records.  A kind of culled down Hot Rocks collection.  All the hits that fit, and it's all killer, absolutely no filler.  The savage young Stones!  Highly recommended.

title: Zeppelin III, beautifully remastered
text: My personal favorite among Led Zep's legendary catalog.  And it has never sounded better to this aging boomer's rock 'n' roll ears.  With that ambient acoustic touch, inspired by the sounds of Crosby, Stills & Nash and The Grateful Dead's American Beauty / Workingman's Dead highwater marks, III soars even as it underplays earlier musical hallmarks.  I've loved this album since buying the LP fifty years ago, and I love it even more in this remastered version.  Very highly recommended.

title: Rock the Casbah, oh yeah!
text: A truly great Clash collection.  As advertised, it's the band's singles set, and that's all right with me.  Upgraded sound, terrific play-list, and an amazing band at its peak.  Rock the Casbah, oh yeah!  All killer, no filler.  Highly recommended.

title: The best of John Mellencamp's first hit-making decade
text: An excellent compilation at a bargain price.  What more could you ask for?  Even if you're strictly a casual fan of John Mellencamp, this one will do the trick.  The best of the first half of his career for under five bucks.  Incredible bargain, really.  The one to get if you just want a touch of JM in your collection.

title: Cowboy at a musical crossroads
text: Thought I was purchasing a new disc, but it turned out to be used:  No shrink-wrap, cracked case, finger smudges on the disc itself.  Docked one star for those issues.  Luckily, though, it plays all right.  "Cowboy" is actually Cowboy, Mach 3, and in many ways is a different band.  More country-rock / commercial radio pop than the earlier versions of this Southern Rock band on Capricorn Records, the home and birthplace of the genre.  Not saying that's a bad thing as it's a quite listenable and enjoyable album.  In the context of 1977, when it was recorded and released however, it was quite out of place and doomed to commercial failure from the start.  Punk was on the rise, disco was rampant on the radio, the classic rock radio format was busy being born, even as the King of Rock 'n' Roll was slipping away in Memphis.  Cowboy, and this LP in particular, deserved better.

title: Catching up with Cowboy's trail bosses
text: Cowboy never reached the level of success its talented membership deserved.  Don't know why, because they had it all: musical chops, solid vocals, engaging songwriting, top of the line production.  It's always a roll of the dice, I suppose, with blind luck outweighing talent in the long run.  "Boyer & Talton" is a pretty terrific collection that centers in on the two main Cowboy movers & shakers.  It ends on a high note with a pair of bonus tracks from the Gregg Allman Tour (Time Will Take Us, Where Can You Go?).  Glad to see it's back in print.  Recommended for fans of Cowboy and Southern Rock in general.

title: Cowboy, still essential Southern Rock after all these years
text: I remember Cowboy from way on back in the mists of time.  Early '70s, the Gregg Allman Tour behind "Laid Back," I believe.  They caught my attention then, and I pretty quickly went out in search of their then-current LP.  Never big sellers, and I don't understand why, but big talents making big music for big albums.  "Reach For The Sky" (also an Allman Brothers LP title) is a fine example of the band's work.  Southern Rock at or near its peak in both production and performance.  Glad this one's back to be enjoyed.

title: Another winning Cowboy Junkies collection
text: Cowboy Junkies don't ever merely cover a song, they rediscover and reinvent it.  "Songs of the Recollection" is the perfect example.  Nine familiar songs are recast in the Junkies mode and all emerge the better for it.  The standouts here include Ooh Las Vegas, No Expectations, Don't Let It Bring You Down, and I've Made Up My Mind To Give Myself To You.  Forty years on, the group just gets better and better.  Highly recommended.

title: The 'Best of' for the serious Cowboy Junkies junkie
text: Contains three of my favorite Junkies' covers (Blue Moon, Sweet Jane, I'm So Lonesome I Could Cry) and misses another one (Working on the Building).  Takes a long, loving look backward at an amazingly consistent covers / originals career.  "The Trinity Sessions" is the one to start with for those just discovering the group, followed closely by this excellent overview compilation.  As with all 'best of' collections, there's room for argument about what's been included and what's been left out.  All in all, however, a solid career retrospective; wish I had picked it up sooner.  Also features excellent notes by Michael Hill.  Highly recommended.

title: Songs for Beginners / Wild Tales 50 + years down the line
text: So many 5-star reviews.  I just don't get it.  I've been a faithful CSN (if less so CSNY) fan since plunking down hard-earned summer job money for Crosby, Stills & Nash back in 1969.  Hooked, I've been a CSN completist ever since.  Even after the trio -- in a very foolhardy turn of events -- painted themselves into a corner, or into the background really, and were rather cruelly referred to as Neil Young's backing singers, I kept on buying.  CSN.  CSNY.  Solo C.  Solo S.  Solo N.  Often solo Y.  C-N.  Manassas.  S-Y Band.  Got 'em all, except some of Neil's new millennium releases.  Crosby, Stills and Nash is a 5-star album, as are Manassas, After the Gold Rush, Wind on the Water.  Songs for Beginners?  Three and a half stars.  Wild Tales?  Three stars.  This live-in-concert presentation of those two LPs is a 3-star release, at best, basically a pleasant if non-essential concert memento.  Fine band, good to very good songs, solid arrangements.  Unfortunately, Nash's 80-year-old vocals have begun to show the wear and tear of the intervening 50-plus years.  I'd have preferred a remixed / remastered two-fer containing the original albums (which I still listen to on my old Atlantic Records LPs).  Recommended for diehard Nash fans and CSN completists only (like myself).

title: Post Poco / SHF Band, the beginnings of Richie Furay's solo career
text: After the relative failure of his Poco masterwork, A Good Feelin' to Know (still a personal favorite of mine), Richie bailed on the band after Crazy Eyes (another fave) to embrace what he expected to be greener ($$) pastures with The Souther-Hillman-Furay Band.  Turned out to be a moderately successful move, but not the Crosby, Stills, Nash jackpot he'd hoped for.  Time to begin a solo career with the David Geffen-run Asylum Records, home of the SHF Band.  The three albums included here are the result.  Not Buffalo Springfield.  Not Poco.  Not even the SHF Band.  Under the radar at best, not the breakthroughs he was still looking for, and total bombs by recording biz commercial standards.  But all three are better than their chart / sales statistics would indicate, and far better than the tepid critical reception they received in the day.  The quality of the material varies, but it is always good to very good, if not excellent.  The playing and arrangements are flawless.  And Richie's amazing vocals are as strong and clear as ever.  Highly recommended to fans of the previously mentioned bands and country-rock fans in general.

title: Unforgettable Eva Cassidy remembered
text: Eva Cassidy.  An acoustic compilation.  Some of her best-loved recordings.  She's gone too soon, but her legacy remains and sustains.  Highly recommended.

title: Steve Forbert: Still Alive & Well on the Arrival of his 22nd (!) album
text: Like Ol' Man River, Mr. Forbert just keeps rollin' along.  Some 44 years down the line from Alive on Arrival, here he is with album number 22.  And this new one, Moving Through America, is definitely a good 'un.  His vocals are a bit worn around the edges (40 years of road work will do that, yeah?), but he's still in the zone and doesn't stray too far from his folk-rock roots.  The songs are very good to excellent and feature his usual clever wordplay and astute observations about life & love in modern America.  And the straightforward, non-fussy musical accompaniment serves him well.  Highly recommended to both Steve Forbert and '70s singer/songwriter fans in general.  I rate it four out of five motel postcards.

title: When the Doobies were brothers and on a very hot streak
text: Wow!  What a double-disc set of Doobie Brothers magic!  My two favorite Doobie albums paired off for maximum listening pleasure.  The Captain and Me took the boys from journeyman rockers to big time headliners thanks to the inclusion of two radio-ready smash hits:  Long Train Runnin' and China Grove.  That album also featured Without You and South City Midnight Lady among its 11 excellent tracks.  The follow-up, What Were Once Vices Are Now Habits, kept the bar high with another pair of huge radio hits:  Another Park, Another Sunday and Black Water.  Vices also included Song to See You Through and Eyes of Silver among its 12-song playlist.  Terrific sound.  Terrific liner notes.  Terrific band at the height of its powers.  Highly recommended.

title: Johnny Cougar grows up to be John Mellencamp
text: Packed double-disc set that's the one to own if you only want one John Mellencamp compilation in your collection.  Leaves any memories of that Johnny Cougar scamp in the dust.  John Mellencamp is an artist now.  Some might feel that a favorite or two has been left out; some might dispute certain new inclusions at the expense of familiar deep cuts.  No matter.  Songs, sound, and performances are all top-notch and sure to please.  Highly recommended by this most casual of Mellencamp fans.

title: When Chicago was still Chicago
text: Great cover, as always.  One of Columbia's wrap-up releases as the band moved on to Full Moon/Warner's, and years of progressively less interesting power ballads.  If You Leave Me Now turned out to be a steady seller throughout the years, actually doing much better than the band's Greatest Hits, Volume Two.  It was bargain-priced (as was the similar Take Me Back to Chicago comp.) and contained enough genuine hits from Chicago's most productive and creative era (Columbia Records years) to make it attractive to diehard and casual fans alike.  Still holds up well, as does Take Me Back to Chicago (if you can find it).  Definitely recommended to Chicago and '70s pop/rock fans.

title: Van the Man!
text: Van the Man!  Two discs, 37 cross-label tracks, pure Van Morrison nirvana.  There'll likely be argument and disappointment about what's included and what's been left out; that's just natural, I suppose.  When that rare an artist -- one of VM's stature -- has his career celebrated with a double-disc compilation, well, there's bound to be personal favorites left behind.  Regardless, this is a killer comp.  Very highly recommended.

title: The Doobies doin' the obvious
text: Southbound is one of THOSE LPs.  You know the kind I'm talkin' 'bout.  An obvious bid to expose a group to a wider market by bringing in a buckboard load of cowboy-hatted current country acts to sing (or sing along with them on) some of their best-known compositions.  It has already worked for the likes of The Beatles, Beach Boys, and Eagles in the past.  This time around, it's The Doobie Brothers' turn to play on the rodeo circuit.  Not especially good, not horrendously bad.  It's just a time-honored exercise in maximizing commerciality through cross-marketing, usually at a career low-point.  Sooner or later, they'll be asked about this dubious project and they'll say they were talked into it.  And they'll be telling the truth.

title: Steve Miller offers fans a peek behind the curtain, and into his audio / visual vault
text: Tremendous package.  The perfect example of the way a career retrospective should be done.  A truly welcome visit to the Steve Miller vault.  Would that he'd revisit his decades-old Pegasus boxset and give it the same kind of treatment (including remixing / remastering).  Lots to like, love, and / or debate about included here.  Very highly recommended to Steve Miller Band longtime / diehard fans.

title: A master lesson from a pair of legends
text: Mavis and Levon.  Staples and Helm.  If you're even remotely interested in that pairing of truly legendary performers, well, you don't need me to go blathering on about how great it is.  Which it is -- great!  A master class in singing and performing.  The sound isn't always all I would've hoped for, and the liner notes are a bit on the scant side.  But the setlist is pure joy and the performances raise the roof like a heavenly revival throughout.  Highly recommended.

title: NGDB still at it after all these years
text: Some 56 or so years down the road, the NGDB is still churning out solid LPs.  Dirt Does Dylan is a good 'un.  Bolstered by second generation musical contributions, Jeff Hanna and Company maintain the usual high NGDB standards.  The playing and singing are top-notch, and the production definitely impresses.  The set list made up of Bob Dylan classics is solid, if a bit predictable.  Actually, a few somewhat under-the-radar titles from the master's catalog might have added some extra flavor to the mix.  Regardless, it's one of the better Dylan the songwriter tributes -- of which there are many.  Recommended, especially to NGDB, Dylan, and folk- / country-rock fans.

title: Disappointing, at best
text: Musically and vocally, Van's still the man.  But oh, those lyrics!  The kindest thing I can say?  Disappointing, and in a big way.  Love the front cover graphics (Invasion of the Body Snatchers), although I'd have to say it's theme cuts a bit too close to the albums vapid lyrical content.  Three pods from me.

title: Surprisingly good LPs from one of America's great '60s / '70s singles bands
text: Great liner notes that explain a lot of the back-story behind this superior Dunhill hit singles machine of the late '60s / early '70s.  Yeah, a singles band, remember them?  It was a desperately un-hip thing for a serious band to be -- singles oriented.  But for about a half-decade, The Grass Roots churned 'em out regularly and without apology.  The four albums that make up this two-disc set prove there was more to the band than 45 rpm top 40 radio hits, and they deserve a much better reputation than they've been saddled with over the years.  Like all the best groups of their era, they progressed with each new release, and grew both as writers and interpreters, and as a band.  Definitely worth checking out, and highly recommended to fans of '60s / '70s folk- and pop-rock.

title: The excellent DRB live in-concert at the Ritz, on the radio
text: Loved this band from the get-go.  Saw them three different times in concert and they were always terrific, even with several member changes by the final show I attended.  The Hillman-Pedersen-Jorgenson talent centerpiece shone brightly regardless of the variations of other players.  Always hoped for an official live album, and I guess this fine radio broadcast will simply have to fill the bill.  Great singing, great playing, great set-list, mostly very good to great sound.  If you were (are) a DRB fan, you're sure to fall for this one.  Just a plain shame that country radio's and MCA Nashville's lack of support brought them to a premature end.  This band wasn't about cowboy hats, line-dancing, or slick country top 40 concessions.  They were about the music, Bakersfield Country-style, and they were the masters.  Highly recommended.

title: CSNY 1974: Disappointing after decades of misplaced hype
text: Sometimes memories should simply be left alone.  I attended Tour '74 with a group of friends (some of them sadly gone now) and we talked about the show for years, decades after.  A highlight of our concert-going experiences.  Fabulous!  Magical.  Absolutely wonderful.  Now we've got the audio proof, right?  Er, ugh, well no, not really.  This release is utterly underwhelming, and it manages to put the lie not only to our collective inner circle memory, but also to the unrelenting Graham Nash hype that preceded its release.  Truly disappointing.  Single disc sampler and the 4-disc box:  Three Peace Symbols.  Strictly for diehard CSNY fanatics.

title: Eric is Derek ... as if we didn't know
text: Unbelievably, Layla was dying on the vine when first released by Atlantic on Atco in the USA in late 1970.  Suddenly, in 1971, there appeared buttons and stickers in record stores (remember them?) and an ad campaign heralding "Eric is Derek!"  Didn't help sales of either Bell Bottom Blues or the radio-ready, edited-down version of Layla on the singles market.  But then in the Spring of 1972, along comes Atco's "History of Eric Clapton," sporting a cover photo of EC playing at "The Concert for Bangla Desh," and released hard-on-the-heels of that smash hit George Harrison & Friends live-in-concert collection.  And BOOM, just like that, Layla is suddenly all over the radio and flying out of the shops.  Finally.  Justifiably.  A bona-fide modern classic.  This 40th Anniversary edition is as great as ever, as well as bigger than ever.  Very highly recommended.

title: One of Clapton's best under-the-radar collaborations
text: Liked this one so much I bought it twice.  One for myself, another for a Clapton fan friend who had been on the fence about it.  She's no longer on the fence -- it's now, she tells me, one of her go-to albums when she needs a lift.  Long a personal favorite of mine, I still can't understand its under-the-radar status among many in Eric Clapton's fandom.  His work here with Wynton Marsalis & Co. is, in a word, magnificent.  Highly recommended.

title: Bobby Rydell: One of the greatest of the pop idol Bobbys
text: Sad to say, his recent passing brought me back to this one for the first time in a long time.  Turned out to be a great listen.  What a talent he was!  Not always great material, but when it was good to very good, look out -- he'd kill it every time.  Of the many '50s / '60s Bobby pop idols (Darin, Goldsboro, Vee, Vinton, et al) he was neck-and-neck with Darin as the king of the hill.  Well, maybe not king, but both certainly princes or dukes.  As Mr. Darin put it so well (and honestly), "if you put all of us Johnny-come-lately types on one corner and Elvis on the opposite corner, all the kids would be rushing on over there with him."  Regardless, give the late Bobby Rydell another chance; you won't be disappointed.

title: Bueno, Raul Malo
text: Great stuff.  Another fine offshoot of the Covid-19 situation.  A full program of 30 low-fi performances spread across two CDs.  If you're a fan of Raul Malo and / or The Mavericks, you're sure to love this one.  Highly recommended.

title: The Rascals come to an end, the solo Felix career begins
text: His solo debut, "Felix Cavaliere," is the most Rascals-sounding of all of Felix's solo LPs.  If memory serves, most of it was written and demoed with the intention of becoming The Rascals' third Columbia album, following the magnificent double-album "Peaceful World" and the fine but not quite equal "The Island of Real."  Wasn't meant to be, as the band broke up in late '72.  I've often thought Columbia could've done well by releasing the Rascals' versions of this material as a variation on "The Byrds (Untitled)" album -- a new studio record paired with a live-in-concert LP, "The Rascals."  I think it may have salvaged the group's waning career back in the day, just as "(Untitled)" had done for Roger McGuinn's then-latest Byrds line-up.  Regardless, Todd Rundgren's heavy-handed co-production aside (as if the great Cavaliere needed help!), there's a great album in here.  I hope someday the original (pre-Rundgren) version will be released.  Destiny is slightly less successful, but certainly funky and fun.  Highly recommended to Felix, Rascals, and early '70s album rock fans.

title: Rushmore: Terrific soundtrack from a terrific film
text: Terrific soundtrack from a terrific film.  Great '60s classics and deep cuts abound.  The music is integral and well-placed throughout the film.  If you've seen the movie, you know exactly what I mean.  However, the soundtrack also works amazingly well as a stand-alone various artists compilation.  Highly recommended.

title: The Band's Greatest Hits supplants The Best of The Band collection
text: If you're only going to have one album by The Band in your collection, I'd suggest The Band (a/k/a The Brown Album).  However, if you're willing to buy another, this is the one I'd suggest.  Hands down, far and away, Greatest Hits is The Band's best single-disc compilation; it supplants 1976's The Best of The Band by a wide margin.  They weren't a "hits" kind of group, so you have to ignore the title and simply go for the content -- which is terrific.  Songs that sounded as if they came from another time at the time of their release -- The Band was always outside the current trend lines -- sound as strong and are as moving as ever.  And they're still outside the lines!  Highly recommended.

title: Harry Nilsson's classic cartoon adventure
text: Harry Nilsson's classic cartoon adventure holds up incredibly well.  The film's message was inclusive (before anyone ever used that descriptive phrase) and it's presented in gentle, musical terms.  You don't have to be a big Nilsson fan to get into this one, and it's a great animated film to share with younger family members.  If memory serves, Dustin Hoffman did the original narration; in this version it's down to Nilsson's buddy Ringo Starr, who does a lovely job of it.  Recommended as nostalgia and as fine family fun.

title: Elvis the movie star, 1956-1969
text: A total of 54 movie-derived tracks spread across three CDs and in chronological order according to soundtrack release dates.  The only thing missing is a booklet with a good set of liner notes and film-era photos.  A blend of big singles charts hits, minor hits, soundtrack EP material, movie / elpee title tracks, this import set makes it obvious that although many (if not most) of his films were low-budget quickies, many a good-to-great recording came down that constantly churning conveyor belt.  While there are soft spots, mostly during the mid-'60s, the material was getting stronger again near the end of his Hollywood run.  By the way, tired and depressed with his position in the business, he turned his back on the movies post-1968 Comeback TV special.  He honored his existing film contracts and then walked away in '69 with Change of Habit.  But the offers kept coming in through the mid-'70s, and he and Colonel kept turning them down.

title: Lindsey Buckingham continues to go his own way.
text: The amazing Mr. Buckingham goes his own way.  And he continues to amaze.  His guitar and vocals haven't lost an inch.  One of the all-time greats in rock 'n' roll.  This one's right up there in quality with his last LP, the one with Christine McVie.  Fleetwood Mac is far less interesting for his loss.  Highly recommended.

title: A worthy successor to his Blues with Friends
text: Blues with Friends, Volume Two, anybody?  Stomping Ground is a worthy successor to that recent Dion classic, and it follows the same basic formula.  Excellent playing.  Very good to great songs.  Star-studded guest vocals and players.  Dion's still amazing voice and guitar.  Recommended to fans of Dion, the blues, and classic duets LPs.

title: Cass County: Perhaps Henley's best solo effort to date
text: Broke this one out for the first time in a long time recently, and what a pleasant surprise it turned out to be.  The closest of any of Don Henley's solo releases to the pre-Joe Walsh Eagles' sound, Cass County is something of a near-classic country-rock album.  The songs, both originals and covers, flow together with the kind of seemingly effortless (but carefully planned and hard-won) grace of the best early Eagles LPs (Eagles, Desperado, On the Border).  I'm especially fond of the Brand-New Tennessee Waltz and Here Come Those Tears covers.  Also, the many Big-Time guest vocalists (Mick Jagger and Alison Krauss among them) add color and perspective to the proceedings, rather than just drawing attention to themselves and becoming a distraction.  All in all, discounting 'best of' compilations of course, Cass County takes its place as Don Henley's strongest solo effort to date.  High praise, indeed.

title: Too many trips to Lu's Jukebox?
text: Fabulous setlist.  Smokin' band.  Less than stellar vocals.  Lu seems to be falling asleep at the wheel much of the time this time around, or maybe it's just one too many trips to the well.  It's number 6 in the series, after all.  For me, the best, most moving moments occur during the first half of the set (the run of Play with Fire, No Expectations, Dead Flowers, and Salt of the Earth), all classic Stones' ballads.  Just may be the least effective of all the Lu's Jukebox releases.

title: The pretty much complete Mamas & Papas collection
text: Amazing when you think about it, but the Mamas & the Papas legend and legacy is based on three LPs: If You Can Believe Your Eyes and Ears, The Mamas & the Papas, and Deliver.  Then came Farewell to the First Golden Era (a greatest hits set), followed by The Papas & the Mamas, and Golden Era, Volume 2 (another hits set), a contractually obligated reunion LP (People Like Us), and a seemingly endless string of compilation packages and re-packages.  Albums four and five (Papas, People) are better than their reviews, but they're both in the long shadow of the first three.  Still, the light never dims on the group's well-earned reputation for taste and quality.  I had this one years ago and loved it.  Loaned it out to a friend, who loaned it to a friend, and I never got it back.  Of course, that's a whole other story!  Right now I'm just glad to have this one back in my collection.  Highly recommended if you can get your hands on a clean copy.

title: The great Hari's hits, just not all of them
text: No argument with what's here, just with what's not.  It would take another full disc to make up the difference.  Maybe there'll eventually be a follow-up -- "George Harrison: This Guitar (Can't Keep from Crying)", perhaps.  In the meantime, this is probably the best available official Hari compilation, and I recommend it highly.

title: The luckiest drummer on Earth's greatest hits, plus
text: A solid 20 tracks of Ringo Starrdust!  Ringo was a hit singles machine in the immediate years that followed the break-up of the Fabs, and this disc has 'em all: It Don't Come Easy, Back Off Boogaloo, Photograph, Oh My My, You're Sixteen, Only You, No-No Song.  It also collects his lesser hits (Hey Baby, A Dose of Rock 'n' Roll, Wrack My Brain, and more), along with one-offs and B-sides (Beaucoups of Blues, Early 1970).  A "must have" compilation for Ringo and Beatles fans.  Highly recommended.

title: Macca, the longest running hitmaking machine among the former Beatles
text: This review is of the two-disc version.  All the hits that fit, and then some.  It's all boss, no dross.  Thirty-nine tracks of McCartney magic spread over a packed pair of CDs.  Not presented in chronological order, which more often than not bugs me, but not here since Sir Paul's writing, playing, and vocals have maintained an incredible high-quality degree throughout his solo career.  One might argue the call a bit as to what's included and what's left out, but there's no arguing the quality of performance throughout both discs.  Very highly recommended.

title: One of his best live discs of the '70s
text: Elvis's second post-1968 comeback live album, recorded during his second residency at the International in Las Vegas.  Recorded (mostly) in February 1970 and released that summer, he was still thrilled to be there, having put the movie years behind with 1969's Change of Habit.  Great energy, great band, great setlist.  He was glorying in performing so much material that seemed to have passed him by during the Hollywood phase of his legendary career.  This expanded version makes an even stronger statement by including some of his then-recent hits that wouldn't last in his concert repertoire for long (In the Ghetto, Don't Cry Daddy, Kentucky Rain), alongside some songs that would become concert staples throughout the '70s (See See Rider, The Wonder of You, Polk Salad Annie, Proud Mary), and some he should have kept in but didn't (Walk a Mile in My Shoes, Release Me, the Yesterday / Hey Jude medley).  At the beginning of his career Elvis was asked what kind of music he sang.  "I sing all kinds," was the famous reply.  He proves that was no mere boast in this collection.  Highly recommended.

title: Aloha and Mahalo, Elvis' last stand before the fall
text: One of his career television highlights, yes, ratings-wise, but not among his best live-in-concert recordings.  He trimmed down and looked great (except for the already 'oh, so yesterday' jumpsuit cliche), added some new old songs to the setlist, and ran through a mildly expanded version of one of his standard Vegas shows.  But something was missing, despite all the hoopla; something was missing in him -- that special spark that set him apart from all his contemporaries seemed to be in short supply.  In the video version, when he unclasps the American Eagle cape and tosses it into the crowd, well, that kind of said it all.  To quote a great Bob Dylan lyric from It's Alright, Ma (I'm Only Bleeding) -- Elvis and Mama, there's a psychological riddle still waiting to be solved -- "All right, I've had enough, what else can you show me?"  That sentiment seemed to apply at that moment.  And then the slow, painful, public downfall.  A mere four years later there was the heartbreak that was the "Elvis in Concert" special on CBS.  The King is dead, long live the King.

title: RIP, Poco: Still keepin' the legend alive ...
text: A five-star live album docked one star for being half a reissue.  I had the original double-disc (CD/DVD) but lost it somewhere along the way.  Having just the audio is better than nothing, but the filmed video of the same concert was definitely one of the lures to buying Keepin' the Legend Alive all those years ago.  Still, it's a great 'through the years' setlist and a fabulous line-up of Poco musicians from across the band's storied career.  Led by the long-running duo of Rusty Young and Paul Cotton and featuring original members Richie Furay and George Grantham, among others, the pioneering country-rock band delivers the musical goods, top to bottom, front to back. Sadly, with Rusty, Paul, and George all gone, we won't see their like again.  RIP, Poco.  Highly recommended to longtime Poco-nuts and country-rock fans in general.

title: Viva the great lost Elvis soundtrack album
text: Summer of 1964.  Viva Las Vegas is released during the first wave of Beatlemania and the British Invasion of the US radio airwaves and record charts.  Elvis's biggest hit film of the '60s (due in no small part to his obvious on-screen chemistry with the wonderful Ann-Margret), yet Colonel Tom Parker and RCA opt out releasing a soundtrack LP.  Instead, there was a single (Viva Las Vegas! / What'd I Say?) and a four-song extended play 45.  It's no secret that extended play 45s were already a dead format, so the question has always remained why no LP?  If the Colonel, true to form, wanted no one but Elvis on the album, why not put the same six tracks on Side One and use a half-dozen unissued recordings from his May 1963 sessions on Side Two?  Could've highlighted the movie and soundtrack songs on the front cover and subtitled the LP "Elvis in Hollywood, Las Vegas, and Nashville," or something to that effect.  Could've / would've been a smash; would certainly have outperformed the previous Fun in Acapulco and Kissin' Cousins soundtracks and likely would've matched the success of the soundtrack for the next film, Roustabout, which went all the way to number one.  Truly, a lost opportunity.  Regardless, this disc makes a worthy addition to the Elvis movie music canon.  The sound is very good; the songs are better than most from his later '60s film era; he's engaged and enthusiastic, and the line-up (playlist?) of tracks flows along nicely.  Viva Las Vegas!  Oh yeah, but what might have been.  Highly recommended to fans of Elvis, Elvis movies, and the Sixties pop scene in general.  By the way, IMHO, the duet with A-M on You're the Boss would've made a smash hit single, whether used in the film or not.

title: The underrated Box Tops cooked up a mighty tasty Memphis soul stew
text: Pretty much the complete recorded output by this seriously underrated -- and underappreciated -- 1960s Memphis group.  The 16-to-19-year-old Alex Chilton is a stone wonder as lead vocalist and the band, in and out of sessions at American with the Memphis Boys, always lend him solid support.  The Letter, Neon Rainbow, Cry Like a Baby, Choo-Choo Train, I Met Her in Church, Sweet Cream Ladies, Soul Deep are the best-known singles highlights, but every one of the four albums collected on these two discs offer a wealth of musical treasures.  From great covers (Trains and Boats and Planes, I'm Your Puppet, I Shall Be Released, She Shot a Hole in My Soul), to Alex Chilton originals (I Must Be the Devil, Happy Song, I See Only Sunshine), to lost singles and B-sides (You Keep Tightening Up on Me, King's Highway, Lay Your Shine on Me), the Box Tops cooked up a mighty tasty Memphis soul stew.  The group's cornball name and singles band reputation worked against their being taken seriously in the day; hopefully, collections like this one will work to reappraise their work and reputation.  They should be held in the same high blue-eyed soul esteem as The Rascals and The Righteous Brothers.  Highly recommended.

title: Crosby, Stills & Nash (sans Young): The Greatest Hits
text: Crosby, Stills & Nash (sans Young) Greatest Hits, via Rhino in 2005.  No Neil is just alright with me.  Trouble is, there's nothing post-1982's Daylight Again.  That leaves five full albums unaccounted for, not to mention various "solo" efforts on which the band members supported one another.  No real argument with what's included, except that the playing order is kind of sloppy and definitely not chronological.  But at 19 tracks it's surely a generous single-disc compilation.  I've been hoping for a Volume Two follow-up, but some 17 years down the line that's pretty unlikely.  Still, highly recommended for harmony lovers everywhere.

title: CCR collection aimed at late '60s AM-Radio and jukebox fans
text: The complete CCR singles, a- and b- sides just the way you remember them.  Ruling the airwaves from 1968 through 1972 or so, CCR were defining roots-rock and Americana before the phrases had even been coined.  This compilation collects the hit singles, many of them double a-sides, almost all of them charted titles, and it's like a musical trip back in time to the heady jukebox and AM-Radio days of the late '60s / early '70s.  Bonus DVD contains four music videos.  The set is nicely packaged and presented, with upgraded sound.  Highly recommended to Creedence fans, especially those with a jones for singles mixes.

title: Basically a 'Best of CCR' double-disc set, with live bonus disc
text: CCR has been repackaged so many times as to be considered ludicrous at this point.  Chronicles one and two stand as the best of the best, but Ultimate (2012) runs a close second.  Discs One and Two (20 songs each) cover the meat and potatoes of the story with smash hit singles a- and b- sides galore, along with memorable deep cuts and covers.  Sticklers for historical fact will be disappointed with the play list in that it is more random than chronological.  Still, it's the real thing, and it all sounds great.  Disc Three is a bit of a problem.  Twelve live cuts, none of which rival the studio originals, and the sound is not up to the usual CCR standard.  In addition, most of these live versions were recorded post-Tom Fogerty exit from the band, and the trio arrangements sound a bit thin.  The price is pretty reasonable for a two-CD set, so the third disc is basically a CCR live-in-concert bonus.  All in all, I'm glad to have this one in my collection. Definitely recommended.

title: Very likely the best of the many John Lennon 'Best Of' collections
text: John Lennon was all about the truth, especially in his public life and throughout his solo career.  "Gimme Some Truth" just may be the best compilation covering his post-Beatles career, even if it's not a complete overview of his American chart hits (singles).  The sound is generally terrific (his vocals have been pushed a bit more to the front than on previous official releases) and features such clarity that you get to hear subtle musical flourishes that had been pretty much buried in the mixes over the years.  No argument with what's been included (with the lone exception of the sloppy live-in-concert version of "Come Together," perhaps), but I'm pretty sure that, like me, you'll notice some personal favorites are missing.  Regardless, this one's highly recommended, even if mainly for the improved sound.

title: Gene Clark: This Byrd has flown ... but what a legacy he left behind.
text: An absolutely fabulous 3-disc, 60-song collection.  And a well-deserved tribute to the most mercurial member of the legendary Byrds.  He was in and out and in and out of the band he co-founded so often that fans simply figured he'd be back yet again every time he exited.  Without him, the Byrds always soldiered on, but without the special singer / songwriter magic he brought to the band.  The late, legendary New York disc jockey Pete Fornatale, who I thought the world of, used to say, "If it ain't Roger McGuinn, it ain't The Byrds."  Well, that was true to a certain extent, but without Gene Clark they simply weren't the same Byrds we all knew and loved.  This collection not only serves as verification to that fact, but also explores Clark's post-Byrds career, some of which rivals (and some even surpass) his Byrds contributions.  Discs One and Two make the case perfectly with excellent official release selections from the Byrds and his adventurous, genre-jumping, post-Byrds albums.  Disc Three is largely made up of demos, live tracks, and alternate takes; most of which remain interesting, some even moving.  I highly recommend "Gene Clark Collected" to fans of The Byrds, Americana, '60s folk-rock, and '70s singer/songwriter music.  Finally, the great Gene Clark gets his due.

title: Doobie Bros:  The hits and nothing but the hits
text: Import version of Rhino's 2001 The Doobie Brothers' Greatest Hits, repackaged in a somewhat slicker cover.  Contains the same line-up of songs, 20 in all, in pretty much chronological order according to singles release dates.  All the hits that fit, yeah!  Singles versions of Listen to the Music, Jesus Is Just Alright, Nobody, It Keeps You Runnin', and Dependin' on You; just the way you remember them from the AM airplay on your car radio back in the day.  Takes you from the Tommy Johnston era through the Michael McDonald period, and on to the Johnston comeback years, with Patrick Simmons rockin' along at every turn.  Highly recommended to fans of the Doobies and '70s rock in general.

title: Not your Mom and Pop's Blue Ridge Rangers
text: A 180 from the original Blue Ridge Rangers.  Alone in the studio covering classic bluegrass, country, and gospel numbers vs. a guest star-studded duets celebration of mostly post-1960 country / country-rock / singer-songwriter material.  The purity and pure joy of the original are lacking in this long-delayed sequel, and the star power and high sheen production hinders rather than helps, imho anyway.  My favorite moment is the re-do of Change in the Weather, a lost classic from Fogerty's disappointing "Eye of the Zombie" LP.  This time around, it's been given a near-perfect musical and vocal arrangement.  Let's call this three-and-a-half stars, a mild recommendation.

title: JC Fogerty's post-Blue Ridge Rangers solo debut
text: Like his post-CCR "Blue Ridge Rangers" album, "John Fogerty" is a one-man-band studio effort that has held up incredibly well.  Buoyed by the inclusion of a pair of his most frequently covered solo songs, Almost Saturday Night and Rockin' All Over the World, "John Fogerty" would've made a great Creedence LP back in the day.  Not meant to be, I know, but it's nonetheless meant as a sincere compliment.  The hint of sterility that pervades quite a bit of this set would've been blown right out the studio door by the vaunted CCR rhythm section, for sure.  Still, this is the closest solo Fogerty has come to recreating that amazing Creedence vibe, and it's all the better for it.  Recommended.  But hey, c'mon John, bring out an official release of its intended follow-up LP, "Hoodoo."  Gotta be better than the still in-print CCR swan song, "Mardi Gras," yes?
