title: Fogerty's first one-man-band project still stands tall
text: John Fogerty's first post-CCR release and it's a stone classic.  He's doing his one-man-band thing -- playing all the instruments and singing all the vocals -- and doing it in subtle yet impressive style.  No J.C. Fogerty originals here, it's all covers of classic country, gospel, and bluegrass favorites done up in his own special style.  The Blue Ridge Rangers has held up incredibly well.  Highly recommended.  I only wish he'd allow an official release of the great lost "Hoodoo" album; can't possibly be any more embarrassing than "Eye of the Zombie," right?

title: The remaining Monkees honor the Pre-Fab Four's legacy
text: Went back and replayed this one upon hearing of Mike Nesmith's passing.  Very moving, perhaps in the light of heart-tugging nostalgia, but also incredibly lively and entertaining strictly on its own merits.  Mike and Micky are hitting on all cylinders here; their show's set-list is first-rate, and the musical support is right in-the-pocket throughout.  The then-remaining Monkees duo do / did their cohorts and their communal musical legacy proud.  Highly recommended to Monkees fans, old and new.

title: The Band album that changed the world of rock 'n roll back in 1968
text: The 1968 debut album by The Band.  All it did was to change the musical landscape of Rock 'n' Roll and kickstart a new genre of American music: Americana.  An album I've loved for more than half a century, and have owned in any number of configurations, from LPs to 8-tracks, cassettes to CDs, and various versions of those.  Magnificent in its simplicity -- which positively flew in the face of late '60s Rock -- wonderfully sung, played, and written, "Music from Big Pink" is one landmark Sixties artifact that has withstood the test of time.  Along with the group's second LP (1969's "The Band," a/k/a 'The Brown Album'), The Band set such a high bar of artistic integrity that even they couldn't maintain it.  Truly, one of Rock's brightest shining moments and this 50th Anniversary edition is most highly recommended.

title: The Grateful Dead's greatest musical effort just got better
text: Workingman's Dead is the band's greatest achievement.  Along with its follow-up, American Beauty, which plays like part two of a set, The Grateful Dead set new standards for themselves and the Album Rock radio acts of the era.  The greatly expanded 50th anniversary version also sets new standards -- for reissues of classic LPs.  Excellent graphics, compelling notes, improved remixed and remastered sound, and bodacious bonus material.  If you're already interested in this expanded reissue, I suppose you're just wondering if it's worth the expense.  If you ask me, there's no need to hesitate -- just go ahead and buy it.  You won't be disappointed.  Five timecards punched, and highly recommended.

title: The Dead's American Beauty: Bigger, better, more beautiful than ever
text: Along with Workingman's Dead, American Beauty is The Grateful Dead's best album.  This 50th Anniversary Edition is bigger and better than ever.  The sound improvement is amazing.  It gives you the chance to pick up on many a subtle musical moment you've hardly even noticed before.  The extras are bountiful and beautiful.  The notes informative and interestingly presented.  The graphics are all any long-time fan could hope for.  In short, it's a five star reissue.  Highly recommended!

title: Eric Clapton's Christmas offering
text: I've had this one for a couple of Christmas seasons, and I've played it numerous times.  Enough to know it's a good 'un.  As I recall, I wasn't all that sure about it upon first couple of plays, but it has definitely grown on me over time.  A good blend of classic, traditional, and original Christmas material, with Mr. Clapton in his low-key J.J. Cale-style vocal mode and supported by his usual coterie of top-flight musicians.  If you're a fan of pop culture Christmas releases, this one should be in your collection.  Four Christmas wreaths, and definitely recommended.

title: The Monkees throw one last Christmas Party
text: Bought this one a couple years ago.  Broke it out again today after hearing the sad news of Mike's passing. So, Micky's the last Monkee standing.  A sitcom prophecy comes true.  Recall from the mists of time the old episode where Mick's left alone by the boys and he's singing, "Here I come, walking down the street ... Hey, hey I'm the Monkee ..."  Nostalgia for a more innocent time, pure and simple.  Anyway, if you're a Monkees fan and a Christmas record fan, this is the disc for you.  Good fun.  Good memories.  Good way to remember fallen childhood heroes.  RIP Mike, Davy, and Pete.  Keep the flame aglow, Mick.  Merry Christmas everyone.

title: Willie Nile's American Ride is a trip worth taking.
text: A 2013 release that's so contemporary it could've been issued yesterday.  Filled to the brim with American observations and a sense of new-fashioned Yankee know-how, Willie Nile has delivered a real-deal keeper here.  It's an album for the new Millenium and for the ages.  From openers This Is Our Time and American Ride, to closers Sunrise In New York City and There's No Place Like Home, with pit stops between for modern classics like God Laughs and Holy War, this is an album made up of memorable songs and sharp, clear-eyed writing to be relished and repeated regularly.  A true masterwork, and definitely recommended.

title: The wondrous Martha Velez takes the pulse of American Heartbeat
text: This is the kind of music that never gets the exposure it so richly deserves.  Martha Velez is a national musical treasure, a name everyone should know, but all too few actually do. Tremendous heart, great vocal approach, soulful and soul-stirring to her core.  She takes on a pop-radio classic like the familiar Oh No, Not My Baby, and makes you forget every other version you've ever heard.  Just nails it and makes it her own.  Originally released way on back in 1977, "American Heartbeat" is of its time, yet timeless.  Highly recommended.

title: A well-deserved tribute to the writings of Willie Nile
text: Two discs, 26 tracks, and featuring a roomful of first-class independent artists, "Uncovered" is a well-deserved tribute to the songwriting talents of the great Willie Nile.  I'm generally not a fan of this kind of thing, but this one works wonderfully well.  Maybe it's the artists themselves, who all seem to share Willie's sense of freedom and independent spirit.  Some of the best known among them (Emily Duff, Elliott Murphy, Dan Bern, Richard Barone, Graham Parker, Nils Lofgren, John Gorka, Jen Chapin, Lucy Kaplansky, Richard Shindell, among others) have had similar lengthy careers to Mr. Nile.  Critical acclaim and high expectations from high-profile record labels, followed by abandonment by same labels mere nanoseconds later.  With a little less luck, it's a circumstance that could've derailed Dylan, Springsteen, and any other '60s / '70s singer / songwriter you care to name.  But some of them, like these determined folks, continue to fight the fight and they recognize a kindred spirit in Willie Nile.  Great songs and fine performances, with a genuine sense of comradery permeating the artistic contributions throughout both discs, I highly recommend "Willie Nile Uncovered."

title: Willie Nile reminds us: We're all Children of Paradise
text: Flat out fabulous.  One of Willie Nile's best, and that's saying something.  My brother put me on to this one, by way of the song Gettin' Ugly Out There, and I can't thank him enough.  It was the entree to an altogether incredible listening experience.  The kind of elpee they don't make anymore; oh, yeah, they do!  From the stirring opener, Seeds of a Revolution, to the heart-on-his-sleeve closer, All God's Children, Willie Nile delivers the kind of record I gave up hoping for too many years ago to remember.  Thanks for restoring my faith in the power of Rock 'n' Roll and my sense of artistic expectation, Willie.  This one should be in everyone's collection.  Magnificent!

title: The incomparable Ms. Velez the soul goods in style
text: Another killer collection from the fabulous Martha Velez.  Ten slices of open-hearted, soul-baring singing at its best.  Worth the price of admission simply for her fabulous version of Do Right Woman, Do Right Man, Matinee Weepers is a master class in the art of soulful singing.  But listening and being moved will do just fine.  This weeper's a true keeper.  Highly rcommended.

title: The Stray Cats continue to strut their Rockabilly stuff, live in-concert, from LA to London Town
text: If you dug Stray Cats back then, you're sure to still love 'em now.  Terrific performances, excellent set list, joyfully played and sung.  If you've got a jones for Rockabilly (revival, or original) you'll likely find a lot to like here.  Rockabilly Rock 'n' Roll music was meant to be played live and loud, and The Stray Cats do it up right.  Recommended for rockers of every stripe, everywhere.

title: Neil Diamond's All Time Greatest Hits?  Absolutely!
text: The single disc version.  All killer, no filler.  If you were a fan at any point during the great man's long, legendary career, you'll find plenty to love about this collection.  As a casual observer, you might be surprised at the length and breadth of his solid pop catalogue.  Not your typical singer / songwriter, Diamond wrote songs for his own limited vocal power, and he wrote them to be PERFORMED LIVE and IN-CONCERT.  These studio recordings may seem bare-bones simple to some listeners (compared to his various and many live releases through the years), but these are the versions I grew up with (as singles and on albums) and definitely favor.  Highly recommended.

title: John Denver's first, and best, Greatest Hits collection
text: Released in the first flush of his success as a singer / songwriter, Greatest Hits may seem rather thin and incomplete to the casual observer of John Denver's career.  However, as his first hits comp (and unsure of how many more hits would follow) this 1973 RCA "Best of" is a great reminder of how good he really was from the beginning.  It's also the first JD LP I ever purchased, so there's a certain nostalgia connection at work as well.  Real radio hits mingle here with album deep cuts and his original versions of songs that had been best-sellers for other artists.  Everything considered, it's remained my favorite among all his many compilation discs through the years.  Highly recommended.

title: Essential Elvis?  Absolutely!
text: Two discs packed to the brim with pop music history.  There will be inclusion and omission quibbles, naturally enough, as Elvis' career was always hot on one radio format or another (Pop, R&B, Easy Listening, Country).  So, it's flat-out impossible to cover 'em all and make everyone happy with a two-disc set.  Maybe they should deliver an "Essential" for every format?  That might be the best solution.  Anyway, what is included here is unbelievably impressive.  This guy could sing anything, really, and do it authentically and with conviction.  He was, quite possibly, at his best delivering a sentimental ballad, or a sad lyrical tale of heartbreak and regret.  He was the King of Rock 'n Roll, yes, but so much more.  "The Essential" is a good place to start for the uninitiated.  Highly recommended.

title: Neil Diamond and Christmas -- how can you go wrong?
text: It's a pretty simple concept.  If you like Neil Diamond (who among us doesn't have an ND favorite or two) and you have a jones for Christmas music (again, who doesn't, really?), then this collection is sure to please.  If not you, then someone close to you.  I gave a copy to my good wife, Hannie, along with a similar John Denver Christmas collection, and they've both been in heavy rotation in her car CD-player.  She's very happy.  Me?  I lean more toward Elvis, Frank, Dean, and Bing, but that's okay, too.  Slipping in the occasional Neil Diamond, John Denver, Carpenters disc is just alright with me.  Recommended.

title: Innocent Christmas memories with Elvis
text: I've been spending Christmas with Elvis since Santa brought me the Elvis' Christmas Album LP back in 1965, when I was a 14-year-old newbie to the pop music scene.  While I had been groovin' to the sounds of The Beatles, Beach Boys, Dave Clark Five, Motown, etc. on my AM Radio (WABC and WMCA, mostly), Elvis was something old that was new again to me.  I became a fan thanks to that original Christmas record, and I soon began backtracking through his RCA catalogue following that Christmas, spending lunch money and snow shoveling / lawn cutting earnings on singles, EPs, and LPs over the next couple of years.  This collection brings back many a fond memory of those more innocent times, and while not his best Christmas comp, it'll do.  I know I'll be playing it constantly over the next few weeks.  Highly recommended.

title: You don't have to be a Mellencamp fanatic for this one to hit home ...
text: I'm not a diehard John Mellencamp fan, by any means.  Rain on the Scarecrow and a couple of 'Best of' sets pretty much make up the Mellencamp section of my collection.  But this one's different.  Terrific audio / visual version of a tour I never saw, but now wish I had.  Very interesting set list, mixing the familiar with the then-new, and adding some nice surprises along the way.  If you're more than a casual fan, you're likely all over this one already.  If you're not an especially big fan, like yours truly, you just may be surprised at how much there is to like here.  Highly recommended.

title: The Band's disappointing fourth LP with 50th anniversary bells & whistles
text: Cahoots, The Band's fourth LP, was something of a disappointment when released back in 1971.  Following on the impressive heels of Music from Big Pink (1968), The Band (1969), and to a lesser extent, Stage Fright (1970), Cahoots proved to be the group's weakest effort to date and failed to capture the sizable audience of its predecessors.  It started off strong with two tracks that quickly became in-concert stalwarts for the group, Life Is a Carnival and Bob Dylan's When I Paint My Masterpiece, but then seemed to quickly go south.  Even the Van Morrison contribution, 4% Pantomime, failed to get things back on track.  Keep in mind, this is in comparison to The Band's glorious early history, which was pretty much unmatched up to that time.  Remixing / remastering helps, bringing out heretofore missed or unheard musical subtleties, and on its own (blanking out the group's previous sterling output) Cahoots is a solid three and one-half stars album.  There are bonus studio tracks and alternate versions included, as well as some fine new liner notes.  The live tracks bonus disc (Live at the Olympia Theatre, Paris, May 1971) is interesting, if incomplete; it's also a bootleg recording so the sound is obviously not up to The Band's usual high standards (especially in the current 50th Anniversary series of reissues).  Still, for fans of The Band and completists, it's worth recommending.

title: Croz's expanded debut: Sometimes less is more ...
text: Crosby's first solo disc from way on back in the day.  Kind of misunderstood, even mildly ignored, at the time of its release, If I Could Only Remember My Name's reputation and stature have grown steadily through the decades.  It's now considered a near-classic by fans and critics alike, and justifiably so.  This 50th anniversary two-disc edition celebrates its accumulated reputation in grand style.  The original LP's sound has been both upgraded and improved on disc one, and expanded to include the fine bonus track, Kids and Dogs, as the album's closer.  Disc Two collects demos, out-takes, and alternate versions from the same sessions, but to far less effect.  Disc One will be in my player regularly over the next few months; Disc Two got its first play upon receipt and it'll be a while before I sit through the whole thing again. Truth be told, I'd have been happy to have been able to purchase Disc One as a stand alone.  Sometimes, less is more.  Still, recommended.

title: Donald Fagen's Steely Dan Band may have you reelin' in the years
text: Docked one star because I'm missing Do It Again, childish as that may seem, Northeast Corridor is only the second Steely Dan live disc ever, coming a quarter century after their first in-concert collection, Alive in America.  Dedicated to the late Walter Becker, Northeast Corridor makes a wonderful in-concert tribute to Fagen's long-time musical partner and Steely Dan sidekick; it's also one helluva trip through this band's tremendous history.  Twelve tracks of Steely nirvana, played by a masterful band led by the inimitable Mr. Fagen.  So good it had me Reelin' in the Years!  Highly recommended.

title: Donald Fagen's "The Nightfly Live" is right in the Steely Dan groove
text: Donald Fagen, backed by the current Steely Dan Band, playing the complete version of his debut solo LP, The Nightfly, live in-concert.  In a word, fabulous!  A near perfect companion to his Steely Dan live disc, Northeast Corridor / Steely Dan Live!  Great material, terrific band.  I.G.Y., Ruby Baby, The Nightfly, the entire album, is musically in the groove, with room to breathe.  If you're a fan of the Dan, you'll definitely want to check out Donald Fagen's The Nightfly Live.

title: 'Tattoo' -- the Stones' version of Odds and Sods
text: If you're looking to buy this anniversary edition, you're already pretty familiar with Tattoo You.  It's one of the Stones' greatest LPs, made up of mostly leftover material from various recording sessions -- not unlike The Who favorite, Odds and Sods.  The original LP play-list is as impressive as ever; the sound has been upgraded and improved; the bonus material is Stones' legend worthy.  Start me up and let it rock!  Highly recommended.

title: The Essential Phil Spector?  Absolutely!
text: Doesn't matter what you think of Spector the man, or how / where he ended up in life.  Amateur human being, genius record producer.  Whatever.  The proof of his genius is right here in the grooves.  An absolutely essential collection for anyone with even the slightest interest in the history of American Pop culture.  Very highly recommended.

title: Across a Room crowded with truth, pain, and emotion
text: A number of my friends find Richard Thompson to be an acquired taste; love his guitar playing, not fond of his vocals.  Some of them feel the same way about Bob Dylan; love his songwriting, hate his voice.  Now, I'm not putting Thompson in anywhere near the same category as Dylan, but I'm a fan of both artists.  Well, with Dylan, I guess I'm some kind of superfan, having purchased every LP he's released during his 60-year career.  Across A Crowded Room (1985) is one of my favorite Richard Thompson albums.  When The Spell Is Broken alone is worth the price of admission, imho, and Love in a Faithless Country, She Twists the Knife Again, and Ghosts in the Wind aren't far behind.  This is a stellar kind of break-up album powered by lyrical truths, pain, and emotion.  And while it's no Blood on the Tracks (what album is, really), it's a very powerful musical ride.  Definitely recommended.

title: The Big Bang of the Neil Diamond musical legend
text: The fabulous Neil Diamond, uncut.  As a songwriter, he's delivering amazingly catchy songs for radio, and for other young pop acts to cover.  As a singer / performer, he's learning his craft as he goes, growing in confidence in leaps and bounds in the era covered here (1966-1968).  In many ways, the Bang Years were his best years.  He could rock like he meant it; he could sell a ballad with sheer sincerity; he could experiment with his music and lyrics in subtle, not necessarily radio-ready fashion.  By the mid-'70s, he'd never be this light-of-touch, easy-to-take, and unencumbered by expectation again.  This is the real Neil.  This is the feel of Neil.  This is the Neil meant just for you.  1966 through 1968: The Big Bang of the Neil Diamond story.  Definitely recommended.

title: He's back from the army alright, and he's better than ever
text: Elvis Is Back paired with Something for Everybody, along with non-LP singles from the sessions, adds up to an incredible double-disc set.  Elvis Is Back (1960), along with From Elvis in Memphis (1969), bookend that decade as his two best post-army albums.  On Elvis Is Back (and singles), he shows off his new voice and takes on material from across the pop scene spectrum.  1961's Something for Everybody (again, plus singles) is a bit less successful, but only because the playlist isn't quite as strong.  His vocals are a wonder to behold throughout -- committed, strong or gentle, always in service of the song.  He's like a method actor of music, bringing the full depth and weight of his life experiences to each performance, especially the ballads.  Highly recommended, and not just to dyed-in-the-wool Elvis fans.  This is a great collection for all popular music lovers.

title: Rick Nelson live in concert when he still had something to prove
text: One of my all-time favorite live albums, remastered and expanded in a very big way.  Close to four times the material contained in the original 12-song Decca Records release, "In Concert - The Troubadour, 1969" presents Rick Nelson as a then-contemporary artist, a man on a musical mission.  The mission?  To leave the gnawing "teen idol" tag in the rear-view mirror and take his Stone Canyon Band into the '70s rock scene as something new and markedly different -- a pioneering country-rock band.  Happy to say, mission accomplished.  This is the sound of a still young artist finding himself, redefining himself, and quite simply enjoying the moment.  It's a complete joy to behold.  To my aging boomer ears, this is the best LP he ever created.  Five stars, for sure.  Recommended unequivocally.

title: The Ultimate Rascals: Time/Peace, and then some
text: America's greatest rock 'n' soul band of the Sixties (just possibly the best ever!), The Rascals infamously imploded by 1970 and sadly missed out on the '70s Rock revolution.  Inter-band member squabbles, a move from their comfortable five-year home with Atlantic Records to a more faceless future at Columbia, the loss of two key members (Eddie Brigati and Gene Cornish) as the band (basically Felix Cavaliere, Dino Danelli, and a rotating cast of musical friends) shifted to a jazzier, funkier sound, and unresolved business and managerial issues, all combined to derail The Rascals as the hit-making machine we all know, love, and remember.  "The Ultimate Rascals" plays like "Time/Peace" (their classic 1968 number one greatest hits LP) on steroids.  Twenty memorable tracks of '60s gold on one disc, "The Ultimate" covers all their hit singles, plus; from their 1965 debut, I Ain't Gonna Eat Out My Heart Anymore, through to their final Top 40 hit, 1969's Carry Me Back, it's a rockin' good ride.  It would be nice to have these classics (Good Lovin', Groovin', How Can I Be Sure, A Girl Like You, A Beautiful Morning, People Got To Be Free, etc.) remixed and remastered, yes.  But even as is (and the sound isn't bad, it could just be so much better a listening experience if cleaned up) this is proof positive as to why The Rascals are justifiably Rock 'n' Roll Hall of Fame members.  Highly recommended!

title: Norah Jones Live ... Will We Meet Again?
text: Three and a half stars.  An old reviewer's adage comes to mind: If you like this kind of thing, this is the kind of thing you'll like.  Nice set, nicely presented, and no real surprises.  Its very predictability undermines the concept of a live in-concert performance recording.  Pleasant enough, yes, and Norah Jones diehards will love it, I'm sure.  For the more casual fan, however, it'll likely feel like a lost opportunity.  'Till We Met Again, or Will We Meet Again?  Only time will tell.

title: A magical evening with Suzanne Vega
text: What a wonderful musical ride for Suzanne Vega / New York City music scene fans.  Ms. Vega is an entrancing and thoroughly engaging cafe / club-style performer and a seemingly natural New York raconteur.  Songs and set-ups keep it all cooking and steadily entertaining.  Some of my favorite moments include Frank and Ava, Tom's Diner, Marlene on the Wall, and her magnificent cover of Lou Reed's Walk on the Wild Side.  Intimate and intricate, and always entertaining, An Evening of New York Songs and Stories ranks with Suzanne Vega's very best.  Wish it came packaged with a visual companion piece.  Highly recommended, especially to those looking for a truly native New Yorker musical experience.

title: For Albert Hammond, when it rained, it really poured
text: Albert Hammond may have made his best living as a hit-making songwriter (99 Miles from L.A., The Air That I Breathe, Names, Tags, Numbers & Labels), but he was no slouch as a recording artist either.  This twofer makes a strong case for the recording artist side of his musical abilities.  While the main draw here is obviously his classy and classic 1972 hit single, It Never Rains in Southern California, there are plenty of other '70s radio play-worthy tracks on both albums to keep you interested all the way through.  Among the standouts included: Down by the River, If You Gotta Break Another Heart, The Free Electric Band, The Peacemaker, and For the Peace of All Mankind, most of them minor chart hits for him.  Recommended for fans of '70s pop / rock radio.

title: Lost Treasure: The wondrous Martha Velez
text: A dear old friend, Sandy Mac, had the "Fiends & Angels" LP back in the day and absolutely played it to death in the apartment I shared with my buddies L.A and Barry back in the early '70s.  This was a couple of years after the album came out, but it was totally new to us.  We all learned to love it.  Great times, great album.  This twofer brings back a lot of fond memories, but it's the music, not the memories, that matter.  Terrific line-up of songs, great musicians (some very famous), interesting arrangements, and Martha's off-the-main-path vocal approach combine to deliver a very memorable musical ride.  "Escape From Babylon," from a few years later, is her Bob Marley excursion.  And while it's very different from the late-Sixties blues-based rock of "Fiends & Angels," it's a complete match in the quality of songs, arrangements, musical support, and star-power.  Martha's vocals, although more restrained this time around, remain eloquent, emotional, and evocative.  A highly recommended lost treasure.

title: Behold Lauren Daigle's lovely Christmas collection
text: Lauren Daigle's Behold: A Christmas Collection is a lovely blend of pop and Christmas classics, along with time-honored seasonal spirituals.  Songs as disparate as Jingle Bells, Winter Wonderland and Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas mix comfortably with traditional spiritual favorites like Silent Night, O Come All Ye Faithful and Away In a Manger, along with pop classics like White Christmas and Little Drummer Boy.  All 13 tracks delivered in fine Yuletide style and seasonal good cheer.  Recommended.

title: A lovely Christmas season session with Norah Jones
text: Christmas with Ms. Jones, what could it possibly be but a warm, pleasant musical experience.  She does a great job livening up even the most familiar holiday material, from across the pop genre color spectrum: Blue Christmas, White Christmas,  Winter Wonderland, Run Rudolph Run.  The set opens with the one-two Yule punch of Christmas Calling and Christmas Don't Be Late, and she winds it down 12 tracks later with a lovely, lucky 13 take on What Are You Doing New Year's Eve?  Charming Christmas fare.  Recommended.

title: The Strip in another time, another place, another groove.
text: Takes me back to way back when.  Another time, another world, another memory dream.  77 Sunset Strip was the coolest show on television, and Kookie was its cooler than ice youth audience draw.  Thus, the Edd Byrnes tracks are nostalgic fun, while the Sunset Strip soundtrack-related material stands up incredibly well.  If you were a fan -- whether a highbrow or a hipster -- this'll be right in your familiar groove wheelhouse.  Like dig it, Dad!

title: Gerry Rafferty's American peak
text: City To City has always been a personal favorite, with Night Owl a fine but less impactful follow-up.  I don't believe there's a weak track on the former, but the latter (despite including excellent tracks like Days Gone Down and Get It Right Next Time) suffers a bit in comparison.  But then, City To City is buoyed by classic Rafferty songcraft the likes of Baker Street, Right Down The Line, and Home And Dry, to name just a few. Neither LP has ever sounded as good as they do in this fine two-disc set.  Definitely recommended.

title: On E Street in 1979, the moment when the great man became legend
text: A signpost moment in Springsteen's career.  Marking the transition from hometown hero turned rock star, to international superstar.  Darkness On The Edge Of Town had gone to number one a year earlier following a nearly three year recording lay-off (contract lawsuits) after his Born To Run break-out, and the release of The River was about a year in the offing.  In the meantime, Bruce Springsteen & The E Street Band were continuing to build on and expand their already heady reputation as the top touring act of the time.  Along comes the multi-artists No Nukes benefit concerts, and these Jersey Shore upstarts blow every other act off the stage, bar none, securing a live-in-concert rep that continues to shine on into the 21st Century.  The sound is very good, and the film has been cleaned up considerably.  Recommended, most heavily for Bruce Tramps, but for '70s rockers in general.

title: As advertised in the title: Lu's Rockin' Little Christmas
text: Three and one-half stars.  Not a classic Christmas album by any means, but it's not coal in your stocking bad either.  Like most holiday collections, if you like the artist you'll likely like their Christmas offering.  Me, I like Lucinda Williams, ergo, I like the disc.  Won't be in heavy holiday rotation on my player, but it'll get plenty of spins, as they used to say.  Lu's no Grinch!

title: Eric Clapton is one rock 'n' roll veteran still performing near the top of his game ...
text: To my ears anyway, The Lady In The Balcony (Lockdown Sessions) is easily Clapton's best album since 2015's celebratory Slowhand At 70 (Live At The Royal Albert Hall), maybe even his best in a couple of decades.  Heavily weighted toward his acoustic side, The Lockdown Sessions plays as a kind of decades-delayed sequel to the guitar master's Unplugged masterpiece.  The setlist is well thought out; the stripped-down musical accompaniment is top-notch throughout; the players and performances are uniformly stellar, and Clapton's singing and playing remain as near-flawless as ever.  I've said it before, but it bears repeating.  Many of the musical sidebar stories of the dreaded Covid-19 pandemic lockdown era will be remembered as amazingly special moments of relief, release, but never resignation.  The Lady In The Balcony will surely attest to that.  Ten stars (five each for both the audio and the video).  Very highly recommended.

title: Tepid '90s country arrangements, but reunion mission accomplished
text: A tribute album, of sorts.  Adapting Eagles favorites from a kind of country-rock Nirvana to run-of-the-mill, bland '90s country radio-ready fodder is not my idea of a true "tribute."  However, the interest generated by this LP is said to have contributed to the reformation of said Eagles.  So, tepid performances or not, mission accomplished.  Still, can't recommend this one; go for the band's Hell Freezes Over instead.

title: From Elvis in Nashville, one last time
text: I'm sure that when these 1971 sessions took place, no one expected them to be Elvis' final tracks from Nashville.  But they turned out to be, simple as that.  Handled with a lighter touch, a surer hand, however you want to look at it, some solid LPs could've come out of this recording session.  Two actually did; however, if you're not into Christmas and / or Gospel music both The Wonderful World of Christmas and He Touched Me probably slipped by largely unnoticed.  This despite the Christmas album being a multi-platinum annual success and the Gospel record scoring Elvis one of his three Grammy Awards (all for sacred recordings) and being a steady (eventually platinum) selling catalog title.  Seems Elvis was listening to a lot of commercial folk music from the Sixties at the time  -- and covering many of the tunes he'd been grooving to during this session -- and he and producer Felton Jarvis could easily have put together a sequel to the previous year's very well-received Elvis Country album.  Songs written by Bob Dylan, Gordon Lightfoot, Buffy Sainte Marie, and Kris Kristofferson, coupled with traditionals like Amazing Grace, could have been the core of a solid Elvis Folk 'n' Country LP.  In addition, an audacious contemporary pop album along the lines of 1970's very successful That's The Way It Is was also within reach.  Instead of throwaway one-off singles, tracks like I'm Leavin' and It's Only Love could have been the centerpieces of that new pop LP, along with as yet (then) unreleased recordings with a contemporary feel (Love Me, Love The Life I Lead, We Can Make The Morning), and well-chosen covers (Fools Rush In, Padre).  Sadly, not to be.  Following on the heels of one of his lesser LPs (Love Letters From Elvis), 1972's Elvis Now and 1973's Elvis seemed like throwaways, which they essentially were.  Happy to say, the 1971 Nashville Session situation is somewhat salvaged and celebrated here.  This four-disc sequel to From Elvis In Nashville does its best to put it all right, and mostly succeeds.  Stripping off the Felton Jarvis (although Elvis-approved, remember) dross and gloss once again works wonders.  The spotlight remains on Elvis' vocals and his band's incredible playing throughout, and it's a revelation.  Do I love it?  Absolutely!  Will everyone else?  Not likely.  But for hardcore Elvis fans (especially when you're trying to make the case to the non-fan) this one's essential.

title: Heading forward by looking back, Fogerty delivers one of his best solo albums ever.
text: Terrific J. C. Fogerty songs (CCR and solo years), vocals, and performances.  Excellent, simpatico  guests.  A rare and nearly perfect duets collection.  A 14-track set that's lean, rocking and dross-free, including a pair of (then) new non-duets (Mystic Highway, Train of Fools).  If you're a longtime Fogerty and / or Creedence fan like yours truly, you'll find yourself in roots rock heaven here.  He really has written songs for everyone.  Glad I revisited this one recently.  Highly recommended.

title: America's early history still sounds fresh
text: History is the America album we all had in our collections back in the day.  Even casual fans who usually put the group down as CSNY knock-offs (something I never agreed with) had a bit of a jones for this one.  George Martin put it together for the group's first-ever greatest hits collection, and it played better and more smoothly than any of their regular LPs.  Sounds great, catchy as ever.  Earwigs like A Horse With No Name, Daisy Jane, and Lonely People continue to sound incredibly fresh, some half-century down the road.  Recommended, especially to fans of '70s pop-rock.

title: Don McLean's AMerican Pie, an early peak or an albatross?
text: Huge success is a double-edged sword, right?  One of the best examples is Don McLean's American Pie.  A tremendously big record that became his blessing and his curse.  Blessed with such a gigantic hit, cursed by the shadow it cast on all his later work.  My late, older brother, Mickey, loved the album jacket's McLean-penned poem dedicated to Hopalong Cassidy.  It captured a moment, he said, and was better than just about any of the songs included on the LP.  Me, I liked the fact that the LP was dedicated to Buddy Holly, even though I couldn't find his influence anywhere but in the American Pie lyrical references. While nothing on the album comes close to the title track epic, in my opinion, Vincent, Winterwood, Everybody Loves Me, Baby, among others, hold up very well, indeed.  But American Pie, love it or hate it, continues to cast a decades-long shadow.

title: JT's amazing Sweet Baby follow-up ... Mud Slide, I'm dependin' on you
text: Taylor's third album release, and the superior (to my ears, anyway), immediate follow-up to Sweet Baby James.  To me, it's his best, most fully realized album.  His singing, playing, and songwriting are all incredible here, and the band's accompaniment is always in the groove.  Includes three of my all-time favorite James Taylor songs in Mud Slide Slim, Hey Mister, That's Me Up On The Jukebox, and Long Ago and Far Away; not to mention his stellar cover of Carole King's You've Got A Friend.  Felt like a beautiful gift when I first bought it back in 1971, and it remains a wonderful listen fifty years on.  Recommended without reservation.

title: Carole King's Hits: As Billed
text: For once the title gets it absolutely right.  Carole King: Her Greatest Hits (Songs of Long Ago) delivers.  We're talking performance hits here, not her Goffin-King Brill Building smashes as a songwriter.  The '70s Laurel Canyon vibe is alive & well throughout this 14-track compilation, and the remastering job is phenomenal.  Tracks one through twelve perfectly make the case; the hits and nothing but the hits, though, sadly, not in chronological order.  These include I Feel The Earth Move, It's Too Late, Jazzman, So Far Away, Smackwater Jack, etc.  The two bonus tracks (13 and 14) are fine live-in-concert versions of Eventually and (You Make Me Feel Like) A Natural Woman.  They all hold up incredibly well.  Highly recommended.

title: The only BS&T collection you need
text: For a very quick moment in the history of pop music, Blood, Sweat & Tears were the kings of the hill.  A split second later, they were also rans.  But for that all-too-brief moment, You've Made Me So Very Happy, And When I Die,  Spinning Wheel, and a handful of other horns-driven singles ruled the charts and the airwaves.  By the time Blood, Sweat & Tears 3 was released, they were already fading.  Everything released afterwards was met with total apathy by radio, retail, and most sadly of all, their original fan base.  Stick with this one; all the great hits, plus.

title: The Byrds: Absolutely Essential
text: A great introduction to one of America's premiere bands.  Takes you through the group's amazing musical journey from folk-rock (Mr. Tambourine Man, All I Really Want To Do), to country-rock (Chestnut Mare, Ballad of Easy Rider), and their many side trips in-between (Eight Miles High, Mr. Spaceman, Lady Friend).  Just about, that is.  Unfortunately, no tracks from BYRDS, their 1973 reunion LP on Asylum, but it manages to add three rather superfluous 1990 recordings (Paths of Victory, From A Distance, Love That Never Dies).  The sound is very good for 1960s / '70s recordings remastered in the 1990s, and the playlist is somewhere beyond memorable.  Highly recommended,

title: Pearl: Janis Joplin's farewell masterpiece
text: Janis Joplin's greatest album achievement, imho.  Takes me back to 1971 and wonderful memories of my time in El Paso, Texas every time I listen to it.  Having been drafted and ending up at Fort Bliss rather than Vietnam was one of the times I knew for sure that somebody up there was watching out for me.  Pure, dumb luck, or an answer to prayers, who knows?  This was one of the LPs that carried me through.  Beyond the nostalgia, it's quite simply a musical masterpiece; not a bad track to be found.  What an amazing note to go out on!  I hope Janis is RIP, singing and smiling and sharing good times with her buds in some far better place.  Highly recommended.

title: Jackie DeShannon: Finding and owning her own 'New Image'
text: Not exactly the equal of BGO's recent Jackie DeShannon "Me About You / Laurel Canyon / Put A Little Love In Your Heart / To Be Free:" double-disc set.  Yet this older "In The Wind / Are You Ready For This? / New Image / What The World Needs Now Is Love" two-cd set manages to point up some of the very same troubles Jackie had to face in her early career.  Fighting for her own individuality in the male-dominated Sixties  Pop Music scene, and dealing with record and radio execs who were often anywhere but in-the-moment and simpatico with her musical aspirations, one couldn't help but understand and relate to her sense of frustration.  And Imperial Records, home to many a hit 45 by mid-Sixties teen favorites like Ricky Nelson and Johnny Rivers, didn't appear to have a clue about how to promote her.  The title of this set's third of four albums included clearly tells the tale: "New Image."  The label was forever chasing a new image for Jackie D, but it was ultimately up to her to find and develop her own image.  Which she did, clearly, by the time of "Me About You" / "Laurel Canyon."  The four elpees that make up this set trace her journey of discovery up to that point (released successively in 1965, 1966, 1967, 1968).  The Bob Dylan dominated "In the Wind" is a folk-rock revelation; "Are You Ready For This?" blends Jackie D originals with Bacharach/David, Chip Taylor, and other then-new songwriters' material.  "New Image" is her version of an Adult Contemporary album ("I'll Be Seeing You," "A Sunday Kind of Love,"  "Night and Day"); "What The World Needs Now Is Love" basically packages the title smash with cherry-picked tunes from previous LP releases ("You Don't Have To Say You Love Me," "It's All In The Game," "Call Me," etc.).  Recommended to fans of Jackie DeShannon and Sixties Pop in general.

title: The one Bob Seger / Silver Bullet Band compilation you need in your collection.
text: An absolute killer Bob Seger collection whether you're a casual or hardcore fan.  All the hits that fit, and then some.  Renders his two previous greatest hits releases superfluous.  This is the one to get if you only have room for one Silver Bullet Band compilation in your collection.  Great '70s / '80s classic rock 'n' roll never forgets.  Now, get back to work on your Night Moves.  Highly recommended.

title: Always ahead of the curve, Jackie was Laurel Canyon before the Canyon was cool
text: Jackie DeShannon was ahead of her time as well as ahead of the musical curve.  That's the takeaway from the four LPs that make up this excellent two-disc set from BGO.  Before Carole King: Writer, before the glorious Tapestry, before Carly and Sweet Judy Blue Eyes and oh so many others, there was Jackie paving the way. Though struggling to be noticed in the male-dominated '60s pop music scene, she delivered a string of terrific LPs in Me About You (March 1968), Laurel Canyon (October '68), Put A Little Love In Your Heart (October 1969), and To Be Free: (March 1970).  Fine originals, well-chosen covers, highlighting new, upcoming songwriters & players, she was almost always in the pocket.  Sad thing was, not enough people were paying attention at the time.  Today, she should be remembered and acknowledged in that rarified circle of legends like Carole, Carly, Judy, and Joni, rather than as a kind of second stringer.  She was / is just that good, really.  Highly recommended, especially the Disc One twofer Me About You and Laurel Canyon.

title: The great Dion keeps on chooglin'
text: Dion just keeps on chooglin'.  A terrific late-career highpoint in a legendary master's musical journey.  And for once, the guests aren't just for the marquee value; they genuinely contribute.  Excellent effort by The Wanderer; it would be considered a near-classic no matter when it came along in his magical career.  Highly recommended.

title: TP / Heartbreakers: The hits and nothing but the hits
text: If you're looking for the hits and nothing but the hits, this is the Tom Petty / Heartbreakers compilation for you.  All the career highlights from a magnificent rock 'n roll life, and then some.  If you only need one Tom Petty set in your collection, well, here it is.  Highly recommended for new fans and old.  RIP, Tom.

title: Chicago Live '75, done in by inconsistent sound engineering
text: The band at its peak but, as others have pointed out, the sound here is a problem.  Inconsistent, at best, which is a shame because Chicago was at its horn-driven, rocking best around this time.  With better sound engineering this would likely have been considered the group's best live-in-concert collection.  As is though,  for dyed-in-the-wool Chicago fans only.

title: Spoonful film soundtracks: What was, is, and might have been
text: The ever adventurous Spoonful dipping their toes into film soundtrack work, with mixed results.  On the upside, contains a pair of John Sebastian's greatest songs in Darling, Be Home Soon and the lesser known gem, Respoken.  There's also a rocking full band version of You're a Big Boy Now (re-recorded in a solo version for 1970's "John B. Sebastian" LP), and the beautiful harmonica-driven band instrumental Amy's Theme.  There's also a lot of semi-dross, colorless film soundtrack music.  Had they added Darling, Be Home Soon and Respoken to their late 1967 "Everything Playing" swansong LP with Sebastian, it would likely have been a bigger hit, and a more fondly remembered farewell.  Three and one-half stars, and recommended for the aforementioned titles.

title: The great Jim Croce, done too soon ...
text: Very good Croce compilation.  I still prefer the first posthumously released Best of (the classic "Photographs & Memories"), but this is also a good place to start for novices.  It's the same 14-song classic playlist, just reissued in less impressive packaging.  Sound is good, playlist impeccable and nicely programmed, Croce's performances still alternately humorous, sentimental, and deeply touching.  And at a bargain price!  Highly recommended, of course.

title: The life & times of a singer / songwriter legend
text: Croce's second solo album was (and is) every bit the equal to his "You Don't Mess Around With Jim" debut.  Very good to great songs, excellent performances, lyrics that run the gamut from comical to heartbreaking.  Life and times we can all relate to.  Sounds as fresh and relevant today as it did upon its release, almost five decades ago.  The great ones never really get old.  Highly recommended.

title: Jim Croce's masterful outside the box debut LP
text: This was our first introduction to the music of Jim Croce for many of us, myself included.  Great single, fine album, an auspicious beginning to an important -- and all too brief -- career.  A masterful songwriter and storyteller from the get-go, the album and Jim himself, remain singer / songwriter touchstones.  Highly recommended.

title: A long way from "McCartney," and not in a good way ...
text: A long way from 1970's "McCartney" (one of my personal favorites), and not in a good way.  For me, it was a struggle to get through it, but I did listen twice, all the way through, before reviewing.  And all I can say is, my, oh, my, how the mighty have fallen.  I've enjoyed a lot of Paul's latter career work, but not this time around.  I'll keep it in my collection as I am a kind of completist, but it's unlikely to be played again any time soon.  Not exactly a ringing endorsement, I know.  For diehards only.

title: Expanded bells & whistles Almost Famous soundtrack rocks the house
text: Great expanded soundtrack from one of the best rock movies, ever.  Bigger, deeper, plenty of new bells & whistles.  If you love the movie like I do, this is a must-have.  Highly recommended for all rock 'n' roll daydreamers like yours truly.  Crank it up and rock the house!

title: Keep those TP variations comin'
text: Another variation on one of the late rocker's greatest solo efforts.  Keep 'em coming.  RIP, TP, still great, still missed, still loved.

title: Lennon.  POB.  A raging, righteous masterwork.
text: Lennon's Primal Scream album in all its raging glory.  Bigger, sounding better than ever, and still raging after all these years.  Listening again in awe and wonder, I'm reminded of Bob Dylan's quote about his own "Blood On The Tracks" masterpiece.  Paraphrasing, of course, I don't understand how people can say they enjoy that kind of pain.  Same here.  Painful.  Angry.  Magnificent.

title: The Flatlanders:  An Americana Treasure
text: Classic Americana from a classy Americana semi-supergroup.  A great blend of classic covers and originals.  The kind of music that will help you get through a tough day, or night.  The kind of album they don't make anymore, and yet here one is.  Takes me back to the pre-Garth Brooks / slick cowboy-hatted pre-fabs country radio has been promoting over the last couple of decades.  And I embrace this Treasure Of Love heartily; I'm betting you will too.  Definitely recommended.

title: Can we call this three-and-a-half stars?
text: With this edition of her Jukebox series, Lucinda Williams takes on some of the great Southern Soul songs of the '60s and '70s.  Not exactly great results, but certainly better than mediocre.  Let's call it three-and-a-half stars.  Fans will likely embrace her Americana-style covers of these Memphis / Muscle Shoals classics; purists will probably find them somewhat lacking.  I've got one foot each in both camps.  Definitely recommended to Lu and Americana fans, less so for those who hold a special space in their hearts for sweet Southern Soul music.

title: The country side of Lu's Jukebox collections
text: Another of Lu's Jukebox entries, and a good one.  Interesting song choices, very good performances.  A definite keeper.  She takes on a number of classic country songs, among them several well-regarded tunes that Elvis Presley also covered memorably during the later stages of his legendary career. Lu's approach is about a 180 from the King's, but she gets the job done in subtle, yet heart-tugging fashion.  Recommended to / for Lucinda Williams and Americana fans.

title: Dylan's Back Pages: Just may be Lu's best Jukebox effort
text: I'm a sucker for a well-done, well-chosen covers collection, especially when its a set of Bob Dylan songs being covered.  Lucinda Williams delivers a good one here.  Her voice is well-suited to Dylan's masterful songwriting, and she makes the best of it here.  I've played it through front-to back three times in a row, and it seems to get better with every run through.  Right up there with (and almost the equal of) Chrissie Hynde's recent "Standing in the Doorway" tip o' the hat to the great songwriting master.  Recommended.

title: Emmylou hitting one of her many Americana peaks
text: Right up there with Emmylou's award-winning "At The Ryman" from 1991, if memory serves.  "Ramble in Music City: The Lost Concert 1990" is a stunning live-in-concert recording.  Why it remained on the shelf, so to speak, is a true Nashville mystery.  Great, well-paced set-list, great Nash Ramblers performances, great material.  If you have, or remember fondly, the Ryman disc, you're sure to be thrilled to ramble along with this one.  Highly recommended.

title: The hype was deserved this time around
text: Since the band had no new album in the chute for its massive 1974 tour, this compilation was hastily put together to have something to promote.  For once, the hype was deserved.  Great 'Best of' collection filled with hit singles, FM-radio deep cuts, and the only album (at that time) where you could find the Ohio / Find The Cost Of Freedom 45 rpm single.  Not to mention Joni Mitchell's fabulous cover art.  So Far has stood the test of time as the definitive CSNY collection. I only wish its companion piece sequel, CSN: Replay, was also available as a remastered CD as it's nearly as good -- even without Y.

title: Loggins & Messina: The Best of Friends, and then some ...
text: Went to one of the shows on the reunion tour that hyped this collection.  Back in 2005 maybe?  Amazingly great show as I recall, especially considering almost three decades had passed since their amicable break-up.  Pretty-near flawless compilation, too.  At a full 18 songs and clocking in at nearly 80 minutes long, Sittin' In Again successfully supplants and replaces their old Best Of Friends retrospective.  Much improved sound, a well-programmed setlist, and songs that have stood the test of time, Sittin' In Again is a great place to start for the uninitiated, and a solid overview of the boys' wildly successful '70s heyday for long-time fans.  Neither artist has ever sounded better, before or after the L&M years.  Highly recommended.

title: Doobies' "Liberte" the band's best in decades
text: Plays like one-half each of two different albums, but adds up to the Doobie Brothers' best new LP in decades, maybe since the band's '70s heyday.  Tom Johnston lays down the Doobie Boogie here and evermore, taking us back to the glorious days when Listen To The Music, China Grove, and Long Train Runnin' ruled both the AM and FM airwaves.  Pat Simmons brings his own special variation on the singer / songwriter genre to his new contributions, harking back to his Black Water, South City Midnight Lady groove, only now with an added touch of wisdom and maybe even melancholy.  It all adds up to two different approaches combining to make one terrific album.  Highly recommended.

title: Sheryl Crow: Tired at the Ryman
text: Live, but just barely.  Tired at the Ryman is more like it.  Out of new ideas, maybe?  Get the feeling we've been down this road one too many times before.  For Sheryl Crow diehards only.

title: Willie Nile's winning streak continues
text: Willie Nile's late career winning streak continues with The Day The Earth Stood Still.  Right up there with Children of Paradise and American Ride, he delivers great rock 'n' roll in the best sense: rockin' the house music, an open rock 'n' roll heart, a touch of punk attitude, and an unbelievably deft way with a lyric, with his on-the-sleeve social conscience always shining through.  Keep on keepin' on, Willie, keep this amazing, continued American Music ride going.  Highly recommended.

title: Mason Proffit:  Still Wanted!
text: Just as I remembered them from way on way back then.  Mason Proffit was one of my favorite country-rock bands back in the '70s.  Goin' back doesn't always turn out to be as pretty a scene as you remember, but in this particular case it has all held up wonderfully well.  Mason Proffit: Wanted sounds amazingly fresh for a 50-year-old album. Glad to have one of my favorite long lost LPs back in my collection on CD.  Big thanks & kudos to Wounded Bird Records for bringing it back.  Recommended to other country-rockers from the day.

title: The foundation of James Taylor's on-going and legendary career
text:
Anyone thinking of purchasing this set already has the JT lowdown. Suffice to say, the six Warner Brothers discs that make up this mini-box, well known as they are to fans, have never sounded better (to these aging boomer's ears anyway). Docked one star for not including the best selling LP of his career, Greatest Hits.
This means you miss out on his superior re-makes of Apple tunes Something In the Way She Moves and Carolina In My Mind, as well as his legendary kick-butt live take of Steamroller -- all essential in my opinion. Still, highly recommended.

title: Dreaming along with Karen Black ...
text: What a lovely surprise.  I was aware of Karen Black, of course; mostly from her appearances in big films like Five Easy Pieces and Nashville.  I was far less in-the-know about her shadowy singing career.  Wow, this collection is a true eye (ear?) opener.  Often haunting, almost always touching, these musical notes from across the years from the late '70s film star point to an alternate trail of what might have been.  Definitely recommended to fans of singer / songwriters in the Carole King / Judy Collins vein.  Glad I bought it.

title: Those Unbeatable Beatles, Fab as ever!
text: What a fabulous package!  Terrific book.  Timeless music.  Clever cover designs and replications.  Provocative liner notes.  It's The Beatles so, of course, everything is given the first class touch.  The new Let It Be mix is a wonder; the Let It Be EP is a great stand-alone item; Glyn Johns' Get Back mix makes you realize the true genius of the late Phil Spector, and the various odds-and-sods alternates, outtakes, and rehearsals provide fly-on-the-wall insider glimpses behind the curtain of the Greatest Show On Earth ... still!!  Absolutely fabulous!!  If you can afford the big box, don't hesitiate.  It just may restore your sense of wonder in these troubled times.

title: The Beatles' Let It Be ... One More Time
text: The much maligned Phil Spector salvaged Let It Be album has always remained a favorite of mine, critical reaction be damned.  Here in this expanded two-disc sampler version of the Deluxe Box Edition it sounds better than ever (to these aging ears, anyway).  And it's accompanied on Disc Two with a lot of bonus tracks; unreleased, alternates, etc.  Great fun, but I wish they'd  paired it off instead with Glyn Johns' previously unreleased Get Back LP mix (included in the Big Box}.  Would've made for interesting comparison listening.  Go with the box if you can afford it, or put it on your Christmas list and let a near and dear one pick it up for you ...

title: John Sebastian haplessly exploring his glory days
text: Two fine musicians, a setlist of near legendary songs, and a stellar supporting cast pay tribute to John B. Sebastian's songwriting skills.  Nice enough idea, especially since he's one of America's greatest living tunesmiths.  By a group of Sebastian's '60s / '70s contemporaries and / or some of the many artists he's influenced through the years it'd make perfect sense.  But with him (and his decades-long damaged vocals) leading the way, I have just one question -- Why bother?  These recordings not only don't touch the sound and glory of the originals (Spoonful or solo), they're not even in the parking lot outside the ballpark.  I've often wondered why he didn't let bygones by bygones and re-join the Spoons once his voice was gone; Joe Butler could still sing pretty well and Sebastian could've led a twilight version of his career peak band through a grace note ending.  Instead, he unleashes another recording showcasing his diminished vocal approach.  Three stars for the songs and musicianship.  Recommended for diehards only.

title: Rod the genuine Rocker
text: Rod Stewart's Mercury Years are to his career what Elvis Presley's Sun Records releases are to his legacy.  Before being smoothed out, repackaged, and sold to the highest bidder, Elvis was a raw young talent, finding his way, and learning as he went under the watchful eye of Sam Phillips and with the tremendous support and generosity of Scotty Moore, Bill Black, and (eventually) D.J. Fontana.  Rod, having done a great deal of musical learning and turning in the decade before Mercury, was backed by Faces and still on the learning curve.  Like early Elvis, he was making the greatest music of his career, the foundation of just about everything that would follow to such great success and sometimes even critical acclaim.  This one's for the ages, for sure, Rod rocking at his peak of power.  I only wish they would have included Coast To Coast, the great lost Rod Stewart / Faces live in-concert album of the mid-'70s.  Highly recommended.

title: Cracked jewel case and second-go-round shrink wrap aside ...
text: Bought this thinking it was new.  Cracked jewel case, bogus second-time-around shrink-wrapping, and fingerprints on the playing side of the disc proved me wrong.  Still, plays fine and it's the late, great Aretha Franklin's vocals with The Royal Philharmonic Orchestra's backing, so who am I to complain ... right?  Music, five stars; this particular package / experience, two-and-one-half stars.

title: Plays like The Great Lost Bob Dylan Album of the '80s ...
text: Having already reviewed the big box version, I'll keep this brief.  This two-disc, kind of "Best of the Best" sampler edition makes an excellent listening experience all its own.  I've played it for a couple of Dylan fan friends through my in-car system and they, like me, consider it a fine stand-alone Dylan album.  As far as the era goes, truly troubling in its day, this double-disc plays like The Great Lost Bob Dylan album of the '80s.  If you're a fan but not willing to go for the cost of the big set, this makes an amazingly satisfying substitute.  Highly recommended.

title: Deluxe "Feel Flows" -- A Won Won Wonderful Beach Boys collection
text: Aural surfing adventure through one of my favorite Beach Boys periods (1969-1971). Brian's somewhere in the shadows most of the time, and it's up to the Boys (especially Carl and Dennis) to step out from behind his massive musical shadow and totally step it up. And they do, all of them, working together (Produced by The Beach Boys) as a solid band unit in a truly joyous team effort.  Excellent songs, excellent sound, excellent packaging, totally excellent musical experience.  This one's won won wonderful.  Highly recommended.

title: Number 16 is one of the best in Uncle Bobby's Bootleg Series
text: All right, yeah, I've always heard those opinions from people supposedly "in the know" that cranky ol' Uncle Bobby tended to undermine his LP releases by holding back the best songs.  Didn't know what to believe for sure, 'til now that is.  Lord almighty, this is a great collection.  Mind-blowing, really.  Out-takes are mostly fabulous, alternate versions generally outshine released versions, the live cuts are killer, and it all adds up to an alternate universe version of Bob Dylan in the '80s.  To yours truly, the Empire Burlesque alternates alone would be worth the price of admission, but there's more, so much more.  The book, photos, and liner notes are all first-rate, top of the line.  Bootleg Series, Volume16 (!) ranks right up there with the best of the series.  Great package!  Highly recommended.

title: Ths Country-Rock pioneers deliver on these early Poco classics
text: Poco was peaking (DeLIVErin') and at their peak (Crazy Eyes) on this pair of country-rock classics, two of my all-time favorite Poco albums.  DeLIVErin' (1971) is one of the best of the many live-in-concert LPs of the '70s, while Crazy Eyes (1973) stretched the band creatively and proved to be Richie Furay's last as the band's erstwhile leader.  As exits go, he went out on a high note.  Beautifully packaged with interesting liner notes, original release photos and graphics, and BGO's usual fine sound production, this two-on-one disc is an aural joy from start (I Guess You Made It) to finish (Let's Dance Tonight).  Definitely recommended for fans of that '70s Cali country-rock sound.

title: The Beach Boys breaking away from Brian's shadow
text: One of my favorite Beach Boys eras.  With Brian cooling out in the shadows for the most part, the other Boys had to step up, or basically drop out of the new '70s music scene.  Did they step it up?  Oh, yeah, did they ever.  This two-disc set is a joy for the heart and the ear.  Very good to great songs, live tracks, out-takes, and peeks behind the scenes, "Feel Flows" gives a wide-angle view of the group in transition, from AM-Radio pop heroes to explorers of the new Sounds of the Seventies, band-defining vocal harmonies always intact.  For me, Surf's Up gets the edge, but Sunflower is also a near-total joy.  If you're already a fan, prepare for some kind of Beach Boys Nirvana -- it's that good.  Highly recommended!

title: "All Things Must Pass" remains a stunning classic, 50 years on
text: I've loved this album for fifty years.  It holds up incredibly well.  It's as wonderful as ever.  No nostalgia here; well, maybe just a touch.  From a time when the music really mattered, this music stood out like a beacon of light and hope.  And it still does.  A stunning, sometimes soothing Rock classic.  Thank you, George, you're still loved, still missed, still leading the way.  If you're thinking of purchasing this one, my friend, stop thinking about it and go ahead and do it.  You won't be disappointed.

title: In Concert, it's the same classic Fleetwood Mac, only tougher
text: Had this one as a two-LP set way on way back when.  Lost it as a loaner, or in one of my frequent apartment moves when I was much younger (and less sedentary) in the day.  Always liked it.  Fleetwood Mac, this particular version anyway,  came across much tougher live-in-concert than they did on studio recordings.  And in the post-punk late '70s, the band (Lindsey Buckingham, in particular) seemed to have something to prove.  Now a 3-CD extravaganza, "Fleetwood Mac Live" delivers a healthy, hefty slice of '70s FM-Rock history in all its multi-platinum glory.  Sometimes less is more, sure, but in this case more really fills in some of the original release's blank spots.  The mighty, mighty Mac, monster success 'though they were as smooth Cali pop-rockers, were out to prove that they could really ROCK, rough edges and all, and they do it here.  If you're a fan of the band, you'll want this new, improved, expanded version of the classic "FML" in your collection.

title: The great Glen Campbell in concert, one last time
text: Some artists you just don't really appreciate 'til it's too late.  That's been my experience with Glen Campbell.  I always liked him in the late '60s / early-to-mid '70s as far as his singles on the radio went, but the only albums of his I ever bought were Greatest Hits / Best of collections.  My loss.  I've been rediscovering him since his tragic, but noble, passing.  He was a great singer and a monster guitarist, as well as a musical team player.  He may have gotten lost occasionally as far as his choices in material went, but his early work with Jim Webb can't be questioned and his later expanding horizon efforts are all well-worth checking out.  This live-in-concert set, his last, was recorded at the legendary Troubadour and covers the full spectrum of his amazing career:  The hits he wove with Jim Webb (By the Time I Get to Phoenix, Galveston, Wichita Lineman), John Hartford (Gentle on My Mind), the number one career-defining smash Rhinestone Cowboy, covers of Tom Petty (Angel Dream, Walls (Circus)), John Lennon (Grow Old With Me), and on and on.  I'm so glad I finally clued myself in.  RIP, Mr. Campbell, give my best to Elvis.  Highly recommended.

title: Blues Traveler's Traveler's Blues is Big Blues Fun
text: Big fun!  Oh, yeah!  Great Blues Traveler covers set.  Terrific set list, and a brace of excellent guests, including Warren Haynes, Mickey Raphael, Rita Wilson, Keb' Mo', among many others.  My favorites among the set's ten tracks:  Sittin' on Top of the World, Roadhouse Blues, Call Me the Breeze, Trouble in Mind.  From the liner notes: "... Blues Traveler would like to thank the original masters who've made these songs legend ..."  Well, that's fine and good, but it's also a kind of hollow tip o' the hat since nowhere in the liners will you find any songwriter, original artist, or publishing credits.  Highly recommended, anyway.

title: Native Sons: Los Lobos and the power of good music
text: One of the very few things we can count on in the ever crazier world we live in is the power of good music to lift our spirits, rejuvenate our souls, and elevate our mental outlooks.  And one of the very few bands we can always count on for all the above (and more) is the great, the wondrous, the "in a zone all their own," Los Lobos.  Native Sons is a wonderful record; with the exception of the title track, a covers LP, yes, which I always love when done right -- and it rarely gets done any righter than this.  Not your typical covers collection, either, as there's a unifying flow to these recordings that makes the album stand as a solid long-player all its own.  My favorite tracks: Bluebird / For What It's Worth, Jamaica Say You Will, Sail On, Sailor, The World Is A Ghetto, and the great original, Native Son.  Highly recommended.

title: Standing in the Doorway with Chrissie Hynde and Bob Dylan
text: The Covid-19 era will undoubtedly go down in history as one of the great scourges of humankind in modern times, yet there will also be a number of positive sidebar stories.  One of those stories will be about the proliferation of stripped-down, DIY musical moments that lifted our spirits and lightened our load during these most trying of times.  Chrissie Hynde's ode (owed?) to Bob Dylan, Standing in the Doorway is a prime example.  Covers albums can be tricky;  Bob Dylan covers albums can be heaven (Fairport Convention's A Tree With Roots), they can be hell (The Hollies Sing Dylan),  or they can land in some limbo in-between (Charlie Daniels Band's Off The Grid: Doin' It Dylan).  Standing in the Doorway leans closer to heaven.  Nine Dylan classics from across his storied 60-year career sung and played with undeniable heart, sensitivity, and commitment.  Chrissie Hynde works real magic here, deftly avoiding cliche and paralyzing respect for the original arrangements, bringing instead her own history and world of experiences to tracks ranging from the familiar (Sweetheart Like You), to the relatively obscure (In The Summertime), to the untouchably classic (Blind Willie McTell).  My personal favorites:  Don't Fall Apart On Me Tonight, Every Grain of Sand.  Highly recommended.

title: Laura Nyro:  always and ever an Angel in the Dark
text: The absolute wonder that is / was the great Laura Nyro.  Always and ever an Angel in the Dark.  Simple and to the point:  Won, Won, Wonderful ...

title: Wallflowers' "Exit Wounds" marks a stunning re-entry
text: I'm totally digging this new version of Wallflowers!  Excepting Jakob Dylan, this is a whole new band, and it's a great one!  The female backing on four cuts is provided by the great Shelby Lynne, and the band's lead guitarist is none other than Val McCallum, David's son, also a member of Jackson Browne's stellar touring outfit.  All songs are by Jakob Dylan (some Bob-worthy lines in there, too), and all of them are very good to excellent.  "Exit Wounds" will be in heavy rotation in my home system for some time to come.  Highly recommended.

title: Shannon McNally's heartfelt tip o' the cowboy hat to the late, great Waylon Jennings
text: Great singer.  Great interpreter.  Really good covers album.  I also have Small Town Talk, her Bobby Charles covers disc, which is terrific and gets the slight nod over this Waylon Jennings salute / project.  On this one, my favorites include We Had It All, I Ain't Living Long Like This, Only Daddy That'll Walk The Line, and You Asked Me To.  The last title was famously-- and beautifully --  covered by Elvis on his 1975 Promised Land LP.  Come to think, I'd love to hear a Shannon McNally covers set of Presley's more country-oriented material from the post-1968 comeback era (Memphis, Nashville, Stax, Hollywood, Graceland) sessions.  In the meantime, dig into Shannon's tasty The Waylon Sessions.

title: She's The One soundtrack, reconfigured
text: She's The One soundtrack LP, reconfigured.  And a pretty wonderful thing it is, too.  A sweet tip of the hat to the late, great T.P.  And a much deserved loose salute it is, too.  Highly recommended, even if you already own the soundtrack disc, like yours truly.

title: John Hiatt's Leftover Feelings -- in a word, magnificent ...
text: If this is what twilight sounds like, then I'll go forward into my 70s proud and unafraid.  The great John Hiatt, hooked up with quite possibly the best musical support of his life in The Jerry Douglas Band, is still at the top of his game as a singer / songwriter / storyteller.  Leftover Feelings?  In a word, magnificent, not a lame horse in this corral.  Long may he continue to run ...

title: The Dead's Arista Years remain one of my favorite roads taken along their long musical journey
text: I know I'm in the minority here, but The Dead's Arista years have always been among my favorites on the band's long and ever-changing musical journey.  While Go To Heaven and In The Dark rank a notch higher on my list, Shakedown Street has always held a special place in my heart.  Music that helps you get through tough personal times is like that -- memorable and buoyant in a kind of inexplicable, mysterious way.  Their tip o' the hat take on The Rascals' great hit cover of Good Lovin' never fails to bring a smile to my face; the title track became an instant fave from the first time I heard it on the late, lamented 102.7 WNEW-FW, where Rock lived once upon a long time ago, and I Need A Miracle, well, what can you say about a song that kept you going through all kind and manner of bad times?  Miraculous, maybe, yeah!  Stunning cover art intact, beautifully remastered, and a handful of bonus tracks only serve to make things even better.  Thanks, Rhino, you've done it again!

title: Jackson Browne's back, and he never disappoints
text: With his first full album of new material since 2014's solid Standing In The Breach, Jackson Browne's Downhill From Everywhere reaffirms his status as a master songwriter, storyteller, and chronicler of his times.  It's a rich and diverse collection of songs, and Browne, who has always wisely written with his own vocal limitations in mind, delivers them all with his usual taste and special care.  The musical backing is quietly impressive and in the pocket throughout; this just may be one of the finest bands he's ever worked with.  Downhill From Everywhere and A Little Too Soon To Say made an excellent teaser single; other standouts among the set's ten tracks include  Still Looking For Something, A Human Touch (NOT the Springsteen song!), and The Dreamer.  Definitely recommended.

title: Al Jardine & Co. deliver the best non-Beach Boys Beach Boys live set ever
text: Al Jardine, Family & Friends' Live in Las Vegas is a joy from start to finish.  It is, to this aging Beach Boys fan anyway, the best live album the Beach Boys never delivered.  The 1999 set covers not only the usual commercial highlights of the band's storied career, but the risky, artistic high-water mark tracks as well.  Among the Family & Friends: Matt and Adam Jardine, Carnie and Wendy Wilson, Billy Hinsche, Bobby Figueroa, and Ed Carter.  All told, 27 tracks of Beach Boys Nirvana.  If you can track one down, don't hesitate, just buy it!  Highly recommended!

title: A.J. Croce's By Request?  Absolutely!
text: Being a genuine sucker for well-chosen cover song collections, A.J. Croce's By Request is right in my wheelhouse.  The songs are great, the arrangements loose and limber, and Croce's singing / performing is right on the money.  My personal favorites: Nothing From Nothing, Ooh Child, San Diego Serenade, Sail On Sailor.  More, please.

title: David Crosby's solo winning streak continues with For Free
text: David Crosby's late life / late career artistic winning streak continues with For Free.  It's a truly fine record, not a bad track to be found, although some pieces are stronger than others, naturally.  James Raymond has proven to be a wonderful blessing for Croz, in more ways than musical I'm sure.  Who'd have guessed that the fallout from the well publicized CSNY break-up a few years back would be a solo career rebirth for Mr. Crosby?  Well, here's the latest installment.  Bless him for sharing and ... long may he run!

title: The great Three Dog Night gets the cheese please treatment
text: The live set is fun and of its time (mid '70s) but thoroughly enjoyable even if you're not a big TDN fan.  The five-song ep modernizes the band's sound (modern as in thirty years ago), but the harmonies and three lead vocalist approach remains unmistakable, some fine material too.  The letdown is in the sound -- it's less than stellar, for sure.  I'd swear I hear some pops and static, as if it was mastered from someone's old personal LP.  Glad to finally have It's A Jungle on disc and in my collection, but really disappointed in the cheesy way it's presented.

title: Classy Three Dog Night, cheesy presentation
text: Purchased this for the two Three Dog Night LPs I never had -- Coming Down Your Way and American Pastime.  While hardly classic albums, they still get that classy Three Dog Night touch.  Slammed by the hip rock critics of the time upon release (even more so than the usual TDN slough offs), both sets are much better than expected, although not always up to the band's usual high standards in cover material.  The problem is presentation:  No notes, no credits, simply front and back cover replications.  And the sound is dubious, at best -- appears to have been recorded off an LP, certainly not from anyone's idea of master tapes.  I'm glad to have these old LPs on disc and in my collection, but I'll keep looking for a better reissue somewhere down the line.

title: Still impressive, but nearing the last gasp of Elvis's "comeback" years
text: Sped up (to fit on one vinyl LP) and rushed out (within two weeks of the event), As Recorded Live At MSG represented another in a long line of Elvis milestones, in more ways than one.  A double-edged sword scenario because while the rush release meant big sales in the wake of this landmark MSG event, it also was the death knell for the already announced Standing Room Only (which was to work as a soundtrack to the film that became Elvis On Tour).  In true Colonel Tom Parker style (or lack thereof), the On Tour singles (Burning Love / It's A Matter of Time, Separate Ways / Always On My Mind) were unleashed on LP in the RCA Camden budget market!  Even the MSG LP cover shot was meant for the SRO soundtrack, so it fails to represent the shows people who bought the LP would've already seen.  IMHO, the better solution would've been a double LP:  MSG paired with SRO, featuring the massive Burning Love hit (as well as its  Top 20 follow-up, Separate Ways), it would've made this an even bigger smash hit album.  Or, RCA could have staggered the release of two separate LPs a bit, a la the previous 1970/71 That's The Way It Is and Elvis Country albums.  For this Legacy release, MSG is paired with another MSG performance, released long after the fact as An Afternoon in The Garden.  To these aging Elvis fan ears, Afternoon is a bit looser, a bit rowdier, a bit more fun.  I'd still like to see Standing Room Only released and readily available as a standard catalogue item (as opposed to the ridiculously priced FTD collectors' edition) just for posterity and to help make some kind of sense out of Elvis's recording legacy, if nothing else.  Meanwhile, The Garden pairing?  Highly recommended!

title: Elvis in Nashville and Las Vegas ... before the inevitable slide
text: That's The Way It Is was released as the soundtrack to the 1970 concert film / documentary of the same name.  In truth, it's neither a soundtrack nor a live album, but a collection mostly made up of Nashville studio recordings, some with applause tacked on for atmosphere.  No harm, no foul, as it's a pretty great studio album regardless.  Disc Two is the eye (ear?) opener here: the full, previously unreleased Dinner Show from August 12, 1970, during his third Las Vegas season since his 1968 television 'comeback' special.  The eventual performing-by-rote slide seems a long way off here, as Elvis mixes plenty of new material amidst the old hits and delivers a masterful, well thought out set.
