Opening with That's All Right and closing 16 songs later with Can't Help Falling in Love, Elvis and his amazing cast of thousands TCB Band deliver the goods BIG TIME and as only he could.  Definitely recommended!!

title: "Elvis Country" :  Presley's most consistent album of the '70s
text:
Hands down, far and away, Elvis Country is Presley's best 1970s LP. Consistently great material, stellar musical backing, and a committed Elvis. Tied together as a concept by its cover (front, anyway) and the threading of the old traditional I Was Born About 10,000 Years Ago throughout the bands, one seemed to know it was saying something musically important right from the get go. As an album artist (something nobody ever accused him of during his lifetime -- he was a singles guy!) he'd never reach these heights again. Love Letters From Elvis, the follow-up, definitely suffers in comparison. A collection of mostly left-overs and throwaways from the same sessions, stylistically all over the map, it basically died on the commercial vine, despite a handful of fine moments (the title song remake, a raving, nearly out-of-control Got My Mojo Working, the beautiful Only Believe). Paired together, and with bonus cuts (including 1971 singles A- and B- sides Where Did They Go, Lord, The Sound of Your Cry, Rags To Riches), these 1971
albums (remastered) never sounded better. Elvis Country is still the one with the edge. Highly recommended!

title: Dave Mason's Alone Together: One of the all-time great solo debuts in classic rock
text: Alone Together, Dave Mason's 1970 debut solo effort, was a stunning surprise back in the day, and it remains a stunningly beautiful album to this very day, some half-century after I first bought it.  Eight tracks of '70s classic rock bliss, it is of its time but certainly not locked in time.  Mason's songwriting is very good to excellent throughout, and the production, playing, and singing are first-rate all the way.  My personal favorites: Can't Stop Worrying, Can't Stop Loving, Shouldn't Have Took More Than You Gave, Look At You Look At Me; there's not a clinker to be found.  If he had had better career management at the start, Dave Mason would be remembered as a superstar rather than a second-stringer today.  Highly recommended!

title: Steve Miller unleashes a mighty, mighty live one from back in the day
text:
Excellent 1977 concert recording. Steve Miller is that rare artist who is equally adept at both studio productions and the live-in-concert experience. Where has this one been all these years? Stored in his vault.
Released back in the day, it would've been a chart-topper and considered an instant classic. Just happy that it's finally available to take its place alongside longtime favorite '70s live sets like Dave Mason's "Certified Live," The Band's "Rock of Ages," and (dare I say it?) "Frampton Comes Alive." Highly recommended!

title: Didn't he come to bring us all a sense of wonder?
text: Who else could get away with an album title as casual and nondescript as "Latest Record Project Volume One," and manage to deliver a collection that's so good that you're already looking forward to Volume Two?  With the exception of the great Bob Dylan, only Mrs. Morrison's grown-up baby boy ... the walking one and only ... the legendary Belfast Cowboy ... Van the Man!  Van the Man!!  Van the Man!!!  Highly recommended to Van fans, old and new.  This one just may revive your sense of wonder.

title: Papa Nez's Country-Rock for the Ages
text: The beginnings of a genre, by an iconic master talent who was always marching to the beat of a different drummer.  While this music never got the critical kudos, nor the big audience, it so richly deserved, perhaps the passage of time has finally caught up with Nez's artistic vision.  The songwriting is very good to excellent throughout, the vocals are consistently top-notch, and the musical accompaniment nothing short of sterling.  Michael Nesmith & the First National Band, down home, intelligent, and country-rockin' before it was ever considered cool, is just alright with me, oh yeah!

title: Single-disc version of America 50 rates 3 and 1/2 stars
text: This distilled down to a single-disc version of the 50th anniversary celebration collection is missing too many important tracks for a five-star rating.  What's here is very good to excellent, but it's a barely expanded version of the band's '70s classic History: America's Greatest Hits, released some 45 years ago.  Disappointing.

title: Gord's golden touch, obvious from the beginning
text: Some of the production flourishes sound a bit dated now, especially compared to his Warner / Reprise recordings of the following decade.  But the songwriting is consistently poetic and meaningful and his vocal approach is never less than strong and true.  Highly recommended to singer / songwriter fans in general, but especially to '70s Lightfoot followers looking to check out his earlier history.

title: I'd have been all over this one, once upon a long time ago
text: I pretty much gave up on my NY collecting around the time of the recording booth covers disc.  Haven't gone through any withdrawal symptoms either.  There's still a lot of good new music coming down the pike:  Dylan, Petty, Bruce, Croz.  Life is good.  I broke down and bought this one strictly as a gift for a life-long pal o' mine who refuses to give it up when it comes to Mr. Young.  He's one of the last of the true believers, God love him, and to him Archives II will be manna from heaven.  Me?  I'll ask him to make me a burn of whatever he considers to be the main highlights and be satisfied with that.  Keep on rockin' in the free world, yeah!

title: The biggest ain't always the best
text: A great five-star two-fer for the casual fan and the curious.  But not for someone looking for The Best Of Elvis, which has yet to be put together, IMHO.  For a truly "Best" overview you'd have to bypass the obvious radio hits and concentrate on lost singles, the misses, b-sides, and deep cuts.  Think of the stream of solid Elvis singles (considered misses at the time) released during the downturn in his career (pre-'68 Comeback):  Love Letters, Big Boss Man, Guitar Man, U.S. Male, You'll Never Walk Alone; b-sides like Come What May, You Don't Know Me, Hi-Heel Sneakers, Stay Away;  deep album cuts like Tomorrow Is a Long Time, Down in the Alley, I'll Remember You, and more.  And that's just the Sixties!  Great overlooked tracks from the '70s would include the massively underappreciated I'm Leavin', along with It's Only Love, and its flip The Sound of Your Cry, The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face (the b-side of An American Trilogy), I Really Don't Want To Know, the studio versions of I've Lost You and Patch It Up, It's a Matter of Time (the country-rock b-side of Burning Love), and on and on.  And the Fifties?  So many titles left uncollected from various movies, extended players, 45-rpm b-sides, and LP deep cuts.  Put together a pair of 30-track sets collecting the real "Best of Elvis" and you've got yourself an unbeatable 60-song overview of a truly magnificent career / life in popular music.

title: The impossibly amazing beginning of a legendary career
text: Good God almighty, was he -- were we -- ever this young and innocent!!??  A mind-altering, cliche-shattering collection of the classic recordings that reshaped the outlook and futures of the youth of America, and then the world.  Elvis's sense of joy imbues every track, and it's absolutely catching -- you'll feel the joy of youth all over again just grooving to these tracks.  Very highly recommended.

title: John Hammond, Jr. and the soon-to-be Band, plus ...
text: From back in the day (1965), this remains singer / guitarist Hammond's best album, for my money anyway.  Amazing setlist, true-to-the-muse vocals, and stellar musical support throughout.  J. Robbie Robertson, Levon Helm, and Garth Hudson (of Levon & the Hawks, soon to be re-christened The Band), along with Mike Bloomfield (on keys!), Charlie Musselwhite (harmonica), and Jimmy Lewis (bass) offer solid support without ever overwhelming Hammond.  My favorite cuts are Who Do You Love, You Can't Judge a Book By the Cover, Baby, Please Don't Go, and Big Boss Man, but there's not a single clinker to be found among the set's 12-song program.  This is not a trip back in time because it's simply a timeless groove.  Docked one star because the sound could definitely have (should have) been improved.  Recommended.

title: Do YOU believe in magic?  You will when the Spoonful casts its good time musical spell ...
text: The sound is excellent.  The tracks, for the most part, are legendary (here in the US, anyway).  The front cover is one of the best, originally used for 1968's Best of the Lovin' Spoonful, Volume 2 LP.  John Sebastian was never better, before or after, than this golden 1965-68 period as a singer or a songwriter.  And the band lends him stellar support throughout.  My one gripe is that the songs are not chronologically arranged, a minor quibble, I suppose, but  still important to me.  Highly recommended import.

title: A peek behind the door to watch a great musician at work
text: Will this moderately-priced, 3-disc, copyright protection from public domain release appeal to everyone?  Not hardly.  Will it appeal to all Bob Dylan fans?  Not likely.  It will, however, be cherished by those of us who enjoy taking an aural peek behind the scenes to see how our favorite musicians eventually arrived at the finished products we know and love so dearly.  In this case, we get to hear and re-evaluate the evolution of what is likely Bob Dylan's most misunderstood and underappreciated work, Self Portrait, along with its concurrently recorded follow-up (considered a 'comeback' at the time of release), New Morning.  Will this release make it to a regular spot on my personal playlist?  Very unlikely, although there's plenty of fun to be had listening here.  But these discs will find their place in my player whenever I want to reflect on the way things turned out on the officially released LPs from back in 1970 (as well as the Bootleg Series' Another Self Portrait). Good stuff, musically, but not exactly essential listening in the normal meaning of the phrase.  Love the old bootleg package design (outside), photos from the era are excellent, and Michael Simmons booklet essay is brief, on the mark, and informative.

title: The first of the continuing wave of Dire Straits compilations; Money For Nothing, indeed
text: Released in the wake of the tremendously successful Brothers in Arms album, Money For Nothing (1988) was a kind of stop-gap 'best of' issued to placate new-found fans until the next studio release (On Every Street, which would turn out to be the band's last).  The obvious candidates are all here (Sultans of Swing, Down to the Waterline, Tunnel of Love, Romeo and Juliet, Money For Nothing, Walk of Life, Brothers in Arms), along with some extended live tracks, deep cuts, and one head-scratcher of an EP-only release (the extremely slight Twisting By the Pool).  Not bad, but certainly not their best 'greatest.'  For that honor I'd recommend 1998's Sultans of Swing: The Very Best of Dire Straits, the group's most comprehensive single-disc compilation.

title: My favorite Muddy Waters album, ever
text: Love this one, and I have for years, decades.  Had it on LP way on back in the mists of time (mid '70s, 1975/76 maybe?).  Opens with Bobby Charles' great observational classic Why Are People Like That, and we're off and running.  The track-list is exceptional, the playing loose and funky, and the guests contribute without pulling star-tripper shenanigans -- this is Muddy's time to shine.  Levon Helm, Paul Butterfield, Garth Hudson, Fred Carter, among others, keep it all chooglin' along, and the mighty Mister Waters rides along on this musical river of dreams like a master sailor.  For my money, the standouts include Caldonia, Let the Good Times Roll, Kansas City, and the CD bonus track Fox Squirrel.  Highly recommended.

title: Judy's heartfelt tribute to the artistry of Bob Dylan
text: While you may not agree with all the choices Ms. Collins made among the disc's 11 tracks, you won't find any clunkers  among the performances.  Great songs from across Dylan's (Freewheelin' through Empire Burlesque) career, they're all delivered in tasty arrangements centered on Bob's lyrics and Judy's ever-tasteful vocals.  My personal favorites included here are Simple Twist of Fate (I prefer it to the Joan Baez cover), Dark Eyes (the acoustic gem that closed Bob's 'Burlesque' LP), and I Believe in You (a soulful Slow Train Coming classic).  I also love Judy's very personal, self-penned liner notes which end:  "As I sang these songs I looked for you.  I found you.  And I found me."  How can you resist?  I couldn't.  Wish there was a Volume Two.  Highly recommended.

title: The newly remixed, remastered Stage Fright is a revelation
text: The Royal Albert Hall disc is flat-out fabulous.  And since it's The Band without frills, additions, or guests, it's a truer, more honest representation of the original group's in-concert sound and impact than either Rock Of Ages or The Last Waltz.  Stage Fright not only sounds better than ever in this new re-mix, it's a revelation.  You hear so many subtle things, in both vocal and musical nuances, that have been buried in the mix in previous versions, even remastered editions.  And the new tracking order, evidently based on J. Robbie Robertson's original vision from back in the day, actually plays better and makes more sense than the decades-old familiar version (to my ears, anyway).  It now unfolds like a well-paced live set.  I do, however, intend to also hang on to my 2000 Capitol remaster, which features the old summer 1970 LP playing order.  Highly recommended.

title: The first and best of the Jim Croce compilations
text: Wore out a pair of copies of the LP version decades ago.  Have picked up various other "Best of Croce" releases through the years, but I've always felt this one -- maybe because it was the first, in my memory bank anyway --  was the best.  What a mighty, mighty talent he was, gone far too soon and for no comprehensible reason other than fate.  Boy, oh, boy, could he have ever gotten a song or two out of that situation!  The sound is excellent.  The setlist impeccable.  The memories forever.  Highly recommended.

title: Nina Simone: Oh, what a mighty talent!
text: The mighty talent of Nina Simone.  Some of her most essential recordings.  No further comment necessary.  Highly recommended.

title: The Kinks' Phobia is packed but hardly essential
text: Largely forgotten Sony / Columbia album by the Kinks from the early '90s (1993?).  The bonus track ("Did Ya?") is actually the best track on the cd, to my ears anyway.  The record itself is in the vein of one of Ray's grand concepts from the '70s (the RCA years), but it never really gains traction.  Noisy, cluttered, and overlong (falling into the temptation to fill up a CDs nearly 80-minute playing time), Phobia kind of fell victim to the Grunge takeover of the FM-radio airwaves of the era.  There are some memorable tracks (Drift Away, Only a Dream, Scattered), but it's hardly essential Kinks.  Strictly for the diehard Kinks fan.

title: Early post-Humble Pie Peter Frampton years
text: Peter Frampton finding his way, post-Humble Pie.  While he hadn't reached the heights of FRAMPTON (his pre- Comes Alive! breakthrough), both Winds of Change and Frampton's Camel feature tracks that would become concert staples in the coming years: Jumping Jack Flash, It's a Plain Shame, All I Want to Be (Is By Your Side), Lines On My Face, Do You Feel Like We Do, and more.  It's great to hear them in the original studio versions and realize how far they'd come in the live-in-concert performances we all remember so well.  Beautifully packaged with fine sound and excellent liner notes.  Recommended.

title: Clapper's tip o' the hat to Mr. King
text: Had this disc probably 20 years ago and gave it away.  Now I remember why.  It was no great shakes to begin with (to my ears) but sorry, it hasn't exactly aged well.  This is definitely a long way from my favorite Clapton and B.B. King efforts (Layla and other assorted love songs / Live In Cook County Jail).  Kind of forced, stale, and by-the-numbers.  I'll keep it in my collection this time around, but strictly as a completest.  I'm sure it's unlikely to get much play.

title: Peter Frampton Band's bluesy farewell grace note
text: Love the retro cover design, a real throwback to the day and a great indicator of the music presented inside.  Frampton and his band play it pretty much by the rules, which is fine by me.  It's classic blues material, served up in traditional, time-honored style, and featuring just enough outside-the-lines adventure to keep it all interesting.  Well-worth the checking out.  If this turns out to be it, Peter, thanks for all the great musical memories, and thanks also for leaving on a bluesy grace note.

title: Celebrating Frampton's commercial golden years
text: Purchased this as a gift for someone who has been a great friend of mine since the '70s.  He was happy to get it.  The sound is generally very good, the two discs are packed with 16 songs each, mostly well-selected, the notes are no great shakes as they offer little in the way of new info or insights.  The material is heavily weighted towards Frampton, Frampton Comes Alive, and I'm In You, which is fair enough I suppose, since they were his most commercially successful LPs.  However, some of the lesser known tracks are among the most interesting: I Can't Stand It No More, Breaking All The Rules, Lying, You, and his cover of George Harrison's Beatles masterpiece While My Guitar Gently Weeps stand out.  All in all, a pretty fair overview of the Peter Frampton solo career.  Recommended for fans of '70s AM / FM Radio crossover (Classic) Rock.

title: Mark Knopfler & Dire Straits are definitely "on" with On The Night
text: Excellent live recording.  Great sound, crowd-pleasing set-list, and arrangements that leave the band plenty of room to groove.  Highlights include the killer opener, Calling Elvis, an expanded Walk of Life, the Making Movies standout Romeo and Juliet, and the one-two punch finale of Money For Nothing and Brothers in Arms.  And that's only half the record!  Had this one a long time ago and lost it.  I'm so glad to have it back in my collection again.  Definitely recommended.

title: John Denver and Christmas music ... Perfect Together
text: Purchased as a Christmas Stocking-stuffer for my good wife, Hannie, a kind of casual John Denver fan.  She loves it, says it's right up there with the late singer / songwriter's first Greatest Hits collection.  Matter of fact, it's still in her car cd-player, even as we're into week two of 2021.  Can't go wrong with John Denver and classic Christmas music, not at our house anyway.

title: It's Christmas.  It's Darlene Love.  It's a year 'round keeper.
text: Darlene Love.  Christmas music.  What's not to love?  Tis the season for holiday neo-classics, right?!  Worth the price of admission for her beautiful take on The Band's "Christmas Must Be Tonight" alone.  But then there's Tom Petty's "Christmas All Over Again," John & Yoko's "Happy Xmas (War Is Over),"  Charles Brown's "Please Come Home for Christmas," and on and on.  Actually, it's so good you'll probably play it all the year through. Highly recommended.

title: Jimmy B's Covid-19 musical gift is his best in years
text: Covid-19 has been an international nightmare, yes indeed.  But the occasional sidebar story has been surprisingly uplifting.  Such is the case with Jimmy Buffett's latest release, "Songs You Don't Know by Heart," a stripped-down, mostly acoustic-based ramble through some of his best least-known (by the general public anyway) deep cuts.  This is his best record in years, maybe decades.  His singing is stronger and lyrically more connected than since I don't know when, and the low-key musical arrangements serve the songs well, and enhance rather than overwhelm his vocals.  This is a magical kind of album, reinforcing in its simplicity what drew us to Buffett's work in the first place: His terrific songwriting skills.  This is so good, in fact, that I'm  hoping he'll follow it up with a similarly arranged re-take of the entire "Songs You Know by Heart" collection, perhaps with a couple of bonus tracks.  Highly recommended.

title: Columbia was the wrong home for the '70s Rascals
text: They were always out to validate themselves as serious musicians, and they were tired of the "singles band" label that seemed to keep them from FM radio acceptance.  As to the former, they refused to hire a PR maven (someone like Derek Taylor, who helped to rebuild The Byrds' reputation after so many personnel changes); their credo was "It's all there in the music, not in the hype."  Honorable, but misguided.  As to being a singles band, it never hurt The Beatles, Stones, or Creedence Clearwater Revival, among others, but the rock press (as well as FM radio programmers) had never managed to get past the early Rascals in knickers image.  Not just The Rascals' loss, but the audiences, as well, because these guys were flat-out great.  Post- "Time-Peace / The Rascals' Greatest Hits,"  a monumental US chart and sales success, the band doubled-down on their quest to be taken more seriously.  Needless to say, it backfired.  They stretched musically, yes, but their label (Atlantic) lost faith, then interest in them.  When Columbia offered them a cool million $ to switch labels at the end of their current contract, Atlantic refused to counter-offer.  The band signed with Columbia (these two albums being the result), losing singer / lyricist / percussionist Eddie Brigati and singer / guitarist / songwriter Gene Cornish in the process.  Brigati's pop smarts and Cornish's rock feel were immediately missed, as was Arif Mardin's production input.  Big time.  Mardin was this group's George Martin, seriously.  Felix and Dino and a cast of thousands (kidding, of course) delivered the magnificent R&B / jazz-influenced Peaceful World in 1971.  Columbia didn't seem to have a clue what to do with it, as they were expecting variations on the Good Lovin' / Groovin' / People Got to Be Free themes.  A mere ripple in the charts, Peaceful World was seen as a kind of noble failure.  It was followed in 1972 by another adventurous LP, The Island of Real, less of a commercial ripple, another noble failure.  A lot of diehard Rascals fans never accepted the Columbia releases as Rascals records, and simply ignored them.  I would disagree.  In the best of all possible worlds, these records could've been released as Felix & Dino side-projects , while the original Atlantic group stayed together and created more rock 'n' soul classics.  Sad, for all of us, that it didn't work out that way.  Still, highly recommended.  Easily worth the price of admission for the first LPs title track and the second's R&B-tinged Be On the Real Side and Jungle Walk; everything else being sweet icing on the tasty musical cake.

title: Nashville's 1970 answer to 1969 From Elvis In Memphis / Back In Memphis sessions
text: The big differences between the 1969 From Elvis In Memphis / Back In Memphis  sessions sessions and the 1970 Nashville marathon recordings are basically two:  The producers and the material.  Memphis had the great Chips Moman, an independent music veteran and an outsider to the powers-that-be that ran Elvis's music career.  Nashville had Felton Jarvis, Elvis's regular producer since Chet Atkins gave up the reins in 1964.  Chips had a jones for R&B and "feel," Jarvis specialized in sweetening -- strings, horns, backing vocals, usually overwhelming the recordings and underwhelming rock critics and audiences.  Difference / problem number two:  The lack of solid contemporary material for the Nashville sessions.  Nowhere to be found are tracks as strong as Memphis classics In The Ghetto, Suspicious Minds, Don't Cry Daddy, Kentucky Rain, etc.  As far as covers of older and / or newer songs, the sessions hit a break even point.  Stripped of the Jarvis sweetening here, these tracks  sound fresher and punchier than ever before, which brings up another observation.  Isn't it a shame that at this post-comeback highpoint in an already legendary career Elvis seemingly lacked the confidence to simply trust in his voice and his musicians, sweetening be damned?  Still, a master at work, elevating everything he touches.  Highly recommended.

title: The great JC Fogerty's Covid-19 family affair
text: Fogerty's Factory, to this long-time fan's aging ears anyway, is everything the recent 50 Year Trip aspired to be and wasn't -- a terrific, clear-eyed nostalgic look back in celebration of a wonderful career.  A heady blend of Creedence favorites, solo years highlights, and a pair of well-selected covers (Lean On Me, City of New Orleans), this is one factory I'd love to hang out in.  Fogerty, his sons and daughter team up to make a most engaging sound.  Maybe they could've capped it all off with a Fogerty Factory cover of Sly Stone's (It's a) Family Affair; would've been a nice note to end on.  Regardless, this is Mr. Fogerty's best in quite some time; a lovely sidebar to the on-going Covid-19 story.  Highly recommended.

title: David Blue ... he changed his last name too
text: Purchased this one on a kind of nostalgic whim while listening to Bob Dylan & The Band's Planet Waves (where he's referenced in the lyrics of Never Say Goodbye) and The Basement Tapes (where he's featured in the cover photo).  Singer / songwriter / actor / scene-maker, his hipster reputation is better known than his musical contributions.  What is probably his best-known song, Outlaw Man (included here), actually charted in 1973 and was covered to fine effect by Eagles on their Desperado album.  This four-album (1968 - 1976), two-disc set makes a strong case for his singer / songwriter talents.  Of the four LPs included, the middle two (1971's Stories and 1973's Nice Baby and The Angel) are my personal favorites, although These 23 Days in September (1968) and Cupid's Arrow (1976) are both very good, indeed.  Well worth checking out.

title: The one I couldn't do without
text: The best version of the E Street Band, IMHO.  Springsteen's writing classics, and the band is lending them amazing support.  From the opening "The E Street Shuffle", to the closer, "New York City Serenade," it's all killer, not a bit of  filler.  The sense of unbridled joy is catching -- Bruce would never sound this joyful again.  By the time of the next release (Born To Run), Vini Lopez and David Sancious would both be gone, Springsteen would find himself under the wing of Jon Landau, and, seemingly, he'd begun to believe the hype.  This one, however, has never let me down, and it has remained in the Top 5 of my Desert Island Disc list for close to a half-century.  Very highly recommended.

title: Bruce Springsteen's amazing debut
text: Springsteen's amazing debut, and his most New Bob Dylan-esque record.  It's buoyed by the sounds of youth, possibility, and  the rebellion of the early 1970s.  You can practically feel Springsteen's sense of release: he's busting out and up, utterly fearless of failure.  Sounds as fresh today as it did nearly a half-century ago.  I loved it then, and I love it now, probably for different reasons.  Highly recommended.

title: Crosby began to break new ground with this first CPR studio release
text: Back in 1998, when this was first released, it probably seemed like a bit of a lark.  A David Crosby side project away from his CSN day job. After all, the upcoming release (1999's Looking Forward) represented the latest long hoped for, often delayed CSNY reunion.  Thing is, "CPR" turned out to be a far more interesting record for Crosby fans -- and likely a far more satisfying creative outlet for Croz himself.  Looking Forward and the even lesser previous CSN effort (1994's After The Storm) failed to impress, while CPR (and Crosby) just kept right on rolling along.  And it continues to sound fresh and new some 20 plus years down the line.  Recommended.

title: With CPR, who needs CSN?
text: By the time of this release, Crosby's second CPR studio album, it was pretty clear that he'd already outgrown the restrictions of CSN.  The mothership had basically become an oldies act by this time, and Croz seemed bored with it.  CPR was a creative outlet worth his time and effort, and Just Like Gravity stands up incredibly well, some 20 years down the line.  Hooking up with master guitarist Jeff Pevar and reuniting with his talented singer / songwriter / keyboardist son James Raymond proved to be an amazing blessing -- for Crosby & his faithful audience.  Recommended.

title: Big Judy, Big Talent, oh yeah!!
text: "The Elektra Albums" combines two LPs from the day (JUDY HENSKE / HIGH FLYING BIRD) on one 24-track disc.  And it's all killer, no filler, thank you very much.  Singer, actor, interpreter, Ms. Henske comes across as a musical force of nature.  I remember seeing Richie Havens in-concert at Monmouth University (NJ) back in the '90s and he was still filled with awe and admiration when recalling his first time seeing Judy perform High Flying Bird back in the Village in the '60s.  He copped it and kept it in his sets for the next half-century, wisely I might add.  A strikingly tall, big-voiced performer, Judy's talent is as big as her presence.  I'm so glad that my younger brother recently put me on to this Ace release.  Beautifully packaged, with informative notes and excellent sound, it'll likely restore your sense of wonder, as it surely did mine.  Highly Recommended.

title: With the right breaks, Pamela Polland shoulda, coulda, woulda been huge
text: A fine singer / songwriter who, with a bit of luck, could've been in the heady Carole King / Carly Simon league.  A terrific, detailed writer and an excellent, emotive singer,  Ms. Polland was poised for a very big career following her participation in the Joe Cocker / Leon Russell Mad Dogs & Englishmen tour.  She would certainly appeal to fans of the Melissa Manchester / Jackie De Shannon sounds of the early '70s.  But unplanned delays, loss of record label bigwigs' faith,  and changes in the musical winds as the '70s progressed conspired to derail her forward career motion.  Very sad, indeed, but it's never too late to appreciate a fine artist, as this two-disc set proves.  BGO does its usual sterling job here:  Excellent notes, graphics, and sound.  Highly recommended.

title: Eagles Tribute Band??
text: Basically, this is simply an event souvenir, 21st Century EAGLES IN CONCERT.  Except that it's not, really.  It plays like a tribute band with real EAGLES guest stars (founding Eagle Don Henley, replacement Eagles Joe Walsh and Timothy B. Schmit).  Sadly, the spark is long gone, despite the addition of Vince Gill and Glenn Frey's son Deacon.  And man, oh. man, is Don Felder's legendary guitar playing ever missed here!  Then there's the increasingly annoying Joe Walsh "How ya doin'?" moments (yeah, that's plural). Overkill, for sure.  Might have played as comedy relief in-concert, but it doesn't stand up to repeated plays on disc.  It's a  pleasant enough concert keepsake for the diehard fan, I suppose, but it's hardly an essential CD release.

title: Wildflowers, by the great Tom Petty & The Heartbreakers
text: Why this was credited as a Tom Petty solo record back in the day remains a mystery to me, among many others.  Contractual obligations, maybe?  Why his record label balked at the idea of releasing it as a double-album is another all-time head-scratcher.  What I do know is this: Wildflowers is definitely a Tom Petty & the Heartbreakers record, and finally releasing it alongside All The Rest makes it a positively seminal double-album.  Don't hesitate; get it! Very highly recommended.

title: Southside Johnny & The Asbury Jukes, post-Epic Records
text: The Jukes' two best post-Epic LPs .  Neither is a match for the band's creative high-water mark, 1978's Hearts Of Stone.  Both of these LPs are a bit more commercial in approach, but that's not necessarily meant as a knock.  The material is solid, and since Billy Rush had essentially stepped up and taken on songwriting duties for the band in the absence of Miami Steve, the two-on-one CD flows beautifully.  Opening on the rush of All I Want Is Everything and closing with the tender and soulful  It Hurts, The Jukes (1979) / Love Is A Sacrifice (1980) combination plays like a solid double-album.  Excellent sound, notes, and packaging.  Recommended to both Jukes fans and '70s rock fans.

title: Bruce's letter to a younger self?
text: This is the sound of a grizzled veteran songwriter straining for continued significance in the twilight of a legendary career.  Letter To You seems, to this decades-long fan anyway,  like a desperate missive to a much younger, hungrier, happier self.  And the best tracks are at least a half-century old -- Janey Needs A Shooter (the weakest of the three), If I Was The Priest (the strongest), Song For Orphans (the most New Dylan-esque).  I have a very simple litmus test when reviewing a new release by an old favorite.  If this was the first LP I ever bought by this artist, would it lead to the long-time musical connection I've enjoyed with him / her throughout the years?  Sadly, in this case the answer is "nope."  Good, but by no means essential.

title: Elvis at Stax: He sings all kinds ...
text: Proof positive that when his heart was still in it -- and the material being recorded was good to great --  Elvis could still deliver the goods in the mid-'70s.  This well-selected 17-song compilation contains hit singles (Promised Land, If You Talk in Your Sleep, My Boy), near misses (Raised On Rock, For Ol' Times Sake, I've Got a Thing About You Baby), well-chosen covers (Good Time Charlie's Got the Blues, Loving Arms, You Asked Me To), and some very pleasant surprises that should've been hits (I've Got a Feelin' in My Body, Find Out What's Happening).  A tasty gumbo blend of rock, pop, old school R&B, and country, Elvis At Stax embodies one of the young Presley's earliest quotes: "I sing all kinds ..."  Very highly recommended, as is the three-disc slipcase version, which takes the listener behind the scenes and offers further proof that Elvis's artistry was still intact and on display in the post-Aloha '70s.

title: There's a rumor going 'round Nashville ...
text: Terrific collection.  A near-perfect marriage of singer (Rumer), songwriter (Hugh Prestwood), and producer (Fred Mollin).  The record has a kind of Linda Ronstadt - Peter Asher '70s feel in that it's a precise and collaborative production.  But Rumer's warm, often seductive vocals can't help but bring Karen Carpenter (at her best) to mind.  Rumer's vocals work beautifully within the country-based arrangements, and she succeeds in uncovering every emotional nook & nuance inside Prestwood's sage, poetic lyric approach.  Highly Recommended.

title: The Jayhawks deliver a strong collaborative effort with XOXO
text: An excellent follow-up to the band's Back Roads & Abandoned Motels, its inspired reclamation of outside-the-group Gary Louris compositions 2018 project.  This time around though, it's a whole lot more of a collaborative effort, with everyone contributing material to create the whole.  Together, they achieve that classic Jayhawks sound -- rootsy acoustic-based alt-country rock, with shadowy underpinnings of the Beatles, the Beach Boys, and the Burritos.  Very good stuff, indeed.  I've noticed some complaints from some reviewers about missing bonus tracks; my CD lists 12 tracks on the back cover, with a sticker on the front claiming LIMITED EDITION INCLUDES 3 BONUS TRACKS -- and it does!  The extra tracks are: 13.)  Jewel of the Trimbelle, 14.)  Then You Walked Away, and 15.)  Hypocrite's Lament.

title: What can you say that hasn't been said about McCartney?
text: In addition to being one-half of the greatest songwriting team in Rock History, and a major one-fourth of the greatest band ever, Paul McCartney is one of the greatest natural performers of the last half-century.  And what a catalog of songs to choose from to perform in concert!  Absolutely Fab!  Had this one years ago, but lost the discs (!) somewhere along the way (but kept the jewel-case, inserts, and booklets -- go figure).  It's just as great as I remember it, maybe even better.  Great mix of Beatles, Wings, solo, and select covers blended into one beautifully paced, memorable Rock Show -- and it tops the earlier release, Wings Over America (IMHO).  Highly recommended, if you can find it!

title: America's 50th, celebrated !
text: A pretty complete overview of this seriously underappreciated trio / duo's Warner Bros. career, plus.  Ostensibly, it's a celebration of the group's 50th anniversary as recording artists.  Since it was decided to include the Capitol Records smash hit You Can Do Magic though, I have to wonder why it was decided to not include the duo's other Capitol Top 40 hit, The Border, as well as their charting California Dreamin' cover.  Strange, yes?  Matter of fact, a representational track from all their albums would've made more sense in the celebratory circumstance of this three-disc release. Regardless, what is included is very good to excellent material (hits, b-sides, deep cuts, live tracks, and demos), all  beautifully sung and performed, and well-deserving of the five star review.  Highly recommended.

title: Ray's a one-man-BAND on this instant classic
text: Since it arrived in my mailbox, I've played this one at least six times, front-to-back, all the way through.  It's an instant classic, or as I've been telling friends, it's a single-CD Desert Island Disc all on its own.  Great stuff, not a single waste cut in sight.  RLM does it all here; plays all the instruments, sings all the vocals, the songwriting, the arrangements, the production.  Atmospherically, it's a throwback to the music of the late '60s / early '70s; he's like a one-man-BAND at their self-titled, 1969 Brown cover peak.  There are also hints of CSN (debut LP), Neil Young (Harvest-era), and even the great Bob Dylan (Basement Tapes and John Wesley Harding-era) -- an unbelievably potent musical gumbo, to be sure.  Highly recommended ... couldn't you tell??

title: Still Bill ... you betcha!
text: Another '70s classic returns to my collection, thank you very much.  Every bit the equal to the great Just As I Am, Still Bill succeeded in moving Bill Withers' singer/songwriter reputation into the stratosphere -- and justifiably so.  Use Me, Who Is He (And What Is He To You), and his all-time artistic high-water mark, Lean On Me, stretched across the pop music genre landscape, and ensured him a place within the all-time upper tier singer/songwriter firmament.  Still Bill?  Oh, yeah!  One of the greats from one of the greats.  RIP, Mr. Withers, thanks for all the great music.

title: Just As I Am ... the real deal
text: One of my all-time favorite albums of the '70s, and it's just as great as my memories of it.  Bill Withers -- what a great talent he was.  "Just As I Am," exactly right!  Nothing bogus, nothing fake, take him for who he is or just don't bother.  The bona fide real deal.  Just check out his own Harlem and Ain't No Sunshine, the terrific covers of Everybody's Talkin' and Let It Be, and lord almighty, his heartrending Grandma's Hands.  Makes me well up with tears and think of my own late Gram whenever I hear it.  So glad to have an upgraded version of this classic album in my collection.  Highly recommended!

title: Rick's return to Rockabilly
text: Had this one a long time ago, but lost it somewhere along the way.  Always liked it, the performances are really good, but it's no "In Concert at The Troubadour, 1969."  On that one he had something to prove, that he was still alive, well, and relevant, and prove it he did, in grand style with the first and greatest Stone Canyon Band.  Here on "Live 1983-1985" he's still singing and playing like he means it, but with its rather safe and predictable set-list, there doesn't seem to be anything at stake.  Heck, he even plays his classic comeback single, Garden Party, without any sense of irony -- it's just another one of the hits to be played.  The thing that bugs me about this release is that it's so chopped up; there's no sense of a continuous concert flow even attempted by whoever it was that put it together.  Performance, applause, dead space, next song, repeat.  A bit of production care could've made it a much more meaningful aural experience.  Regardless, it's good to know that Rick was still delivering the in-concert musical goods right to the very end.  RIP, Mr. Rick Nelson, you truly were a 20th Century troubadour.

title: Mighty and delicate: Sagittarius' Present Tense, plus
text: Boy Howdy, does this one take me back!  A friend / bandmate of mine had the original Columbia LP back in the Fall of '68, following the previous year's Summer of Love.  Great love-in of an LP that never gained the traction it deserved.  Perhaps it came out a bit too late?  I hesitate to use the phrase Sunshine Pop because there's so much more to it than that.  The brain-trust of successful producer / songwriters Gary Usher and Curt Boettcher, the album boasts elements of The Association, The Beach Boys, The Left Banke, Spanky & Our Gang, The Turtles, and more, blended into its own unique mighty, yet delicate sound scape.  Half of this release's 20-song playlist is made up of previously unreleased tracks and / or alternate versions, but not to worry, as  combined with the original LP material included here it's all of a won, won, wonderful piece.  Recommended to fans of aurally adventurous late '60s harmony groups.  Me, I'm loving it.

title: Ruthanne Friedman's guitar & vocal debut LP, plus
text: Her late '60s A & M sessions failed to gel into a debut LP, so it was back to the drawing board for a solid set of sessions and a genuine debut with Reprise Records in 1970.  Considering the singer/songwriter takeover of the early '70s airwaves and record charts, it should have resulted in a smash.  Guitar and vocals simplicity rule the day, a wise decision on the part of producer Joe Wissert, to my way of thinking anyway.  The songs are good, to very good, to great, and the bare & basic aural settings serve the songs -- and Ruthanne's vocals -- well.  Following the LPs original 12 tracks, there's a pair of more produced recordings (not nearly as effective as what went before), followed by a whole other album's worth of tracks recorded at the same sessions as the debut.  I found my way to this artist while reading up on The Association (she wrote Windy) and I'm really glad that I did.  Highly recommended.

title: Everyone knows it's ... Ruthann??
text: She wrote the great Association smash hit Windy.  Although rather atypical of her songwriter's songbook, it should have propelled her into a better known singer / songwriter career; that it didn't is a real head-scratcher.  From the A & M sessions that should've resulted in her debut album (but obviously didn't!), "Windy: A Ruthann Friedman Songbook" will have you wondering why.  She had the songs, the chops, the voice, the connections, the whole package; that it didn't happen for her only serves to point up what a roll of the dice the record business was / is.  If you're a fan of the '60s Cali singer / songwriter era, this one's for you.  Why more of these songs haven't been covered is yet another record biz mystery.  Good stuff.  Highly recommended.

title: And then along came Tandyn ...
text: "Tandyn Almer" was one of those names that turned up in parenthesis underneath the titles of some of my favorite recordings (the Association's Along Comes Mary, the Beach Boys' Sail On, Sailor and Marcella).  He was a songwriter, yes, but as far as I knew, not a singer / songwriter.  I guess that's just what makes this disc feel like such a find -- he was a singer / songwriter, of sorts.  This collection of, for lack of a better phrase, well-produced demos is an eye and ear-opener.  And while nothing here jumps off the disc like another Along Comes Mary or Marcella, there's plenty of good, to very good, to great songs to enjoy and play what-might-have-been games with (matching his songs with bands that might have done well to cover them).  Among my favorites:  Find Yourself (the opener), There's Gotta Be a Way, Alice Designs, and Where Will They Go.  Highly recommended for fans of late '60s - early '70s pop / rock.

title: Russ Giguere takes you back to a time when the music really mattered
text: Is this a lost classic?  No, not really.  But it is a quality artifact from an era when record labels (remember them?) gave artists room to breathe, freedom to create, and an opportunity to grow in their craft.  Here we have a group of good to great songs, all beautifully played and sung, and produced with heart and care.  Recorded with the rest of the band, it would've made an excellent studio follow-up to either 1969's "The Association" or 1970's double "Live."  As a Russ Giguere solo elpee,  it's an engaging, varied and entertaining side-project, much of it anticipating the soon-to-happen country-rock boom of the '70s.  Highly recommended to fellow fans of Southern California Pop / Rock.

title: Dylan continues to amaze with Rough and Rowdy Ways
text: There are great singers, great songwriters, great singer/songwriters.  And then there's Bob Dylan -- in a zone all his own, the greatest of them all.  Nearly 60 years into his justifiably legendary career, he delivers yet another late career highwater mark LP with Rough & Rowdy Ways.  We've all heard the epic Murder Most Foul, and that track alone would make it worth the price of admission.  The fact that "Murder …" is packaged as a stand-alone disc here makes two points very clear: The strong, atmospheric nine-song album succeeds in standing on its own bluesy ground quite nicely, thank you; and "Murder …" is a masterwork beyond anything we have a right to expect at this point in Mr. Dylan's life and career.  Absolutely amazing, but don't take my word for it.  Jump right in and find out for yourself …

title: False Unknown Legend
text: Finally officially released after some 45 years of hype, this is disappointing in the extreme.  Homegrown is the missing link connecting Harvest and Comes A Time?  Nah, I don't think so.  I bought into the "lost classic" hype as heavily as any other diehard N.Y. fan I know, and that's what really makes this hard to handle.  It's not like Homegrown is just another of Neil's more recent bombs (I know, he's gotta follow his muse, right?); it's the fact that it's supposed to have been this great classic work from his salad days that was sacrificed in the name of Tonight's The Night.  Turns out that was a wise exchange, after all.  I've given it three plays, front to back, all the way through.  I won't be returning to it anytime soon.

title: Latter day Byrds in flight
text: One of the first Byrds LPs I ever bought, even though it was the latter day group nearing the end of the band's long flight.  Purchased it again on 8-track, then cassette for car purposes (always preferred LPs at home) and eventually had it on CD.  Lost it somewhere along the way -- during one of my many moves from apartment to apartment back in the '70s/'80s -- and always kind of missed it.  So, purchasing it again as a near-perfect used disc was a no-brainer.  Glad to have it back in my collection again, for the nostalgia as well as the great music.

title: JT's Greatest is greater than ever
text: A contractual obligation release that turned into a defining career album moment, James Taylor's Greatest Hits was a kiss-off to Warner Bros as he moved on to a lucrative new deal with Columbia Records.  Funny thing is, it turned out to be an amazing gold, platinum, and diamond-certified fare-thee-well to his former label.  I've owned it on record, 8-track, cassette, and CD, and it has been a staple when gift-giving to family, friends, and romances throughout the years and configurations.  This newly-released, Peter Asher-supervised remaster is hands-down, far and away the best version yet.  The sound is crisp and intimate, the separation perfectly executed, and Taylor's vocals (just slightly in front in this mix) have never sounded warmer or more assured.  Even the fade-outs have been improved; they're much clearer, and they last longer, so that the playouts reveal musical subtleties utterly unnoticed until now.  Oh, yes, the fold-out white cover replicates the original 1976 release right down to the non-glossy, textured paper sleeve.  Five balding stars and highly recommended.  JT's best just got better …

title: Jukes: Meanwhile, Back in Jersey ...
text: Completes my Jukes trifecta (joining The Fever: The Remastered Epic Recordings and The Mercury Years).  While none of these discs reach the heights of the band's greatest elpee (the remarkable final Epic release, Hearts of Stone), all three are solid journeyman efforts by one of the hardest working stage acts in rock 'n' roll.  Messin' With the Blues (produced by the great E Street Band bass player Garry Tallent) does just that; instead of doing a covers album of classic blues tunes, Southside and the gang deliver a steaming set of mostly originals, with a few tasty covers thrown in (Tom Waits' great Gin-Soaked Boy a standout).  Going To Jukesville is a throwback to the Jukes' roots, and it has the feel of an artist finding his way back home.  Among its highlights: Baby Don't Lie, I Won't Sing, and the Goffin  / King classic No Easy Way Down.  Into The Harbour just may be the best of the trio.  A carefully blended mix of tasty covers and Jukes originals, the disc plays like a well-planned live set.  The band takes on the Stones (Happy), Tom Waits (Hang Down Your Head), Richard Thompson (Tear-Stained Letter), and Delbert McClinton (When Rita Leaves) and delivers the goods every time.  They also deliver a boat-load of solid originals, including Dancing on the Edge of the World, The Time Between (with contributions from ex-Rascal Felix Cavaliere), and the terrific title song.  Very good to great music, well-produced, played and sung, nicely packaged, and at a bargain price -- who could ask for more?  Highly recommended to Jukes fans and lovers of real, made from the heart rock 'n roll.

title: Excellent post-James Gang, pre-Eagles Joe Walsh
text: I believe this was Joe's first proper "solo" album.  I purchased the LP back in the day on the basis of his work within the James Gang, having been a big fan of early '70s rock radio favorites Walk Away and Midnight Man, both of which were huge FM hits in El Paso when I lived there back in 1971.  Initially, I'll admit that I was a bit underwhelmed by Barnstorm because I didn't hear a Walk Away or Midnight Man-type track on the LP. I hardly even noticed when it went missing during one of my many apartment moves.  A bit further on up the road, however, and after getting into his The Smoker You Drink LP, I went out and repurchased Barnstorm and began to really appreciate its highpoints, of which there are many.  It just may be Joe Walsh's quietest work, but in many ways, it may also be one of his deepest.  Glad to finally have it on CD and back in my collection.

title: FBB soaring live at the Fillmore East
text: Excellent concert offering.  Great set list, great performance. Love it!  Wish I had been there.  The Fillmore East was a great venue to take in a show, I know.  This comes from the Wolfgang's Vault concert archives (the late, great Bill Graham), so you know the sound is about as good as it can be.  From the same archive, but the Fillmore West, there's a terrific Rascals concert from May, 1971 in which the reconstituted (Columbia Records) version of the band serves up a tasty and soulful resume of their Atlantic/CBS career up to Peaceful World.  I'm still hoping that it too will see the light of day some one of these fine days.  In the meantime, dig into the FBB authorized bootleg at the Fillmore East.  You won't be disappointed.

title: Rick Nelson, bandmember
text: The one thing that Rick Nelson was that his musical hero Elvis Presley wasn't?  Simply a member of the band, and that's brilliantly displayed here.  I'm not knocking Elvis, my own first, strongest, and longest-lasting musical hero, here.  His fame, vocal talent, and stage presence were simply too huge to overcome -- much as I'm sure he'd have liked to, at times.  But Rick, a teen idol at odds and ends in the post-Beatles era, decided to take a different route.  After a series of flop releases (including a pair of terrific country-related LPs that failed commercially), Rick put together the Stone Canyon Band and found his second act in Rock 'n' Roll.  Working in the band format, he not only found his way back into the singles charts (She Belongs to Me, Easy to Be Free), but released perhaps the best album of his long career, Rick Nelson In Concert.  He was a country-rock pioneer, and it served him well.  Commercially, the Stone Canyon Band years peaked with Garden Party, but they soldiered on for a couple of more albums and many a tour.  This bargain-priced, 23-track collection presents the highlights, and they are many (in addition to the aforementioned titles).  Dylan covers stand out (If You Gotta Go, Go Now, Love Minus Zero/No Limit, Just Like a Woman, I Shall Be Released), along with Windfall, Rock & Roll Lady, Life, Fadeaway, Wild Nights in Tulsa, and his tip of the hat to Elvis, a terrific cover of Mystery Train.  Well worth checking out.  Highly recommended.

title: Who is the real Bob Dylan?  This'll help you find him.
text: A great set with which to introduce Dylan to the uninitiated.  Three discs filled to the brim with highlights from the master songwriter's five decades-plus career.  Intelligently programmed, beautifully mastered, and touching just about every musical / lyrical base, The Real Bob Dylan will make you realize that there have been many "real moments" throughout the great man's legendary career.  But no one can pin him down -- and that's a good thing.  Three great discs (44 tracks) and at a bargain price; what a deal!  Highly recommended.

title: Three discs (49 tracks) of Elvis at his best, and at a bargain price!
text: What gets lost in the legend and the lurid tales of life-gone-wrong for the King (a title he hated and was forever trying to escape), is the plain fact that at his best -- and in my opinion that was in the Sixties -- this guy could sing anything.  And I mean with authority and authenticity.  I love the fact that these three discs span the spectrum -- hit singles, classic b-sides, album deep cuts, soundtrack songs, television and live-in-concert performances.  Wisely, it circumvents the obvious, over-anthologized hit titles (like It's Now or Never, Are You Lonesome To-night?) to include lesser, but no less satisfying titles (like Such a Night, Devil in Disguise, She's Not You).  It also features great, if somewhat forgotten flipsides (like Witchcraft, You'll Be Gone, Blue River), deep-cut ballads (like I'll Remember You, Gentle on My Mind -- yes, done as a soulful ballad!), and some great blues and r&b (like Long Black Limousine, Reconsider Baby, Stranger in My Own Hometown).  Three discs filled to the brim with great music at a bargain price; who could ask for anything more?  Highly recommended.

title: Sadly, not as advertised
text: Three discs of Beach Boys Nirvana, which should've resulted in a five star review.  However, this package isn't what was advertised.  It's supposed to come in a three-panel slip-case with the new, much-improved cover art (pictured).  Sadly, it's the same old package I've owned for years.  So, music: 5 stars; unimproved packaging takes it down to three.  Disappointing.

title: Album: 5 stars / Packaging takes it down
text: Along with Holland, my favorite '70s Beach Boys album.  Terrific contributions from everyone, especially Carl, Alan, and of course, Brian; not to mention the absolutely classic album cover art.  Five stars for the long player, but the new packaging is not as advertised.  There's supposed to be a book(let), which is non-existent.  Great music (with all the Boys picking up the slack left them by Brian), very disappointing repackaging (the back cover photo isn't even era-correct!).  Three stars.

title: Smile and say Cheese, Dave
text: One of my all-time favorite '60s bands (and their fans) given the short-shrift with a cheesy, abridged recycling of The Hits, the packed, vastly superior 28-track 2008 compilation.  This 16-track compilation (15 actually, since the last title, Universal Love, is inexplicably missing), All The Hits, hardly lives up to its title since a dozen or more chart hits are MIA.  The notes and packaging are also recycled.  There's no real improvement in the sound -- to my ears, anyway -- and the track-list is basically a title-by-title replication of the first half of (2008) The Hits.  Like all too few other classic '60s groups, Dave Clark has always maintained control / ownership of his band's masters / recordings.  That being the case, this cheesy collection is a real head-scratcher.  Very disappointing.

title: Alex Chilton's Rock 'n' Soul beginnings with the Box Tops
text: Still in his teens, Alex Chilton & the Box Tops cooked-up a hearty brand of Memphis rock 'n' soul stew from the very beginning with The Letter.  Once the band broke through with that 1967 classic, well, there was just no stopping that flow of soulful singles:  Neon Rainbow, Cry Like a Baby, Choo-Choo Train, Soul Deep, and the out of left field classics I Met Her in Church and Sweet Cream Ladies, Forward March.  They're all included here, along with great b-sides (Fields of Clover, People Gonna Talk), deep cuts (She Shot a Hole in My Soul, Happy Times), and lost singles (I Shall Be Released, Turn On a Dream).  A killer collection by anyone's standards, and at a bargain price.  Highly recommended.

title: The Best of Cilla Black's Sixties Brit Hits
text: Ordered this as a gift for my better half after we watched the Cilla bio flick on Acorn.  Neither of us knew much about her or her career (just "You're My World," really), so the picture was a real eye-opener.  Anyway, this is a pretty terrific -- and complete -- hits overview for a single-disc compilation.  Highlights include her excellent versions of Anyone Who Had a Heart, Alfie, It's For You, and the aforementioned US hit, You're My World.  Good, if brief, liner notes, very good remastered sound, solid 14-song track list.  Highly recommended for fans of '60s British pop -- and who among us isn't?

title: The Left Banke is, was, and evermore will be The Real Thing
text: Had this one on LP way on way back when. Always liked it a lot, but loaned it out and never got it back somewhere along the way.  Walk Away, Renee and Pretty Ballerina sound as fresh, baroque, and tastefully soulful as ever, and the rest of the disc is of a piece.  So glad to have this one back in my collection.  Recommended '60s listening.

title: An American Treasure redefines a collection of American Standards
text: I'll keep this simple and to the point.  Instead of taking the routine (and overdone) "Sings the American Songbook" route, by way of performance and arrangements he turns these American classics into James Taylor songs.  If, like yours truly, you're a life-long JT fan, you're sure to find a lot to love about this new collection of old favorites.  Give it a try; I don't think you'll be disappointed.  Highly recommended.

title: The Band -- just as great as ever
text: One of my all-time favorite albums, only bigger.  Disc 2 includes the group's Woodstock set in its best sound to date.  The other extras are fun and nice to have, if non-essential.  This record changed my life back in 1969, and has remained a constant aural / artistic companion for more than a half-century.  I was a teen when I first bought the LP, and now I'm a retired old guy, and it means as much to me as ever.  The great works never fade away …

title: It's getting tired, Mr. Fogerty, really
text: The question with this release is, why bother?  The Walmart-only double-disc version is the one to get if you're really interested, as it tips its hat to Woodstock with some cleverly chosen covers.  This singular, stand-alone disc is less compelling, with a 19-song setlist that covers the Creedence canon and manages to sneak in a trio of Fogerty solo years hits (Rock and Roll Girls, Centerfield, The Old Man Down the Road -- all from the Centerfield album).  None of it essential, especially considering the far superior live sets (CCR and solo) that are already available.  For diehards only; casual fans should probably take a pass.

title: Mavericks play the hits,  bar band-style
text: As covers albums go, this is a very good one, indeed, but it's hardly essential.  However, it is the Mavericks, so you know the playlist stretches across the musical spectrum, and it's all well-played, superbly sung, beautifully produced -- and a whole lot of fun.  My personal faves: Before the Next Teardrop Falls, Hungry Heart, Don't Be Cruel, and Blue Eyes Crying in the Rain.

title: Listen to the '70s music ... Yeah!
text: Another gift purchase for a dear friend.  She loved it; the Doobies are right in her '70s musical wheelhouse.  All the hits that fit, plus.  She says that she even likes the handful of remixed versions included at disc's end, but actually prefers the originals.  Tells me this one's getting a lot of repeat plays in her car disc-player, alternating play-time between Doobies, Eagles, Chicago, and Moody Blues.  Seems it's a '70s world on any given day.  Who would've thought?

title: This disc's in heavy auto-player rotation ...
text: Another gift purchase that was a big hit.  She was very happy because all her major favorites were included, though not in chronological release order (minor quibble).  She tells me its been in regular rotation in her car disc-player, which is a very good sign.  Excellent collection; excellent price; couldn't be happier.  Thanks.

title: The perfect gift for the casual Chicage fan ...
text: Purchased as a gift.  She was very happy with the fact that the collection crossed various eras / aspects of Chicago's very long and successful career.  Power ballads, '70s pop-radio hits, FM-rock radio classics, etc.  The sound is good, packaging perfect. All in all, the perfect gift for the casual Chicago fan.

title: Dylan and Cash: Perfectly imperfect together
text: In complete agreement with Stuart Jefferson's well-written and well thought out review.  Little to add except that the Ken Burns PBS documentary (which featured episodes heavily slanted toward Cash as Country's King) will likely cause added interest in this particular Bootleg Series release.

title: Springsteen's Redundant Western Stars
text: The completist within me said "buy it;" my natural tendency to question my own motives said "it's redundant."  And the critic within says, "His less than stellar performance of Rhinestone Cowboy hardly justifies the cost of the purchase."  If you don't already have the very recently released studio version, this is well worth your time, money and effort.  If you do -- and you're not a completist, like me -- probably wise to take a pass.

title: The second half of Poco's Epic Years nicely collected
text: If you're reading this odds are you're already aware of Poco.  They're the kind of little band that gets into both your ear and your heart; the many tough breaks they went through over the years only served to endear them even more to their loyal fan-base.  They could've called themselves the Dangerfields, since they've always been taken for granted and shown little in the way of respect, commercially or critically.  Where this collection begins (their fifth album), Jimmy Messina had already left the group and begun his successful run with Kenny Loggins; previously, Randy Meisner had left the band to work with Rick Nelson's Stone Canyon Band and then the Eagles.  The relative failure of 1972's A Good Feelin' To Know made Richie Furay antsy to move on, realizing he wasn't ever going to achieve his desired Crosby, Stills, Nash and Young-style payday with Poco.  Having come to that realization, he knew he'd be gone after the 1973 follow-up album (Crazy Eyes).  Choosing not to replace him, the four remaining members stepped it up and carried on as a self-contained country-rock quartet with Paul Cotton, Rusty Young and Timothy B. Schmit ably taking on songwriting responsibilities on 1974's Seven and Cantamos.  The fifth disc contained here is the Epic's revenge release, the still very enjoyable Poco Live, recorded in 1974 and released in '76 to compete in the marketplace with their then-current ABC release, Rose Of Cimarron.  This collection is well put together:  Nicely packaged, solid liner notes and graphics, very good sound.  Hearing these tracks in the way they were originally released -- in album form -- and listening in chronological order, one can't help but smile and be thankful for this little band that could -- and wonder what might have been.  Highly recommended.  Hopefully, they'll follow up and collect the first four Poco Epic releases in a similarly impressive collection.

title: Van the Man is back!
text: Following hard on the worn heels of four consecutive (largely) covers discs, Van Morrison finally delivers the real follow-up to his wonderful Keep Me Singing disc (2016), and it's his best in years.  Three Chords & The Truth finds Van back in the singer / songwriter game -- all originals and one traditional with new Morrison lyrics -- and he's very near the top of his game.  A very hands on record, in addition to the sterling band and his own terrific vocals Van's all over the musical landscape -- on acoustic and electric guitars, electric piano, and sax.  This record is pure joy and a most welcome return to form.  I give it five smiling Irish eyes, yes indeed!

title: Remastered?  Not this Pretender ...
text: Listed as a remastered import on Amazon, this cd came as a very big disappointment.  Import, yes; remastered, no way.  One of the great albums of the '70s, musically, is a five star release.  Being hoodwinked into re-buying it by claiming it's a remaster when it's not, well, fool me once, shame on you, fool me twice ...

title: Jakob Dylan's Heartfelt Tribute to the Legendary Laurel Canyon
text: I am loving this soundtrack.  Essentially a tribute album to a time / place / artistic ideal, it plays like a Jakob Dylan solo LP, featuring memorably gorgeous (frequently male / female) duets throughout the 13-track ride.  A fresh coat of paint on classics by the likes of The Byrds, The Mamas and The Papas, The Beach Boys, The Buffalo Springfield, Love, The Association, The Turtles, and even The Monkees,  breathes new life into time-honored, landmark songs like Go Where You Wanna Go, You Showed Me, In My Room, Never My Love, Questions, and Expecting to Fly.  The male / female duets often uncover new meaning and feeling (I was especially drawn to You Showed Me with Cat Power, In My Room with Fiona Apple, and Never My Love with Norah Jones), while Beck's contributions to The Byrds' tracks (Bells of Rhymney and Goin' Back) are among the LP's standout moments.  Two constants are at work here: Jakob Dylan and great songs.  Neither lets you down.  Already one of my all-time favorite covers discs, right up there with Chris Isaak's Beyond The Sun.

title: An unprecedented run, all the way around
text: First the autobiography, then the Broadway run, the Netflix taping, and now this audio release to keep it all fresh and in perspective.  Amazing!  Bruce Springsteen operates in a class all his own, and in the same way I feel about Bob Dylan, I'm just lucky to be alive at the same time to witness his artistry.  Not a collection I'll necessarily play endlessly (like I did Born To Run, The River, and others when I was a much younger man), but one I'll take the time to savor again and again over the years -- like a fine bottle of wine for special occasions.  Thanks, Bruce, for taking us along and sharing your amazing life's journey.

title: The Rolling Thunder Revue stills lives in the head and the heart
text: Maybe you had to be there, I don't know, but it's always been one of my favorite periods in Bob Dylan's great career.  All tied-up with personal history, I suppose.  Planet Waves found me newly single following the disintegration of a foolish teen-age marriage; Before The Flood was both a nostalgic look back and a breath of fresh future air -- and a rockin' good time with The Band, as well.  Blood On The Tracks felt as if Uncle Bobby had been reading my mail and then airing the tawdry details in public -- cutting to the bone and drawing blood, as promised in the title.  Rolling Thunder (including Desire and Hard Rain) were triumphs of art, determination, and courage over crass commercial concerns; something true and real and definitely needed in the light (darkness?) of my first rock 'n' roll hero's (Elvis) tragic and very public fall from grace at this very same time.  Dylan singing and playing with righteous anger (Hurricane), heartbreak and resignation (One More Cup of Coffee), his deft sense of humor and romance intact in matters of the heart (Romance in Durango), facing marital challenges (Isis), celebrating marital bliss (Sara), and on and on.  Backed by a wonder band that's up to -- and always there to meet -- every  musical challenge, punctuated throughout by Scarlett Rivera's otherworldly violin fills.  And the tour's event in Montreal (December 4, 1975) seems (to me) to celebrate my then-new love (Patti, 1975-80, and remembered with affection to this very day) and my 25th birthday.  Really, I've just got to love it.  Beautifully packaged; terrific photos and notes; great, great music.  Thanks Bob, 44 years later!

title: Western Snoozer
text:
First of all let me say I've been on the Springsteen Train -- if not from the very beginning -- since before his Columbia Records deal. Saw The Bruce Springsteen Band for the first time in 1972 at the Captain's Garter in Neptune, NJ and it was magic, simply magic. I was a still wet-behind-the-ears 21-year-old, but I was musically wise enough to know the stuff of greatness when I saw it, up close and personal. I've been on board and attended countless concerts and purchased every BS album since. I'm a long way from my twenties now, and so unfortunately is Brucie; seems as if the fire has dimmed a bit for the both of us. Utilizing his usual solo work approach (you know, the thick-tongued- Okie variation on Woody), while drenching the set in strings, he lets no lyrical cliché go unused in this '70s country pastiche. Ignore the Sony PR / personal management hype. Here, Springsteen is neither up to Jimmy Webb's amazing songwriting artistry, nor does his singing come even close to Glen Campbell's unforgettable vocals. Look, I'm a collector and a completist, so I'm happy enough to have this set in my collection, and it won't be the first BS disc that doesn't get a lot of play in my house. I know I can't expect anything close to Greetings, Wild & Innocent, or Darkness at this stage, but this one still definitely comes as a disappointment. A real snoozer; and boring is a word I never thought I'd use to describe a new Bruce Springsteen release.
8/2/2019 Update: Felled by a serious summer cold, I've spent the last few days giving Western Stars far more spins than I would ever have expected when I wrote the above review. To borrow another time-worn cliché, it takes a big man to admit he's made a big mistake. Er, uh, that would be me. Digging deep into the latest BS set, I've discovered many a gem hidden among the lyrical Western clichés that make up these subtle songs -- like scripts to some favorite old westerns from my youth. And the sweeping strings? The soundtracks punctuating the beauty of those (to me) memory-filled classics. The Jimmy Webb / Glen Campbell comparisons probably pointed me in the wrong direction from the get-go; Bruce was never going to match those legendary songs / vocals. Instead, Western Stars is a tip of the hat to western ideals: Movies like The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance and Lonely Are The Brave; TV series like the half-remembered Stoney Burke and Wide Country, mixed with a bit of Sam Shepard , John Ford, Howard Hawks -- and a whole lot of Bruce Springsteen. An album about mortality that, in its own quiet way, will rank right up there with Bob Dylan's Time Out Of Mind on my list of great statements from the greatest artists. Five Stars, belatedly ...

title: The roots run deep within Fairport Convention's Dylan covers set
text: Love this one, may turn out to be my favorite Dylan covers set.  Also love the cover art; takes me back in memory to the old Columbia Records LP artwork.  This one's a keeper, for sure.

title: A pair of sadly underrated late-career Rascals albums
text: By the time these two excellent albums were originally released (1969/1971),  the Rascals had fallen out of favor with their record label (Atlantic) as the label's management had fallen in love with Crosby, Stills, Nash (& Young) and were riding the FM airwaves with Blind Faith, Iron Butterfly, etc.  And therefore 1969's "See" got little in the way of promotion despite including three hit singles in the title track, Carry Me Back, and Hold On.  The album also features the band's killer cover of Temptation's 'Bout to Get Me, which stands as one of the great lost shoulda/coulda/woulda been smash hits of 1969/70.  "Search and Nearness" (1971) is very nearly its match in quality, but Atlantic let it die on the vine with no promotion at all, cutting out the album barely a month into its release.  Why?  Because the Rascals had already basically imploded (the loss of both Eddie Brigati and Gene Cornish), and the Felix Cavaliere and Dino Danelli-led version of the band had already moved on to Columbia Records (the reconstituted group's landmark "Peaceful World" double-album came out within weeks of "Search & Nearness").  Regardless, it's a very good record that features three great but sadly forgotten singles (I Believe, Glory Glory, Right On), Dino Danelli's emergence as songwriter/composer  (Fortunes, Nama), a Gene Cornish country-rock nugget sung by Eddie (You Don't Know), Felix Cavaliere's terrific soul-pop (Ready for Love, Thank You Baby, Almost Home), and Brigati's soul-stirring vocal workout on the oft-recorded Memphis soul smash The Letter, slowed-down, soaring, and almost unrecognizable from the 1967 Box Tops hit version.  After five years of delivering the musical goods, the Rascals, their fans, and both these albums deserved a kinder farewell from Atlantic.  Highly recommended; check 'em out.

title: So long, Van the Man, it's been a great run but now it's over
text: Since the release of 2016's Keep Me Singing (the most recent, and perhaps last, excellent Van Morrison album by the way) Van the Man has off-loaded four consecutive (two in 2017, two in 2018) less-than-inspired sets of mostly covers, with a few Morrison originals thrown (carelessly, I'd have to say) into the mix.  Well, after a five-decade run of something bordering on VM hero-worship, I'm finally done.  The Prophet Speaks is the latest covers set (plus six Van compositions), and it's simply one too many (at the very least).  It's definitely the one that has finally ended my blind faith in this once great artist, as I'll never again buy one of his new releases without benefit of hearing it first.  Guess I'll just have to hard-nose the highway, yes?

title: Where have you gone, Bobbie Gentry?
text: Docked one star for not including Okolona River Bottom Band; still, mind-blowingly great.  She had it all: the voice, the looks, the moves, the talent.  She was the female Elvis who could write her own songs.  Incredibly beautiful and unbelievably talented, the sultry Ms. Gentry's career should have been huge & much longer-lasting.  That she appears to have simply walked away from it all (after just about a decade, or so) is a mystery that'll likely never be solved -- unless and until she decides to divulge her secrets.  Here's hoping that she's happy and healthy and enjoying her anonymous life, with no regrets.  Personally, I'd just like to thank her for that decade of musical wonder ...

title: The SHF Band deserved a better fate
text: For those of us who were around back in the day when these albums were originally released (separately), the critical knock was that the SHF Band was a pre-fab super-group put together by Asylum's David Geffen.  All these decades later I say, so what & who cares?  The music is the thing, and album number one (tracks one through ten here), in particular,  really had it going on.  From Richie Furay's delightfully energetic (and very Poco-like) opener (Fallin' in Love), to J.D. Souther's sterling Border Town, and Chris Hillman's (fresh from his Stephen Stills collaboration in Manassas) memorable Safe at Home, the debut album drew airplay and sales (it went top twenty & gold) despite a critical drubbing.  Trouble in Paradise, their second album (tracks 11 through 19) took an even tougher critical beating and failed to reach the modest success of the debut.  All the bad press blunted fan interest, killed radio support and sales, and eventually caught up with the band -- which broke up soon after.  Truth be told, Trouble in Paradise deserved a better fate; it's every bit as good as the debut album, even if it lacks a Fallin' in Love-like hit single.  Still, it's filled to the brim with fine singing and playing, and very good to excellent material: the musical trifecta of Mexico, Prisoner in Disguise, and the great title track alone make it worth the price of admission.  The new Friday Music two-on-one disc release serves to prove the critics of the day wrong -- these 1974-75 LPs were equally satisfying and of a piece all along.  Highly recommended.

title: The Smithereens' heartfelt farewell comp to brother Pat DiNizio
text: I love great artists doing covers of their musical heroes' ( and influences) classic material, and no one does it better than the Smithereens.  Twenty-two tracks of pure cover song nirvana, staying true to the originals while imbuing them all with that special Smithereens energy and spirit.  Beatles (group and solo), Beach Boys, the Who, Bruce Springsteen, Frank & Nancy Sinatra, Buddy Holly, Sam the Sham, and on & on.  Great listening and great fun, and it's all dedicated to the memory of the late, great Pat DiNizio.  Thanks to the Smithereens for putting this terrific compilation together for all of us to rock out to, remember, and enjoy.

title: The Jayhawks revisit Gary Louris's Back Roads and make them their own
text: While these songs, in the main, had been written by Gary Louris for/with other artists, make no mistake about it, this is definitely a Jayhawks album.  And a very good one at that.  The material feels brand new, not at all recycled, and the tracks hang together seamlessly with the certain easy grace that is the hallmark of the Jayhawks best efforts.  Come Cryin' to Me, Gonna Be a Darkness, and El Dorado have already emerged as personal favorites.  Glad to have added it to my collection.  Highly recommended.

title: Mr. Simon picked the right time to retire
text: Paul Simon revisiting deep cuts from his solo career, and in not particularly exciting, nor interesting arrangements.
