He simply sounds tired, bordering on weary, and the '70s lounge act musical accompaniment does nothing to perk up his weak vocals.  I guess I'm glad to have it to complete my collection, but it's likely to be a dust-collector -- I'll stick to the originals, thank you.  His recently announced retirement suddenly seems like a very good idea from a very wise man.  Thanks for the memories, Mr. Simon, and for all the great music you gave us through the years.

title: Jackie's Stone Cold Soul brings her Capitol Records career to light
text: I remember buying Jackie DeShannon's Songs LP back in 1973.  I got it on the cheap from the cut-out bins at the old WoolCo department store.  Cut-out or not, the album was a revelation:  A well-chosen mix of originals and covers, it was (to these ears) the best album by a female artist since Carole King's masterwork, Tapestry.  Here, the entire Songs album is combined with her other Capitol recordings (including her incredible Chips Moman-produced American Recording Studios Memphis tracks, one-off singles, and previously unreleased tracks) to give a wider, sharper, and deeper Technicolor view of her Capitol career.  And it's a beauty.  Recommended without hesitation to anyone who loves the '70s female singer-songwriter era, great Memphis music magic (think Dusty Springfield, Elvis in Memphis), or just great music.

title: When Jackie walks in the room, she's not just passing through
text: Great.  Jackie hasn't lost her touch.  Terrific low-key performances of some of her best-known material.  But at only eleven tracks and a playing time of just under 37-minutes, it seems a bit light on the playlist; rounded out with another five or so songs ,it would've been a five-star no-brainer.  Still, considering what's here rather than what's not, you've got to be thrilled that Jackie's still in the room.  Highly recommended.

title: Great young new bands are still out there ... if you're looking
text: Great energy.  Great material.  Great singing and playing.  And it's all captured live-in-concert at the legendary Ryman Auditorium.  Wild Feathers brings to mind the music of such past masters as The Band, Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers, and the Eagles; but the group's influences are all blended into its own unique and magical musical gumbo.  The live atmosphere only serves to enhance their terrific material, while also showcasing each member's vocal and instrumental performance skills.  This two-disc set is one hot slice of live Americana.  Highly recommended.

title: From 1968, the Steve Miller Band's great Sailor
text: Contains the Steve Miller Band's most beautiful ballad ever (the exquisite Dear Mary), as well as one of Steve's early signature songs (the rocking, sardonic Living in the USA). There's also portent of the future in the band's cover of Johnny Guitar Watson's Gangster of Love.  Not to mention the fact that with Boz Scaggs and Tim Davis all over the record, this may just have been the strongest ever SMB line-up.  As far as fifty-year-old albums go, this one's well worth checking out.

title: Christie's Yellow River: Like the welcome return of a long lost friend
text: The return of a lost classic; it's like hearing from an old friend you thought you'd lost forever.  Yellow River was one of those records that got me through some very tough times in the era after I'd been drafted into the army back in the early '70s.  Definitely helped me through basic training and AIT, not to mention the move from Jersey to Georgia for Advanced AIT. That song alone is worth the price of admission, but the rest are mostly very good to excellent, and are all well-performed both musically and vocally.  Welcome back to Yellow River, yeah!

title: The Don Nix masterpiece: Living By The Days
text: Owned this on LP way on way back when, back when Don Nix and I were both young men whose futures were in front of them.  I lost it somewhere along the way, probably during one of my many apartment moves of the '70s.  The album was a personal favorite back then, and I'm absolutely thrilled to have the CD version back in my collection.  Given a proper chance, the album (released on the cusp of the '70s Southern Rock breakthrough) should have been huge; that it was not has only enhanced its reputation to near-legendary status.  It has held up incredibly well, and it plays front-to-back, track one (The Shape I'm In) through track nine (My Train's Done Come and Gone) as of a piece -- the way a great early '70s album should.  Highly recommended.

title: J C Fogerty strutting his musical stuff on Deja Vu All Over Again
text: I remember picking this up on its day of release, way on way back when (2004, maybe?).  It was on display among the new CD releases at the Harmony Hut record store (remember them?), and although I hadn't heard a single track and never even knew it was coming out, I bought it simply because it was the great John C Fogerty's new release.  The title track was an instant classic and has remained a personal favorite down through the years ever since; She's Got Baggage will ring true to anyone who has been through a few relationships over time; I Will Walk With You is tender and sweet without ever seeming cloying; Honey Do is the middle-aged guy's theme song, and In the Garden is the near-perfect album closer.  Ten tracks in all and it seems to end too soon -- a surefire sign of a very good record.  Asked why he never did an encore, Elvis is supposed to have said, "always leave 'em wanting more."  The same could be said of John Fogerty's Deja Vu All Over Again.  It's a good 'un!

title: Fogerty's most dated solo album
text: The follow-up to his big-time return, the number one LP Centerfield, expectations were especially high for Eye of the Zombie.  I guess you could say it was almost bound to disappoint, coming out in the shadow of Centerfield's tremendous critical and commercial success.  Needless to say, it did indeed disappoint in every way possible.  The synth-drenched production and session pro backing musicians were decidedly non-Fogerty, and since the album credits read  "arranged and produced by John Fogerty," well, where was the blame to go?  Fogerty re-recorded "Change in the Weather" to much greater acclaim and effect on his second Blue Ridge Rangers record (Rides Again), and I have to wonder if he hasn't been tempted to re-do this entire record.  There are very good to excellent songs throughout the album, buried alive in bad '80s productions and arrangements, but they could all be revived to a second-wind life with the kind of care and dedication Mister Fogerty  lavished on the "... Weather" remake.  Blue Ridge Rangers' Eye of the Zombie, anyone?  Heck, I'd buy it.

title: When is a Dylan Bootleg Series release not a Bootleg Series release?
text: A lifelong Bob Dylan fan (like yours truly) will remember the days of genuine bootlegs: Cheesy packages, no information labels, absolutely terrible to moderately passible sound quality, etc.  For them (us), Dylan's Sony/Columbia Bootleg Series of the last quarter-century-plus has been manna from the vaults.  "Bob Dylan Live, 1962-1966" is not part of the Bootleg Series, and I'm guessing the subtitle (Rare Performances From The Copyright Collections) is meant to explain why.  Previously released or no, the set flows along in mostly chronological order from solo Bob to folk-rocker Dylan, charting both his steady artistic maturation and his leaps-and-bounds growth as a live performer.  Me?  I'm especially fond of disc two, which zeroes in on his switch from child of Woody Guthrie folkie to fully in-charge leader of a great rock 'n' roll band.  The packaging is nice enough, if not up to Bootleg Series standards, with plenty of rare photos, recording site info, and musician credits in the accompanying booklet.  The sound quality varies a bit, but it's mostly very good to excellent.  And there's no arguing with the playlists; I mean, really, this is Bob Dylan -- peaking in performance -- in his early career prime.  Highly recommended.

title: Aerosmith's Gold takes nephew back to his golden years
text: Purchased as part of a birthday gift for my nephew, who absolutely loved this two-disc compilation covering mostly the band's Geffen Records career.  He says the sound quality is very good overall, but the liner notes seem kind of thin.  Still, it takes him back to his "younger days" (he's all of 28!), and he's enjoying both the music and the memories as he drives around town rocking out to his era's Aerosmith.  All in all, a well-intentioned gift; graciously accepted and enjoyed.

title: Live at the Troubadour: The peak of a well-lived life & career
text: A truly magical evening, captured live for posterity; the absolute peak of a wonderful life & career. If you've ever had in interest in the music of Mike Nesmith, or country-rock, over the past half-century, this is a disc that must find its way into your collection.  It is so good that it just may restore your sense of wonder; I know it did mine. Highly recommended.  Thanks, Papa Nez, I offer you my own Loose Salute!

title: The late, great Jesse Ed Davis made a joyful noise
text: I love this collection!  Jesse Ed Davis was one of the premier session guitarists of his generation, his name cropping up in the liner notes of the superstar rockers of the era.  His work with George Harrison springs immediately to mind (he actually recorded & released George's "Sue Me, Sue You Blues" (included here) before the ex-Beatle).  How I missed out on his Atlantic/Atco solo releases back in the day I'll never know; definitely my loss then, my pleasant surprise now.  Among those covered in addition to Harrison: Van Morrison (Crazy Love), Leon Russell (Alcatraz), Merle Haggard (White Line Fever), Levon Helm & Robbie Robertson (Strawberry Wine).  One of his own compositions (included), Make a Joyful Noise, sums things up nicely.  Highly recommended.

title: Gospel Music was Elvis's truest, longest-lasting love
text: As a kid growing up on the East Coast, there was an ad campaign I was exposed to for years:  "You don't have to be Jewish to love Levy's Rye Bread" was the catch-phrase seared into my then-young brain.  And it was so true; it is also applicable to other aspects of life, as well.  Which is the long way around to saying you don't have to be Christian to love Elvis Presley singing gospel music; I actually think he'd have had a happier life if he'd achieved his earlier dream of becoming a member of a gospel quartet.  He's at his most honest and sincere when singing this music, and it's no accident that his three Grammy Award wins were for gospel performances.  Where No One Stands Alone is that rarity -- a collection featuring new backing (music and vocals) and a number of alternate Elvis vocals -- a posthumous Elvis release that's every bit as powerful and moving as just about any recording officially released in his all-too-brief lifetime.  Highly recommended to anyone who loves Elvis, Gospel, or just great music.  Can I get an "Amen," somebody?

title: Little Steven and The Disciples of Soul will restore your faith in Rock 'n' Soul
text: One of the last of the true believers, and man-oh-man, Little Steven and his mighty Disciples of Soul are out to restore your faith in Rock 'n' Soul, too.  And if this amazing three-disc live revival doesn't do the trick, well, you're just beyond the saving.  I absolutely love this set and I recommend it without hesitation.  And by the way, Steven, thanks for all you did to bring the Rascals' Once Upon A Dream to the stage -- it was something I never thought I'd get to see again (the four original Rascals together once more, on-stage and live-in-concert) and it's a production I'll never forget.  You're some kind of miracle worker, man!

title: Steve Miller is no joker, but he plays The Joker in concert
text: The Steve Miller Band plays The Joker Live in Concert, but no-one's telling when or where in the liner notes. It plays like a collection of across-a-tour live tracks, rather than a recording of an original full show.  No matter.  It is indeed The Joker LP, in full and in order, and man, it still rocks, as does the band.  I've had a whole new interest in, and a renewed respect for, Steve Miller ever since he pulled back the curtain on the Rock 'n Roll Hall of Fame a couple years back, and showed up  its powers-that-be for the ego-driven showbiz phonies they really are.  Keep on doing, Steve!

title: Steve Miller Band Live ... at the end of an era
text: This one marked the end of an era -- for both the Steve Miller Band and for the American Pop/Rock scene.  MTV and CDs were taking over, and road warrior rock bands like Steve Miller's were reaching the end of their shelf-life.  I bought this LP within weeks of its original release -- I was still a proud CD holdout -- having seen and been impressed by the group that summer live-in-concert at the Garden State Arts Center (now known as the PNC Bank Arts Center at Garden State -- just rolls off the tongue, right?).  And, yes, some 35 years after the fact, the CD holds up incredibly well.  The set-list is a bit on the short side, but manages to hit most of the hallmarks: early FM-Radio fodder (Living in the USA), the mass audience break-through (The Joker), the genuine AM/FM smashes (Jet Airliner, Take the Money and Run), the giant comeback (Abracadabra).  The band is consistently in the pocket, playing with a kind of telepathic musicality that comes only from years of constant road-work together.  This Edsel import sounds great, is beautifully packaged, and features incisive Joel Selvin notes.  Highly recommended!

title: Steve Miller Band's Rock Love was lost, but now it's found
text: If memory serves, Steve Miller himself hated this LP to the point he refused to allow a compact disc release.  He was recuperating from a serious accident at the time of its release and is said to have had little to do with its actual production.  Still, it has long been a personal favorite of mine (still have the original LP version, though it's a bit furry around the edges), and I'm thrilled to finally have it in my CD collection.  It's a half-live, half-studio set, with almost all of it running on a steady blues power.  Its production and arrangements are '70s throwbacks, sure, but it's also filled to the brim with heart, soul, and a certain innocence that remains incredibly attractive and appealing.  Thanks for this one, Steve, you really shouldn't take it so hard.

title: Graham Nash at his very best ... over the years
text: Having been utterly disappointed with his last critically acclaimed all-new release (the very self-absorbed This Path Tonight), I'm happy to say that I've warmed considerably to this new compilation disc.  Nash is clearly the most commercially-oriented songwriter among the CSN (& sometimes Y) mother-ship, and this collection features just about all the post-Hollies Nash hits that fit.  The second disc is something of an eye/ear-opener, as it is comprised of stripped-down demo versions of the well-known songs on disc one -- great fun to listen to, just not too frequently.  Whereas the first disc's beautifully produced hit tracks will get plenty of play, both at home and in the car stereo (if you still have one!).  Highly recommended.

title: The Moody Blues celebrate 50 years of Days of Future Passed
text: The audio companion to the DVD/BluRay release.  Disc One is the opening nine-song hits set (which is killer); Disc Two is the Days of Future Passed main event, along with the two-song encore (Question, Ride My See-Saw).  It's all beautifully performed by the band, the orchestra, and the backing vocalists and musicians.  If you went to one (or more) of the 50th anniversary celebration shows, it's a great keepsake.  If you're a long-time (or even a casual) fan of the band, it's likely you're going to love it.  Highly recommended.

title: Stick with Brian's brilliantly executed originals with the Wrecking Crew
text: Disappointing.  Like patchwork on the original Brian Wilson productions with the Wrecking Crew -- where the Crew was artistically pure and creatively unencumbered. So, why mess around with the perfection of Brian's original productions?  The concept worked to better effect with the Elvis releases (IMHO), at least on the lesser known deep cuts (There's Always Me, anyone?).  As a Beach Boys completest, I'm glad to add this one to my collection; however, it's unlikely to get very many spins.

title: This was the Youngbloods, back when we were youngbloods ourselves
text: Bought this one on whim, or actually on a wave of nostalgia, shortly after hearing that a dear old friend -- who had given me the original double-album as a 22nd birthday gift, back when we were youngbloods so many years ago -- had recently lost his battle with cancer.  As things turned out though, it was like getting the gift a second time; the music the Youngbloods made while on RCA in the '60s has held up incredibly well.  Get Together was the band's big hit single (in 1969, the second time around) and it's the track they'll always be remembered for, but this tasty 1972  retrospective presents a much wider overview of the group's three album RCA tenure.  Tracks like Beautiful, Sunlight, Quicksand, and Darkness, Darkness would have been high-water marks for any band, and their covers of C.C. Rider, Too Much Monkey Business, and the previously mentioned Get Together, all sound as fresh today as they did so many years ago.  RIP, Brother Dave, thanks for almost five decades of music, memories, and lasting friendship.

title: Recycled Fogerty: Blue Moon Swamp one more time
text: Different front cover art, but otherwise this now BMG-distributed John Fogerty opus is the same as the 2004 Geffen reissue.  Other than the cover, and personally I prefer the original, there are no upgrades: the sound hasn't been altered, and the play-list remains exactly the same, right down to the two bonus tracks included (Just Pickin' and Endless Sleep).  Generally well-received by music critics and moderately successful commercially (made the Top Forty, eventually certified Gold by the RIAA), Blue Moon Swamp is not nearly as good as its reputation (IMHO), and it's not a patch -- in quality or in sales -- on Centerfield. If, like me, you already have the original release and/or the Geffen reissue, this will likely come across as just another recycled Fogerty money-grab. It's as if he's become the "Mister Greed" of Centerfield notoriety.  Kind of sad, yes?

title: The solid distilled version of James Taylor (Live)
text: Culled from his earlier 2-disc "(Live)" set, "(Best Live)" is a stripped-down, no-frills Greatest Hits Live set dominated by performances of tunes from his Warner Brothers catalog (nine of the 12 tracks included here).  The three CBS additions are all noteworthy, Handy Man, Your Smiling Face, and the terrific Shed a Little Light, and the set ends on a high note with Taylor's lovely anthem, Shower the People.  The sound and packaging are very good indeed, with appropriate tour photos, musician & songwriting credits, and liner notes by former JT producer Peter Asher.  A great gift for the casual fan, or one to yourself for your next road trip.  Highly recommended.

title: A glorious afternoon in the Garden with the King
text: The better of the two MSG Elvis live-in-concert releases (IMHO), and available at a bargain price to boot!  The original 1972 live album was rush-released (within 10 days of the event) and it kind of showed -- the audio mix was no-where near the quality of his two previous live in Las Vegas records (1969 and 1970), and even the cover was recycled from the sadly cancelled half-live/half-studio Standing Room Only LP.  An Afternoon in the Garden, however, is beautifully packaged with appropriate to the event photos, excellent notes by Colin Escott, and Elvis in all his ragin' in the early '70s glory. The set-list is a bit looser and so is Elvis, especially as he takes on the rarely performed blues classic "Reconsider, Baby," originally recorded for his 1960 Elvis Is Back LP.  If you're wondering what all the fuss was about before the slide began, this is the one you want to check out. It's highly unlikely that you'll be disappointed.

title: Johnny Rivers' rockin' little contemporary christian excursion
text: A rockin' little contemporary Christian collection that has held up better than anyone might've expected.  Rivers contributes the very good Nowhere Else to Go and takes a songwriting credit for the arrangement on the classic Uncloudy Day.  Sixties Pop and R&B hits like Sam Cooke's A Change Is Gonna Come, the Four Tops' Reach Out, I'll Be There, and Ben E. King's Stand By Me are all given a spiritual shift simply by changing a pronoun or two, and to mostly great effect.  The collection closes on a grace note with a beautiful cover of Dion's Golden Sun, Silver Moon. The sound and packaging are up to BGO's usual high standards, and John O'Regan's liner notes are both interesting and informative.  A most welcome addition to my Johnny Rivers collection.

title: Carole King's most rocking live disc
text: The great songwriter-singer Carole King's most rocking live disc.  Supported by an impressively tight and terrific band, Ms. King gets out from behind the keyboards and takes on the role of cheerleading front person -- and she makes the most of it.  The opener, Hard Rock Café, sets the tone, and in due course she and her band rock out on some of her best-known tunes (Up on the Roof, Smackwater Jack, Jazzman, I Feel the Earth Move), alongside quieter arrangements on her beloved ballads (So Far Away, Beautiful, Will You Love Me Tomorrow, You've Got a Friend).  Docked one star for the rather thin packaging (no photos other than the front cover shot, no musician credits, no liner notes, etc.).

title: Fogerty's latest Centerfield money-grab
text: The material is still mostly great but it's also the same material, including the two bonus tracks (singles b-sides "My Toot Toot," "I Confess").  It basically mimics the 2010 Geffen 25th Anniversary edition, now distributed by BMG with no upgrades in sound or graphics.  A rather disappointing money-grab if you already own it (like yours truly).

title: Sacred Fire just may be Santana's hottest live disc
text: Owned and loved this live-in-concert disc back in the day, when it first came out.  Lost it once in a move from one apartment or another; lost it a second time when I loaned it out and it never came back. Someone in my circle of friends besides me must've also loved it!  Sacred Fire is a perfect title:This is an incredibly exciting, heart-felt, joyous concert experience, with Carlos & Company at the top of their game.  It's a classic example of the in-concert marriage of heart, soul, and spirit between artist and audience. Carlos's guitar has never sounded sweeter (or hotter), while his namesake band is absolutely on fire throughout.  Santana's best live disc (IMHO), and one of my all-time favorite live albums by anyone, anytime  (obviously, right?).  So glad to have it back in my collection.

title: Glenn Frey's very best could've been better
text: The stand-alone single-disc version is very good, but it could've been better.  No argument with what's included, since it contains most of the late Eagle's best known solo career hits. But there are a number of problems, regardless.  First of all, the missing-in-action: I Found Somebody (Glenn's first solo hit), All Those Lies (the third single from No Fun Aloud), True Love (the biggest hit single from Soul Searchin'), and Livin' Right (a 1989 #22 Adult Contemporary Radio airplay hit from Soul Searchin').  Secondarily, the rather random track order.  Hits collections always work better (to my ears, anyway) when their play-lists are presented in chronological order, so that the listener can pick up on the performer's artistic growth and musical changes. Thirdly, the sloppy editing of the compilation-ending live medley, Lyin' Eyes/Take It Easy, which fails to edit out Glenn's acoustic guitar and spoken introduction of the next performance -- which never comes (River of Dreams).  The studio version of the song is included earlier on the disc; so really, they could've either done a better edit at the medley's fade, or moved the studio River of Dreams to the end slot to close the disc.  Still, a lot of great music, and a lot of great memories included here.  Thanks, Glenn, RIP.

title: Eric Andersen: An Essential American Singer-Songwriter
text: If you're only going to have one Eric Andersen set in your collection, this is the one you'll want to get.  An absolutely sterling addition to the 2-CD "The Essential ..." series, this compilation attempts to do the impossible -- to highlight Andersen's multi-label 50-year career over the course of two discs -- and it very nearly succeeds.  Appropriately, Disc One opens with Everything Ain't Been Said and Dusty Box Car Wall from his Vanguard Records debut, then follows through to his Columbia Records treasures (Blue River and Stages: The Lost Album), featuring Andersen favorites like Is It Really Love at All, Blue River, Pearl's Goodtime Blues (for Janis Joplin), Time Run Like a Freight Train, and Woman, She Was Gentle.  Among the guests:  Joni Mitchell, Joan Baez, Dan Fogelberg, Leon Russell, and the great Debbie Green-Andersen.  Disc Two starts with highlights from Andersen's Arista Records tenure, including '70s live versions of Thirsty Boots and Violets of Dawn, Blues Keep Fallin' Like the Rain, and Close the Door Lightly When You Go, before turning to fine Andersen recordings of the more recent past like Belgian Bar, Trouble in Paris, and You Can't Relive the Past.  The compilation ends on a nostalgic note with a duet between Andersen and his late friend and folk-cohort Phil Ochs on Plains of Nebrasky-O.  One two-CD set, no matter how well programmed, simply isn't enough to cover Eric Andersen's legendary career in the kind of depth he deserves, but The Essential Eric Andersen is likely about as close as we're ever going to get.  Highly recommended.

title: Be True To You: Eric Andersen's '70s masterwork
text: Let's get this out of the way from the top: I've always preferred Arista's Be True To You to Sony's Stages: The Lost Album. Even knowing the story of how the master tapes to his follow-up to the great Blue River had somehow been lost in Columbia's vaults back in the day, and he had to re-start from scratch to deliver his Arista debut, Be True To You is the better album (in my opinion).  Great production, smoother sequencing, Andersen's sensitive vocal approach, and his sheer determination to see the project through, combine to elevate Be True To You to classic status.  Its follow-up (Sweet Surprise) isn't nearly as strong; it's a lighter, breezier affair with a mid-'70s country-rock feel.  Following the classic Be True To You playlist on this BGO two-on-one disc, Sweet Surprise plays like nine enjoyable bonus tracks.  Highly recommended.

title: Above the Clouds is a fine tribute to Glenn Frey's solo career
text: Love the Strange Weather/Live in Dublin DVD, a version of which I previously owned on VHS; it's great to finally have a clean, crisp copy of the eye/ear-opening Longbranch/Pennywhistle album in my collection; the Disc One & Two hits and deep cuts have never sounded better.  Two minor quibbles: Why is True Love placed at the end of the second disc, rather than being included on the first (among the hits); and why -- as with every other previous Glenn Frey compilation -- is Glenn's first solo hit, I Found Somebody, completely ignored?  Chronological order, according to release, would've been nice, too.  But what's here is much more important than what's not, and all things being equal, Above the Clouds is a fine tribute to the talents and solo career of the late, great Eagle.  RIP, Glenn ...

title: You're driving me crazy with all the cover collections, Van
text: Van the Man's third collection of covers (jazz and R&B classics, mixed with re-makes of some of his own) in a mind-spinning span of about 12 or 13 months is hands-down, far and away, the best of the bunch.  He sounds engaged if not totally committed, and more importantly, he actually appears to be enjoying himself.  Perhaps working with the great Joey DeFrancesco just brought out the fun in him, who knows.  Classic tunes, first-rate  musicianship, on-the-fly arrangements with space for the vocals to find their groove, You're Driving Me Crazy represents a marked improvement over Van's last release (the lifeless Versatile).  All that being said, an album of all-new Van Morrison material is long overdue and would be most welcome next go 'round, yes?  Three and one-half stars from me.

title: Finally, Elvis is shown the respect he's always deserved
text: I am loving everything about this two-part HBO documentary special, not least of which its wonderful soundtrack.  As a lifelong Elvis fan, I've suffered through RCA's terrible mishandling of his recorded output (pre-Ernst J.), 'Colonel' Tom Parker's "show me the money and the boy's yours" management style/attitude, slapdash money grabs (RCA Camden budget releases, anyone?), salacious so-called tell-all bios, and an unbelievably callous and cruel critical backlash throughout his career (both alive and post-death).  And now (finally!), his story is retold with a new degree of empathy and respect for Elvis the artist/musician.  And all it took was his untimely death at 42, plus the ensuing 40 years. Here's hoping that he's looking down from some better place, wearing that lopsided grin of his, and singing along with every soulful note of "If I Can Dream."  He's earned every bit of this newfound respect, and he earned the right to enjoy it decades ago.  RIP, EP, long may you dream ...

title: Celebrating the circle of musical life with the NGDB
text: The absolute best of the three 50th anniversary NGDB releases, this live-in-concert two-disc cd/dvd set was recorded & filmed at the legendary Ryman Auditorium in Nashville.  How appropriate, yes?  When the band was made up of a group of young long-haired, furry-faced hippie-types all those years ago, they came to Nashville to celebrate and bring together (at that time a seemingly impossible task) the old guard & the new.  A music miracle of sorts, it all worked out wonderfully well; the result being the wildly successful (artistically, critically, commercially) and still much-revered classic, "Will The Circle Be Unbroken?"  The band bridged the generation gap, opened the doors for others to follow, and staked its reputation on that tremendous break-through. Now, four decades and two "Circle" sequels on, they're the established elder statesmen and they're back at the Ryman to celebrate the incredible NGDB journey.  And what a celebration it is!  Guests from along their musical history include former member Jimmy Ibbotson (Ibby's back!), Jackson Browne, Jerry Jeff Walker, Rodney Crowell, John Prine, Alison Krauss, Vince Gill, among many others.  But it's the Dirt Band's show and, as always, they deliver the musical goods.  Highly recommended.

title: NGDB's Anthology: Great collection, too many defective tracks
text: Great collection, but whatever happened to a little thing called "quality control?"  Both discs are packed to the brim (21 tracks on disc one, 18 on disc two), but each CD has three songs w/ dead zones, or what we would've called skips back in the day when the LP ruled.  And this is not a one-off situation; I purchased three (3) copies of NGDB Anthology, one for myself and two as gifts -- all three sets "skip" in the same places.  Disc One: Tracks 14 (Honky Tonkin'), 20 (Mother Earth), and 21 (Bowlegs); Disc Two: Tracks 9 (You Ain't Goin' Nowhere), 17 (Midnight at Woody Creek), and 18 (The Resurrection).  The accompanying CD booklet is lovely and informative; Holly Gleason strikes just the right tone in her notes; the playlists are impeccable on both discs.  But six defective tracks out of a total of 39?  Inexcusible!  Three stars for content & packaging; without the defects it would've been a no-brainer 5-star review.

title: Rusty Young's shining moment
text: For the better part of a half-century, through all kinds of personnel changes and commercial ups-and-downs, Rusty's been the one who has kept Poco going, both in the studio and out on the road pickin', singin' and a-grinnin'.  Waitin' for the Sun is the culmination of his musician's life and artistic dedication; it's also the album long-time Poco fans (Poconuts) always knew he had in him.  The title track and the finale (Gonna Let the Rain) are epic compositions that work on every level (emotional, lyrical, musical, storytelling).  Former Poco band-mates make memorable guest appearances: Richie Furay and Timothy B. Schmit deliver haunting harmony vocals on the touching shuffle, My Friend, while Jimmy Messina (guitar) and George Grantham (percussion) help to funk-up Honey Bee. Current Poco member Jack Sundrud (bass, vocals) is all over the record, in addition to co-producing with Rusty.  Had there not been a falling-out with Paul Cotton, this just may have been a Poco album. As such, it would have been their best in decades.  But this is Rusty Young's shining moment, and he's earned it.

title: Crosby's esoteric musical Lighthouse
text: Musically adventurous and esoteric, lyrically obtuse or in-your-face, tackling often politically-charged topics, Lighthouse seems to be aimed at the diehards, rather than casual Crosby fans. Still, with it's beautiful vocals and engaging musical accompaniment, it's strong enough to continue his impressive stretch of solid late career solo albums.  Whether diehard or casual fan, regardless, Crosby proves once again he doesn't necessarily need Stills, Nash, or Young to make interesting music.

title: Crosby's winning streak continues with Sky Trails
text: The late career artistic winning streak that began with 2014's Croz continues with Sky Trails. This just may be Crosby's strongest and most accessible solo disc since who knows when, perhaps all the way back to his 1971 debut (If I Could Only Remember My Name).  His playing is still absolutely unique, and his vocals continue to defy the passage of time.  For a guy who, for the longest time, was the next best bet to be joining Jim, Janis & Jimi, Crosby remains a vertical man, and a kind of musical miracle.  And we're all the better for it.

title: Solo Croz, it's like he's never been away
text: His first new solo disc since who knows when (Thousand Roads, maybe?), Croz comes as a most pleasant surprise.  With tremendous musical support, most notably from producer/co-writer/keyboardist/vocalist James Raymond (his extremely talented son, as we're all aware by now), Crosby's usual outside-the-box song-craft, and his age-defying vocals -- he still sings like a hipster choirboy -- this record is an absolute joy, start to finish.  Highly recommended.

title: Stills & Collins' Everybody Knows it's a good 'un
text: Once upon a long time ago, this superstar duets effort would likely have arrived as a highly anticipated, major label-supported,  FM radio-ready chartbusting smash hit.  I mean it's the artistic powerhouse behind CSN (&Y) and the folk scene diva who brought Joni Mitchell to the masses (via her hit cover of Both Sides Now), not to forget the pair's legendary love story as celebrated in CSN's Suite: Judy Blue Eyes.  One can only imagine the 1968 impact and possibilities!  Fifty years on, it's a bit of a different story on the anticipation front: There's no real record industry left, nor any hint of the free-form FM radio format that would've welcomed such a release.  And we're all the poorer for it.  "Everybody Knows" is a far better record than any of us had a right to expect, or even hope for.  Stills is in good voice and is as nimble-fingered as ever on guitar; Ms. Collins' vocals remain as lovely, pure and stirring as they ever were.  The musical support is tasty and in the pocket, and the choice of material, while hardly bold, is both strong and appropriate.  Highlights include the Wilburys' classic Handle With Care, Leonard Cohen's oft-covered Everybody Knows, and Stills' own Questions.  It's a good 'un!

title: Denny Doherty's lost classic
text: I love this record!  I've been playing it regularly since it arrived and I keep wondering how the heck I missed it upon its original release all those years ago.  Having been a huge fan of the Mamas & the Papas, I remember being captivated by John Phillips' "John, The Wolf King of L.A." debut (especially the Mississippi single), but somehow Denny's 1971 solo debut, "Watcha Gonna Do," slipped by unnoticed.  My loss. This is a great ahead-of-the-curve debut, anticipating the upcoming country-rock boom that would dominate the mid- to late- Seventies.  The wonderfully catchy original title track (Whatcha Gonna Do) is a shoulda-coulda-woulda been hit that sadly never gained traction at radio; his remake of Got A Feelin' is stunningly effective, and the original closing Beatles medley (Here Comes the Sun/Two of Us/Give Peace a Chance) is an absolute charmer. Six bonus tracks, including a pair by then unknowns Donald Fagen & Walter Becker (Sail the Waterway, Giles of the River), make this reissue all the more interesting and worthy of attention.

title: Bidin' My Time represents a Hillman high watermark
text: A wonderful Chris Hillman album and a poignant farewell for late, great Byrds-loving producer Tom Petty.  With core Desert Rose Band members on board (Herb Pederson as executive producer and singing/playing on every track; the incredible John Jorgenson playing lead guitar on 11 of the collection's 12 tracks), plus Heartbreakers Benmont Tench (piano/organ) and Steve Ferrone (drums) making contributions throughout, Bidin' My Time is a country-rocker's dream project. A very graceful Chris Hillman makes the most of it all, and if this 70-something Americana pioneer never makes another album, he goes out on a high note here.  Highly recommended.

title: Chris Hillman's first steps to a solo career
text: Chris Hillman's first two solo efforts after being a secret weapon-type player in the Byrds, the Burritos, Manassas, and the fan embraced, critic rejected singer/songwriter super-group the Souther Hillman Furay Band.  These two albums (Slippin' Away and Smooth Sailin') were proof positive that Chris was more than ready to step out front to lead his own band.  From Slippin' Away, "Step on Out" foreshadows his later country-rock success with the Desert Rose Band; "Witching Hour" does right by his association with Stephen Stills & Manassas, and "(Take Me in Your) Lifeboat" is a lively harmony-laden bit of bluegrass.  Clear Sailin' is a bit more (over?) produced but also has its share of highlights, including a terrific cover of Danny O'Keefe's "Quits," an interesting take on the old Marvin Gaye Motown hit "Ain't That Peculiar," and the lovely title track and album closer, a Chris Hillman-Rick Roberts co-write.

title: My, oh, my,  how the Mighty Van the Man has fallen
text: Once upon a long time ago, I'd have bet the mortgage that Van the Man could sing an old phone book's listings front to back and make it all seem not only interesting but moving and soulful.  Judging by "Versatile," his second release of mostly half-baked covers released in 2017, I'd have lost that bet big time.  And it breaks my heart to make that admission, having purchased, enjoyed, and often cherished every VM album since "Blowin' Your Mind" all too many decades ago.  I played "Versatile" as soon as it arrived; I could not believe what I was hearing, but I continued to play it through to the end.  Man, was I ever rattled.  I took a break, then went on to play it a second time, again, all the way through and hoping that the replay might change my mind.  It didn't.  Terrible, just terrible; I won't waste any more of my time or energies on this one.  Here's hoping Van takes his time and puts some genuine effort into his next release, whenever and whatever that may be.

title: Steve Miller Band: the Hits and Nothing but the Hits
text: This one caught me by surprise, I must say.  I've always enjoyed the Steve Miller Band, but I wouldn't consider myself anything more than a casual fan.  This two-disc set, however, is something of an eye/ear-opener; not a bad or weak track to be found, even among the handful of live versions of familiar Miller hits included.  Some 40 tracks spread across two discs (though not chronologically arranged, a disappointment), featuring such landmark Miller Band titles as Living in the USA, Space Cowboy, The Joker, Take the Money and Run, Rock 'n Me, Fly Like an Eagle, and Jet Airliner, among many, many others.  It may not be perfect, but it's close; and it's the one to get if you only want one Steve Miller compilation for your collection.

title: John Sebastian at his best from a time when the music really mattered
text: John Sebastian.  Founder/leader of the Lovin' Spoonful, forever identified with the late '60s/early '70s via tie-die & Woodstock, composer/performer of the surprise number one 1976 smash hit "Welcome Back," and one of the all-time great American songwriters.  This single-disc compilation makes for a very satisfying introduction to his five-album solo career on Reprise, and will likely lead newer listeners to seek out the original releases in full.  The 16-track set-list includes his first solo single (She's a Lady), a 1972 non-LP track (Give Us a Break), the full version of his tour-de-force on-the-road suite (The Four of Us), and perhaps his greatest, most covered solo composition (Stories We Could Tell).  The disc ends on a high note with a four-song mini-live set made up of Lovin' Spoonful classics from 1971's "Cheapo-Cheapo Productions Presents Real Live John Sebastian."

title: Glen Campbell's heartbreakingly beautiful farewell
text: A heartbreakingly beautiful farewell.  Glen's magnificent reading of the great Jimmy Webb's Adios closes the record.  How appropriate, since he and Jimmy found early success together and continued to maintain their relationship and that success through a half-century's worth of musical teamwork.  Not a weak track to be found in this collection; but then Glen always had a good ear and was as tasteful a player as he was a vocalist.  It's a rare farewell, indeed.  Safe home, Glen, thanks for all the great music.

title: Peter Cetera's ballad heavy best
text: It's about time, yes?  Peter Cetera's Warner Brothers solo hits have never been collected together in one package until now, some quarter century after his chart-run heyday.  So, despite opting out of Chicago's (his former band) long overdue 2016 Rock 'n' Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony, looks like 2017's the year to take advantage of the accompanying commercial hoopla.  Predictably ballad-heavy, this 14-track compilation still opens with One the Line, a song from Cetera's first (and most rocking) solo album, 1981's Peter Cetera, recorded during one of Chicago's deepest commercial lulls.  From there it's movie ballads (Glory of Love, After All), duets (with Amy Grant, Cher, Chaka Khan), the radio hits (One Good Woman, Restless Heart), and a handful of lesser-known singles (Big Mistake, Best of Times).  All of them well-written, beautifully sung, and impeccably produced.  If only he'd gotten in touch with his inner rocker a bit more often.

title: Lamm's Time Chill is a stone-cold keeper
text: This is a great introduction to Robert Lamm's released-on-the-quiet solo (non-Chicago) career material, 1999 onward.  His lone solo album during Chicago's Columbia Records tenure, Skinny Boy, may not have made the charts, but it certainly had a better chance to hit than his later solo works if only because of Columbia's promotional power.  Its relative failure may have led to the 25-year gap between solo discs.  Regardless, the 15-track Time Chill, A Retrospective is a stone-cold winner, featuring a half-dozen unreleased tracks, five JVE remixes, a taste of his Beckley-Lamm-Wilson side project, and more.  It would really be great if the Chicago mother-ship would pick up on his sense of musical adventure once again.

title: Fleetwood Mac, minus Stevie
text: This one plays like a solid Fleetwood Mac album (Mick Fleetwood and John McVie are all over it), minus Stevie Nicks.  Turnabout is fair play (or so they say), and this one is far superior to 2003's middling at best (and Christine McVie-less) Fleetwood Mac set, Say You Will.  If you're a fan of the  Fleetwood Mac mother-ship, Lindsay Buckingham, and/or Christine McVie, this one's definitely for you.

title: New Lovers and Old Friends 40+ years on
text: Released in the USA as New Lovers and Old Friends back in 1975 (same cover shot and track line-up), Help Me Rhonda (first time on cd!) is the latest re-master in BGO's terrific Johnny Rivers reissue series.  And while it may not be another Realization (arguably Rivers' masterwork), it is yet another solid release in a long line of fine Johnny Rivers albums.  The concept?  New Lovers (covers of then recent songs and songwriters like Christine McVie's Spare Me a Little, Ned Doheny's Postcards from Hollywood), and Old Friends (old favorites like the Four Tops' It's the Same Old Song, the Beach Boys' Help Me Rhonda, Arthur Alexander's You Better Move On) all get that familiar, comfortable Rivers' treatment.  The great Brian Wilson (along with then-wife Marilyn and the Honeys) even turns up to deliver backing vocals on the album's hit remake of his own Help Me Rhonda.  Great to have this one finally available on cd.

title: Sunshine Tomorrow, Sunshine Today
text: A treasure trove of previously unreleased tracks, outtakes, and live material, this two-disc set is a must-have for diehard longtime Brian Wilson/Beach Boys fans, myself included.  The stereo version of the Wild Honey album, which opens this compilation, is an eye- and ear-opening delight from start to finish.  The Wild Honey and Smiley Smile Sessions take the listener behind the scenes, fly-on-the-studio-wall style, to get an insider's view of how things were changing within the band in 1967.  And finally, Lei'd in Hawaii, the long talked about, never released "live" follow-up to the band's wildly successful "Beach Boys Concert" album, makes its debut.  Even some fifty years after Capitol rejected its release, Lei'd  in Hawaii makes it all worth the price of admission.  Don't even hesitate if you're a BB fan; order this one now, you won't be disappointed.

title: Big Star: shoulda coulda woulda been a '70s superstar band
text: This one I absolutely love; very possibly the best Big Star compilation, in terms of both sound and selections.  I'm loving the six single versions included (which I've never before even heard, let alone owned), and their classics remain so (Back of a Car, Thank You Friends, Ballad of El Goodo).  All in all, sixteen slices of the greatest rock 'n' roll you probably never heard on your radio.  Most likely the best little unknown (yet hugely influential) band ever.

title: The Beau Brummels' best never sounded better
text: This is an excellent compilation, covering the Singles history of one of my all-time personal favorite bands of the Sixties.  Hits all the high points (Laugh, Laugh, Just a Little, You Tell Me Why), and then some, and all in superior upgraded sound.  The Beau Brummels have never sounded better.  Unfortunately, the band isn't nearly as well-known, critically acclaimed, or appreciated as it should be; this is a great place to start.

title: The Rascals rule once more
text: One of the greatest bands of the Sixties, and definitely the best blue-eyed soul group America has ever produced, gets the mono/stereo complete singles A & B sides treatment.  Across the set's two discs and 47 tracks, we see/hear the Rascals grow from A-list cover band (Good Lovin', Slow Down, Mustang Sally), to hit-making self-produced songsmiths (You Better Run, Lonely Too Long, How Can I be Sure?), to ambitious and adventurous trend-setters (Groovin', It's Wonderful, A Beautiful Morning), and outspoken social commentators (People Got to Be Free, A Ray of Hope, See).  Ed Osborne delivers the goods in his well-observed liner notes; Mike Milchner's remastering is peerless; Claire Morales's booklet design, which includes replications of the band's Atlantic picture sleeves, is pure eye-candy for long-time fans like yours truly.  The Atlantic years were definitely the band's high-water mark, both commercially and creatively.  But the lesser Columbia singles (Jungle Walk, Love Me, Lucky Day) are also a blast to hear and appreciate, even after all these years.

title: The Jukes' seminal Epic years
text: The great first three Jukes albums, plus the band's much sought after promo only "Live at the Bottom Line," finally presented together in one terrific two-disc package. The beautifully remastered sound, the upgraded graphics, and especially Chris Morris's lively & incisive liner notes, all combine to make this one the "must have" collection for longtime fans of Southside Johnny & the Asbury Jukes.  The Epic years were seminal, with Steven  Van Zandt at the production helm and Bruce Springsteen's song-craft and musical influence very much in evidence, the band were in very good hands and they excelled.  The first and second LPs were a total blast, cut from the same rocking R&B cloth, and featuring such memorable tracks as "I Don't Want to Go Home," "The Fever," "Without Love," "Love on the Wrong Side of Town," and "This Time It's for Real."  The third and final Epic studio album, "Hearts of Stone," stands tall as the Jukes' masterpiece, as effective & affecting today as it was upon its original 1978 release.  Yeah, baby, this time it's for real.  Indeed.

title: Dave Mason: like reconnecting with a long lost friend
text: Long Lost Friend is a generous (19 tracks) & well-chosen single-disc representation of the great Dave Mason's (1973-1979) Columbia Records career.  It's a nicely designed package, featuring excellent liner notes written by William Ruhlmann.  This 1995 compilation was produced by the great Bob Irwin and mastered by Vic Anesini.  For a 22-year-old cd release, its sound has held up incredibly well.  At its current bargain price, it's just about the best single-disc Dave Mason retrospective available, although you'd have to look elsewhere for his original (pre-Columbia) Blue Thumb Records material.

title: Check out the new & improved  Delaney & Bonnie Motel
text: Their greatest album achievement, expanded, upgraded, and improved.  The previously unreleased tracks are a revelation; the sound has been vastly improved; the liner notes (featuring quotes from recent interviews) are well-written and informative, without ever going the fan-boy route.  I've got a never-ending love for this one.  Maybe you will, too.

title: 16 track compilation celebrates the artistry of the late Gerry Rafferty
text: It's a real shame that the late Gerry Rafferty's body of work is both underrated by music critics and underappreciated by the general public. Despite the over-the-top success of a pair of stone cold multi-radio format classics in "Stuck in the Middle with You" and "Baker Street," Rafferty's reputation as a musician's musician and songwriter's songwriter has for the most part failed to transfer into the mega-sales of superstar status.  Don't hold it against him.  "The Very Best of/United Artistry" (a clever bit of wordplay, based on the fact that his biggest solo years were spent on the UA label) will not right past wrongs, critically or commercially, but it stands tall as an excellent sampler, easily the best (and best sounding) single-disc Gerry  Rafferty compilation currently available.  All the hits that fit and then some, 16 tracks in all, including Stealers Wheel's "Stuck in the Middle," "Baker Street," "Right Down the Line," and "Get It Right Next Time."  Give this one a try; you won't be disappointed.

title: Greatest Radio Hits is true to its no-nonsense title
text: This is the one I buy for friends/relatives when I need to pick up a quick gift. Great music & lyrics, lively singing & playing by Hornsby, or as we call him here in New Jersey, the other Bruce.  His best loved, most well-known tunes, conveniently collected in one place, with informative notes by Gary Graff, as well as individual track-by-track breakdowns. These fifteen tracks make a superior single-disc compilation, and at a bargain price, no less!

title: 21 NGDB tracks of pickin', grinnin', & heavenly harmony
text: This is the one you want if you only want one single-disc NGDB compilation for your collection.  The sound is very good to excellent throughout; since it's a cross-label Rhino/WB affair, almost every commercial peak is present & accounted for; and since the NGDB has really always been about the playing, the singing, and the songwriting, it's a great musical ride from start to finish, 21 solid tracks of pickin', grinnin',  and heavenly harmonies.  Essentially an upgraded two-on-one disc that combines the Warner's releases "Twenty Years of Dirt" (1986) and "More Great Dirt" (1989) back-to-back in original tracking order, it covers the band's most commercially successful period.

title: A personal favorite gets even better
text: A personal favorite gets even better.  It has been expanded (w/ tracks from the same sessions) & offers improved, upgraded  sound.  Mr. Kristofferson is justifiably proud of this set, and it is very clearly the high water mark of producer Fred Mollin's storied career. These just may be the definitive versions of the works that made Kris' songwriter reputation.

title: The big '70s hits, plus a fly-on-the-wall intimacy
text: I especially love the second disc for its fly-on-the-wall intimacy; the newly sequenced material that makes up disc one has really never sounded better, in my opinion; John Jackson's lively essay (Exile On Lonely Street) is clever, insightful, and informative; and the packaging, almost always low-rent during Elvis's lifetime, is eye-catchingly first-rate.  Let's face it, back in the '60s these 16 tracks would've been an album and a pair of stand-alone singles, certainly not the pair of LPs they were in the '70s.  So, the 16-track disc one works well here because it's of-a-piece, though obviously ballad heavy, and features the hits and the should've been hits (Way Down, She Thinks I Still Care, Pledging My Love, For The Heart, Hurt, Moody Blue).  Disc two manages to dispel the prevailing image of a depressed, bored, uninvolved Elvis; this guy's in great spirits, cracking on himself and his band mates, laughing, joking, yet obviously in charge and leading the musical way.  Is this material new to FTD fans and EAP completists?  Probably not.  Regardless, this one's a keeper.

title: Barbara Fasano: Busy Working Magic
text: There are plenty of talented singers, but all too few who can somehow manage to inhabit a lyric like a method actor disappearing into a role and emerging as a totally different character.  That's quite a trick to pull off.  But that's the magic of Barbara Fasano.  She's a gifted vocalist with great taste and an unerring ear for what's right for her (from Irving Berlin, to Joni Mitchell, to Jimmy Webb), as proven here and on earlier collections such as Written in the Stars (music by Harold Arlen) and the eclectic The Girls of Summer.  Having recently seen her perform at Birdland (NYC) with her husband and musical partner Eric Comstock, I can only say that the musical magic she weaves so well on record seems even stronger in person.

title: Tallent's joyous Break Time brings along the R 'n' Roll fun
text: The great E Street Band bassist Garry W Tallent may never earn his living as a vocalist, but he proves here that he can certainly carry his weight as a songwriter.  Lots of old-school rockabilly, country, and rock 'n' roll melodies and attitude, dovetail perfectly with his sharp, witty and playful lyric approach to make one of the best Americana/roots LPs released so far this year.  And unlike his Boss's more recent work, Garry's joyful album is actually a fun listen.  If only Elvis was still with us, I'd say, "Hey E, check this sucker out, man; maybe you ought to record the whole damn thing."  Break Time is that good.

title: Singer's singer Nicolette Larson gets the classic BGO reissue treatment
text: The late, great singer's singer gets the excellent BGO reissue treatment.  Her first three Warner Bros LPs packaged together as a slip-cased two-CD set, featuring BGO's usual beautifully re-mastered sound, interesting and informative liner notes, with in-depth musician/songwriter credits, commentary, and photos.  Her stunning debut LP, "Nicolette," which kicked off with her smash hit cover of Neil Young's "Lotta Love," proved to be a tough act to follow, commercially speaking.  Artistically and creatively, however, she maintained the same high watermark throughout her Warner Bros years, and beyond.  Both "In the Nick of Time"  (no relation whatsoever to Bonnie Raitt's Grammy-sweeping Capitol Records comeback) and "Radioland" succeed in keeping pace with the high standards set by her eponymous debut, even if neither set hit the same commercial peaks as "Nicolette."  Placed (and played) side-by-side in this two-disc set, however, their quality is seamless, and the material of a piece.  Highly recommended to anyone who loves great singing and great playing in that classic '70s Southern California style.

title: Stills continues decade-long roll, with a little help from his friends
text: Not to slight the great Kenny Wayne Shepherd & Barry Goldberg, but I made this purchase based on Stephen Stills' decade-long artistic and creative upswing which began with 2005's genre-jumping comeback album, "Man Alive!"  That was followed by 2009's excellent "Live at Shepherd's Bush," a half-acoustic, half-electric cd/dvd package; the aborted Rick Rubin-produced CSN covers project; the live two-cd/dvd set "Crosby, Stills & Nash 2012," on which Stills continued to shine on brightly, and of course 2013's "Can't Get Enough," the Rides rollicking blues-rockin' debut cd.  "Pierced Arrow" is a more than worthy follow-up, with Stills in fine voice (never thought I'd be typing that phrase again!), and the entire group in sync and rocking the blues.  If you got into the first Rides collection, you'll be sure to want/like the new one.  Highly recommended.

title: Nash lumbers down an all too familiar musical path
text: Lame in the extreme.  Derivative melodies, trite lyrics, unimaginative arrangements.  Has this guy ever met a musical/lyrical cliché he wouldn't stoop to use?  His strength has always been high harmony; as a lead vocalist he's limited and often sounds strained and harsh, even more evident at age 74.  The accompanying in-concert dvd shows him to be an engaging, if lightweight performer, with a bloated sense of self-importance and a penchant for namedropping.  Some artists (James Taylor and Neil Young come immediately to mind) have successfully toured using the stripped-down (two-man) live approach attempted here; Nash bravely makes the effort but doesn't quite pull it off.

title: Dhani and company pay tribute to the late, great Hari
text: An interesting cross-section of talented artists pay tribute to the music of the late, great Hari.  If you're a big George Harrison fan, as I certainly am, you'll find this package hard-to-resist.  The Bluray's picture is unbelievably crisp; the audio is equally as impressive in its clarity.  The performances are from-the-heart and respectful across the board, without ever feeling like stodgy by-the-numbers remakes.  Every listener will be certain to have his/her own favorites, based largely on the breadth of George's songwriting skills and the wide-ranging line-up of artists involved.  You really gotta tip your hat to Dhani Harrison: he not only promotes his Dad's music, but protects his legacy.  Well-done all around.

title: Catherine Howe's mid '70s two-fer a most pleasant surprise
text: Wow!  What a pleasant surprise this one turned out to be.  I'd somehow missed this terrific artist her first time around (mid-1970s), so I guess I'm playing a bit of catch-up here.  But thanks to BGO Records, that great import reissue label, it's a catch-up game well worth the playing.  The crisp remastering lends the tracks a certain uncluttered clarity, without sacrificing vocal warmth or musical textures.  The arrangements, which run the gamut from singer-songwriter simplicity (Castle Gate) to quasi-disco (Hot Night) to Laurel Canyon-style country-rock (Bob Dylan's To Be Alone With You), are tasteful and mostly piano-based.  They serve to surround and support, but never overpower, Catherine Howe's timeless songs and heart-felt vocals.  Among my personal favorites: Loving Arms (her cover is the song that led me to this two-fer), title track Harry, and the beautiful When The Sparrow Flies.  Great stuff.  More, please!

title: Welcome Back, "Harry!"
text: I've been looking to replace HARRY for years; very hard to find at a reasonable price.  I already have the 2000 Buddha/BMG NSN reissue, which is great; but for me, HARRY is the real deal reason for buying this two-fer.  Great Nilsson songs (The Puppy Song, I Guess The Lord Must Be In New York City) and performances (including Mother Nature's Son, Mr. Bojangles, and Simon Smith And The Amazing Dancing Bear, a trio of Harry's best covers); excellent sound; informative liner notes, with the original album cover art faithfully reproduced, and at a bargain price.  Who could possibly ask for more?

title: The Mamas and The Papas collection we've been waiting for
text: This is the one we've all been waiting for.  Despite decade upon decade of reissues, repackages, reshuffled greatest hits titles, etc., it has taken nearly a half-century to get it right.  Remembering that the group was anchored in that magical era when singles ruled both the radio airwaves and the pop charts (think: Lovin' Spoonful, Rascals, Motown, etc.), this two-disc set represents the definitive The Mamas and The Papas career overview.  Thanks to Real Gone Music, we can now finally enjoy 'em the way we originally heard 'em, lo these many, many years ago.  All the hits that fit (group and solo) in chronological order, according to single release, in their original, pristine 45-rpm mono mixes.  Glorious mono sound, excellent liner notes, wonderful memories abound.  California dreaming, anyone?  It doesn't get any better than this.

title: The Essential Dave Mason, really!
text: I've wondered for years why Sony Music has never released a two-disc Dave Mason Columbia Records career compilation in its very popular "The Essential ..."  series.  Well, that's now a moot question, thanks to Real Gone Music's excellent new Dave Mason release, The Columbia Years: The Definitive Anthology.  Thirty tracks are spread over the two discs; they're chronologically arranged and beautifully remastered; every one of his Columbia Records albums is represented, with the tracks from Certified Live programmed to play together like an unbelievably impressive 5-song mini-concert.  The notes are informative, and Mason's comments are interesting, if a bit distant.  My only real quibble: the omission of Warm and Tender Love (the great Percy Sledge classic covered on Mariposa de Oro), which originally served as a beautiful a cappella intro to his hit cover of Will You Still Love Me Tomorrow.  That having been said, this one really is the essential Columbia-era Dave Mason.

title: Just about the best single-disc Rascals hits set
text: This is just about the perfect single-disc Rascals greatest hits compilation.  Every Atlantic Records chart hit, sans two, arranged chronologically, and presented in their original glorious single mixes.  Rhino could've made this THE PERFECT RASCALS' GREATEST HITS set simply by bookending 1970's Hold On, and 1971's Right On, on either side of 1970's Glory, Glory.  Those two additions would've resulted in all 18 Rascals Atlantic A-sides being together, in chronological order according to singles release, in one killer single-disc collection.  Even as it stands, these 16 tracks make the case for the Rascals as the premier rock 'n' soul band of the Sixties; just maybe, the best blue-eyed soul band ever.

title: One of Linda's all-time best, remastered
text: The late-1974 album that took Linda Ronstadt from journeywoman country-rock opening act to international superstar headliner in 1975.  This beautifully packaged tri-fold cover re-mastered cd version replicates the original LP's artwork and tracking order.  It also expands the playing time by including two bonus tracks, the Mono Single versions of her smash hits You're No Good and When Will I Be Loved.  The high-water mark of Linda's early career, and one of her all-time best.

title: One great live recording
text: This is one of those albums you wish you'd hung on to.  Lost the LP back in the day, during one move or another, and I've been looking for a CD replacement for years.  Here it is, and I'm so happy to have this one back.  Nanci's in fine voice and seems charmingly at-home on the concert stage.  Great backing band, excellent set-list, enthusiastic audience, and beautifully recorded.  Who could ask for more?

title: Off the Grid disappoints
text: Had high hopes for this one. The title (Off The Grid) would imply taking on some of Uncle Bobby's more unusual compositions, and/or delivering something new and different in their musical arrangements, or both.  How about neither?  This is a very safe record: the standard selections everyone always seems to cover, and not a single surprise in the vocals or arrangements.  Mister Charlie can't make a totally uninteresting record; he's just too fine a musician.  Gotta say this one's a bit of a disappointment.

title: The ballad of Emmylou and Gram
text: Had this one years ago on LP, and always considered it to be one of Emmylou's greatest achievements.  So glad to have finally found a reasonably priced CD reissue; it's great to have this one back in my collection.  Emmylou's own version of a country-rock concept album (a la Willie Nelson's Red-Headed Stranger, perhaps?), some say The Ballad of Sally Rose is a thinly disguised musical memoir of her complex relationship with her late mentor, Gram Parsons.  Maybe yes; maybe no; only Emmylou would know for sure, and she's still not talking.  Regardless, as one of her first stabs at songwriting (in partnership with co-producer Paul Kennerley), and taking on a complete album's worth of material with a unifying theme and a pronounced storytelling arc, this 1985 effort is an absolute stunner.  And it even produced some country radio hits: Rhythm Guitar, Timberline, White Line).  A stone classic.

title: Nanci Griffith's complete MCA studio output
text: With the obvious exception of her 1988 live disc (One Fair Summer Evening), this compilation collects Nanci Griffith's entire MCA Records output onto two packed discs.  If you're a fan, you'll love it; if not, you probably won't be interested anyway.  For the casual fan and the curious, there's always The MCA Years - A Retrospective (1993), or From A Distance: The Very Best of (2002), a pair of well-selected single- disc collections covering the same (1986-1993) era, only to lesser effect.

title: Steve Earle live and kickin' with the Dukes
text: Had this great rockin' live disc years ago.  Loaned it out to a friend, lost touch with her, and never saw it again.  Good to have it back in my collection.  Kick-butt backing band and killer versions of his Devil's Right Hand, I Ain't Ever Satisfied, Copperhead Road, and Guitar Town, as well as some inventive, unexpected covers (She's About a Mover, Dead Flowers).  Steve Earle & the Dukes, Yeah!

title: The Essential Bob Dylan, updated and upgraded
text: The Essential Uncle Bobby, updated.  Perhaps Sony should do an Essential Dylan two-disc set for each decade; I mean, really, his voice, his writing, his whole approach to studio recording, his live-in-concert performances, have all gone through so many phases and changes that it's damn near impossible to compile a satisfying two-disc career overview.  Still, you can't really argue with what's here, only scratch your head at what's missing.  A goldmine for the casual fan, and a fine introduction for the uninitiated.  Five Stars.

title: A mid '80s blast via the Power Station
text: Cheesy packaging and lack of liner notes aside, this is a pretty complete comp for a group that released so few recordings.  Everything you could possibly want or need is here, including the big hits (Some Like It Hot, Get It On (Bang a Gong), Communication (Club Mix), The Heat is On), a Beatles cover (George Harrison's Taxman), and an unreleased live Motown cover (Dancing in the Street).  A true blast from the mid-Eighties past.

title: Hollies Epic Anthology needs an audio apgrade
text: This is a five-star compilation disc in desperate need of an audio upgrade; thus, my four-star rating.  I love the Epic Records-era Hollies, with or without Graham Nash.  This set is pretty much chronologically arranged, which definitely adds to the CDs appeal. The listener is given the chance to see (hear?) the group's vaunted harmonies going through changes and becoming more intricate over time.  The big hits are all here (Carrie-Anne, King Midas in Reverse, Jennifer Eccles, Sorry Suzanne, He Ain't Heavy, He's My Brother, Long Cool Woman (in a Black Dress), Long Dark Road, The Air That I Breathe); as well as some great lesser-known Hollies tracks (Bruce Springsteen's Sandy (4th of July, Asbury Park), Another Night).  And at this bargain-basement price, how can you possibly go wrong?

title: Yes's audio and commercial peak
text: 90125 isn't exactly a favorite of longtime, diehard Yes fans, but to the more casual fan, like yours truly, it's one of their best.  This expanded remaster is the one to get: the sound has never been better, and the bonuses are bountiful, including various versions of Leave It and the extended remix of Owner of a Lonely Heart.  Yes, indeed!

title: This one's the classic Yes Album
text: The classic Yes album, remastered and expanded; the one we (East Coast Tri-Staters) all heard over and over again on the late, lamented 102.7 WNEW-FM, where rock lives... I'm no Prog-Rock maven, but this is the one I've always loved. I've Seen All Good People, yeah!  Great to have it back, and sounding better than ever.

title: Fleetwood Mac's turning point - Bare Trees
text: This is the one we all owned back in 1972, before Buckingham-Nicks.  And a great album it was/is: Bob Welch hit his personal high-water mark with this specific recording of Sentimental Lady (his later solo hit version doesn't hold a candle); Christine McVie hints at things to come with her excellent vocal/composition Spare Me a Little of Your Love; plus, there's FM-radio ready tracks in the day like Bare Trees, Danny's Chant, and Thoughts on a Grey Day.  This is the album that made me a life-long Fleetwood Mac fan.  Maybe you, too?

title: The best of the Airplane's early flights
text: Remastered and expanded version of the band's first - and best - compilation album.  They were just way too counter-culture cool to call it what it really was (their "best of" LP); just as they were loathe to admit that they were making radio-ready hits for the masses.  Some 45 years down the line, does anybody really care about the slightly embarassed tongue-in-cheek title?  I think not.  Fact is, this is the one to get: a solid, 17-song, single-disc overview of the Airplane's early flights.  All great material, not a waste cut to be found.

title: Oh, waitress, underwhelming service
text: Purchased as a Christmas gift for our 25-year-old nephew, who is quite the Sara B fan; however, he seemed a bit underwhelmed at Christmas.  Perhaps he's moving on (finally!)?  Ah, wouldn't that be nice ...

title: Ten Years After, 45 years later
text: The one we all owned by Ten Years After, from back in 1971.  The band was riding high on the concert circuit and on FM-radio platlists, due in no small part to their show-stopping, career-making appearance in the Woodstock movie of 1970.  Newly signed to Columbia (Big Timin' it!), they hit the airwaves like never before with I'd Love to Change the World and Baby, Won't You Let Me Rock 'n' Roll You.  And, even back then, hit singles sold albums...

title: Their career was like Quicksilver
text: Largely forgotten about today, Quicksilver Messenger Service was a hugely important band back in the early days of FM-Rock radio,  They weren't a "hits" band, which was supposed to be cool back then; thus, their reputation has faded along with the free-form radio format they were such an integral part of.  This remastered 12-track set will give you an audio glimpse as to what the band was capable of: Who Do You Love, Fresh Air, What About Me, Just for Love, rank among the highlights.

title: Classic Joe South Masters
text: Joe South was one of those '60s artists who should have had a much bigger career, in my opinion.  A terrific songwriter, his tunes were covered by genre-crossing artists to much radio and chart success (Lynn Anderson's version of Rose Garden, Deep Purple's take on Hush, Billy Joe Royal's smash hits Down in the Boondocks and I Knew You When, the Raiders' Birds of a Feather, etc.).  Like his contemporary great Tony Joe White, Joe South saw less success on the singer side of his singer/songwriter career label.  But he had some big ones: Walk a Mile in My Shoes, Games People Play, Don't It Make You Want to Go Home, Children.  They're all present and accounted for in this excellent remastered 12-track disc's set-list.  Great stuff that'll leave you wanting more.

title: Time has come to get psychedelicicized again
text: How great is was to have our souls psychedelicized by the Chambers Brothers back in 1968!  Time Has Come Today was one helluva trip, even if you never touched the stuff...  This remastered, expanded reissue takes me back, way on back in time, to days of incense and innocence; to an era when free-form FM-Radio was in its infancy; to a day when the music mattered, and all things seemed possible. And the music's pretty damn impressive, as well: Time Has Come Today (both the long album version and the single edit), their heart-stopping vocal showcase take on People Get Ready, and a killer version of In the Midnight Hour, among many other standouts.  Great to have this one back in my collection.

title: Jefferson Starship's Golden Years
text: Had the picture disc version of the LP (w/ the Bonus single included) back in the day, and I always figured it was about the most consistent album Jefferson Starship ever released.  Their regular studio albums always seemed to include a certain amount of dross; Gold, on the other hand, is all killer, no filler. The bonus single from the days of vinyl is now a part of the 12-track set-list.  Excellent re-mastered sound, too.

title: Starship's Platinum & Gold Hits Collection
text: This is the one to get if you're looking for a single Starship hits set for your collection.  The 12-track set-list covers all of the big ones (We Built This City, Sara, Nothing's Gonna Stop Us Now, Tomorrow Doesn't Matter Tonight), and then some.  Good stuff.  Great fun.

title: Carly Simon's Greatest Hits, Etc Live
text: Greatest Hits Live?  Well, not really.  This is actually Arista's edited down, 11-track, rearranged set-list, CD-version of Carly's HBO (and video) concert special, Live From Martha's Vineyard.  While the disc does indeed include performances of a half-dozen of Carly's greatest hits, many of her other well-known tunes (which were included in the HBO concert special) were left off this soundtrack CD in favor of then-current material from her Arista debut (1987's Coming Around Again).  Since the concert performance clocks in at just about 70 minutes (easily fitting a single-disc release), Arista's cut-and-paste approach makes no real sense.  Surely, Ms. Simon and her audience deserve better.

title: The best single-disc America hits set
text: The one to get if you're only planning to have one America set in your collection.  All the familiar Warner Brothers hits are here, along with their  biggest Capitol Records singles, a couple of newer previously unreleased titles, and even the band's minor chart hit cover of California Dreamin'.  CSNY-lite?  That's always been the knock on these guys, but I don't think it's deserved.  They've outlasted the critical backlash; they've survived the inevitable commercial peaks and valleys, and their recordings have withstood the test of time.  One listen to this 22-song set will provide all the audio proof you'll need.

title: Sam Cooke, the Smoothest of Soul Men
text: This is the one that first introduced many of us to the late, great Sam Cooke.  It's also one of the first LPs I ever owned, purchased with my own hard earned lawn-mowing cash way on back in the mists of time.  This re-mastered reissue, with an expanded track list, isn't getting five stars for its nostalgia value, however; this just happens to be great music that holds up incredibly well.  Sam Cooke was, is, and will always be the smoothest of soul men; the man who wrote the book of soul; the soulful gospel-based singer who defined the genre.  A monumental talent, and one of the all-time great "Best Of" compilations.

title: Never too late to appreciate Starship
text: Like far too many other Jefferson Airplane/Starship fans, I chose not to give this version of the Starship a fair listen back in the day, simply because the onetime counterculture band had "gone commercial."  As if the group ever wanted to not sell records, right?  Cut off nose; spite face cliche.  Listening now, I realize that many of us were missing out on some great fun -- even though radio/video hits like We Built This City, Sara, and Tomorrow Doesn't Matter Tonight were pretty much everywhere.  Glad I finally (!) changed my way of thinking.  Good stuff!

title: Pure Prairie League's commercial and artistic peaks
text: Another gift purchase for my classic rock-lovin' niece, who was very happy to receive it.  This particular compilation includes tracks from the band's more commercial radio-ready Vince Gill years, in addition to familiar material from the group's artistic peak with RCA back in the mid-Seventies.  Overall, a pretty good career overview.

title: The Monkees trio rerun is another rip-off
text: Another Monkees rerun.  This is the same remastered trio reissue Rhino unleashed years ago.  Once again, the music and packaging is just fine, but I'm definitely feeling ripped-off.

title: This Monkees duo release is basically a rerun
text: Feelin' a bit ripped-off here.  Aren't these the same exact remasters that Rhino reissued years ago?  The music and packaging is fine, but it's definitely something akin to a Monkees rerun...

title: More of Silver Bullet's Best
text: Purchased as a gift for my classic rock loving niece, who was thrilled with it.  All the other hits that fit, including some of the lesser-known radio and soundtrack smashes (Beautiful Loser, Shakedown, Understanding).  This 2003 compilation adds up to a worthy follow-up to 1994's Greatest Hits.

title: The King goes Royal Philharmonic
text: These Elvis vocals w/ different backing track projects can be dicey (anyone remember the disaster that was I Was The One, in which his rockabilly classics were given updated '80s backing?), and there's been a number of them through the years.  For the most part, though, this one actually works.
