The best tracks are the least well-known -- Neil Diamond's And the Grass Won't Pay No Mind, Don Robertson's There's Always Me -- as well as some of his better '70s LP cover tunes (You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin', Bridge Over Troubled Water, An American Trilogy).  All things considered, fans can breath a sigh of relief and enjoy: this one's a keeper.

title: Pass the Dixie Chicken and listen
text: For Lowell George and Little Feat, this third album was the charm.  Dixie Chicken, originally released in 1973, was and still remains the band's best studio album and greatest overall achievement.  George's songwriting was at a peak, his vocals would never be better, and the band itself was on fire.  A number of the Feat's all-time classics first appeared on this disc: Two Trains, Roll Um Easy, Fat Man in the Bathtub, and the oft-covered title track leading the way.  Lowell George, another of the would-be greats, another one who burned out far too soon.

title: Sweet Soulful Sheryl
text: I bought this at the suggestion of a friend who happens to be a big-time Sheryl Crow fan, which I have to say I'm not -- I'm more of the casual "greatest hits" / "live" disc kind of Crow fan.  Have to say this one came as something of a sweet, soulful surprise; not a bad track to be found on this 2010 release, right down to the bonus J-5 cover, I Want You Back.  Glad to have this one in my collection, even if I got here six years late!

title: Bargain-priced Stealers Wheel compilation
text: Don't let the cheesy packaging deceive; this 18-track single-disc 1998 compilation boasts excellent sound; an imaginative track list that gives equal props to both Gerry Rafferty and Joe Egan; and manages to hit all the high spots (including the worldwide smash title track, Everyone's Agreed That Everything'll Turn Out Fine, You Put Something Better Inside of Me, and Star), as well as highlighting many lesser-known gems.  The brief liner notes give us a kind of shorthand history of the band, but little in the way of  insight or inspiration.  Still, its a bargain-priced introduction to an extremely talented, trouble-plagued band that should have had a much longer shelf-life.

title: The ever-evolving, high-flying Byrds
text: The title says it all.  It's the ever-changing, high-flying Byrds, and it's the band's complete Columbia Records album output.  And these are the expanded, reissued remastered cd versions, and at a bargain-basement price, no less.  I purchased this box-set as a gift for a longtime Byrds fan friend who had put off buying it for quite some time; needless to say, said Byrds fan is currently flying eight miles high...  The box-set arrived a day ahead of the scheduled delivery date and in brand-new shrink-wrapped condition, as promised.  Thanks!

title: Otis Redding's soul man master class
text: The great man's posthumously-released pop-chart/pop-radio breakthrough, remastered,  While the track-list may seem like a bit of a mish-mosh, the overall power of the music cannot be denied.  The title track remains both timeless and classic, with Mr. Redding's quietly powerful lead vocal emerging as a two-and-a-half minute soul man's master class.  Other highlights include Otis's stirring takes on Nobody Knows You (When You're Down and Out), The Glory of Love, and Ole Man Trouble.  RIP, Mr. Redding.

title: Guess Who's original "Best of," plus three
text: The first Guess Who album I ever purchased, and it remains a stunner.  The band's most consistent LP, now with upgraded sound and three bonus singles included on the CD, "Best of" makes the case for the Guess Who as the most prolific and soulful singles-oriented band since the Rascals.  And that's a high compliment, indeed.  Among hits sets, I'd put this 1971 release right up there with 1968's Time Peace: The Rascals Greatest Hits.

title: The Guess Who's American breakthrough album
text: I've always preferred the previous LP (Canned Wheat) and the follow-up album (Share the Land) to this one.  Granted, American Woman was the band's big breakthrough LP, and it did have some incredible moments (the title track/single, the stunning No Time remake, the No Sugar Tonight-New Mother Nature medley, the dynamic When Friends Fall Out).  But there were also waste cuts and an over-use of the American Woman motif.  It's about half a great album, I'd say, padded out with too much lesser material.  And most of the great stuff would soon appear on the group's first "Best of," a year or so later.

title: Rafferty's most complete "Best of" compilation
text: This is the one to get if you want only one Gerry Rafferty compilation in your cd collection.  It touches all the career bases; contains all the major group (Stealers Wheel) and solo hits; boasts excellent sound, and offers informative liner notes.  Raven has done it again!

title: Peter Frampton's solo studio breakthrough
text: This was the album that introduced many of us to Peter Frampton.  It was all over the FM rock radio airwaves back in the day (1975), and many of the songs from this LP were showcased on (and actually paved the way for) his massively successful follow-up, Frampton Comes Alive!  The studio versions of tracks like Show Me the Way; Baby, I Love Your Way, and (I'll Give You) Money still sound great, and the "Frampton" cd will take you back to a more innocent, pre-pop idol Peter Frampton.  This one's a keeper.

title: Fotomaker, the great lost power pop supergroup
text: How this band of elite rock 'n' soul (ex-Rascals) and pop-rock (ex-Raspberries) players failed to make the superstar-level Big Time remains an unsolved mystery to many, including yours truly.  Fotomaker really had it all: the look, the experience, the material, the musical chops, even the right record label (Atlantic).  Given even a quick cursory listen, this terrific 16-track compilation will have power pop fans old and new scratching their heads in amazement and wondering what could've possibly gone wrong back in the day.  Buy it; try it; you won't be disappointed.

title: Otis, my man!
text: Otis, my man!  This cat was a force of nature, especially when on stage, caught live in concert.  What a tragedy that he was taken so soon.  A powerhouse performance of soulful emotion, Live in Europe has been a personal favorite for decades - dating back to a time when we'd listen in awe as the tape played its way through on our rather cheesy car 8-track.  Good time memories and great soul music.  RIP, Otis.

title: Harry Nilsson's last farewell
text: Harry, after his wondrous voice was broken.  Not up to his peak standards (by a long shot), but it's his final album statement; therefore, I'm glad to have it added to my collection.  RIP, Harry.

title: Norah's Covers leaves you wanting more
text: Being a sucker for both Norah Jones and cover tune discs, this purchase was something a no-brainer.  It arrived ahead of schedule and shrink-wrapped new, as promised.  The cd cover is a bit on the cheesy side, and while the track list is definitely enjoyable and impressive, the running time comes up kind of short.  The old cliché goes "less is more," but in this case, at least, less leaves you wanting more.  And I guess that could be construed as a good thing.

title: Great Elvis vocals at a bargain price
text: Inspirational shouldn't be confused with Elvis's sacred recordings, although some of his best-known spirituals are included in the disc's 20-song track list.  These '60s and '70s performances run the musical gamut: From memorable Top 40 hits (If I Can Dream, Crying in the Chapel, In the Ghetto), to pop covers (Put Your Hand in the Hand, Bridge Over Troubled Water, Neil Diamond's lovely And the Grass Won't Pay No Mind); from  country classics (A Thing Called Love, If That Isn't Love, Larry Gatlin's desperate prayer Help Me), to Broadway musical showstoppers (You'll Never Walk Alone, The Impossible Dream); from Irish vocal workouts (Danny Boy, I'll Take You Home Again Kathleen), to his Grammy-winning Gospel  signature tune (How Great Thou Art).  Docked one star for not presenting the program in chronological order, a tack that would've accented Elvis's artistic growth as both vocalist and serious interpreter.

title: The Guess Who at their peak
text: Purchased as replacement for my old LP version, long lost but always a favorite.  Guess Who's best and most consistent album to my way of thinking.  The Iconoclassic release is flat-out fabulous!  Crisp, clean sounding mix, and the harmony vocals have never sounded more heavenly.  Includes three bonus tracks, including the single version of Hang on to Your Life and the forgotten Hand Me Down World b-side, Runnin' Down the Street.  Quite possibly the best Guess Who line-up, ever.

title: A survivor's lost angel
text: He's no angel, just ask him!  But he sings like some kind of lost angel with the blues, someone who has faced it all -- good, bad, indifferent -- and come out on the other side all the better for the experience.  No, it's not up to the impossibly high standard set by Laid Back all those many years ago; but it's a survivor's record, and it's much more (and much better) than any of us had a right to expect upon its original release back in 1987.  Amazingly, almost 30 years on, it still has the emotional power to move you.  I'd say it has held up incredibly well.

title: A live keeper from Croz and company
text: As live records go, this one's a keeper.  Quite probably Crosby's most focused in-concert recording outside the CSNY Mothership. And the set list covers just about every phase of Croz's storied career: Material ranging from Byrds, CSN, CSNY, Crosby-Nash, solo LPs, and CPR, all sounding sharp and of-a-piece as delivered by this crack band. I'm really happy to have this fine live double-disc set in my collection.

title: The motel shot heard 'round the world
text: Hands down, far and away, 1971's Motel Shot is/was Delaney & Bonnie & Friends's greatest album achievement.  I've been looking for a reasonably priced cd replacement (for my long-lost original vinyl LP) for years (decades, really), and having finally found it/ordered it/ received it from Amazon I can only say it does not disappoint -- it's actually better than I even remembered!  Great vocals.  Great playing.  Great material.  And its very atmospheric production approach makes it feel timeless.  And it actually arrived a day ahead of schedule; couldn't be happier with the service or the product.  Thanks!

title: CCR Trio rockin' it  live in '71
text: The only officially released live disc (that I'm aware of) by the post-Tom Fogerty-exit trio version of CCR, and it positively rocks.  The sound is better than I remembered from the old vinyl double-album; the set list is mightily impressive, featuring the familiar hits and concert performance staples, as well as the band's (then) most recent single release, Sweet Hitch-Hiker b/w (Stu Cook's) Door to Door.  J.C. Fogerty's in fine form on lead vocals and guitar, and the Stu Cook-Doug Clifford rhythm section has never sounded tighter.  This disc is much better than its reputation; I'm glad I decided to give it a listen with fresh ears.

title: Carole's still making people happy
text: Purchased as a gift for a friend, who was absolutely thrilled with it.  Much preferred this deluxe two-disc version to the single cd version she already owned.  Everybody's happy, and love makes the world go 'round ...

title: Bargain-priced EpicYears Allman Bros anthology
text: Mycology is a well-selected single-disc overview of The Allman Brothers Band's surprisingly sturdy tenure with Epic Records.  No more, no less.  If you're looking for a solid introduction to the band's Epic output, this is the one to get.  Simple as that.

title: Early Canned Heat jammin'
text: Were these guys actually the template for the many jam bands that followed?  Always had a soft spot for Canned Heat, especially this early era in the band's long history.  On the Road Again was my introduction to their blues-based boogie sound, coming over the late Sixties AM airwaves on my cheesy car radio, way on way back when.  The music holds up incredibly well, my own personal nostalgia aside; most of these tracks have aged well, like vintage wine.

title: A hit and miss overview of Harry's RCA years
text: Not the most complete Harry Nilsson compilation, but a good place to start for the uninitiated.  Harry's biggest hits are mostly all here; unfortunately, they're not chronologically arranged, which can be jarring as both his songwriting and vocal skills went through many changes over the course of his RCA career.  Nevertheless, I purchased this particular disc as a gift for a friend and it was very well received, indeed.  RIP, Harry.

title: Another fine Gregg Allman Band offering
text: Another really fine effort from Gregg's Epic Records career.  Somehow this one slipped past me unnoticed upon first release.  However, like his great I'm No Angel album of the year before, it's jam-packed with great singing, great playing, and some very good-to-great songs.  And at a bargain price, you just can't lose.  Favorite tracks:  Slip Away, Island, Before the Bullets Fly.

title: Alvin Lee's in very good company
text: Bought this on a whim.  I had the LP a long time ago, but lost it somewhere along the way during one move or another.  Always liked this one a lot, as it wasn't your typical Ten Years After boogie.  Good material, great playing, and some fine vocals as well.  Glad to have this one back in my collection!

title: Back to a time when the music mattered
text: Never say never, I know, but it's a heartbreaking shame that the surviving members of CCR will never play together again.  This killer concert takes me back to another CCR show, one my friends and I caught at Madison Square Garden in 1970.  Openers were Wilbert Harrison and Booker T and the MGs, with CCR headlining in all their raging youthful glory.  Very similar set list to this cd, as I recall, and it was a no nonsense, all killer, no filler kind of concert.  Great performances.  Great songs.  Great fun from a time when the music mattered.

title: Hari's on Tour Express backing band
text: This was the album Tom Scott was hyping on George Harrison's Tour '74.  Tom Cat was actually part of the Hari's on Tour Express set list.  An impulse buy that I don't regret one bit.  Very good-to-great material, delivered in typically slick, yet funky L.A. Express style.

title: A Beacon in Wishbone's catalogue
text: Had the vinyl version back in the day, and I always loved the Ballad of the Beacon track.  The rest of the cd is better than I remembered, but Ballad ... is the keeper and the reason I ordered the disc in the first place.  Takes me back to kinder, gentler, younger days...

title: All the PPL Hits That Fit -- Live!
text: This band was made to make a live record!  I had this on vinyl many years ago, and it was always a personal favorite.  Great to have it back, on disc and in upgraded sound.  Highly recommended!

title: Pure Prairie League Lets It Fly
text: I'd forgotten how much I liked this band until I picked up the recent Bustin' Out/Two Lane Highway two-fer.  So, purchasing this two-disc three-fer follow-up was a no-brainer for me.  Best of' and Greatest Hits collections are good and useful as far as they go, but to get a real feel for a band or artist's career output it always helps to listen to the original releases in the way they were intended to be heard.  Yes?  I have to say I'm lovin' these discs; PPL set a certain level of fun-filled country-rock artistry on their first two LPs in 1975 and managed to maintain their enthusiasm and achieve their artistic goals throughout these 1976-78 sets.  This in spite of their record label's blundering and/or disinterest.  Excellent packaging, interesting liner notes, and upgraded sound.  Who could ask for more?

title: Pure Prairie League's Lost Classics
text: Pure Prairie League's first two ("lost") country-rock classics paired as a one-disc two-fer.  These guys were a great, loose, eager-to-please mid-Seventies band who had the misfortune to be signed to RCA, a label that didn't even know how to market Elvis Presley or Willie Nelson, let alone a square-peg-in-a-round-hole act like PPL.  Despite RCA's blundering mismarketing, Bustin' Out's Falling In and Out of Love/Amie would not be denied.  The single became a huge AM radio hit, an FM radio staple, and spearheaded the album's charge up the charts and eventual gold record status.  About six months later the band followed-up with Two Lane Highway, and once again, their label dropped the ball.  The LP's title track received massive FM radio airplay, but the RCA marketing team failed to turn it into a hit single.  So, despite peaking inside the top 25 on Billboard's album chart, the Two Lane Highway LP quickly crashed and burned.  Together, these two albums blend perfectly as one, a 20-track slice of 1975 country-rock pie.  To quote a catch-phrase from that bygone era, "Try it, you'll like it!"

title: Poco's Hit 'n' Miss Atlantic Years
text: As a long-time Poco fan, and as something of a collecting completist, it's great to have these two Atlantic albums paired on one disc by the BGO Records imprint.  Ghost Town is the better of the two titles, continuing with the commercially and artistically successful ABC/MCA Cowboys & Englishmen line-up.  Shoot for the Moon was singled out as the AC radio hit, while Rusty Young's title track stands as one of his best-ever compositions.  Despite having former Poco members Richie Furay, Timothy B. Schmit and George Grantham on board for backing vocals, and boasting some very strong Young and Paul Cotton songwriting, Inamorata suffers from its over-reliance on slick 80s production choices.  Cotton's Days Gone By provided the AC radio hit, and Young's Save a Corner of Your Heart was the missed opportunity.  Too bad this line-up never re-recorded the Inamorata LP in an acoustic, unplugged version.  The material definitely deserved a second chance.

title: Raven Gathers Three Melanie Classics
text:
I owned these three titles back in the days of vinyl, but hadn't heard them in years (decades, really). Really took me back in time; lots of good memories. Raven has done its usual excellent job in packaging the three LPs as a two-disc set, with the bonus of the full-length 7:48
version of Lay Down (Candles in the Rain), in addition to the more familiar 3:47 hit single version. The upgraded sound is a major plus throughout, but especially on the studio tracks. Ian McFarlane's notes are interesting and informative, but one correction, if I may: The Ink Well coffee house where Jersey Girl Melanie Safka sometimes performed was located in West End (not West Inn), NJ. A unique talent; it's a pleasure to have these classic Melanie albums back in my collection, especially in such crisp, clear sound.

title: Gettin' Gritty with NDGB
text: The final two Warner Bros albums, paired by BGO on one disc.  The updated sound is clean and crisp; the material mostly very good to excellent; John O'Regan's liners are informative and band-friendly, without coming across like fawning fan-boy notes.  Workin' Band (tracks 11 thru 22) gets the edge and is most welcome (first time I've ever owned it on CD!), while the more readily available Hold On is certainly no slouch, boasting country chart hits Fishin' in the Dark and Baby's Got a Hold on Me, as well as Bruce Springsteen's then-rare Angelyne.  All in all, a pretty great twofer.

title: Bang for Your Buck
text: Probably the best of the late-career Stones releases.  The band sounds committed, the songs are of very good to great quality, they have something to say, and they rock.  As they said back in the day, "Made loud, to be played loud!"

title: Who knew?
text: While I've always admired Benmont Tench for his subtle yet quietly impressive keyboard work w/ the Heartbreakers (and others), I had no clue that he was such a clever and insightful lyricist.  His thin, whispery lead vocals bring Bob Dylan to mind; but it's Uncle Bobby as if his voice has been filtered through the ghost of the great, great George Harrison.  I love this record!

title: Macca in the heart of the country
text: I purchased this CD on a whim, and it turned out to be a thoroughly enjoyable tribute to Sir Paul's songwriting and his musical roots in American rock 'n' roll.  It's no secret that Paul and the other Beatles were deeply influenced in their formative years by American musical icons like Elvis, Buddy, the Everlys, Carl Perkins, and many other pioneers of rock, and this tribute disc returns the favor by recasting many a familiar McCartney (Beatles, Wings, or solo) tune in an Americana  musical setting.  Great good fun, indeed.

title: Derek's secret musical weapon
text: Great stuff from Derek & the Dominos' not-so-secret weapon.  How these two (2) LPs got lost upon their original release is a mystery.

title: The Everlys would be thrilled
text: This is such a great record that I'll give it the ultimate compliment:  At thirteen (13) tracks, it seems far too short!  Seems as if Dawn McCarthy & Bonnie 'Prince' Billy were born to sing together, and making the LP all the more interesting, they don't just cover the obvious Everly Brothers hits. Here's hoping there's a sequel in the offing.

title: Not quite the Pixies, but pretty decent
text:
I got this album because of the comparisons everyone seemed to be making to The Pixies. But rather than the slack-jawed awe I had the first time I heard the Pixies, the Shackletons gave me a nostalgic appreciation. I was lucky enough to live through the hey day of the Minneapolis music scene and the band they reminded of most is Trip Shakespeare (predesecer of Semisonic.) They have quirky lyrics and good melodies, and doing stuff other people just aren't doing with their music.

A big part of this nostalgia is because the sound is not overly polished. It seems very much like the music I heard in the bars in my pre-parenthood days. It is good music, but it is more raw than most albums are allowed to be these days.

All in all, a pretty good album.

title: Brilliant in the Movie, So-so standing alone.
text:
Richard Thompson and the other musicians did a great job of creating this soundtrack to go along with Werner Herzog's movie. If you want to appreciate it, watch the movie. When it is not accompanying the movie, it seems a little disjointedly moody and ambient, and doesn't seem to play well track to track.

There are some gems on the album, the main title track is great and Coyotes is a great cowboy classic, but the brilliance of the soundtrack was when it was joined to the film. Perhaps the best thing to do is buy a couple of tracks through itunes and skip buying the album.

Again, brilliant work for its intended use, not so great on its own. Also, if you get a chance, watch the music featurette on the Grizzly Man DVD. It's interesting, especially if you are a Richard Thompson fan.

title: So Relaxing; Takes Me Back to Living in the Farmhouse
text:
When I was in college I lived in my parents’ old farmhouse which had a tin roof. The sound of the rain on that tin roof is probably one of the most soothing sounds I have ever heard in my lifetime and I slept like the dead when it rained at night. The house is gone now and I have moved into a modern house with a normal shingle roof, so I do not get the benefit of listening to the rain on the roof like I did in college. I still like the sound of the rain, but in my bedroom I do not hear the rain when it is coming down most of the time. This CD gives me the opportunity to listen to the rain whenever I want now, which not only helps me to sleep but also provides a very relaxing background in my day.

This CD is a single track – one 60-minute recording of nothing but gentle but steady rain falling. As I listen to the recording, I try to identify what the rain is striking as it falls. Some sounds like hitting wet pavement. Some sounds like hitting shallow puddles. Some sounds like hitting a window. It all sounds like it was recorded outside and most sounds are very distinct and clear. It is not the same sound as what rain on a tin roof makes but it is as relaxing.

In my home office I have my computer set up with a Bluetooth speaker with a spacial sound feature so it spreads out the sound to make it more natural. With this configuration, the rain sounds so clear, so fresh and natural that it really relaxes me as I work. Yes, this is a CD marketed primarily as a sleep aid, but it is highly relaxing as background noise.

As a sleep aid, it works well for me. I usually use a large, steady fan to lull me to sleep, but I like the sound of the rain more than the sound of the fan and the rain takes me back to that farmhouse.

This is one of the most relaxing CDs I have ever owned. The recording of the rain reminds me of the rain on the roof of the house my parents owned several years ago, but it also helps me to sleep at night and relax during the day.

title: Fall Asleep More Relaxed
text:
I have struggled with sleepless nights for years, sometimes getting 3 hours or less when I am particularly anxious or have too much to do. I have tried seeing a doctor about my lack of sleep and that did not pan out well for me either. I was willing to try this CD – I really had nothing to lose – and though I honestly did not have especially high expectations it really does help me fall asleep.

The first track on the CD is relaxing and has a woman's voice instructing on breathing technique and relaxation. This is reminiscent of a yoga class I had in college, though it was a bit more formalized. From there, the CD goes into tracks with guitar music with wave sounds in the background. Being interested in really giving this CD a chance I complied with the instructions of the first track and was conscious enough to hear the second track start but faded off before the third track started. I have no idea what the other tracks sound like as I have not listened to the CD in the daytime when I am fully awake.

Does it make me sleep better? Well, yes, to a point. The CD does make me fall asleep faster and I am definitely less anxious when I drift off, but I still find myself waking up in the night. I don't wake up with a jolt, though, and I am not disoriented when I wake up as I often am in the night. This is a good step in the right direction. I will work with this CD some more and update this review after I have worked with it several nights in a row.

I cannot say definitively that this CD makes me sleep better, but it does make me more relaxed so I can fall asleep more easily. That's a win for me. Time will tell if it will be a huge help, but the results I have seen so far are promising. This is more than the doctor was able to do for me.

title: 4 Strings found their winning formula again
text:
Contrary to the item's listing, it was released in 2005, not 2025... So, it is available now.

This CD single is very reminiscent of their debut CD "Believe". They have found their original sound again, a relief for fans that were disappointed in their second CD "Turn it Around". There are seven mixes of Sunrise on this CD, and every one of them is superb, due mostly to a primary keyboard melody that remains unchanged between the mixes. Some mixes are a little better than others, and some have vocals where others do not, but none can be mistaken for being produced by a different group. And for those that have vocals - Vanessa (yes, it's definitely her) does a phenomenal job.

Any true 4 Strings fan will want this CD. Although it is just one song with 7 different mixes, it rivals "Believe" in being among their best work.

Even if you are not a big fan of Howard, you might still like seeing how he had to fight his way to the top of the pile against mainstream media and the FCC.

You will get to see the very personal sensitive side of Howard on screen. Too fun, and too funny!

title: A GEM
text:
If there is only one Manilow CD that is a must to own, it is this one. This is a Manilow unlike the one known to pop audiences. Gone is Mandy, Copa Cabana & I Write The Songs. Instead, the listener is transported to a smokey bar after last call. The crowd is thinning and the piano man begins to sing from the depths of his broken heart. He is accompanied in duet by Sarah Vaughan on one track and Mel Torme on another and is joined by some of the jazz greats who back him up on this journey through the heartache of lost love.

Thirty odd years ago, I heard the duet with Mel Torme being played as I shopped in my local grocery store. I raced to the nearest record store to find the album. I found one copy buried among all the other Manilow vinyl. I purchased it on the spot. Years later, after wearing the grooves to a frazzle, I replaced it on CD. I can't put in words how much I love this CD. Recently, I signed on to Spotify, one of the many free music sources. Just today, I was adding to my cache of music and decided to check out what was available by Manilow, when, to my surprise, I came across this "remastered" version of 2am Paradise Cafe. As I started listening to it, my ears pricked up. I was hearing instrumentals I never caught before. The singing sounded more poignant, if that could be possible. I found myself swept away in an experience that far surpassed the original. But because this CD had no English translation, I was unaware. I did have some hope for Malafemmena which I recalled as a passionately sung song of my younger years. Alas, Bocelli seemed barely awake through it. Love Me Tender? The only song sung in English... no passion, no feeling. There was only one song that made the cost of this CD almost worth it and that was La Vie En Rose w/ a blending in of Edith Piaf voice, but even there, the woman dead so many years, had more energy than Bocelli. If this is all that he has left in his voice to give and will continue with these outdated orchestrations, I'll tune to American Idol and hope for new talent. title: One of my sisters-in-law bought me a Waylon Jennings LP ...
text: One of my sisters-in-law bought me a Waylon Jennings LP in the 1970s for Christmas. I was to be forever changed. Just a teen then, I soon found myself locked and loaded for Waylon and the Waylors. Later in life on a show boat in Kansas City, I would hear of Waylon's last performance. Not too long later sitting in my Phoenix home, the news came the Hero of Honky Tonks had crossed from this life to the next. It was brought to mind at the time in this album, the music reflected on Waylon and how he and Jessie had it all, and then some!

title: You like pure, raw country

title: Done in raw, true to the bone fashion. ...

In true homage to he and his father's friend George Jones, the younger Jennings drives home a tribute no one else quiet could. Because most folks didn't have first hand experience dealing with the opossum!

title: It is the best way to uncover generations of history
text: Waylon has always been a hero. A legend, music singers are made of. As goes with The Taker/Tulsa. Any student of the musical arts should make it a point to study Waylon Jennings, Buddy Holly, Patsy Cline, George Jones and Jerry Lee Lewis. It is the best way to uncover generations of history, document the changing attitudes toward acceptances and understand what it is to live with demons and still be succesful...too much so at times.

title: I Give it an AAA+
text: In many media reviews I read poor reviews of this set of recordings originally mastered in the 1980's. But it ranked Bill Board Country Chart #1 and #2 spots the first half of April 2014! With "She Use To Love Me, A Lot," the Man in Black is spot on in the performance and his voice is coldly honest. Throw in a duet with June Carter Cash and you get a double daily. Still there is more! When you hear Johnny chatting and laughing, just before he and Waylon Jennings get rhythm, with "I'm Moving On" and the CD shoots clearly "Out Among The Stars!" Going to show the critics missed the mark by not knowing who they were talking about.

title: Right for the Time is Right for Me!
text: Waylon - raw emotion and thumb strumming sound can be clearly enjoyed in true Waylon Style! I could only imagine if Waylon was promoting the CD today, how he'd say..."if you don't have it you should!" I came to appreciate Waylon later in his career, however his biography should be studied by fans of any style of music and could be with Right For The Time!

title: This is my 3rd CD of And Along Came Jones, the other 2 wore out.
text: Kept in my truck are three CD's, among them is And Along Came Jones. I wore two previous CD's out and this is my third replacement that speaks volumes of how much play time the CD received!

title: True Country at It's Core, Jones' Style
text:
George Jones brings the raw emotions to the core of songs on Heartaches and Hangovers. Singing with feeling as though he was living through the song as he sang it.

For hard core country fans, you will delight in the style that Jones retained from his Starday recording days. True, brutal, plain ole country boy picked off a dirt road in Southeast Texas.

For those looking for todays other country, you won't find the gimics in George Jones. George is the real deal and has real country music roots that taper directly off Hank Williams Sr!

From Jones, came Johnny Paycheck, Vern Gosdin and few other good ole boys. Few of which you will see on anything called country music television or radio of today. To know what country is...you have to look at Jones...he is a study in country music. He didn't just sing it - he lived it!

title: Paycheck Sings Borrowed Tunes...On a Test Run...
text: Johnny Paycheck has been a favorite for me since he first appeared in George Jones' band in the early 1960's. In this collection he locks the first song with Take This Job and Shove It! From there he shares his versions of tunes from George Jones, John Conlee, Merle Haggard and Waylon Jennings. Paycheck is best known for taking a song and making it his own, which he mastered with the "Old Violin!" This album appears to be a test run on his quest to accomplish what he would leave as being his mark on the world.

text: I was not expecting Pearl Jam but was expecting something akin to the Into the Wild Soundtrack which was brilliant and captured the spirit of that film.  I was initially put off by this album since it did not resemble Into the Wild or anything that Vedder had previously done.  After listening I sat the CD aside as one of those mistakes one makes in buying something based totally on unrealized expectations.  After a few days I pulled it out and played again and found I really liked some of the music.  I played it again and discovered that I really liked the entire album and have listened to it enough I can sing along just like I do with Pearl Jam albums or Into the Wild.  Not every Pearl Jam fan will like this but only Eddie Vedder has the guts and the talent to do this kind of CD and be entertaining - at least I have been totally entertained.  The lesson - if after listening to this and not enjoying it, give it a second or third try and it will begin to grow on you.

title: Grand and Glorious
text: Nearly 50 years ago when I was a preteen I first heard this album on vinyl.  I was overwhelmed by the rich harmonies and the passion in which the songs were sung.  Part of the reason that I became interested in the history of the American Civil War (War Between the States) was directly related to this album.  For purists this will not fill their needs since it is a Choir singing and not a group sitting around a campfire waiting for battle.  But, it is a remarkable collection of songs that represent one of the saddest chapters in American history.  And for me, I can close my eyes and almost smell the smoke of that campfire.

title: Great Album
text: After listening to Give Up the Ghost, I purchased this album as well as her first album (self titled).  I can see her development from album to album (gave her third album 5 stars).  The common thread in all of her albums is her incredible voice which brings both passion and feeling.  But, with each album there is a sense of growing maturity to her music and lyric choices.  The title song (The Story) is powerful and the messages delivered in each song in this CD are just as meaningful as those on her third album.  Listen to the samples but to truly appreciate the talent that Brandi Carlile has, you need to listen to each track in full and let her music embrace and envelope you.  She possesses a chrisma that only a few entertainers can claim. "So many stories of where I've been...And how I got to where I am...But these stories don't mean anything...When you've got no one to tell them to..." (Brandi Carlile's The Story).

title: Amazing...
text: Idina Menzel has such a marvelously rich voice that it is hard to find fault with this album.  But here it is:  it is 38 minutes long which is far too short.  Just as I am looking forward to the next song, the CD is completed.  But, I think if the CD was 3 hours and 38 minutes long I would still be craving more.  My first experience with Menzel was the musical CD Wicked and I became overwhelmed by every song that she was a part of.  I watched a video of her singing I Stand and based on that song alone decided to purchase this album.  I had some trepidations as to whether the rest of it would live up to my expectations.  I was so pleasantly surprised that her powerful and melodic voice carried this CD from the first song (I Stand) through the last song (Perfumes and Promises). Idina captures the essence of Broadway Musicals as well as Pop Music in this effort. I am convinced that whatever she elects to sing would be just as great as every other song that I have ever heard her sing. What's missing in my life is more available music from her to listen to. So, I will continue to relish in listening to this CD until another Menzel masterpiece becomes available.

Starting with the the first selection, Looking Out, through the final selection, Oh Dear, Carlile tells stories of youth, mistakes made and ultimately hope.  Although not credited on the CD, the song Caroline features Elton John in a duet (shared by her on the PBS program). One message from Brandi Carlile:  "When you're outside looking in - You belong to someone - And when you feel like giving in - And the coming of the end - Like your heart could break in two - Someone loves you."  From Looking Out. Eleven songs on this CD provide this kind of impactful lyrics in every song along with Carlile's beautiful voice to spread her messages.

title: A desert island disc
text: A solid record. Gleason started (along with AD co-lead vocalist Warren Ham) as a sideman for John Elefante era Kansas, after which they shared lead vocal duties in Kerry Livgren and Dave Hope ’s short-lived post-Kansas “solo” effort - AD. After that band’s sadly abbreviated life, Gleason released Children of Choices which was produced by (also ex-Kansas) John Elefante and his brother Dino. The Elefantes owned and operated Pakaderm Records as well as one of the most successful studios in Nashville and produced a string of successful CCM releases by artists such as Petra as well as John Elefante’s own solo work and collaborative band Mastedon and others. Their excellent work is also amply demonstrated on CoC. Songwriting is solid and excellent throughout, as are the arrangements and production. If you’re familiar with Gleason’s vocal work with AD, you may be pleasantly surprised by his punchier and more in-your face work here. One can only wonder how AD’s output might have benefitted from the Elefante brothers’ involvement. (Not to denigrate Livgren’s own substantial production skills by any means). Sadly, Gleason’s musical efforts faded away shortly after CoC. He released a small amount of material which apparently suffered from lack of publicity. Nearly thirty years later, Children still stands as a high water mark of 80’s power pop CCM.

title: Not their best
text: As has been said in other reviews, DR is okay, but not one of TFK's best. One of the aspects that truly makes most of their catalog stand out is an unflagging optimism. "Stardust we are... close to divine...". On Desolation Rose, that optimism has been replaced with a decidedly gloomier outlook. (Read Stolt's comments in the main description to get a better idea where he's coming from here.) Sorry... I think it's more effective to inspire listeners than the reverse. On top of that, even the music seems thinner here. Gone are the grandiose themes, replaced by more pedestrian music sporting predictable changes and time signatures. It's not that "fiddly bits" are necessarily always better, but after repeated listens, there just isn't much here to hold your attention. Is this better than most of what passes for music on the pop charts? Absolutely, but that isn't saying much. I'll stick with "Stardust We Are", "Space Revolver" or even "Banks of Eden" for something a little more recent. These guys can (and usually do) do better.

title: a mostly weak effort
text:
I guess I have to stand with the opposition on this one - River of Souls is a mostly weak effort from a singer, songwriter and musician who is often capable of so much better. Specifically, it's the cheesy drum machine (whatever happened to Russ Kunkel?), the me-too world music of "Serengeti Moon", the too-obvious keyboard and synth patches all over the place, and the preachy politics of "Voice For Peace" and "Holy Road". The title track is a near miss for me - it takes the smooth jazz dentist's office music factor farther than I want to go on a Dan Fogelberg album. "All There Is" has "I need a hit" written all over it. (am I the only one who finds the idea of a millionaire pop star lecturing a billionaire real estate magnate a bit ludicrous?)
Still, there are at least a couple stand out tracks, even here. "Magic Every Moment" is a joyful song that's difficult to get out of your head once you've heard it. "The Minstrel" - a gorgeous and haunting love song to Dan's beloved sailboat Minstrel is worth the cost of the disc all by itself. Those two tracks are still worth the price of admission, but overall, River of Souls falls far short of Nether Lands, Souvenirs, and even Phoenix.

title: a pleasant surprise
text: I'm another one who doesn't typically buy Christmas releases. Just thinking of horrid holiday fare like "Last Christmas, I Gave You My Heart", "Baby Please Come Home for Christmas" and "Grandma Got Run Over By a Reindeer" is nearly enough to make me go into self imposed audio exile until after New Year's. When I got the email from Amazon to pre-order the New Enya release I didn't think for a moment. I love Enya's music so I ordered first and checked it out afterward. Oh no, a Christmas CD... Ah well, too late. I decided to give her a chance. I'm glad I did. This isn't your typical remake of a dozen hackneyed holiday hits. While there are a couple of well known Christmas tunes here (a gorgeous Gaelic rendition of Silent Night and a haunting rendition of O Come O come Emmanuel) the rest are more subtle in sticking to the theme, so I'll be able to enjoy them in August as well as December. I was a little disappointed in Amarantine - the arrangements didn't vary much from song to song and seemed a little predictable. I'm happy to say that "And Winter Came" is a step in the right direction. The arrangements are more varied (though there's nothing startling here if you're familiar with Enya's catalog - that's a good thing to my ears.) and there's even a tasty electric guitar solo in the playful "My! My! Time Flies!". Well done Enya, Nicky and Roma.

title: Home Free and nearly a Home Run
text:
Dan's first album, released in 1972 when he was just 21 hints at things to come. It has a more organic feel than much of his later work, but many of his trademarks are already on display here - the impeccable acoustic guitar work, the stacked harmonies and the introspective lyrics. Home Free has a somewhat more country feel than most of his later work, with the possible exception of High Country Snows. Standout tracks - well, it's a cop out to say it, but it's true - pretty much all of them.

Some random thoughts:
To the Morning is one of my all time favorite DF songs. Like so many Fogelberg songs, I have a cherished memory that goes with it and I can't hear the song without recalling the memory.
In "Stars" (which was recently lovingly covered by Alison Krauss) you'll find one of the earliest examples of Dan's occasionally quirky phrasing:
"stars fall every time a lover has to face the truth, and far too many stars have fell on me..."
Dan was quoted in an interview once as saying that he didn't play Stars much anymore because of the voyeuristic aspect of the song.
I heard him remark once in a concert that Looking for a Lady was written when he was in a particularly... ah, "amorous" frame of mind. (that wasn't the word he used) I've never been able to listen to that song the same way since.
Dan said Wysteria was a song written about a ghost.
The only track I don't care for is the one that many people seem to think is a standout - The River. I realize this bit of criticism won't earn me points from other Dan fans, but the whole effect to my ears is that of a high school boy trying to write something "important". While the lyrics are occasionally interesting, The music is in large part a tired 3 chord riff supporting an uninspired wah wah guitar solo. The track just doesn't seem to fit with the rest of the album, either stylistically or in terms of quality.
That having been said, Home Free overall is an amazing freshman effort and full of gems that are often overlooked due to the lack of initial commercial success the release received.

title: more of the same
text: By "more of the same" I mean no insult - if you're buying an Enya CD, chances are you know what to expect, and you'd be unhappy to discover she'd gone off in some radically different direction. No worries about that here. I happen to like Enya, and Amarantine fits quite comfortably with the rest of her catalog. Lush mixes featuring rich synth pads and Lexicon soaked vocal choirs, pizzicato strings, and Enya's soft, soothing voice floating over it all. If you like Enya, you'll like Amarantine, though this isn't among her best releases, in my opinion.  While this is an entirely enjoyable disc, to my ears there are no standout tracks - not a "Storms In Africa" or "China Roses" among the bunch.

title: rootkit and recycled music
text:
First the rootkit - many Sony/BMG music CD's install a 'rootkit' - a commonly used hacker backdoor trick - on your Windows PC if you play them on your computer. This disc employs a different but still invasive method licensed by Sony from Sunncomm. It's not just a matter of copy protection, it's a matter of security, performance and system stability. Sony/BMG CD's will negatively impact all three. Don't buy this CD for that reason alone, or at the very least, don't play it on your Windows PC.

Second, the music. I used to be a big fan of Santana (the guitarist and the band) and Supernatural, although a weaker effort than the 'old' Santana, gave me hope that Carlos might be on the return. 'All That I Am' is a disappointing step in the other direction. It literally sounds like the tracks were recorded and Carlos came in on his lunch hour and improvised solos over the top of a finished mix. His tone is wretched, his playing is uninspired and his contribution is more name than music. Want to hear some passion, some fire, some *real* Santana? Go find Abraxas or one of his band releases from the early 70's. Skip this watered down, computer trashing, phoned in muzak.
