I've literally listened to and mentally dissected this album hundreds - if not thousands - of times and I hear something new each time. Of course the rhythm section, and especially Bill Evans on piano, add significantly to the music. If you are a drummer you can also discern the different approaches by Connie Kay and Philly Joe Jones. I tend to favor Kay's playing on the tracks on which he is playing because his approach is more delicate. However, Jones perfectly fit the music on the tracks on which he played.

Tracks 1 through 3 and 5 through 7 were recorded in NYC on December 30, 1958 with Baker accompanied by Herbie Mann on flute, Pepper Adams on baritone sax, and a rhythm section comprised of Bill Evans on piano, Kenny Burrell on guitar, Paul Chambers on bass and Connie Kay on drums.

Tracks 4 and 8 through 10 were recorded in NYC on January 19, 1959 with the same line-up except Philly Joe Jones has the drum chair.

The remaining five tracks are from the album titled [[ASIN:B000UBOUA0 Plays The Best Of Lerner & Loewe]]. These are selected tracks and not the entire album - just the session in which Bill Evans participated.

Again, to me the beauty of the music is mainly due to the richness of tone from Baker's trumpet, augmented by Pepper Adams' baritone sax. The baritone perfectly harmonizes with the lower registers in which Baker is playing on this album. I am sure that his earlier stint with Gerry Mulligan influenced him enough to create a sound that complemented (and was complemented by) the baritone sax.

Herbie Mann on flute and tenor sax, and Zoot Sims on alto and tenor sax round out the front line. While the melody flows from Baker on each track, the harmony from Adams, Mann and Sims adds a lot of texture to the music. I also love the contrast between the baritone sax and the higher register instruments, and especially Mann's flute and Sims' alto sax. The rhythm section features Bill Evans, backed by Earl May on bass and Cliff Jarvis on drums. These tracks were recorded for Riverside at the Reeves Sound Studios on July 21, 1959.

title: Ellis leading the Oscar Peterson Trio Plus
text:
This is one of the swingingest and hardest driving examples of just about any album I can think of that contained both Ellis and Peterson. The ensemble is interesting. Harry Edison on trumpet give each track a slightly traditional flavor (or what was going by the name Mainstream Jazz during the mid 1950s). Jimmy Giuffre, who switches among clarinet, tenor and baritone sax enhances Edison's playing with a tinge of West Coast style thrown in. The remaining core ensemble is the Oscar Peterson Trio, with Peterson on piano, Herb Ellis - the leader - on guitar and Ray Brown on bass. Alvin Stoller was brought in as drummer for the two sessions that resulted in this album.

Instead of my trying to describe the music give the sound samples on this page a listen. The entire ensemble is on fire and Ellis is actually pushing them. It's a rare occasion to hear Peterson being pushed on, but that is what seems to be happening. The arrangements are first rate too.

The album was recorded in two sessions less than a week apart in Los Angeles for the Clef label (the precursor to Verve.) The first session produced the first four tracks with the core ensemble mentioned above on December 28, 1955. The remaining tracks were recorded on January 3, 1956 with Charlie Mariano added on alto sax.

title: Oscar does the Count justice
text:
Being both a Basie and Oscar Peterson fan I just had to have this album. Peterson and his ensemble (Ray Brown on bass, Herb Ellis on guitar and Buddy Rich on drums) capture the essence of Basie's signature songs, but with their own touch.

Listening to Lester Leaps In without a tenor saxophone in the group was a little weird at first, but even that track is done in a manner that should being a smile to Pres' face. Make no mistake, Herb Ellis is no Freddie Green and Buddy Rich's style is vastly different from Papa Jo Jones (not to mention the differences between Ray Brown and Walter Page). On the other hand, the fact that a quartet could swing as hard as the Basie band AND pull off each song in a manner that does it justice is a laudable feat. Give the sound samples on this page a listen and hear for yourself. Resist the urge to compare this to Basie performances because that is apples and oranges. Frankly I admire the way this ensemble pulls off this album.

This was recorded for Norman Granz' Clef label (forerunner to Verve) in Los Angeles on December 27, 1955. Not only does the quartet do a remarkable job, they did it in a single session. They don't make musicians like that anymore.

title: Short,  but great
text:
At a few seconds short of forty one minutes this album is almost a tease. On the other hand it's both historic and great music. The historic aspect is this is the first of four collaborations between Peterson and Jackson and it presages the ones to come.

Listen to the sound samples on this page and even those short snippets will reveal the magic of this album. I am not going to try to dissect the music or impose my personal taste on you, but if you love swinging and tight quartets with a piano and vibraphone in front you will be more than pleased with this album.

While I promised to not dissect the music I will say that the intensity that Jackson brings to the performances match the backing trio - Peterson and bassist Ray Brown in particular were renown for intensity even on ballads, and drummer Ed Thigpen fit right into that as well. So the chemistry among the four is natural and one of the reasons why this album appeals to me.

The album was recorded for Verve in NYC over the course of two sessions (September 15 and 18, 1961.) Sadly there were five unissued tracks from the sessions, two of which are logged as 'untitled Peterson originals' that I would have loved to have been included in a reissue. Regardless, the music that is on this album is definitely worthwhile.

title: Two well known and one lesser known plays
text:
This set is a tribute to shows and plays, starting off with My Fair Lady that debuted in 1956 on Broadway with music by Frederick Loewe. The next album in this set is the soundtrack from Porgy and Bess that debuted on Broadway in 1935 with music by George Gershwin DuBose Heyward and Ira Gershwin. The final album is Fiorello! that was first performed on Broadway in 1959 with music by Jerry Bock.

I do not consider any of the albums in this set to be essential to most Peterson fans, although they are a valued addition to my personal music library. Listen to the sound samples on this page and decide for yourself. All of the albums were recorded in the 1959-1960 time frame when sound tracks from musicals were popular, so there is a commercial aspect to each of the albums in this set.

Here is what the set contains: Disc One, Tracks 1 through 7 are the album titled [[ASIN:B004MFNA7O Oscar Peterson Plays My Fair Lady]] that was recorded for Verve at Universal Recording in Chicago on November 20 and 21, 1958. This album features Peterson backed by Ray Brown on bass and Gene Gammage on drums (Ed Thigpen had not joined the trio as drummer so Gammage is strictly interim.)

Tracks 8 through 12, and 1 through 5 on Disc Two are the album titled [[ASIN:B000VZFWO8 Plays Porgy And Bess]] that were recorded in Los Angeles on October 12, 1959. This line up is the classic Peterson/Brown/Thigpen edition of the trio.

The remaining tracks are the album titled [[ASIN:B000VZKRUW Fiorello]] that was recorded in Los Angeles in January 1960. This album is the soundtrack from a musical about NYC mayor Fiorello LaGuardia, which is consistent with the overall theme of this set. The trio is the classic Peterson/Brown/Thigpen line up.

title: One of my favorite Peterson Trio sets
text:
If I had to choose a box set of Peterson's work to take to a desert island this would probably be my choice. I say 'probably' because there are a few other sets that I own that would compete for my attention. However, this is on the short list and one of the reasons is the diversity of songs. Two, Whisper Not and I Remember Clifford, are rare examples of Peterson interpreting some of my favorites.

This set contains four previously published albums, plus thirteen tracks that were never released prior to this set. The entire contents of this set was recorded over the course of July 27 through August 6, 1961 and clock in at just over five hours and fifteen minutes. The albums in this set are:
1: [[ASIN:B000W25AG0 The Trio Live From Chicago]]
2: [[ASIN:B000VZMS8Q The Sound Of The Trio]]
3 and 4: [[ASIN:B00BJ9NF94 Put on a Happy Face + Something Warm. Live at the London House]] (this two album set contains both of the remaining four.)
You can listen to sound samples on each of the above album product pages. There is some background noise, which a fellow Amazon reviewer who was there explained. That reviewer, Julie Swedien Johnson, was there with her father Bruce who was the engineer. She related that her father, "went insane, going from table to table shushing people. There was nothing he could do to edit out the noise but it's a stellar album." I agree that it's a stellar album set. She also related that both Bill Evans and Lionel Hampton dropped by for some of the performances. She was not clear about whether she was there both nights, but I suspect that she was. One other piece of information that she revealed was her father spent his own money for the stereo tapes for the recordings because studio executives thought stereo was a gimmick. I am guessing that she was referring to Richard Seidel who was the producer for the sessions.

The sound samples cited above will provide a good idea of the energy and sound quality of the tracks in this set. For me this is a coin toss for best ever Oscar Peterson Trio set, but with the classic trio of Peterson, Ray Brown on bass and Ed Thigpen on drums it's probably their best recorded live work. The reason I am not going to claim that it's my absolute favorite is I am also partial to the trio when Herb Ellis was on guitar in lieu of a drummer. Regardless, if you are a Peterson fan you cannot go wrong with this.

title: Nice sampler of original songbook albums circa 1952/1954
text:
This album is a compilation of Peterson's earlier Songbook albums that he recorded in 1952 and 1954 for the Mercury and Clefs labels. All were at the behest of Norman Granz.

The tracks here are drawn from the Arlen, Berlin, Ellington, Kern, McHugh, Porter, Warren and Gershwin songbooks. These albums were recorded in Los Angeles. The subset of tracks on this album are an excellent sampling of what's on the individual source albums. The 1952 sessions feature Peterson, Ray Brown on bass and Barney Kessel on guitar. The 1954 sessions have Herb Ellis replacing Kessel. Their styles are sufficiently different to stand out. While I generally prefer Ellis, Kessel's playing on the 1952 tracks appeal to me more. That said, the sound quality is very good considering when these tracks were originally recorded.

Note: these songbooks would be repeated with the classic trio (Peterson, Ray Brown on bass and Ed Thigpen on drums) in 1959. While many of the songs are repeated in the 1959 set of albums, both have merit. I own both collections of the albums of which this one is a mere subset, and I am forever tossing a coin when I need to choose a 1952-54 or 59 songbooks.

If you are a Peterson fan chances are that you already have these albums. If you just discovering Peterson and want a sampling of Peterson in your collection this is a great place to start.

title: Porter + Sinatra
text:
This is actually two complete albums and a bonus track. The albums were recorded a few months and a continent apart, and feature what I call the classic trio comprised of Peterson, Ray Brown on bass and Ed Thigpen on drums.

Since there are no track list or sound samples on this page at the time of this review I will provide the tracks and links to both albums that have sound samples on their product pages.

The sound quality of this CD is excellent. The label, Masterworks Singles, appears to be a quality label that is new to me. Here are the tracks, albums or sources, and session dates:

[[ASIN:B000VZKP2C Oscar Peterson Plays The Cole Porter Songbook]] was recorded at Universal Recording in Chicago during a marathon set of sessions spanning July 14 through August 9, 1959. Tracks are:
1. In the Still of the Night
2. It's All Right with Me
3. Love for Sale
4. Just One of Those Things
5. I've Got You Under My Skin
6. Everytime We Say Goodbye
7. Night and Day
8. Easy to Love
9. Why Can't You Behave
10. I Love Paris
11. I Concentrate on You
12. It's De-Lovely

[[ASIN:B000VZPH7K A Jazz Portrait Of Frank Sinatra]] was recorded in Paris, France on May 18, 1959. In less than three months after the session that produced this album the trio would go to Chicago and produce ten classic albums, including the Porter album above. Tracks are:
13. You Make Me Feel So Young
14. Come Dance with Me
15. Learnin' the Blues
16. Witchcraft
17. The Tender Trap
18. Saturday Night (Is the Loneliest Night of the Week)
19. Just in Time
20. It Happened in Monterey
21. I Get a Kick Out of You
22. All of Me
23. Birth of the Blues
24. How About You?

The bonus track is live and believed to be from a London House, Chicago performance that was recorded during a run at that venue on July 28 and 29, 1961. The track is a Cole Porter tune that was released on a 1962 album titled Something Warm:
25. I Love You

title: Great double album set from both of Peterson's songbooks series
text:
This is a two album tribute set that features Peterson's 1959 Richard Rogers Songbook album, and an earlier album titled Oscar Peterson Plays Richard Rodgers and released as Clef MGC 624. Every song on this album is a standard from the Great American Songbook, and both Peterson led trios did each one the justice it deserves.

You will notice a difference between the first twelve tracks, which are from the 1959 album, and the bonus tracks that were from the early 1950s. Some of that is due to the difference in recording technologies that had improved in the ensuing years between albums, but also in the trio format itself. The bonus tracks feature Barney Kessel on guitar, while on the 1959 tracks drummer Ed Thigpen has replaced Kessel. That means that the harmonies between Peterson and Kessel are not present on the earlier music. So the trade-off is richer music for sound quality. You be the judge.

Run through the sound samples on this page to hear what the tracks sound like, including comparing and contrasting the two different trio configurations. The musical differences between the trio with a guitarist and the one with a drummer are dramatic. This makes the album a wonderful study in contrasts for any musician or student since the track lists are virtually the same for both sets of tracks.

For my fellow jazz geeks here are the dates, locations and personnel. On the 52-53 bonus tracks the line-up is Oscar Peterson backed by Ray Brown on bass and Barney Kessel on guitar. On the 1959 tracks (the first twelve on this album) drummer Ed Thigpen - one of my personal inspirations - replaces Kessel.

The first twelve albums were recorded at Universal Recording Studios in Chicago during a marathon set of recording sessions that took place between July 14 and August 9, 1959. Those sessions resulted in ten albums, nine of which were tribute albums covering various songbooks. The bonus tracks were recorded in Los Angeles on December 6, 1953, except for Thou Swell, which was recorded in Los Angeles in June, 1952, and Manhattan, which was recorded in Los Angeles on December 10, 1953.

title: Truly superb small group jazz
text:
This is a treasure of six and a quarter hours of some of the tightest, swingingest small group music I own. Considering that these sessions took place in 1953-54 with the relatively crude state of recording technology the sound quality is amazing. Whoever remastered these discs knew their stuff.

Run through the sound samples on this page for a taste of what's in the set. I had some reservations about Buddy Rich who can be a little wild, but except for a few tracks (like Air Mail Special where he just HAD to do an extended solo), he is supporting the music. His brushwork on tracks where he uses them is masterful.

While I tend to prefer the quartet tracks the two quintet ensembles in this set are as satisfying to my ears. Here are the three ensembles in this set:
Quartet: Lionel Hampton on vibraphone, Oscar Peterson on piano, Ray Brown on bass and Buddy Rich on drums.

Quintet 1: the quartet plus Buddy DeFranco on clarinet.

Qintet 2: the quartet plus Herb Ellis on guitar (and Hamp on vocals).

Here are the sessions and which group played on them:
========
DISC ONE
========
Tracks 1 through 6: Quartet in NYC on September 2, 1953; Tracks 7 through 9: Quartet at the Fine Sound Studios in NYC on April 12, 1954.
========
DISC TWO
========
A continuation of the April 12 session.
========
DISC THREE
========
Quintet 1at the Fine Sound Studios in NYC on NYC, April 13, 1954
========
DISC FOUR
========
Tracks 1 through 10 Quartet in NYC on September 13, 1954. Tracks 11 and 12, Quintet 2 in NYC on September 15, 1954.
========
DISC FIVE
========
Continuation of September 15, 1954 session.

title: Early Peterson with vocals
text:
This is one of three albums I know of that feature Peterson on vocals, and it's a gem. His voice is practically identical to Nat King Cole's.

Sadly there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review because the music and vocals are wonderful. Some critics have panned this album, but I disagree. Perhaps I rated it so highly because of the rarity, but I like to think my rating reflects the music. Of course my personal taste comes into it as well. What is not in dispute is the sound quality on this particular CD. Universal Japan did an excellent job of remastering and re-releasing this album.

In addition to missing sound samples the track listing is also not on this page (at the time of this review). I am providing it so you know what the album contains:
1. I'm Glad There Is You 3:00
2. Polka Dots And Moonbeams 3:16
3. One For My Baby 3:20
4. I Hear Music 2:31
5. Autumn In New York 4:03
6. I Can't Give You Anything But Love 3:10
7. Spring Is Here 2:50
8. These Foolish Things 4:41
9. From This Moment On 2:58
10. The Things We Did Last Summer 4:03
11. Too Marvelous For Words 2:52
12. But Not For Me 2:29

The album was recorded over the course of three sessions. Actually, I believe the last two tracks were thrown in because they were recorded two years earlier. Here are the dates and places for each session: Tracks 1 through 7 were recorded on May 21, 1953 in NYC with Peterson on piano and vocals, Barney Kessel on guitar and Ray Brown on bass. Tracks 8 and 9 were recorded on April 27, 1954 in Los Angeles with Peterson on piano, Herb Ellis on guitar and Ray Brown on bass. The last two tracks were recorded on February 26, 1952 in Los Angeles with Peterson on piano and vocals, Barney Kessel on guitar and Ray Brown on bass.

title: And a voice to sing with
text:
This is rare because it's one of three albums (that I know of) that feature Peterson performing vocals. His voice is surprisingly good, which begs the question regarding why he so rarely sang on recordings. Regardless, he does Nat King Cole justice. Interestingly Cole was also a reluctant vocalist earlier in his career, but once he started he shifted his performances on that aspect. Like Peterson, Cole was a virtuoso pianist, but that's another story.

Run through the sound samples on this page (I am reviewing the CD version) and you will be treated to some of Peterson's vocals, as well as some excellent musicianship in both big band and trio formats. Five of the tracks are big band arrangements by Manny Albam who is also credited as the orchestra leader. The album was recorded in two sessions - one on each coast - for the Limelight label.

Tracks 1, 3, 5, 8 and 10 are big band arrangements that were recorded at the A&R Recording Studio in NYC on November 13, 1965. These tracks feature a front line comprised of John Frosk, Joe Newman, Ernie Royal and Daniel Stiles on trumpet with the latter two also on flugelhorn, a trombone section comprised of Wayne Andre, Jimmy Cleveland and J.J. Johnson with Tony Studd on bass trombone, and a wind/reed section comprised of Seldon Powell and Jerome Richardson on tenor and bass flute, Jerry Dodgion and Phil Woods on alto saxophone and Marvin Holladay on baritone saxophone. The rhythm section was co-led by Hank Jones and Peterson swapping on piano, Barry Galbraith on guitar, Richard Davis on bass and Mel Lewis on drums. Peterson also is the vocalist.

The remaining tracks are a trio format that was recorded in Los Angeles on October 28, 1965 with Peterson on vocals and piano, Herb Ellis on guitar and Ray Brown on bass.

title: A hidden gem
text:
This one nearly escaped me and I am a Mingus fan. This is Mingus at his creative best as an arranger in my opinion. Not only does he manage to orchestrate and lead an ensemble of alto, tenor and baritone saxophones, but manages to arrange in such a manner that each musician has a piece that showcases his talent. I am sure that this was somewhat open as a jam session, but I am equally sure Mingus had some definite guidelines for each musician.

I am reviewing the CD version of this album, and there are no sound samples on that page at the time of this review. I encourage you to listen to the samples on the MP3 album's page at [[ASIN:B00123KE3M Mingus At Carnegie Hall]]. You will only get a hint of what's on the album, but enough to make a purchase decision.

One thing is the music swings like crazy. Yes, sometimes the melody of the two Ellington tunes gets lost in the more creative phrases, but it never ceases to swing, and Mingus should get credit for doing the Duke proud on the two tracks that comprise this album.

The core rhythm section is Don Pullen on piano, Mingus on bass and Dannie Richmond on drums. The front line is Jon Faddis on trumpet, and a saxophone section comprised of Charles McPherson solely on alto saxophone, with John Handy on alto and tenor, Roland Kirk on alto (his 'stritch is a straight Buescher alto) and tenor, George Adams solely on tenor saxophone and Hamiet Bluiett on baritone saxophone.

This album was recorded live a la JATP style (although it's not a Jazz At The Philharmonic performance) at Carnegie Hall on January 19, 1974. I would not classify this as an essential album for Mingus fans, but as another reviewer pointed out, if you are a saxophonist this is must-have.

title: Large ensemble, but DeFranco and Peterson are not lost in it
text:
I received this album as a part of a value-priced set and was a little taken aback when I first listened to it. It seemed too commercial. On subsequent playings the interplay between DeFranco's clarinet and Peterson's piano is simply amazing. It's one of the most impressive displays of musicianship I have heard, but it may take a few run throughs to hear it in its full genius.

Since there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review), you can hear all ten tracks that were originally released on this page: [[ASIN:B000VZMQOM Buddy Defranco And Oscar Peterson Play George Gershwin]]. The CD that I am reviewing has two alternate takes from the original session.

This was first recorded for the Norgran label (later to morph into Verve where it was reissued). The recording session spanned two days in Los Angeles (December 6 and 7, 1954) and feature DeFranco with Peterson's trio at the time comprised of Herb Ellis on guitar and Ray Brown on bass, augmented by Bobby White on drums. In addition to the core ensemble, there is a fairly large brass and reed section as well as strings backing the group. The brass and reed section is comprised of Harry Betts, Nick DiMaio, Murray McEachern, Dick Noel, Tommy Pederson on trombone and Dick DeRisi on French horn, and DeFranco leading a section comprised of Marty Berman, Jack Dumont, Herman Glunker, Jules Jacobs on reed (and woodwind) instruments. Interestingly the backing ensemble punctuates, but manage to not overwhelm the focus on DeFranco and Peterson.

title: Two full albums + bonus track
text:
This set has two otherwise out-of-print albums that Peterson recorded for Verve, plus a single bonus track that was recorded live. The line-ups of all three sources are different, but the unique aspect of this album is Peterson adds his vocals to tracks 2, 6, 10 and 12.

Although there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review you can hear snippets of most of the tracks on these two MP3 album pages: [[ASIN:B000W11KWO Soft Sands]] and [[ASIN:B004MFNA7O Oscar Peterson Plays My Fair Lady]]. Let those guide you.

Here are the specifics about each album:
Tracks 1 through 12 are the album Soft Sands and were recorded in Los Angeles over the course of two sessions on March 28 and July 31, 1957. This is a quartet format with Peterson backed by Herb Ellis on guitar, Ray Brown on bass and Stan Levey on drums.

Tracks 13 through 19 are the album titled Plays My Fair Lady and were recorded in Chicago with Peterson backed by Ray Brown on bass and Gene Gammage on drums.

The bonus track, 20, was recorded live at the Playboy Jazz Festival in Chicago on August 8, 1959 and features what I call the classic trio with Peterson and Brown joined by Ed Thigpen on drums.

This CD clocks in at a total 1 hour and 18 minutes. If you are missing these from your Oscar Peterson collection this set is an easy way to get two otherwise out-of-print (and enjoyable) albums.

title: Essential for musicians and perfect for anyone who loves great music
text:
Peterson and trio do a masterful job of adapting West Side Story to a trio setting, and that is why I claimed it's essential for musicians. Taking a full orchestra score and rearranging it to piano, bass and drums is one aspect of the genius contained within this short album (it clocks in at just thirty-five minutes. Compare the original, [[ASIN:B0000027WF West Side Story (1961 Film Soundtrack)]], to this album you will have a great appreciation for Peterson's arrangement for a trio. More importantly, he manages distill down the original score unto seven songs - for a trio no less - and perform them in a way that I am sure pleased Leonard Bernstein.

There are no samples at the time of this review, but they can be heard here: [[ASIN:B000W21EQA West Side Story]]. I definitely encourage you to give those a listen.

Back to the music itself: Peterson handles the melody lines (ably assisted by Ray Brown on bass in places). It's Brown and drummer Ed Thigpen who add significantly to the tracks because the West Side Story suite requires a strong and complex rhythmic foundation. The way Brown and Thigpen interpreted and provided it in this trio setting is nothing short of remarkable in my opinion. As a drummer I have dissected this album musically many times and remain in awe of it.

Musically - to my ears - this album is as fresh and relevant today as it was over a half century ago when it was first recorded for Verve in NYC during two sessions spanning January 24 and 25, 1962.

title: Wonderful music; poor mastering
text:
Up front: my reason for the reduced rating is uneven sound quality, which is even more frustrating given the superb playing on every track. It's not terrible, but just enough to irritate me and detract from the total enjoyment of listening to a master play the compositions of masters.

This set contains three of the 1951/52 and 1959 songbooks Peterson recorded for Norman Granz. The 1951 tracks feature Peterson on piano, accompanied by Barney Kessel on guitar and Ray Brown on bass. The 1959 tracks are what I call the classic trio with Kessel replaced by drummer Ed Thigpen. Note that the problems I complained about are mainly in the 1951 tracks. I know there are better recordings and masterings out there because I own other albums where those tracks are pristine.

The first disc in this set is the Cole Porter songbook. The 1951 tracks were recorded for the Mercury label and stretched out over three sessions in Los Angeles in November 1951, and February and December 1952. The 1959 tracks were recorded in a marathon session for Verve at the Universal Recording studio in Chicago between July 14 and August 9, 1959. All or the 1959 tracks in this set as well as some other albums were recorded during this session.

Disc Two is the Ellington songbook that was recorded in Los Angeles for Mercury in December 1952 and Verve during the Chicago session I mentioned above.

Disc Three is the Gershwin songbook that was recorded during the same time frames and locations as the Ellington one.

Had the earlier material been better mastered this would easily be a five star set. Personally I would have chosen the same three sets (there are also songbooks for Irving Berlin, Jerome Kern for the 51/52 and 59 albums, and additional ones for Richard Rogers, Harry Warren, Harold Arlen and Jimmy McHugh from the 1959 releases that are still available as individual albums and in other sets.

A final note: the quality of the musicianship is, for me, a coin toss. I love both editions of the trio represented in this set and on some days I prefer the Petterson/Kessel/Brown renditions and others the Peterson/Brown/Thigpen ones. That is a matter of personal preference. If you search for each of the individual albums here in digital music you will find product pages with sound samples that will give you a better idea of the music.

title: A cookin' session
text:
Up front this is one of my favorite albums and I admit to being biased. Lester Young is my most significant musical inspiration. Not something you would expect from a drummer, but it's true. More importantly, he is perfectly paired with Peterson and the backing ensemble. What makes this work so well is Young's tone and phrasing, and the way he and Peterson complement one another. Some of the magic is also from Ray Brown's keen understanding of melody (something that is not often found in a bassist), and the rich harmonic support Kessel adds.

Since there are sound samples on this page let those guide you. Do note that the bonus track for It Takes Two to Tango is risque and probably not fit for playing around young ears.

Oscar's trio comprised of bassist Ray Brown and guitarist Barney Kessel was augmented by J. C. Heard on drums to 'fatten' the sound. Frankly I think Oscar, Ray and Barney would have done just fine on their own. A drummerless trio was a proven formula for them and would continue to be for another seven years. I do think that Heard does add something special though.

This album contains every track that was recorded on August 4, 1952 in NYC. Some sites claim November 1952, but digging into a few discographies and cross referencing information I am going with the August date. This was originally recorded for Norman Granz' Norgran label, which would eventually morph into Verve. Also, this album represents every track, including a fragment of I Can't Get Started on track 14 that was recorded during the session.

title: A compliation of Songbook tracks
text:
This album is a compilation of Peterson's earlier Songbook albums that he recorded in 1952 for the Mercury label (and at the behest of Norman Granz who would form the Clef label, which would morph into Verve.) Note: these songbooks would be repeated with the classic trio (Peterson, Ray Brown on bass and Ed Thigpen on drums) in 1959. While many of the songs are repeated in the 1959 set of albums, both have merit. I own both collections of the albums of which this one is a mere subset, and I am forever tossing a coin when I need to choose a 1952 or 59 songbook.

The tracks here are drawn from the Berlin, Ellington, Kern, Porter and Gershwin songbooks. Eight of the tracks are from Ellington, six from Gershwin, two from Berlin, two from Porter and one from Kern. All of the tracks were recorded in Los Angeles in December 1952, and all feature Peterson on piano, accompanied by Barney Kessel on guitar and Ray Brown on bass.

Sound quality on this album is very good or better. While I personally would have preferred a more even distribution of tracks from all of the songbooks I cannot complain. Each selection is a classic, and each is played beautifully. It's a shame there are no sound samples on this page to showcase that aspect of this collection. If you are a Peterson fan chances are that you already have these albums. If you just discovering Peterson and want a sampling of Peterson in your collection this is a great place to start.

title: Very early OP in a duet
text:
I received this album as a part of a value-priced set titled [[ASIN:B00KBZ74O4 Oscar Peterson & Friends]] and loved the sparseness of each track. At first I though it was Peterson solo, but there was a bass in the mix. More about who played that instrument and on which tracks below.

There are no sound samples on the CD version's product page, but you can listen to sound samples on this page: [[ASIN:B004A6HISM Keyboard]]. If you opt for the MP3 version there is some background noise that sounds like the transfer was made as a needle drop from a worn LP. The CD's sound quality in the set I own has better fidelity.

This was recorded during the second session for the Clef label (forerunner to Verve) that also produced [[ASIN:B00PBN414W Tenderly]]. Peterson is not only a virtuoso pianist, but also an incredibly prolific force in the studio with a long history of marathon sessions that resulted in more than a single album per day. This one is no exception. He cut this entire album in NYC on May 8, 1950, along with tracks from the aforementioned Tenderly. On the first eight tracks the bassist accompanying Peterson is Major Holley, with Ray Brown replacing him on the final four.

Run through the sound samples linked above and you can hear the subtle differences between Peterson with Holley and with Brown backing him. It's more than bass playing alone - he and Ray brown connect on a level that would not be heard again until Peterson began collaborating with Niels-Henning Ørsted Pedersen.

The main reason why I highly recommend this album is Peterson had only been recording for five years when it was made. Already his style was mature and he had a signature sound that would be refined throughout his career, but can be traced back to his performances on this album.

title: A glimpse into the future
text:
Sadly there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review) because you could hear some of the old as well as a hint of what would be coming. Specifically, on Milestones (track 4) would hear the genesis of So What, which is one of the most memorable tracks from the later Kind of Blue album. Another thing is Milestones is a clear indication of Davis' move towards modal arrangements at that point in his career.

Most of this album, though, is the the more familiar work he did for Prestige before moving to Columbia. This album, though, swings a lot more and part of it is the rhythm section that started the classic quintet that morphed into this sextet with the addition of Cannonball Adderley on alto sax. This would be the last of that particular rhythm section, and when Kind of Blue would be recorded - replaced by Wynton Kelley and Bill Evans on piano, and Jimmy Cobb on bass. Paul Chambers would be the bridge that holds Davis' rhythm sections, past and present, together.

One of the reasons why I lamented the lack of sound samples on this page is the swinging and cooking rendition of Monk's Straight No Chaser. While there is a lot to commend every track on this album, that particular one is my personal favorite. Red Garland literally shines on piano, with Paul Chambers and drummer Philly Joe Jones swinging like crazy. Miles, Coltrane and Adderley are perfect on it. That is not to say this is the best track. It's just my personal favorite and is based on my specific tastes. I will go on a limb and say that there is not a single dud on the entire album, which thankfully includes three alternate takes that were not on the original release.

This album was recorded for Columbia in their 30th Street studio in NYC on February 4 and March 4, 1958. Personally I feel it is one of Davis' essential recordings for both the music and as a window into what would be a transitional period for him.

title: Launch of the classic quintet
text:
In some ways this album has historic value as the genesis of Davis' classic quintet. Of course the musical value is the main reason why this is essential for Davis fans. For me Davis' Prestige years are my favorite (and, yes, I acknowledge the great things he did when he joined Columbia.)

The musicians in this line-up are all perfectly matched to Davis' style during this period. Indeed, Coltrane in particular probably influenced Davis' evolution (a constant in Miles' career) beginning with the session that produced this album. As for the rhythm section of Red Garland on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Philly Joe Jones on drums, they were the perfect foundation. Garland and Chambers, in particular, are strong, and Jones - Davis' favorite drummer - adds a lot to this album as well.

Run through the sound samples on this page for a taste of what this album is all about. Coltrane, in particular, is a little more restrained here than on other albums he would record with Davis, but you can hear hints of his sheets of sound that would emerge later. Also, pay careful attention to Garland and Philly Joe, as well as Chamber's amazing bass work that holds things together. This album is unfortunately short, but it foreshadows the final albums Davis would cut for Prestige so he could move over to Columbia.

This entire album was recorded in a single session at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on November 16, 1955. It clocks in at just 33:47, but can be thought of as a seque or intro to Cookin', Relaxin', Workin' and Steamin'. It's definitely in that class of excellence in my opinion and represents my favorite period in Davis' career.

title: Truly unique for Davis
text:
This album is interesting for a number of reasons. Foremost, the ensemble is odd for what Davis was doing in this period. I actually cannot think of a time when he included both a trombone and a vibraphone. The trombone makes sense because it matches the lower registers which Davis had a penchant for (as well as the minor keys he also seemed to favor.) Plus Charles Mingus - both bassist on this album and co-owner of the Debut label that published this album - seemed to favor trombones.

Combined with a vibraphone the entire album has a sound that is vastly different from any other Davis recorded - or that I remember him recording. Some critics cite the cool jazz aspect of this album. To be honest, this does not have any relation to that genre. If anything it's a tribute to Monk's 'Round Midnight (a song Davis recorded nineteen times in his career and played many more.) Listen to the sound samples on this page for evidence of that. The entire album is pensive and the arrangements seem more inspired by Monk's composition than any other album Davis recorded. The trombone on some tracks foreshadows some of Mingus' later albums, including Ah Um, so I am sure he had a hand in writing the arrangements as well.

To be honest, this is not typical Miles Davis fare, and it probably is not the nest album for someone who is just digging into his body of work. For musicians it's worth a listen, especially fans of Davis because it shows another side of his creativity.

The album was recorded for the Debut label at the Audio-Video Studios in NYC on July 9, 1955. That label was a joint venture among Mingus, his wife Cecilia and drummer Max Roach. The ensemble on this album is comprised of Davis on trumpet, Britt Woodman on trombone, Teddy Edwards on vibraphone, Charles Mingus on bass and Elvin Jones on drums.

title: Miles in a quartet setting
text:
I love this album for a number of reasons, but foremost is the fact that Oscar Pettiford is on bass. The stories about Pettiford being intoxicated during the session may or may not be apocryphal, but a listen of the sound samples is telling. His playing - impaired or not - is superb, as are the performances of the entire quartet.

This is the first session with Red Garland on piano who is another of my favorite musicians, and having Philly Joe Jones on drums is the icing on the cake so to speak.

In addition to superb musicianship this album covers a range of musical styles from ballads to blues to up tempo. Nothing boring about the track list or the sequence. I love track 3, I Didn't, which is an answer to Monk's Well, You Needn't. In fact, as a drummer I especially love that song because of how smoothly and adroitly Philly Joe Jones switches from sticks to brushes and back, and his brushwork on Green Haze.

If you are a Davis fan this is an album to own if for no other reason than the quartet format and the personnel who are on it. Of course, the music is great. It was recorded in a single session for Prestige at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on June 7, 1955.

title: Miles and Monk in the studio
text:
This album was actually recorded in two different sessions nearly two years apart. The bulk of the album is from the same session that produced [[ASIN:B0014DM8OS Bag's Groove]], which is a great companion album to this one. The remaining track, 'Round Midnight, is from a session twenty-two months later that was Davis' big push to meet contractual commitments with Prestige so he could move to the Columbia label. For such hurried work and the fact that even the first session was recorded in a signal day, the music is remarkable. In my opinion, anyway.

Run through the sound samples on this page to get a sense of the music. I think that Davis' Prestige years are his golden ones. Yes, he produced some remarkable stuff for Columbia, including Kind of Blue, which is still a best selling jazz album, but the stuff on this album is Davis during one of his many transition points in his career. The sound samples should tell you everything you need to know.

On all but 'Round Midnight the album was recorded in Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on December 24, 1954. The ensemble is Davis on trumpet and Milt Jackson on vibraphone out front, with Monk on piano leading a rhythm section comprised of Percy Heath on bass and Kenny Clarke on drums. Some accounts describe conflict between Davis and Monk during this session, but I am not going to get into that. This was the only studio session where Davis and Monk worked together, and Monk's music is well represented with two of the five total tracks.

'Round Midnight was recorded in the same studio on October 26, 1956 with a different line-up. This session has Davis joined by John Coltrane on tenor sax as the front line with Red Garland on piano leading a rhythm section comprised of Paul Chambers on bass and Philly Joe Jones on drums.

title: Great music as long as you are looking for the CD only
text:
1 star for the product and 5 for the music. Sound odd? At the time of this review the autorip feature is linked to a totally different album that contains two only tracks. That album is [[ASIN:B002B10HKO Bag's Groove]]. Note: the Bag's Groove on the two-track MP3 album is from a January 3, 1959 radio broadcast from Birdland and features Miles accompanied by Cannonball Adderley on alto sax, John Coltrane o n tenor sax, and a rhythm section comprised of Wynton Kelly on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Jimmy Cobb on drums. The second track on that album is also from a Birdland radio broadcast dated May 3, 1952, featuring Miles with Jackie McLean on alto sax, Don Elliot on vibraphone, Gil Coggins on piano, Connie Henry on bass and Connie Kay on drums.

Bottom line: if you do not care about getting this album immediately you actually make out because the erroneously cross-linked album actually adds to this one and you will be getting a second album for free. If you are expecting to get this CD immediately, though, you are going to feel cheated. Still, for the music it's an easy five stars in my opinion.

This album was recoded for Prestige at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on June 29, 1954 (tracks 2 through 7) and December 24, 1954 (tracks 1 and 2). The album was not released until 1957.

One reason why I rate this album so highly is the line-up. The first two tracks, two takes of Bag's Groove, have Davis accompanied by its composer Milt Jackson on vibraphone, backed by a rhythm section comprised by Thelonious Monk on piano, Percy Heath on bass and Kenny Clarke on drums.

On the remaining tracks Davis is accompanied by Sonny Rollins on tenor sax, and backed by a powerful rhythm section comprised of Horace Silver on piano, Percy Heath on bass and Kenny Clarke on drums.

Both sessions produced some excellent music and it's a shame there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review. The performances by all musicians participating in the sessions are uniformly excellent. I especially love the contrast between Monk on the first two tracks and Silver on the remaining ones.

An interesting aspect of this album is Davis allows sideman Rollins to contribute three of his own compositions to the second session (tracks 3, 4 and 6). According to some sources I checked the compositions were not complete during the start of the session with Rollins refining them as he went along. All three went on to become jazz standards is a short time, so this particular album has a place in jazz history as well as being a collection of excellent music. It also captures Davis approach before he segues into his modal phase. He would reinvent himself many times, but this happens to be one of my favorite periods in his career.

title: Truly spectacular
text:
I have long awaited the rerelease of this album because it's sort of the holy grail of some of Harris' recorded work and has been long out of print. On one level I have outgrown bebop, but on another I can never escape because two of my top three favorite pianists are Bud Powell and Thelonious Monk. Of course Tad Dameron is on my short list. This album is Harris performing Dameron's songbook, but in a manner that is fresh. Yes, I listen to the older recordings and love them, but some days they sound a little on the archiac side. Harris on this album sweeps away the cobwebs.

To be sure, part of the reason why I love this album is the backing ensemble, both of whom smooth the flow out a bit. Listen to Dameron and his rhythm section and compare to bassist Gene Taylor and drummer Leroy Williams here. They may not be as exciting as the ryhthm sections in which Dameron served, but they definitely add to the music on this album and give it polish for more modern listeners.

Here, though, Harris is taking Dameron's compositions and making them his own. He makes no effort to mimic Dameron. In fact, you can hear more of Bud Powell's influence in this album. It's a pity that there are no sound samples (at the time of this review) because if you are a Dameron fan you will love what a genius he was through Harris' interpretations of his work, and what a virtuoso pianist and genius Harris is as well.

This album was recorded for the Xanadu label at the RCA studios in NYC on June 4, 1975 and clocks in at 41:53. Truly a masterpiece if you are a Dameron fan or a Harris fan.

title: JATP performances (not all with Miles)
text:
This is a great set from an historical perspective, but I am unsure of the 'pedigree' of this Green Corner label's release since there is no evidence that these were licensed from Verve, which was the label sponsoring the Jazz at the Philharmonic concerts at the time. That issue aside, the sound quality is decent and the music will delight any Miles Davis fan. I have always liked Davis live and the line-up is predictable on most of the tracks. Having Sonny Stitt on alto sax on the October 15, 1960 concert is somewhat unique for a Davis Quintet, but is also a delight as far as I am concerned.

At the time of this review there is scant information about the contents, dates and places on each disc in this set. Before I delve into those details I want to disclose that there are six tracks in this set that do not include Davis. Those are tracks 7 and 8 from disc one and tracks 6 through 9 on disc three. I am mentioning this because the title of the set implies otherwise. Another thing is the bonus tracks on disc three were not recorded in Holland, but instead in Germany.

Some of the front line personnel will change depending on the concerts and dates, but the rhythm section is the same on every track: Wynton Kelly on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Jimmy Cobb on drums. Here is what each disc contains:
========
DISC ONE
========
01 Introduction By Norman Granz 0:44
02 If I Were A Bell 12:05
03 Fran-Dance 7:24
04 So What 10:23
05 All Blues 12:56
06 The Theme 0:58
07 Whisper Not 8:32
08 Ease It 12:21
Total time is 65:26 minutes. The first six tracks are from the Concertgebouw performance in Amsterdam on April 9, 1960 with the full quintet (Davis, John Coltrane on tenor sax and the rhythm section. The final two tracks is from the same venue, but on October 15, 1960 and are performed my the rhythm section functioning as a piano jazz trio.
========
DISC TWO
========
01 Introduction by Norman Granz 1:28
02 But Not For Me 11:12
03 Walkin' 15:20
04 All Of You 15:20
05 So What 9:00 ?
06 The Theme 0:50
07 Stardust 4:08
08 Old Folks 3:46
09 All Blues 12:36
10 The Theme 1:23
Total time is 75:08 minutes. This disc contains the October 15, 1960 concert at the Concertgebouw in Amsterdam and features Davis, Sonny Stitt on alto sax, and the rhythm section.
========
DISC THREE
========
01 So What 17:37
02 `Round Midnight 5:44
03 On Green Dolphin Street 12:27
04 Walkin' 9:09
05 The Theme 0:50
06 On Green Dolphin Street 8:55
07 Autumn Leaves/What's New/Moonlight In Vermont 6:22
08 Walkin' 7:16
09 The Theme 3:31
Total time is 71:55 minutes. The first five tracks are from a separate April 9, 1960 concert at the Kurhaus in Scheveningen. These tracks feature Davis, Coltrane and the rhythm section. The remaining four tracks are a bonus from an earlier concert in Dusseldorf, Germany on March 28, 1960. Davis is not present on these tracks, which feature Coltrane and the rhythm section. Stan Getz is sitting in on tenor sax on the Moonlight in Vermont segment of the medley on track 7.

If you are a fan of Davis or Coltrane this is nice to have. I would not deem it to be essential and there are parts of what this set contains on other albums, so if you have an extensive collection you may already own some of the content. Still, it's a bargain if you don't own any of this material.

title: Mix of hard bop and West Coast styles
text:
I found one of the original copies of this album at an estate sale and while my copy is used the music and sound quality are excellent. This is a good blend of East and West coast styles, with a distinct hard bop edge. Sadly there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review because they would have conveyed in seconds what I cannot describe in words. If you are familiar with Mulligan's mid-1950s work (or Zoot Sims during the same time frame) you have an idea of the music.

While this album was released by the Fontana label in 1964, all of the sessions were recorded in NYC in 1955 and 1956 for the EmArcy label. I'll list the sessions in a comment to this review.

Also at the time of this review there is no track listing on this page. Here are the tracks and times. Total play time is 44:40 on my copy.
A1 Igloo 6:50
A2 Sweet And Lovely 2:40
A3 Ain't It The Truth 5:15
A4 Lollypop 5:48
B1 The Lady Is A Tramp 5:10
B2 Makin' Whoopee 3:57
B3 Apple Core 5:23
B4 Bernie's Tune 6:40

The core group appearing on all of the tracks is comprised of Mulligan on baritone sax, Zoot Sims on tenor sax, Bob Brookmeyer on valve trombone, and Dave Bailey on drums. Bassist Bill Crow is on tracks A1, A3, A4, B2 with Peck Morrison in the bass chair on the remaining tracks. John Eardley is on trumpet on tracks A2, A3, B1, B3, B4 and Don Ferrara is on trumpet on the remaining tracks.

I won't claim that this is an essential album, but I will say that it's enjoyable and one that showcases the synergy among Mulligan, Sims and Brookmeyer in particular, and the entire ensembles in general.

title: One of my favorite Costa albums
text:
Sadly there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review), nor is there a track listing. Here is what is on this album:
1. House of Blue Lights
2. My Funny Valentine
3. Diane
4. Annabelle
5. When I Fall in Love
6. What's to Ya

The title track is a Gigi Gryce composition, not the hit composed by Don Raye and Freddie Slack in 1946. Also, tracks 4 and 6 are Costa compositions. It's Costa's approach to each song that I love about this album. The musical approach tends towards modal, but it swings like crazy. This is a treasure for a few reasons. Number one is it's the last recorded work by Costa as a leader. Second, his rhythm section is rock solid. Wendell Marshall on bass is especially strong on the entire album, and Paul Motian on drums is one of my inspirations. I especially love Motian's brushwork and the way he adds to Costa's approach to the music.

Sound quality is superb. The recording and mixing impart a vivid sound that allows you to hear every note played by the trio. More importantly each instrument is perfectly placed in the mix.

This album was recorded in NYC for the Dot label on January 29 and February 2, 1959. It clocks in at 40:15 and is - in my opinion - an essential album for Costa fans. In fact, I also deem it essential for drummers who are either fans of Motian or are mastering the art of brush playing because this contains a wealth of ideas for that.

title: An entire album plus bonus tracks
text:
The first six tracks are the original title album that was recorded live for the Contemporary label at the Lighthouse on May 15, 1953. The front line is comprised of Shorty Rogers on trumpet, Milt Bernhart on trombone, and Bob Cooper and Jimmy Giuffre on tenor sax. The rhythm section features Marty Paich on piano, Howard Rumsey on bass and Shelly Manne on drums.

Basically this is more of a jam session than a planned recording, and the energy is definitely pouring from this album. I'll admit that the sound quality is not stellar, but it's also not terrible. I still awarded five stars because this is truly the birth of the West Coast jazz sound. However, there is a healthy dose of East Coast influence in the music because the West Coast style was just evolving.

Sadly there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review to truly convey the essence of the music. If you are familiar with Shorty Rogers work in the 1950s these tracks are stamped with his signature sound, which seems to dominate any ensemble in which he is playing.

The final three tracks are from a live session at the Lighthouse that was recorded for Contemporary on September 13, 1953. These tracks were intended for albums titled Chet Baker And The Lighthouse All-Stars - Witch Doctor and Howard Rumsey's Lighthouse All-Stars - Mexican Passport, but did not make the release. They feature a front line of Chet Baker and Rolf Ericson on trumpet and Bud Shank on alto sax. The rhythm section features Lorraine Geller (tracks 7 and 9) and Claude Williamson (track 8) on piano, Rumsey on bass and Max Roach on drums. These tracks have a more definite West Coast jazz feel although they were only recorded four months after the first six tracks.

title: Not your average jazz piano trio
text:
I have a few of Higgins's albums, and count myself among his fans. This one is full of musical twists and turns. It goes from pensive tracks to heavily swinging ones, but nothing in your face.

Listen to the sound samples on this page for a taste because you will be treated to snippets of tracks ranging from Cole Porter to Bach and Rachmaninoff - and a lot of territory in between. Eclectic? Perhaps, but strangely the song selection seems to cohesively fit into some unknown theme.

One thing I especially love is the constant interplay between Higgins and bassist Don Wilmer. That alone makes this album worthwhile for any musician. Drummer James Martin is an active participant in the music more than a mere time keeper, and his playing can go from quiet fire to subdued. Whatever the music calls for he provides.

This entire album was recorded in just two days (March 25 and 26, 1996) for Sunnyside at the New River Studios in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. To my ears it's a gem and if you are a fan (or bassist or jazz musician) it's well worth grabbing.

title: Shows McPartland's incredible jazz chops
text:
I discovered this at a local thrift shop in good condition. I wasn't expecting much, but was in for a delightful surprise as soon as I played it. Not just because the vinyl was in decent condition from a play perspective, but also because of McPartland's chops.

McPartland was well established at NYC's Hickory House when this studio album was recorded for Capitol on July 25 and 30, 1956. For some reason her regular bassist, Bill Crow, is replaced by William Britto on this album, but here drummer at the time, Joe Morello, is on it. Morello had been with her since 1953, but was shortly to be recruited by Dave Brubeck.

The focus of this album is McPartland and her virtuoso piano work. Her skill as a musician has sadly been overshadowed by her Piano Jazz radio program for NPR, and this album refocuses the attention on just what an incredible musician she was.

Britto does a competent job on bass and easily locks in with Morello. If you are a drummer accustomed to jaw dropping displays by Morello you may be a little disappointed in how he stays in the background on this album. Personally I am not in the least disappointed because he displays both taste and incredible brushwork on most of the tracks.

Since there is no track list (at the time of this review) here is what the album contains:

A1 Stompin' At The Savoy
A2 The Things We Did Last Summer
A3 Bohemia After Dark
A4 Dream A Little Dream Of Me
A5 Hallelujah!
B1 The Baron
B2 This Love Of Mine
B3 Carioca
B4 Symphony
B5 There'll Be Other Times

The last track is a McPartland composition, which I think stands out nicely among the standards that comprise the rest of the album. Total time is 36:18 of delightful music and incredible musicianship on the part of every member of the trio.
