title: Maybe not the absolute best, but darn good
text:
Like all 'best of' and 'greatest hits' compilations this one is not all inclusive. However, I can say that if a friend asked me to recommend an album representative of the Andrews Sisters I would probably recommend this one.

What surprises me is there are tracks in this collection that are from the late 1930s, yet the sound quality is very good. Also, the song selection contains the material that a fan would immediately associate with the sisters. Since there are sound samples on this page the best way to get a sense of the sound quality and the songs is to run through those.

While this is a nostalgic album for folks my age (I am 66 at the time of this review and grew up listening to my parents play this music), the music itself is timeless. The likes of Christina Aguilera has covered some of their music relatively recently, and the Puppini Sisters have crafted their entire act to have the sound and feel of the sisters (although they are not a tribute group.) That speaks volumes about the quality of the music, but the real value if you are a musician is the songs on this album are a study in both arrangements and harmony. Especially the latter.

If you are a fan you probably have all of the material on this album. If you are just 'discovering' the sisters this is a wonderful starting point for a collection of their better known work.

title: One of my favorite Mann albums
text:
I was inspired to write this review because my pianist and I were mesmerized listening to this album enroute to a gig today. In particular the harmonic genius displayed on the five tracks that feature Jack Nimitz on baritone saxophone and bass clarinet, and Urbie Green on trombone are reason enough to get this album.

It's interesting that Mann opted for mainly lower register instruments for most of this album. That is part of the reason why it's my top pick for Mann's work. Some of the harmonization between Mann and Nimitz, especially with Mann also on bass clarinet while Nimitz is on baritone sax seems impossible, but they pull it off wonderfully. Another highlight is how Green harmonizes with his trombone (not to mention some of his solo work.) The icing is Joe Puma on guitar who adds a lot to the mix, as well as Oscar Pettiford on bass who manages to move things along. Charlie Smith is a special case for me. I first came across him on a video clip from a 1952 TV program where he was the drummer backing Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie on Hot House. I was so taken with his playing that I have snapped up nearly every album on which he played. On this particular album his brush work on track 2, When The Sun Comes Out, is so unique and spot on for the music that I have played it over and over to get a sense of what he is actually doing.

The three tracks without Nimitz and Green are 3, 6 and 8. They are stand outs as well, but the five that contain the full ensemble are pure gold in my opinion. As another review has mentioned, Lazy Bones is a great rendition. It's certainly different from any other rendition that I have ever heard, but it is a perfect vehicle for the harmonization I mentioned above. You can listen to sound samples of these tracks on a double album set titled [[ASIN:B0055WHK92 Let Me Tell You]].

This album was recorded for Riverside in two sessions at the Reeves Sound Studios in NYC. The first session was on April 1, 1957 and produced all of the tracks with the full ensemble, and the second session was without Nimitz and Green, which produced tracks 3,6 and 8.

title: Advanced playing for 1953
text:
This jam session - which what it was - was recorded for the Contemporary label on February 21, 1953 at the Lighthouse. At the time jazz was in both a confused state and in transition. Part was due to bebop not capturing the mainstream, emergence of R&B and other factors. Also, the music on this album was quite different from what the east coast musicians were playing. There were shared ideas because many Lighthouse sessions featured NYC musicians, but the music on this album was more melodic and flowing compared to what a lot of eastern recordings were offering.

Sadly there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review), and describing music with words has never been my strong suit. If I had to pick a favorite track (and my choices change with my mood), right now it would be All the Things You Are. It features Shorty Rogers on trumpet with Hampton Hawes on piano comping behind them before taking a ride himself. I love Hawes, but he is only on this, Morgan Davis and La Soncailli on the album. The other tracks feature Frank Patchen on piano.

The rest of the line-up are Bob Cooper and Jimmy Giuffre on tenor sax, Milt Bernhart on trombone, Lighthouse owner Howard Rumsey on bass and Shelly Manne on drums. Carlos Vidal is on congas on Viva Zapata.

Recording quality is excellent considering the era, and the music has a distinct West Coast flavor. The crowd noise is not overly loud and adds to the ambiance. If you find this album to your liking I strongly recommend checking out [[ASIN:B00000605J Sunday Jazz A La Lighthouse, Vol. 2]], which was recorded not long after this album in May and September with a slightly different line-up. The line-up is different, but the flavor of the music isn't.

title: Beautiful and eclectic collection of tracks
text:
This album is a beautifully arranged and performed set of standards. Some folks claim Higgins' approach is close to Bill Evans, but I disagree. For one thing, each track on this album has a different energy (for lack of a better way of putting it). The tempos and rhythms are vastly different from Evans' body of recorded work and I am an Evans fan who has most of his albums.

Sadly there are no sound files at the time of this review, but you can find a few tracks from this album by searching the web. If you are unfamiliar with Higgins' style and playing those will give you a good idea about this album.

Another aspect that I love is the rhythm section backing Higgins. I will confess that I know little to nothing about bassist Jay Leonhart or drummer Mark Taylor, but they are both superb on this album. I especially admire Taylor's brush work. Of course Leonhart is also locked in to both Higgins and Taylor and provides the perfect pulse regardless of tempo.

The LP of this album was issued with only eight tracks, so I am guessing that the additional ones were intended for CD only. This and three other albums were recorded for Venus (a Japanese label) at the Clinton Studio in NYC on June 18 through 21, 2005. Different sources claim October 14 through 17, 2006, but I am trusting the source claiming 2005. The other albums that were recorded during the sessions are [[ASIN:B0029NYFMU Secret Love]], [[ASIN:B0029NYFK2 A Lovely Way To Spend An Evening]] and [[ASIN:B0029NYFNY You Are Too Beautiful]], each of which are a continuation of this one in mood and performance. To be honest you cannot go wrong with any of them, but I opted to review this one because I happen to be listening to it (again) as I write this review.

title: Great tracks from three days in Japan
text:
This album sticks strictly to Harris and his rhythm section live over a three day period in April 1976. There were other recordings made by Harris during these three live performances, but they were in quartet and quintet formats, and are not included on this album. All of the tracks were recorded for the Xanadu label with Harris backed by Sam Jones on bass and Leroy Williams on drums.

The first three tracks were recorded on April 1, 1976 at Yubin Chokin Hall in Tokyo. There is some dispute over the exact date in discographies I checked, with one pointing out that the eleven day gap between these tracks and the next set is an overly long time. Regardless, after dispensing with a standard Harris goes right into two bebop anthems and does them justice.

Tracks 4 through 7 were recorded at the same venue on April 12. During this performance there were five tracks that are not included here, but feature Jimmy Raney on guitar.

All of the remaining tracks were recorded at Sun Plaza Hall in Tokyo on April 14, 1976. It's the trio on all but Fukai Aijo where Harris is solo. The entire performance was divided among Harris and his trio, and performances led by Charles McPherson and Jimmy Raney. Sadly there are two tracks not included where McPherson and Raney join with the trio on alto sax and guitar respectively.

Overall this is an excellent showcase for Harris' talents (as well as Jones and Williams.) The tracks are a nice mix of standards, bebop anthems and two of Harris' own compositions (A Soft Spot and Fukai Aijo). Personally I would rank this album as essential for any Harris fan. The choice of music and musicianship are excellent. And while I somewhat lament the lack of the quartet and quintet tracks that were recorded during the Japan tour, I understand why they were not included because Harris is at his best in a trio format

title: Early, live performances with two incarnations of the quartet
text:
At the time of this review there are different albums linked to the same body of reviews, which can be confusing. This is unfortunately common here so be aware that the album that I am reviewing is on this page: [[ASIN:B00BGETM1M The Dave Brubeck Quartet In Europe]]. It shares no tracks or even date and location with the MP3 version, so if you are on that page this review will not make sense.

This is a double album set that contains the Copenhagen concert from March 5, 1958 that was recorded live for Columbia records and released as an catalog number CL 1168. This performance is the classic quartet line-up comprised on Dave Brubeck on piano, Paul Desmond on alto sax, Gene Wright on bass and Joe Morello on drums. Since there is no track list at the time of this review I am providing it so you can clearly note the difference between this album and others that are erroneously cross linked to it. Also it will give you an idea of the actual contents because the first song does not show up on any other of the quartet's albums.
1. Wonderful Copenhagen
2. My One Habit Is Falling In Love
3. Tangerine
4. The Wright Groove
5. Like Someone In Love
6. Watusi Drums
Like most of the live albums this one has a lot of energy, and two of my favorite songs (Tangerine and The Wright Groove). While my favorites are subjective, if you are a fan you will probably enjoy this album. Especially if you like their live albums.

The remaining tracks are an album titled Dave Brubeck Quartet Live Featuring Paul Desmond. This is an earlier line-up that has Brubeck and Desmond backed by Bob Bates on bass and Joe Dodge on drums. If you are not familiar with the earlier line-ups of the quartet do not write this one off because some of the great albums by the quartet were recorded before the Wright/Morello rhythm section (for example, Jazz Goes to College and the Oberlin concert.) Regardless, tracking down the actual date of this one is an exercise in futility. My two most referenced discography sites for Brubeck disagree not only with each other, but what the liner notes of this album claim. The liner notes say NYC, September 1956. A Brubeck-specific site claims 1954 (Bates was not with the quarter during that year), and jazzdisco org claims Italy 1956. The problem with that is the quartet was not in Italy at that time, although a reissue was made by an Italian label that probably accounts for that confusion. I am going to say 1956. To most folks this is probably too pedantic, but we jazz fanatics need this information to ensure that albums we desire are not a repackaging of something we already have. The tracks of this album are:
1. Shis Kebab
2. Fare Thee Well, Annabelle
3. Don't Worry 'Bout Me
4. Lover Come Back To Me
5. Royal Garden Blues
6. How High The Moon
7. Love Walked In

This album was recorded for the bandstand label with a total time of 1:18:31. The sound quality of both albums in this set is very good considering they are live performances that were recorded nearly sixty years ago.

title: Half of a two live engagement
text:
There are a few things about this album and I want to get one out of the way first. This is a different side of Hawes' playing. He is more subdued and interactive on this album than he is on others, and if you are deeper into his earlier work you will be taken slightly aback. Give the album a chance because after a few listens it will grow on you. Or, at least it did me and I hate change.

The other thing you need to know that this and a companion album titled [[ASIN:B000000YZP I'm All Smiles]] were both recorded for Contemporary at Mitchell's Studio Club in Los Angeles on April 30 and May 1, 1966. Discographies I have cross checked do not show which tracks were recorded on which sets, or even days. I will say that the mood shifts from one album to the other and I am not sure if it is because of selective editing or if they were, indeed, different days (or sets).

What I do know is there is a telepathic bond among Hawes, bassist Red Mitchell and drummer Donald Bailey. It goes deeper than mere interplay - there are new nuances between and among them that I hear each time I play this (and the other) album, which lately has been often.

Sadly there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review). There are tracks from each album that will surface if you diligently search them out on the web, but there is nothing like listening to both this and the other album back-to- back. I will forewarn you that if you are a Hawes fan who loves his earlier work this is going to take you aback the first time you hear it. If you take the time to listen without judgement and when you can devote your ears and mind to it you may grow to appreciate it as I have. Inside is another view of Hawes' genius.

title: A different side of Hawes
text:
You'd swear that Hawes was channeling Bill Evans on this album, and when I first heard it I was a little disappointed. The more I listened the more I realized the true depth of his genius. More importantly I started to search any albums with Donald Bailey on drums because he and Red Mitchell are connected to Hawes on this album at a level non-musicians cannot fathom.

This is one of two albums that were recorded simultaneously for Contemporary at Mitchell's Studio Club in Los Angeles on April 30 and May 1, 1966 (the other is [[ASIN:B000000YPD Seance]]). I do not know if one album is set one and the other set two, or if the tracks are mixed, but the two are relatively seamless. The mood changes on Seance, so perhaps it's sets from two different days.

Unfortunately there are no sound samples at the time of this review because they would give a good idea of the music and how different this (and Seance) are from more of Hawes' other albums. I will say that if you take the chance and get this album, and you dislike it upon first listen, give it a chance. Set it aside for a time when you can sit back and listen without interruption or distraction. It grew on me, and it may on you.

title: Great collaboration
text:
This is the second album featuring Brubeck with a trio and Gerry Mulligan as guest artist after the break up of the Quartet. The line-up is - to me - powerful with Jack Six on bass and Alan Dawson on drums. I loved Joe Morello as drummer with the Quartet, but Dawson is a chops monster as well. Their technical abilities are close, but styles are different. As for Six replacing Gene Wright on bass, again, I love both, but Six picks up an electric bass that adds a dimension to this album that Wright's double bass would not. Both are exceptional bassists, but different in approach.

As long as I am comparing, I will say that while Paul Desmond and his alto sax were the soul of the Quartet (in my opinion), Mulligan and his baritone sax are incredible here. Especially on the tracks on which Six is playing electric bass. Moreover, even Brubeck gets into the act with an electric piano on a track.

Sadly there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review and this album is out of print. Also, there is no track list, so I am proividing that:
A1 Limehouse Blues 4:47
A2 Journey 8:56
A3 Cross Ties 11:07
B1 Broke Blues 4:57
B2 Things Ain't What They Used To Be 7:21
B3 Movin' Out 5:33
B4 Blues Roots 6:50

Five of the seven tracks were composed by either Brubeck, Mulligan or producer Teo Macero. Brubeck composed Cross Ties and Movin' Out, Mulligan composed Journey and Macero composed Broke Blues. Brubeck and Mulligan share composer credits for Blues Roots. The remaining two titles are standards with Limehouse Blues by Furber and Braham (and one of Django Reinhardt's signature songs) and the Mercer Ellington (Duke's son) tune, Things Ain't What They Used to Be.

This album was recorded for Columbia in NYC on October 4 and December 13, 1968. It is no longer in print and I was fortunate enough to find my copy in VG condition at a local thrift shop. If you are a Brubeck or Mulligan fan this is worth tracking down.

title: Clever title and intriguing music
text:
I acquired this gem like most other vinyl albums by rummaging through thrift shop bins. Honestly I had never heard of this album and I have a large Brubeck collection. The music is uniformly excellent on every track, but the real essence of this album is the riddle(s).

According to the liner notes (written by Brubeck) the riddle(s) are 'to discover the thematic relationship of each of the tunes. The second riddle is to detect which parts of the music are written, and which are improvised.' Therein lies the value and pleasure of this album - there is a coherent theme to the tracks in both content and sequence, which makes listening not only a pleasure, but an intellectual exercise. The latter is optional. If you just want to sit back and listen the music will consume you anyway. There is nothing abstract or strange about this album. For one thing Bill Smith on clarinet is both a classical and a jazz musician. Having Brubeck along with Joe Morello on drums and Gene Wright on bass providing a rhythmic foundation that swings is perfect backing. Normally I would lament the Quartet sans Paul Desmond, but not in this case. Smith brings something great to the session and gives the 'Quartet' a slightly different character.

A search of the web will reveal some of the tracks from this album (the title track is apparently both prevalent and popular), but you will have to snag the album to hear the entire set. And while songs can stand alone, listening to this album in the sequence and in its entirety will reveal a lot more than the songs in isolation. In that respect this is a synergistic collection of tracks.

Since there is no track list (at the time of this review) I am going to provide it:
A1 Hey, Ho, Anybody Home? 5:22
A2 The Twig 4:15
A3 Blue Ground 5:40
A4 Offshoot 2:38
B1 Swingin' 'Round 7:35
B2 Quiet Mood 6:00
B3 The Riddle 3:56
B4 Yet We Shall Be Merry 3:36

This album was recorded in NYC for Columbia on August 12, 1959 and released in 1960. If you can get your hands on a copy of this album it may just become a favorite. For the time being my copy is getting a lot of play.

title: A seminal Puma album
text:
This and [[ASIN:B005L0KBKI The Jazz Guitar of Joe Puma]]are a great start of a Joe Puma library. If you are on the CD's product page there are no sound samples at the time of this review. I recommend checking out the MP3 version at [[ASIN:B00HJ19UPY Wild Kitten (Bonus Track Version)]]. That format has additional tracks that the CD lacks, but those tracks can be found on The Jazz Guitar of Joe Puma that I mentioned above. Between the two, you will get a lot of Puma's work in different musical settings.

Tracks are basically the original album of Wild Kitten with two bonus tracks from a Various Artists album released by the Harmony label in 1956.

The main album, tracks 1 through 8, were recorded during two separate sessions with two line-ups for the Dawn label in 1957. The first session in NYC was on February 25 and features Puma with Mat Mathews on accordion, Whitey Mitchell on bass and Shadow Wilson on drums. The tracks recorded during that session are 2 through 4 and 7. Tracks 1, 5, 6 and 8 were recorded during an unspecified date in February with the same line-up except Oscar Pettiford replaces Mitchell on bass.

As a previous review mentioned, Mathews on accordion manages to go off on a few tangents, but for me the tracks with Pettiford redeem it, and also Shadow Wilson makes this album worthwhile for me because he is one of my influences.

The last two tracks are included as a bonus and are from an album titled Various Artists - Modern Jazz Festival that was recorded for and released by Harmony. The actual recording was in NYC on June 13, 1956 and features Puma with Tom Stewart on baritone horn, Steve Lacy on soprano saxophone, Herbie Mann on tenor saxophone, Whitey Mitchell on bass and Herb Wasserman on drums.

title: Excellent collection of Puma's work as leader and sideman
text:
This album is a jazz guitarist's dream for a few reasons. Foremost, it highlights Puma's earlier work, but also provides an opportunity on some tracks to compare him to other established and rising stars of the instrument. More importantly, it places Puma in a number of different musical contexts, so it is not only enjoyable listening, it's also a trove is musical ideas for jazz guitarists.

If you are on the CD's product page refer to the MP3 version's page at [[ASIN:B005L0KBKI The Jazz Guitar of Joe Puma]], which contains both a track list and sound samples. I am not going to repeat the track titles here because it's redundant. The sound samples will give you a good idea of the music on this album.

The first eight tracks are an opportunity to hear Puma with fellow guitarist Barry Galbraith on an album titled Joe Puma - East Coast Jazz/3 that was recorded for the Bethlehem label in NYC on November 30, 1954. Along with the two guitarists are Don Elliot on vibraphone, Vinnie Burke and Teddy Sommer on drums.

Tracks 9 through 12 have Puma paired with another top guitarist, Dick Garcia, and both are backed by Danny Martucci on bass and Al Levitt on drums. These tracks are from an album titled Jimmy Raney/Chuck Wayne/Joe Puma/Dick Garcia - The Four Most Guitars that was recorded for ABC-Paramont at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on December 18, 1955. Raney and Wayne do not appear with Garcia and Puma on the source album, which itself is a compilation. It's a pity that never happened, but these and the first tracks do give some context to Puma's style compared to both Galbraith and Garcia.

Track 13 is a single track from a Vinnie Burk album titled The Vinnie Burke All-Stars that was recorded for ABC-Paramont in NYC on July 22, 1956. Puma is backed by Eddie Costa on piano, Vinnie Burk on bass and Jimmy Campbell on drums.

The remaining tracks are from an album titled Joe Puma Quartet And Trio that was recorded for the Jubilee label in late summer 1957 in NYC. I could not pinpoint an exact date. Tracks 14 through 16 feature a trio with Puma backed by Eddie Costa on vibraphone and Oscar Pettiford in bass. The remaining three tracks feature a quartet with Puma backed by Bill Evans on piano, Oscar Pettiford on bass and Paul Motian on drums.

title: Incredible performances on each track
text:
First, I want to acknowledge that Thompson is only one of two soprano saxophonists who truly impress me. For the record the other is Sidney Bechet. Unlike Bechet who used a lot of vibrato to control the unruly instrument, Thompson manages to make do what we wants without masking the inherent out-of-tune nature of the instrument. He is also masterful on tenor sax on this album, but it's the soprano work that makes this a gem.

The backing ensemble also could not have been better chosen. While I am not very familiar with bassist Richard Davis he is excellent on this album. Hank Jones is the perfect choice of pianist. I am a long time fan and I just love how he keeps the music flowing. Drummer Connie Kay of MJQ fame is one of my major influences, so having him in the rhythm section is a major plus for me.

Unfortunately there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review), so you'll have to trust me when I say this album is worth it. The music itself is not in the least subdued - it's fiery in quiet way in spots - but it is overall a fairly mellow album. Not elevator music by any stretch, but not in your face. I mentioned that Jones' piano kept it all flowing and that is the best way I can describe it.

At the time of this review this page also lacked a track list. Here it is, along with track times:
1. In a Sentimental Mood (5:49)
2. Fly With the Wind (4:01)
3. Mid-Nite Oil (5:08)
4. Reminiscent (4:04)
5. Mumba Neua (4:47)
6. I Forgot to Remember (6:36)
7. Prey-Loot (4:05)
8. Invitation (4:55)

Total time comes in at 39:25, and all but the first and last tracks are Thompson's own compositions. The album was recorded for Prestige in a single session at Rudy van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs, NJ studio on September 15, 1964. If you are a Thompson fan (or soprano saxophonist) this is definitely a must-have album in my opinion.

title: Early McRae backed by two iconic arrangers
text:
This was McRae's fourth album and her second for the Decca label. The music is beautifully arranged by Tadd Dameron and Jimmy Mundy, both of whom led backing orchestras on this album. In that respect this album has two distinct flavors. Dameron's tracks (1, 3, 5 and 6) have a big band feel, while the remaining tracks credited to Mundy include a lush layer of strings.

Since there are multiple versions of this album you need to know that I am reviewing this one: [[ASIN:B000051TM5 Blue Moon]]. At the time of this review there are sound samples on the product page, so instead of my trying to describe the music let those convey what is on this album. For the record I much prefer Dameron's arrangements, but when this album was recorded and released in 1956 Mundy's tracks were more in keeping with mainstream tastes. Not that Mundy didn't know a thing about swinging big band arrangements since he did the Goodman arrangement of Louis Prima's Sing, Sing, Sing that took down the house at Goodman's 1937 Carnegie Hall concert that became the swing era's anthem.

Arrangements and backing orchestras aside, the focus of this album is McRae and even at this early stage of her career it's apparent from the tracks on this album that she was a rising star. While her voice would continue to improve like a fine wine throughout her career, she had already established her own sound and it shows on this album. If you are a fan this early material is well worth getting.

The entire album was recorded in NYC in just three sessions spanning March 28 through 30, 1956, with Dameron's four tracks on the 28th and the remaining ones by Mundy on the other two sessions.

title: Truly one of McRae's best
text:
I discovered this album by accident and was stunned that I did not know about it before. Of the collection of McRae's albums I own - dozens - this one stands out as one of her best. I won't say 'the best' because that is a matter of personal taste, but I will say that if you are a fan and do not own this one you are missing an essential album from her body of work.

Since there are sound samples on this page (I am on the CD version's page at [[ASIN:B0000034QO Any Old Time]]) give those a listen to hear what I am trying to say. Her voice is slightly lower in pitch at this point in her career, but to me it adds a lot of nuance to her delivery of every song. More importantly, her backing ensemble is one of the best. Add in Clifford Jordon to her own quartet and McRae's vocals are perfectly showcased to my ears.

Her quartet during this period and on this album was comprised of Eric Gunnison on piano, John Collins on guitar, Scott Colley on bass and Mark Pulice on drums. While the ensemble is tight and Jordon's tenor saxophone adds a lot to this album, Collins' guitar and especially Colley's bass work stand out.

This album was recorded in NYC on June 23, 1986 for Denon (a Japanese label) and released the same year. How it took me until 2015 to 'discover' it is a mystery, but rest assured it is getting a lot of play time.

title: Three entire albums plus much more of early Wes
text:
This is a comprehensive set of albums and parts of other albums from 1955 to 1958. Along with [[ASIN:B00UXDJ0CS Echoes of Indiana Avenue]] this is a great foundation of Wes' beginnings (although he as a sideman on a number of recordings dating back to 1948 through 1955 with Lionel Hampton and a handful of others).

If you are in the CD product page jump to the MP3 version to hear sound samples at [[ASIN:B00CFAHJAM The Montgomeryland Sessions]]. Most of the tracks here feature Wes with his brothers, and some are from albums in which he is a sideman. Here is a rundown on the source albums:

On Disc One the first seven tracks are from the album titled [[ASIN:B00O3TG1NY The Montgomery Brothers Plus Five Others]] that was recorded for World Pacific in Indianapolis on December 30, 1957. The front line is Freddy Hubbard on trumpet, Wayman Atkinson and Alonzo Johnson on tenor sax and Wes on guitar. The rhythm section is Buddy Montgomery on vibraphone, Joe Bradley on piano, Monk Montgomery on electric bass and Paul Parker on drums.

Tracks 8 through 14 are the Pacific Jazz label titled Montgomeryland that was recorded in Los Angeles on April 18, 1958. This album features the great Harold Land on tenor sax backed by Wes, and a rhythm section comprised of Buddy on piano, Monk on electric bass and Tony Bazley on drums.

Track 15 is from a Columbia compilation album titled Almost Forgotten that was recorded in NYC on June 15, 1955. It features Wes with tenor saxophonist Alonzo Johnson backed by Buddy on piano Monk on electric bass and Robert Johnson on drums.

Disc Two starts with tracks 1 through 4 from an album titled Monk Montgomery/Wes Montgomery/Buddy Montgomery - Montgomeryland that was recorded for the Pacific Jazz label in Los Angeles on October 1, 1959. This line up features Pony Poindexter on alto sax on tracks 2 through 5, and Wes backed by brothers Buddy on piano, Monk on electric bass and Louis Hayes on drums.

Tracks 5 through 10 are from a Masterworks album titled Kismet that was recorded for World Pacific at the Forum Theatre in Los Angeles on April 22, 1958. Wes is backed by brothers Buddy on vibraphone and Monk on electric bass, Richie Crabtree on piano and Benny Barth on drums.

The remaining tracks are from a Jon Hendricks album titled [[ASIN:B000TEVFCE A Good Git-Together]] that was recorded at Fugazi Hall in San Francisco on October, 1959 (the actual date of the discography I checked was not given.) These tracks feature Jon Hendricks as leader and vocals, Pony Poindexter on alto sax and vocals, Wes on guitar, Gildo Mahones on piano, brother Monk on electric bass and Walter Bolden on drums.

Disc One clocks in at 77:44 and Disc Two at 79:08 for a total of 2:36:43 of Wes' roots. If you are a fan this is actually essential in my opinion.

title: A great collaboration between Shearing and the Montgomery brothers
text:
I came across this album nearly pristine condition at a local thrift shop. Compared to my CD version this original has three less tracks, but the sound quality is much warmer and enjoyable (to my ears).

If you want to hear snippets of how the Montgomery brothers and George Shearing melded into a great session listen to the sound samples of the MP3 version of this album at [[ASIN:B007Z5372G George Shearing & The Montgomery Brothers]]. Since I am a fan of both this album gets a lot of play in my rotation. While I love Wes alone, I have always enjoyed his playing when his talented brothers were in the mix as well.

At the time of this review there was no track listing on this product page and since this has the original tracks I am going to provide it (plus track times):
SIDE A
A1 Love Walked In 2:10
A2 Love For Sale 3:32
A3 No Hard Feelings 3:45
A4 Enchanted 3:41
A5 Stranger In Paradise 4:47
SIDE B
B1 The Lamp Is Low 2:11
B2 Double Deal 3:47
B3 And Then I Wrote 3:15
B4 Darn That Dream 4:18
B5 Lois Ann 3:08
B6 Mambo In Chimes 2:26

Compare those to the existing CD and MP3 albums, most of which have bonus tracks that this one lacks.

This album was recorded for the Jazzland label at the United Recording Studios in Los Angeles on October 9 and 10, 1961. If you are a Wes Montgomery fan this would be his last album for Jazzland because he moved to the Riverside label shortly after. He would also not record with his brothers again until his last recorded performance via a television broadcast from Detroit, in 1968.

The core line up for all tracks are Wes and Shearing on guitar and piano, backed by Buddy Montgomery on vibraphone, Monk Montgomery on bass and Walter Perkins on drums. On tracks A5, B1 and B6 additional percussion is performed by Armando Peraza and Ricardo Chimelis on bongos and congas (and Chimelis also on timbales).

title: Powell personified
text:
While I personally do not buy into the common claim that Powell was starting a decline around the time the 1953 performances on this album were recorded I have to admit that he is strong here. Part of the reason why this album is so excellent is his backing. With Oscar Pettiford on bass and Roy Haynes on drums he has a dream rhythm section who understood the music and provided exceptional support.

While there are no sound samples on this page you can get a good idea of the music on this album from samples on an album that was recorded about two weeks later: [[ASIN:B0013AT05C Inner Fires]]. Powell's playing is practically identical, and that album also features Haynes on drums, but Charles Mingus on bass instead of Pettiford who is on this one.

As expected, there is a heavy bop undercurrent in the music, but these are not cookie-cutter performances. The entire trio obviously put their hearts into each note, and no matter how many times you hear Powell play a tune there is going to be something different and innovative that you've never heard before. Same for Pettiford and Haynes. Especially Pettiford who I think is perfect for this set of sessions.

The sessions are a series of radio broadcasts by WJZ radio from Birdland in NYC. The first five tracks were broadcast live on March 21, 1953 and the remainder were broadcast on the 23rd. Interestingly these tracks were not released until 1977, and when they were released it was by a label that would not exist until 1964 (ESP Disk). Thankfully these have survived and they sound quality is better than I expected considering they were from a radio broadcast in the early 1950s.

title: Nice find and back in print
text:
I never had the pleasure of hearing the original recordings, but when this was re-released by the Solar label in October 2014 I managed to purchase a copy before the end of the year. I have a number of mid-1960s albums and videos of Monk from this particular period and this is among the better recorded performances.

Sadly there are no sound samples or track list on this page at the time of this review. The tracks from both CDs come in at a total of 1:49:36. The tracks are:

========

05 Epistrophy #1
Total Time: 46:56
========
DISC TWO
========

These tracks feature Monk backed by Ernie Henry on alto saxophone, Paul Chambers on bass and Willie Jones on drums.

The sound quality is above average for a live recording, and although the group had a heavy schedule during this period they were especially tight for this performance. In fact, the schedule probably is why the were so good, because they had recorded in France at various studios and broadcasts on March 18, 20 and 23 prior to this Swiss performance.

title: Perfect mood music
text:
I pull this out on rainy days or when I want to create a mood. Garland could have easily pulled this album off solo, but I am happy he opted for a trio format. I am not familiar with bassist Larry Ridley, but do admire his playing on this album. Drummer Frank Gant is on other albums I own (Yusef Lateef and Ahmad Jamal) and is a known quantity to me. I have long admired his brushwork and count him as an influence so his participation on this album is one of a few reasons why I rated it so highly.

The main reason I awarded five stars is Garland's playing. He has repeatedly been called lyrical by critics and that quality shows here. Of course he can swing a ballad, adding a level of interest that can get your feet tapping. That is no mean feat for the material he plays here, which are all standards. In fact, all of the major names are covered: Hammerstein, Kern, Carmichael, Hart, Gershwin, Berlin, Ellington and Strayhorn to name but a few. In other words, these are not boring ballads, but quality compositions performed by a tight jazz trio.

Listen to the sound samples on this page for a taste of the music. On each Garland's unmistakable style practically leaps out, so if you are a fan you are not going to be disappointed. Even if you think nearly forty minutes of back-to-back ballads are boring, I assure you, Garland's arrangements and the trio's performance on the entire album is anything but. Relaxing, yes. Even romantic if that is the mood you are trying to create.

This album was recorded in a single session for the Jazzland label in the Plaza Sound Studios in NYC on November 30, 1961.

title: A treasure on many levels
text:
As blasphemous as it may sound, the sound quality on this album is decent, but the mix leaves something to be desired. Still, having an extra 150 minutes of Garland (with Philly Joe Jones on drums and Leroy Vinnegar on bass no less) is a welcome addition to my library. These tracks join the 132 tracks I already owned from various Red Garland albums and compilations.

I mentioned that the mix is a little less than optimum. Part of that is Philly Joe is a little too prominent on most of the tracks. To be fair, part of that is Philly Joe's own style. On the other hand it's a treat to be able to hear Vinnegar's every bass note on every track. I have more than a few albums with Vinnegar (including a very special one with guitarist Oscar Moore), and this is the first album where I can truly enjoy his genius on bass.

Sadly there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review) because the playing is spectacular. Music aside, one of the main reasons why I awarded this album five stars is because of the booklet that comes with it. A lot of it's testimonials from older and younger musicians, but there are nuggets of insight into Garland the musician and man. As another reviewer has mentioned, it's a shame there is no biography on Garland. However, he has not exactly faded into obscurity as others (including editorial reviews) imply. I am certainly a big fan, and most of those in my circle are or they at least are familiar with his body of work. And that brings me to another reason why I rated this album so highly - the music was deemed to have been lost or not recorded and now we have 150 more minutes of Garland's recorded output (as well as Jones' and Vinnegar's).

If you are a fan this is truly essential if for no other reason then it adds to the body of work. If you are just discovering Garland I personally recommend [[ASIN:B000E1NWV4 At The Prelude [2 CD]]], or any of his studio albums from the Prestige era, and especially those he recorded with Paul Chambers on bass and Art Taylor on drums. But you cannot go wrong with this one too!

title: Excellent study in rhythm sections
text:
I have owned a copy of this album on one form or another for literally decades. One of the interesting things about it is the way the rhythm sections change. While Bell is the anchor on bass (and tuba on some tracks), the piano and drums are marked contrasts because there are two different pianists and three drummers. Also, do not let the word, 'Trio' on the album cover fool you because this album also has a trombonist who also switches to vibraphone (Tyree Glenn) on some tracks.

Bottom line, the music is fuller than the album cover implies and is more than you would expect. At the time of this review there is no track list on the CD version's product page; however, if you switch to the MP3 album's product page at [[ASIN:B00EHMF0E8 After the Party's Over]] you can see the track listing as well as listen to snippets of each track. That will reveal more about the music than I can possibly describe in words.

This album was recorded for RCA in NYC between June and July, 1958. Bell, as mentioned, is the only constant since he is the session leader and is on every track. He plays both double bass and tuba.

Hank Jones is the pianist on tracks 1 through 3, 5, 9 and 10. Jones is backed by brother Elvin Jones on drums on tracks 2 and 10, and by Ed Thigpen on tracks 1, 3, 5 and 9.

Charles Bateman is the pianist on tracks 4 and 6 through 8. He is backed by Charlie Smith on drums.

For me one of the main reasons why I love this album is I can compare and contrast three superb drummers, one of whom is sadly forgotten (Smith), but who should be a household name like Thigpen and Jones. More importantly, the contrast between Bateman and Hank Jones has a strong effect on both the bass and drums - especially when the bass is provided by a tuba instead of a string instrument. If you are a musician it's definitely a study in texture, and when you add in Glenn's contributions it's difficult to believe you are only listening to a quartet.

title: My favorite Ashby album
text:
This is the third of eleven albums that Ashby recorded as a leader. All of her albums, including those on which she is a sidewoman, are worth checking out, but this one is my favorite. I cannot pinpoint exactly why other than personal taste, but I am sure the fact that a favorite drummer (Roy Haynes) is on it. I am also taken with each performance by Frank Wess on flute. He and Ashby lock in as a duo with the rhythm section of Haynes and bassist Herman Wright providing a rhythmic fabric and pulse that allows Ashby and Wess to play off one another. By the time this was recorded She and Wess were quite familiar with each others playing since he was also on her first two albums as a leader.

It's a shame that there are no sound samples on this page because the music swings - this is not elevator music by any stretch. Also, there is no track list on this page at the time of this review so I am including it. The album's eight tracks clock in at 39:26:

1. Rascallity 3:54
2. You'd Be So Nice to Come Home To 3:59
3. It's a Minor Thing 3:56
4. Yesterdays 4:22
5. Bohemia After Dark 6:19
6. Taboo 6:15
7. Autumn in Rome 5:33
8. Alone Together 4:58

Tracks 1 and 3 are Ashby's own compositions and the remaining tracks are well known standards. This album was recorded in a single session for the New Jazz label at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on September 19, 1958 and released later that year.

title: Nice blend of R&B and Jazz
text:
This album reminds me more of a fusion of R&B and jazz. It has a certain R&B feel, but also a definite swing and jazz feel. The best way to get a feel for the music itself is to listen to the sound samples. If you are on the CD's product page those and the track list are missing at the time of this review, but can be found on this page: [[ASIN:B001AX9A6G Milt & Hal (Paris, 1968)]].

This is really an album led by tenor saxophonist Hal Singer, which accounts for the generous amount of R&B in the music. Not that Milt Buckner was moving it in the other direction because Buckner was comfortable in a number of musical settings including jazz, jump blues, and R&B. The pairing of Singer and Buckner gives this album a nice flavor as evidenced by the sound samples.

Other members of the ensemble are John Letman on trumpet and Tiny Grimes on guitar. Letman was also a session leader because his album, [[ASIN:B001AX9AKC A Funky Day In Paris]], was also being recorded during the same sessions and the entire ensemble appears on both. Having the great Tiny Grimes on guitar is pure icing on a rather delicious cake.

This was one of the first Black and Blue label's releases and worth grabbing if you are a guitarist or B3 player because of Grimes and Buckner. However, it's not limited to that - it's great music from an era when jazz was morphing into other styles. The album was recorded in a two day set of sessions on July 31 and August 1, 1968 in Boulogne, France. It was originally released with the first six tracks on this album, with alternate takes and previously unissued tracks that are bonuses on this one. This and the Letman album I linked to above make a great pair because the music is consistent across the two albums.

title: One of my favorite albums of Porgy and Bess
text:
Like most jazz musicians I love every Gershwin title on this album, all of which have long since become standards. This album has been in my collection for ages, and the ensemble is first rate. I am more of a piano type, but having Lowe lead this group is a serendipity because his guitar work fits the arrangements so perfectly. But it's his arrangements that truly make this album stand out from among many others dedicated to Porgy and Bess.

At the time of this review there is no track listing, so I am providing it. Total time comes in at 32:49. While it may seem short by today's standards that was the norm for albums during the late 1950s.
Tracks:
01. Summertime ... 4:46
02. Bess, You Is My Woman Now ... 3:05
03. I Loves You, Porgy ... 4:57
04. I Got Plenty O' Nuttin' ... 2:50
05. Oh Bess, Oh Where's My Bess? ... 2:18
06. Red Headed Woman ... 2:22
07. My Man's Gone Now ... 3:24
08. It Takes a Long Pull to Get There ... 2:46
09. It Ain't Necessarily So ... 3:11
10. There's a Boat Dat's Leavin' Soon for New York ... 3:10

All but three tracks feature Lowe on guitar backed by Art Farmer on trumpet, Don Elliott on mellophone and vibraphone, Tony Scott on clarinet and baritone saxophone, Ben Webster on tenor saxophone, George Duvivier on bass and Osie Johnson on drums.

On tracks 3, 5 and 10 the ensemble is in trio format with Lowe backed by George Duvivier on bass and Ed Shaughnessy on drums and vibraphone.

This album was recorded for RCA in NYC on July 16 and 17 and October 3, 1958, and released the same year. For me it's the penultimate version of the Porgy and Bess score. That's a matter of personal taste, but even if you find a different album of the score more appealing the chances are that you will still like this one for the arrangements and performances.

title: A gem among gems
text:
It pays to browse thrift shops because I came across this gem in near pristine condition. I am a Three Sounds fan and this is otherwise out-of-print, hence the title. It is a gem. At the time of this review there is no track list. I am including it here:
A1 When I Fall In Love
A2 Parker's Pad
A3 Blues After Dark
A4 I Got It Bad And That Ain't Good
B1 Straight No Chaser
B2 I Let A Song Go Out Of My Heart
B3 It Could Happen To You
B4 Two Bass Hit
Note that Gene Harris - pianist and band leader - managed to include one of his own compositions (Parker's Pad), and also sprinkled a generous helping of Ellington and standards. I was surprised to find a Monk tune, Straight No chaser, and delighted to discover the John Lewis and Dizzy Gillespie collaboration titled Two Bass Hit. Lest I forget, Benny Golson's Blues After Dark is a real treat as well.

Since this album is out of print and the only copies available are used the sound quality is definitely going to depend on condition. A pristine copy link the one I own, even run through a cheap turntable like my [[ASIN:B00OPEYLPC 3 speed USB Turntable vinyl Record Player]] is an enjoyable listen.

The album was recorded for Bluenote at Rudy van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs, NJ studio in a single session on June 28, 1960. It clocks in at 38:51 and features the original Three Sounds line-up with Harris backed by Andrew Simpkins on bass and Bill Dowdy on drums. If you are a Three Sounds (or Gene Harris) fan this will not disappoint.

title: Format makes all the difference
text:
I am reviewing the Hybrid SACD format of this album ([[ASIN:B0002T21VK We Get Requsts]]) that was mastered by the late George Marino at Sterling Sound. While this is a pricey format it's worth every penny to an audiophile and is so different in sound quality that it's like listening to a different album altogether.

As for the content - the song selection and musicianship - its merits are in the ear and taste of the beholder. I personally love the songs and the way Peterson, bassist Ray Brown and drummer Ed Thigpen interpreted and performed them. You can judge that aspect of the album by checking out one of the other format product pages which contain sound samples. Go to the MP3 album's product page at [[ASIN:B000W29836 We Get Requests]] for samples of the content. Remember, that the sound quality will not be anywhere close, but the content will alert you to whether or not the songs are to your taste.

A few notes about why the sound is superior and background information on the original sessions. Up until Marino remastered this particular edition reissues were being made from the original stereo masters, which had started to deteriorate. Marino 'discovered' the original three track and found that it was pristine. He used that to remaster this particular edition and if you've listened to other copies of this album and compare them to this one you will hear a dramatic difference and improvement. Is it worth it? That is a decision that only you can make. If you are an audiophile I am guessing it is.

This was recorded for Verve over the course of three sessions in NYC on October 19 and 20, and November 20, 1964.

title: Original format not reissue with bonus tracks
text:
While there is nothing wrong with the fact that this is missing the two bonus tracks included with the reissue I wanted to point out that this is the original format as released on December 11, 1961. This album clocks in at 41:45.

Although there are no sound samples on this page you can listen to them on the MP3 version's page at [[ASIN:B00138J9FA Someday My Prince Will Come]] (which also contains the two bonus tracks). Let the samples guide you in a purchase decision.

While this album is touted as a sextet, only the first track is in that format, which has Davis on trumpet, John Coltrane and Hank Mobley on tenor sax, and a rhythm section comprised of Wynton Kelly on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Jimmy Cobb on drums. The remaining tracks are a quintet with Davis, Mobley and the rhythm section (except track 5 in which Coltrane replaces Mobley on tenor sax.)

Three of the tracks are Davis compositions and three are either standards or well known and covered by others. More than a few musicians have covered Someday My Prince Will Come, which is a delightful 3/4 tune that remains popular with jazz musicians. Davis' compositions are tracks 3, 4 and 5.

The entire album (including the bonus tracks if you opt for the expanded version to which I linked above) were recorded for Columbia in three sessions at their 30th Street Studios in NYC. The first session on March 7, 1961 yielded Pfrancing and Drang-Dog, followed by a March March 20 session (Someday My Prince Will Come and Old Folks), with the remaining two tracks cut the next day on March 21. If you do opt for the bonus track album the track titled Blues No. 2 was recorded during the March 21 session with Philly Joe Jones on drums; the alternate take of Someday My Prince Will Come was recorded during the March 20 session.

title: I forecast enjoyment
text:
This is a transparently themed album with every track having to do with weather, including one Christmas song (Winter Wonderland). Actually, the tracks seem to complement one another. Not one does not seem to fit musically. This is solid fare for jazz piano trios, and even in late May as I write this Winter Wonderland seems strangely appropriate.

The sound samples on the CD's product page at [[ASIN:B000000YAS All Kinds Of Weather]] convey all you need to know if you are on the fence about getting this album. If you are a Red Garland fan there are no surprises.

I've never been disappointed in any album that features Garland as leader, and especially those from his Prestige years. The trio here is the familiar Paul Chambers on bass and Art Taylor on drums. One thing I love is Taylor is a prolific drummer who shows up on a number of recordings during the 50s and 60s because he was normally a chameleon who did anything a producer or session leader requested. Here he is under the music, but his brushwork is simply beautiful. Also, the engineer, Rudy van Gelder, seemed to evenly mix all three musicians so that they were using their own dynamic control to level the sound.

This album clocks in at a little under forty minutes and was recorded in a single session at van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on November 27, 1958. If you love piano jazz trios this is a gem in my opinion.

title: This is still great nearly 60 years later
text:
This album is a compilation of Day's hits singles dating back to 1952 (hence the tracks labeled '78RPM version'.) The mono version of this album was released in late 1958 and released in stereo in 1962. However, what is important is this single compilation has some of Day's best pop work, much of which are from films.

Sound quality is surprisingly good considering how long this album has been in print and the age of some of the source tracks. If you are familiar with Day or are a boomer like me this will be very familiar. Run through the sound samples on the MP3 album's page at [[ASIN:B00136NTTY Doris Day's Greatest Hits]] to hear what I am trying to convey. Those are sufficient for both the sound quality and musical content. I am not going to cite my favorite tracks or try to dissect the music. For one thing 'favorite' is a subjective term, and for another I always come off as pretentious when I try to describe music in words - especially when the sound samples I cited do a far batter job.

I will say that if I had to recommend a single Doris Day album to someone wanting to know more about her music this would be it. It's also a safe recommendation for folks in my age range who want a dose of nostalgia (I was born in 1948.) To be sure, there are other aspects of Day as a vocalist that are only hinted at on this album. For example, while she was extremely popular as a mainstream vocalist during her heyday, she was also a superb jazz vocalist who could swing in both large and small ensembles. For that I recommend [[ASIN:B0097ID9W2 Best Vocal Jazz of All Time: The Essential Doris Day]]. There is some crossover between that album and this regarding style, but if you are more interested in her as a jazz vocalist that is the one to get. Or a starting point. But if you want the best of Day as a pop singer this album has withstood the test of time and will probably still be making Columbia money long after I have departed this world.

title: A delightful romp through genres
text:
Musically this is all over the map. Collett and his trio manage to seamlessly segue from one sub genre to another, mixing Monk, Tadd Dameron and Benny Golson with Basie, Strayhorn and even Bill Evans. Oddly it all fits perfectly.

Sadly there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review), but the music is beautifully arranged - one of Collett's strong points - and wonderfully played. On this album he is ably backed by Bob Magnusson on bass and Joe LaBarbera on drums. I have a few other albums pairing Collett and LaBarbera, but Magnusson is new to me. All three are not only flawless together, but forceful as well.

I love the song selections. One can only imaging the mental shifting required of the trio to go from Lush Life to Topsy. Or to get into the Monk medley. Many of the compositions are unsprisingly by pianists like Monk, Randy Weston, Tadd Dameron, Bill Evans and Joe Zawinul, but some are by folks like Billy Strayhorn (a virtuoso pianist, but an even more important composer), tenor saxophonist Benny Golson who has contributed some exceptional compositions and standards, and even Clifford Brown whose Joy Spring kicks off this album. In fact, when you consider Collett who is both a great pianist and arranger the track list begins to make sense.

Like the other albums I have by Collett this one was recorded in Los Angeles. Specifically it was recorded at Sage & Studio in just two days on November 3 and 4, 1997. Although [[ASIN:B0040PZKOW Music From the Movies]] is the album that get me interested in Collett in the first place, this one sealed the deal because of the interpretation and performance of a diverse set of songs.

title: Two albums that showcase Day's talent as a pop singer
text:
This double set showcases the pop side of Day circa mid 1950s. She had a gift for singing big band, jazz and pop arrangements and could deliver in any of those genres. The albums in this set are more pop and definitely easy listening.

Unfortunately there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review, so it's difficult to convey the music. I will say that the first twelve tracks are from a smaller ensemble, but strings were either present at the session or dubbed in later. Of the two albums, this is my personal favorite. Tracks 13 through 24 - the Day By Night album - have a much larger backing ensemble and is great for romantic background music. Actually the entire album serves as that, and if you are a boomer this set has a very definite nostalgia appeal.

The first album (Day By Day; tracks 1 through 12) was recorded for Columbia in 1956 and released towards the end of that year on December 17, 1956. The second album was recorded the next year and released eleven months later on November 11, 1957. Both albums were conducted by Paul Weston who played a significant collaborative role in each album.

If you want to explore Day's jazzier side I also recommend [[ASIN:B0097ID9W2 Best Vocal Jazz of All Time: The Essential Doris Day]], which truly showcases her talent in that genre as well as her versatility as a vocalist.

title: One of my favorite Turrentine albums
text:
This and [[ASIN:B00004TR14 Complete Blue Hour Sessions]] are probably my two top picks for Turrentine albums. I am actually listening to this one as I write this review (my second pass for the CD this morning.)

One reason why I love this one is the line-up. Of course having wife Shirley Scott cooking on the B3 is not only a driving force, but Turrentine's own forceful playing. I have always loved his tone and phrasing, so when you add Kenny Burrell's guitar to the mix and Bob Crenshaw's bass the music takes on a life of its own. I am not as familiar with Otis Finch, the drummer, but do admire his playing. He can do a shuffle with the best of them, but can swing like mad when the music requires it, so I will be digging deeper into his background.

Basically there is nothing I can say to describe the music that the sound samples on this page cannot say better. Do give those a run through.

I mentioned that I also love Turrentine on the album titled Complete Blue Hour Sessions. The contrast between that one and this is significant. On the Blue Hour sessions he is backed by a straight ahead jazz trio - The Three Sounds - with the great Gene Harris on piano. While that album has a strong blues infusion, it's still more jazz whereas this one is funky and has Turrentine's (and Scott's) imprint all over it. Both are great albums, but for different reasons.

For my fellow music geeks, this was recorded Bluenote during a single day at Rudy van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs, NJ studio on January 24, 1964 and released the same year. If you are only now discovering Turrentine this is a good starting point. If you are already a fan this is yet another treasure he and Scott recorded and worth grabbing.

title: Ella's first full filmed concert and some excellent backing ensembles
text:
Other reviews have provided set lists from each performances as well as personnel, so I am going to confine my review to why I keep returning to it.

First, it's a treat to see Ella backed by quartets instead of larger ensembles that backed her on some albums during this period. She seems to be more connected to both the music and audience in this context.

A personal reason for me is as a jazz drummer I could contrast two of my influences - Papa Jo Jones on the Belgium segment and Gus Johnson on the Sweden one. It is also a treat to see bassist Ray Brown (on the Belgium segment) so up close and personal, as well as Tommy Flanagan on piano on the Sweden one.

The music during both segments is swinging (as you would expect from Ella), although the Belgium performance was more so in my opinion. Or perhaps it seemed that way because there was a lot more energy. Plus, on the last song of the Belgium performance Oscar Peterson sits in on piano and Roy Eldridge joins in to make it a quintet and things truly take off.

I mentioned that the Belgium set had more energy. That, of course, is a personal opinion. And if so, I think that is balanced by the pure musicality of the Sweden set, which was too short for me. I was truly immersed in both Flanagan's piano and Johnson's tasteful drumming.

Video quality is a bit spotty, especially for the Sweden segment which seemed to be overlit, but still good enough to savor the performances. Sound quality is excellent (considering) for both segments.

Bottom line, though, is if you are an Ella fan this is essential. If for no other reason than the first segment is the first whole performance of her ever captured on video. But also for the music, musicians and even capturing audience response to her during this period.

title: Galbraith's only album as a leader
text:
This album was recorded for Deca during the course of thrree sessions in January 1958 and released the same year. One of the main reasons why I love this album, aside from Galbraith, of course, is it features Bobby Jasper on flute on all tracks. He is one of my favorite flautists, although he passed away way too soon in his career. This is Galbraith's only album as a leader (but certainly not as a sideman considering that he participated in 594 during nhis prolific career.)

The best way to get a feel for this album is to run through the sound samples on the MP3 version's product page at [[ASIN:B00B3BD8Y0 Guitar And the Wind]]. This is relaxing music, but it is not 'elevator' music by any stretch. At least not to me. Let your ears and personal taste decide from the samples.

Through all three sessions the core group was comprised of Galbraith on guitar, Eddie Costa on piano and celeste, Milt Hinton on bass and Osie Johnson on drums (the latter two were as prolific as sidemen as Galbraith.)

All three sessions were recorded in NYC. On the January 16, 1958 one the core ensemble is joined by Urbie Green, Frank Rehak and Chauncey Welsch on trombone and Dick Hixson on bass trombone. This session produced tracks 1, 4, 8 and 12.

During the January 21 session the core ensemble is joined by Phil Bodner on flute, clarinet and bass clarinet, Romeo Penque on flute, oboe and clarinet and Spencer Sinatra on flute and clarinet. This session produced tracks 2, 6, 7, 10.

The remaining tracks were performed by the core ensemble on January 28, and led by Galbraith.

title: Two albums plus 4 tracks from an extended play
text:
This is two full LPs and a 4-track extended play record that clocks in at a few seconds over an hour and fifteen minutes. The LPs are from late 1959 and the EP is from 1955.

While there are no sound samples or a track list for this album on this page at the time of this review, you can find both on this product page: [[ASIN:B00VDO966Q Music From "Some Like It Hot" (Bonus Track Version)]]. This music is inspired by the movie [[ASIN:B004778YJG Some Like It Hot]]. Indeed, the first twelve tracks are the sound track. The remaining tracks fit in and if you live 'Dixieland' or traditional jazz you will love this album.

Run through the sound samples on the page I linked to get a good feel for the music. For me this is somewhat nostalgic because I was eleven when the soundtrack was released and there was a minor resurgence of dixieland music that had caught my interest (which is one reason why I love this particular album.)

Here are the source albums and personnel for the tracks (which I am going to repeat here for clarification):

title: An eccletic collection of tracks
text:
The tracks on this album range from a Chopin waltz to bebop, with a sprinkling of that I can only call 'free jazz' or music that was starting to bubble up as such around the time this album was recorded on January 21 and 22, 1958 at Contemporary's Studio in Los Angeles.

What truly makes this special is Feldman's vibraphone work, and, of course, having Scott LaFaro on bass. Not to be overlooked is the great Stan Levey on drums. If you are asking, 'Stan who?" Levey played with Dizzy Gillespie at 16, as well as Charlie Parker (who was also a room mate for over a year), George Shearing, Coleman Hawkins and even Thelonious Monk. In fact, Levey suggested 'Bebop', track 6 on this album, and he had first played it with Dizzy in 1945. Interestingly, Levey also contributed the cover photo of the album.

It's sad that there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review). You can do a search on the web and find most of the tracks to get a better sense of this album's musical aspects. To some it may not be coherent enough, although to me personally I love it and think it fits together perfectly. Also note that at the time of this review there is no track list on this page. Here is what the album contains:
01. Serpent's Tooth
02. Waltz
03. Chasing Shadows
04. Flamingo
05. S'Posin'
06. Bebop
07. (There Is No) Greater Love
08. Too Blue
09. Minor Lament
10. Satin Doll

Three of the tracks - Chasing Shadows, Too Blue Victor and Minor Lament - are Feldman's compositions. He also did the arrangement of Frederic Chopin's Waltz (track 2). The remaining tracks are by the likes of Miles Davis, Duke Ellington and others and add a wonderful seasoningto this album.

title: Another Getz milestone
text:
I've been a Getz fan for over a half century, and vividly remember when this album was first released (the same year I joined the Navy). I view this as his third phase segueing from an identifiable Lester Young influence to Brazilian and into this freer style. Actually, there was a short bridge between the Lester Young influenced style and the Bossa Nova phase, but it flew by quickly.

Listen to the sound samples on this page and you will hear Getz backed by a rhythm section along the same lines as Scott LaFaro and Paul Motian backing Bill Evans or Herbie Hancock, Ron Carter and Tony Williams backing Miles Davis and Wayne Shorter. The rhythm is free and flowing, even on tracks like O Grande Amor where the rhythm section is loosely tied to formula of Brazilian music. On this album Chick Corea on piano, Ron Carter on bass and Grady Tate on drums prove to be on the same level as the aforementioned rhythm sections.In fact, this album serves as a study in flow and interplay backing a front line melody instrument played by the likes of Getz.

I do want to point out that the credits on the track listing (at the time of this review) make no sense whatsoever. For example, tracks 1, 4 and 5 credit Bill Evans and Chick Corea and Stan Getz. First, Evans is nowhere near this album, and second, composer credits for tracks 1 and 5 go to Corea, to Jobim and DeMoraes for track 2, to Mike Gibbs for track 3 and to Dizzy Gillespie for track 4.

This album was recorded for Verve in just two days (March 21 and 30, 1967) at Rudy van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs, NJ studio. It's certainly a transitional album for Getz, and is a bit on the short side at 37:29, but is recommended for die hard fans.

title: Simply Desmond with perfect backing
text:
I only wish this product page had sound samples (it does not at the time of this review.) It is also missing the track list, which I will fill in:
1. Glad To Be Unhappy
2. Poor Butterfly
3. Stranger In Town
4. A Taste Of Honey
5. Any Other Time
6. Hi-Lili, Hi-Lo
7. Angel Eyes

Do note that other albums have three additional tracks that were recorded during the same sessions, but never made it to the initial release of this album. See [[ASIN:B00005IAWT Glad to Be Unhappy]] if you want the entire set of songs. This album, though, stands out as better from a sound and mix perspective (to my ears). Regardless of which version you choose, I do not believe that you will be disappointed if you are a Desmond fan.

The music is simply exquisite and showcases Desmond's style like no other album I own featuring him. One of the reasons why I rated this album so highly is he is backed by some excellent musicians who truly complement Desmond's playing. Jim Hall's guitar is as though he and Desmond were soul mates, and Gene Wright on track 2 and Gene Cherico on the remaining tracks are perfect. Lest I forget, Connie Kay (of the Modern Jazz Quartet) is similarly perfectly matched to Desmond and the rest of the ensemble. In fact if I had to pick drummers, it would have come down to either Key or Ed Thigpen, both of whom were masters of brush playing that is the essence of this music, and good taste.

All of the tracks were recorded for RCA in their Studio "A" and Webster Hall facilities in NYC on June 6, 1963 (track 2), and the remaining in 1964 on July 13, August 20 and September 4 and 8.

title: A rare treat
text:
These tracks have been in the can since 1962 and show the jazzier side of Anderson. For we fans this release of her live performances at the Penthouse Club in Seattle is truly a treat.

Listen to the sound samples on the MP3 version of this album's page at [[ASIN:B00T5Z0LEG Ernestine Anderson Swings The Penthouse]]. The recordings are surprisingly good considering that no major label that I was able to track down is behind the original recordings. This was recorded in Anderson's home town (she was born in Texas, but grew up in Seattle), and is during the same period after an acrimonious parting from Mercury after which recording and work became scarce. I wish I knew more, but the liner notes are scant and so is information from the usual sources.

One thing that stands out aside from her great delivery of standards is the fact that she is backed by a piano and drums. No bass, yet the music is full and rich. Part of that is because of her vocal presence and part is the left hand of pianist Dick Palombi. Drummer Bill Richardson does a superb job of creating a rhythmic fabric for every track. His playing is tasteful and ideal for this ensemble.

The tracks come from three individual performances from 1962, and indicate that Anderson was either a regular or had a long run at the Penthouse Club: February 7 and October 24 and 31.

This period is like a black hole in Anderson's career, so if anyone knows more about these performances and who recorded them please make a comment to this review because I have hit a dead end. Of course I am grateful that this album was released because the music is excellent and truly swings as the title promises.

title: Rare, with less than stellar sound (but worth it for some of us)
text:
This was a thrift shop find for me and I was fortunate that the LP was in excellent condition with no scratches. Even with the condition the mix seemed a little muffled and that may be because of the live recording and the engineer at the time.

The real reason to grab this album is it has Booker Little on trumpet. Of course, there are other reasons for we die hard jazz fans. In addition to Little I was intrigued that not only Ray Draper is on tuba, but Art Davis is on double bass. To be honest I am not as familiar with Davis, but generally tubas were the 'bass' of traditional jazz and Dixieland bands and bass replaced it. Having both instruments in an ensemble - and not stepping on each other - is interesting and music bears that out.

While there are no sound samples (or even a track list) on this page you can access both on the MP3 version of this album's product page at [[ASIN:B0049QNE0E Max Roach + 4 At Newport]]. Note that some discographies list six tracks - that is because the original label - EmArcy - reissued this album with a bonus track titled Deeds, Not Words that is from the same July 6, 1958 performance at the Newport Jazz Festival.

In addition to Roach and the other members I mentioned above the ensemble also includes George Coleman on tenor sax. The entire performance is hard bop (yes, with a tuba), and if the sound quality were better it would easily be mainstream. As it is, this is mainly of interest to Booker Little and Ray Draper fans.

title: Candlelight and wine
text:
As a jazz musician I normally eschew arrangements that include strings, especially when the core musicians are swinging ones with great jazz chops. I make an exception with this album. Chalk it up to my Italian blood and Sagittarius sign, but this is one of the albums I pull out late at night when I am romantically inclined.

While eight of the tracks do have lush orchestral backing, all of them have some great rhythm sections backing Krall who beautifully interprets every song. Before I get into the pedantic details give the sound samples on this page a listen to get a sense of this album. It's Krall's fifth, but is different from her previous ones in a lot of ways. Let the sound samples speak for the music.

There are some interesting facts, though. For one thing, track 13 is a Clint Eastwood composition (along with co writers Carole Bayer Sager and Linda Thompson-Jenner), and is from Eastwood's movie, [[ASIN:B001QWE5G6 True Crime (1999)]]. Russel Malone is on guitar on all of the remaining tracks, and West Coast drummer and vibraphonist Larry Bunker is on vibraphone on tracks 3 and 6. Krall's strongest rhythm section - bassist John Clayton and drummer Jeff Hamilton - are on tracks 1, 3, 5 and 10 to 12. Bassist Ben Wolfe is on tracks 2, 6, 8 and 9, and drummer Lewis Nash is on tracks 6 and 8. Tony DiPalma is mainly behind the orchestral arrangements and ensembles backing Krall, but Johnny Mandel's hand is in this production as well.

Bottom line: even if you dislike string arrangements give this one a chance. It may be a tad on the commercial side, but still swings and should appeal to those who are hopeless romantics at heart.

title: Possibly one of Alexander's best albums
text:
While my personal favorite album will always be [[ASIN:B00I5XKEDM Montreux Alexander]] because it was the one that introduced me to him, this one is probably his best. Of course that is subjective and we all have favorites. I will say that if you are a fan this album will be on your short list.

Listen to the sound samples on this page. The music is solid and not only from Alexander. Andy Simpkins on bass has long been a favorite of mine because I am a Three Sounds fan too and Simpkins was an integral part of that trio with his very distinctive bass sound. I am somewhat familiar with Frank Gant as a drummer. I cannot pick him out blindfolded like I can some drummers, but love his style. I know him mainly from his work with Yusef Lateef and the decade he spent with Ahmad Jamal, the latter of which honed him for this album because his playing behind Alexander is impeccable.

The last three tracks on this album were not released on the original album, but were recorded during the same January 22 1979 studio session at the Polydor KK studios in Tokyo.

Regardless of how you personally rank this album if you are a fan you're missing out if you do not already own it.

title: Essential even today
text:
Regardless of what kind of music you play, if you are a drummer who wants to truly craft melodic solos and fills this album is essential listening.

At the time of this review the CD that I am reviewing has no sound samples on its product page, but you can listen to sound samples on the MP3 album's page at [[ASIN:B00260R352 Drums Unlimited]]. The CD has a bonus track that the MP3 album lacks (at the time of this review), which is a second take of In The Red [A Xmas Carol]. But the real value is listening to how Roach crafts grooves that are melodic, even on the three tracks on the album where is is not accompanied, yet still manages to tell a story with his drums.

He is accompanied on tracks 2, 4 and 6 by Freddie Hubbard on trumpet, Roland Alexander on soprano saxophone (track 4 only), James Spaulding on alto saxophone, Ronnie Mathews on piano and Jayme Merritt on bass. Hubbard and Merritt had extensive experience with drummers in Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers, and the entire ensemble is perfect for this album.

All of the tracks were recorded at Atlantic's NYC studios on October 14 and 20, 1965 (tracks 1, 2, 4 and 6), and April 25, 1966 (tracks 3 and 5), The solo tracks are The Drum Also Waltzes (a 3/4 masterpiece that is worth the price of the entire album in my opinion), Drums Unlimited and For Big Sid, the latter a tribute to the great Sid Catlett.

title: High energy performances
text:
Note: I am reviewing the CD album titled [[ASIN:B00004XNJZ After You've Gone]] that is erroneously credited to Teddy Wilson at the time of this review. Moreover, at the time of this review this album is also erroneously linked to yet another Teddy Wilson album that is on MP3 format.

This album is the 1974 Concord Jazz Festival and features the following line-up: Sweets Edison on trumpet and Plas Johnson on tenor sax, backed by George Duke on piano, Herb Ellis on guitar, Ray Brown on bass and Jake Hanna on drums.

Until discovering this CD on an auction site I had been listening to the vinyl LP version. This CD's sound quality is as good as the LP (taking into account that the LP has a naturally warmer sound.) I wanted this to preserve the LP and am not disappointed in it.

The music is like of the of the better JATP concerts - full of energy, superb musicianship and some great selections. And improvisation, of course. In addition to some excellent music there is a bit of humor in the recordings as well. Specifically on Mitch's Lament and Detour Ahead Herb Ellis introduces the songs since he is the composer and mentions the ASCAP fees he expects from the live performance. Other tracks written by performers are Home Grown (Harry 'Sweets' Edison) and Fatty McSlatty (Ray Brown).

title: Great collaboration that builds on earlier excursions out of 4/4
text:
I am a staunch fan of both McCann and the Modern Jazz Quartet, so this album practically called my name when I cam across it. Since the CD's product page does not have a track list or sound samples at the time of this review please refer to this page for both: [[ASIN:B008WFNA8E Jazz Waltz]].

The sound samples are indicative of both the sound quality and the music. I love it because it's a rare album that is filled with 3/4 time music. Granted, Max Roach did a total 3/4 album six years prior when [[ASIN:B0007KVAYS Jazz in 3/4 Time]] was released in 1957, but this one has a more funky quality where Roach's earlier album straddled hard bop and straight ahead. So it boils down to a matter of taste. Also, this album takes the foundation Roach built and extends it, so in a way it also pays homage.

But, it's all about the music and to my ears this is truly ground breaking and somehow got lost in the shuffle because I only recently discovered it.
