I would love to nail down the exact dates, but McCann's discography as well as Pacific Jazz information is scant. I do know this album was recorded at the Pacific Jazz studios in Los Angeles in late 1963 and subsequently released by both Pacific Jazz (PJ-81). World Pacific also released a 45 RPM with Spanish Castles and Bluesette on sides A and B.

Personnel are McCann and Joe Sample on keys (both on piano and organ with McCann also credited with electric piano), Wayne Henderson on trombone, Wilton Felder on tenor sax, Bobby Haynes on bass and Stix Hopper on drums.

title: Alexander's second album
text:
That this is still in print is a miracle, and if you are a fan it's worth adding to your library. In fact, if you still have a turntable you can also get Alexander's debut album: [[ASIN:B006LMZBD2 Alexander The Great]].

At the time of this review there are no sound samples or even a track list on this page. I can rectify the missing track list:
01 Spunky 2:39
02 Naturally 3:35
03 Jamaican Shake 2:25
04 Heartstrings 3:33
05 Taggies Tune 4:14
06 Rattlesnake 2:30
07 Whisper Not 3:58
08 I'm An Old Cow Hand 2:32
09 Little Children Of Peru 2:50
10 Spirit Of Foo Foo 4:45

It's interesting that if you listen to Alexander today, then go back to this album (or even the debut one), you can hear a lot of his influences that have stuck with him throughout his career. At the top of the list is Les McCann, but he is no McCann clone. Monty has his own style and it was was already established in his earliest recordings including this one.

This album was recorded during the course of 1964 and 1964, with eight of the tracks in Los Angeles and two in NYC. What's interesting is Pacific Jazz for whom this album was recorded allowed him to include four of his own compositions (Spunky, Jamaican Shake, Rattlesnake and Spirit of Foo Foo.) More interesting is guitarist Scott Turner who is on the Los Angeles sessions has one of his compositions on the album (Little Children Of Peru). I mention this because studios were not as liberal with new artists and usually insisted on standards and more popular songs that would sell albums.

The first session in Los Angeles was recorded during unspecified dates in 1964-65 at the World Pacific Studios. Alexander's rhythm section on these sessions was Victor Gaskin on bass and Paul Humphrey on drums, with Scott Turner on guitar on track 7 only. Two of the songs - Heartstrings and Rattlesnake - were recorded during the second session at the Plaza Sound Studios in NYC during the same period. For those two songs Alexander is backed by Gene Bertoncini on guitar, Bob Cranshaw on bass and Bruno Carr on drums.

A final note: the mastering and sound quality on this CD is excellent.

title: More subdued than their 1976 debut, but solid live performance
text:
This is supposed to be the reunion from the trio's Montreaux debut seven years earlier. However, if you own [[ASIN:B00I5XKEDM Montreux Alexander]] and are looking for the same wild, propulsive music you'll be disappointed. On the other hand, if you want to enjoy Alexander backed by John Clayton on bass and Jeff Hamilton on drums playing with incredible musicality this is a great album/

To be sure, Alexander does go off on musical excursions throughout this album because it's in his nature. The only pity is there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review because the contrast between the 1976 performance and this one is significant.

Frankly I love both performances with the Clayton'Hamilton rhythm section because they manage to take whatever Alexander is playing to another level. Both Clayton and Hamilton are nearly telepathic, but there is also a strong connection between Clayton and Alexander that is on every album they have ever done.Evidence of that is the duo album Alexander and Clayton did titled [[ASIN:B00I5JSK28 The Duke Ellington Song Book]]. But I digress. Here the trio may not be as wild as the Montreaux concert, but are as solid. If anything, they are even more solid here because they add a richness to the songs on this album that are as much based on the set list as their own personal growth as musicians in the ensuing seven years.

This album was recorded love at the Club Manufaktur in Germany on May 27, 19i83. The sound quality is uniformly excellent and the trio is in the forefront of the mix with no extraneous or ambient club noise to detract from the performance. More importantly, the mixing places all three musicians in balance with one another. This is definitely an album for fans of the Alexander/Clayton/Hamilton edition of the trio.

title: Jazz dripping with blues
text:
I've been both a Ray Brown and Gene Harris fan since I was a teenager (I am now 66), so this album is special to me. Most of my earlier Brown recordings were from his Oscar Peterson Trio days and my Harris ones from when he led The Three Sounds. Frankly I had always thought that pairing Brown with Peterson or Harris with Three Sounds bassist Andrew Simpkins were perfect. However, the synergy between Brown and Harris on this album is incredible.

Run through the sound samples on this page for a taste of what I am trying to say. What Brown brings to the table is an intensity and a jazz feel that only a handful of bassists have. Of course he could play the blues with the best of them. Harris, on the other hand, infused everything with blues, even when he was playing straight ahead jazz, so the pairing is perfect.

To be honest I am not as familiar with the drummer (Gerryck King), but I admire his playing on this album. He is there with Harris and Brown and plays exactly what the music requires. Considering Brown's intensity and Harris' touch that is no easy task for a drummer to support without messing up the flow. King manages to pull it off with aplomb and considerable musicality.

On track 5 Emily Remler and Red Holloway join in. It's a curious mix that seems to fit - Remler's guitar playing shows Wes Montgomery's influence that dovetails nicely with Brown's style, and Holloway's R&B style on tenor sax is a great complement to Harris' piano.

The album was recorded in August 1984 at the Coast Recorders in San Francisco. The sound quality is as excellent as the music itself. If you are a fan of any of the musicians on this album you will not be disappointed. Actually, you won't be disappointed. Period.

title: Excellent music and interesting arrangements
text:
I am thankful that this album is back in print. Like most of Alexander's recordings as a leader there is scant information regarding when and where. I was able to track down that this was recorded originally for the MPS label on March 29, 1983 in Villigen, Germany.

Facts, though, are not as important as the music, and you can listen to sound samples on the MP3 album's page at [[ASIN:B00I5JSK28 The Duke Ellington Song Book]]. It's just Alexander on a Steinway concert grand piano and John Clayton on bass running through Ellington's (and Billy Strayhorn's) body of gems. Actually, there are more collaborators than Strayhorn on the songs, and East Side, West Side is a Phil Moore composition (not to be confused with the 1890s song technically titled Sidewalks of New York that is commonly called East Side, West Side.)

Alexander stays close to Ellington's renditions and Clayton is simply amazing as an accompanist. I love the fact that on some selections Clayton takes over the melody while Alexander comps against it. On all tracks the arrangements and playing are what one would expect from both if you are an Alexander and/or Clayton fan.

If you are a drummer this album has even more value because it's the perfect play along - a 'minus one' tool as well as great listening. In fact any musician will get a lot from this album through critical listening, but this is definitely not just for musicians.

title: Difficult to find and one of Alexander's best trios
text:
While I personally love Alexander's trio with John Clayton on bass and Jeff Hamilton on drums, the combining of Herb Ellis on guitar and Ray Brown on bass is delightful. This album - three album set really - literally cooks. I only wish there were sound samples on this page to provide a taste because I am sure most folks would be hooked.

This is comprised of three albums. Tracks 1 through 9 on Disc One is the album titled [[ASIN:B0000006E6 Triple Treat]] that was recorded for Concord during March 1982 at Sounds Creation in Osaka, Japan.

Tracks 10 through 13 on Disc One and 1 through 3 on Disc Two are the album titled [[ASIN:B0000006GQ Triple Treat 2]] that was recorded live for Concord during June 1987 at The Loa in Santa Monica, CA. John Frigo on violin join Alexander, Ellis and Brown on Disc One's track 13 and the first three tracks on Disc Two.

The remaining tracks are the album titled [[ASIN:B0000006I2 Triple Threat 3]]. They were recorded live at The Loa in Santa Monica during the same June 1987 performances and also feature Frigo on tracks 9 through 12 on this disc.

This is high energy piano jazz trio sans drums, but the added spice of jazz violin on some tracks. It ranks high on my list of Monty Alexander albums, and equally high on my list of albums I play for friends to demonstrate how insanely intense a small jazz group can be.

title: Perfect voice and true lounge music
text:
I found this album completely by accident when I was looking up various renditions of Miami Beach Rhumba for a rehearsal. The track was actually on Youtube and piqued my interest enough to spring for the entire album. What a serendipity because I discovered what our friends Down Under already knew - Seidel is an amazing vocalist and pianist, and this album is a treasure trove of beautifully arranged music.

Sadly there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review. There is also no track listing, but I can rectify that. The following fourteen tracks come in at a few minutes under an hour:
01 Moonglow
02 If They Asked Me I Could Write a Book
03 Always
04 Midnight Sun
05 Miami Beach Rhumba
06 Canadian Sunset
07 Whatever Lola Wants
08 Lullaby of Birdland
09 Cow Cow Boogie
10 Trolley Song
11 Cry Me a River
12 The Breeze and I
13 Somewhere Over the Rainbow
14 Dream

Note that all of the arrangements on this album feature strings backing an exceptional jazz ensemble. Seidel is on piano as well as vocals, but most of the tracks feature pianist Kevin Hunt, with Chuck Morgan on guitar, Ben Jones on saxophone, brother David Seidel on bass, Adam Pache on drums and Fabian Hevia on other percussion.

Seidel's voice resembles Doris Day to my ears. She is certainly not a Doris Day clone, but the similarities are there. For me that is part of this album's (and Seidel's) appeal because I have always contended that Day was an underrated vocalist. But comparisons aside, the music on this album is simply superb and if you drop the strings the arrangements are still excellent. Actually, I am on the fence about the stings. As a jazz musician I eschew them on principle, but have to admit that they add a certain lushness to this album and they do make it perfect for easy listening.

If you know who Seidel is then you probably know about this album since it was released in 2003. If, like me, you are just discovering her, this is an excellent collection of her work.

title: Outstanding performances
text:
My copy was discovered at a local Goodwill and I was fortunate that the LP was in pristine condition. The music is like of the of the better JATP concerts - full of energy, superb musicianship and some great selections. And improvisation, of course.

I would rate the sound quality as excellent (dependent upon the condition of the LP). There is a CD version of this concert floating around too. I have not actually heard a copy so cannot say if the mastering is as good as it is on this LP.

At the time of this review there is no track list on this page. Here is what the LP contains:

SIDE A
A1 After You've Gone...7:55
A2 Mitch's Lament...7:46
A3 Home Grown...5:52
SIDE B
B1 Mood Indigo...5:28
B2 Detour Ahead...6:22
B3 Fatty McSlatty...9:40
B4 Flintstones II...5:38

In addition to some excellent music there is a bit of humor in the recordings as well. Specifically on Mitch's Lament and Detour Ahead Herb Ellis introduces the songs since he is the composer and mentions the ASCAP fees he expects from the live performance. Other tracks written by performers are Home Grown (Harry 'Sweets' Edison) and Fatty McSlatty (Ray Brown).

Performances are from the 1974 Concord Jazz Festival and feature the following line-up: Sweets Edison on trumpet and Plas Johnson on tenor sax, backed by George Duke on piano, Herb Ellis on guitar, Ray Brown on bass and Jake Hanna on drums.

title: A great set of performances with one of Monk's better quartets
text:
Nearly all of Monk's recorded output from 1963 through 1967 were live performances. All stand out as superb (to my biased ears), but this one is among my favorites.

I'll confess that my favorite rhythm section during this period was the John Ore (bass) and Frankie Dunlop (drums), but my second favorite is on this album and is comprised of Larry Gales on bass and Ben Riley on drums. Both Dunlop and Riley are major influences on my own approach to drums, so this particular album is special from that perspective. If goes without Saying that Charlie Rouse's tenor saxophone is the perfect complement to Monk's playing.

Run through the sound samples on this page (if you are on the CD's product page they can be heard on the MP3's product page at [[ASIN:B0013AWWGG Live At The Jazz Workshop - Complete]]. Those snippets onvey the essence of the music on this album, which clocks in at a few minutes less than two and a half hours.

One of the reasons this is one of my top favorite live Monk albums (from this era anyway) is how tight the rhythm section is, and the latitude Monk gives the entire ensemble. It seems as though this edition of the quartet had come into its own, and Monk also seems inspired by the energy and interplay among them.

This album supposedly contains everything recorded for Columbia during the quartet's November 3 and 4, 1964 performances at the Jazz Workshop is San Francisco. I checked one of my referenced discography sites and the tracks in this page and the ones known to have been recorded match so I am inclined to believe that this is all that was captured.

title: More than just the Sunset Eyes sessions
text:
The tracks in this set share one commoin point: Edwards' rhythm section is comprised of Joe Castro on piano, Leroy Vinnegar on bass and Billy Higgins on drums. Higgins lends vocals to one track and Gloria Smyth to two others (cited below). Many of the tracks are in other albums from Pacific Jazz, but surprisingly this set also contains a Joe Castro led album for Atlantic, a compilation album that also featured Sonny Rollins (whose tracks are not included here), and even tracks from a 1958 TV broadcast.

Listen to the sound samples on this page to gauge the music, which I think is excellent on every track. I also think that Fresh Sounds did their usual excellent job of ensuring the best possible sound quality.

Here are the sources for each track:
========
DISC ONE
========
Trsacks 1 through 3 are from a TV broadcast from KABC-TV, Stars Of Jazz on December 15, 1958.

Tracks 4 through 9 are the Joe Castro led album titled Groove Funk Soul that was recorded for Atlantic Records at the Radio Recorders studio in Los Angeles on July 18, 1959

Tracks 10 and 11 are from the Gloria Smyth album titled Like Soul! recorded for the Pacific Jazz label at Sound Enterprises in Los Angeles on September 12, 1959. Smyth is the female vocalist on these tracks.

Tracks 12 and 13 were recorded at the Falcon's Lair in Los Angeles on an unspecified 1958 date and released by the Metrojazz label as Sonny Rollins At Music Inn/Teddy Edwards At Falcon's Lair With Joe Castro. These tracks are the only two by Edwards and his rhythm section on the album.
========
DISC TWO
========
Tracks 1 through 6 were recorded at the Rex Productions Studio in Los Angeles on August 16, 1960. The vocals on track 2 is drummer Billy Higgins.

The remaining tracks were recorded for the album titled Teddy's Ready! for the Contemporary label at their Los Angeles studio on August 17, 1960.

title: Two album set from 59-60
text:
Smith was still active into the 2000s, yet the two albums in this set were not exactly his earliest works. Smith had released nineteen or twenty albums prior to the two in this set. Both of these albums were recorded for Verve at the United Recorders studio in Los Angeles.

If you are on the CD's product page there are no sound samples at the time of this review. You can listen to them on the digital album's page at [[ASIN:B00Q804O1W The Paul Smith Trio & Quartet. The Big Men / The Sound of Music]], and they will give you an idea of the great music this set contains.

The first eleven tracks are the album titled The Big Men, and the first two tracks are Smith's own compositions. They were recorded in two sessions on December 8 and 9, 1959 and feature one of my favorite Los Angeles rhythm sections backing Smith: Leroy Vinnegar on bass and Stan Levey on drums (Levey was an early bebop pioneer who played with Dizzy Gillespie at 16 and was Bird's room mate for a period.)

Tracks 11 through 21 are the album titled The Sound of Music that was recorded a month later in a single session on January 8, 1960. Here Smith is backed by another rhythm section of luminaries featuring Barney Kessel on guitar, Morty Corb on bass and Irv Cottler on drums.

As an aside, if you are a Paul Smith fan and want to explore more of his work I highly recommend the following compilation: [[ASIN:B00E44GL0G Essential Jazz Magic]]. That collection was my introduction to Smith's incredible playing and body of work, and it led me to this (and other) albums which I will be reviewing in the coming months.

title: I purchased this because of Edwards and McCann and got a lot more than expected
text:
This album is a collection of tracks recorded by Edwards on three albums. Two albums are led by Edwards and the third is led by Gloria Smyth. All of the recordings were done between March and May 1960, and they were recorded in Los Angeles for the Pacific Jazz and World Pacific labels.

The backing ensembles are all first rate. The real bonus in this collection - for me - is stumbling across Smyth. Edard's tenor sax matches her voice in the same sway that Lester Young's did Billie Holiday's. Don't misunderstand. Edwards had his own style and Smyth was no Lady Day clone, but musically she and Edwards were as perfectly matched - to my ears anyway. Give the sound samples a run through and you will hear what I am trying to describe on tracks 8 through 11 and 17 through 19.

All of the tracks were drawn from four sessions at the Rex Productions Studio in Los Angeles. Tracks 1 through 11 were recorded on May 2, 1960. Of those, tracks 1 through 7 found their way on Edwards' Pacific Jazz album titled It's About Time, and tracks 8 through 11 were recorded for Smyth's World Pacific album titled Like Soul!. Personnel on both albums are Edwards on tenor sax backed by Les McCann on piano, Leroy Vinnegar on bass and Ron Jefferson on drums (with Smyth on tracks8 through 11).

Tracks 12 through 15 were recorded on March 21, 1960 for Edwards' Sunset Eyes album (tracks 13 and 14 during that session did not make it to the album). Here Edwards is backed by Amos Trice on piano, Leroy Vinnegar on bass and Tony Bazley on drums.

Tracks 16 through 19 were recorded on March 23, 1960, with track 16 going to the Sunset Eyes album and the remaining tracks to Smyth's Like Soul! album. Edwards backed by Ronnie Ball on piano, Ben Tucker on bass and Al Levitt on drums are on all tracks, with Smyth on the final three.

There are so many outstanding musicians on this album that alone make it worthwhile. McCann and Ball on particular stand out as incredible pianists (and Trice is no slouch either). The bassists are like a who's who on that instrument and the drummers are all exceptional. Plus Smyth's vocals!

title: Great live perforamane from three different albums
text:
I want to note that RCB's February 27, 2015 review is accurate regarding sound quality. I can only guess what Fresh Sounds had to work with to remaster this album, but this is one of the very few albums I have from that label that is spotty. You can pick up hints of the sound quality from the sound samples on this page. You can also pick up hints about the performances and that is why I gave this album five stars anyway. If you are an audiophile this is probably going to rank in the one or two star category, so please bear that in mind before ordering.

For me it's all about the music, and this is live McCann at his best. Early McCann anyway. This album represents everything that was recorded live at the Bit coffeehouse in Los Angeles. McCann has his McCann Ltd. drummer, Ron Jefferson, but his trio's bassist (Herbie Lewis) is replaced by West Coast great Leroy Vinnegar. The album is actually a compilation of three different Pacific Jazz albums that among them contain all of the tracks that were recorded live on July 16 and 17, 1960.

Tracks 1 through 9 are the original album titled Les McCann Ltd. Plays The Shout. Track 10 is from a Pacific Jazz compilation of various artists titled This Is The Blues, Vol. 1, and the final three tracks are from another album titled From the Top of the Barrel that features four other tracks from McCann's performances at San Francisco's Jazz Workshop that were recorded in December 1960. The missing four tracks can be found on the album titled [[ASIN:B008ILPD1O Les McCann Ltd. in San Francisco]], but they feature McCann's own bassist, Herbie Lewis.

Bottom line: the sound quality may be spotty and the crowd noise a distraction, but the music is excellent and this does represent everything that was recorded at the Bit on those two July nights - all of which was previously scattered among three albums.

title: Original album + five bonus tracks
text:
This is the original Verve album titled 'Stuff Smith' (Verve MGV 8206), plus five bonus tracks. The first six tracks are the ones that comprise the original album, tracks 7 through 9 are takes from the same sessions, and the final two tracks are from the session that produced 'Have Violin, Will Swing'.

The music on the first nine tracks have an expected unity since the backing ensemble is comprised of Oscar Peterson on piano, Barney Kessel on guitar, Ray Brown on bass and Alvin Stoller on drums. All but Stoller have solos on the various tracks, but not to the exclusion of totally supporting Smith. Since there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review), you can listen to the first six tracks on this album's product page: [[ASIN:B00481S8WE Stuff Smith]]. All of the first nine tracks are along the same musical lines.

Personnel backing Smith on the final two tracks are West Coast stalwarts Carl Perkins on piano not to be confused with the rockabilly guitarist of the same name), Red Callender on bass and Oscar Bradley on drums.

Tracks 1 through 9 on March 7 and 12, 1957 at the Glen Glenn Studios in Los Angeles. Tracks 10 and 11 were recorded at the Capitol Studios on Los Angeles on February 5, 1957.

title: All of Corbin's known recorded output
text:
This album contains all of Corbin's known recorded work. I mention this because he did at least three broadcasts from Birdland in 1961 (one in September and two in December), and there may be transcriptions or privately recorded tapes laying around.

At the time of this review there are no track lists or sound samples on this page - you can access both on the MP3 format of this album at [[ASIN:B00S0OY66C The Driving New Jazz Piano of Harold Corbin. Soul Brother]]. I was unfamiliar with Corbin until I stumbled across this album. The scant bio and other information claims that he was heavily influenced by Erroll Garner. That is evident in the tracks on this album, but his style also has more than a hint of classical. He tends to 'concertize' on some of the tracks (a term my bandleader/pianist uses to describe a style influenced by classical training.) That element is certainly there.

The album is very short at just over thirty seven minutes, but is packed with some excellent playing. Corbin is backed by Spanky DeBrest on bass and Eddie Campbell on drums. I am very familiar with DeBrest's playing because he surfaces on some of the 1950s Jazz Messenger albums. His playing here is solid. I am not familiar with Campbell, but am impressed by his playing.

The first ten tracks on this album were recorded in NYC for the Roulette label in June, 1961 and released as The Driving New Jazz Piano of Harold Corbin (SR 52079). The remaining two tracks were recorded prior to the main album - they led to the Roulette contract - in Philadelphia as the A and B sides of a 45 RPM record for the Twentieth Century label.

title: Uncanny recreation
text:
I am a big Bix fan, and especially anything he recorded with Frankie Trumbauer who was Lester Young's inspiration. This album manages to recreate the sound and vibe while avoiding a note-for-note performance. That is one of the main reasons why I awarded it five stars.

The best way to compare this album to the real thing is to run through the sound samples on this page, then jump to [[ASIN:B006MXVBXE The Complete Collection]], which is more representative of Bix (and Tram) since it is a comprehensive collection of their recordings. The similarities in style are uncanny. Note that the song selections are different since this album is designed to recreate with Bix would have sounded like on an album of Gershwin tunes.

One of the main success factors of the authentic sound is the musicians. Three - Dick Hyman, Tom Pletcher and Eddie Metz Jr. - are well versed in this style of music. Hyman is an encyclopedia of both knowledge and playing styles, Pletcher is a staunch Bix devotee, and Metz is one of the most versatile drummers who is more at home in tradtional jazz than many living drummers. It's as though the album was a labor of love for them.

In addition to Hyman's piano, Pletcher's coronet and Metz' drums, the rest of the members of the ensemble are perfect. Dan Levinson is certainly versed in the music and not only does a remarkable job on clarinet, but actually uses a C melody saxophone like Tram. Bob Leary's guitar (and banjo) are also authentic. One can hear shades of Eddie Lang in the guitar. What truly added to this was Vince Giordano's bass saxophone. The latter has a deep, tuba sound like bands from Bix's era, but allows faster notes unlike a tuba. I am guessing that Hyman thought that up. Regardless, it was yet another touch that makes this album so great (to my ears anyway).

If you are a Bix fan this album keeps the spirit of his music alive with a great deal of integrity.

title: Great quartet album
text:
This is an excellent Teddy Edwards album featuring him leading a quartet of mainly West Coast jazz luminaries. Since there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review you can listen to them on tracks 13 through 21 on this two-album set: [[ASIN:B00MHQRKA8 Love Moods - Good Gravy]].

One of my reasons for rating this album so highly is it features Phineas Newborn, Jr. on piano on the first two tracks. He is a personal favorite. The remaining tracks feature the lesser known (but excellent) Danny Horton on piano leading a rhythm section comprised of Leroy Vinnegar on bass and Milt Turner on drums. Vinnegar is another reason why I rated this album so highly because he was one of the top West Coast bassists whom I have on a number of other albums and have grown to admire.

This album was recorded for the Contemporary label in Los Angeles on August 23 through 25, 1961. If you are a Teddy Edwards fan it's a treat because as the sound samples I mentioned above convey, his playing is exquisite and the rhythm section is perfect behind him.

title: Great vocals backed by Teddy Edwards' Septet and Quartet
text:
Discovering this album was a serendipity because I was digging into the works of pianist Phineas Newborn, Jr. when I stumbled across it. Stewart's voice - to me - is incredible. While there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review you can listen to them on a double album set's product page at [[ASIN:B00MHQRKA8 Love Moods - Good Gravy]]. If you are new to Stewart's vocals be prepared to be delighted.

The backing ensembles on this album are led by tenor saxophonist Teddy Edwards and are comprised of some of the finest West Coast jazz musicians of the era. On the first four tracks, recorded for Contemporary on January 20, 1961, Stewart backed by the Teddy Edwards Septet comprised of Edwards on tenor saxophone, Jack Sheldon on trumpet, Frank Rosolino on trombone, Art Pepper on alto saxophone, Pete Jolly on piano, Jimmy Bond on bass and Frank Butler on drums.

On the remaining tracks Stewart is backed by the Teddy Edwards Quartet comprised of Teddy Edwards on tenor saxophone, Phineas Newborn, Jr. on piano, Leroy Vinnegar on bass and Milt Turner on drums. These tracks were recorded on August 21 and 22, 1961.

This has quickly become one of my frequently played albums and has made me a staunch fan of Stewart.

title: Billie Holiday live in Cologne, Germany
text:
At the time of this review this album, a vinyl version of [[ASIN:B00LYX2UC8 Lady Love by Billie Holiday]], is erroneously cross-linked to a CD album by the same title by Lou Rawls. I am reviewing the Billie Holiday album.

This is a live performance of Billie at the Jazz Club U.S.A. in Cologne, Germany on January 5, 1954. Since the track list is not listed on this page (at the time of this review) I am including it because there were two ensembles backing Billie on this album. Tracks A1 through A8 feature Billie backed by Carl Drinkard on piano, Red Mitchell on bass and Elaine Leighton on drums. These tracks are:
A1 Announcement by Leonard Feather 0:26
A2 Blue Moon 2:08
A3 All Of Me 1:38
A4 My Man 2:45
A5 Them There Eyes 1:30
A6 I Cried For You 3:10
A7 What A Little Moonlight Can Do 2:25
A8 I Cover The Waterfront 3:10

The final tracks - all on Side B - feature a much larger ensemble coming out at the performance and backing her. Here she is backed by Buddy DeFranco on clarinet, Red Norvo on vibraphone, Sonny Clark on piano, Jimmy Raney on guitar, Red Mitchell on bass and Elaine Leighton on drums. The track titles are:
B1 Billie's Blues 11:28
B2 Lover Come Back To Me 6:35

This album was recorded for and released by United Artists as UAJ 14014. The sound quality is very good, but not spectacular, and the music is energetic. This is not an essential album, but one die hard fans will appreciate.

title: Recorded in 1952, released in 1956 and timeless today
text:
This album started life as eight tracks from a Clef Records 10" that was recorded in Los Angeles on March 26, 1952 and released as [[ASIN:B000WLMNTS Billie Holiday Sings]]. When Clef morphed into Verve this album was rereleased with four additional tracks from an April 1952 session. This album has all of those tracks plus others that were recorded during both sessions, including an alternate take of Autumn in New York.

Instead or trying to describe the music or the sound quality, run through the sound samples that have been added to this page and let those convey the essence of this album. I will say that Billie is powerful and this album all the more enjoyable because of the ensembles backing her.

The first session on March 26 was recorded at Radio Recorders in Los Angeles. She is backed by Charlie Shavers on trumpet and Flip Phillips on tenor saxophone, and a solid rhythm section comprised of Oscar Peterson on piano, Barney Kessel on guitar, Ray Brown on bass and Alvin Stoller on drums.

For the April session the recordings were made at an unspecified location (probably Radio Recorders as well) with the same backing ensemble except J. C. Heard replaces Stoller on drums.

This is classic Lady Day in my opinion and a great album that every fan should own. In fact I would have no qualms introducing potential fans to her work with this one.

title: Poor sound quality on many tracks, but pure gold for fans
text:
This set of tracks range from 1944 to 1949 and most are taken from transcription discs from live broadcasts. Some are probably private recordings based on the diminished sound quality. Regardless, if you are a die hard fan this album provides insights into her sound on stage. The entire album clocks in at a few seconds short of forty minutes.

Here is a rundown on the tracks and when and where they were recorded:

Tracks 1 and 2 were recorded at the Apollo Theater in NYC on December 15, 1945. The backing ensemble is the Apollo orchestra featuring Hot Lips Page.

Track 3 is the oldest track that is taken from the Esquire First Annual Concert in NYC on January 18, 1944. Billie is backed by the Coleman Hawkins All Star Band.

Tracks 4 through 12 were recorded in Los Angeles in early 1949 and feature Billie backed by Red Norvo's orchestra.

Track 13 was recorded in NYC on Jenuary 13, 1947 with Billie backed by Teddy Wilson and his orchestra.

Track 14 was recorded in Los Angeles some time in 1949 (I could not nail the date), and features Billie backed by Percy Faith and his orchestra.

This is not for everybody because of the sound quality, but even with that flaw it captures the magic of Billie's voice on every track. I cannot bring myself to subtract a star because I get a lot of enjoyment from this set of performances. If you are an audiophile, though, you may want to pass it by.

title: All of the tracks and takes from both Mulligan collaborations
text:
This is a complete set of tracks from two sets of recording sessions in NYC for the World Pacific label.

Before describing the sessions, since there are no sound samples on this page at the time go to [[ASIN:B006RCWD78 Sings a Song With Mulligan! (Bonus Track Version)]] and take a listen. While that MP3 album has additional tracks it also contains all of the ones this CD does and you can hear before making a final purchase decision.

Tracks 6 through 16 comprise what was recorded during the first set of sessions on December 11 and 12, 1957. They feature Ross backed by Mulligan's quartet that was comprised of Mulligan on baritone sax, Chet Baker on trumpet, Henry Grimes on bass and Dave Bailey on drums.

The second session was recorded in a single day on September 25, 1958, and has Ross backed by a different Mulligan quartet comprised of Mulligan on baritone sax, Art Farmer on trumpet, Bill Crow on bass and Dave Bailey on drums. The tracks from this session are the first five on the CD.

You need not be a Ross or a Mulligan (or Baker) fan to appreciate this album. It's just as hip and swinging today as it was when recorded in the late 1950s. Plus it has Henry Grimes on most of the tracks, so if you have followed his life and career you will know what a treasure he is, as well as one of those rare individuals who had a spectacular comeback after being lost in obscurity for nearly a half century.

title: London House 1961 oiriginally recorded for Verve
text:
Note: this review is for the CD version of this album at the following product page: [[ASIN:B00CL1C6F8 The Trio: Live From Chicago (2 CD)]]. At the time of this review the bonus tracks on this album differ from the bonus tracks on the MP3 version at [[ASIN:B00BKRT2S8 The Trio. Live from Chicago (with Ray Brown & Ed Thigpen) [Bonus Track Version]]], although the core tracks are identical.

If you are on the CD's product page you can listen to sound samples on the MP3's page. Those capture the energy of the performances. For the first seven tracks on each album they were recorded on July 28 and 29, 1961 at the London House in Chicago. This is the classic OP trio with Ray Brown on bass and Ed Thigpen on drums and as intense as they normally are, they are at their pinnacle on those nights. In my opinion, anyway.

The bonus tracks on Disc Two are taken from August and October 1961 performances at the London House. All of the tracks were originally recorded for Verve, although this and the MP3 version are credited to a different label. That said, the mastering and sound quality of this CD set are excellent to my ears.

Oscar Peterson Trio fans will love this set. Indeed, it is one of the better live albums for that Peterson/Brown/Thigpen lineups and one that I recommend to friends who want to delve into the trio's larger body of work.

title: Some unreleased gems (12 are Wilson's own)
text:
If you are a Teddy Wilson fan this album is important because none of the material had been previously released, and because twelve of the tracks are his own compositions. As another reviewer stated the tracks on this album are from old albums made for radio broadcast by the Keystone Broadcasting System. The unreleased discs came from Wilson's estate, and was subsequently compiled into this album and released in 1997.

Considering the period in which these tracks were recorded the sound quality is simply amazing (to my ears). Whoever mastered this set knew what they were doing and were obviously working from pristine discs because this is much more than a 'needle drop' transfer.

Listen to the sound samples on the MP3 version's product page at [[ASIN:B0012PAIEU Solo Piano - The Keystone Transcriptions]]. This album clocks in at just under an hour and five minutes of Wilson's characteristic playing. Personally, knowing that these were all intended for radio broadcast makes them special to me because none of them are duplicates in my extensive collection of Wilson's albums. Indeed, many of the songs are one-off titles that show up nowhere else.

Another thing that I love is the fact that twelve of the twenty-six tracks are Wilson's own compositions. Those are tracks 4 through 6, 9, 11, 14 through 16, 20 and 23 credited solely to Wilson with co-composer credits on tracks 12 with Harold Adamson and 13 with Haven Johnson.

Overall, this is truly essential for die hard Wilson fans such as myself, as well as for anyone who enjoys great piano playing.

title: Remains a favorite
text:
I keep coming back to this album for various reasons during the nearly twenty years that I have owned it. One of the reasons is I am also a Nat King Cole fan, but another is Krall has matured and evolved musically and I sometimes revisit this to remind myself of her beginnings.

Actually, this is her third album, so she was maturing when it was recorded. While the sound samples on this page convey the music, they do not provide enough time to hear just how identical Krall's phrasing is to Nat King Cole's. That part of her playing continues to this day, so hearing this early album gives you a good sense of the foundations of her later music.

Her backing ensemble is perfect - in my opinion - for the music, and especially the fact that percussion is very minimal and confined to Boulevard of Broken Dreams where it does add to the song.. The real essence - again, in my opinion, is the synergy among Krall, Paul Keller on bass and Russell Malone on guitar. They come close to capturing the magic of what I consider to be the best Nat King Cole Trio line-up with Johnny Miller on bass and Oscar Moore on guitar. Make no mistake, they wisely did not try to replicate that trio, but did manage to play in the same spirit.

For folks like myself who care about such things, this album was recorded in only six days between October 3 and 8, 1995 at The Power Station (now Avatar Studios) in NYC. Krall is on every track except If I Had You where Benny Green takes over on piano. The only track with percussion features Steve Kroon.

title: Jazz session superstar compilation from three 1956 albums
text:
This is a compilation drawn from three 1956 albums that were recorded over the course of four sessions for Epic in NYC. Before I delve into the boring details of the sessions, give the sound samples on the MP3 format of this album a listen at [[ASIN:B005MH8VGQ The New York Rhythm Section]]. That page also contains the track list of the 21 songs that are included in the nearly 71 minutes of music.

The source albums for this compilation are out of print. Tracks here are from The Rhythm Section (Epic LN3271), After Hours Jazz (Epic LN3339P) and Rhythm Plus One (Epic LN3297).. These albums were recorded on April 16 and 25, and May 3 and 8, 1956.

Personnel comprising the core rhythm section are Hank Jones on piano, Barry Galbraith on guitar, Milt Hinton on bass and Osie Johnson on drums. They were the NY jazz equivalent of the Los Angeles rock session gods known as the Wrecking Crew. Trombonist Jimmy Cleveland appears on four tracks (three from Rhythm Plus one: Wolf Talk, Sahara, and Blues, and Jimmy's Tune on After Hours Jazz.)

If you are a member of a jazz rhythm section this is a great album to study because the music and playing certainly stand the test of time. The recording quality is excellent and the individual musicians are true masters of their respective instruments. You need not be a musician to enjoy this album, though, because it's enjoyable across the board.

title: Ella unadorned
text:
This two album set is truly pure Ella because it strips away all supporting ensembles except for the great Ellis Larkins backing her on piano. If you are a big Ella fan you will find the absence of strings, swing bands or even piano trios refreshing because there is nothing between you and her talent but an exceptionally well played piano.

Another thing I love is this is Ella in the early 1950s, and her style and voice had been tempered by the evolving music before it settled down after the bebop phase.

The best way to gauge this album if you are making a purchase decision is to go through the sound samples on this page. There is sufficient play to hear the essence of this set, and the sound quality is surprisingly good for the era. Both albums were recorded for the Decca label and both feature just Fitzgerald and Larkins.

Tracks 1 through 8 are the out-of-print album titled Ella Sings Gershwin that was recorded on September 11, 1950. The remaining tracks are the album titled [[ASIN:B000W0AG2K Songs in a Mellow Mood]] that was recorded on March 29 and 30, 1954.

If you are a fan this is must have in my opinion. If you enjoy excellent piano/vocalist duos this should delight you.

title: Comprehensive survey of evolution of jazz piano
text:
Note: I am reviewing the physical media set and not the MP3 version, so this review contains references to a DVD that is included in the physical media set. The focus of this set is on jazz and the roots from which it sprang (ragtime and stride). Boogie and other contributing or ancillary styles are included. More about that below.

This set is nearly breathtaking in scope and you will probably be repeating both the CDs and the DVD that are included as you read through the booklet.

What I love is this can be used as an educational tool or just for entertaining listening. The DVD, of course, is aimed at pianists or other interested musicians. Although I am a drummer I came away with a keener understanding of what the various pianists that I back are doing musically, so this is not only for pianists.

The CDs are Hyman himself displaying his versatility with many styles as well as his amazing chops. The man is definitely a virtuoso, and a wealth of knowledge on top of that. Here is a rundown on the CDs:

DISC ONE covers ragtime and stride with an emphasis on Jelly Roll Morton (and his ideas about the 'Spanish Tinge', James P. Johnson (father of stride), Earl Hines and early Mary Lou Williams.

DISC TWO tin pan alley with an emphasis on Gershwin, novelty piano styles, boogie woogie, and James P. Johnson;s disciples (Fats Waller, Willie 'The Lion' Smith and two giants who changed playing: Art Tatum and Teddy Wilson. Note: in fairness to Earl Hines on Disc One one can make a case that Himes is the real father of jazz piano.

DISC THREE delves into swing with a focus on both Duke Ellington and Count Basie, Erroll Garner, early bebop (Bud Powell, Monk, etc.) and blues.

DISC FOUR: Monk and a plethora of other beboppers, then a grand tour of some important pianists who followed from Lenny Tristano to Bill Evans.

DISC FIVE is a catch all much like the infamous Disc Ten is in [[ASIN:B000BITUEI Jazz : A Film By Ken Burns]]. A lot of material is compressed into this disc and not every majoy pianist can be cited. Still, it's enough to pique your interest.

DVD: this is a favorite because Hyman gives mini lessons that focus on the key styles of some of the most influential pianists that are covered in the CDs. Not only are style and technique covered, but some anecdotes and historical context are provided to bring the lessons alive.

Finally, the booklet augments and serves as a brief road map to the discs in this set. I found it to be an important and integral part of this set, but I am a musician and stuff like that fascinates me.

If you are a pianist you will also want to grab [[ASIN:1617740195 Dick Hyman's Century of Jazz Piano - Transcribed! - Instructional Book/DVD]], which augments this set - note for note.

title: Perfect ending
text:
This album was Brown's last as a leader and - to me - a fitting end mark to a remarkable career. Before proceeding with my take I want to say that this album was panned by some critics for not having a drummer. As a drummer I can say that one was not required, and would have probably broken the spell that the music holds for me personally. If you happen to be a drummer, think of this is one of those 'Minus One' play-along albums and dig in.

Sadly there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review. Each track, especially on the first disc, is a mini masterpiece and a shining example of what a jazz trio should be. In particular, Alexander's piano work is more subdued than what he is known for, but it worked beautifully in this context. Brown's bass is unmistakable with his characteristic tone and feel. The big surprise for me is Malone's guitar work. I am familiar with him from his work with Diana Krall, but here he has the opportunity to play in such a nuanced style that he won me over completely. I am not especially fond of guitars, but Malone has earned a place on my short list of favorite guitarists.

A few notes. First, it's easy to compare this trio to other ones in which Brown was a member and especially the Oscar Peterson Trio when Herb Ellis was a member. The music here is totally different in character. For one thing Alexander has a style that is completely different. On the other hand you can hear a touch of Herb Ellis in Malone's playing, although you can probably trace that back to Oscar Moore, who influenced Charlie Christian who in turn had a major influence on Ellis. The common thread, though, is Brown.

Disc Two of this set does contain a few tracks with some great drummers like Jeff Hamilton and Lewis Nash. For some reason the track list for that CD is not included in the product description (at the time of this review), so I will include it here:
01. Tin Tin Deo (Brown with Monty Alexander and Russell Malone) (10:34)
02. CRS-Craft (Brown with Monty Alexander and Russell Malone) (8:09)
03. Tanga (Brown with Monty Alexander, Benny Green, Jeff Hamilton and Russell Malone) (4:18)
04. En Estate (Brown with Monty Alexander and Russell Malone)(7:32)
05. Bye Bye Blackbird (Brown with Monty Alexander, Benny Green and Russell Malone)(10:35)
06. Blue Monk (Brown with Monty Alexander, John Clayton, Russell Malone and Christian McBride) (7:58)
07. St. Louis Blues (Brown with Monty Alexander, Russell Malone and Lewis Nash) (7:11)
08. Lament (Brown with Monty Alexander, Geoff Keezer, Russell Malone andKarriem Riggins) (8:17)
09. Get Happy (Brown with Monty Alexander, John Clayton, Russell Malone and Christian McBride (4:02)
10. Mysterioso (Brown with Monty Alexander, John Clayton, Russell Malone and Christian McBride (8:14)

If you love Ray Brown or jazz piano trios, or just exceptional music this set is a delight. It's worth every penny for the first disc, and the second one is icing on a very delicious cake.

title: A gem
text:
I'm both a Bill Evans and a flute fan, so this collaboration is one of my gems. Need I attempt to describe Evans' playing? It's especially typical for this part of his career, and provides beautiful support to Steig.

Jeremy Steig is pensive and his playing seems to favor the lower registers. Of course, the rhythm section that is comprised of Eddie Gomez on bass and Marty Morell on drums also adds to what I consider to be magic on this album.

It was recorded in NYC for Verve over the course of four sessions in 1969 (January 30, February 3 and 5, and March 11). Sadly there are no sound samples at the time of this review on this page nor on the album to which I linked. The tracks are:
1. Straight, No Chaser
2. Lover Man
3. What's New
4. Autumn Leaves
5. Time Out For Chris
6. Love Theme From Spartacus
7. So What

Before making a final purchase decision check out [[ASIN:B0013UXYN6 Bill Evans with the Flutists: What's New / Nirvana]], which contains this album as well as Evans' collaboration with Herbie Mann. On that album you can compare and contrast the vastly different styles and musical approaches of two great flautists. Either way, though, you cannot go wrong.

title: Another transition moment in Evans' body of work
text:
I have my favorite editions of Evans' trios, which include such pairings as Scott LaFaro on bass and Paul Motian on drums, as well as Eddie Gomez on bass and Marty Morell on drums. This rhythm section, though, is intriguing because it features Jack DeJohnette on drums opposite Gomez.

Normally when there are sound samples available I recommend letting those guide folks who are trying to decide. The CD product page is missing them, but you can listen to snippets on the MP3 album's product page at [[ASIN:B000VZO2ZS Bill Evans - At The Montreux Jazz Festival]]. In this case, though, the sound samples do not begin to convey the music. Partly because Evans give both Gomez and DeJohnette a lot of leeway and they take it. Of course, Evans characteristically gave his rhythm sections a lot of space and especially on this album you can hear some amazing solo work.

I especially like DeJohnette's work, both in a supporting role as well as in a solo context. He is a virtuoso pianist (and composer) in his own right and it's powerful to listen to how connected he is to Evans ... and Gomez. In fact, one critic thought the highlight of this album was the interplay between Evans and Gomez. I am taking a contrary view and not just because I am a drummer. I do think, though, that nobody will disagree that Evans was in fine form and the real center of this performance.

Another reason why I love this album is it's somewhat off the beaten path of Evans' work and when I first discovered it I felt as though I found a diamond in the rough.

A few parting notes: the difference between this CD version and the MP3 version to which I linked is this one contains an extra performance of Walkin' that the MP3 album lacks. It was performed live for Verve on June 15, 1968 and is one of those Bill Evans albums that true fans will enjoy.

title: Bill Evans and an opportunity to compare and contrast Jeremy Steig and Herbie Mann
text:
I own the two albums that comprise this set so when I was given this as a gift I had both the time and opportunity to hear two greats back-to-back. The first seven tracks are the album titled [[ASIN:B004Q84XPK Whats New]] that was recorded in NYC for Verve over the course of four sessions in 1969 (January 30, February 3 and 5, and March 11). Sadly there are no sound samples at the time of this review on this page nor on the album to which I linked. The tracks are:
1. Straight, No Chaser
2. Lover Man
3. What's New
4. Autumn Leaves
5. Time Out For Chris
6. Love Theme From Spartacus
7. So What

There is a marked difference between Jeremy Steig's playing on these tracks and Mann's on the remainder of the album. For one thing Steig is more pensive and his playing seems to favor the lower registers. Another difference is the rhythm section that is comprised of Eddie Gomez on bass and Marty Morell on drums. They are quite different from the the Chuck Israels/Paul Motian pairing on the next six tracks. S

Those remaining tracks comprise the album titled [[ASIN:B00124JEX2 Nirvana]]. It features Herbie Mann on flute and his approach is more swinging and, frankly, more in-your-face energy. I am not saying one is better than the other, but the differences between the two flautists and the albums are like night and day. Plus Chuck Israels on bass and Paul Motian on drums are two different musicians than Gomez and Morell. Another factor is this album was recorded seven years earlier when jazz itself was changing. The good news about these tracks, though, is both the listing and sound samples are available on the product page to which I linked, Let those and your ears guide you regarding the value of the Nirvana part of this album. Nirvana was recorded in NYC for Atlantic on December 8, 1961 and May 4, 1962.

For me the keystone is Bill Evans, although I also have a sizable Herbie Mann album collection. Steig is a real treat, and especially when heard next to tracks that feature Mann with Evans as the common denominator.

title: A real gem
text:
Since this particular CD is out of print and priced in the stratosphere at the time of this review I am going to cover the content and sidestep value and pricing issues. I do want to say that the mastering on this JVC disc is superb.

While there are no sound samples or even a track list on this product page at the time of this review you can find both on this page: [[ASIN:B000UBOPR8 Loose Blues]]. That is the original name of the album and for convenience I am also including the track list and times here:
1. Loose Bloose 7:07
2. Loose Bloose 5:34
3. Time Remembered 6:02
4. Funkallero 6:13
5. My Bells 5:24
6. There Came You 5:52
7 Fudgesickle Built for Four 4:31
8. Fun Ride 5:15
Total run time: 45:46

Let the sound samples on the Loose Blues page convey the music. And for the record, the real title should have been 'Loose Bloose' based on the title track, but for some reason was released as Loose Blues.

All of the tracks are Evans' own compositions, and his playing is excellent. It's the line-up of backing musicians who truly make this album magic. Zoot Sims on tenor sax adds a lot of depth to Evans' arrangements and the chemistry is certainly evident between the two. Jim Hall on guitar is pure magic in my opinion, and Ron Carter and Philly Joe Jones are a rock solid rhythm section. While I love the LaFaro/Motian and Gomez /Morell bassist and drummer pairings of Evans' better trios, Carter and Jones are perfect for this session.

This album was originally recorded for the Milestone label in the Nola Penthouse Sound Studios in NYC on August 21 and 22, 1962. It was shelved until 1982 when it was first released.

If you can find this JVC reissue at a reasonable price I recommend grabbing it for the sound quality. If not, you probably won't be disappointed by the MP3 album I linked above.

title: Not essential, but great music and energy
text:
I recently unearthed my copy of this excellent live performance and wonder why I had not ripped it to my phone a long time ago. It's a shame that there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review) because there is an ambiance from Ronnie Scott's club and patrons, as well as the playing itself that gives this album energy.

To be honest, this is not Evans' best album, but to my ears it's good enough to snag if you can obtain a copy at a reasonable price. Evans' playing is typical for what he was doing in the mid 1960s. On the plus side, this album captures him at his consistent best playing standards. Some of his live performances, especially the lesser known ones like this one, could be spotty. So the fact that he is in full command of his powers on this album makes it worthwhile.

Evans is also backed by a solid rhythm section: Chuck Israels on bass and Larry Bunker on drums, I've been a long time fan of Bunker who adds a lot to the performance (and forgive my bias).

For reference the first five tracks were recorded on March 2, 1965 and 6 through 9 on March 11 at Ronnie Scott's in London. Les Tomkins conducted the interview excerpt on track 10 on January 4, 1972. In fact, I have heard (but have not confirmed) that Tomkins recorded the sets that comprise this album for personal use. If that's the case the sound quality is surprisingly good for a 'bootleg.'

As I said, this is not essential, but if you are a Bill Evans fan it's highly recommended.

title: Great album
text:
I am reviewing the album and not the value since the asking price for this out-of-print gem is about two hundred bucks at the time of this review. These pop up for sale at more reasonable prices on auction sites and other places.

The reason why I awarded this five stars is mainly because of Paul Smith's incredible piano work. I own a number of his albums and love the way he manages to 'concertize' standards, yet still swing.

Sadly there are no sound samples on this page, but the recording quality is excellent on the CD that I own. Another thing that makes this a five star recording is the rhythm section. Ray Brown on bass should not require an introduction, but if you are new to jazz he was an integral part of the Oscar Peterson Trio, and has recorded with virtually everyone. Drummer Louie Bellson is known for his chops, but also for his ability to play tastefully in smaller ensembles. He is perfect here.

Back to Smith's style that I mentioned above. The tracks on this album are prime examples of that style. Here is the complete track list with starting times for the CD version:
1. The Lady Is a Tramp 00:00
2. Yesterdays 04:24
3. Everything Happens to Me 09:51
4. On a Clear Day 13:27
5. Surrey With the Fringe on Top 17:15
6. My Heart Stood Still 20:38
7. Chicago 26:28
8. Lover 29:58

The total length is 34:44. The album was originally recorded in Los Angeles on March 17 and 18, 1978 for the Discwasher Recordings label and issued as DR 001 DD. If you do happen to be a Paul Smith fan and find this at a decent price I recommend grabbing it. Also, if you do a search on the web for videos and include Smith, Brown, Bellson and Intensive Care in your search criteria you will be rewarded with some tracks with which you can judge the music for yourself.

title: Beautiful playing and superb sound quality
text:
A few notes about the music. This is actually from two albums, only one of which features Tatum. The first ten tracks and the last one feature Webster with Tatum and was his last recorded work before he passed away two months later. Tracks 11 through 14 are taken from a Webster led album that features Webster with Teddy Wilson on piano.

To be honest I have a lot of Tatum in my library, but most of the tracks feature him laying down a superhuman barrage of notes. Here he 'concertizes' most of the selections and plays with the same beauty as Webster.

I could go on and on about the music itself, but instead I recommend that you listen to the sound samples (if you are in the CD version's product page go to [[ASIN:B0089SZYZQ The Art Tatum and Ben Webster Quartet (Bonus Track Version)]], which also contains the track list that is not on the CD's page.)

I've owned the albums that comprise this one in one incarnation or the other for over twenty years. In fact I am listening to it again as I write this review. I've always loved Webster's playing - he has a big, virile sound, but can also deliver a ballad with such delicacy and beauty that it's moving. Most of his playing on this album is the latter.

Sound quality is absolutely superb on this CD. This was initially mastered by Fresh Sound Records, a label that I've come to trust.

I mentioned that this is actually two albums. Here is the breakdown of the who, when and where.

Tracks 1-7 are the album titled Ben Webster-Art Tatum Quartet. They were recorded for Verve in Los Angeles on September 11, 1956. Backing Webster and Tatum are Red Callender on bass and Bill Douglas on drums.

Tracks 8 through 10 are alternate takes from the September 11 session that were not released on the original album.

Tracks 11 through 14 are from the album titled Music For Loving that was recorded for Verve's predecessor label (NOGRAN) in NYC on on March 30, 1954. Webster is paired with Teddy Wilson on piano and backed by Ray Brown on bass and Papa Jo Jones on drums.

Track 15 is Tatum solo that was recorded in Los Angeles on December 29, 1953.

title: A.K.A. Keep on Blowin'
text:
This is a laid back and soulful album that just flows. That's not to say that it's all mellow because some of the tracks are plain cookin', but there is a difference between Jack McDuff on organ on this album and the better known Jimmy Smith's more aggressive approach. Neither is better than the other - just different.

Another reason why this is laid back when the music calls for it is guitarist Bill Jennings. I love his playing and own a number of albums that feature him as leader. He has a touch and approach that somehow combines blues, jazz, R&B and funk (even before there was such a word applied to music). It all shows on every track on this album.

Finally, Willis Jackson's smooth and soulful tenor sax is the magic ingredient. The interplay between and among McDuff, Willis and Jennings is a joy and can draw you in.

Rounding out the rhythm section are three bassists (Milt Hinton on Keep On A' Blowin'), Wendell Marshall on On The Sunny Side Of The Street and Blue Strollin') and Tommy Potter on the remining tracks. Buck Clark is credited with the congas on Keep On A' Blowin' and Alvin Johnson on drums.

Since there is no track listing on this page at the time of this review I'll provide it:
SIDE A
A1 Keep On A' Blowin'
A2 How Deep Is The Ocean
A3 On The Sunny Side Of The Street
SIDE B
B1 Blue Strollin'
B2 The Man I Love
B3 A Smooth One

As for the music quality, I am loathe to comment since I am using a cheap turntable. To my ears though is is more than adequate, but I cannot tell how good (or bad) this vinyl would sound on high-end gear.

This album was recorded for Prestige at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack and Englewood Cliffs, NJ studio over the course of three sessions (May 25 and November 9, 1959 and February 26, 1960). For the total jazz geek A2, B2 and B3 were all recorded in the Hackensack studio during the May 25 session, and the remaining tracks in the [then new] Englewood Cliffs studio (A3 and B1 on November 9 and A1 during the February 26 session).

title: Another delight in my growing collection of Parrott's albums
text:
If you are a fan I need not say much, but if you are just now discovring Nicki Parrott and do not know which album to get this one is more up tempo than [[ASIN:B0046EDACQ Fly Me to the Moon]]. On the other hand, that one has lusher arrangements that include her sister Lisa on both baritone and soprano saxophones. This one, though truly flows.

I've heard other albums she has released, as well as enjoyed live video clips of her with luminaries like Les Paul and Rossano Sportiello and this one has the energy of her live performances. Not that her other albums are not superb also because I would hate to have to choose just one.

What I love about this one is the arrangements are more straightforward and allow you to hear the many nuances she brings to songs. And nuances she brings becuase on a track like Cry Me A River she evokes Julie London's iconic delivery, but manages to make it her own as well. On Nicki's Blues her vocals are true blues and easily sells that particular song. In fact, I would be hard pressed to pick a favorite track, but Moon River and Takin' A Chance On Love keep popping into my head.

Sadly there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review. You can hear some of the songs on this album if you search Youtube, but the entire album is so delightful that a few songs will only whet your appetite.

In addition to Nicki I have come to respect the pianist and the drummer (John Di Martino on piano and Billy Drummond on drums) who are on a lot of her albums. Both are excellent and as a fellow drummer I acknowledge Drummond as a true master who plays with a lot of taste. Tenor saxophonist Harry Allen is also on more than a few of her albums and is to her what Lester Young was to Billie (in my opinion - I am drawing an analogy instead of a comparison). Rounding out the ensemble here is Paul Myers who added a lot to the music.

Overall this is probably one of my favorite Parrott albums, if for no other reason than it showcases her versatility as a vocalist and a bassist. It also has more raw energy (to my ears) than her other albums - but that's just me.

title: I've quickly become a fan
text:
I came to Parrott via a Youtube video of her and Les Paul, which led to some of her collaborations with Rossano Sportiello. From there I was hooked and this album validates that.

At the time of this review there is no track list, nor are there any sound samples. I an remedy the first omission by providing the list below. As for describing the music I will do my best.

Most of the tracks are at slower tempos than I am accustomed to for the songs. For example, the intro to Bei Mir Bist Du Schoen segues into a much slower rendition than just about any other version I have heard. Even Waltzing Matilda from Parrott's home country of Australia seems a bit on the slow side. I am not complaining because every track has a sensuality that comes from the arrangements, the lavish use of tenor and baritone saxophones, and Parrott's delivery.

Nicki's sister Lisa is on baritone and sporano sax on this album, paired with Harry Allen on tenor. The rhythm section is John Di Martino on piano, Mark Sganga on guitar, Nicki on bass and Billy Drummond on drums. The entire ensemble is tight, which is not easy at the languorous at which they are playing.

One other note: Nicki has a distinct vocal style, but on I Never Had A Chance I swear she was channeling Anita O'Day.

Here is the track list, which is lacking at the time of this review:
1. Bei Mir Bist Du Schoen
2. I Love The Way You're Breakin' My Heart
3. Do It Again
4. Fly Me To The Moon
5. La Vie En Rose
6. Waltzing Matilda
7. I Never Had A Chance
8. Evil Gal Blues
9. For All We Know
10. Charade
11. I Never Dreamed You'd Leave In Summer
12. Them There Eyes
13. Two For The Road

title: Excellent live performance
text:
I own a lot of Humes' performances on albums and individual tracks going back to 1941 (with Don Byas at Minton's in NYC). This performance, though, captures her energy in a live setting as a much more mature vocalist.

Give the sound samples on this page a run through and you will hear what I was trying to convey above the energy of this too-short performance. Humes has just turned 61 when this album was recorded on July 2, 1974 at the Montreux Jazz Festival.

What intrigues me about this album is both Earl Hines and Jay McShann are credited as pianists. I honestly cannot tell them apart and I can usually hear Hines' signature style as well as McShann's. I will say they the piano backing on all songs is extraordinary. In fact whichever of the two played on the first track did a masterful job.

The other musicians backing Humes are Buddy Tate on tenor sax, Jimmy Woode on bass and Ed Thigpen on drums. Tate added as lot, as did Woode's bass. The big surprise is Thigpen who is known as 'Mr. Taste' for his subtle playing and brushwork playing some heavy backbeats.

If you are a Helen Humes fan this may not be an essential album, but it's fun. Her singing is in excellent form and the backing ensemble cooks.

title: Ranks high on my favorite Getz and Evans lists
text:
I am a fan of both Getz and Evans, so this is a treat for me. I am going to refrain from comparing it to [[ASIN:B000W1QNLW Stan Getz and Bill Evans]] because both featured leaders had matured musically by the time this album was recorded, and I dislike comparing studio albums like the 1964 one to live recordings like this.

The best way to determine if this album is for you is to listen to the sound samples. To me the playing is in top form for Getz and Evans. You can still hear echoes of Lester Young in Getz' playing, even though he had evolved considerably. And there is a throwback of Evans' playing to the Kind of Blue sessions. But in the main - despite the infamous Stan's Blues episode - there is a real synergy between the two.

More than just Getz and Evans, I love this for both Eddie Gomez's bass work and Marty Morell's drumming. Morrel, in particular, has been an influence, so I take every opportunity to listen to him. I also hold Gomez in the highest regard as a musician and his playing on this album is incredible. In fact, I've probably spent more time delving into their roles on this album than I have Getz and Evans.

This album was actually recorded from two different performances, with the six tracks from the Middelheim Jazz Festival in Belgium on August 16, 1974, sandwiched between the first and last two tracks from a live performance from the Laren International Jazz Festival in the Netherlands on August 9, 1874. I do not know the model of the piano used at the August 16, 1974 performance, but the sound and tone of that instrument captivated me when I first heard this album. Of course Bill Evans had much to do with it.

If you are a fan of either Getz or Evans (or both) this is a worthwhile album. If you are a bassist or drummer, you will learn much from Gomez and Morell's playing too. For me this is a five star delight.

title: Superb collaboration
text:
I'm both a Shearing and a Montgomery fan, so this CD is a real treat for me. I especially love Wes with his brothers because there is a telepathic magic in ensembles featuring all three together. On this one brother Buddy - who is more frequently on piano - gives up that seat to Shearing and plays vibraphone. Brother Monk is on bass and Walter Perkins is on drums.

Listen to the sound samples on the MP3 version of this album's product page at [[ASIN:B007Z5372G George Shearing & The Montgomery Brothers]]. You'll clearly hear Shearing's imprint on some of the tracks, as well as the classic sound of the Montgomery Brothers. Note that that version of this album is missing the three alternate takes, which as another reviewer mentioned are very different renditions from one another.

The album was recorded for the Jazzland label at the United Recording Studios in Los Angeles on October 9 and 10, 1961. If you are a Wes Montgomery fan this would be his last album for Jazzland because he moved to the Riverside label shortly after. He would also not record with his brothers again until his last recorded performance via a television broadcast from Detroit, in 1968. In that respect this is a somewhat important album from an historical context as well as a great listen.

title: Two complete albums from 1959 and 1960
text:
I've always loved Wes' playing during this era. Actually, my favorite recordings go back even farther to the mid 1950s, but the two albums contained in this set have energy that was not always present on his later recordings.

These recordings were made in both quartet and trio settings, but only the first five tracks feature the Montgomery brothers. Sadly there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review). However, you can listen to samples of the first five tracks on another compilation album titled [[ASIN:B008JERYF8 Quartet Studio Sessions]], and the remaining tracks from the source album that is still in print. While I have my own opinions of the music, you'd be better served by listening to the sound samples and deciding for yourself.

Tracks 1 through 5 are the out-of-print album titled The Montgomery Brothers that was recorded for the Fantasy label in San Francisco during July, 1960 (some sources claim November). Wes is backed by brothers Buddy on piano and Monk on Fender electric bass, with Lawrence Marable on drums.

The remaining tracks are the album titled [[ASIN:B000000Y21 Dynamic New Sound]] that was recorded for Riverside at the Reeves Sound Studios in NYC on October 5 and 6, 1959. The source album to which I linked has sound samples. Here Wes is backed by Mel Rhyne on organ and Paul Parker on drums.

If you are a fan of early Wes I also recommend the album titled [[ASIN:B000LZUUMM Beginnings]] that also features the Monk brothers on every track. That album spans 1957 through 1959 and is a natural segue into this one.

title: My introduction to Nicki's talent
text:
I stumbled across this quite by accident and was drawn from the first note on the first track. Most female vocalists covering standards opt for backing by a piano trio, or a quartet that adds a guitar. Parrott is backed by those plus her sister Lisa on wind instruments and an additional tenor saxophonist. This ensemble brings a deeper level or richness to the sound.

The music swings like crazy on every track, and Nicki's bass work is as superb as her vocals in my opinion. Unfortunately there are no sound samples on this page, but you can find entire tracks from this album in Youtube. Any of them will give you a flavor of the music on this album. My personal favorite is Dark Eyes, although she did an excellent job with Black Coffee and Fever.

Indeed, the choice of songs is another reason why I awarded this album five stars. It has the obligatory standards, but also some pop tunes like Our Day Will Come and jump blues like Alright, Okay, You Win. The track list is not provided on this page at the time of this review so I am including it in a comment.

This album was recorded for the Japanese label Venus Records at Avatar Studio in NYC on December 17 through 19, 2009 and released Apr 21, 2010. Nicki's bass and vocals are accompanied (and backed) by her sister lisa on baritone and soprano saxophones, and bass clarinet, Harry Allen on tenor sax, John Di Martino on piano, Paul Myers on guitar and Dion Parson on drums.

title: Hardman's last album as a leader
text:
I've been a long time Bill Hardman fan and as I listen to his contributions to albums led by others as well as his own I am stuck by his evolution as a musician. This one is the book end to his first album as a leader - a 1961 masterpiece for Savoy titled [[ASIN:B008LNWBR8 The Bill Hardman Quintet. Saying Something]]. Contrasting that album against this one is a perfect way to gauge Hardman's professional growth on his instrument.

On this album his sound has mellowed out. This is partially because of his musical direction over the years and partly because of the arrangements and accompanying instruments. Especially the low end from Robin Eubanks' trombone and Paul Brown's bass. I am not as familiar with the rhythm section, which also includes Mickey Tucker on piano and Leroy Williams on drums, but I love their playing. Junior Cook and Hardman had a long history together so their near telepathic collaborations are expected.

The best way to gauge this music is to listen to the sound samples on this page. If you are familiar with Hardman's hard bop from earlier years and his stints with the Jazz Messengers, this one has a different vibe. It flows with ease, but still has intensity. I've always loved Hardman's tone and phrasing, and here it's at its peak. Unfortunately he would be gone in less than a year and a half after recording this album - and at a relatively young age - so there is no telling how much more his music would have changed had he even reached the tender age of 65. As it is, this is a gift to fans and an album that I consider to be essential.

It was recorded in Copenhagen on July 7, 1989 for the Steeplechase label. Some early releases of this album contained only the first six tracks, although all were recorded during the same session.

title: A short-lived Jazz Messenger line-up, but a gem
text:
I got this album when I purchased a two album set titled [[ASIN:B007KLY8W8 Tough! + Hard Bop + 1 Bonus Track]] and on that page you can listen to sound samples of tracks 1 through 5 and 9 on this one.

One of the reasons why I rated this so high is the line-up. I have been a Bill Hardman fan for quite sometime and own some of the albums that he led. I find his tone and phrasing to be remarkable for a trumpeter who is unfairly obscure. I also like the fact that this edition of the Jazz Messengers features Jackie McLean on alto sax. Blakey had a penchant for tenor saxophonists, so on the rare occasions in the early years when he used an alto instead is a treat for me. The remaining line-up on this album - including the bonus tracks - are Sam Dockerty on piano, Spanky DeBrest on bass and Blakey on drums. As a rhythm section that are as strong and driving as any Jazz Messenger line-up before or since.

The bonus tracks (6 through 8) are from an album titled [[ASIN:B00489O61I Drum Suite]] that was recorded during the same December 12 and 13, 1956 sessions as Hard Bop. The same line-up too. You can listen to sound samples of those tracks on the linked product page.

All of the tracks - main album and bonus - were recorded for Columbia in NYC, and all are incredibly rhythmic. As a side note, the Gershwin Medley on track 9 was recorded for inclusion on this album, but was not on the original release, This is one of three recordings that Blakey did of that medley (here, on the album titled Tough! and one on a KABC-TV Stars Of Jazz episode that first aired on October 29, 1956.)

If you are a Jazz Messengers fan chances are this album is missing from your library. Listen to the sound samples on the pages I linked above and hear for yourself why you should have it in your playlist!

title: Two albums by one of the lesser known Jazz Messengers line-ups
text:
I happen to be a fan of Bill Hardman whose trumpet has a beautiful tone to my ears. I have albums he led after this one, and I first 'discovered' him on a different Jazz Messenger album than the two that comprise this set. Of course, the rest of the line-up is also excellent.

The sound samples on this page will convey all you need to hear to make a purchase decision. This is typical Jazz Messenger fare on one level, but there are a few twists and turns that set this set apart. One, of course, is Hardman, and another is McLean's alto sax. Blakey usually (but not always) had tenor saxophonists in his line-ups, and McLean (and Lou Donaldson in the pre-Jazz Messenger line-up that featured Clifford Brown briefly) are notable exceptions. The rhythm section on all of the tracks are Sam Dockerty on piano, Spanky DeBrest on bass and Blakey on drums.

Here is what this album contains:
Tracks 1 through 5 are the album titled [[ASIN:B009R50YRS Tough]] that was recorded in the Swedien Recording Studio in Minneapolis sometime in the spring of 1957. Engineer Bruce Swedien's daughter and fellow Amazon reviewer, Julie Swedien Johnson, confirmed that this was just before the family moved to Chicago. So for me, having a friend who has firsthand knowledge of the session adds an interesting dimension to these tracks. The track titled Gershwin Medley is comprised of Rhapsody In Blue/Summertime/Someone To Watch Over Me/ The Man I Love. This album was released by the Cadet label as LP 4049.
