The remaining tracks are the album titled [[ASIN:B000VSBX8Y Hard Bop]] that was recorded for Columbia in NYC on December 12 and 13 1956. Tracks 6 through 9 and 11 were recorded on the 12th and track 10 on the 13th.

Note: the album description is a little confusing about then the Gershwin Medley on track 11 was recorded. It was, in fact, recorded during the December 12 session, but not released on the original album. It contains the same song sequence as the one on track 5, but is about a minute shorter.

If you are a Jazz Messengers fan this is a set of albums that seem to have fallen through the cracks. For me it's a gem and ranks on my short list of favorite JM albums. Let the sound samples guide you.

title: Hardman's first album as a leader
text:
I first took notice of Hardman on a Jazz Messengers album titled [[ASIN:B00000HZF0 Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers With Thelonious Monk]] (he is also featured on another JM album titled [[ASIN:B005C8F1V8 Ritual]]), but his playing was overshadowed by the other musicians. Here Hardman's playing is in front and his talents can be truly appreciated.

Give the sound samples on this page a listen and you will hear what I mean. I love Hardman's tone and phrasing. But the rest of the ensemble is also excellent. I admit that this is probably the first time (to my knowledge) that I have heard pianist Ronnie Mathews, and I am impressed. The rest of the rhythm section are very familiar - Bob Cunningham on bass on Capers and It Ain't Happened Yet, with Doug Watkins on the rest of the track, and Jimmy Cobb on drums. And I love Sonny Red's alto sax. I will confess that I am not that familiar with Red's work either. All of my previous recordings featuring Hardman had him paired with Jackie McLean on alto, but Red is a credible player.

This was Hardman's debut album that he recorded for the Savoy label in Newark, NJ on October 18, 1961. It's a shame he had not recorded more frequently as a leader because his playing is first rate, a fact to which this album attests.

title: Some amazing trio work with drums dubbed in later
text:
I've recently been digging into Pate's 1950s recordings when his focus was on jazz. This features him in a live setting at the Blue Note in Chicago.

Since there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review I am going to include them here:
01. Dancing On The Ceiling
02. What A Difference A Day Made
03. It Might As Well Be Spring
04. Falling In Love With Love
05. All The Time
06. Old Devil Moon
07. I Surrender Dear
08. Yvonne
09. Tea For Two
10. Pennies From Heaven
11. Carmen's Chaser
12. Slaughter On Tenth Avenue

It truly is a shame that there are no sound samples because the highlight [in my opinion] is Floyd Morris on piano. In fact, I first heard of him when I played this album and have added him to my list of greats who are sadly forgotten. Of course Pate is a force to be reckoned with on bass, and his playing is awesome on this album. I do wish he were a little more prominent in the mix, but you can still hear his every note.

This album was actually recorded as a trio with Wilbur Wynne on guitar (another unsung, monster player). The drums were later dubbed in by Johnny Whited (this information comes from Armin Büttner who maintains a page on Pate's discography).

According to Büttner this album was recorded for the Salem label during the period of July 3 through 10, 1956. Some sources cite January, 1957, but I am more disposed to believe Büttner who appears to be knowledgeable of Pate's career.

If you are looking for Pate's earlier jazz recordings this one is a shining example of his work. A lot of his albums feature the better known Ronnell Bright on piano who happens to be among my favorites. However, Floyd Morris on this album is easily Bright's equal in my opinion.

title: Purchased for Ronnell Bright's participation and discovered much more
text:
I was drawn to this album because it featured Ronnell Bright on piano. I got a lot more than I bargained for: some excellent trio work led by bassist and composer Pate. His bass work is excellent and a match for Bright's piano, but his composing skills are also showcased in this compilation. Of the twenty four tracks a full third - eight - are Pate's compositions.

For some reason there are no sound samples nor a track listing on this CD version's product page, but both are on the MP3 album's page at [[ASIN:B00IH6POHI Johnnie Pate Trio. Complete Recordings 1955-1956]]. Give those a run through to get a feel for both the music and the sound quality.

The albums and and singles that comprise this set are long out of print, so this is a wonderful find. I cross checked the album information with a Swiss site devoted to jazz documentation. Pate's recordings are well documented by Armin Büttner, although there are gaps in dates and locations. However, if you do a search for Pate and Büttner you;ll be rewarded with a full list of Pate's early work.

Here is what this compilation contains. Tracks 1 through 8 are from an album titled Johnnie Pate Trio that was recorded in Chicago sometime in 1955 for the Talisman label and released as TLP-1. This features Pate on bass, Bright on piano and Charles Walton on drums. All three provide vocals on track 1.

The remaining tracks were recorded for the Gig label in Chicago on January 28, 1956. These tracks are an album titled Subtle Sounds (tracks 9 through 20), and two double sided singles for tracks 21 through 24. The same personnel are on these tracks, with all three providing vocals on tracks 11 and 24, and a female vocalist named Gwen Stevens on vocals on tracks 19 and 22.

If you know who Pate is, then I do not have to sell you on the merits of this album. If you are a Bright fan, his playing is as exceptional here as on his other albums. For me it's another discovery that is taking me down a wonderful path.

title: Startling voice
text:
I have only recently stumbled across Dane's work and was blown away by her voice. I had assumed that she was African American and long dead, but she is blond and still alive as I write this review. Moreover, she was not only a jazz and blues vocalist, but also a guitarist and folk singer!

Both of albums in this set were recorded in 1959 and 1962, respectively, and truly showcase facets of her talent. There are no sound samples on this (CD version) product page at the time of this review, but there are for the MP3 version at [[ASIN:B00CLS17HY "Livin' with the Blues". Barbara Dane with Earl Fatha Hines and His Orchestra Plus "On My Way" With Kenny Whitson Quartet]]. Give those a listen to hear what I am trying to say about Dane's voice and ability to deliver blues songs. If you are already familiar with her work please forgive my gushing because I have only recently 'discovered' her.

The first ten tracks are the album titled [[ASIN:B008CIMXEI Livin' With The Blues]] that was recorded for the Dot label at the Master Recorders studio in Los Angeles on January 9 and 12, 1959. She is backed by an Earl Hines led ensemble featuring Hines on piano, Benny Carter on trumpet, Herbie Harper and John Halliburton on trombone and Plas Johnson on tenor sax. The rhythm section was comprised of Leroy Vinnegar on bass and Shelly Manne on drums.

Tracks 11 through 22 are the album titled [[ASIN:B00DR2WDVW On My Way]] that was recorded in Los Angeles for Capitol over the course of five sessions (April 23 through 26, and 28, 1962). Dane is backed by Kenny Whitson Quartet.

title: Not your typical West Coast fare
text:
Randi (like his peer Paul Smith) were not your typical West Coast jazz pianists as the two albums that comprise this set attest. Both albums are out of print, and I am grateful that Fresh Sounds has not only reissued them, but also for the fantastic remastering.

If you are on the CD version's product page there are no track listings, nor sound samples. There are on the digital version's page at [[ASIN:B00KHUMOHK Don Randi Trio. Feelin' Like Blues / Where Do We Go from Here?]]. Even the short snippets will convey just how unique Randi is. My band leader is a pianist and she was spellbound by the inventive playing and technique. I have to agree.

In addition to Randi, his bassists and drummers on the two albums are not only excellent and perfect for the music, but on tracks 8 through 15 are none other than Leroy Vinnegar on bass and Mel Lewis on drums. What a delight. Of course, the bassist and drummer on the first seven tracks are also excellent. I will confess that I am not very familiar with them (Hersh Hamel on bass and Gene Stone on drums), but their performances were also excellent.

The albums were recorded in Los Angeles. Feelin' Like Blues (tracks 1 through 7) was recorded for World Pacific at the Rex Productions Studio on August 9, 1960. Randi is backed by Hersh Hamel on bass and Gene Stone on drums. Where Do We Go from Here was recorded at Radio Recorders on February 1, 1962 with Randi backed by Leroy Vinnegar on bass and Mel Lewis on drums.

If you are not familiar with Randi, but love piano trio jazz I cannot recommend this album highly enough. If you are a pianist you would be missing out if you do not grab it! For Paul Smith whom I mentioned above this album is a great starting place: [[ASIN:B00E44GL0G Essential Jazz Magic]].

title: Very early work circa 1939-51
text:
This 97 track collection is exhaustive for Shearing's early years, but only the most avid fans will love it. It does showcase Shearing's many influences and base of experience, including him on accordion, and in ensembles of various sizes.

The set is divided among four discs, and the songs are in chronological order. Sound quality is as good as can be expected considering the state of recording technology and techniques during the period covered. The quality improves successively from the first disc to the last. The booklet that comes with this set is as valuable as the songs if you are an avid fan. It is one of the better discographies covering his first decade that I have come across.

At the time of this review the track listing is continuous, but there is a product photo that shows the back of the packaging and the way the songs are divided up. I am going to provide the ensembles, dates and locations of the tracks on each disc, but ask that you refer to the photo for the tracks. That will keep this review from consuming this entire page, while providing sufficient details about the tracks for you to make a purchase decision. You can also listen to some of the sound samples on a much smaller compilation that is a subset of this one: [[ASIN:B002PZ5NC8 The Best of George Shearing]].
=========
DISC ONE
=========
Tracks 1 through 4 were recorded in London on March 2, 1939 and feature Shearing on piano and accordion, Leonard Feather on piano and Carlo Krahmer on drums.
Tracks 5 through 8 were recorded in London on March 3, 1941 with Shearing solo.
Tracks 9 and 10 were recorded in London on April 9, 1941 featuring Stephane Grappelli and his Quartet with Grappellion violin, Shearingon piano, Jack Llewellyn on guitar, George Gibbs on bass and Dave Fullerton on drums.
Tracks 11 through 13 were recorded in London on April 23, 1941 with Shearing solo.
Tracks 14 and 15 were recorded in London on July 19, 1941 featuring the Radio Rhythm Club Sextet with Harry Parry on clarinet, Roy Marsh on vibraphone, Shearing on piano, Frank Deniz on guitar, Sam Molineaux on bass and Ben Edwards on drums.
Tracks 16 through 19 were recorded in London on August 1, 1941 with Shearing solo.
Tracks 20 and 21 were recorded in London on December 9, 1941 with Shearing solo.
Tracks 22 and 23 were recorded in London on January 28, 1942 with Shearing Solo.
=========
DISC TWO
=========
Tracks 1 through 11 were all recorded in London and feature Shearing solo. Tracks 1 through 4 were recorded on April 28, 1942, 5 through 8 on December 12, 1942, and tracks 9 through 11 on December 21, 1943.
Tracks 12 through 15 were recorded in London on February 14, 1944 and features the George Shearing Sextet with Kenny Baker on trumpet, Harry Hayes on alto sax, Aubrey Frank on tenor sax, Shearing on piano, Tommy Bromley on bass and Carlo Krahmer on drums.
Track 16 was recorded in London on December 18, 1944 with Shearing on piano with Frank Weir and his Astor Club Seven.
Tracks 17 and 18 are undated and assumed to have been recorded in London. They feature Shearing on piano backed by Allan Hodgkins on guitar and Carlo Krahmer on drums.
Tracks 19 through 22 are the George Shearing Trio featuring Shearing on piano backed by Gene Ramey on bass and Cozy Cole on drums. All were recorded in NYC, with 19 and 20 on February 3, 1947 and 21 and 22 on February 23, 1947.
Tracks 23 and 24 were recorded in NYC on December 23, 1947 with Shearing backed by Curley Russell on bass and Denzil Best on drums.
=========
DISC THREE
=========
Tracks 1 and 2 were recorded during the same session from the preceding disc in NYC on December 23, 1947. They feature Shearing backed by Curley Russell on bass and Denzil Best on drums.
Tracks 3 through 9 were recorded in London on November 26, 1948 with Shearing backed by Jack Fallon on bass and Norman Burns on drums.
Tracks 10 through 25 were recorded in NYC over the course of three sessions and feature the George Shearing Quintet comprised of Marjorie Hyams on vibraphone, Shearing on piano and accordion, Chuck Wayne on guitar, John Levy on bass and Denzil Best on drums. Tracks 10 through 17 were recorded on January 31, 1949, tracks 18 through 21 were recorded on February 17, 1949 (with Hyams on piano on track 18), and the remainder on June 28, 1949.
=========
DISC FOUR
=========
Tracks 1 through 18 were recorded in five sessions in NYC. They feature the George Shearing Quintet comprised of Marjorie Hyams on vibraphone, Shearing on piano, Chuck Wayne on guitar, John Levy on bass and Denzil Best on drums. Tracks 1 through 4 were recorded on July 27, 1949, 5 through 8 on December 12, 1949, 9 through 11 on April 3, 1950, 12 through 14 on April 4, 1950, and 15 through 18 on July 5, 1950.
Tracks 19 and 20 were recorded in NYC on February 5 and 7, 1951 by the George Shearing Quintet with Don Elliott on xylophone on track 19 and vibraphone on track 20, backed by Shearing on piano, Chuck Wayne on guitar, John Levy on bass and Denzil Best on drums.
Track 21 was recorded in NYC on October 2, 1951 by the George Shearing Quintet featuring Joe Roland on vibraphone, Shearing on piano, Chuck Wayne on guitar, Al McKibbon on bass and Denzil Best on drums.
Tracks 22 and 23 were recorded in Los Angeles on October 10, 1951 by the George Shearing Quintet with the same personnel except Dick Evans is on bass and Billy Erskine is on vocals.
Tracks 24 through 26 were recorded in NYC on December 18, 1951 by the George Shearing Quintet featuring Joe Roland on vibraphone, Shearing on piano, Chuck Wayne on guitar, Al McKibbon on bass and Denzil Best on drums.

title: Excellent collection of Young's earlier work
text:
The albums in this compilation were recorded in Chicago between 1956 and 1962 and encompass Young's trio recordings that were released for the Argo and Vee-Jay labels. The set is just a few seconds short of two hours and thirty-seven minutes, so you are getting a lot of Young's music.

What makes this collection special is all of the albums are out-of-print, so having them on a single compilation is a real treasure. As usual Fresh Sounds has done a remarkable job of remastering the originals, so the sound quality is as excellent as the music itself. Unfortunately there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review, but you can hear them in a different order on this album: [[ASIN:B00BMLFV1E Essential Jazz Masters]]. Note: the sound quality of that album does not approach the quality of this two disc set.

This is a two disc set and here is what's one each:
========
Disc One
========
The first ten tracks are the album titled Young John Young that was released as Argo LP 612. They were recorded in Chicago in 1956 (I could not track down the exact studio or date). Young in backed by Herbert Brown on bass and Larry Jackson on drums.

Tracks 11 through 21 are the album titled Opus de Funk that was recorded in Chicago on November 19 and 21, 1957 and released as Vee-Jay VJS 3060. Young is backed by Herbert Brown on bass and Larry Jackson on drums.
========
Disc Two
========
Tracks 1 through 12 are the album titled Themes and Things that was released as Argo LP 692. They feature Young backed by Bill Yancey on bass and Philip Thomas on drums drums and were recorded at the Ter-Mar Recording Studios in Chicago on June 6 and 7, 1961.

The remaining tracks are the album titled A Touch Of Pepper that was recorded on November 29 and December 4, 1962 at the Ter-Mar Recording Studios in Chicago. Young is backed by Sam Kidd on bass and Philip Thomas on drums.

title: Two great performances + two rare tracks
text:
The first four tracks on this album are from the album titled [[ASIN:B00000K278 Newport]] and are the only tracks on that album that were performed by the Quartet on July 6, 1956. Note: the other three tracks from that album feature J. J. Johnson and Kai Winding performing during their set. This would be Joe Dodge's last Newport Jazz Festival performance sine he was replaced by Joe Morello four months later. Norman Bates is the bassist for this performance, and, of course Dave Brubeck is on piano and Paul Desmond on alto sax.

Tracks 5 through 8 were recorded three years later on July 5, 1959 at the festival and feature the classic line up with Eugene Wright on bass and Joe Morello on drums backing Brubeck and Desmond. The difference in the rhythm sections between the two performances is like night and day.

Wrapping the album up are two bonus tracks that was recorded live on February 28, 1958 in Hannover, Germany during their European tour that year. This, too, features the classic Quartet. To the best of my knowledge these tracks do not show up in any other albums. Indeed, they are not listed in the discographies I consult when I an cross-referencing information.

For casual listening this is not what I consider to be an essential album. For avid fans like myself it's enjoyable, and as a drummer I do appreciate the contrast between the Bates/Dodge rhythm section and the Wright/Morello one. While the latter is vastly more technically proficient and key to some of the amazing albums the Quartet would release, the 1956 Quartet was better suited to backing Paul Desmond in my opinion. On the other hand there would never have been Time Out with the older Quartet. Wright and Morello made it possible for Brubeck and Desmond to take the quartet to a whole new level.

title: Shearing's first decade
text:
This is Shearing's earliest work that was recorded between 1939 and 1949 and feature him in some interesting musical settings.

The tracks range from early work with Leonard Feather in the late 1930s, to collaborations with Stephane Grappelli, through to bebop era collaborations with some of the pioneers of that genre like bassist Curley Russell and drummer Denzil Best. In fact, some of the tracks feature Shearing on accordion! Most of the tracks were recorded for the Decca and Savoy labels.

While there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review), there are on this MP3 album: [[ASIN:B002PZ5NC8 The Best of George Shearing]] (it contains the same tracks, but in a different order.) Those will give you a feel for the music. Some of the tracks are less than perfect from an engineering perspective, but are still listenable. Bear in mind that this material was recorded sixty five to seventy five years ago on relatively crude technology. I am not making excuses for this, but do want to set expectations.

This collection is filled with surprises (and to be honest a few duds, bot those are in the ear of the beholder). If you are a fan who want to dig a little deeper into his beginnings, as well as to chart his evolution as a musician this album is worthwhile.

title: When I'm stressed I pull this out. When I need inspiration this is my source
text:
I cannot begin to express how much I love this album and will not bore you with contrived banter. What this contains that previous albums of that performance do not are some alternate takes and announcements that did not make the final cut in post production. The two previous albums, both released by Riverside in 1961, that contained parts of this performance are:

[[ASIN:B003YOMN68 Waltz for Debby]] tracks are: Disc One, tracks 4, 7 and 8; Disc Two, tracks 4, 6, 8, 9 and 10; and Disc Three, tracks 1 and 3.

[[ASIN:B001D6OKJ2 Sunday at the Village Vanguard]] tracks are Disc One, tracks 3 and 9; Disc Two, tracks 1 through 3 and 7; Disc Three, tracks 2, 3, 5 and 6.

Although there are no sound samples on this product page at the time of this review you can listen to them on the MP3 version's page at [[ASIN:B007CSETZU The Complete Live At The Village Vanguard 1961 MP3]]. There is a certain ambiance that the two source albums seem to lack. Also, it's a treat to listen to the entire three sets (or at least everything that was recorded). Even the voices and chatter of the audience in the background add to the listening experience if you want to relive the performances.

This is also the last recorded performance by Scott LaFaro who would be dead less than two weeks later. He is one of my favorite bassists and when you add drummer Paul Motian into the equation this is probably the Best Bill Evans line-up ever.

Since this set reflects the actual sequence in which the tracks were performed, the discs are divided by sets. The afternoon sets one and two are on Disc One, the first two evening sets are on Disc Two and the final evening set is on Disc Three.

This is definitely a treasure for fans and if you do not already own both source albums this is the one that I recommend.

title: Fifteen years of Lady Day
text:
This set spans a good many of Billie's studio recordings from December 18, 1933 to December 10, 1948. Moreover, they are in chronological order, but there are some gaps. One is the July 24, 1938 session for Bluebird with her backed by Artie Shaw and his Orchestra. Another is an important April 20, 1939 Commodore session in which she was backed by Frank Newton & Café Society Band and introduced the studio version of Strange Fruit.

However, the gaps do not terribly detract from this collection because the sound quality is decent. My definition of 'decent' takes into account the state of recording equipment and techniques during the era in which these tracks were recorded (sixty-five to eighty years ago!) There are nine hours and fifteen minutes of music in the set.

I do not know why the label did not provide discography information since it's relatively easy to find. I compiled the following information in an afternoon, so it could not be hard. I left out the personnel for each session, although if you request specifics for a track or session in a comment I can provide it. You can correlate the tracks to which I am referring below to the photo on the top of this page of the back of the box that lists them for each disc. Here is what this set contains:

Disc One: Starts with her very first studio recording sessions backed by the Benny Goodman Orchestra and recorded for Columbia in NYC. The first two tracks are from two different sessions (November 27 and December 18, 1933. The remaining tracks on this disc are from 1935 and early 1936 sessions led by Teddy Wilson for Brunswick. These sessions were in NYC between July 2 and December 3, 1935; and January and July 1936.

Disc Two: Picks up in the same June 30, 1936 session that ended Disc One. This was also recorded for Brunswick and led by the Teddy Wilson Orchestra. The songs are in chronological order spanning June 30 through November 19, 1936, with the last three songs credited to Billie Holiday and her Orchestra from a January 12, 1937 session for Vocalion in NYC.

Disc Three: The first two songs are from the same January 12, 1937 session that concluded Disc Two. The remaining tracks are from Brunswick sessions in NYC that are once again led by Teddy Wilson and his orchestra spanning January 25 through May 11, 1937.

Disc Four: The first track is the last track recorded from the May 11, 1937 session that ended on Disc Three. The next four tracks are credited to Billie Holiday and her orchestra for Vocalion in NYC on June 15, 1937. The next four tracks are from a September 13 session by Billie Holiday and her orchestra, followed by four tracks for Brunswick on November 1, 1937 with Teddy Wilson and his orchestra backing Billie. The final two tracks are also for Brunswick led by Teddy Wilson on January 6, 1938 in NYC.

Disc Five: The first two tracks are from the same January 6, 1938 session that concludes Disc Four. The next sixteen tracks are from three Vocalion sessions in NYC credited to Billy Holiday and her orchestra that took place in NYC on January 12, May 11, June 23 and September 15, 1938. The final track on this disc is from an October 31 session for Brunswick with Teddy Wilson and his orchestra backing Billie.

Disc Six: This disc starts with the remaining track from the October 31, 1938 session that concluded the previous disc. The next eight tracks are also for Brunswick and led by Teddy Wilson on November 9 and 28, 1938. The next two tracks are credited to Billie Holiday and her orchestra and were recorded for Vocalion on January 20, 1939. On January 30 she records the next four songs for Brunswick backed by Teddy Wilson, and finishes up the tracks on this disc for Vocalion on March 21, 1939 as Billie Holiday and her orchestra.

Disc Seven: The first track is from the March 21, 1939 from Disc Six. Sadly this disc omits an entire April 20, 1939 Commodore session that contains her first recorded rendition of Strange Fruit and s few other iconic songs. Instead, it skips ahead to eight tracks cut for Vocalion with her orchestra on July 5 and December 13, 1939. The next four tracks are also for Vocalion and were recorded on February 29, 1940 with her orchestra. The remaining tracks on this disc are from two sessions recorded by her and her orchestra for Okeh in NYC on June 7 and September 12, 1940.

Disc Eight: The first two tracks pick up from the September 12, 1940 session on the previous disc. The next two tracks are from an October 15, 1940 session for Okeh in NYC led by Benny Carter and his All Star Orchestra. These tracks were supposed to be for a concept album of W. C. Handy songs, but was never completed. The next eight tracks are from March 21 and May 9, 1941 sessions for Okeh in NYC featuring Eddie Heywood and his Orchestra. The next four tracks are led by Teddy Wilson for Columbia in NYC on August 7, 1941. The last three tracks were recorded for Columbia and led my Teddy Wilson on February 10, 1942.

Disc Nine: The first track was recorded for Capitol in Los Angeles on June 12, 1942. Billie is backed by Paul Whitman's orchestra and her last studio session before the 1942-1944 American Federation of Musicians recording ban. All but the last two tracks are from NYC sessions for Commodore led by Eddie Heywood and his Orchestra. These sessions span March 25, April 1 and 8, 1944. The last two tracks were recorded for Decca in NYC on October 4 and November 8, 1944. Billie is backed by Toots Camarata and his Orchestra.

Disc Ten: The first three tracks are from an August 14, 1945 session for Decca led by Bob Haggart and his Orchestra. The next three tracks were recorded for Decca on January 22, 1946 with Billy backed by Bill Stegmeyer and his Orchestra. The next two tracks were recorded for Decca in NYC on April 9, 1946. Billie is backed by Billy Kyle and his Trio. Her last 1946 session produced the next two tracks on December 27; John Simmons and his Orchestra backed her on this session. The next four songs represent her total studio output in 1947. These tracks were recorded for Decca on February 13, 1947 with Bob Haggart and his Orchestra backing her. The remaining tracks were recorded on December 10, 1948 for Decca in NYC. She is backed by Bobby Tucker and his trio.

title: One of the greats you may have never heard of
text:
This collection has brought me a lot of listening pleasure. All three of the albums in this are out-of-print, making this collection a real treasure (especially for local fans from the DC area.)

It contains a smoking hot live set and two equally enjoyable studio albums. All of the tracks in this colletion were recorded for Riverside in 1960 and 61. What I love is that it contains six Morgan compositions: For Pete's Sake, Like Lois, See What I Mean, Meditation, Bash! and Settlin' In.

While there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review you can listen to all of the tracks (in a different order) on this page: [[ASIN:B009U2B7CO Essential Jazz Masters]]. A quick run through will quickly convey why I think that Morgan's talents deserved wider recognition. I am grateful that the three albums that comprise this set have been reissued and even more grateful that Fresh Sounds Records took the time to remaster them so that you can hear Morgan at his [recorded] best Here is what this album contains:
========
DISC ONE
========
Tracks 1 through 8 are the album titled At The Showboat that was recorded live at the Showboat in Washington, DC on May 4, 1960. Morgan is backed by Keter Betts on bass and Bertell Knox on drums.

Tracks 9 through 12 are the album titled See What I Mean that was recorded at the Plaza Sound Studios in NYC on October 31, 1960. Morgan is again backed by Keter Betts on bass and Bertell Knox on drums.
========
DISC TWO
========
Tracks 1 through 4 are a continuation of See What I Mean from Disc One.

Tracks 5 through 14 are the album titled Settlin' In that was recorded at the Bell Sound Studios in NYC on May 17, 1961. Morgan is backed by Joe Benjamin on bass and Ben Riley on drums.

title: A hidden gem
text:
I only recently 'discovered' this album and had to double check that it's actually Bill Evans on piano. Although there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review), the music needs much more than a snippet of sound per track to appreciate.

This is not the same fare as Evans with Scott LaFaro and Paul Morian or even Chuck Israelis and Paul Motian. Evsn's touch is almost jaunty, and Monty Budwig has a more laid back style than LaFaro or Israelis. As a drummer I was drawn into Shelly Manne's playing here. He is his melodic and inventive self. I will admit that there was an uncharacteristic hint of bebop in his playing, but that kept me interested.

If you want to hear Evans in an entirely different context this is the album to get. I am a big fan and may be biased, but I think it's must-have for fans of either Evans or Manne (or both).

Most sources claim that this album was recorded in NYC, but in fact it was cut in Rudy van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs, NJ studio on August 14, 1962. At the time of this review there is no track list on this product page, so I am including it here:

TRACK
1: The Washington Twist (6:30)
2: Danny Boy (3:43)
3: Let's Go Back to the Waltz (4:33)
4: With a Song in My Heart (9:13)
5: Goodbye (5:11)
6: I Believe in You (5:51)

title: Beautiful music; beautiful remastering
text:
The sound quality of this disc is well worth the premium price if you have the gear to do it justice. I spend too much time listening to MP3 files on my phone piped through bluetooth, and when I put this disc on my 'real' system I am reminded of what I am missing. The only thing better would be a pristine copy of the original vinyl.

However, the music is superb and the pairing of Mulligan's baritone sax with Monk's approach to playing between the cracks is a joy to my ears. Although there are no sound samples on this page you can listen to them here: [[ASIN:B00DUIA1YO Mulligan Meets Monk [Original Jazz Classics Remasters]]]. Bear in mind that the sound quality of this disc is vastly superior to the samples on that page.

The original album was released by Riverside with six tracks, four of which were Monk compositions (or co-compositions), one - Decidely - by Mulligan and one standard (Sweet and Lovely). This album contains the core tracks and alternate takes. It was recorded for Riverside at the Reeves Sound Studios in NYC on August 12 and 13 1957.

In addition to Monk and Mulligan, additional magic of the album comes from the rhythm section. As a drummer Shadow Wilson is a near deity and his performance here bears that out. In fact, if you are a drummer, this album is like getting a mini lesson in dynamics, swing and groove. Wilbur Ware on bass is also key to the sound of this album. He truly understood Monk and his music, backing him on three 1957 albums (including this one), plus one in 1961.

This album may be off the beaten path of those deemed essential for either Monk or Mulligan, but I personally love it. In fact, it is one I recommend to friends who want to dig further into Monk's music. As a parting note that is more trivia than anything else, Mulligan, Monk and Ware were all among the 57 musicians present for the iconic 1958 photo titled [[ASIN:B000LJPKH8 Art Kane A Great Day in Harlem Jazz Portrait 1958 Photo Poster Print]]

title: Value-priced collection of gems
text:
This set features most of Davis' earliest albums for Columbia (some still recorded when he was with Prestige, but with their permission.) The sound quality is very good, and the albums selected for inclusion are nearly all essential in my opinion.

If you are just getting into Davis, this is a good starting place. To be honest I am as fond of his Prestige albums as I am of these, but it's hard to argue against any album in this collection. For one thing, Kind of Blue is included here and is one of four albums that every jazz lover should own. It's also one of the essentials for any Miles Davis fan.

Although there are no sound samples on this page each of the source albums to which I linked below have samples on their product pages. For a complete track listing see the back cover image above. Here is what the set contains:
========
DISC ONE
========
Tracks 1 through 6: [[ASIN:B00IT5FY2M 'Round About Midnight]], which kicks off Davis' Columbia period as well as solidifying the classic quintet (Davis on trumpet, John Coltrane on tenor sax, Red Garland on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Philly Joe Jones on drums.) This album was recorded over the course of three sessions at Columbia's 30th Street Studios in NYC. The three sessions spanned eleven months: October 26, 1955, and June 5 and September 10, 1956, but the album was not released until early 1957.

Tracks 7 through 16: [[ASIN:B00138F1B6 Miles Ahead]], the second album Davis recorded for Columbia was recorded over the course of five sessions at Columbia's 30 Street Studios. This album features Davis and the Gil Evans Orchestra, which featured Davis on fluglehorn accompanied by a trumpet section comprised of Johnny Carisi, Bernie Glow, Taft Jordan, Louis Mucci and Ernie Royal. The trombone section included Joe Bennett, Jimmy Cleveland and Frank Rehak with Tom Mitchell on bass trombone. Jim Buffington, Tony Miranda and Willie Ruff were on french horn with Bill Barber on tuba. The wind ensemble was comprised of Edwin Caine, Sid Cooper and Romeo Penque on flute and clarinet, Danny Bank on bass clarinet, and Lee Konitz on alto sax. The rhythm section was Paul Chambers on bass and Art Taylor on drums. The sessions for this album spanned May 6, 10, 23 and 27, and August 22, 1957.
========
DISC TWO
========
Tracks 1 through 13: [[ASIN:B004AE0NL8 Porgy And Bess]], is another Miles Davis and Gil Evans Orchestra studio album recorded for Columbia at their 30th Street Studios in NYC. This album was recorded in a number of sessions in July and August, 1958 and entail a large ensemble. Davis is on both fluglehorn and trumpet, accompanied by a trumpet section comprised of Johnny Coles, Bernie Glow, Louis Mucci and Ernie Royal. The trombone section was comprised of Joe Bennett, Jimmy Cleveland, Frank Rehak, with Dick Hixson on bass trombone. Additional brass was provided by Willie Ruff, Gunther Schuller and Julius Watkins on French horn, and Bill Barber on tuba. The wind section was comprised of Phil Bodner and Romeo Penque on flute, Danny Bank on bass clarinet, and Cannonball Adderley on alto sax. The rhythm section was Paul Chambers on bass and Art Taylor on drums.

Tracks 14 and 15 are the first two tracks of [[ASIN:B00IS4187Y Kind Of Blue]], which was one of four 1959 albums that changed jazz. This album was distinguished by it's foray into model jazz and remains one of the best selling jazz albums of all time (ranked up there with one of the other four albums from 1959 - Dave Brubeck Quartet's Time Out - and is reason enough to own this set if you are just getting into Davis or jazz in general. This album was recorded for Columbia at their 30th Street Studios on March 2 and April 22, 1959. Davis leads on trumpet accompanied by John Coltrane on tenor sax and Cannonball Adderley on alto. Bill Evans is on piano on all of the tracks except for Freddie Freeloader, on which Wynton Kelly plays. Paul Chambers is on bass and Jimmy Cobb on drums.
=========
DISC THREE
=========
The first three tracks are a continuation of Kind of Blue from Disc two.

All of the remaining five tracks are [[ASIN:B00IT5GD5Y Sketches of Spain]], which was recorded at Columbia's 30th Street Studios on November 20, 1959 and March 10, 1960. This is another Miles Davis with the Gil Evans Orchestra album with a large backing ensemble. Davis is on fluglehorn and trumpet accompanied by a trumpet section comprised of Bernie Glow, Taft Jordan, Louis Mucci and Ernie Royal. Trombone section was Dick Hixson and Frank Rehak, augmented by John Barrows, Jim Buffington and Earl Chapin on French horn and Jimmy McAllister on tuba. Wind instruments were Albert Block and Eddie Caine on flute, Harold Feldman on oboe and clarinet, and Danny Bank on bass clarinet. The harpist was Janet Putman. The rhythm section was comprised of Paul chambers on bass, Jimmy Cobb on drums and Elvin Jones on percussion.

title: A hodge podge of eras, but a delightful one
text:
I've owned this CD for well over a dozen years and continue to listen to it. As for the music, that is all over the map ranging from Bessie Smith in the 20s or early 30s, to contemporary artists like the power trio of Marcia Ball, Angela Strehli and Lou Ann Barton on the very first track. By the way, Bessie's predecessor and influence, Ma Rainey, is also included, as are her peers from her era, Mammie Smith, Victoria Spivey, Ida Cox and Sippie Wallace. And, of course, Alberta Hunter who had a major comeback in the 1980s.

One of the reasons why I love this album is I learned of so many artists whom I would not have otherwise known about. For example, Marcia Ball and Rory Block. It also opened my eyes and ears to Saffire (Uppity Blues Women) who became one of my passions.

Another reason is it rekindled my interest in Nina Simone and Ruth Brown. I was familiar with them, but had drifted away until I heard them on this album and was inspired to dig out old albums and buy some new ones.

Considering that some of the tracks were recorded eighty plus years ago on relatively crude equipment, the overall sound quality is darn good. Whoever engineered the remastering knew their stuff.

If you are new to blues and R&B, take a chance with this one because you'll discover some great examples by some sadly forgotten stars of yesteryear. If you are familiar with the genre, I am willing to bet that you will find some gems that you never knew existed.

title: Cements Rollins' piano-less trio concept
text:
This is Rollins' third recording that employs his piano-less trio format and it establishes his sound in that format. Before going further note that there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review. I am a firm believer that samples are the best way to convey the essence of an album because they strip away all subjectivity. You can listen to the six tracks on this album on this page: [[ASIN:B0017YZIKK Freedom Suite]].

One of the reasons why I believe that this is not only a five star album, but one of Rollins' essential recordings is because the rhythm section features two of the most melodic musicians on the scene: Oscar Pettiford on bass and Max Roach on drums. Of course Rollins' inventive playing also factors into that, and here he truly stretches on this entire album. I am sure that Pettiford and Roach behind him were inspiring him to reach for those musical heights.

Another reason why I am so enthusiastic about this album is it builds upon two earlier ones that introduced his piano-less trio format: [[ASIN:B003D5GWRY Way Out West]] and [[ASIN:B000TDGAFW A Night At The Village Vanguard]]. Neither this nor the other two are musically similar beyond the format because Rollins' approach to music is ever evolving.

This album is as it was originally released without the bonus tracks reissues include. All of the tracks except Freedom Suite were recorded for Riverside in NYC on February 11, 1958 (Freedom Suite was recorded in NYC on March 7, 1958).

title: Smokin' album that should be better known
text:
Rollins' prolific output makes it hard to keep track of some of this earlier work. To me this one is spectacular, if for no other reason than track 8 on which he plays solo. I could babble on about this album, but would probably come across as a pretentious jerk, so let the sound samples sell you on it if you are on the fence.

To me every track is worth playing and playing again. The line-up changes on each of the three sessions that produced this album. It's if Rollins is continuously experimenting. The first session was recorded on June 11, 1957. It features Rollins backed by Sonny Clark on piano (and a real treat to hear), Percy Heath on bass and Roy Haynes on drums. The tracks from this session are 5, 6 and 8 with Clark, Heath and Haynes on 5 and 6 and Rollins solo on 8.

On the second session (June 12, 1957) Rollins is again backed by Clark, Heath and Haynes, who are on all four tracks recorded that day (2, 3, 4 and 9).

The final session was recorded on June 19, 1957 and has Rollins backed by Clark and Haynes, with Paul Chambers taking over the bass duties. On this one the full ensemble plays on tracks 1 and 10, but Rollins uses only Chambers and Haynes on track 4. This is not unusual because he had pioneered the piano-less trio using drums and bass three months earlier on the album titled [[ASIN:B003D5GWRY Way Out West]]. It worked on that album and it works on these tracks.

This album was recorded for Riverside at the Reeves Sound Studios in NYC and released the same year as catalog number RLP 12-241. Track 10 was not on the original LP release. It is one of the delightful gems that I discovered when I was digging into Rollins' earlier recordings and one I recommend to fans.

title: Title album + NJF tracks from 1957
text:
This is the title album that is otherwise out-of-print plus five tracks Wilson's trio played at the Newport Jazz Festival during their July 6, 1957 performance.

To get a taste of this album listen to the sound samples on this page. The recordings are clear and beautifully mastered. The material encompasses most of Wilson's signature tunes, and the musicianship on every track is impeccable. The sole track on which Gerry Mulligan appears is one of my favorites.

The original album comprised of the first twelve tracks was recorded in NYC for Verve on August 12, 1957 (catalog numnber MGV 8330). It features Wilson backed by Arvell Shaw on bass and Roy Burness on drums.

Bonus tracks - 13 through 17 - that were recorded on July 6 feature Wilson backed by Milt Hinton on bass and Specs Powell on drums. Gerry Mulligan joins them with his bartione sax on Sweet Georgia Brown. These tracks were released by Verve as The Teddy Wilson Trio And Gerry Mulligan Quartet At Newport (catalog number MGV 8235).

This is not what I would call an essential album, but it does provide a few minutes over an hour of quintessential Teddy Wilson, both in the studio and live. If you are a fan do not pass it up. If you are new to Wilson, this is a good a place as any to start.

title: Compete album + sides 1 and 2 of an EP
text:
This is all of the tracks laid down for both Clef (Norman Granz' label) and an EP recorded for Columbia two days later. Both were record in Los Angeles.

Before proceeding, there are sound samples of a digital version of this album titled [[ASIN:B00BCYSKTQ The Complete 1955 Session (with Lionel Hampton & Teddy Wilson)]]. Please refer to those because they describe the actual music on this album far better than I.

Tracks 1 through 6 are an out of print LP titled Gene Krupa - Lionel Hampton - Teddy Wilson Play Selections From "The Benny Goodman Story" on which Gene, Hamp and Teddy (backed by Red Callender on bass) play the tunes they recorded for the 1955 movie, the [[ASIN:B0074JOVUU Gene Krupa Story]]. This album was recorded on July 31, 1955 and released the same year as Clef MGC 681.

Tracks 7 and 8 are from an extended play (EP) 45 RPM record titled Strollin' Along that was released by Columbia as catalog number SEB 10086. These two sides were recorded by the same personnel on August 2, 1955.

I've uploaded customer-supplied images for the covers and liner notes for the album and EP, which provides some interesting information about each. The music is excellent and at a few seconds less than fifty-seven minutes is a great way to spend almost an hour.

title: Great two-album set
text:
This set contains an out-of-print album titled Then They Wrote and one that is still available titled [[ASIN:B00ABL40JA Mr Wilson And Mr Gershwin]]. They were both recorded in 1959 (one in January and the other in December), and feature Wilson backed by drummer Bert Dahlander on both, and bassist Major Holley on the first twelve tracks and Al Lucas on the remaining ones.

Both albums are different from one another in key ways. First, Major Holley on the first album has a far more prominent place in the mix than Al Lucas does on the second album. Second, the first album is a tribute to some of Wilson's influences and includes a representative song composed by each and played by Wilson (Wilson also includes one of his own compositions - Sunday Morning - in the set.) The second album is a collection of standards that showcase Wilson's own style and interpretation.

Tracks 1 through 12 comprise Then They Wrote. Unfortunately there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review, but be aware that Wilson manages to play each song in his own style while being true to the originals. That's some balancing act, and he is aided on a number by Holley's energetic approach to bass. This is an interesting contrast to Bert Dahlander's more subtle drumming on this album (and the other one in this set.) This album was recorded for Columbia in NYC on December 3, 11 and 12, 1959. I'll list the track titles and composer for each in a comment to this review.

The remaining tracks are the album titled Mr Wilson And Mr Gershwin. This album allows you to hear Wilson's every note and nuance. I love hearing his light touch and almost silvery tone that were his alone. The product page for this album (linked above) does have sound samples and I encourage you to give them a listen. The album was recorded for Columbia in NYC on January 19 and 21, 1959.

If you are a Teddy Wilson fan this is a great set, especially the ability to obtain the out--of-print Then They Wrote. Another bonus about this set is you can compare and contrast Wilson in two very different musical setting. Both are trios, but the goals are different.

title: Back out west
text:
This is like being in West Coast jazz heaven, and is a fitting book end to Rollins' 1957 album titled [[ASIN:B003D5GWRY Way Out West]]. There are a few twists in this one though. While the first West coast album was his debut as a piano-less trio, this one features Hampton Hawes on piano on all but one track, and adds Victor Feldman on vibraphone on track 4 (You).

Rollins' apparently was experimenting with ensemble formats because on How High the Moon he opts to be backed only by Barney Kessel on bass and West Coast legend Leroy Vinnegar on bass. For a trio without a pianist or drummer they have a surprisingly full sound. For some reason he dispenses with drums on In The Chapel In The Moonlight, and while I love Shelly Manne, the song works well without him.

The core ensemble is Rollins backed by Kessell, Hawes, Vinnegar and Manne, so it's like a who's who on that coast. Let the sound samples convey the essence of this album because they do so far better than I can with mere words. The bottom line is this is yet another glimpse into Rollins' ever evolving musical vision, experimentation and evolution. Personally I find that aspect fascinating, and the music superb.

Background: recorded for Contemporary in their Los Angeles studios in three consecutive sessions on October 20 through 22, 1958.

title: Establishes Rollins' vision
text:
This is the third recording Rollins made with his unique piano-less trio, and this one cements this particular format. The preceding two albums debuting this format are as different from this one as they are from each other: [[ASIN:B003D5GWRY Way Out West]] and [[ASIN:B000TDGAFW A Night At The Village Vanguard]].

I consider this one to be essential because the rhythm section features two of the most melodic musicians on the scene: Oscar Pettiford on bass and Max Roach on drums. As a drummer those two are reason enough for me to get this album, but as a musician it's a joy to hear Rollins reinventing himself yet again. He truly stretches on this entire album, and I am sure that Pettiford and Roach behind him were inspiring him to reach.

The only way to get any sense of this album is to listen to the sound samples on this page. Granted, they are only tantalizing tidbits, but should be enough to reinforce what I am trying to say. Indeed, there is nothing I can say that will convey more information than the samples.

Note that this has extra takes that the original album did not have. Al of the tracks except Freedom Suite were recorded for Riverside in NYC on February 11, 1958 (Freedom Suite was recorded in NYC on March 7, 1958). I mentioned that I consider this to be an essential album, but not just for Rollins's fans. If you are a fan of Pettiford and/or Roach it's equally important because both are well showcased here. It's a spectacular recording for anyone who loves jazz from the era.

title: Hardbop with a nostalgic feel
text:
This is a fun album that clocks in at just under thirty eight minutes. What makes this special - aside form Dizzy and the two Sonnys - is the rhythm section led by Ray Bryant. I am a big fan of Bryant, so part of my gushing about the music and the five star rating is pure bias.

Listen to the sound samples for a good idea of the music. What you will not hear is how track 3 unfolds because there is no way a few seconds of the sample will convey the 3:19 intro played mainly by Ray Bryant on piano backed brother Tommy on bass and Charlie Persip on drums before Dizzy's trumpet, and Stitt's and Rollins's tenor saxophones come in.

The rest of the tracks are hard bop, with a definite bebop edge (especially on the last track.) I also love Dizzy's vocals on track 1. In fact, this is the one track that gives everyone a chance to stretch and swing. It's more straight ahead than the other tracks, and the rhythm section is strong. It's obvious that everyone is having fun.

For my fellow jazz geeks: this was recorded for Verve at Nola Studios in NYC on December 19, 1957 and released shortly afterwards in 1958.

title: Rollins' second album featuring a pianoless trio
text:
This is the perfect follow-on album to [[ASIN:B0038M61I2 Way Out West]] because it reinforces Rollin's innovative approach to using a piano-less trio. The Way Out West album was when Rollins introduced that format, but between that one and this album all of Rollins' other recordings featured pianists (Horace Silver, Sonny Clark, Thelonious Monk, Hank Jones and a few others.) This one comes back to the original format.

The sound samples on this page give a nice flavor of this album. All but the first two tracks were from the evening set which featured Rollins backed by Wilbur Ware on bass and Elvin Jones on drums. The first two tracks feature Don Bailey on bass and Pete LaRoca on drums, and it's easy to hear the difference between the two rhythm sections.

It goes without saying that from a rhythm section perspective Ware and Jones dominate this album. Plus you get a foreshadowing of Jones' approach when he joins Coltrane in 1960. However, that does not mean that the central force is not Rollins because he is the focal of every song. The rhythm section is secondary.

More importantly, the contrast between the more melodic rhythm section in Way Out West and the polyrhythmic one on this recording is striking. So is Rollins' playing, so if you compare the two albums you can get a sense of Rollins' evolution as a musician in a very short period of time.

I am sure that this album, like Way Out West, influenced Ornette Coleman who would also use a piano-less ensemble when he recorded his seminal [[ASIN:B0048ZLH1Y The Shape Of Jazz To Come]]. That was one of the four albums released in 1959 that changed jazz, and that particular one was notable for its lack of a chordal instrument - something that Rollins pioneered on this album and Way Out West before it. Therein lies the importance of this one on one level. On another level this album captures the ambiance and magic of the live performance at the Village Vanguard on November 3, 1957. In fact, of all of the live albums I own by any artist, this one stands out as one of the few that makes you feel as though you were there.

title: Innovative on a number of levels
text:
There are some excellent reviews going back to 2000 that cover this album exhaustively. My perspective is the format that Rollins came up with and used for the first time on one of his recordings: pianoless trios that used a bassist and drummer to back Rollins. This is the first of his albums to employ that format and it was a pretty daring move back in 1957.

Before I get too far off track give the sound samples on this page a listen. Some reviews have complained about the mix, but I suspect that this is exactly how Rollins intended the album to sound, but 1957 recording technology was not up to it. At any rate, the mix brings to the fore Ray Brown's bass, which has an unmistakable tone and style to begin with. What captivated me, though, is Shelly Manne's incredible percussion. He was one of the few drum kit players who could come up with not only the right groove, but incorporate effects into it. I've studied his playing extensively and this album epitomizes his unique style. If you are a drummer this is an essential album.

Back to why this is an innovative album: I sincerely believe that this album was an influence on Ornette Coleman when he recorded [[ASIN:B0048ZLH1Y The Shape Of Jazz To Come]] (which is one of four albums released in 1959 that changes jazz forever.) One of the things that made that 1959 album groundbreaking is the lack of chordal instruments, and specifically a piano. So Rollins approach is innovative by any standard for the era, even if my theory about influencing Coleman is wrong.

A few other items that are only of interest to my fellow jazz geeks is this was recorded in Contemporary's Los Angeles studios on March 7, 1957 and released the same year. This album differs from the original in that it has additional takes from that session. Rollins would follow this pianoless trio concept up with a recorded live performance on November 3, 1957 that was released as [[ASIN:B000TDGAFW A Night At The Village Vanguard]]. I highly recommend that album as well.

title: Williamson is like a fine wine
text:
I own most of Williamson's earlier recordings from the early-to-mid 1950s through the 1960s, so I have a good point of comparison to the tracks on this album. His earlier recordings were well grounded in bebop, and characterized by the tempos and changes of that genre. This album is almost lush in comparison. His approach to music when this was recorded had aged in the best sense of the word.

It's a shame that there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review because fans who are familiar with Williamson's earlier work could hear how he evolved musically forty years after his earlier recordings. For me both the song selection and Williamson's trio make this special.

The song selection is fun. All have some connection with exotic places, although not all south of US borders. As Time Goes By evokes Rick's in Casablanca, and Embraceable You is not pinned to any one geographic location. I normally do not reveal favorites, but on this album it's a toss-up between Corcovado (which does fit the album's theme) and the aforementioned As Time Goes By.

It's the trio that makes this special in my opinion. Andrew Simpkins has long been one of my favorite bassists because I am a big fan of The Three Sounds in which he spent well over a decade adding his distinctive bottom. His playing here is as good as anything he did with The Three Sounds and adds a lot to every track. Al Heath on drums is another of my favorites. I first came across him on a Sonny Rollins performance and loved his playing. On this album he displays the same mastery that he did for Rollins (and Dexter Gordon, John Coltrane and a plethora of others.) In other words, if ever there was a trio that meshed this one is it.

This album was recorded for the Japanese label, Venus, at the Bakery Recording Studio in Los Angeles on December, 15 , 1992. If you are a Williamson fan this album is a genuine treat. If for no other reason than to hear how the edgy music he was playing in the 1950s had evolved into a more complex, mature sound that is a delight to hear and a pleasure to enjoy.

title: Williamson magic circa 1995
text:
This album was recorded for the Japanese label Venus in New Jersey on April 22 and 23, 1995. To say that I am a Claude Williamson fan is an understatement, but most of his recordings in my library are from the 50s and 60s. When I heard the title track from this album I had to have it and it does not disappoint.

It's a shame that there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review. For one thing, the mix and sound quality are spectacular (although bassist Bill Crow is a little too prominent in the mix in my opinion.) If I had to pick a favorite track it would probably be Manhattan and bassist Crow does truly shine on it.

This is definitely evidence that Williamson's playing is like a fine wine that keeps improving with age. When I discovered his earlier work (you can hear a lot of it on [[ASIN:B004ODE45G Essential Jazz Masters]]) it was a jaw dropping experience for me. This album is even better than any of his earlier stuff in my opinion.

In addition to Bill Crow on bass Williamson is backed by David Jones on drums. I confess that I know little about him, but I love his approach to drums. The entire trio is spectacular on every track.

title: Four great albums
text:
Wright has long been one of my favorite pianists and the opportunity to grab four of his albums is a five star event in itself. All of the tracks in this set were recorded in a relatively short span in 1960 and 61. Three of the albums were recorded for Prestige and the fourth was for the Status label.

Interestingly, of the thirty one tracks Wright composed twelve and co-composed an additional three. Considering that he was not as well known, that is tribute to him as a composer because producers and record companies do not normally allow lesser known musicians that lattitude. He may have been lesser known, but he was definitely not lesser in any sense of the word.

Listen to the sound samples to hear how incredible each track is. In addition to superlative music, Fresh Sounds has done an excellent job of mastering (not to mention making these albums once again available).

All four albums were recorded at Rudy van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs, NJ studio. Here are the albums and some backfround:
========
DISC ONE
========
Tracks 1 through 7 are the album titled South Side Soul that was recorded for Prestige on August 30, 1960. Wright is backed by Wendell Roberts on bass and Walter McCants on drums.

Tracks 8 through 15 are the album titled Nice `N' Tasty that was recorded for Prestige on November 8, 1960. Wright is backed hy Wendell Marshall on bass and J. C. Heard on drums.
========
DISC TWO
========
Tracks 1 through 8 are the album titled Makin' Out. This is the only album that is not in trio format in this set. It was recorded for Prestige on June 23, 1961. Eddy Williams is on the front line on tenor sax backed by Wright, Wendell Marshall on bass and Roy Brooks on drums.

Tracks 9 through 16 are the album titled The Last Amen that was recorded for the Status and New Jazz labels on December 19, 1961. Wright is backed by Eugene Taylor on bass and Walter McCants on drums.

If you are new to Wright's work this is the perfect place to start. If you are a fan and have worn out your vinyl albums this is mastered good enough to replace them. It is not the same as vinyl, but is a close second.

title: Two album set from 54-55
text:
This is an two album set that was originally recorded for Capitol at their Melrose Avenue studios in Los Angeles. Both source albums were recorded under the auspices of Stan Kenton's 'Presents Jazz' imprint for the label.

Although there are three different rhythm sections spanning the two albums, the focus is clearly on Williamson's playing. He manages to play with blazing speed and a light touch that reminds me of Teddy Wilson (to an extent), as well as the ability to play the high keys for the same authority as Ahmad Jamal. I am not comparing Williamson to either of those, but did want to point out some of his signature sound and the best way is by analogy.

The sound samples on this page say far more about the music than I can with mere words. Let those be your guide.

The first eleven tracks are from an out-of-print album titled Stan Kenton Presents Jazz: Claude Williamson. They were recorded in June and July, 1954, and feature Williamson backed by Curtis Counce on bass and Stan Levey on drums. Counce's bass is truly superb as is Levey's drumming.

[[ASIN:B0059L04JM Keys West]] comprises the rest of the album that was recorded in two sessions in May, 1955. The tracks on this album feature two rock solid rhythm sections, with Williamson backed by Max Bennett on bass and Stan Levey on drums on tracks 14, 16 and 17, and backed by Buddy Clark on bass and Larry Bunker on drums on the remaining tracks.

The sound quality on this disc is up to Fresh Sounds usual high standards. I awarded five stars because this set resurrects one out-of-print album, and has been remastered to perfection (to my ears).

title: Excellent 2-album set from 1956
text:
This is a double album set that was recorded in 1956 for the Bethlehem label. Although there are no sound samples or track list on this page (at the time of this review), you can find both on the MP3 version albums page at [[ASIN:B005MVI6FS Complete 1956 Studio Sessions]]. Give those a run through to hear the incredible music in this set.

Here are the source albums and some background information:

Tracks 1 through 9 are the album titled [[ASIN:B00BEIBBOQ Claude Williamson]] that was recorded at the Radio Recorders studio in Los Angeles on January 19, 1956. It features Williamson's lightning fast playing with a superb backing rhythm section comprised of Don Prell on bass and Chuck Flores on drums.

Tracks 10 through 21 are the album titled [[ASIN:B00004WH7R Round Midnight]] that was recorded at the Radio Recorders Studio in Los Angeles on December 3, 4 and 5, 1956. He is backed by Red Mitchell on bass and Mel Lewis on drums.

I would be hard pressed to pick a favorite alum from the two in this set because the rhythm sections on each are wonderful. Each is different, but both stand out in their own special way. The centerpiece on each track is Williamson who plays fast and light, and manages to make the higher notes stand out like few other pianists. Let the sound samples and your ears guide you because there is nothing I can say that will convey as much information as those.

If you are a Claude Williamson fan this is a set that deserves a place in your library (if you do not already own them.)

title: Excellent interpretation of standards
text:
This entire album is a collection of some of my personal favorite standards, so my five star rating is completely subjective. The mastering, like all of the reissues by Fresh Sounds, is superb. I own a fair number of Williamson's albums and this one is on my short list of favorites.

One of the reasons why I am drawn to this one - aside from the song titles - is Chuck Flores on drums. His playing is fluid and tasteful, but also forceful. That may sound like a contradiction, but if you listen to the sound samples you will get a sonic glimpse of what I am trying to describe. I've spent hours studying his playing on this album and I learn something new each time I listen.

However, this is not a drummer's album. To me it's a template for any jazz piano trio. As mentioned, the song selection is hard to argue against, and the trio is tight. Williamson literally glides across the keys, and Flores and bassist Duke Morgan are with him on every note.

At less than thirty minutes this album definitely left me wanting more. However, what this lacks in listening time it makes up in musicianship. If you are a pianist or member of a jazz rhythm section this is worth its weight in gold in my opinion. If you are a fan or aficionado the pleasure is intense.

For fans, this was originally recorded in Los Angeles for the Contract label in 1961.

title: One of my favorite Williamson Trio albums
text:
This album was recorded for Bethlehem at the Radio Recorders Studio in Los Angeles on December 3, 4 and 5, 1956 and is an excellent example of Williamson's work in the mid 1950s. It's one of my favorite Claude Williamson Trio albums for a number of reasons (all subjective, of course). His piano technique tops the list of reasons. He is extraordinarily fast and can play the highest notes with the same authority as Ahmad Jamal. One of my favorite tracks is 'Round Midnight that features Williamson solo. He nails Monk's pensive feeling in every note.

There are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review, but you can listen to them by going to the following album: [[ASIN:B004ODE45G Essential Jazz Masters]]. That album contains every track on this one and more. The tracks to listen to are on Disc One (tracks 4, 6, 17, 18 and 26) and Disc Two (tracks 3, 8 through 11, 15 and 24).

While Williamson's playing is my primary reason for awarding this album five stars, his backing rhythm section is a close second. He is backed by Red Mitchell on bass and Mel Lewis on drums and the synergy among the three is pure magic. Both Mitchell and Lewis have no problems keeping with with some of Williamson's high speed playing, and both add their own distinctive touches to the music. In particular, Lewis is well worth picking out in the mix if you are a drummer because of his unique approach to rhythm.

title: The album that made me a fan
text:
This is the first Elias album I ever heard and was instantly smitten by her musicianship and voice. It was only later that I delved into her larger body of Brazilian material.

She practically channels Bill Evans on piano, but it's her vocals that make this album special to me. Having her husband Marc Johnson on bass and Joey Baron on drums round out the experience. Although I knew Johnson actually played with Evans, for some reason I kept imagining he and Baron as Scott LaFaro and Paul Motian - my favorite Evans trio line-up. Perhaps it is merely evidence of my mind going in my old age, since both Johnson and Baron have their own musical styles, but I caught glimmers of LaFaro and Motian in their playing the same as I could clearly hear Evans himself in Elias' playing.

Sadly there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review, but you can run through them on this page: [[ASIN:B0011XHATO Something For You MP3]]. Let those and your ears guide you because you can hear enough of each track to make up your mind if this album is for you. I mention this because I notice that some of Elias' fans are not as enchanted with her when she steps outside her Brazilian heritage. For me, it's the standards and tributes that I most love (although I love her Bossa albums too.)

One final note: this and [[ASIN:B00BXUG0KU I Thought About You (A Tribute To Chet Baker)]] get a lot of play in my home, but I think that a tribute to George Shearing would be a natural for her and an incredible gift to music in general. One can only hope.

title: Great music delivered in style
text:
A few other reviewers have done a marvelous job of dissecting this album, so I will confine this review to two things: personal impressions and the reasons why I awarded it five stars.

I was drawn to the album because it is a tribute to Chet Baker and I am a fan. I was skeptical that Elias could do a credible job with some of Baker's signature tunes, but she did something better: she made each song on this album her own. To me that is the best possible tribute and it epitomizes her own talent (not to mention validating the timeless value of each song that was selected.)

Another thing I love about this album is the backing ensemble. The swinging energy reminds me of a young Chet at the Trade Winds in the Los Angeles suburb of Inglewood, or with Gerry Mulligan (although there is no baritone sax on this album the fresh energy is).

For some reason there are no sound samples on the CD album's product page at the time of this review. If you are on that page go to the MP3 version at [[ASIN:B00CSSRPGY I Thought About You (A Tribute To Chet Baker) [+digital booklet]]] and listen to the sound samples. Those say it all. You can hear Elias' distinctive phrasing and the way she enunciates the words, as well as the backing ensemble. Also take the time to read RBSProds's excellent May 28, 2013 review, which provides rich background details.

If you do not own any of Elias' albums this is a great place to start. If you are a Chet Baker fan this album is one of the most loving tributes I have the pleasure of owning. Of course, if you do not know much about either Elias or Baker, this is still a wonderfully performed collection of some iconic songs. Either way you cannot lose.

title: Certainly different, but a matter of personal taste
text:
I fall on the side of folks who love this album. Krall has evolved considerably since the mid 1990s and this album marks one more step in her evolution as not only a musician, but as an entertainer.

There is nothing I can possibly write that will supplant the value of the sound samples on this page. Listen to those, especially if you are a fan, because the entire essence of this album is conveyed in a few seconds per track sample. Like what you hear? Grab the album. Not what you were expecting? Wait for her next album.

The reason I personally love this album is I listen to the same source albums from the 20s and 30s that apparently influenced Krall and inspired her to do this album. The music is true to the originals, although some of the tracks seem a bit heavy on amplification. Perhaps the producer wanted to modernize the sound a little for younger audiences. I love the song selection. Indeed, the trio I perform in does most of the material on this album, so there is a level of both validation and comfort listening to it.

Bottom line: art - and music is art - is what the beholder perceives. It's OK to not like this album, and is equally OK to love it. Personal tastes aside, the musicianship is superb and the taste of whoever selected the material is impeccable. Liking it is optional.

title: First Trio recordings
text:
This album features Cole's first trio comprised of Oscar Moore on guitar and Wesley Prince on bass. All of the tracks were recorded for Decca towards the end of 1940 and through 1941.

While I personally prefer the slightly later trio that features Johnny Miller on bass, that is a personal preference and not a reflection of the configuration on this album. Indeed, the era in which these tracks were recorded was dominated by big band with some smaller ensembles like Louis Jordan starting to emerge. But trios were practically unheard of, so the tracks here are like ground zero for not only trios in general, but Nat King Cole in particular.

The sound quality is very good considering the era in which these tracks were recorded and the state of the art for equipment and techniques. Here is the rundown on each track regarding locations and dates:

Tracks 1 through 4 were recorded in Los Angeles on December 6, 1940.

Tracks 5 through 8 were recorded in NYC on October 22, 1941.

Tracks 9 through 12 were recorded in Chicago on March 14, 1941'

Tracks 13 through 16 were recorded in NYC on July 16, 1941.

For fans who want to go to the roots of Cole's work this is a good starting point.

title: Early Capitol years
text:
This collection contains tracks plucked from most of the trio's recording sessions for Capitol. By the time these were made the original bassist, Wesley Prince, was replaced by Johnny Miller who is on all but one track. Also, the trio is augmented by a drummer on track 20. Nearly all of the tracks were recorded in Los Angeles, and all feature songs familiar to fans. This is a perfect companion to [[ASIN:B000003N4L Hit That Jive Jack: Trio 1940-41]], which is his Decca years.

It's a pity that there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review) because they pack so much information into a few seconds of sound. The sound quality is surprisingly good for 1940s recordings and become successively better on the final tracks.

I've tracked down the recording sessions from which the tracks are taken. Except where noted, the trio is comprised of Bat backed by Oscar Moore on guitar and Johnny Miller on bass.

1942: Track 1 features Cole and Moore with bassist Red Callender and was recorded at the C.P. MacGregor Studios on Los Angeles on October 11, 1942.

1943: Tracks 2 through 4 were recorded at the same studio on November 30, 1943 with tracks 5 through 7 on December 15, 1943.

1944: Track 8, which was recorded in the same studio as the previous ones on March 6, 1944.

1945: Track 9 was recorded at the Radio Recorders studio in Los Angles on April 13, 1945. Tracks 10 through 12 were recorded at the same location on May 19, 1945.

Tracks 13 and 14 were recorded at the WMCA Radio Station in NYC on October 11, 1945, and tracks 15 and 18 were recorded there on December 4, 1945.

1946: Track 16 was recorded at the Radio Recorders studio in Los Angeles on March 15, 1946; track 17 at the same studio on April 11, and track 19 on April 18.

Track 20 was recorded with the trio plus drummer Jack "The Bear" Parker at the WMCA Radio Station in NYC on August 19, 1946. Track 21 was recorded there on August 22 (without Parker).

The last track was recorded at the Pathe Studios in NYC on December 18, 1946.

title: Some of Nat's earliest recorded work
text:
Both the historical and musical value of this album make it worthwhile for fans. This is Cole's fourth album. He had previously recorded one for the Davis & Schwegler label in Los Angeles in 1939, another for the Ammor label in 1940, and the third for Savoy the same year. These recordings were mainly quartets backing vocalists.

This album, though, features Cole's first trio on the first seventeen tracks. All were recorded for Decca with Cole backed by Oscar Moore on guitar and Wesley Prince on bass. The remaining tracks are led by Cole's brother Eddie.

The sound samples on this page convey both the music and sound quality. To my ears the sound is excellent considering the relatively crude recording equipment and techniques used when these tracks were recorded.

The frst five tracks were recorded in Los Angeles on December 6, 1940.

Tracks 6 through 9 were recorded in Chicago on March 14, 1941

Tracks 10 through 13 were recorded in NYC on July 16, 1941 and 14 through 17 were recorded there on October 22, 1941.

Tracks 18 through 22 feature Nat with his brother's group called Eddie Cole's Solid Swingers, featuring Nat on piano, brother Eddie on bass and vocals and Jimmy Adams on drums backing a front line comprised of Kenneth Roane on trumpet, Tommy Thompson on alto and tenor sax and Bill Wright on tenor sax.

title: Early Wilson and a great album
text:
This the second album Wilson recorded and it ranks up there among my favorites for a few reasons. First the arrangements are perfectly matched to each song. Billy May downshifted on a few tunes with respect to ensembles, but I think it had more to do with Wilson's approach to each song than anything else. Listen to the sound samples on this page and you will hear what I mean.

My reason for loving this album (indeed Wilson's first four albums) is the choice of material. In some ways this is a continuation of her first album, [[ASIN:B0072CQEF4 Like in Love]], because the material was well established. Indeed, some of the tracks were the domain of other vocalists, but Wilson took them and made them her own, which is an impressive feat. Two that come to mind are Teach Me Tonight, which Dinah Washington defined and What a Little Moonlight Can Do, which was a throwaway that Billie Holiday transformed into a hit. Regardless, Wilson did both of those songs justice and laid claim to Guess Who I Saw Today which would forever be associated with her.

The personnel backing her were even wiser choices than the song list. For one, Ben Webster's tenor sax is strategically used on four tracks. He was known for two things: a big, virile sound on solos and the ability to deliver ballads with a sensitivity and tenderness that brimmed with emotion. That was what made him perfect on this album. I also loved Justin Gordon on flute and Jack Marshall on guitar because they, too, augmented Wilson's vocals in key places. Of course the remainder of the ensemble read like a who's who of West Coast musicians and if anyone if interested in the full personnel list I will include it in comments. I usually weave them into reviews, but here I want to focus on the few reasons why I love the album.

title: Essential for any jazz fan
text:
You need not be a Nancy Wilson or Cannonball Adderley fan to love this album, but if you are this is a must-have album. The original album only had eleven tracks, on which Wilson performed on all of the odd numbered ones and Adderley's Quintet playing instrumentals on the even numbered ones. This release contains a bonus track (Little Unhappy Boy) and is sequenced differently than the original. Here Wilson is on the first seven tracks backed by Adderley's quintet, which then performs the last five tracks without Wilson.

Fortunately there are sound samples on this page because I cannot put into words the magic of the entire album, not the synergy between Adderly's group and Wilson.
