I will say that Joe Zawinul's piano is a major factor in that magic and synergy. He had a knack for backing female vocalists, including Dinah Washington, and his playing behind Wilson is inspiring.

The album was recorded in 1961 for Capitol in NYC, with two days allocated to Wilson on June 27 and 29,) and a month later for just the quintet on August 23 and 24. Aside from Cannonball on alto sax and Zawinul on piano, the quintet also consisted of brother Nat on cornet, Sam Jones on bass (who is the composer of Unit 7) and Louis Hayes on drums.

One final note: although much of the material is comprised of standards there is a surprisingly large number of songs composed by members of the quintet. In addition to Sam Jones' composition, other members of the quintet had composer credits too: Cannonball composed Never Say Yes, and is co-composer on The Old Country, Nat composed Teaneck and Zawinul co-composed One Man's Dream.

title: A loving tribute
text:
What makes this album remarkable is how beautifully Bryant plays the compositions and styles of some of his own favorite pianists. Considering that Bryant had his own signature style this album is testimony to his virtuosity. But this is more than a mere homage or display of versatility: the music is nicely played with Bryant ably backed by Ray Drummond on bass and and Winard Harper on drums. To nbe honest I am not familiar with either of them, but their playing is impeccable.

Sadly there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review), because the music is what makes this a five star album. It's not what I would consider one of Bryant's essential albums, but it certainly provides more insight into him as a musician and person and that makes it valuable to fans.

This album was recorded for the JVC label in NYC on June 26 and 27, 1997. For folks who are curious about the fellow pianists that Bryant honored in this album I will include the list and the associated tracks in a comment to this review.

title: Original album plus bonus trancs sans Bryant
text:
This is an interesting album because it marks Carter's first album as a leader (in fact she is listed as the leader on eight of the tracks), as well as Bryant's (four tracks are credited to the Ray Bryant Trio).

In addition to twelve tracks that were originally released, this album contains seven bonus tracks. Note that Bryant is not on all but one of the bonus tracks.I will sort those out below.

Since there are sound samples on this page use those as your primary guide regarding your personal like or dislike of this album. I personally love it, but I am a staunch Ray Bryant fan and I also love Betty Carter's vocals. Another thing I love is some of Bryant's own compositions made it to this album. Considering that he was 24 at the time the recordings were made that is an unusual endorsement on the label's and producer's parts. Those tracks are Sneaking Around, Threesome and Bryant's Folly.

The track listing reflects the 1996 reissue of this album, with some of the bonus tracks leading off. Here are the sessions that produced the tracks:

On the Original Album:
Tracks 5 through 9 and 11 through 13 were recorded in two sessions in NYC for the Epic label on May 13 and 16, 1955. Carter is backed by Bryant's trio with Wendell Marshall on bass and Papa Jo Jones on drums. The flautist on three tracks is Jerome Richardson.

Tracks 14, 15 and 17 were recorded on June 1, 1955 in NYC with Bryant backed by his trio (Marshall and Jones), and tracks 16 and 18 a month later on July 1, 1955 by the same trio. Bryant's Folly did not make it to the original album and is considered to be a bonus track.

Bonus Tracks: 1 through 4, 10, 16 and 19 are from Carter's second album titled Social Call and were recorded in NYC for Epic on April 25, 1956. Carter is backed by a big band led by Gigi Gryce, but Bryant is not on these tracks. The pianist is Hank Jones.

title: Breathtaking jazz piano trio work
text:
I needed a single track to learn for an upcoming gig (Golden Earrings) and got caught up in the beauty of every track on this album. Give the sound samples a listen. If you hear them the way that I do, this album epitomizes what jazz piano trios should sound like. Bryant's bassist and drummer (Ike Isaacs and Specs Wright) are the perfect backing for Bryant's playing. I especially love Wright's brushwork, but Isaacs' bass is simply amazing too. I am quite familiar with Wright, but need to dig up more albums that feature Issacs because there is something about his playing that grabs me.

Of course, the focus should be on Bryant, and for me it is. Plus, his piano is perfectly placed in the mix, so you can savor each note. While the tracks are mostly by some of Bryant's contemporaries like John Lewis, Gerald Wiggins, Clifford Brown, etc., two of the tracks are his own compositions: Blues Changes and Splittin'.

This album was recorded for Prestige in Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio in 1956 (I cannot pin down the exact date), and released in April 1957. For me personally it is one of many from what I consider to be Prestige's golden era. At any rate, it is a perfect example of how great a jazz piano trio can be with the right leader and backing musicians.

title: A Gem
text:
This album came after a fifteen month gap in recording (and it would be another five years before Newborn would return to the studio). But that's trivia. What is important is the music on every track on this album. There are no duds, and the song selection is solid because they allow Newborn to show his talents in a number of tempos and styles. None of the tracks are his compositions, although bassist Leroy Vinnegar had a hand in composing Hard to Find.

Sadly there are no sound samples on this page. If you are familiar with Newborn's music you will not be surprised by anything on this album, but if you are a pianist and this album is your first exposure, be prepared for a few jaw dropping moments.

On the topic of sound, my copy seems to have a less than perfect mix. Newborn's piano is in front where it should be, but Frank Butler's drums are a too on top of Leroy Vinnegar's bass to my ears. Granted, the drums are a louder instrument, but there is less balance between them and the bass than I would have preferred. Since that is purely subjective on my part I am keeping my rating at five stars because Newborn is loud and clear and the playing of all three is remarkable.

This was recorded for Contemporary in their Los Angeles studios on April 1, 1964, fifteen months after he recorded [[ASIN:B000000YLK Great Jazz Piano of Phineas Newborn Jr.]] (Vinnegar was the bassist on that album too.) On this (and that one) Newborn was at the height of his playing, which makes this album another essential one for fans.

title: One incredible hour
text:
I absolutely had to have this video because of the Phineas Newborn Jr. episode and struck gold because Jimmy Smith's segment is just as incredible.

The video quality of both segments is excellent. Both are in black and white, and are crystal clear visually. The sound is surprisingly good coming from early 1960s TV programs. I am assuming that there was a lot of transferring and remastering magic before this DVD was released.

As I mentioned the main reason I purchased this DVD is for the Newborn segment. I am a big fan of his, and have also been long intrigued by drummer Kenny Dennis' technique. This clip did not disappoint because there were ample shots of all three musicians, including Dennis. His drum technique is centered on the snare drum, very similar to the first generation of jazz drummers who used press rolls to keep time. Al McKibbon's bass work is also a treat. All three epitomize the best in jazz piano trio musicianship.

I keep forgetting just what a treasure Jimmy Smith was, so the next clip was a reminder that I had far too little of his music in my library (I rectified that by purchasing [[ASIN:B003GE69LG Kind of Smith]].) He, guitarist Quentin Warren, and drummer Donald Bailey turned in an amazing performance that stands on its own merits. What I mean by that is this segment alone was worth the cost of the DVD to me.

title: One of the essential albums for fans
text:
By the time Newborn recorded this album he was a veteran leader as well as incredible sideman. If you are a fan I will only bore you with my gushing. If you are new to Newborn and his music you are in for a treat.

Sadly there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review, but there are three from this album on a compilation titled [[ASIN:B00845BMUK The Very Best Oo Phineas Newborn Jr]]. (tracks 2, 6 and 26 on that page correspond to Theme for Basie, New Blues and Four.)

The music on this album is incredible. Newborn is backed by two rhythm sections. On the November 21, 1961 that produced the first five tracks on this album he is ably backed by Sam Jones on bass and Louis Hayes on bass. As an aside, this session also resulted in tracks for another album titled [[ASIN:B000000Y9W World of Piano]].

Tracks 6 through 9 were recorded on September 12, 1962 with Newborn backed by Leroy Vinnegar on bass and Milt Turner on drums.

This album was recorded for Contemporary Records in their Los Angeles studios and offers some of Newborn's best work from this period. Some folks accused him of being too technical, but to my ears he played from his heart with gifts that few have. Both of this trios are perfectly matched to his playing, which makes this album all the more enjoyable.

title: Dazzling
text:
This is Newborn's fourth album as a leader and like every other album on which he led or supported his playing is simply dazzling. Although there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review) you can hear these tracks by going to this compilation - [[ASIN:B00845BMUK The Very Best of Phineas Newborn Jr.]] - and running through the sound samples for tracks 3, 7, 8, 15, 19, 20, 22 and 23.

While Newborn's playing is ample reason to grab this album, his skills as a composer are evidenced by three songs on the album that he composed: Juicy Lucy, For Carl and Cabu. The remaining tracks are covers of some great songs that allow him to stretch out and show his virtuoso piano chops. These range from some fiery bebop numbers by Bird and Diz, to a gorgeous rendition of Billy Strayhorn's Lush Life.

The first four tracks were recorded at Contemporary's Los Angeles studio on October 16, 1961. Newborn is backed by Paul Chambers on bass and Philly Joe Jones on drums. The remaining tracks were recorded in the same studio on November 21, 1961 with Newborn backed by Sam Jones on bass and Louis Hayes on drums.

If you are a fan this is one of the essential albums to own. If you are a pianist and are just now exploring Newborn be prepared for some jaw dropping moments.

title: McGhee with some LA stalwarts
text:
I snapped up this album the minute I heard it. Although I could ramble on about the music, there are sound samples that do that better than I. If you are on the CD's product page just jump to this page and run through the samples: [[ASIN:B005NUUJCG Maggie's Back in Town MP3]].

At less than forty-five minutes this album leaves you wanting more. What I love is not only McGhee's playing, but the incredible rhythm section backing him. One of my personal favorites is Phineas Newborn Jr. who is on piano. He easily keeps up with McGhee. In fact, listen to Demon Chase with a critical ear and you will hear what I am talking about. Bassist Leroy Vinnegar and drummer Shelly Manne are also exceptional here.

Not only does this album showcase McGhee's considerable talents on trumpet, but the aforementioned Demon Chase is evidence of his compositional skills. While at first I lamented the absence of Teddy Edwards' tenor sax on this album I am now happy that he is not on the album. My reason is there is a certain magic in the music that comes from McGhee backed by only rhythm section. Too many of my other recording have him with Edwards, Bird and even big band settings.

This album was recorded in a single session for Contemporary in Los Angeles on June 26, 1961. For some reason it was not released until 1964. Of the albums I have led by or featuring McGhee this one seems to get the most play time, so five easy stars.

title: Mance is firmly established
text:
This is Mance's second album as a leader and by the time he recorded this he had a solid twelve year track record as both a valued sideman and leader. While the choice or material consists of mostly standards or work of established musicians like Ellington, Mary Lou Williams and Jay McShann, two of the tracks are Mance compositions: The Uptown and Playhouse.

The value of this particular reissue CD is the sound quality, which is excellent. In addition, since this album is otherwise out of print, there are only a few other sources to obtain it, and all are compilations. For some reason there is no track list on this page (at the time of this review), so I am including it here:
1. The Uptown
2. Ralph's New Blues
3. Main Stem
4. Darling, Je Vous Aime Beaucoup
5. Playhouse
6. Sweet And Lovely
7. Oo-Bla-Dee
8. I Didn't Care
9. Swingmatism

For the music itself the best way to get a sense of it is to listen to sound samples. While there are none on this page you can hear them by running through the first nine tracks on this compilation: [[ASIN:B008JER3WW The Soulful Piano of Junior Mance / Big Chief! / Junior Mance Trio At the Village Vanguard]]. There is nothing I can write that will take the place of the actual music on that page. Let those samples and your ears guide you. Do note, though, that the sound quality of this CD is better than the sound on that MP3 album.

This album was recorded for the Jazzland label in NYC on October 25, 1960 and features Ben Tucker on bass and Bobby Thomas on drums backing Mance.

title: Mingus' last album as a performer
text:
This is Mingus' final appearance as a performer on a recording. True, he was involved with three other albums the following year, but that involvement was as composer and conductor.

Before I go further, listen to the sound samples on the MP3 version of this albums product page at [[ASIN:B001NB1F5Y His Final Work (MP3)]] (there are no samples on the CD's product page at the time of this review.) There is nothing I can possibly write that will convey as much information about the music on this album than the short snippets of sound from the samples. And I will not try since I'll only come across as pretentious when your own ears can hear the essence of the music.

I love Hamp's participation in this work. I've always been a fan and hearing a collaboration between Mingus and him is a treat. In fact this album is something of an endpoint since Mingus was in Hampton's orchestra in 1947 and 48, and did not perform with him again until this album.

Other members of this ensemble are a front line comprised of Woody Shaw and Jack Walrath on trumpet, Peter Matt on French horn, Gerry Mulligan on soprano and baritone saxophones, and Ricky Ford and Paul Jeffrey on tenor sax. The rhythm section is comprised of Lionel Hampton on vibes, Bob Neloms on piano, Mingus on bass and Dannie Richmond on drums.

This album was recorded in a single session in NYC on September 6, 1977 for the Who's Who in Jazz label. It was also released as Lionel Hampton Presents The Music Of Charles Mingus, but Mingus is definitely the leader. Arranger credits go to tenor saxophonist Paul Jeffrey, although the arrangements definitely bear Mingus' touch. I would not call this an essential Mingus work, but it's a solid one for those of us who are avid fans.

title: A.K.A. Jazzical Moods
text:
This is the original title of what eventually became retitled as [[ASIN:B000UBHGN8 Jazzical Moods]] that was recorded for the Bethlehem label in NYC in December 1954 and released in 1955.

What I love about this album is that it is early Mingus establishing his own vision and path. In fact, this was his second album (the first was [[ASIN:B00320SGU6 Jazz Composers Workshop]].) Most of the sound samples for this album are on a compilation titled [[ASIN:B005AUZU1Y Back Home With Charlie - [The Dave Cash Collection]]]. Go to that page and listen to tracks 2, 5, 7, 8 and 11. On those can already hear the genesis of Mingus' later work.

This album is certainly an experiment. For example it features Jackson Wiley on cello on What is This Thing Called Love and Minor Intrusion. Mingus switches to piano on Four Hands, and Thad Jones joins the ensemble as trumpeter on What is This Thing Called Love, Minor Intrusion and Spur of the Moment.

The core of the ensemble is comprised of John LaPorta on clarinet and alto sax, Teo Macero on tenor sax, Mingus on bass and Clem DeRosa on drums.

If you are a Mingus fan this is an insightful examination of his early work as a leader and one that I recommend.

title: Actually three albums with the bonus tracks
text:
This is the title album, plus two other albums on which Mingus is a side man. You can listen to sound samples of the tracks from the title album (the first seven tracks here) on an MP3 album titled [[ASIN:B005AUZU1Y Back Home With Charlie - [The Dave Cash Collection]]].

What I love about these tracks is it's Hampton Hawes on piano, Mingus on bass and his musical soulmate, Dannie Richmond on drums. Hawes brings a definite flavor of the West Coast to the ensemble, although Mingus is at ease with that sound having grown up on that coast as well. This is Mingus unadorned. His more complex compositions and playing are not as evident as on his subsequent work. This album was recorded for the Jubilee label in NYC in a single session on July 9, 1957.

Tracks 8 through 11 were recorded for Savoy in NYC on January 30, 1955 for an album titled The John Mehegan Trio/Quartet (Savoy MG 15054). Mehegan is the leader on piano, with Mingus on bass and Kenny Clarke on drums.

The remaining tracks are the album titled Teddy Charles - The Word From Bird that was led by Teddy Charles for Atlantic. This one was recorded in NYC on November 12, 1956 and features Charles on vibes, Hall Overton on piano, Mingus on bass and
Ed Shaughnessy on drums.

This is one of Mingus' albums that is off the beaten path, as well as two other albums that were recorded in the same approximate time frame. It's definitely a find for we hard core fans, but is not essential by any stretch of the imagination.

title: Teddy in a small(er) ensemble setting
text:
These tracks were never intended for sale so they are a great find. If you are on the CD version's product page there are no sound samples (at the time of this review), but you can run through them on this page: [[ASIN:B0019C28LM The Complete Associated Transcriptions 1944]]. As you can hear the sound quality is surprisingly good for the era and especially since these tracks were meant for radio broadcast.

One other thing you will note is the tracks are all much longer than the normal three minutes for recordings intended to be released on record. Some are approaching five minutes, and the bulk are in the three and a half to four and a half minutes, which is a dead giveaway regarding radio transcriptions.

These were all recorded in NYC during a single session on June 15, 1944. The ensemble has a very similar sound to Benny Goodman's small groups, which is no accident since Wilson was a member of those as well.

The line-up is Chu Berry on trumpet, Benny Morton on trombone and Edmond Hall on clarinet, with Wilson, Slam Stewart on bass and Big Sid Catlett on drums holding down the rhythm section.

If you are a Teddy Wilson fan this is an album that does not show up in discographies. I love it for the obvious influence Goodman's ensembles had on him, but he remains his own man because you can hear his own sound that put him on the map during the mid 1930s when he was backing Billy Holiday as well.

title: Mance's debut album as a leader
text:
By the time Mance made this recording debut as a leader he was a veteran performer who had been recording as a sideman for about twelve years. A run through the sound samples on the [[ASIN:B008FTBOM6 Junior (MP3 Album)]] product page makes one wonder why he didn't lead sessions before this one.

Tracks 1 through 10 on the CD version comprise the original album as it was first released by Verve. They were recorded in a single session in NYC on April 9, 1959. Mance is backed by Ray Brown on bass and Lex Humphries on drums.

There are two additional tracks on the MP3 version (both product pages share the same reviews at the time this was written), so if you are on the CD version's page you may want to check out the link I placed above.

The bonus tracks are from an out-of-print 4-LP set titled Mercury 40Th Anniversary V.S.O.P. that was released by Mercury Records in 1984 to commemorate their fortieth anniversary. The tracks are from Disc 2, Side 2 and were recorded for Mercury in March 1954. They feature Mance backed by Israel Crosby on bass and Buddy Smith on drums.

If you are a Mance fan and want to augment this album with the ones that quickly followed in the early 1960s I highly recommend [[ASIN:B00755IDM0 The Junior Mance Trio. (The Soulful Piano of Junior Mance / Big Chief! / At the Village Vanguard / Birdland Broadcast Performances)]]. That one picks up where this left off and features Mance's early stint Riverside's Jazzland subsidiary.

title: Early Mance
text:
Note: This review is for the album titled [[ASIN:B00CXS3L3K 3 Classic Albums Plus - Junior Mance]], which is cross linked to a similar set of Shelly Manne albums at the time of this review.

This set contains Mance's earliest albums as a leader. You are actually getting almost four complete albums instead of the three claimed. I love it when labels err on the side of the customer, and in this case the value is truly high. For one thing, the sound quality is superb. I own a number of sets released by Avid and have never had cause to complain.

title: Most of Powell's 1950s work as a leader
text:

What makes this set valuable is the individual albums are now out-of-print, so you can get nearly two and three quarters of an hour of Powell's music at an affordable price.

I rate the sound quality as very good plus. In fact, I have a number of sets from Avid and have been happy with all of them. This one is no exception. title: Breathtaking
text:
I love this album for the same reason why I am drawn to Sonny Rollins: three of the five tracks are pianoless. Don't get me wrong, piano is one of my favorite instruments (I earn my living performing with piano-centric ensembles and most of the music to which I listen is led by pianists.) But a tenor sax backed by just a bass and drums shifts the entire focus to that instrument. In that respect Coltrane shines without any buffer between him and the listener.

Instead of reading my babbling give the sound samples on this page a listen. On the first three tracks there is enough music from the samples to convey that I mean by a pianoless trio. The remaining two tracks will showcase Coltrane in larger ensembles and you can clearly hear why I prefer the more minimalist arrangements. Of course, that is a personal preference on my part and your experience may be different. The bottom line is although this was released in 1961 it is still Trane from his Prestige period circa 1957 to early 1958.

Do not let my reference to Rollins send you on a tangent. Rollins was experimenting with the pianoless trio concept when this album was recorded, but the absence of piano on this album's first three tracks is due to Red Garland missing the August 16, 1957 recording session when those tracks were made and not by design.

For the record, the other tracks were recorded on May 31, 1957 (I Hear A Rhapsody) and January 10, 1958 (Lush Life). All of the sessions were at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio and feature the following personnel: May, Coltrane is backed by Red Garland on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Louis Hayes on drums. August he is backed by Earl May on bass and Art Taylor on drums, and January he is accompanied by Donald Byrd on trumpet and backed by Red Garland on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Tootie Heath on drums.

In many ways this album provides a rare glimpse into Trane's playing from tracks 1 through 3, as well as his compositional genius on Trane's Slo Blues, which is the only track on this album that he wrote.

title: Excellent showcase for Kuhn's talent
text:
This album is Kuhn's first as a leader and truly showcases his playing and preferred musical style. Although there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review) you can hear them on the MP3 version of this album at [[ASIN:B005L4W5QC Rolf Kuhn and His Sound of Jazz]]. Let those guide you because describing this music is difficult. I think of it as small ensemble swing with a West coast jazz vibe.

Thanks to Fresh Sounds Records (once again) for not only reissuing lost gems, but for their spectacular mastering. The sound quality of this CD is probably better than the original issue.

Since there is no track list on this page at the time of this review I am going to provide one because the personnel change on some of the tracks. I have that information, but cannot find the exact dates or studio where this was recorded, and from the personnel it looks like there was more than one session. Here are the tracks:
1. Istambul
2. Waltzing Matilda
3. Lady Of Spain
4. Canadian Sunset
5. South Of The Border
6. Atlanta, GA
7. A Touch Of Berlin
8. Manhattan
9. Chicago
10. Caravan

This is clearly a theme album with travel or geography as the anchor. I love the song selection and the arrangements. This is a fun album that will keep your foot tapping. It was recorded originally for the Urania label in NYC sometime in 1960 and features the following personnel:
Tracks 1, 5, 6 and 9 are Kuhn on clarinet and Jack Shelton on guitar, backed by John Bunch on piano, Chuck Wayne on guitar, Henry Grimes on bass and Ray Mosca on drums.
Tracks 3 and 7 are the same personnel, except Shelton drops out and Jim Hall replaces Chuck Wayne on guitar.
Tracks 2, 4, 8 and 10 feature yet another line up with Kuhn on clarinet, Bunch on piano and organ, George Duvivier on bass and Don Lamond on drums (although Jim Hall rejoins this ensemble on track 10).

title: The soul mate of Flight to Denmark
text:
It's hard to separate this album from [[ASIN:B000027UPE Flight To Denmark]] since they both recorded during the same two sessions in Copenhagen on November 25 and December 2, 1973. Like that album, this one has Jordan's signature style, but a more flowing approach to music than his earlier work. It does foreshadow his later evolution, although you could always hear echoes of his earlier work with Bird, Art Blakey and others.

Although this and Flight of Denmark share some common tracks the value of both albums is the amazing rhythm section that is comprised of Mads Vinding on bass and Ed Thigpen on drums. In particular, Thigpen's presence on the album is a treat because he is one of my major influences. Another treat is Vinding's bass in the mix, which is more prominent on this and the 'Denmark' album. If you are a bassist this alone is reason to grab this and the companion album.

The best way to evaluate this album is to run through the sound samples on this page. They give a definite flavor of the music, as well as the high quality sound of the album itself.

Overall mood of this album is laid back and relaxing. The way Jordan's notes flow and Vinding and Thigpen back him brings me a lot of pleasure, and the more I listen, the more I hear something special in this album. Plus the song selection contains many of my favorites. If you love Jordan you are sure to enjoy this album.

title: Relaxing, but Jordan's signature style is there
text:
First, this album begs to be combined with [[ASIN:B000027UOO Two Loves]] because they were recorded together over the course of two sessions in Copenhagen on November 25 and December 2, 1973. The two albums share common tracks, but some titles are not duplicates, but different takes. In fact, as you scan the track list here you will see that.

Listen to the sound samples first. They will convey the essence of the music better than I can describe, but I want to provide a few personal comments about this album. Mads Vinding's bass is fairly prominent in the mix on most tracks and this is the first opportunity that I have had to truly dig into his playing. I've heard him on numerous other recordings, but apparently I never really listened with the critical ear that this album provides. His tone and approach is quite unique and this album is why I have moved him up into my relatively small pantheon of bassists.

Jordan's playing has his signature style, with a hint of his fire here and there, but is also relaxing. Part of the reason is the choice of songs, but even On Green Dolphin Street, which normally is played with a Latin groove in the A section and a swing feel in the B section, is more of a swing feel in both sections. The fire emerges on a few tracks like Jordu, but for the most part this album has a different mood.

I'd be remiss if I failed to mention how much I enjoyed Ed Thigpen's drumming on this album. He has been a strong influence on my own professional growth, and he adds his usual tasteful touch to every track here. He is not as prominent in the mix, but he is exactly where he should be in it.

Overall this is one of my treasured Duke Jordan albums. While most of his peers who started out in bebop sort of lost their relevance, Jordan evolved and remained completely relevant his entire career, and this 1973 album is a mid career showcase of his work.

title: An overlooked Jazz Messengers album
text:
Although there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review, you can listen to most of the tracks on an album credited to Duke Jordan (adding to the confusion because it implies he is the pianist on all tracks) with the same title: [[ASIN:B00ASPPC64 Les Liasons Dangereuses (MP3 album)]]. Not all of the tracks are on that one, but it will give you a good idea of the music.

The interesting (and confusing) thing about this album is it's a partial soundtrack to the movie of the same title, [[ASIN:B00007KK1S Les Liaisons Dangereuses DVD]]. Thelonious Monk composed and performed the score, but that music has never been released on a record.

This album is only part of the soundtrack and is the score for the extended party scene, and is often credited to Duke Jordan. He composed all but one track (Prelude in Blue), but the pianist is Bobby Timmons on all but one track (the same one that Jordan did not compose, but played on).

In fact, this is an Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers album with the following line-up: Lee Morgan on cornet (a departure from trumpet), Barney Wilen on tenor and soprano sax, and the rhythm section that includes Timmons and Jordan on piano, Jymie Merritt on bass, Art Blakey on drums and additional percussion by Tommy Lopez and Willie Rodriguez on congas, and Johnny Rodriguez n bongos. It was recorded for the French label, Fontana, at Nola's Penthouse Sound Studios in NYC on July 28 & 29, 1959.

While this is not an essential Jazz Messengers album, it's a fun listen and hard core fans will love it. And for the record, Monk recorded his contributions to the soundtrack at the same studio on July 27, 1959, with charlie Rouse and Wilen on tenor sax, Sam Jones on bass and Art Taylor on drums. I am hoping those tracks will eventually be released.

title: Annie with a West Coast vibe
text:

Foremost this is Ross backed by predominately West Coast musicians. That alone guarantees a different aspect of her talent. title: Sound quality is not spectacular; music is
text:
Although there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review you can listen to them on a Ralph Sutton compilation titled [[ASIN:B004ZSTAL8 Piano Jazz Essentials]] that has nearly all of the tracks that this album contains. Let those tracks guide you with respect to the music because mere words cannot begin to describe Roberts' and Sutton's playing. They need to be heard. The sound quality on that one is better, but it is missing some of the tracks that this one contains.

The fact that this album contains six tracks by Lucky Roberts is reason enough to award it five stars, although you can mentally subtract one for less than great sound. Since these are but of a handful of Roberts' recordings that he made in his long life (he would pass twenty-two years later in 1968), there is historical significance to this album too. Roberts' tracks were recorded in NYC on May 21, 1946 and if you have never heard his actual playing each track is jaw-dropping.

Ralph Sutton occupies the remaining tracks - all recorded in a January 22, 1949 and a June 11, 1952 session, both in NYC. His 1949 session produced tracks 7 through 11 and feature Sutton solo. The remaining tracks feature him accompanied by drummer George Wettling.

A piece of trivia to end this review: both Roberts and Sutton's drummer on this album (Wettling) were featured in Art Kane's iconic 1958 photograph titled [[ASIN:B000LJPKH8 Art Kane A Great Day in Harlem Jazz Portrait 1958 Photo]].

title: Focus on Jordan with some Bud balancing it out
text:
This is really a Duke Jordan album with the first tracks from a January 28, 1954 session he recorded for a number of labels including Disques Swing, Prestige and the usual suspects. Most of the tracks wound up on 'Various Artists' compilations.

What I love is the focus on Jordan and his playing, with just enough of Bud Powell tagged on the end of the album to compare and contrast. Of course Powell's powers were declining by the time his four tracks were recorded in Paris on October 14, 1960. However, for this session Powell was in good form. There is much talk about how his work after the early 1950s was not so hot. The last four tracks dispel that notion because his playing was truly inspired.

On the Duke Jordan tracks his rhythm section is the rock solid Gene Ramey on bass and the equally excellent Lee Abrams on drums. Powell is backed by a stellar rhythm section too: the legendary French bassist Pierre Michelot and Kenny Clarke who is the father of bebop drumming. In other words, this album is a collection of rhythm section powerhouses if nothing else.

However, it is truly much more than just rhythm sections. The bebop vibe is strong on every track (no surprise), but the structure and form is modernized and streamlined, and the pianos of both artists are cooking. It's a shame that there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review) because a few seconds from each track would easily compel a fan to grab this album.

title: Cobb backed by a great rhythm section
text:
At the time of this review the CD version's product page of this two album set is missing both sound samples and a track list. I am adding the track list in a comment to this review for the benefit of those reading this on the CD's product page.

The albums that comprise this set are [[ASIN:B001DGGWY8 Sizzlin']] (tracks 1,2,4,7,10 and 13) and the out-of-print album titled Ballads by Cobb (tracks 3,5,6,8,9,11 and 12). I have no idea why Fresh Sounds Records interleaved the tracks from the two albums that way, but they sure made up for it in mastering. The sound on the CD version is excellent! Go to the MP3 version of this album's product page (if you are not there already) at [[ASIN:B00IXKPUZO Arnett Cobb: Blues & Ballads (feat. Red Garland's Trio)]] and run through the sound samples. The music speaks for itself and the short snippets of the samples are truly representative of both the music and the sound quality.

What I love is the consistency of both albums. One reason, of course, is they were recorded in two consecutive days, and another is the signature sound of Red Garland on piano on both albums. I am fairly sure that is why Fresh Sounds was able to get away with mixing the tracks from both. Yet another reason for the homogenous sound is the fact that both albums were recorded by Rudy van Gelder at his Englewood Cliffs, NJ studio. The quality certainly bears the imprint of his unique touch.

Sizzlin' was recorded on October 31, 1960 with Cobb's tenor sax backed by Garland's trio with George Tucker on bass and J.C. Heard on drums. Ballads by Cobb was recorded the next day on November 1, 1960 with George Duvivier taking Tucker's place in bass.

This is definitely a Cobb led session that is credited to the Arnett Cobb Quartet, but Red Garland fans will also want this in their libraries. If you listen carefully you can hear subtle changes in jazz of the era because this album has an touch of R&B in it.

title: An absolute delight
text:
I first encountered this album as part of a much larger compilation titled [[ASIN:B0051V6UNE The Ultimate Jazz Collection]] (which I also highly recommend if you are a Red Garland fan). Before getting distracted by my following commentary, give the sound samples on this page a listen. They say far more about this album than anything I can possibly write below. Even the false start on Lil' Darling' contains something of musical value to my ears, but I am admittedly biased towards Red Garland's playing.

The music is fantastic, but only after I got this album did things start falling into place. For one thing I was unaware of this particular live date, nor the fact that the bassist and drummer here were Jimmy Rowser and Specs Wright. Finding that out answered a lot of questions I had because Wright in particular is a fairly aggressive drummer for a piano jazz trio member circa 1959.

Another thing I love is the playing has a consistent quality throughout. Part of that is because all three sets from the October 2, 1959 performance are here, including tracks that Prestige did not issue originally. The tracks are not in the order in which they were performed, but that is not a real issue in my opinion.

If you are a Red Garland fan this is some of his best recorded work as a leader. This particular set captures him outside of the studio recordings for which he is better known, and if you are a pianist or musician who has excellent listening skills you will hear humor in his playing on this particular date.

title: A bright spot in music
text:
Sorry for the pun in the title. I stumbled across Bright after reading posts and interviews by one of my favorite writers - Marc Myers - who inspired me to search out more of Bright's work. I am glad I did. This is a set of three albums that features Bright during the mid-to-late 1950s. This two-disc set clocks in at 78:29 and 33:53 respectively.

The sound samples on this page say it all with respect to the music. Fresh Sounds Records has worked their typical magic on remastering, which should assuage any concerns that you have about sound quality. You will not be disappointed!

Here are the source albums and background information on the tracks:
========
DISC ONE
========
Track 1 is from an various artists compilation that was issued by the Epic label as After Hours Jazz. This track was recorded in Chicago on June 12, 1956 with Bright backed by Wilbur Wynne on guitar and Willard Nelson on drums.

Tracks 2 through 9 are the album titled [[ASIN:B000001CT0 Brights Spot]] that was recorded for the Regent label at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on September 26, 1956. Bright is backed by Kenny Burrell on guitar and Leonard Gaskin on bass. This album was reissued by Savoy.

Tracks 10 through 21 are the out-of-print album titled Bright Flight that was recorded for the Vanguard label during two sessions in NYC on March 2 and November 27, 1957. Bright is backed by Benjamin on bass and Bill Clark on drums.
========
DISC TWO
========
The entire disc is the album titled [[ASIN:B003B4SP04 Ronnell Bright Trio]], which was recorded in Paris, France for the Polydor label on June 5, 1958. Bright is backed by Richard Davis on bass and Art Morgan on drums.

If you are new to Bright this is a perfect starting point. The only thing disappointing is the injustice of Bright not being better known because the music is exceptional and he certainly should be a household name. For some of the reasons why do a search of the web using the keywords Ronnell Bright and Marc Myers. You will be rewarded with a wealth of information and should be even more inspired to purchase this album!

Tracks 1, 4, 6, 7 and 8 were recorded on March 25 with Ross backed by Zoot Sims on tenor sax, Russ Freeman on piano, Jim Hall on guitar, Monte Budwig on bass and Mel Lewis on drums.
