title: Her first two decades
text:
This is an excellent collection of the first two decades of Maxine's career. The four discs in this set are chronological and cover her most important recordings between 1937 and 1956.

Sound quality is as good as can be expected, especially on the first three discs in this set, some of which are approaching eighty years old. Unlike some compilation sets, this one comes with extensive documentation regarding the source albums and sessions, including musicians backing her. For those of us who are obsessive about such information this alone is worth the price of the set.

Here is a rundown of what this set contains with respect to backing orchestras and time frames. If you want detained information about specific tracks leave your question in a comment and I will do my best to answer it.

Disc One contains tracks recorded from June 1937 through March 1939 (most, though, were in 1938). Maxine was backed by orchestras led by Claude Thornhill or John Kirby.

Disc Two picks up where the first one left off, with coverage of 1939 through 1942. John Kirby's orchestra, as well as Benny Carter's dominate the backing ensembles and these tracks are where Maxine and Charlie Shavers first connect.

Disc Three picks up in March 1942 with the first few tracks, then skips to 1944 with the Cedric Wallace Orchestra. Next are two tracks in 1944 with Teddy Wilson's quintet (and one of the best renditions of E'vry Time We Say Goodbye I have ever heard), then backing by groups large and small led by Benny Carter, Sylvan Schulman, Elis Larkins and Vic Ash from 44 to 1954.

Disc Four covers 1955 and 1956, and is dominated by Charlie Shavers led ensembles, with an excellent set of tracks featuring Dick Hyman.

This is an exceptional collection of Maxine's earlier work, and although there are no sound samples on this page, you can listen to many of these tracks on this MP3 album: [[ASIN:B00274DZ18 The Very Best Of]]

title: Amazing line-ups and exceptional music
text:
Although there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review), you can listen to the tracks on the MP3 version's product page at [[ASIN:B00CHI5UV2 Randy Weston Trio]], or by visiting each of the individual source album pages. This album clocks in at a few minutes over two hours.

The sound samples provide a sonic glimpse of the music, but the CD version of this album - this one - is superbly mastered and the sound quality is excellent. What I love, aside from Cecil Payne's lush baritone sax is the fact that one of my favorite bassists, Ahmed Abdul-Malik, is on every track. Of course, Weston's piano is another reason to grab this album. The drummers featured (Wilbert Hogan and Willie Jones) are both exceptionally competent and fit right into the stellar ensembles on each track.

I am going to let the sound samples speak for this three album set. They convey the essence of the music far better than I can describe with words. Here are the source albums and the background information on each:

Tracks 1 through 8 on Disc One are the album titled [[ASIN:B00BNQUH1W With These Hands]], which was recorded for Riverside at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on March 14 and 21, 1956. The album is credited as the Randy Weston Trio With Cecil Payne, with Payne's baritone on all tracks except 2 and 4, and Weston on piano backed by Ahmed Abdul-Malik on bass and Wilbert Hogan on drums.

The remaining six tracks on Disc One and the first three on Disc Two are the album titled [[ASIN:B00BNUCZH2 Modern Art of Jazz]]that was recorded for the Dawn label. Disc One, Tracks 10, 12 and 14 and Disc Two, Track 1 were recorded in NYC on November 21, 1956. Personnel for this session are Ray Copeland on trumpet and Cecil Payne on both baritone and alto saxophones, backed by Weston on piano, Ahmed Abdul-Malik on bass and Wilbert Hogan on drums. Disc One, tracks 9, 11 and 13, and Disc Two, Track 2 were recorded the next day by the trio featuring Weston on piano, Ahmed Abdul-Malik on bass and Willie Jones on drums. Disc Two, Track 3 was recorded during this session too, but for the Harmony label.

Tracks 4 through 11 on Disc Two are the album titled [[ASIN:B00BNEIF90 Jazz á la Bohemia]] that was recorded for Riverside live at the Cafe Bohemia in NYC on October 14, 1956. This album is also credited to the Randy Weston Trio With Cecil Payne, with Payne on baritone sax, and Weston and Ahmed Abdul-Malik holding down the rhythm section with drummer Al Dreares.

title: A collection of some of the bebop greats
text:
Since this album only includes greats who recorded for Savoy or its affiliates there are some omissions. Regardless, this set gathers some household names like Bud Powell, Horace Silver and Lennie Tristano, and some whose names have been sadly forgotten by many. All of the pianists in this collection, though, were highly regarded in their day and among we jazz geeks continue to be highly regarded to this day.

It's a shame that there is scant information on this product page at the time of this review, but I have tracked down dates, personnel and locations for the tracks. I only wish there were sound samples, but each of the pianists in this collection have MP3 albums on this site where you can listen to the actual tracks included here. Linking to those is a giant undertaking and I am limited to ten links in this review, so I am going to sidestep that. A search of each artist and a selected track title here will yield links to sound samples that are in other albums.

Some gems include tracks by Herbie Nichols, Dodo Marmarosa and George Wallington. Not because they are necessarily better (that is too subjective), but they deserve more recognition than they receive today. Pay particular attention to Nichols because his style is truly unique. Every pianist in the collection, though, is amazing. Here is what this set contains:

Tracks 1 through 3 are credited to The Be Bop Boys, which was the ad hoc group Bud Powell recorded these tracks with. Track 1 was recorded in NYC on August 23, 1946. It's also known by the more common title, Bouncing with Bud, and has a front line comprised of Kenny Dorham on trumpet and Sonny Stitt on alto sax. Bud leads a rhythm section comprised of Al Hall on bass and Wallace Bishop on drums. The other two tracks were recorded in NYC on September 4, 1946 and feature the same line up, except Kenny Clarke is on drums.

Tracks 4 through 7 were recorded in NYC on October 23, 1947, and feature Lennie Tristano backed by Billy Bauer on guitar and John Levy on bass.

Tracks 8 through 11 were recorded in NYC on March 6, 1952 and feature Herbie Nichols backed by Danny Baker on guitar, Chocolate Williams on bass (and vocals on track 11) and Shadow Wilson on drums.

Tracks 12 through 15 were recorded in Pittsburgh on July 21, 1950 with Dodo Marmarosa backed by Thomas Mandrus on bass and Joe Wallace on drums.

Tracks 16 through 19 were recorded in NYC on November 21, 1951 with George Wallington backed by Curly Russell on bass and Max Roach on drums.

Tracks 20 through 22 were recorded at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on January 30, 1956. The front line is comprised of Donald Byrd on trumpet and John LaPorta on alto sax. Horace Silver leads the rhythm section comprised of Wendell Marshall on bass and Kenny Clarke on drums.

title: Great music and an histroical event in jazz
text:
The first seven tracks were recorded at the Fine Studios in NYC on October 28 and 29, 1959 and have both historical and musical significance. Historically those two sessions are credited as the first collaboration among Bill Evans, bassist Scott LaFaro and drummer Paul Motian who would form their own trio that would be regarded as the very best one led by Evans.

Musically this album showcases Tony Scott's compositional skills as well as his virtuoso command of a number of instruments. Listen to the sound samples for an idea about the music itself. Thematically this album pays homage to Scott's heroes. Most of these tracks were also released on an album titled Dedications.

The full Evans/LaFaro/Motian trio only appears on tracks 1, 4 and 5, backing Scott on Clarinet. Track 2 is Scott solo on clarinet and baritone sax and on track 3 Scott takes over on piano backed by LaFaro on bass and Motian on drums. Tracks 6 and 7 is a duo of Scott on clarinet and Evans on piano.

The final two tracks were recorded sometime in 1958. I was unable to track down specifics other than Scott is solo on guitar on track 8, and on clarinet backed by Juan Sastre on guitar.

To my ears each track contains not only amazing compositions, but also a showcase for Scott's mufti-instrumental talents. He is sadly less known than the sidemen whom he picked for this album. In fact, not three months after this session Evans, LaFaro and Motian were so solidified as a trio that they recorded and released [[ASIN:B00492ANTS Portrait In Jazz]], which went on to become a seminal album.

title: A great compilation of Monk/Coltrane collaborations from 1957
text:
This is a compilation of tracks from 1957 sessions that are collaborations between Monk and Coltrane. Track 6 is a notable exception because it feature Monk solo. All of the tracks are actually outtakes from three different studio albums (I will provide background information below).

I am not going to dissect the music because it has not only been ably done by some very articulate reviews here, and also the sound samples describe more about the music in a few brief seconds per track than thousands of words.

From a personal perspective I love this album because Coltrane's approach to music - at least as a co-leader and sideman during this period - is straight ahead. By the time this album was released in 1961 Coltrane had started to go in musical directions that broke new ground. It also was evolving away from his performances on the five tracks he is on in this collection.

Another reason why I love this album is there are three tracks that feature one of my favorite drummers: Shadow Wilson. By the time this album was released he had been deceased for two years, so the tracks are part of his legacy.

Finally, the two tracks featuring a larger ensemble that included both Coltrans and Coleman Hawkins on tenor sax is a study in contrasts between Hawkins who practically invented the jazz vocabulary for jazz tenor sax, and Coltrane who would add significantly to that vocabulary.

Here are the source sessions for the tracks on this album:

Tracks 1, 2 and 4 were recorded at the Reeves Sound Studios in NYC during July, 1957. Coltrane is both accompanied by and backed by Monk with Wilbur Ware on bass and Shadow Wilson on drums.

Tracks 3 and 5 were recorded at the Reeves Sound Studios in NYC on June 26, 1957 and feature a front line comprised of Coltrane and Hawkins on tenor sax, Gigi Gryce on alto sax and Ray Copeland on trumpet. The rhythm section is Monk, Wilbur Ware on bass and Art Blakey on drums.

Track 6 is Monk solo and was recorded at the Reeves Sound Studios in NYC on April 12, 1957.

title: CD is the expanded version with excellent sound and music
text:
This is the original 13-track album titled [[ASIN:B001V6GB8C Mary Lou Williams Trio At Rick's Café Americain, Chicago]] plus fourteen additional tracks. If you are looking at the MP3 version (the album to which I linked) know that the CD version is more complete. If you are on the product page for the CD version of this album ([[ASIN:B004NHRGZI At Ricks Cafe Americain]]) you will get everything that was recorded live at Rick's Café Americain in Chicago on November 14, 1979.

What I love is this is a rare musical glimpse at Williams in a live setting backed by a trio. Her own playing is magical to my ears, and her backing musicians comprised of Milton Suggs on bass and Drashear Khalid on drums do a superb job of supporting her. Go to the MP3 version of the album to listen to sound samples of the thirteen tracks that were originally released. Those will convey the overall essence of both the gig and the quality of the recordings. Personally I love the sound quality. The mix is beautifully done with every instrument where it should be and every note clear.

The original album's thirteen tracks were all standards, with co-composer credits on What's Your Story Morning Glory going to her. This one contains five more of Williams' own compositions, plus tracks featuring her solo.

Here is a cross-reference of the tracks on this expanded album that were on the original thirteen track release: Disc One, tracks 7 through 11 and 14. Disc Two, tracks 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10 and 11.

title: Jeep in command
text:
This album grabs me from the very first note. No matter how many times I listen to it, the music transports me to a special place. Run through the sound samples for a taste of what this incredible album offers. I know that Hodges is the leader, but to me it's the sophistication of Ellington with a dose of blues.

One of the reasons I keep coming back to this music is how beautifully the rhythm sections on each of the tracks perform. On three of the tracks Duke himself leads the rhythm section (1, 2 and 4), with Billy Strayhorn leading on the remaining tracks. Papa Jo Jones on drums on all tracks is a key ingredient. He manages to provide the perfect groove to every tune. Of course bassists Al Hall on tracks 1, 2 and 4, and Wendell Marshall on the rest of the album add a solid pulse that glues the rhythm sections together.

Hodge's creamy alto tone is another reason for my love affair with this album. On tracks 1, 2 and 4 he is accompanied by Harry "Sweets" Edison on trumpet who adds a bluesy Kansas City flavor to those tracks. He is also accompanied by Les Spann on guitar (and flute) on those tracks. The remaining tracks shift slightly with Hodges accompanied by Ben Webster on tenor sax and Roy Eldridge's trumpet. Lawrence Brown's trombone adds more bottom to these tracks and the sound is noticeably different.

The album was recorded for Verve in two sessions, both in NYC. Tracks 1, 2 and 4 were recorded at the Columbia Studios on February 26, 1959 while the remaining tracks were recorded at the Nola Studios earlier on August 14, 1958.

title: Original album plus bonus tracks: superb music!
text:
I rank Paul Desmond up there with the greatest alto saxophonists, and Gerry Mulligan is among not my favorite baritone saxophonists, but composers as well. Both are inventive musicians and pairing them with the other members of their backing ensembles equals perfection in my mind.

Before I bore you with my take on the music, let the sound samples from the MP3 version of this album convey the music: [[ASIN:B0081M0DDI Two Of A Mind]]. There is just under seventy-four minutes of music, with over forty from the original six tracks and the remaining from the bonus tracks.

On the original album, recorded at RCA's Studio A in NYC, the first six tracks were recorded in three sessions. Each of which featured backing by incredible rhythm sections. The bassists on those tracks are Wendell Marshall on tracks 1 and 2, and John Beal on track 4, and Connie Kay on drums. Kay is one of the most sensitive drummers I have studied and is absolutely perfect (especially behind Desmond's alto sax.)

Completing the original albums, Joe Benjamin is the bassist and Mel Lewis is the drummer on tracks 3,5 and 6. They both back Desmond and Mulligan on one of the bonus tracks as well (track 9).

I am not sure when the bonus tracks were recorded. While the original six were recorded on June 22, July 3 and August 13, 1962 there is no discography showing when or where the remaining ones were laid down. Track 9 was probably made during the original sessions, but the personnel on tracks 8, 10 and 11 are different. On those Jim Hall's guitar adds a lot to the ensemble, with Ed Shaughnessy on drums. Interestingly, on track 11, which is a fragmented alternate take, Mulligan is on piano and Desmond is on baritone sax.

For me this is a delightful album featuring two stellar saxophonists who are backed by exceptional rhythm sections. If you are a fan or either Desmond or Mulligan (or both) you will enjoy this album.

Since there is no track list on this page at the time of this review I am including it in a comment below.

title: A great collaboration
text:
Normally I prefer Chet accompanied by a baritone sax because that instrument is a perfect complement to his penchant for playing in lower registers. However, there is something compelling about Chet and Art Pepper's alto sax. To be honest I cannot put my finger on it. Perhaps it's not just a lower register instrument, but an Eb one that seems to go with Baker's trumpet. Regardless, this album is a gem to my ears on a number of levels.

Foremost, this is some of the best West Coast jazz in my collection. A run through the sound samples clearly reveals that this is two different albums, but with musicians of a like mind. If you are on the CD version's page there are no sound samples at the time of this review. To listen to them go to this page: [[ASIN:B005L0K7JI Complete Playboys Sessions, 1956]].

The first five tracks were recorded at the Forum Theater in Los Angeles on July 26, 1956. Baker and Pepper are accompanied by Richie Kamuca on tenor sax, and backed by Pete Jolly on piano, Leroy Vinnegar on bass and Stan Levey on drums.

All of the remaining tracks were recorded at the Radio Recorders studio in Los Angeles on October 31, 1956. Baker and Pepper are accompanied by Phil Urso on tenor sax and backed by Carl Perkins on piano, Curtis Counce on bass and Lawrence Marable on drums.

One of the reasons to purchase this album - aside from being a Chet Baker and/or Art Pepper fan - is this album represents the only tracks they recorded together. The music epitomizes the best of West Coast jazz (in my opinion), and the rhythm sections of the two ensembles are different enough to contrast West Coast sub styles.

title: For diehard fans; not an essential album
text:
Frankly I purchased this album because it features Artt Frank on drums (he is credited as 'Art' but uses the second T in his name these days.) Of course, I purchased it for Chet too.

While I am not disappointed in the drumming on the album, the overall music itself lacks the soul that Chet exhibits when he is truly 'on'. The music also has a slight bebop feel, which took me by surprise. Indeed, you can pick some of that up from the short sound samples on this page. While the music lacks soul, there are a few moments of brilliance scattered throughout the 1:17:46 of music.

The main reason I subtracted a star, aside from the less than stellar performance, is the sound quality is a little below Fresh Sound Records' normal standards. The reissue label usually leads the pack when it comes to sound, so I have to assume that the masters from which they made this were in poor shape. Listenable, but in a bootleg sort of way.

This performance was recorded live at the Backstreet Club in New Haven, CT on February 19, 1980. Chet is backed by Drew Salperto on piano, Mike Formanek on bass and Artt Frank on drums. Frank was one of a very few drummers that Chet admired and his performance on this album shows why. If you are a die hard fan or a drummer this is an excellent album, otherwise you can safely pass it by.

title: Live performance by my favorite trio
text:
Of all of the trios Baker led this one is my personal favorite. There is almost a telepathic communion between Baker and guitarist Philip Catherine, with bassist Jean-Louis Rassinfosse also in the conversation.

This album was recorded live at the Seventh Jazz Festival in Munster, Germany on June 21, 1985. Although I personally like Baker's studio sessions more than his live performances this one is an exception. The trio is hot, and their set list runs slightly over an hour. I love the eclectic approach to the music, including the definite Bossa feel of the last track.

Unfortunately there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review), but you can listen to snippets from the MP3 version's product page at [[ASIN:B008SOJOWK Chet Baker Trio: Strollin']]. That album also contains a track that this one does not (Funk In Deep Freeze).

One of the reasons this performance is so tight is it was sandwiched in between two studio sessions on June 6 and 25, 1985 in Belgium. Those sessions produced what I consider to be the greatest album from this particular trio - [[ASIN:B000027LIV Chet's Choice]] - but to my ears this album ranks right up there with that one. In fact in my opinion any album that features this line up is a treasure. That is merely a reflection of my personal taste, so listen to the sound samples and not my babbling.

title: Great soundtrack from a great video
text:
This is the sound track from the fifty-five minute video titled [[ASIN:B0052Y0FPE Baker, Chet - Candy]]. I own both: this CD has been ripped to my phone so I can play it anywhere, and the video for when I want to enjoy Chet on an entirely different level.

Unfortunately there are no sound samples on this page. The only vocal is on the first track, Candy, followed by some excellent instrumental performances. Chet is ably backed by Michel Graillier on piano and Jean-Louis Rassinfosse on bass. The overall mood is informal, but the musicianship is not compromised in any way. Each musician pours his heart and soul into each selection.

I love the laid back feeling that the music imparts, and if you are fortunate enough to watch the video the visual will show why. Baker and his trio are relaxed and enjoying what they are doing.

The music is late life Chet, and his playing is both pensive and full of vitality. I am sure the setting helped (this was recorded in the Sonet Record library in Lindingo, Sweden on June 30th, 1985.) If you are a fan of Chet's mainly instrumental work you will love this. If you are a die hard fan you may want to consider getting this album and the video.

title: One of my 'essential' Baker albums
text:
Since there are sound samples on this page I'll spare you a barrage of hyperbole and gushing. I too often come off as pretentious when describing music and the sound samples convey more than I can possibly put into words.

I will give you a few reasons why I love this album, which will make sense as you cycle through the samples. Foremost is the rich tone from Baker's trumpet, augmented by Pepper Adams' baritone sax that perfectly harmonizes with the lower registers in which Baker is playing on this album. Baker always sounded best when paired with a baritone sax, and possibly his earlier stint with Gerry Mulligan influenced him enough to create a sound that complemented (and was complemented by) that instrument. Regardless, he and Adams here are pure magic to my ears.

I also love Herbie Mann on flute and tenor sax, and Zoot Sims on alto and tenor sax, which round out the front line. While the melody flows from Baker on each track, the harmony from Adams, Mann and Sims adds a lot of texture to the music. What makes it all work, in my opinion, is the contrast between the baritone sax and the higher register instruments, and especially Mann's flute and Sims' alto sax.

Half of the album features Bob Corwin on piano leading the rhythm section and half features Bill Evans, backed by Earl May on bass and Cliff Jarvis on drums. I am ashamed to admit that I know little of Jarvis' work, but he is excellent on this album.

The tracks featuring Evans on piano are I Could Have Danced All Night, Thank Heaven For Little Girls, I Talk To The Trees and Show Me . These were recorded for Riverside at the Reeves Sound Studios on July 21, 1959. The remaining tracks feature Corwin on piano and were recorded at the same studio the next day.

I promised not to gush and broke that. Forgive my enthusiasm - I am old and sometimes cannot help myself. If you are a Chet Baker fan, though, I am reasonably sure you will agree with me.

title: Evidence of Baker's powers late in his career
text:
Although this is not an album that I would consider to be essential, it is a great listen and is unmistakable evidence that Baker still had considerable powers as a musician late in his career.

Some folks - even fans - are a little put off by his singing. I am not and his vocal performances on this album are a source of delight for me. If you do not like Baker's vocals, you are not going to change your mind with this album, but if you do, you may find some of the tracks here to be gems. I agree with John W. Levin's June 8, 2013 review that Baker's rendition of For All We Know is powerfully moving.

Instead of buying into my personal tastes let the sound samples on this page convince you one way or the other. I am betting, though, that if you are a Chet Baker fan you will find the sound samples compelling enough to grab this album. See below for two other albums that were recorded during this session.

One thing I truly love about this album is the simple backing by Harold Danko on piano, Jon Burr on bass and Ben Riley on drums. This superb rhythm section provides a sensitive backing and rhythmic foundation for Baker's trumpet and voice.

This album was recorded in Holland over the course of three sessions from December 17 through 19, 1986 and is one of three albums from the sessions. The other two are [[ASIN:B000026GVI As Time Goes By]], also by the Timeless label and worth checking out, and an out-of-print album for Polydor titled Singin' In The Midnight.

title: Five complete albums plus bonuses
text:
This compilation contains five complete albums led by either Red Garland (three of the albums) or John Coltrane. All were recorded in 1957 and 58 for Prestige at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio.

This is both my personal favorite era and label for jazz, but it may not necessarily be yours. I will say that regardless of your favorite era, if you love circa 1950s jazz you will probably love this album.

Three of the albums are from a single 1957 mega-session, while the rest are from individual sessions. Here is what is on the album:

From the November 15, 1957 session led by Red Garland and his quintet that is comprised of Donald Byrd on trumpet, John Coltrane on tenor sax, Garland on piano, Jamil Nasser on bass (known as George Joyner when these tracks were recorded) and Art Taylor on drums:
[[ASIN:B00D1ZG6CM All Mornin' Long]] is Disc One, tracks 1 and 2, and Disc Two, track 2. These three tracks clock in at a total time of 37:20.

[[ASIN:B000SQJ2NW Soul Junction]] is Disc One, tracks 3, 4, 6 and 8, and Disc Two track 1. These five tracks closk in at 42:21.

[[ASIN:B000000YJF High Pressure]] is Disc One, tracks 5 and 7, and Disc Two, tracks 4, 5 and 6. These five tracks clock in at 43:58.

From the 1958 sessions, all credited to the John Coltrane Quintet:
January 10, 1958: [[ASIN:B000000Z1X Believer]] is Disc Three, tracks 2 through 5 and Disc 4, track 1. Personnel on this album are: Coltrane on tenor sax, Donald Byrd on trumpet, Red Garland on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Louis Hayes on drums.

May 23, 1958: [[ASIN:B001GUNIQQ Black Pearls]] is Disc Three, Track 6 and Disc Four, tracks 2 and 3. This features Coltrane on tenor sax, Donald Byrd on trumpet, Red Garland on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Art Taylor on drums.

Bonus Tracks are from a John Coltrane Quintet session for Prestige on December 26, 1958. These tracks are scattered among a number of albums and all feature Trane on tenor sax accompanied by Freddie Hubbard on trumpet, and backed by Red Garland on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Art Taylor on drums.

title: Not an essential album, but still worth checking out
text:
The music in this album reminds me a lot of Chet in the late 1950s. The music literally flows from his trumpet. His vocals on this album are among his best in my opinion. His phrasing is superb, both on his trumpet and his vocals. I am sure that this was an ad hoc session, but he is backed by an ensemble that is perfect for the song selection. In fact, it's the piano trio backing that gives this album an intimate sound and feeling.

Listen to the sound samples on this page. It's easy to get lost in the sheer beauty of the album, and the samples are only a tantalizing taste of what is contained within. Some folks lament that Baker's powers had declined in his later years, but this 1986 album refutes that notion. Of course I am a staunch fan and am somewhat biased, so let the samples guide you.

This was recorded in Holland over the course of three sessions from December 17 through 19, 1986. Baker is backed by Harold Danko on piano, Jon Burr on bass and Ben Riley on drums. This is one of three albums from the sessions. The other two are [[ASIN:B000026GW8 Cool Cat]], also by the Timeless label and worth checking out, and an out-of-print album for Polydor titled Singin' In The Midnight.

While this is not an essential album by any stretch, it is a relaxing listen and evidence that Chet still 'had it' late in his career.

title: Beautiful music beautifully played
text:
Reviewer Afuro nailed it in the August 18, 2013 review when he stated that this is essential for fans. I own a lot of Baker's albums and this is one I play for friends who want to hear him at his best.

Sadly there is no track list on this page at the time of this review. I will put one in a comment below. Also, there are no sound samples, but you can listen to snippets from each track here: [[ASIN:B000UBOUA0 Plays The Best Of Lerner & Loewe]]. As you cycle through the samples on that page you will be treated to a richness of tone from Baker's trumpet, augmented by Pepper Adams' baritone sax that perfectly harmonizes with the lower registers in which Baker is playing on this album. Baker always sounded best when paired with a baritone sax, and possibly his earlier stint with Gerry Mulligan influenced him enough to create a sound that complemented (and was complemented by) that instrument. Regardless, he and Adams here are pure magic to my ears.

Herbie Mann on flute and tenor sax, and Zoot Sims on alto and tenor sax round out the front line. While the melody flows from Baker on each track, the harmony from Adams, Mann and Sims adds a lot of texture to the music. I also love the contrast between the baritone sax and the higher register instruments, and especially Mann's flute and Sims' alto sax.

Lest I forget, the rhythm section is another reason why I love this album. Half of the album features Bob Corwin on piano leading the rhythm section and half features Bill Evans, backed by Earl May on bass and Cliff Jarvis on drums. I am ashamed to admit that I know little of Jarvis' work, but he is excellent on this album.

The tracks featuring Evans on piano are I Could Have Danced All Night, Thank Heaven For Little Girls, I Talk To The Trees and Show Me . These were recorded for Riverside at the Reeves Sound Studios on July 21, 1959. The remaining tracks feature Corwin on piano and were recorded at the same studio the next day.

title: Norvo in transition
text:
This album is all of the tracks that the Norvo/Farlow/Mingus incarnation of Norvo's trio recorded for Savoy in 1950. For Mingus and to a degree Farlow this period in their careers was one in which they were perfecting their sound. For Norvo this is another milestone in his evolution as a relevant musician, which would continue for decades.

The sound samples on this page are the best gauge of the music this album contains. In addition to glimpses into a young Charles Mingus' already incredible touch on bass, this provides insights into both Norvo and Farlow.

Norvo is characteristically quiet. Still, he is energetic and swinging which are also hallmarks of his playing. Farlow's approach to music here is laid back, with flowing notes punctuated by pure fire. This is a nice counter to Norvo's playing.

What should strike most listeners, though, is the synergy among the three during the sessions that produced this album. Each brings key strengths and fills in gaps left by by the other two.

Nine of the tracks in this collection found their way into an album titled [[ASIN:B00A2BK1NS MOVE!]] Surprisingly, only three of the tracks in this collection were recorded in Los Angeles. They are Cheek To Cheek, Night And Day and Time And Tide, which were recorded on May 3, 1950. All of the other tracks were recorded in Chicago on October 13 the same year.

title: East meets west
text:
Note: At the time of this review, this CD is cross-linked with one of the two albums contained in this set. This review is for the album titled [[ASIN:B00004WJZR Nobody Else But Me / Blue & Sentimental]].

The two albums in this set are Betty Bennett's [[ASIN:B0058ZENIW Nobody Else But Me]] and Lurlean Hunter's [[ASIN:B00260USPE Blue & Sentimental]], both of which were recorded for and released by Atlantic Records.

While there are no sound samples on this page the product pages for the two source albums linked above contain them. Those will give you an idea about the music as well as the incredibly great vocals by both of the artists. Frankly I knew very little about Bennett until getting this album solely for Hunter's tracks. It exposed me to a new (to me) vocalist and has inspired me to track down more of her work. Moreover, the music is as different as the two coasts on which the respective albums were recorded. The first twelve tracks were recorded in Los Angeles in 1955 and feature a very different approach to jazz than the remaining tracks that were performed by New York-based musicians five years later. The contrast is another reason why I love this album.

Here are the details of each of the two albums:

Nobody Else But Me was recorded at the Capitol Studios in Los Angeles on October 6 and 7, 1955. Betty Bennett's vocals are backed by Shorty Rogers on trumpet and flugelhorn, Frank Rosolino on trombone, Harry Klee on alto sax, Bob Cooper on tenor sax and Jimmy Giuffre on baritone sax. Andre Previn on piano led the rhythm section backed by Barney Kessel on guitar, Ralph Pena on bass and Shelly Manne on drums (Irv Cottler has the drums on some of the tracks.)

Blue And Sentimental was recorded at Atlantic's NYC studio on August 12 and 23, 1960. Lurlean Hunter's vocals are backed by Harry Edison on trumpet, Rudy Rutherford on clarinet and Bud Freeman on tenor sax. Jimmy Jones on piano led the rhythm section backed by Jim Hall on guitar George Duvivier on bass and Don Lamond on drums. Trigger Alpert is the bassist on some of the tracks.

Two schools of jazz are represented - West Coast cool for Bennett and East Coast with a definite old school swing vibe for Hunter. Yet, as different as they are, there is a nice, seamless feel to the tracks in this set. If you love female jazz vocalists this is a great two-album set to add to your library.

title: Previn and some West Coast giants collaborate
text:
This is a collection of tracks from one complete album and part of another that are a collaboration between Andre Previn and Shorty Rogers.

Sadly there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review. This is typical West Coast jazz that has Rogers' sound woven throughout every track. If you are familiar with Rogers (or most of the musicians who would show up at the Lighthouse or other venues) then you have a sense of the music. Previn's piano adds a lot to the already large ensemble, and on the last seven tracks we are treated to vocals by Previn's wife, Betty Bennett. For those I have linked to the source album that does contain sound samples.

At the time of this review there is no track list on this page. To save space I will provide that in a comment to this review. The sound quality of this album is superb and typical of the great job Fresh Sound Records has done of the growing number or reissues that I own from that label.

The complete album is comprised of tracks 1 through 13. It is the now out-of-print LP titled Collaboration that was recorded for RCA in Los Angeles over the course of three 1954 sessions. The March 30, 1954 session has a front line comprised of Shorty Rogers on trumpet, Milt Bernhart on trombone, Bud Shank on alto sax and flute, Bob Cooper on tenor sax and Jimmy Giuffre on baritone sax. Previn's piano leads the rhythm sectoon with Al Hendrickson on guitar, Joe Mondragon on bass and Shelly Manne on drums. The same personnel are on the June 14, 1954 except Curtis Conce is on bass. The final session on September 14, 1954 has Mondragon back on bass, but with Jack Marshall taking over from Hendrickson on guitar.

Tracks 14 through 20 are from the album titled [[ASIN:B0058ZENIW Nobody Else But Me]] that was recorded for Atlantic at the Capitol Studios in Los Angeles on October 6 and 7, 1955. Tracks 14, 17, 18 and 20 were recorded during the October 6 session with Betty Bennett's vocals backed by Shorty Rogers on trumpet and flugelhorn, Frank Rosolino on trombone, Harry Klee on alto sax, Bob Cooper on tenor sax and Jimmy Giuffre on baritone sax. Andre Previn on piano led the rhythm section backed by Barney Kessel on guitar, Ralph Pena on bass and Shelly Manne on drums.

The remaining three tracks (15, 16 and 19) were recorded at the same studio with the same line up except Irv Cottler replaces Shelly Manne on drums.

title: Perfect timing ... and a great listen!
text:
This is one of my favorite Previn jazz albums for a few reasons. Foremost, I love piano trio formats. Previn had the ability to cross boundaries from classical to pop to jazz. He was always at his best in whichever genre he happened to be performing when accompanied or backed by top musicians from that area. With Red Mitchell on bass and Shelly Manne on drums, Previn is backed by two musicians who add just the right amount of swing and excellent taste.

Second, I am a fan of just about everything composed or scored by Rogers and Hart, and one song on this album - Bewitched - is one of my all time favorites.

The sound samples on this page will convey the music itself and even the short snippets will cue you about Previn's interpretation.

What amazes me is Previn was in the studio recording this album only two days after the movie from which this album is the soundtrack was released. True, the music was written back in 1940 for the play, but timing for the movie's remake and release is - to me - extraordinary. The movie made its debut on October 25, 1957 and Previn, Mitchell and Manne walked into Contemporary Records' Los Angeles studio on October 28 and knocked this album out in two days.

If you love West Coast jazz and especially in piano trio format this is a nice listen. The sound samples attest to that. If you also love Rogers and Hart tunes, then you have an even more compelling reason to purchase this.

title: The [West Coast] jazz side of Previn
text:
This set is a West Coast jazz fan's dream come true. Most of the tracks are from in-print albums featuring Previn in a trio format, with one out-of-print album that features him leading the rhythm section of a much larger ensemble.

All of the albums, though, are beautifully reproduced here with decent sound quality. To be sure, these are not audiophile recordings, but neither are they needle-drop transfers from worn LPs. All pre-date stereo, so if you are new to recordings from this era you may think there is something wrong with the sound.

Like most of these value-priced sets this one is short on documentation, and is even missing the track list from this product page (at the time of this review.) I will fill in the gaps below, and on three of the albums I have linked to the source album pages that have sound samples. This is a perfect starter set for Previn's jazz work, as well as a wonderful intro to West Coast jazz. Here is what you get:
========
DISC ONE
========
Tracks 1 through 8 are the album titled [[ASIN:B007Z52C6I West Side Story]] that was recorded in Los Angeles for the Contemporary label on August 24 and 25, 1959. Previn is backed by Red Mitchell on bass and Shelly Manne on drums. The track titles are:

The March 30, 1954 session has a front line comprised of Shorty Rogers on trumpet, Milt Bernhart on trombone, Bud Shank on alto sax and flute, Bob Cooper on tenor sax and Jimmy Giuffre on baritone sax. Previn's piano leads the rhythm sectoon with Al Hendrickson on guitar, Joe Mondragon on bass and Shelly Manne on drums. The same personnel are on the June 14, 1954 except Curtis Conce is on bass. title: An historical artifact with one of the best renditions of Stardust
text:
I have to agree with Dennis C's July 1, 2006 statement that the rendition of Stardust on this album is one of the best ever. Indeed, it's that track from a Youtube video that drew me to this album in the first place. Helen Humes is featured on that and the second track and her vocals add to the listening pleasure.

My real reason for falling in love with this album is Don Byas' tenor sax. The tone is lush and gorgeous, and his trademark blend of blues and swing. Here he is part of a core group who are creating something new - bebop - and that is the value of this album.

The sound samples on this page will reveal marginal sound quality, but energetic music. The sound quality is because this was recorded by an amateur - a college student named Jerry Newman - who lugged a portable disc recorder into Minton's and captured what were jam sessions. One problem is the trumpets and saxophones, and Humes' vocals are pretty clear, but the rhythm sections are way down in the mix. One fortunate happenstance if Monk's playing on track 2 is clear, including his solo.

While most sources lump all of the tracks on this album into a collection of sessions in 1941 with Byas accompanied by Joe Guy in trumpet and backed by Thelonious Monk on piano and Kenny Clarke on drums, only four of the tracks include that line-up (1 and 2, and 5 and 6). And even then all of the musicians present on those tracks are not known. Monk is the only musician who is identified on five of the six tracks and is probably on all of them. Here is who is known to be on each track:

Tracks 1, 2, 5 and 6 have Joe Guy on trumpet accompanied by Don Byas on tenor sax. Monk is on piano with Kenny Clarke on drums. Humes, as mentioned, is the vocalist on tracks 1 and 2, but unidentified are the second trumpet on track 1 and the second tenor sax on track 2. The bassist on all four of these tracks is unknown.

Track 3 is the mystery - it shows up on no discographies (and I have searched exhaustively to no avail.)

Track 4 is actually Roy Eldridge on trumpet and Herbie Fields on tenor sax backed by Monk on piano. The bassist and drummer on this track are unknown.

title: Norvo, Farlow and Mingus for the Savoy label
text:
This is more than the title album - it's a complete collection of the songs the trio recorded for Savoy in 1950. Although there is no track list or sound samples on this page at the time of this review, you can listen to the samples on this page: [[ASIN:B000001CUA Red Norvo Trio with Tal Farlow and Charles Mingus: The Savoy Sessions]]. The tracks are listed below (they are in a different order on the linked page.

Most folks gyrate to this album because it has early Mingus, but the music is much more than that. Norvo had a quiet, but energetic and swinging, style, and his playing is truly spectacular on these tracks. Farlow, too, had a laid back approach to music on his guitar and the synergy among the three during the sessions that produced this album is spectacular to my ears. Do not take my word - go to the linked page and run through the sound samples.

Here are the tracks that are included in this album:

02 Night and day 4:07
03 September Song 3:32
04 Time and tide 2:32
05 Move 2:36
06 I've Got You Under My Skin 2:22
07 I Get a Kick Out of You 2:25
08 I'll Remember April 3:25
09 I Can't Believe That You're in Love With Me 2:52
10 Little White Lies
11 Zing! Went the Strings of My Heart 3:26
12 Have You Met Miss Jones
13 If I Had You 4:06
14 Godchild 4:47
15 I'm Yours 4:02
16 Mood indigo 3:29
17 Swedish Pastry 2:25

Tracks 1, 3, 5 through 9, 11, 13, 14, and 16 and 17 are from the original album titled [[ASIN:B00A2BK1NS MOVE! Red Norvo Trio LP]].
