Cheek To Cheek, Night And Day and Time And Tide were recorded in Los Angeles on May 3, 1950 and the other tracks were recorded in Chicago on October 13 the same year.

This is definitely a gem for fans or Norvo, Farlow or Mingus, and clocks in at an enjoyable 63:41.

title: Complete for the Norvo/Farlow/Mitchell edition of the trio
text:
Since there is no track listing on this page (at the time of this review) here is what is on the album. Please refer to the list as I discuss background information.
01. Who Cares?
02. Let's Fall In Love
03. Old Devil Moon
04. Cabin In The Sky
05. How Am I To Know?
06. That Old Black Magic
07. What Is This Thing Called Love?
08. I Brung You Finjans For Your Zarf
09. My Funny Valentine
10. Lullaby Of Birdland
11. Farewell To Alms
12. Tea For Two
13. Lullaby Of The Leaves
14. Sweet Georgia Brown
15. Tenderly
16. I Remember You
17. Skylark

If you are a fan or jazz lover this is laid back, but tight. It's almost as though the trio is communicating by telepathy. They are obviously having fun, but are also serious about their music. I have always been a Norvo fan because of his light touch, and little or no vibrato on his vibraphone. Farlow's flowing guitar fits into the middle with Mitchell's bass keeping the pulse going.

This is a not all of Norvo's trio recordings, but is focused on his work with Tal Farlow on guitar and Red Mitchell on bass. As such this is a collection of the complete recordings of that group, including previously unissued tracks.

The first ten tracks are from the album titled [[ASIN:B0049YZDZU Red Norvo With Strings]] that was recorded for the Fantasy label in Los Angeles on October 6 and 7, 1955. You can listen to sound samples for those tracks by following the link I provided. Tracks 11 through 14 are from the same session, but were not released. By the way, the only strings featured on that album are the six on Farlow's guitar and the four on Mitchell's bass.

Tracks 15 through 17 were recorded for Decca for the out-of-print album titled Dancing on the Ceiling. These were recorded in Los Angeles on July 1 and October 16, 1952. The reason the full album is not included is Tal Farlow is only on those tracks, and was replaced by guitarist Jim Raney on the remainder of that album.

While this is not the end all/be all of Norvo's trio recordings, it is an excellent cache of music from one of his tightest trios.

title: Short and beautiful
text:
Note: I am reviewing the CD version of [[ASIN:B000046PW2 Songs From the Heart]], which contains six additional bonus tracks that the MP3 version lacks. Since reviews for both products are cross linked (at the time of this review) I wanted to clarify that to save confusion and disappointment.

This is Hartman's first album as a leader and it's a puzzle why he did not receive wider acclaim. If you listen to the sound samples on the MP3 version's page at [[ASIN:B00HFN2BGG Songs From The Heart]] you will hear not only his rich voice, but soulful ability to convey the meanings of each song. That's a rare gift and the sound samples clearly show he had it.

Not all tracks fit a coherent romantic theme (Ain't Misbehavin' is an example of one that does not), but all come across as romantic. Perhaps it's the sensual quality of Hartman's voice. For me Howard McGhee's trumpet added the perfect backing for Hartman's voice, and the rhythm section comprised of Ralph Sharon on piano, Jay Cave on bass and Christy Febbo on drums support Hartman (and McGhee) with sensitivity.

This album was recorded for Bethlehem at the Beltone Studios in NYC during October 1955. The original release in 1956 contained twelve tracks, so this CD version is definitely a gem for fans and collectors who want to hear the complete sessions, including the previously unissued alternate takes.

title: One of a handful of albums I use for romantic moods
text:
When it comes to mood setting I go with one of two choices: something by Chet Baker or something by Johnny Hartman. To be honest, this is the album that gets the most play because there is something about Hartman's voice and ability to deliver lyrics that is compelling. As for the mood setting, all I can say is that this album has proven to be surprisingly effective in that department.

As a hopeless romantic every track is perfect. As a musician I am equally enchanted with the music, but also impressed with the sensitivity each member of Hartman's backing ensemble displayed. The core group - Hank Jones on piano, Milt Hinton on bass and Hank's brother Elvin on drums - provided the right tone and feel for each song. Jim Hall and Kenny Burrell swapping on guitar added to the magic because both had styles that were well suited to ballads. The surprise (to me) was how Illinois Jaquet handled this material on tenor sax. He is known for far more energetic playing, but handled the songs he backed with the same sensitivity and lyricism that Lester Young gave Billie Holiday.

I could blather on about each track, but I would be indulging in a boring exercise. Listen to the sound samples to truly get a feel for the music on this album. At the time of this review there are no samples on the CD version's page, but you can listen to them here: [[ASIN:B000W197AG I Just Dropped By To Say Hello]].

This album was recorded for Impulse five months after Hartman's collaboration with John Coltrane for the same label. This one was recorded at Rudy van Gender's Englewood Cliffs, NJ studio on October 9 and 17, 1963. It's a tad under thirty-three minutes, but what a wonderful listen!

title: Almost two complete albums
text:
This album clocks in at 76:28 and is a delight, if for no other reason than to compare and contrast some giants of tenor sax from the period. Since this page is missing a track listing and sound samples at the time of this review here is what is on this expanded album:
01. Tenor Conclave 11:06
02. Just You, Just Me 9:30
03. Bob's Boys 8:22
04. How Deep Is The Ocean? 15:06
05. Cattin' 7:23
06. Sunday 6:59
07. Anatomy 8:52
08. Vodka 9:06

Tracks 1 through 4 are the original album, and you can listen to sound samples on this page: [[ASIN:B000UBQOGS Tenor Conclave]]. That album is essentially a Prestige blowing session with Trane, Mobley, Sims and Cohn backed by Red Garland's trio comprised of Garland on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Art Taylor on drums. This album was recorded at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on September 7, 1956.

The remaining tracks are from the album titled [[ASIN:B000UBLVY8 Cattin' With Coltrane And Quinichette]] that was recorded for Prestige at the same studio on May 17, 1957. You can listen to sound samples on that page. This is not the complete album, only the tracks that feature Trane are included here (Exactly Like You and Tea For Two are the missing titles). The session features Trane with Paul Quinichette on tenor sax, and backed by an interesting rhythm section comprised of Mal Waldron on piano, Julian Euell on bass and Ed Thigpen on drums.

title: A personal favorite
text:
This album is difficult to find (it goes in and out of print) and the only other album that contains it is a set that is missing a track. I love the sound quality of this CD and fully agree with the September 24, 2013 review's comments regarding that factor.

Ray Bryant is one of my favorite pianists and this album gets a lot of play time in my car and house. While I love Bryant in larger ensembles, especially his collaborations with Coleman Hawkins, he truly shines in trio settings or solo. This album has both. All of the tracks, except 7, feature him driving a trio, with track 7 featuring him solo. If you are a fan you will appreciate this album because so much of Bryant's recorded word from this period was as a sideman.

There are no sound samples nor a track listing on this page at the time of this review. You can hear samples of each track on this page: [[ASIN:B008JESUG0 Con Alma & Little Susie]] (unfortunately that album is missing track 7), and the tracks are:
01. Con Alma ...6:55
02. Milestones ...4:10
03. 'Round Midnight ...3:51
04. Django ...5:38
05. Nuts And Bolts ...3:05
06. Cubano Chant ...4:22
07. Ill Wind ...3:12
08. Autumn Leaves ...5:22
09. C Jam Blues ...4:22

One final note: track 4 was not issued on the original album. Apparently Columbia deemed it unsuitable, but it is included here and is a gem in and of itself. This album was recorded at Columbia's 30th Street Studio in NYC in two sessions. The first, which produced Milestones and Django, was on November 25, 1960 and features Bryant backed by Arthur Harper on bass and Mickey Roker on drums. The second session was recorded on January 26, 1961, with Bill Lee replacing Harper on bass.

title: Five albums ... plus!
text:
I purchased this mainly for the Ray Bryant collaborations and was treated to a much wider range of familiar and quasi-familiar musicians. This set is comprised of five albums that feature both Byrant and Coleman Hawkins circa 1958-59, and includes two bonus tracks that are icing in the cake.

Although there are no sound samples or track listing on the CD's product page (the format that I am reviewing) you can listen to the sound samples and see the track list at [[ASIN:B00FPEBBE0 Complete Recordings]]. This album set clocks in at 3:51:33, which is divided across the three discs as 78:57 (Disc One), 76:31 (Disc Two) and 76:18 (Disc Three). That's a lot of great music for the money, and they sound samples convey that fact more effectively than anything I can put in words.

Here is what the set contains:
========
DISC ONE
========
Tracks 1 through 7 are the album titled [[ASIN:B000UBK08Q Soul]] that was recorded for Prestige at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on November 7, 1958. The session was recorded as the Coleman Hawkins Quintet with Hawkins on tenor sax, backed by Bryant on piano, Kenny Burrell on guitar, Wendell Marshall on bass and Ossie Johnson on drums,

Tracks 8 through 11 are the album titled [[ASIN:B000000Z0A Blues Groove]] that was recorded for Prestige at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on February 28, 1958. The session was credited to the Tiny Grimes and Coleman Hawkins Sextet, with Coleman Hawkins on tenor sax and Musa Kaleem on flute, backed by Bryant on piano, Tiny Grimes on guitar, Earl Wormack on bass and Teagle Fleming Jr. on drums.
========
DISC TWO
========
Tracks 1 through 3 are a continuation of Blues Groove from Disc One.

Tracks three through 8 are the album titled [[ASIN:B000000YGD Hawk Eyes]] that was recorded for Prestige at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on April 3, 1959. The session is credited to the Coleman Hawkins Sextet with Hawkins on tenor sax and Charlie Shavers on trumpet forming the front line, backed by Bryant on piano, Tiny Grimes on guitar, George Duvivier on bass and Ossie Johnson on drums.

Track 9 through 11 are the album titled [[ASIN:B0089F9W2U Stasch]] that was recorded for the Swingville and Prestige labels at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on February 5, 1959. This session is credited to the The Prestige Blues-Swingers with a large front line comprised of Hawkins on tenor sax, Idrees Sulieman on trumpet, Jerome Richardson on alto sax and flute, and Pepper Adams on baritone sax. The rhythm section is Bryant on piano, Wendell Marshall on bass and Walter Bolden on drums.
========
DISC THREE
========
Tracks 1 through 3 are a continuation of Stasch from Disc Two.

Tracks 4 through 9 are the album titled [[ASIN:B000SQJ2IC At Newport Live]] that was recorded live for Verve on July 5, 1957 at the Newport Jazz Festival. This line-up has a front line comprised of Hawkins on tenor sax, Roy Eldridge on trumpet (and drums on Sweet Georgia Brown) and Pete Brown on alto sax. Bryant leads the rhythm section on piano, with Al McKibbon on bass and Papa Jo Jones on drums.

The last two tracks are bonus tracks that were recorded live at the 1959 Newport Jazz Festival on July 3 and feature Hawkins on tenor accompanied by Roy Eldridge on trumpet and backed by Bryant on piano, brother Tony on bass and Oliver Jackson on drums.

title: I keep coming back to this album
text:
Disclaimer: I am a mid-1950s Prestige junkie so this album has a lot of appeal to me personally. To be totally objective this is not an essential album by any stretch, but for folks like myself who believe that this and other Prestige albums are from a golden age the music is compelling.

Run through the sound samples on this page. That is the best way to determine whether I am some crazy or there is merit to my fondness for this album. As you cycle through the sound samples you will probably notice that track 2 is not the full sextet, but a trio with Tommy Flanagan on piano, Doug Watkins on bass and Louis Hayes on drums. All of the remaining tracks feature that core trio with John Coltrane on tenor sax and Idrees Sulieman on trumpet forming a front line, and Kenny Burrell on guitar adding a new dimension to the rhythm section. This is classic music from Prestige during the era.

This is one of the The Prestige All Stars sessions with no real featured artist. It is more of a promo type recording that labels back in that era recorded. It was recorded for Prestige at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on April 18, 1957. It was released two years later on both the Original Jazz Classic and Prestige labels. This may not be on the short list of many jazz fans as a desert island album, but it's nonetheless a great listen.

title: Excellent collaborations and some rare bonus tracks
text:
If you are in the CD version of this album's product page there are no sound samples nor track lists at the time of this review. You can get both on this page: [[ASIN:B002VJYUX6 All Star Groups - Three Classic Albums Plus (Meets Monk / Meets Stan Getz / The Gerry Mulligan-Paul Desmond Quartet)]].

The sound samples convey the sound quality and the essence of the music on this two-disc set. My set had no flaws in the physical media (and if you are purchasing the MP3 version this is not an issue), and the music quality was acceptable. By that I mean an audiophile will be better off purchasing vinyl copies of the albums, but for casual listening this set is not terrible.

There is little in the way of documentation, so I tracked down the basics of each source album. Note that the three albums in this set are as originally released. Some of the source albums to which I have linked below are reissues with bonus tracks that were not released on the original albums. Also note that on the jewel case cover art there is mention of Bob Brookmeyer - he does not appear on any of the tracks in this set.

Here is what you get:
========
DISC ONE
========
Tracks 1 through 6 are the album titled [[ASIN:B00ABQGUWA Mulligan Meets Monk]] that was recorded for Riverside at the Reeves Sound Studios in NYC on August 12 and 13, 1957. Mulligan is in the front line with Thelonious Monk on piano, Wilbur Ware on bass and Shadow Wilson on drums forming a solid rhythm section behind him.

Tracks 7 through 12 are the album titled [[ASIN:B00492GEIW Gerry Mulligan Meets Stan Getz]] that was recorded for Verve in Los Angeles on October 12, 1957. Mulligan and Getz (both swapping on tenor and baritone sax) are the front line backed by Lou Levy on piano, Ray Brown on bass and Stan Levey on drums.
========
DISC TWO
========
Tracks 1 through 7 are the album titled [[ASIN:B002BORI30 Blues In Time]] that was recorded for Verve during two sessions on August 2, 1957 at the Capitol Tower Studios in Los Angeles and on August 27, 1957 at the Fine Sound Studio in NYC. Mulligan's baritone sax and Desmond's alto sax are backed by Joe Benjamin on bass and Dave Bailey on drums.

Tracks 8 through 10 are from a longer album titled [[ASIN:B00F3LOL24 The Teddy Wilson Trio & Gerry Mulligan Quartet With Bob Brookmeyer At Newport]] from the 1957 Newport Jazz Festival. With Mulligan on baritone sitting in with Teddy Wilson on piano, Milt Hinton on bass and Specs Powell on drums.

Track 11, Don't Get Around Much Anymore, is from the album titled 'Gerry Mulligan with the Marian McPartland Trio' that was recorded at the 1958 Newport Jazz Festival on July 3. Mulligan is sitting in with Marian McPartland on piano, Milt Hinton on bass and Ed Shaughnessy on drums. sound sample: B002VK50B6

Track 12, Prima Bara Dubla, is from the album titled 'Newport 1958: Duke Ellington and his Orchestra featuring Gerry Mulligan.' Hearing Mulligan together with the 'father of baritone sax' - Harry Carney - makes this track a true gem in this set.

I am adding the complete track list for both discs in this set as a comment to assist folks who are on the CD version's product page. See below.

title: Early Ellis and West Coast jazz - essential for guitarists
text:
While these albums are not in chronological order on the two discs that comprise this set, they are well mastered and have very good to excellent sound. Of course they are not audiophile quality, so take that into account.

Since there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review I have linked to the source albums, most of which have sound samples on their respective product pages. Also, because the set is a little light on documentation I am providing discography information. Do note that these albums are as originally released. Reissues subsequent releases often contain alternate takes and bonus tracks that are not included in this set.

Here is what the set contains:
========
DISC ONE
========
Source of the first eight tracks is the album titled [[ASIN:B0000046TM Nothing But The Blues]] that was recorded in Los Angeles for Verve on October 11, 1957. Ellis is accompanied by Stan Getz on tenor sax, Roy Eldridge on trumpet, Ray Brown on bass and Stan Levey on drums.

The remaining seven tracks are the album titled [[ASIN:B00000K1HX Herb Ellis Meets Jimmy Giuffre]] that was recorded for Verve in Los Angeles on March 26, 1959. Ellis is accompanied by Jimmy Giuffre and Richie Kamuca on tenor sax (with Giuffre also on baritone sax), Bud Shank on alto sax, Lou Levy on piano, Jim Hall also on guitar, Joe Mondragon on bass and Stan Levey on drums.
========
DISC TWO
========
The first track is continued from Herb Ellis Meets Jimmy Giuffre from Disc One.

[[ASIN:B000CIXCD2 Ellis in Wonderland]] is the source of the next eight tracks that were recorded for Norgran in Los Angeles on December 28, 1955. This was Ellis' debut album and included Harry Edison on trumpet, Jimmy Giuffre on clarinet, tenor and baritone sax, and a rhythm section comprised of Oscar Peterson on piano, Ray Brown on bass and Alvin Stoller on drums.

[[ASIN:B000VZO5PK Thank You, Charlie Christian]] comprises the remaining tracks that were recorded for Verve in Los Angeles on June 1 and 2, 1960. Ellis is accompanied by Frank Strazzeri on piano, Harry Babasin on cello, Chuck Berghofer on bass and Kenny Hume on drums.

title: Great guitar and great West Coast jazz
text:
This is a wonderful find for guitarists who wish to study Kessel's style as well as jazz fans who love jazz from the early-to-mid 1950s and especially West Coast Jazz. In fact you can practically chronicle the nascent West Coast scene from the four albums contained in this set.

Sound quality is surprisingly good considering the crude recording equipment and techniques in the early 1950s. Note that if the sound separation sounds funny to you there was no such thing as stereo when these albums were recorded. Regardless, the sound is rich (to my ears) and short of tracking down the vinyl copies of these albums is about as good as you are going to get.

The four albums are provided on two discs. While this package is somewhat short on documentation I have tracked down the discographies so you can enjoy not only the music, but know who performed. I have also linked to the source albums and two of those have sound samples on their product pages. Here are the albums, all of which were recorded in Los Angeles for the Contemporary label:
========
DISC ONE
========
[[ASIN:B000000Y8V Easy Like]] is the first twelve tracks that was recorded in three sessions: Tenderly, Bernardo, Vicky's Dream and Just Squeeze Me were recorded on November 14, 1953 by Bud Shank on alto sax and flute, Arnold Ross on piano, Kessel on guitar, Harry Babasin on bass and Shelly Manne on drums.

The same ensemble was on the second session on December 19, 1953, which recorded Lullaby Of Birdland, What Is There To Say, Salute To Charlie Christian and I Let A Song Go Out Of My Heart.

For the final session that was recorded on February 23, 1956 the line-up is Buddy Collette on alto sax and flute, Claude Williamson on piano, Kessel on guitar, Red Mitchell on bass and Shelly Manne on drums. The tracks from this session are: Easy Like, That's All, April In Paris and North Of The Border.

[[ASIN:B000000YDE Kessel Plays Standards]] comprises tracks 13 through 24. There are sound samples on that album's product page. This was recorded in three sessions, the first of which was on June 4, 1954 with Bob Cooper on tenor sax and oboe, Claude Williamson on piano, Kessel on guitar, Monty Budwig on bass and Shelly Manne on drums. Tracks from this session are Speak Low, On A Slow Boat To China, Prelude To A Kiss and A Foggy Day.

On July 1, 1954 the same personnel recorded Love Is Here To Stay, How Long Has This Been Going On, Barney's Blues and 64 Bars On Wilshire.

The final session was over a year later on September 12, 1955 and features Bob Cooper on tenor sax and oboe, Hampton Hawes on piano, Kessel on guitar, Red Mitchell on bass and Chuck Thompson on drums. Tracks from this session are My Old Flame, Jeepers Creepers, You Stepped Out Of A Dream and I Didn't Know What Time It Was.
========
DISC TWO
========
[[ASIN:B00000GBSG To Swing Or Not to Swing]] is made up of the first ten tracks that were recorded in two sessions. The source album has sound samples. On March 28, 1955 Happy Feeling, Wail Street and Contemporary Blues were recorded by Harry Sweets Edison on trumpet, Bill Perkins on tenor sax, Jimmy Rowles on piano, Kessel and Al Hendrickson on guitar, Red Mitchell on bass and Shelly Manne on drums.

The second session was recorded on July 26, 1955 and produced Begin The Blues, Louisiana, Embraceable You, Indiana, Moten Swing, Midnight Sun, Don't Blame Me and 12th Street Rag . This line up also has Harry Sweets Edison on trumpet, with Georgie Auld on tenor sax, Jimmy Rowles on piano, Kessel and Al Hendrickson on guitar, Red Mitchell on bass and Irv Cottler on drums.

[[ASIN:B000000YY0 Music to Listen to]] are the remaining tracks and was recorded in three sessions. The first session on August 6, 1956 recorded Makin' Whoopee, Gone With The Wind, I Love You and Fascinating Rhythm. The line-up for this session was Buddy Collette on flute, alto flute and clarinet, Junie Cobb on oboe and English horn, George W. Smith on clarinet, Justin Gordon on clarinet and bass clarinet and Howard Terry on clarinet, bass clarinet and bassoon. The rhythm section was Andre Previn on piano, Kessel on guitar, Buddy Clark on bass and Shelly Manne on drums.

The second session on October 15, 1956 featured a slightly different ensemble comprised of Ted Nash on flute and clarinet, Junie Cobb on oboe and English horn, George W. Smith on clarinet, Justin Gordon on clarinet and bass clarinet and Howard Terry on clarinet, bass clarinet and bassoon. The rhythm was comprised of Jimmy Rowles on piano, Kessel on guitar, Red Mitchell on bass and Shelly Manne on drums. Tracks from this session: Cheerful Little Earful, My Reverie, Blues For A Playboy and Carioca.

For the third session the line up is the same as above except Claude Williamson is on piano. Tracks are Love Is For The Very Young, Mountain Greenery, Indian Summer and Laura.

title: One of  my favorite collaborations between Trane and Burrell
text:
This album and [[ASIN:B0002IQFUE Cats]] are two outstanding collaborations between John Coltrane and Kenny Burrell. Of the two I would have to toss a coin to pick a favorite. You can let the sound samples on this page help you decide about this album. Compare it to Cats that I mentioned and you will hear a striking similarity in how musically on the same page Trane and Burrell were.

I love this particular album because it allows Coltrane to stretch a bit, and it scales down on 'Why Was I Born?' to a duet between Coltrane and Burrell, which is further evidence of the synergy between the two during this period. Of course, the core rhythm section on the remaining tracks - Tommy Flanagan on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Jimmy cobb on drums - are perfect for both Coltrans and Burrell.

Another thing I love is this is from one of my favorite periods in US jazz. It has that vibe that clearly shows the Prestige imprint on the music. Oc course this album also has the Rudy van Gelder touch since it was recorded in his Hackensack, NJ studio on March 7, 1958.

title: A Prestige classic from their belle epoque
text:
This is what I consider to be jazz from one of the golden eras, in this case Prestige recordings from the mid 1950s. If you are on the CD's product page there are no sound samples at the time of this review, but you can listen to them on this page: [[ASIN:B000UAWHC4 The Cats]].

As you cycle through the sound samples you will probably notice that track 2 is not the full sextet, but a trio with Tommy Flanagan on piano, Doug Watkins on bass and Louis Hayes on drums. All of the remaining tracks feature that core trio with John Coltrane on tenor sax and Idrees Sulieman on trumpet forming a front line, and Kenny Burrell on guitar adding a new dimension to the rhythm section. This is classic music from Prestige during the era.

While this album was recorded for Prestige at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on April 18, 1957. It was released two years later on both the Original Jazz Classic and Prestige labels. However, the ensemble recorded as 'The Prestige All Stars', which indeed the line-up is. This may not be on the short list of many jazz fans as a desert island album, but it's nonetheless a great listen.

title: I consider it to be the definitive interpretation
text:
Bernstein proved his genius when he and Stephen Sondheim scored the musical, but Johnny Richards' arrangement took this to a new level.

I love the instrumentation as much as I do the arrangements. Richards was determined to include mellophones in the arrangement, which is also heavy with trumpets. This worked out beautifully in the performance of the arrangements, and the lower register mellophone fit in beautifully with the other lower register instruments which make up the bulk of the ensemble. In fact, the majority of the instrumentation is bottom end types, including bass and baritone saxophones, trombones and a tuba (to name but a few). Even the percussion section contains tympani.

Listen to the sound samples on this page for a gauge of the music itself. In fact, if you compare this album to the original film sound track, [[ASIN:B0000027WF West Side Story (1961 Film Soundtrack)]], you will immediately notice that Richards left out any woodwind instruments that Bernstein and Sondheim included (although there is a relatively large reed section.)

Another thing I love is this album swings. The original score was ideal for adapting to jazz and swing style music, and Richards' arrangement (and Kenton's conducting and ensemble) pulled it off perfectly. That is the main reason why I claimed that this is the definitive interpretation in the title.

One final note: If you play (or love) trumpet, Conte Candoli's solos shine. Since most of the instrumentation is in lower registers Candoli's solos practically float on top of the music. If you are a musician, composer or arranger there is a goldmine of ideas on this album. If you are a fan who loves great music you will be rewarded.

title: A favorite rendition of a favorite score
text:
I grew up listening to the original soundtrack because my parents purchased it in 1961 as soon as it was released and played it frequently. If you compare the original, [[ASIN:B0000027WF West Side Story (1961 Film Soundtrack)]], to this album you will have a great appreciation for Peterson's arrangement for a trio. More importantly, he manages distill down the original score unto seven songs - for a trio no less - and perform them in a way that I am sure pleased Leonard Bernstein.

The best way to gauge this album (and to hear what I am trying to describe regarding how Peterson and his trio remained true to the score) listen to the sound samples on this page. Note: if you are in the CD version's product page it has no samples at the time of this review, but they can be heard here: [[ASIN:B000W21EQA West Side Story]].

While Peterson handles the melody lines (ably assisted by Ray Brown on bass in places), it's Brown and drummer Ed Thigpen who shoulder a large load tool. The entire West Side Story suite required a strong and complex rhythmic foundation and the way Brown and Thigpen interpreted and provided it in this trio setting is nothing short of remarkable in my opinion. As a drummer I have dissected this album musically many times and remain in awe of it.

Although this clocks in at a scant thirty five minutes it's one of my favorite Oscar Peterson albums. It certainly epitomizes his genius (as well as the musicianship of Peterson, Brown and Thigpen), and to my ears this album stands the test of time. It is as fresh and relevant today as it was over a half century ago when it was first recorded for Verve in NYC during two sessions spanning January 24 and 25, 1962.

title: I would not have hand picked a better quartet!
text:
This album is a personal treasure on many levels. Of course Hawes on piano is the centerpiece, but every other member deserves equal billing in my opinion.

While my preferences are subjective, I believe than any jazz aficionado who runs through the sound samples on this page will be taken by the music. Harold Land on tenor sax is on the mark on every track, and I seriously doubt that Scott LaFaro needs an introduction to most of the prospective buyers on this page. As a drummer having Frank Butler included in the line-up is like putting a cherry on top for me because I have long admired (and studied) his approach to drums. He does not disappoint here.

It was originally recorded for the Contemporary label in Los Angeles on Los March 17, 1958. Although the six tracks come in at a scant 45:42 it's still three quarters of an hour of four musicians giving it their all. Dissect it if you are a musician or just sit back and enjoy if you are a fan who loves jazz. It's all good.

title: Interesting transitional album
text:
This album was recorded for Riverside over the course of three sessions in NYC on October 27, 28 and 30, 1959. The most striking aspect is the change in the way Kelly approached vocals. I have a feeling that she was experimenting and the differences can be heard by listening to the sound samples on this page and comparing it to her earlier work with Pat Moran (listen to the sound samples marked Bev Kelly on [[ASIN:B004SAW5PG Essential Jazz Masters]] for examples, as well as her singing a mere year after this album on a live album titled [[ASIN:B00000I8ZQ In Person]]. There are no sound samples on the latter, but if you search the web you will find complete tracks.

While her approach to vocals is different on this album, you can still her her basic vocal qualities. I would have no problem picking her out in a blind test, and her vocals are well supported by the ensembles that backed her on these sessions. I especially like Jerome Richardson's tenor sax and flute on tracks 1, 6, 7 and 10. However, it's also wonderful to hear Harry Sweets Edison backing her on tracks 1, 2 and 8).

The core musicians who were present on every session were Jimmy Jones on piano, Kenny Burrell on guitar and Milt Hinton on bass. Those three now only formed the nucleus of a powerhouse rhythm section, but added melodic and harmonic dimensions that supported Kelly's vocals in the best possible way. The drummers changed for each session, but they were among the best session drummers in NYC at the time. In particular, Ossie Johnson on tracks 1, 6, 7 and 10 was probably the most sensitive of the drummers on these sessions. That is not to say that Roy Haynes' treatment of 4, 5, 9 and 11 were not excellent because Haynes (who is still playing as of the date of this review) played superbly as did Johnny Cresci on tracks 2, 3 and 8.

If you are a fan of Kelly then you will quickly recognize that she is in a transition regarding her vocals. Personally I love the way she handled every song and view this as an essential album if you want to hear her ability to handle mood music and ballads with the best of them.

title: Full of energy
text:
This live album was recorded at the Coffee Gallery in San Francisco on October 14, 1960 and showcases Kelly's musical growth after her earlier stints with Pat Moran. While the Moran collaborations were excellent - especially those that featured Scott LaFaro on bass - her singing had matured a little more by the time she made this album.

The tragedy is there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review, because the album is brimming with energy and Kelly is backed by what I consider to be an excellent quartet comprised of Pony Poindexter on alto sax and a rhythm section led by Flip Nunez on piano, Johnny Allen on bass and Tony Johnson on drums.

If you are a fan of Kelly's work, and especially her earlier recordings, you will probably love this album. Another reviewed compared her to Anita O'Day. While they are vastly different musically, I will agree that if you like O'Day you will also like Kelly and this album in particular. If for no other reason than the album sounds both intimate and full of energy. I know those are conflicting terms, but in the absence of sound samples that is the only way I can describe it.

title: Two Pat Moran Albums in a single set
text:
This is a two-album set of Pat Moran's quartet recordings for the Bethlehem label in 1956 and 1957. Although there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review you can listen to samples of most of the tracks on the following album: [[ASIN:B004SAW5PG Essential Jazz Masters]].

What makes this two-disc set special is the sound quality, which is superb. Also, the music is more than a mere quartet - all members contribute vocals, which is a totally different sound than Moran's trios - especially recordings that back Bev Kelly. Indeed, the vocals on both of the discs that comprise this album sound lush compared to Moran's smaller group work, and disc two has a richer ensemble that takes the sound in a different musical direction entirely.

Here is what is on the two discs:
========
DISC ONE
========
This disc contains the album titled [[ASIN:B000CSUY38 Quartet]] that was recorded in Los Angeles for the Bethlehem label during May 1956. This album features Moran on piano and vocals, Beverly Kelly as vocalist, plus her bassist John Doling and drummer Johnny Whited who contribute vocals as well.
01. This Can't Be Love
02. A Foggy Day
03. What a Difference a Day Makes
04. Have You Met Miss Jones
05. I Should Care
06. Gone With the Wind
07. Someone Loves Me
08. The Best Things In Life Are Free
08. Sunday Kind of Love
10. Medley: Spring Is Here/It Might As Well Be Spring
11. Two Sleep People
12. Pick Yourself Up
========
DISC TWO
========
This disc contains the album titled While At Birdland that was recorded for Bethlehem in NYC in April 1957. Most of these tracks feature a large ensemble with a front line backing Beverly Kelly on vocals as well as the rhythm section members who are also contributing vocals for a rich harmony. The front line is comprised of Burt Collins on trumpet, Earl Swope on trombone, Sam Most on flute, and Dick Meldonian and Anthony Ortega on alto sax, and the rhythm section is led by Moran on piano and backing vocals, John Doling on bass and vocals, Johnny Whited on drums and vocals. Oscar Pettiford is on bass on some of the tracks.
01. Thou Swell
02. Have You Met Miss Jones
03. Lover Man
04. Jor-Du
05. It Never Entered My Mind
06. Come Rain or Come Shine
07. I'll Be Around
08. Just Squeeze Me
08. I Can't Get Started
10. Lullaby of the Leaves
11. I'll Remember April
12. Mother McCree
13. Well You Needn't
14. Lady is a Tramp
15. The Four

title: Patti Moran McCoy circa 1956
text:
Note: this review is for the single disc album titled [[ASIN:B007S3Q5LK The Pat Moran Quartet]] that is incorrectly cross-linked to a double album titled [[ASIN:B000RG14R0 Pat Moran Quartet]]. The names are confusing and the fact that the two albums are lumped into the same product description is even more confusing. The album this review covers is the one with the light blue cover.

It's always a treat for me to stumble upon Moran's recordings and especially when she has Beverly Kelly on vocals. This album features not only Kelly as vocalist, but also Moran (she went by Pat Moran when this was recorded), plus her bassist John Doling and drummer Johnny Whited contribute vocals as well.

The music showcases Moran's virtuoso piano style, but the surprise is how well her rhythm section performs. I mean this in the best way because in 1957 she would employ bass legend Scott LaFaro and one would think that he would eclipse any other bassist. In fact he does, but that does not mean that Doling is not superb because he is on every track, as is Whited on drums.

While there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review), you can listen to samples on this product page: [[ASIN:B004SAW5PG Essential Jazz Masters]]. The tracks that correspond to those on this album are:
Disc 1: tracks 4, 8, 12, 15, 16, 17, 20 and 23.
Disc 2: tracks 9, 16, 17 and 23

This album is a cut above mid 1950s jazz piano trios, which this essentially is, plus Kelly as the primary vocalist. It's Moran's piano that makes this well worth checking out (although Kelly's voice is appealing.) Moran was still active as Patti Moran McCoy the last time I checked, although her focus is on Christian music.

The album itself was recorded in Los Angeles for the Bethlehem label during May 1956.

title: Miles in his early Prestige era
text:
I love this album for a few reasons. Foremost is I love everything he did during his Prestige era, and I am also a big fan of the rhythm sections on this album. To add icing, four of the tracks have Zoot Sims who is one of my favorite tenor saxophonists. But my love for this album is not based on those four tracks - for reasons that reflect my personal taste in music I love every track.

What is lacking is the sound quality. While this album has obviously been restored and remastered the original recordings were made on relatively crude equipment in the early 1950s. That pre-dates stereo, so the separation is going to sound a little artificial. Listen to the sound samples to get a sense of that aspect. Or, better, invest the eighty-nine cents and purchase this album as a contiguous MP3 file with no separate tracks: [[ASIN:B0064WO8KG 01 - Miles Davis - Horns - Full Set]]. If you do not like the sound quality on that, you can skip this one.

The album itself was recorded in two separate sessions over a two year period - January 17, 1951 and February 19, 1953 - and released in 1956. Interestingly Miles added a trombone to each of the ensembles, and the added low end from that instrument gives this album a cohesiveness that any other one comprised of sessions so widely spaced and by different personnel would have lacked.

Of the two sessions, the track sequence starts with the newest and ends with the older session. Tracks 1 through 4 were recorded at the Beltone Studios in NYC during the February 19, 1953 session. The front line is Davis on trumpet, Sonny Truitt on trombone, and Al Cohn and Zoot Sims on tenor sax. The rhythm section is John Lewis on piano, Leonard Gaskin on bass and Kenny Clarke on drums.

The remaining tracks were recorded at the Apex Studios in NYC on January 17, 1951, and feature Davis on trumpet backed by Bennie Green on trombone and Sonny Rollins on tenor sax. The rhythm section is John Lewis on piano, Percy Heath on bass and Roy Haynes on drums.

title: Excellent early Brownie with some superb tracks featuring Elmo Hope
text:
This is actually a two album set that was compiled and released in 1956 by Blue Note after Brown's untimely death. The source albums were both recorded in 1953.

Although there are no sound samples on this page you can listen to snippets from each track here: [[ASIN:B000T1CT8G Memorial Album (The Rudy Van Gelder Edition)]].

Some critics claim that this set is not as good as the work Brown did with Max Roach. I am not going to argue the point, but why I put this set on the same level is pianist Elmo Hope is on tracks ten through eighteen and his playing is simply superb. All of the tracks feature top notch front lines and equally stellar rhythm sections, so any debate about the relative value of this album is more an exercise in subjectivity. It's all good in my opinion.

The first nine tracks are the out-of-print album titled New Star on the Horizon that was recorded for Blue Note at Audio-Video Studios in NYC on August 28, 1953. The front line on this album features Brown on trumpet, Gigi Gryce on alto sax and flute, and Charlie Rouse on tenor sax. The rhythm section is John Lewis on piano, Percy Heath on bass and Art Blakey on drums.

Tracks 10 through 18 are the out-of-print album titled Donaldson/Clifford Brown New Faces-New Sounds. They were recorded for Blue Note at the WOR Studios in NYC, June 9, 1953 and feature Brown on trumpet and Lou Donaldson on alto sax as the front line, with a rock solid rhythm section led by Elmo Hope on piano, Percy Heath on bass and Philly Joe Jones on drums.

title: Hope's debut album as a leader
text:
The sound quality of this particular album is less than optimal, but the music is superb. This is Hope's debut as a leader, which was recorded for Prestige at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on July 28, 1955. Hope is backed by John Ore on bass and Willie Jones on drums.

When this was recorded Hope was thirty and had a stellar reputation among his peers and critics. This album is evidence of his genius on piano, and marginal sound or not, is an album that a fan should own.

Although there are no sound samples on this page you can listen to them by going to [[ASIN:B004TZD4WI Ultimate Jazz Masters '53 - '61 by Elmo Hope]] and listening to tracks 1, 7, 8, 9, 15, 17, 20, 24, 35 and 36, which correspond to the tracks on this album. From those you can get a sense of the music as well as the sound quality, which is about par with the quality of this album.

If you are an Elmo Hope fan this is definitely an album to have in your collection. It is also on Disc One of a value-priced set of Hope albums titled [[ASIN:B0085Z5AWU Six Classic Albums]], which you may want to consider before making a final purchase decision.

title: Eclectic and delightful
text:
First, at the time of this review the CD version of this album is erroneously linked to an MP3 album titled [[ASIN:B005MI6YSW The Complete Unedited Sweets At The Haig 1953]]. This review is for an album titled [[ASIN:B000050FMI Hollywood & Newport, 1957-1958]]. That said, this is the album to check out if you have eclectic tastes. Although there are no sound samples or track listing on this page at the time of this review you can listen to samples on this page: [[ASIN:B004B51S1U Hollywood & Newport Live]]. You will get a sense of why I claim this is eclectic from those, but the sound quality on this CD is light years ahead of the MP3 album to which I linked.

This album provides a glimpse into what I call 'jazz off the beaten path' that had been mostly in the background in the mid 1950s. Giuffre's trios were almost jazz chamber music, and along the same experimental lines as what Chico Hamilton, Herbie Mann and a handful of others were doing. The tracks on this album are evidence of the inroads it made [surprisingly] into mainstream, as well as how the music has withstood the test of time. That it sounds contemporary by today's standards over fifty-five years later is proof of the genius of Giuffre's musical vision.

Here are the tracks:
1. Gotta Dance ... 2:19
2. Four Brothers ... 2:40
3. Two Kind If Blues ... 4:46
4. Pony Express ... 5:27
5. Down Home ... 5:34
6. The Lonely Time ... 3:19
7. That's The Way It Is ... 5:31
8. Waltz ... 3:42
9. Pony Express ... 4:40
10.The Train And The River ... 4:46

The first five tracks are from live TV performances. The program was called Stars of Jazz - way ahead of its time - and originally produced by KABC TV in Los Angeles. Tracks 1 through 3 are from episode 27 that was broadcast on January 7, 1957. Giuffre is featured on clarinet, and tenor and baritone sax, and accompanied by Jim Hall on guitar and Ralph Peña on bass.

Tracks 4 and 5 were recorded over twenty-two months later on episode 121 of the same program on October 27, 1958. By this time Guiffre's trio had Bob Brookmeyer taking over the low end with a valve trombone that obviated the need for a bass.

The final half of this album features the Giuffre-Hall-Brookmeyer line-up live on July 4 at the 1958 Newport Jazz Festival. In fact, track 10 was immortalized in video in Bert Stern's [[ASIN:B00003OSU4 Jazz on a Summer's Day]].

title: A fitting tribute to Bernstein
text:
This album contains seven Leonard Bernstein compositions that are associated with four musicals that Bernstein scored. Although there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review) you can listen to them on this album: [[ASIN:B008DM4Z58 Essential Jazz Masters]] (tracks 2, 4, 7, 12, 24, 25 and 27).

The songs that are associated with Bernstein's scores (and the associated musicals) are:
Tracks 1 and 3 (America and Tonight) from West Side Story (1957).
Tracks 2 and 5 (Lonely Town and Lucky To Be Me) from On the Town (1944).
Track 4 (It's Love) from Wonderful Town (1953),
Tracks 6 and 7 (Glitter And Be Gay and Make Our Garden Grow) from Candide (1956).

For me this is one of my favorite Tommy Flanagan albums, and certainly one that showcases his style on both pensive ballads and a few up tempo tracks. The sound samples on the page I provided will convey the range about what I speak.

This album was recorded in NYC for Blue Note on March 10, 1959. Flanagan is backed by Joe Benjamin on bass and Elvin Jones on drums. If there ever was a 'desert island' Flanagan album this one would be on my personal short list.

title: A rare glimpse at a young Flanagan
text:
Flanagan was twenty-seven when he led this session in Stockholm, Sweden on August 15, 1957. His playing, though, has a maturity and virtuosity than is beyond his years.

The best way to describe what I am trying to say about the music on this album is through sound samples. Although there are none on this page at the time of this review, you can listen to them on this page: [[ASIN:B008DM4Z58 Essential Jazz Masters]]. On that page listen to tracks 3, 11, 14, 16, 19, 20, 22, 28 and 29, which are the all of the tracks on this album except for the alternate takes.

While Flanagan's performances on this album are exceptional, his bassist and drummer made significant contributions to the music as well. Bassist Wilbur Little has a nice touch and, of course, Elvin Jones on drums for already a master when this album was recorded. I especially admire Jones' brushwork and control of dynamics. He would later evolved into a much heavier drummer who mastered polyrhythms, but on these tracks his playing is subtle.

This particular album is on my personal short list of Flanagan albums to own. Listen to the sound samples on the page to which I linked above and you may agree.

title: Simply beautiful
text:
I acquired this album as part of a larger set titled [[ASIN:B008DM4Z58 Essential Jazz Masters by the Tommy Flanagan Trio]]. The music, as the sound samples will attest, is on the mellow side and showcases Flanagan's ability to handle ballads with sensitivity.

Ironically this album was recorded for the Moodsville label. I say this because this is one of the albums I grab when I want to set a relaxed and/or romantic mood.

While Flanagan's piano is the center of this album, credit is also due to bassist Tommy Potter and drummer Roy Haynes. Both support the music with the same sensitivity as Flanagan, and if you are a drummer you will appreciate this side of Haynes who has massive chops (he is still active as of the date of this review), but was also a master of brushwork and playing dynamics.

This album was recorded at Rudy van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs, NJ studio on May 18, 1960. To my ears it sounds as fresh today as it did fifty-three years ago when the album was first released. I am betting it will still be viable music fifty years from now because the arrangements and playing are timeless.

title: More complete than the original Riverside recordings
text:
This album is a dream come true for me, and probably for other Monk fans, and especially those of us who love his collaborations with Charlie Rouse. For me this two hour set of albums has additional value because I am also a fan of Frankie Dunlop who is on drums. Add in John Ore on bass and the supporting musicians are one of Monk's classic ensembles.

What makes me rave is the fact that the original Riverside albums did not capture the complete concerts (although the Milan album came close). This set does. The cherry on top is the fact that Fresh Sound Records has taken pains to ensure the best sound quality.

As you check out the track list I want to invite your attention to an interesting fact: on the songs that are not Monk originals he is solo on piano. So songs like April in Paris, Body And Soul, etc. are without backing.

While there are no sound samples on this page you can listen to samples of most of the tracks by going to the source album product pages.

All of Disc One and the first two tracks on Disc Two are from the live April 18, 1961 performance at the L'Olympia in Paris. The original album, [[ASIN:B000UB336C Monk In France]], contained only tracks 3 through 7, 9, 11 and 12. You can listen to samples of those tracks on that product page. This set, though, has the full concert in the same sequence as the original concert.

The remaining tracks on Disc Two are from three days later on April 21, 1961 at the Teatro Lirico in Milan. The source album for this concert, [[ASIN:B000UB07WA Thelonious Monk In Italy]], has sound samples for the concert minus the opening introduction.

Since this is the only complete record of both live performances you may want this set even if you have the original Riverside albums (and especially the Live in France one.) If for no other reason than the magic that Fresh Sound Records worked on the sound.

title: The original + bonus tracks from a different period
text:
This is the original album, which was released by Verve with eleven tracks in 1962, plus five bonus tracks from 1951 through 1961 that fit the theme of this album.

There is no track list or sound samples on this page at the time of this review. You can listen to samples of the original album on this page: [[ASIN:B00397F0WY Night Train]]. The original album tracks are as follow:
01. Happy-Go-Lucky Local (AKA 'Night Train')
02. C-Jam Blues
03. Georgia On My Mind
04. Bags' Groove
05. Moten Swing
06. Easy Does It
07. The Honeydripper
08. Things Ain't What They Used To Be
09. I Got It Bad (And That Ain't Good)
10. Band Call
11. Hymn To Freedom

There were recorded in the Radio Recorders Studios in Los Angeles on December 15 and 16, 1962. This is the classic version of the trio with Beterson backed by Ray Brown on bass and Ed Thigpen on drums. They literally cooked on every track, and Peterson gave Brown and Thigpen plenty of space. Indeed, Brown's bass is not merely playing rhythm, but it complementing the melody and at points adding harmony. Thigpen's drumming on both brushes and sticks is breathtaking (at least to me).

The bonus tracks are:
12. Easy Does It from an Los Angeles session for Verve on December 27, 1955 that features an early trio comprised of Peterson backed by Herb Ellis on guitar and Ray Brown on bass, plus Buddy Rich joining in on drums.

Tracks 13 and 14 - Things Ain't What They Used To Be and and I Got It Bad (and that ain't good) - are from a marathon set of sessions for Verve in Chicago from July 14 through August 9, 1959 that produced a number of theme albums. The personnel are Peterson backed by Brown and Thigpen.

Track 15, Band Call, is from a live performance at the London House in Chicago on July 28, 1961 and features Peterson backed by Brown and Thigpen.

The final track, C Jam Blues, is from one of Norman Granz' Jazz At The Philharmonic concerts. This one was live at Carnegie Hall on September 13, 1952 and features an early incarnation of the trio with Peterson backed by Barney Kessel on guitar and Ray Brown on bass.

This album clocks in at 1:13:26 and is a delightful listen all the way through. I love the main tracks, but the bonus tracks are also a good fit the the original material. Definitely an essential album for OP fans.

title: A classic concert, but J. J. Johnson is only on three tracks despite the title
text:
First, the label's marketing department appears to have run amok because despite the title this album only contains three tracks featuring J. J. Johnson. That said, this is still a worthwhile buy because this is Norman Granz' grand experiment of putting on a jazz concert in a major venue. This debut of the Jazz at the Philharmonic performances would continue for thirteen years of both concerts and tours.

This album contains almost a full hour of high energy performances at the first Jazz At The Philharmonic (JATP) concert at Philharmonic Auditorium in Los Angeles. All but one track in this set were recorded on July 2, 1944.

What makes this set special to some folks, myself included, is the three tracks that feature Nat King Cole on piano and Les Paul on guitar. You can get a hint of the white hot energy from the sound samples, but you need to hear each track in its entirety to fully appreciate the music.

The first track is from the July 30, 1944 concert that features Cappy Oliver on trumpet backed by Maxwell Davis and Illinois Jacquet on tenor sax, with a rhythm section comprised of Nat King Cole on piano, Red Callender on bass and Lee Young on drums.

On track 2 the line-up changes to Shorty Sherlock on trumpet with Illinois Jacquet and Jac McVea on tenor sax. The rhythm section isNat King Cole on piano, Les Paul on guitar, Johnny Miller on bass (some discographies cite Red Callender), and Lee Young on drums.

Tracks 3 through 5 feature a front line comprised of J.J. Johnson on trombone, and Illinois Jacquet and Jac McVea on tenor sax, with backing by Nat King Cole on piano, Les Paul on guitar, Johnny Miller on bass and Lee Young on drums.

title: Timmons outside the Jazz Messengers - mostly early 1960s
text:
This is an excellent glimpse into Timmons' work outside of the Jazz Messengers and covers mostly the early 1960s with one track from 1957. The sound quality on the four discs that comprise this set is uniformly excellent. Some of the Real Gone Jazz 'Classic Albums' sets I own are inconsistent, but this collection is well mastered to my ears.

At the time of this review there are no sound samples or track listings on this page. I am providing that information so you will know exactly what you will be getting. In the case of sound samples I am linking to source albums that, with one exception, contain them.

The biggest of this set is you have an opportunity to hear Timmons in a variety of musical settings. The more I listen to these discs the more I appreciate his playing. It's sad that he is not better known. One final note: there is another compilation of tracks on an album titled [[ASIN:B0089YBBCU Essential Jazz Masters by Bobby Timmons]] that is over three and a half hours long. There is some overlap between this album and that one, but there is enough unique material to justify purchasing both.

title: Some of Ellington's purest blues compositions
text:
When I first heard this album I was actually dumb stuck. It sounded more like something Basie would have recorded, but the compositions and arrangements definitely have Ellington's imprint.

Listen to the sound samples on this page. The music is incredible, and if nothing else is clear evidence that had Ellington lived to be one hundred his powers would still be incredible. I am not sure what the catalyst behind this album was. He was composing and leading small and medium ensembles during this period, and his output was - as always - thematic.

I especially love the first six tracks, which feature Johnny Hodges and some of Duke's other super stars. Those tracks were recorded in 1967 in a single session at the RCA Studios in NYC on March 15, 1967. The remaining tracks would be put on hold for three years, and the last two would be recorded a mere two months after Hodges passed away.

Tracks 7 through 9 were recorded in Las Vegas on January 7, 1970, and the final two tracks on July 15, 1970 at the National Recording Studio in NYC.

The line-ups are as interesting as the compositions and arrangements. But with Ellington they go hand-in-hand because he always composed for specific musicians. The first session for tracks 1 through 6 the ensemble featured a front line comprised of Cat Anderson on trumpet, Lawrence Brown on trombone, Johnny Hodges on alto sax, Paul Gonsalves on tenor sax and Harry Carney on baritone sax. The rhythm section consisted of Duke on piano, John Lamb on bass and Rufus 'Speedy' Jones on drums.

The Las Vegas session featured a front line made up of Willie Cook on trumpet, Lawrence Brown on trombone, Paul Gonsalves on tenor sax and Wild Bill Davis on organ. The rhythm section has Victor Gaskin and Paul Kondziela replacing Lamb on bass with Duke and Jones on piano and drums.

The final session has Cat Anderson on trumpet (track 11), Paul Gonsalves on tenor sax on track 10 and replaced by Harold Ashby on track 11, Norris Turney on flute on track 10, and Joe Benjamin on bass with Duke on piano and Jones on drums.

If you love the blues Ellington style, and especially Duke in smaller ensembles this is a great album.

title: A treasure
text:
Parts of the concert have been floating around for years. My first exposure was a video of Philly Joe Jones sitting in for the much younger Paris Wright on Nutty that was part of a DVD of Jazz drummers that was published by Hudson Music. Other snippets of the concert are scattered all over Youtube, but Disc Two, the DVD, has it in its entirety and if you are a Monk fan that alone is reason to spring for this set.

I love the way the sound has been enhanced on the CD - Disc One - which is superior to the concert footage. Regardless, though, this is a wonderful glimpse of Monk because it portrays him has uncharacteristically grounded and mature.

The ensemble features Charlie Rouse on tenor sax, but two 'kids' on bass and drums. Philly Joe's solo is well worth studying if you are a drummer. Also, both Hygelund and Wright are surprisingly solid as a rhythm section, and Rouse is at the top of his game.

One last comment - there is an interview on the DVD that is conducted by Jacques B. Hess (a bassist himself and a critic). In some ways it's comical because despite Hess' every effort to engage Monk and elicit insight and answers Monk reverted to his eccentric self. If you are a fan it's one more data point that shows where Monk was at as both a musician and a human being near the end of his career.

title: Two complete albums plus four bonus tracks
text:
This album contains two very different albums with two things in common: they both feature Oscar Moore on guitar and the music is excellent. In additon there are four bonus tracks that were released as A and B sides on two 78 RPM records.

Unfortunately there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review, but you can listen to them - in a different order - on this album's product page: [[ASIN:B00BN03KFS Have You Met Inez Jones?]]. Note that album does not contain the four bonus tracks that are included on this one.

On the first nineteen tracks the first track and all of the even numbered ones after it (1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16 and 18) are the out-of-print album titled Have You Met Inez Jones.There tracks This album was recorded for Riverside Master Recorders in Los Angeles on May 27, 1957, and released as Riverside catalog number RLP 12-819. Jones is backed by some West coast heavies: Carl Perkins on piano, Oscar Moore on guitar, Curtis Counce on bass and Bill Douglas on drums.

The remaining odd numbered tracks to 19 (3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 17 and 19) are the album titled Presenting Oscar Moore. Here the spotlight is solely on Moore who is accompanied by bassist Leroy Vinnegar who is a West Coast legend in his own right. It would seem that these tracks with just a string duo would sound thin compared to the ones that feature Jones backed by a quartet, but they do not. This album was recorded for the Omegatape label at the Audio Arts Studios in Los Angeles on December 12 and 14, 1956, and released as catalog number ST 7012. One note about this album is the sound quality is far superior to the version I linked above.

The final four tracks feature Jones backed by Howard Biggs on piano, Red Callender on bass and Chico Hamilton on drums. There were recorded for the Victor label at the Radio Recorders studio in Los Angeles on July 17, 1952.

Obviously this album is a gem for guitarists and especially Oscar Moore fans, but Jones' incredible vocals add a lot of value to the listening experience too.

title: Uncanny (and exquisite)
text:
This album is uncanny because I thought it truly was Day on vocals, and exquisite because of the music and song selection. Many of my fellow jazz snobs (and I am definitely a snob) dismiss Doris Day and have little (or no) knowledge of Raney. It's their loss.

I was born in 1948, so grew up not only listening to Day, but the songs on this album are burned into my DNA. Raney's interpretation and performance of the tracks are simply amazing. When I first heard this album I would have bet money and body parts it was, in fact, Doris Day. Fortunately nobody took me up on it.

Listen to the sound samples on this album. If you are younger you may discover more than one song that will resonate with you. More importantly, Raney's voice is exquisite. Although Raney has been performing since 1954 and this album sounds like it's from that era, it was recorded in 2006 (at Captiol's Los Angeles studios.)

There is a large orchestra backing Raney on this album and I will provide a list to anyone who requests it. For me, though, one of the two drummers - Clayton Cameron - is one of my great influences, so that adds value for me personally. For the record the other drummer who is on some of the tracks is Joe LaBarbera who is no slouch either.

Above I mentioned that Day is often dismissed as a serious jazz vocalist. Listen to her rendition of Ellington's Mood Indigo for evidence that she was every bit a jazz vocalist. That Raney opted to cover some of Day's best known tunes is the lure that hooked me as one of her fans.

title: Delightful collection of tracks
text:
Rare is a strong word, but live describes the tracks in this album. All but three are from a Los Angeles TV show titled Stars of Jazz and hosted by Bobby Troupe. The station for those tracks was KABC-TV.

The sound samples on this page not only reveal some great West Coast jazz, but also a surprisingly good sound quality. I can only surmise that someone who knew what they were doing remixed and remastered the tracks because they sound a lot richer than what would have been the norm for mid-50s TV.

Here are the dates and line-ups. I'll call out the only tracks that are not from the broadcasts below:

Tracks 1, 3 and 8 through 10 are from April 7, 1958. Of those, 1, 3 and 10 feature LaFaro with the Richie Kamuca Quintet with Frank Rosolino on trombone and Richie Kamuca on tenor sax. The rhythm section is LaFaro with Victor Feldman on piano and Stan Levey on drums.
Tracks 8 and 9 have LaFaro backing Ruth Price on vocals with the Victor Feldman Trio comprised of Feldman on piano, LaFaro on bass and Stan Levey on drums.

Tracks 2, 5 and 12 Victor Feldman Trio on November 3, 1958. They feature Victor Feldman on vibraphone and piano, LaFaro on bass and Stan Levey on drums.

One of the three tracks not from the TV broadcasts is track 4. It was recorded in a local and popular jazz record store called Bob Andrew's Recordville in Redondo Beach, CA on October 9, 1958. It features LaFaro backed by Victor Feldman on piano and Stan Levey on drums.

The other two tracks not from the TV broadcasts are tracks 6 and 7. These were recorded in San Francisco on February 8, 1958 by the Stan Getz/Cal Tjader Sextet. The line-up is Stan Getz on tenor sax, Cal Tjader on vibraphone, Vince Guaraldi on piano, Eddie Duran on guitar, LaFaro on bass and Billy Higgins on drums.

Track 11 is from a Stars of Jazz broadcast in 1958. I cannot pin down the date for this one, but if anyone knows please post it in a comment to this review. (UPDATE: Dan Stewart who read this review contacted me with the information: recorded on 6/30/58 and issued on Calliope 3002.) The line-up is Cal Tjader on vibraphone, Vince Guaraldi on piano, LaFaro on bass, Billy Higgins on drums and Bernard Verlardi on congas.

title: One of a dearth of Joe Gordon performaces
text:
If you're a fan of Joe Gordon then this is an essential album because it's one of a literal handful that feature him as a leader. More importantly, the three tracks on this album on which he appears is from a rare live performance at the Lighthouse Cafe in Hermosa Beach (a suburb city of Los Angeles.) Note: contrary to claims that those three tracks are from the San Francisco performance at the Black Hawk on September 22, 1959, they are, indeed, from the July 31, 1960 date at the Lighthouse.

If you are on the product page for the CD version of this album there are no sound samples or a track list. You can listen to snippets of each track on the MP3 album's page at [[ASIN:B005OH0GTE West Coast Days]] .

The first three tracks feature a line up comprised of Gordon on trumpet and Richie Kamuca on tenor sax, backed by a rhythm section consisting of Russ Freeman on piano, Monty Budwig on bass and Shelly Manne on drums. Manne is the leader and it's his voice making the introductions.

Tracks four and five were recorded two years earlier at the Lighthouse in September 1958. This is billed as the Victor Feldman Quartet, with Richie Kamuca on tenor sax, Victor Feldman on piano, Scott Lafaro on bass and Stan Levey on drums.

Although this album has only five tracks it clocks in a few minutes short of an hour. For Joe Gordon fans the three tracks featuring him make this album a gem for fans, and the fact that Scott LaFaro is on two of the tracks is icing on the cake. This is West Coast jazz at its finest in my opinion and the sound quality on the CD is as good as it gets.

title: A wonderful sampler of Evans' work
text:
This is a great sampler for folks who want to explore some of Evans' best work. It contains six complete albums as originally released (without bonus tracks or alternate tracks on later reissues), plus some great performances from Birdland.

Except where I note below, the albums were recorded for the Riverside label. What I especially love about this set is a good many tracks feature what many (including myself) consider to be the best trio, with Evans backed by Scott LaFaro on bass and Paul Motian on drums.

Sound quality is a notch above most box sets from Proper. I own a lot of their sets and for the most part the quality across the board is acceptable. The quality of the sound in this one is superb.

At the time of this review there are no track list nor sound samples. I am going to link to the source album, most of which have sound samples on their respective product pages, as well as provide a track list for each of the four discs in this set. Here is what you will be getting:
