title: Point and counterpoint
text:
This is the first of three collaborations between Edison and Webster and it my favorite. There is something about Webster's tone on this album that touches me. He had a wide range to begin with, and could knock you over with his virile, in-your-face sound or melt you with a ballad. Here he manages to capture a lyricism on his tenor that I have not heard on any of his other recordings, and he does it on every track.

Edison's mostly muted trumpet is the perfect counterpoint to Webster, but every musician on this session made it special. I love Barney Kessel's guitar, which came in at the perfect time with the perfect notes, and Jimmy Rowles' piano added comping when needed, melody when there was space and harmony in measured doses. The rhythm section - Joe Mondragon on bass and Alvin Stoller - gave a distinct West Coast flavor to the album.

I could babble on about the music, but the more I do the more pretentious I sound. Listen to the sound samples on this page for a real idea about the music. I will say that on most of the tracks Webster is the dominating force.

The album was recorded in Los Angeles on September 4, 1956. The other two albums on which Edison and Webster collaborated are [[ASIN:B007U8TF2E Gee Baby Ain't I Good to You]] (recorded for Verve on March 5, 1957) and [[ASIN:B00138D3D4 Ben And "Sweets"]] (recorded for CBS Records on June 6 and 7, 1962).

title: A hidden gem
text:
I first heard this album today when a friend played it and was blown away. I am familiar with Bishop's work as a sideman, but did not suspect his power as a leader and in front.

Although there are sound samples on this page that describe the music better than I possible can, I feel compelled to add a few observations. First, it takes entire tracks to hear the synergy among Bishop, bassist Jimmy Garrison and drummer G. T. Hogan. I am familiar with Garrison, but this is the first time I paid attention to Hogan and am impressed. His brushwork is masterful, and I love the way he and Garrison lock in to support Bishop out front.

Some of the song selections are on the mark. I especially love Blues in the Closet, which Oscar Pettiford wrote and Bud Powell made his own. I can hear Bishop channeling Powell on that track, but he has his own sound. In fact, there are more than faint echoes of Bishop's bebop past here, but the music has a more straight ahead feel that Garrison and Hogan smooth out.

Interestingly this is Bishop's first album as a leader and the tracks were recorded on March 13 and 14, 1961. For some reason the March 13 tracks were recorded for the Muse label and released as [[ASIN:B0000561W9 Speak Low]] while the ones on March 14 were recorded for Black Lion and released under this album's title. That accounts for all of the alternate take included here.

title: Amazing sound and even more amazing music
text:
First: the sound quality of this CD is unreal. It's as though I am actually in the same room, which is all the more amazing considering my medium-range gear. I can only imagine what this album sounds like with a true audiophile set-up.

I've long been a fan of Young and Holt, and added Monteiro immediately after listening to an earlier album titled [[ASIN:B0060ZJ4M4 Montreux]] that featured the three of them. This album is at least the equal of that one, and perhaps better. It's always a treat to listen to Eldee Young sing and he does not disappoint on What a Wonderful World. Not that the other musicians are slouches because everyone on this disc is in top form.

Take a minute to run through the sound samples on this page. You will hear some excellent music. What you will not hear if you are purchasing the disc version of this album is the sound quality about which I gushed about above. Even if you opt for the MP3 version of the album you are still in for a musical treat.

Jeremy Monteiro's piano style is hard to nail down. He can swing with the best of them, and in places has a lush sound. If you are coming to this as Young and Holt fans from their Ramsey Lewis days you will find that they support Monteiro as well as they did Lewis. What I love is the way that O'Donel Levy's guitar augments the two tracks he plays on (Falling In Love With Love and What a Wonderful World), and Ernie Watts' contributions on tenor sax on Falling In Love With Love and alto sax on Surrey With a Fringe on Top.)

My only complaint is the 41:21 playing time whets my appetite and leaves me wanting more.

title: White hot and live
text:
This album was an unexpected delight. I purchased it because I am a long time fan of Eldee Young and Red Holt (and the Ramsey Lewis Trio in which they were the rhythm section for a decade.) This album opened my eyes to some younger musicians who were carrying the torch forward. More about that below.

Take the time to listen to the sound samples on this page. You can hear the energy and even get a hint of the fun the musicians are having on stage. However, you will not be treated to some of the amazing improvisations from the sound samples - for those you need to listen to the full tracks. A great example is Stormy Monday. It is closer to T-Bone Walker's original composition, but the thirteen plus minute rendition here goes way off course in a good way with bassist Eldee Young on vocals that weave in a back story to the lyrics. The rest of the album is like this also.

Every note is sizzling. Every solo is jaw dropping. If you have read some of my other music reviews you know I am not given to hyperbole, but the music on this album inspires it. Part of the reason is that I have watched live clips from the 1988 performance that is captured on this album and the combination visual plus the music does inspire.

This was recorded late night/very early morning of July 17/18, 1988 at the Montreux Jazz Festival in Switzerland. The core ensemble is Singapore's 'swing king' Jeremy Monteiro on piano, Eldee Young on bass and Redd Holt on drums. They are accompanied by O'Donel Levy on guitar and John Stubbelfield on tenor sax.

title: Beautiful mastering and sound quality
text:
I want to disclose that I have only recently discovered Jane Fielding and instantly became a fan. This two album set showcases her perfectly because she is portrayed in a few different settings.

At the time of this review there are no sound samples on this page. You can listen to her on a different MP3 compilation that contains all of these tracks, but in a different order: [[ASIN:B009X8YO5M Vocal & Jazz Essentials]]. While the tracks on that album do not separate the original album tracks they will give you an idea of the different musical settings in which Fielding performs on this compilation. Note that the sound quality of this CD is vastly superior to the sound of that MP3 album to which I linked.

[[ASIN:B0040N5KYY Embers Glow Jane Fielding]] comprise the first ten tracks. That album was recorded at the Capitol Studios in Los Angeles during two sessions: tracks 1, 2, 7, 8 and 10 were recorded in March 1956 and tracks 3 through 6 and 9 the previous month. On the February session she was backed by the Kenny Drew Quintet comprised of Joe Maini on alto sax, Ted Efantis on tenor sax, Kenny Drew on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Lawrence Marable on drums. Leroy Vinnegar replaced Chambers on the March session.

The next ten tracks, 11 through 20, are the album titled [[ASIN:B00501YQPE Jazz Trio for Voice, Piano, and String Bass]] that was recorded at the Capitol Studios in Los Angeles on August 29, 1955. Again she is backed by some giants: Lou Levy on piano and Red Mitchell on bass. However they did not carry her. On the contrary, she used that sparse backing to showcase her chops. These tracks are my personal favorites on the album.

Wrapping up with the last two tracks, which are a bonus from a TV broadcast from a KABC-TV program titled Stars Of Jazz on March 4, 1957. According to some sources these tracks are Fielding accompanied solely by Bobby Hammack on piano. However, you can also clearly hear guitar and bass accompaniment, which turns out to be Herb Ellis on guitar and Ray Brown on bass.

title: Superb compilation of six albums for Clark fans
text:
I was inspired to obtain this set at the suggestion of an Amazon customer whose nom de plume is Tout en chantant. While waiting for my order I discovered that a friend has this set so I borrowed it and have been listening to it for hours.

There are six albums plus one lone track from a seventh on the four discs contained in this set. The sound quality exceeded my expectations and I am not new to the Proper box sets. All of my other sets from this label are good-to-very good and this is VG or better. Do be aware that most of the original albums were recorded in mono or a 'sort of' stereo, and the sound here reflects that.

The six albums are as originally released. Therefore there are no bonus tracks or alternate takes in this set. Some of the source albums I am citing do have those so if you visit the individual product pages to listen to sound samples or read reviews for each album you may notice more tracks that this set contains. Releases and reissues today typically include tracks that were not released on the original albums.

Here is what this set contains. Please refer to the track listing on this page for titles and visit the albums linked for sound samples.
===========
DISC ONE
===========
The first seven tracks are from an album titled [[ASIN:B0094JXZFA 1954 Memorial Album]] that was recorded for the Xanadu label. Tracks 1 through 5 are Clark solo and were recorded at Randi Hultin's home in Oslo, Norway on January 15, 1954, and tracks 6 and 7 were recorded at the Penguin Club in the Sinsen Restaurant in Oslo on January 16, 1954. For that performance Clark is backed by Ivar Borsum on bass and Bobby White on drums.

Track 8 is from an album titled [[ASIN:B000002X6W Together!]] that was recorded for Xanadu in Paris on February 6, 1954. Clark is accompanied by Jimmy Raney on guitar and backed by Red Mitchell on bass and Bobby White on drums.

Tracks 9 through 12 are the Blue Note album titled [[ASIN:B000T087GK Dial S For Sonny]] that was recorded at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on July 21, 1957. The front line is Art Farmer on trumpet, Curtis Fuller on trombone and Hank Mobley on tenor sax. Clark's piano is leading the rhythm section comprised of Wilbur Ware on bass and Louis Hayes on drums.
===========
DISC TWO
===========
The first two tracks are a continuation of Dial S For Sonny from Disc One.

Tracks 3 through 7 is the Blue Note album titled [[ASIN:B000TRXO1Q Sonny's Crib]] that was recorded at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on September 1, 1957. Donald Byrd on trumpet, Curtis Fuller on trombone and John Coltrane on tenor sax form the front line while Clark on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Art Taylor on drums hold down the rhythm section.

Tracks 8 and 9 are the Blue Note album titled [[ASIN:B000SZ11V4 Sonny Clark Trio]] that was recorded at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on October 13, 1957. This is a trio with Clark backed by Paul Chambers on bass and Philly Joe Jones on drums.
===========
DISC THREE
===========
The first four tracks are a continuation of Sonny Clark Trio from Disc Two.

Tracks 5 through 8 are the original four tracks released on the Blue Note album titled [[ASIN:B000TEPJJY Cool Struttin']]. This album was recorded at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on January 5, 1958. Art Farmer on trumpet and Jackie McLean on alto sax are the front line with Clark's piano backed by Paul Chambers on bass and Philly Joe Jones on drums forming the rhythm section.

The last track, 9, is the Out-of-print Blue Note album titled [[ASIN:B002CK3GVQ The Art of the Trio]] that is continued on Disc four. This is a trio featuring Clark backed by bassist Jymie Merritt and drummer Wes Landers. This rare album was recorded at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on November 16, 1958.
===========
DISC FOUR
===========
The first five tracks are continued from the album titled The Art of the Trio from Disc Three.

Tracks 6 through 13 are from an album titled [[ASIN:B00491PE2A Sonny Clark Trio]] that was recorded for the Time label at the Capitol Studios in NYC on March 23, 1960. Clark is backed by George Duvivier on bass and Max Roach on drums.

title: Unique gem of a recording that was not intended for release
text:
This is a wonderful collection of tracks that I am grateful to String Jazz Records for tracking down and releasing. Granted, it took nearly forty years after it was recorded, but to my ears is worth the wait.

While there are no sound samples on this page you can hear six or the tracks on an album that has tracks from this session as bonus tracks: [[ASIN:B00C90VKO4 The Trio]]. Listen to tracks 9 through 14, which are identical to the same tracks contained here.

What I love is the musical maturity of a group that deserves to be pulled out of obscurity. The members are Walter Norris on piano, Hal Gaylor on bass (and cello on track 8), and Billy Bean on guitar. They manage to hold down the melody, harmony and rhythm that rivals Nat King Cole's early line-up featuring Oscar Moore on guitar and Johnny Miller on bass. A quick run through of the sound samples will attest to that.

This was originally recorded as a demo in a log cabin that all three shared in Greenwood Lakes, NY in 1961 and 1961. Although this is essentially a home recording the tracks have excellent sound quality. As a musician I have learned a lot from analyzing the trio's approach to harmony and melody, and how they provided a solid rhythmic base upon which the music floated. As a drummer it's humbling to know how unimportant my instrument is when the other musicians are cooking along. But as a listener this is just great jazz performed by musicians who should be better known.

title: Special? You bet!
text:
Strange as it may seem I am a drummer who loves jazz that feature ensembles that have no drummer. More about that below. I want to say that this trio is amazing in that they manage to hold down the melody, harmony and rhythm that rivals Nat King Cole's early line-up featuring Oscar Moore on guitar and Johnny Miller on bass. Here it's Walter Norris on piano, Hal Gaylor on bass and Billy Bean on guitar.

Before I proceed with background information take a moment to listen to the sound samples on this page. Even though each is a few seconds, there is enough to give you a tantalizing taste of the music. As for sound quality, it is superb. This reissue label, Fresh Sound Records, has never disappointed me.

The first eight tracks are the album titled [[ASIN:B000UBVKY4 The Trio]] that was recorded for Riverside at the Plaza Sound Studios in NYC on June 6 and 30, 1961. A treat is track six on which Gaylor switches to cello. He had played with jazz cellist great Fred Katz, so I suspect that Gaylor was inspired by those collaborations to play cello on that track.

The remaining tracks are six of the eight from an album titled [[ASIN:B00004NH9X Trio: Rediscovered]] that was released by the String Jazz label in 1999 or 2000. These tracks were recorded as a demo in a log cabin that all three shared in Greenwood Lakes, NY in 1961 and 1961. Even these have excellent sound quality.

I mentioned above that I loved music that had no drummer. There are two reasons for this: (1) as a drummer I can play along, and (2) it serves to show me that I can be replaced by musicians with a strong sense of rhythm. Actually, there is a third reason when it comes to this album: it's an excellent study of melody and harmony floating on a rhythmic foundation that is created by a piano, guitar and bass. All that aside, it's plain good listening too.

title: A panorama of Katz' music as a leader  circa 1958-59
text:
This album portrays Fred Katz as one of the most versatile jazz musicians of the late 1950s. He is also unique in that he played a non-traditional (for jazz) instrument, but could hold his own in classical as well as jazz performances. The man could definitely swing! This album showcases three vastly different approaches to music from Katz' genius of arranging, composing and leading.

While there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review I have linked to the source album product pages that do contain those samples. As you listen to them you will be treated to such a wide range of musical styles that it's hard to believe they come from the leadership and vision of one man.

All of the albums in this set were recorded in Los Angeles at the Decca studios in 1958 and 1959. Here are details about each album that comprise this set:
=========
DISC ONE
=========
Tracks 1 through 12 are the album titled [[ASIN:B00BNQVJ9G Soul Cello]] that was recorded over the course of four sessions in January 1958. Each session featured a different line-up, yet the music is cohesive and seamless. This album is like a Chico Hamilton album, but led by Katz. In fact on most of the tracks it's a virtual Chico Hamilton line-up, including Hamilton on drums!

Tracks 1, 4 through 7 and 11 were recorded on January 22, 1958 and feature Katz accompanied by both Paul Horn and Buddy Collette on alto sax, Harry Klee and Bill Green on flute, and a rhythm section comprised of Calvin Jackson on piano, John Pisano on guitar, Hal Gaylor on bass and Chico Hamilton on drums.

Tracks 2, 3, 8 through 10 and 12 were recorded on January 15, 1958 and feature Katz accompanied by Paul Horn on flute and clarinet, Ann Stockton on harp and the same rhythm section as above.

Track 13 was recorded on January 24, 1958 and features Katz accompanied by John Pisano and Billy Bean on guitar, Gene Estes on vibraphone, and backed by Hal Gaylor on bass and Larry Bunker on drums.

Track 14 was recorded on January 30, 1958 and features an unusual (for jazz) string section comprised of Katz, Raphael Kramer and Edgar Lustgarten on cello, Alexander Neiman and Irving Manning on viola, John Pisano and Billy Bean on guitar and Hal Gaynor on bass. Calvin Jackson is on piano and Chico Hamilton is on drums.

The final two tracks, 15 and 16, are from the album titled [[ASIN:B00BCEUAF8 4-5-6 Trio]]. Where the first album in this set is close to what Chico Hamilton was doing at the time, this set is a radical departure. It's an unusual string trio and innovative for the period in which it was recorded originally recorded for Decca in Los Angeles on May 26, 1958. Fred Katz is on cello, John Pisano is on guitar and Hal Gaylor is on bass.
=========
DISC TWO
=========
The first seven tracks are a continuation of the 4-5-6 Trio album.

All of the remaining tracks are from the album titled [[ASIN:B00BC6410G Katz and His Jammers]] that has a definite West Coast jazz feel. The core ensemble for two of the three sessions featured Katz on cello, Don Fagerquist on trumpet, Gene Estes on vibraphone and Leroy Vinnegar on bass. On tracks 8, 10 and 13, which were recorded in the March 12, 1959 session the drummer is Lenny McBrowne. Tracks 9, 12 and 15 were recorded on May 26, 1959 with Billy Higgins on drums. On the final session, August 28, 1959, Pete Candoli is on trumpet and Frank Butler had the drum chair. This session recorded tracks 11, 14, 16 and 17.

title: Some outstanding collaborations
text:
This is a four disc set that contains eight albums (listed below). The entire collection clocks in at 4:52:35 and spans sessions from 1955 through 1959. The actual albums were released as late as 1961.)

The burning question is how is the sound quality? I have played the discs numerous times and have not discovered any flaws like skips that plague some of the sets from Real Gone Jazz. The sound quality is more than adequate to my ears as well. Note that nearly all of the albums pre-date true stereo.

All tracks are from the original releases and do not include alternate takes and bonus tracks that reissues now contain. Note that there are no Modern Jazz Quartet sessions, which is as it should be because there are a plethora of their albums that also feature Jackson. Here his heavy blues influenced playing comes to the fore - something that was not evident in most of his MJQ albums. Indeed, what I love about this set is it includes two album collaborations with Ray Charles, Jackson's ad hoc quintet with John Coltrane, and some great ensembles comprised of luminaries such as Joe Newman, Art Farmer and Lucky Thompson.

Another common question is what does this set contain? I have taken the time to track down the albums, dates and personnel to make this a more valuable album for fans.
==========
DISC ONE
==========
The first six tracks are the album titled [[ASIN:B002DEUUPG Milt Jackson]] that was recorded for Prestige at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio on May 20, 1955. Jackson is backed by Horace Silver on piano, Percy Heath on bass and Connie Kay on drums.

Tracks 7 through 13 are the album titled [[ASIN:B0026DTNRU Plenty, Plenty Soul]] that was recorded in NYC for Atlantic. This album was recorded in two sessions in NYC. Tracks 7 through 9 were recorded on January 7, 1957. This session featured a large ensemble with a front line comprised of Joe Newman on trumpet, Jimmy Cleveland on trombone, Cannonball Adderley (credited as Ronnie Peters for contractual reasons) on alto sax, Frank Foster on tenor sax and Sahib Shihab on baritone sax. Jackson with Horace Silver on piano, Percy Heath on bass and Art Blakey on drums rounded out the rhythm section.

Tracks 10 through 13 were recorded on January 5, 1957 with Jackson accompanied by Joe Newman on trumpet, Lucky Thompson in tenor sax, and a rhythm section comprised of Horace Silver on piano, Oscar Pettiford on bass and Connie Kay on drums.
==========
DISC TWO
==========
Tracks 1 through 4 are the album titled [[ASIN:B0049QSQ4S Jackson's-Ville]] that was recorded in NYC for the Savoy label on January 23, 1956. Jackson is accompanied by Lucky Thompson on tenor sax and backed by Hank Jones on piano, Wendell Marshall on bass and Kenny Clarke on drums.

Tracks 5 through 10 comprise one of two collaborations between Jackson and Ray Charles. This out-of-print album titled Soul Brothers was recorded for Atlantic in NYC on September 12, 1957. Ray Charles is on both piano and alto sax, with Billy Mitchell on tenor sax. When Charles is on alto sax Jackson fills in on piano (as well as guitar on some tracks). Skeeter Best is also on guitar, with Oscar Pettiford on bass and Connie Kay on drums.
==========
DISC THREE
==========
Tracks 1 through 6 are the album titled [[ASIN:B002617IK6 Bean Bags]]that is a collaboration between Jackson and tenor sax great Coleman Hawkins. This was recorded in NYC for Atlantic on September 12, 1958. Jackson and Hawkins hold down the front line with Tommy Flanagan on piano, Kenny Burrell on guitar, Eddie Jones on bass and Connie Kay on drums.

Tracks 7 through 12 are the album titled [[ASIN:B000005HDN Bags' Opus]] that was recorded for United Artists at Nola's Penthouse Sound Studios in NYC on December 28 and 29, 1958. Jackson is accompanied by Art Farmer on trumpet, Benny Golson on tenor sax, and backed by Tommy Flanagan on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Connie Kay on drums.
==========
DISC FOUR
==========
Tracks 1 through 5 are the album titled [[ASIN:B00123NWEA Bags & Trane]] that was recorded in NYC for Atlantic on January 15, 1959. The line-up is Jackson with John Coltrane on tenor sax, backed by Hank Jones on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Connie Kay on drums.

The remaining tracks are Jackson's second collaboration with Ray Charles that was recorded for Atlantic and released as [[ASIN:B0086XFFSK Soul Meeting]].

Tracks 6 through 8 and 10 were recorded in NYC on April 10, 1958 with Ray Charles on alto sax, electric piano and piano, Jackson on vibes and piano when Charles is on alto sax, Kenny Burrell on guitar, Percy Heath on bass and Art Taylor on drums.

Tracks 9 and 11 are from the Soul Brothers session above on September 12, 1957.

title: Superb remastering of Reys' international debut
text:
This is the album that started Reys on the road to being acclaimed as Europe's First lady of Jazz. In fact it was track 3, My funny Valentine, that caught George Avakian's attention at Columbia Records, which ultimately resulted in this album. Prior to that she had recorded two albums in her native Holland in 1953, but was not well known outside a relatively small circle. This album changed that.

Although there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review you can listen to them on the MP3 version of this album at [[ASIN:B0048Q1AVA The Cool Voice Of Rita Reys]]. The first six tracks of this album were recorded at the Phonogram Studios in Hilversum, Holland. The leader, drummer Wessel Ilcken, was Rita's husband. The three sessions feature three different line-ups:

Tracks 1, 2 and 4 were recorded on February 16, 1956 with Reys backed by Ack Van Rooyen on trumpet, Herman Schoonderwalt on baritone sax, Rob Madna on piano, Dick Bezemer on bass and Wessel Ilcken on drums.

Track 3 is the song that put Reys on the map by garnering the attention of Columbia Records' George Avakian. This track was recorded on January 17, 1955. Reys is backed by Dick Bezemer on trombone, Toon Van Vliet on tenor sax, Gerard Van Rooyen on piano, Chris Bender on bass and Wessel Ilcken on drums.

Tracks 5 and 6 were recorded on August 16, 1955. Reys is backed by Gerard Van Rooyen on trumpet, Toon Van Vliet on tenor sax, Rob Madna on piano, Dick Bezemer on bass and Wessel Ilcken on drums.

The remaining tracks were recorded in NYC in two sessions at the Columbia studios. Tracks 7, 8, 10 and 12 were recorded on May 3, 1956 and feature Reys backed by Donald Byrd on trumpet, Hank Mobley on tenor sax, Horace Silver on piano, Doug Watkins on bass and Art Blakey on drums.

Tracks 9 and 11 were recorded on June 25, 1956 with Reys backed by the Jazz Messengers with Donald Byrd on trumpet, Ira Sullivan on tenor sax, Kenny Drew on piano, Wilbur Ware on bass and Art Blakey on drums.

title: Incredible sound quality
text:
What makes this CD worth every penny is the sound quality, which is second only to vinyl in my opinion. It will certainly please any audiophile.

The album itself is really three complete albums recorded for the Transition label over a one year period between December 2, 1955 and December 8, 1956. Not only does this feature some out-of-print Donald Byrd albums, all of which also feature Doug Watkins on bass, but it also contains Watkins' debut album as a leader.

I will not repeat the track list here because you can find it (and sound samples representing the music, but not the sound quality) on an MP3 version of this album at [[ASIN:B000TGZFU0 Donald Byrd And Doug Watkins - The Transition Sessions]]. Note that while that album has 24-bit mastering there is still a certain amount of loss that is associated with the MP3 format.

The following is background information about the tracks contained in this album because they are somewhat special given their rarity.

DISC ONE: the first six tracks comprise the album titled [[ASIN:B0046K0U78 Bird's Eye View]] that was recorded in Harvard Square in Cambridge, MA on December 2, 1955. This album features a front line of Byrd and Joe Gordon on trumpet (Gordon is only on the first four tracks), Hank Mobley on tenor on tracks 1, 4 and 5, and backed by Horace Silver on piano, Watkins on bass and Art Blakey on drums.

Tracks 7 through 10, and 6 and 7 on DISC TWO are the album titled [[ASIN:B00005RGWF Byrd Blows on Beacon Hill]] that was recorded at Steve Fassett's home in the Beacon Hill section of Boston on May 7, 1956. This features Byrd on trumpet backed by Ray Santisi on piano, Watkins on bass and Jimmy Zitano on drums.

DISC TWO starts off with tracks 1 through 5 comprising Watkins' debut album as a leader titled [[ASIN:B0046K0U7I Watkins At Large]]. It was recorded in NYC on December 8, 1956 and features Donald Byrd on trumpet accompanied by Hank Mobley on tenor sax, with Duke Jordan on piano, Kenny Burrell on guitar, Watkins on bass and Art Taylor on drums (Panonica is Donald Byrd, backed by Duke Jordan, Watkins and Art Taylor.)

The last two tracks go with tracks 7 through 10 on Disc One from the album titled Byrd Blows on Beacon Hill.

title: Watkins' first album as a leader
text:
Watkins was only 22 when he led the recording session for this album. It was recorded in NYC on December 8, 1956 for a now obscure label called Transition. While the label is long forgotten the tracks are still in circulation because Blue Note purchased the Transition catalog.

However, what makes this album special is the line-up, which is comprised of some heavy stars: Donald Byrd on trumpet accompanied by Hank Mobley on tenor sax, with Duke Jordan on piano, Kenny Burrell on guitar, Watkins on bass and Art Taylor on drums.

While this page lacks sound samples of a track list at the time of this review you can listen to samples on a larger compilation titled [[ASIN:B000TGZFU0 Donald Byrd And Doug Watkins - The Transition Sessions]] (they are the first five tracks on Disc Two.) Here is the track list:
1. Phil T. McNasty's Blues 4:56
2. More Of The Same 10:04
3. Panonica 3:51
4. Return To Paradise 12:49
5. Phinupi 9:23

Note that on track 3, Panonica. the ensemble scales down to a quartet; Donald Byrd, backed by Duke Jordan, Watkins and Art Taylor. Also, the other album that Watkins recorded as a leader, [[ASIN:B001ZMWUMI Soulnik]], features him on cello. Even if you are focusing on his bass work that is still a great album to track down. This one is essential for bassists and Watkins fans.

title: Exceptional sound quality
text:
Considering that this set was recorded in the mid-1940s on relatively crude equipment the sound quality is simply superb. The collection is from a series of radio transcriptions (discs made for later broadcast) that were cut between and March 1946 and June 1947.

Listen to the sound samples on this page to hear what I mean about the sound quality. However, it's the music that makes this set worthwhile. One reason I am particularly fond of this set is I am a big fan of Oscar Pettiford, the bassist who replaced Jimmy Blanton after his untimely death. Pettiford is on every track and the tracks have been so skillfully mixed that you can pick him out (or any other musician) if you happen to want to study this for its musical value as well as the entertainment and listening pleasure it provides.

If there is any interest I can add the full line-ups for each session as a comment to this review. Here is the information about when and where the tracks were recorded:
===========
DISC ONE
===========
Tracks 1 through 13 and 15 were recorded at a Capitol Radio Transcriptions recording session at WMCA Studios in NYC on March 28, 1946.
Tracks 14, 16 through 19, 20, 21 and 23 were recorded at a Capitol Radio Transcriptions recording session at Hollywood Studios in Los Angeles on July 11, 1946.
===========
DISC TWO
===========
Tracks 1 through 6 were recorded at the same Los Angeles studio as above on July 16, 1946.
Tracks 7 through 16 were recorded the next day in July 17 at the same studio.
Tracks 17 through 20 were recorded at Capitol Radio Transcriptions recording session at Pathe Studios in NYC on January 7, 1947.
===========
DISC THREE
===========
Tracks 1 through 3 continued from the January 7, 1947 session on Disc Two.
Tracks 4 through 13 were recorded at the same studio on June 9, 1947.
Remaining tracks, 14 through 21, were also recorded at the same studio on June 10, 1947.

If you are an Ellington fan this is a treasure trove of performances because many of the transcription discs have long since disappeared. These have obviously been remastered because the sound quality and mix are superior to what was possible when they were recorded. However, the music is the focus and it's pure Ellington with some excellent line-ups.

title: Another evening with Jutta at the Hickory House
text:
This is a companion album to [[ASIN:B000TLYFII At Hickory House 1]] that captures the performance the night after that one was recorded. This performance was on April 6, 1956 and has the same line-up of Peter Ind on bass and Ed Thigpen on drums backing Hipp.

The sound quality of this CD is superb. Unfortunately there are no sound samples on this page to hear both the quality and the beautiful playing of the entire ensemble. Hipp plays ballads and faster tempo material with fluidity and swing. I've always enjoyed her approach to jazz piano because while she was definitely a talent who played with feeling, she also had a recognizable style that was her own.

With backing by Ind and Thigpen it should go without saying that each track is impeccable. Ind was normally a more aggressive bassist, but subsumed his incredible chops to supporting the music and Hipp's renditions of the standards in the set list. I am sure that Thigpen's renowned tasteful approach was a factor in Ind's restraint, and if you are a drummer his playing is well worth studying on this and Volume 1 of this engagement.

Since there is no track list on this page at the time of this review I am including one to give an idea of the range of music on this disc:

01. Gone with the Wind
02. After Hours
03. The Squirrel
04. We'll Be Together Again
05. Horacio
06. I Married an Angel
07. Moonlight in Vermont
08. Star Eyes
09. If I Had You
10. My Heart Stood Still

Bottom line: this is an essential album for Jutta Hipp fans and a perfect companion disc to Volume 1.

title: Valuable for Jutta Hipp fans
text:
I am not going to recite Hipp's history nor lament the fact that she quit a promising career in jazz for other pursuits. If you are on this page you probably already know those stories.

This is one set of a running engagement she had at NYC's Hickory House in 1956. This and the companion album, [[ASIN:B002SVPN1K At Hickory House Vol. 2]], are among the very few recordings of Hipp's superb piano style in a trio setting. Sadly there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review because the sound quality is solid, and the musicianship is excellent.

She is backed by one of my favorite drummers - Ed Thigpen - whose style is both tasteful and always fit the music. Bassist Peter Ind is surprisingly restrained on these tracks. His typical style was more aggressive, but his playing on these tracks is as understated as Thigpen's.

The music runs from ballads to livelier fare and just about every imaginable tempo is covered in the impressive song selection. Since there is no track list on this page (at the time of this review) I am including one so you can get an idea of the songs from this April 5, 1956 performance:

01. Introduction by Leonard Feather
02. Take Me in Your Arms
03. Dear Old Stockholm
04. Billie's Bounce
05. I'll Remember April
06. Lady Bird
07. Mad About the Boy
08. Ain't Misbehavin'
09. These Foolish Things
10. Jeepers Creepers
11. The Moon Was Yellow

If you are a Jutta Hipp fan this is an essential album, if for no other reason than it's one of the few examples of her playing in a trio ensemble. If you are a drummer Ed thigpen's playing and especially his brushwork are well worth studying.

title: Rare tracks and even rarer orchestrations
text:
Not only are the tracks on this album a rare find, but some of the line-ups are interesting. For example, the very first track is Pettiford in a duo with a trumpet, and tracks 13 and 14 feature a front line comprised of four baritone saxophones. However, all tracks are treasures because Pettiford is prominent in the mix and his genius shines brightly.

If you are on the CD version's page there is no track list nor sound samples (at the time of this review). You can see the track names and listen to sound samples on the MP3 version's product page at [[ASIN:B00BK6HSV2 Oscar Pettiford: Lost Tapes - Germany 1958/1959]]. There you can hear what I am struggling to describe in words with respect to the unique nature of the music on this album.

Since there is scant background information about the performances I have tracked it down. Note the line-ups for each track because there is a certain boldness in the way the front lines are assembled.

Track 1 is from a July 15, 1959 session recorded in the SWF Baden-Baden studio in an interesting duo of Pettiford on bass and Dusko Goykovic on trumpet.

Track 2 is the same session, but the line-up is Lucky Thompson on soprano sax, Hans Hammerschmid on piano, Pettiford on bass and Hartwig Bartz on drums.

Tracks 3, 5 and 6 were recorded in the SWF Baden-Baden studio on June 14, 1959 and feature Pettiford on bass, Rolf Kuhn on clarinet and Jimmy Pratt on drums.

Tracks 4 and 7 are from the same session with Hans Koller on tenor sax added to the line-up.

Tracks 8 through 10 were recorded on February 24, 1959 at the SWF Baden-Baden studio featuring Hans Koller on tenor sax, Attila Zoller on guitar, Pettiford on bass and Jimmy Pratt on drums.

Tracks 11 through 14 were recorded on December 2, 1958 at the SWF Baden-Baden studio. Tracks 11 and 12 feature Hans Koller on tenor sax, Attila Zoller on guitar, Pettiford on bass and Kenny Clarke on drums. Tracks 13 and 14 are a treat because Pettiford is on bass and cello with an interesting baritone sax section comprised of Hans Koller, Helmut Brandt, Rudi Flierl and Johnny Feigl. Hans Hammerschmid on piano and Kenny Clarke on drums round out the rhythm section.

The final two tracks are from a live radio broadcast from Stadthalle, Karlsruhe, Germany on December 3, 1958 that features Hans Koller on tenor sax, Hans Hammerschmid on piano, Attila Zoller on guitar, Pettiford on bass and Kenny Clarke on drums.

title: Greal album with some equally great bonus tracks
text:
This is the original title album plus all of Quinichette's participation on another album that was led by Gene Roland. Sadly, at the time of this review there are no sound samples. I lament that because this album showcases Quinichette in both large and smaller ensembles, and he holds his own in both settings. The sound quality of this CD is very good. To my ears it is mixed perfectly and reflects the mid-50s mono technologies used to record this album. That means that the stereo effects is going to sound odd if you are not accustomed to albums from this era.

The first eight tracks are the original title album that was recorded for the Dawn label in NYC on July 16, 1956. This album features Quinichette on tenor sax accompanied by Bill Graham on alto and baritone saxophones, a trumpet section comprised of Reunald Jones, Thad Jones and Joe Newman, and Henry coker on trombone. The rhythm section is a powerhouse lef by Nat Pierce on piano, Freddie Green on guitar, Eddie Jones on bass, and Sonny Payne on drums.

Bonus tracks are from an album titled Jazzville, Vol. 4 released by the Dawn label in 1959. The leader on these tracks is Gene Roland.

Suitcase and Minor Scene were recorded in NYC on August 20, 1959 with an ensemble comprised of Gene Roland and Johnny Carisi on trumpet, Robbie Swope on trombone, Dick Meldonian on alto sax, Quinichette on tenor sax, Nat Pierce on piano, Dudley Watson on bass and Walter Nolan on drums.

Colonel Hodge was recorded in NYC on August 26, 1957 and features Gene Roland on trumpet, Quinichette on tenor sax, Nat Pierce on piano, Freddie Green on guitar, Wendell Marshall on bass and Sonny Payne on drums.

The Creeper was recorded in NYC on August 13, 1957 with Gene Roland on trumpet, Quinichette on tenor sax, Nat Pierce on piano, Doyle Salathiel on guitar, Oscar Pettiford on bass and Osie Johnson on drums.

title: The oriiginal album plus some great bonus tracks
text:
The nine tracks that comprise the original album feature Quinichette in straight ahead and Afro-Cuban ensenbles. These tracks show his versatility as a musician as well as his ability to make different styles of music his own. Here he is much more than a Lester Young clone. Although there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review you can listen to most of the tracks on the product page of a compilation album titled [[ASIN:B0052ZPJ2W Essential Jazz Moods]].

All of the original tracks for the title album were recorded over the course of two sessions that were recorded in 1954. Both sessions were recorded at the Fine Sound Studios in NYC.

The November 4 session recorded tracks 1 through 5 with a front line comprised of Quinichette on tenor sax and Sam Most on flute, backed by Sir Charles Thompson on piano, Jerome Darr and Barry Gabbraith on guitar, Paul Chambers on bass and Harold Wing on bass.

Tracks 6 through 9 were recorded on November 22 with Quinichette on tenor sax accompanied by Herbie Mann on flute and tenor sax, and backed by a large rhythm section comprised of Jimmy Jones on piano, Al Hall on bass, Tommy Lopez on congas,Manny Oquendo on bongos and Willie Rodriguez on timbales.

The remaining tracks are bonus tracks not included on the original album. Track 10 was recorded in NYC in July 1954 with Quinichette on tenor sax, backed by Jimmy Jones on piano (some discographies claim John Williams), Jerome Darr on guitar, Milt Hinton on bass and Gus Johnson on drums.

Tracks 11 through 17 were recorded at the Fulton Recording studio in NYC on January 30, 1952. The session features Quinichette as leader and on tenor sax accompanied by Buck Clayton on trumpet and Dicky Wells on Trombone. The rhythm section was comprised of Count Basie on both piano and organ, Freddie Green on guitar, Walter Page on bass and Gus Johnson on drums.

title: Quinichette channeling Pres with strong Kansas City vibe
text:
This is an excellent compilation of Quinichette's work in the early 1950s. Most of the tracks feature him with various alumni of Basie's band so the music has a definite Kansas City vibe. You can listen to sound samples of most (but not all) of the tracks on the product page for [[ASIN:B000W1W97Y The Vice Pres]]. The sound quality of this album is very close to what is conveyed on that album's product page.

Although the November 16, 2010 review has a very helpful track listing I am going to repeat the tracks here along with when, where and by whom they were recorded. I hate to clutter up this page like that, but feel that it's easier to get that information than jumping back and forth to associate track titles with the source information.

The first four tracks were recorded at the Reeves Sound Studios in NYC on October 5, 1951. Quinichette's tenor sax is backed by Kenny Drew on piano, Bill Doggett on organ, Freddie Green on guitar, Jimmy Lewis on bass and Gus Johnson on drums.
1. Cross Fire
2. Sandstone
3. Prevue
4. No Time

Tracks 5 through 11 were recorded at the Fulton Recording studio in NYC on January 30, 1952. The session features Quinichette as leader and on tenor sax accompanied by Buck Clayton on trumpet and Dicky Wells on Trombone. The rhythm section was comprised of Count Basie on both piano and organ, Freddie Green on guitar, Walter Page on bass and Gus Johnson on drums.
5. Shad Roe
6. Paul's Bunion
7. Crew Cut
8. The Hook
9. Samie
10. I'll Always Be In Love With You
11. Sequel

Tracks 12 through 15 were recorded at Fine Sound Studios in NYC during July, 1952. The front line of the large ensemble is comprised of Quinichette on tenor sax accompanied by Marshall Royal and Ernie Wilkin on alto sax, Charlie Fowlkes on baritone sax, and Joe Newman and Henry Coker on trumpet and trombone respectively. The rhythm section is led by Bobby Tucker on piano, with Freddie Green on guitar, Jimmy Lewis and Al McKibbon on bass (depending on track) and Gus Johnson on drums.
12. Bustin Suds
13. Let's Make It
14. P Q
15. Bot Bot

Tracks 16 through 19 were recorded in NYC in December 1952 and feature Quinichette backed by Kenny Drew on piano, Freddie Green on guitar, Gene Ramey on bass and Gus Johnson on drums.
16. Green Is Blue
