title: Vintage Quinichette including part of his debut album
text:
Before I launch into a boring recital of the discography and source albums that comprise this compilation listen to the sound samples. Two things will leap out at fans familiar with Quinichette's work: (1) the selections showcase his incredible talent, and (2) even the crude recording technology and techniques of the early 1950s managed to capture his exquisite tone.

If you are not familiar with Quinichette's playing it is difficult to distinguish him from Lester Young. Indeed, I would be hard pressed to take the blindfold test and I am a big fan of Young who went by the moniker 'Pres'. About half of the tracks in this compilation are from Quinichette's debut album titled The Vice Pres, so early on he was considered to be heavily influenced by Young's playing.

Here is what is on the album: about one and a half albums, plus a bonus track from yet another recording session. Since this makes no pretense to be anything but a compilation I am not going to subtract a star because the tracks are interleaved. It's somewhat frustrating if you own the original albums, but it's also a boon for anyone who wants to know Quinichette's music.

Tracks 1, 5, 7, 8, 11, 12 and 16 are from Quinichette's debut album titled [[ASIN:B00004VXG3 The Vice Pres]]. These tracks were recorded at the Fulton Recording studio on NYC on January 30, 1952 and features Quinichette as leader and on tenor sax accompanied by Buck Clayton on trumpet and Dicky Wells on Trombone. The rhythm section was comprised of Count Basie on both piano and organ, Freddie Green on guitar, Walter Page on bass and Gus Johnson on drums.

The rest of the tracks, except for Sunday (track 4), comprise the out-of-print album titled Moods that was recorded at the Fine Sound Studios in NYC on November 4 and 22, 1954. The November 4 session recorded tracks 1, 6, 9 and 14 with a front line comprised of Quinichette on tenor sax and Sam Most on flute, backed by Sir Charles Thompson on piano, Jerome Darr and Barry Gabbraith on guitar, Paul Chambers on bass and Harold Wing on bass.

Except track 4, the remaining tracks were recorded at the same studio on November 22 with Quinichette on tenor sax accompanied by Herbie Mann on flute and tenor sax, and backed by a large rhythm section comprised of Jimmy Jones on piano, Al Hall on bass, Tommy Lopez on congas,Manny Oquendo on bongos and Willie Rodriguez on timbales.

Sunday, track 4, was recorded in NYC in July 1954 with Quinichette on tenor sax, backed by Jimmy Jones on piano (some discographies claim John Williams), Jerome Darr on guitar, Milt Hinton on bass and Gus Johnson on drums.

title: Superb arrangements beautifully performed
text:
Quinichette and Rouse are the front line for this outstanding album. Defining the music is difficult. It's certainly straight ahead, but falls short of hard bop. The arrangements succeeded in showcasing Quinichette and Rouse in a musical setting. I love the contrasts between the two as well, but the key strength is this album is tenor sax heaven.

Give the sound samples a listen. While the music in a macro sense has a wonderful structure and flow, what bubbles to the top are the distinctly different tones Quinichette and Rouse get from their instruments.

I also love the backing ensemble. On all but two tracks the rhythm section is comprised of Wynton Kelly on piano, Wendell Marshall on bass and Ed Thigpen on drums. Those main tracks were recorded for the Bethlehem label in NYC on August 29, 1957. Tracks 2 and 7 were recorded a little over a week later in NYC on September 8, 1957. On those Hank Jones replaces Kelly on piano and Freddie Green joins the rhythm secion on guitar. He does the same remarkable job that he did for decades for Basie. His playing does not stand out, but it adds immeasurably to the music and changes those two tracks.

If you love tenor sax this is a great album becuase the front line provides perfornances on each track that are sensitive, musical and have exquisite tone. The backing on every track is perfect for the music and fully support what Quinichette and Rouse are playing.

title: Better late than never - early Chet
text:
Why this live performance set in the can for thirty-two years is a mystery to me. It set in the vault until it was finally released in 1985. Better late than never. This features very early Chet who is accompanied by the who's who of West Coast jazz. In fact as you run through the sound samples you will clearly hear that this is anything but the stereotypical, 'cool' music we are led to believe epitomized that style. The entire ensemble is on fire.

As you listen to the sound samples you will hear a bump or distinct shift on the last two tracks. That is because there was a personnel shift in which Bob Cooper replaces Jimmy Giuffre on tenor sax in the front line and the pianist and drummer are replaced by Claude Williamson and Shelly Manne respectively.

The core tracks feature a front line comprised of Baker and Rolf Ericson on trumpet, Bud Shank on alto and baritone sax and Jimmy Giuffre on tenor sax. The rhythm section features Russ Freeman on piano, Howard Rumsey on bass and Max Roach on drums.

This album was recorded for the Contemporary label at Howard Rumsey's Lighthouse Cafe in Hermosa Beach, CA on September 13, 1953. There is another album, recorded for the Fantasy label, that was recorded at the venue on the same day with an expanded line-up that is also worth checking out: [[ASIN:B000UBN0BK At Last!]]

title: West Coast jazz at its finest
text:
I have always loved this album (the real title is Jam for Your Bread) because of the distinct West Coast vibe. Listen to the sound samples on the MP3 version of this album (correctly named) to get a sense of the music: [[ASIN:B00BEQZ47S Jam for Your Bread]].

While I love Mitchell's bass work - the initial reason I purchased it - the centerpiece for me is Hampton Hawes on piano. I've always enjoyed Hawes' playing, but on this album he is exceptional in that he holds down both the rhythm section while participating in the front line comprised of Conte Candoli on trumpet and Joe Maini who is on alto and tenor sax. Those two are on every track except 2, 7 and 9 on which Hawes, Mitchell on bass and Chuck Thompson on drums perform superbly as a jazz piano trio.

For a studio album the energy is high. In fact it sounds a lot like a typical night at Howard Rumsey's Lighthouse Cafe, so the fact that a studio album could have fooled me had I not known better is a tribute to the music and musicians. This was recorded for Bethlehem Records in Los Angeles on September 27, 1955 and is an excellent example of Mitchell's bass technique. The mix if perfect as is the sound quality.

title: Oscar with a talented group of Danish musicians
text:
This was one of Oscar's final albums before his untimely death two months after this album was recorded. The ensemble is comprised of some Danish musicians of whom I know very little, but their talent is unmistakable.

Listen to the sound samples for evidence of the musicianship and how well the arrangements are written. I am especially fond of the composition of the ensemble, which features a front line of trumpet, tenor sax and vibraphone, and a rhythm section comprised of piano, bass (and cello), and drums.

This album was recorded in Copenhagen, Denmark on July 5 and 6, 1960. Personnel are Allan Botchinsky on trumpet, Erik Nordstrom on tenor sax, Louis Hjulmand on vibraphone, Jan Johansson on piano, Pettiford on bass and cello and Jorn Elniff on drums.

While this is not essential for fans we musicians will pick up ideas. I particularly like how the front like can shift with Hjulmand's vibraphone alternating between melody and rhythm, and the addition of Pettiford's cello that belongs more in the front line than the rhythm section.

title: Synergy + energy = great album
text:
I have been fans of both Ray Brown and Gene Harris for decades and this album is one of my favorite collaborations between the two masters. However, the secret ingredients is how well Al Grey's trombone fits into the mix and Ron Eschete's guitar work, which alternates from supportive, Freddie Green style playing to pyrotechnics. Grady Tate on drums is, as always, tasteful. There is a reason why he, Brown and Harris were a unit onto themselves.

Run through the sound samples on this page and you will be treated to how Brown and Grey solidly hold down the bottom, while Harris and Eschete weave in melody and harmony. On this album I especially love Harris' playing, both on an acoustic piano and a Fender Rhodes. Harris was a blues pianist in his soul, and on my earlier albums with him leading his original group - The Three Sounds - he would sometimes play a piano with one hand and a celesta with the other. The Rhodes used on this album gave him a more expanded sound palette and adds greatly to the music.

From a purely personal and subjective perspective I love every track because of the song selection. Most are my favorites regardless of who plays them, but the way they are arranged and performed here make this album one of my favorites. Much of that - for me - stems from the way the ensemble is put together and much how the musicians performed.

For fellow jazz geeks who track such things this album was recorded at the Classic Sound Studio in NYC on May 1985. I normally do not listen to much music recorded after the mid 1960s, but this album and a handful of others are exceptions.

title: Great educational aid or casual listening for Swing fans
text:
This set is more of an educational tool or for the listening pleasure of swing fans. It has a heavy emphasis on traditional jazz, earlier swing and more regimented big band. There are a few examples of bebop and even a West Coast jazz track.

At a little over five hours of music this set is a bargain. The sound quality is acceptable, but not particularly exceptional. That is understandable considering that most of the tracks are from eras in which recording technology and techniques were crude.

The music is roughly chronological, so for a jazz appreciation course this would make an excellent foundation of listening and study material. And it is fun to put the discs in a mult-disc player and indulge yourself with some great music performed by some top bands of a golden age. It's a fun collection, but not a particularly essential one. What I love is the list of bands represented in this four disc collection. I will provide a list in a comment to this review because it's impressive.

As for arrangers, many of the names are actually hidden and show up nowhere in the scant documentation. What I mean by that is you may see a track credited to Chick Webb and his orchestra, but chances are that the arranging genius behind the performance is Edgar Sampson. The same goes for Andy Kirk and His Clouds of
Joy. Chances are that Mary Lou Williams did the arranging. And while Benny Goodman - well represented in this collection - did some arrangements some of his best material was arranged by Fletcher Henderson (who is represented on some of the tracks under his own band.)

I need to note that the lack of documentation regarding arrangers is not the fault of Proper as much as it is the way the industry works. Compose a song or write lyrics and you get credit and royalties. Arrange the song and nobody but insiders seem to know who you are. Also, there are gray areas. Consider Count Basie who is represented in this collection. His success was to begin with the song's melody, then leave it up to individual musicians to embellish with 'head' arrangements. So when you listen to those tracks in this collection the question is who, really, deserves arranger credit?

That is not to say that there are no arrangers represented. Jelly Roll Morton, Duke Ellington and Glenn Miller, among others, are well represented in this collection and probably arranged the songs on the tracks contained here.

While this page has a complete track listing of the songs on each of the four discs I will add a comment below that matches the actual band to the song title. Bear in mind that I have not cross-referenced the actual arranger for each. Some will be obvious and some will not.

title: The concert that started it all
text:
This album contains Norman Granz' grand experiment of putting on a jazz concert in a major venue. This debut of the Jazz at the Philharmonic performances would continue for thirteen years of both concerts and tours.

According to critics the standouts on this album are Les Paul, Illinois Jacquet and Nat King Cole. Frankly, the entire ensemble on each track literally cooks. There is a raw energy that literally spills over. The sound quality for a circa 1944 live album is surprisingly good too.

While there are no sound samples at the time of this review, you can listen to most of the tracks on this album on on Disc Two of a Nat King Cole album titled [[ASIN:B003KZZ4SK Riffin: The Decca Jatp Keynote & Mercury Recording]]. While the sound quality and mastering are slightly different between the two discs, this music isn't.

All but one track in this set were recorded on July 2, 1944 at the Philharmic Auditorium in Los Angeles. The last track was recorded in the same venue, but on July 30, 1944.

Tracks 1 through 4 feature a front line comprised of J.J. Johnson on trombone, and Illinois Jacquet and Jac McVea on tenor sax, with backing by Nat King Cole on piano, Les Paul on guitar, Johnny Miller on bass and Lee Young on drums.

Track 5 features Shorty Sherlock on trumpet with Illinois Jacquet and Jac McVea on tenor sax. The rhythm section isNat King Cole on piano, Les Paul on guitar, Johnny Miller on bass (some discographies cite Red Callender), and Lee Young on drums. On track 6 the same line-up, but J.J. Johnson on trombone replaces Shorty Sherlock.

Track 7 has the line-up back to Shorty Sherlock on trumpet with Illinois Jacquet and Jac McVea on tenor sax. The rhythm section isNat King Cole on piano, Les Paul on guitar, Johnny Miller on bass (some discographies cite Red Callender), and Lee Young on drums.

Track 8 is from the July 30, 1944 concert that features Cappy Oliver on trumpet backed by Maxwell Davis and Illinois Jacquet on tenor sax, with a rhythm section comprised of Nat King Cole on piano, Red Callender on bass and Lee Young on drums.

If you are new to the Jazz at the Philharmonic (JATP) concerts and tours this one has special value because served as the template for those to come over the next thirteen years. What I love is that there is a freshness to this set of recordings that make it stand out.

title: Tasteful and inventive drumming and some excellent West Coast jazz
text:
Writing this review is a labor of love because Manne is a drummer whom I not only hold in the highest regard, but who is an inspiration as well. These tracks are pure west coast jazz, and most of them are from 1952-53. Some tracks were recorded as late as 1958, and all epitomize Manne's tasteful and inventive drumming.

The discs are beautifully mastered. I have come to depend on Fresh Sounds Records to lavish attention to restoring these out of print gems. Indeed, nearly all of the albums from which these tracks are taken are out of print.

It's a shame that there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review) because they would provide a glimpse into the beauty of the music. Here are the sources and personnel for each album. My information is slightly different from what Fresh Sounds provides. I did cross-reference the following information with my usual sources. Here is what you get:
==========
DISC ONE
==========
The first eight tracks comprise the out-of-print album titled Here's That Manne that was recorded for Dee Gee during two sessions on November 12, 1951 and January 7, 1952. The November session was recorded in Chicago and features a front line comprised of Conte Candoli on trumpet, Bill Russo on trombone, Art Pepper on alto sax and Bob Cooper on tenor sax. The rhythm section is Gene Esposito on piano, Don Bargley on bass and Manne on drums and vocals, accompanied by Shelby Davis on vocals.

The 1952 session was recorded in Los Angeles and features both Conte Candoli and Shorty Rogers on trumpet, Jimmy Giuffre on tenor sax and Bob Gordon on baritone sax. The rhythm section is Frank Patchen on piano, Joe Mondragon on bass and Manne on drums.

Tracks 9 through 16 are from the out-of-print album titled Shelly Manne and His Men, Volume 1 that was recorded for the Contemporary label in Los Angeles on April 6 and July 20, 1953. Personnel on these sessions included Bob Enevoldsen on valve trombone, Bud Shank (tracks 9 through 12) and Art Pepper (tracks 13 through 16) on alto sax, Bob Cooper on tenor sax and Jimmy Giuffre on baritone sax. The rhythm section was comprised of Marty Paich on piano, Joe Mondragon (tracks 9 through 12) and Curtis Counce (tracks 13 throu bass, and Manne on drums.

Tracks 17 through 19 were recorded for Contemporary for an out-of-print album titled Shelly Manne and His Men, Volume 2. These tracks were recorded in Los Angeles in two sessions, the first of which was on December 18, 1953 and featured Don Fagerquist on trumpet, Shorty Rogers flugelhorn, Bob Enevoldsen on valve trombone and Paul Sarmento on tuba. They were backed by Marty Paich on piano, Joe Mondragon on bass and Manne on drums.

The remaining tracks were recorded on May 17, 1954 with a front line comprised of Ollie Mitchell on trumpet, Shorty Rogers flugelhorn, Bob Enevoldsen on valve trombone and Paul Sarmento on tuba. Russ Freeman on piano, Joe Mondragon on bass and Manne on drums.
==========
DISC TWO
==========
The first four tracks are from an album titled B000000Y8T that was recorded in Los Angeles for the Contemporary label on April 6, 1953. The front line is Bob Enevoldsen on valve trombone, Art Pepper on alto sax, Bob Cooper on tenor sax and Jimmy Giuffre on baritone sax. They are backed by Marty Paich on piano, Curtis Counce on bass and Manne on drums.

Tracks 5 and 6 are from the album titled Shelly Manne And His Men, Vol. 6 - Concerto For Clarinet And Combo that was recorded in Los Angeles on December 6, 1955. Personnel are Stu Williamson on trumpet and valve trombone, Bill Holman on tenor sax, with backing by Russ Freeman on piano, Leroy Vinnegar on bass and Manne on drums.

Tracks 7 through 13 are from the album titled Shelly Manne And His Men, Vol. 4 - Swinging Sounds that was recorded on January 19 and 26, 1956. This ensemble features Stu Williamson on trumpet and valve trombone, Charlie Mariano on alto sax, Russ Freeman on piano, Leroy Vinnegar on bass and Manne on drums.

Track 14 has the same personnel and was recorded on Los Angeles, CA, February 2, 1956

The final two tracks were recorded in Los Angeles for Shelly Manne And His Men, Vol. 5 - More Swinging Sounds on August 15 and 16, 1956. Personnel are Stu Williamson on trumpet and valve trombone, Charlie Mariano on alto sax, Russ Freeman on piano, Leroy Vinnegar on bass and Manne on drums.
==========
DISC THREE
==========
The first six tracks are from the same Vol. 5 - More Swinging Sounds album that capped Disc Two. Tracks 1 and 2 are from the August 15 and 16, 1956 sessions cited above, while tracks 3 through 6 are from a July 16, 1956 session. The same personnel as the previous disc.

With the exception of track 11, the remaining tracks are from Shelly Manne And His Men, Vol. 7 - The Gambit that spans four sessions between January 1957 and February 1958. Personnel are Stu Williamson on trumpet and valve trombone, Charlie Mariano on alto sax, Russ Freeman on piano, Monty Budwig on bass and Manne on drums.

Track 11 was recorded in Los Angeles on July 25, 1957 and features Stu Williamson on trumpet and valve trombone, Charlie Mariano on alto sax, Russ Freeman on piano, Monty Budwig on bass and Manne on drums.

title: Over three and a half hours of less known (but not lesser) music by Nat King Cole
text:
This is an incredible find for any avid Nat King Cole fan, and especially those of us who are drawn more to his earlier trio and jazz recordings.

The tracks span a relatively short period - 1941 through 1946 - and feature some of his early trio work, a brief stint with his brother Eddie's group, and some smoking track from the very first Jazz at the Philharmonic. The final disc in this set has Nat backing Dexter Gordon in a relatively rare set of recordings, then a more widely known collaboration with Lester Young and Buddy Rich. The final tracks in this set are leftovers from the Keynoters session that capped off Disc One.

Listen to the sound samples, which are especially important if you are purchasing the CD version of this set because they not only give a hint about the music, but also about the recording quality. Here is what is in the set with respect to a discography:
==========
DISC ONE
==========
The first seventeen tracks are from original trio recordings cut for the Decca label in the 1940-41 timeframe. All feature Nat backed by Oscar Moore on guitar and Wesley Prince on bass. Tracks 1 through 5 were recorded in Los Angeles on December 6, 1940. Tracks 6 through 9 were recorded in Chicago on March 14, 1941, and 10 through 17 were recorded in NYC on July 16 and October 22, 1941.

Tracks 18 through 22 feature Nat with his brother's group called Eddie Cole's Solid Swingers, featuring Nat on piano, brother Eddie on bass and vocals and Jimmy Adams on drums backing a front line comprised of Kenneth Roane on trumpet, Tommy Thompson on alto and tenor sax and Bill Wright on tenor sax.

The remaining tracks feature Nat with the Keynoters. These tracks were recorded in Los Angeles on February 16, 1946 and feature Willie Smith on alto sax, Red Callender on bass and Jackie Mills on drums.
==========
DISC TWO
==========
This is the first Jazz At The Philharmonic concert that was produced by Norman Granz at the Philharmonic Auditorium in Los Angeles. Most of the tracks are from the first day, July 2, 1944.

The highlight of these tracks, aside from hearing Nat's true virtuosity on the piano, is the presence of Les Paul. I already had these tracks on a large set of JATP performances, but many folks have never heard him in this musical context. If you are one of those then this disc along may be reason enough to purchase this set.

Here are the musicians who are also on these tracks: Shorty Sherlock on trumpet, Illinois Jacquet and Jack McVea on tenor sax, Les Paul on guitar, Nat on piano, Red Callender and Johnny Miller on bass (depending on track) and Lee Young on drums.
==========
DISC THREE
==========
The first four tracks are a relatively rare session recorded in Los Angeles in July 1944. The front line is Dexter Gordon on tenor sax, Harry 'Sweets' Edison on trumpet, and a rhythm section comprised of Nat on piano, Johnny Miller on bass (some discographies credit Red Callender) and Juicy Owens on drums.

Tracks 5 through 13 is a fairly well known collaboration that was recorded at the Radio Recorders studios in Los Angeles in the March-April, 1946 timeframe. The recording was released as Giants 3 and features Lester Young on tenor sax, Nat on piano and Buddy Rich on drums.

Tracks 14 through 16 are additional takes from the Keynoters session that capped off Disc One. These are from the same February 16, 1946 session and the same personnel: Willie Smith on alto sax, Red Callender on bass and Jackie Mills on drums.

If you are a fan you can get an idea of this compilation's value from the combination of discography and sound samples. It is probably not essential to a casual fan, but for we die hards this is a must-have collection of some of Nat's less known work.

title: An outstanding life retrospective
text:
While this set is missing the earliest years, it does a wonderful job of covering the highlights of Nat King Cole's work from 1943 until his last recordings in 1964. Granted, there are omissions, but for the most part this set literally allows you to hear him evolve as an entertainer and musician.

For the record, my favorite period is the earlier Trio years and I have a few collections that cover those very well. I sometimes forget just how masterful he was when it came to tapping into the public mind and arranging songs that captivated listeners of all walks of life. Therein lies the true value of this album to me: it reintroduced me to NKC's genius for entertaining instead of just his side as a jazz musician. Of course he excelled at both, and both sides are represented in this collection, although the focus is more on his pop material.

At the time of this review there are no sound samples on the CD set's product page, but there are on the MP3 collection here: [[ASIN:B001AM2P4Q Nat King Cole]]. Give those a listen to get a feel for the music and arrangements. Basically you will get nearly five hours of music that should delight anyone. One additional feature of the physical CD set is the booklet, which contains a complete discography of each track in this set. That information includes dates and personnel, which are invaluable to folks like me who have an extensive collection of Nat's material and want to keep track of the renditions of each song.

The tracks are chronological. Here are a few notes on each disc:
Disc One covers 1943 through 1949, and not all of it is strictly Trio recordings. For example, the song You Can Depend on Me that was recorded on March 30, 1945 has Nat as part of an ensemble called the Capitol International Jazzmen that was comprised of Bill Coleman on trumpet, Buster Bailey on clarinet, Benny Carter on alto sax, Coleman Hawkins on tenor sax, Oscar Moore on guitar, John Kirby on bass and Max Roach on drums. Another example is The Christmas Song that was Recorded on August 19, 1946. It features the trio, plus a drummer (Jack 'The Bear' Parker), and a string ensemble.

Disc Two picks up in 1949 and continues through 1953. You can hear the music changing over to a wider appeal. The tracks start to become pop productions with more orchestration.

Disc Three continues with 1953 and ends at 1958, so the material is truly cherry picked from five years of recordings. By this time Nat is firmly established as a superstar with total cross over appeal. Remember that at the time the airwaves were practically segregated.

Disc Four starts out with some 1958 tracks and ends with Nat's last recordings in 1964.

title: Nice compilation of Nat's pop years, plus some earlier work
text:
I purchased this album in late 1999 and woke me up to the fact that he was much more than a pop artist. To me sure, his pop material dominates this album, which culminates in a posthumous duet with daughter Natalie on the last track.

While there are no sound samples on this page you can listen to them on the MP3 version of this album: [[ASIN:B001AVWJUW The Unforgettable Nat King Cole]]. For some reason that one contains an extra track. However, what is important is to get a sense of the sound quality and the music itself. To my ears the sound is excellent. Most of the music has orchestral arrangements, including stings, so if you are more of a fan of his Trio recordings you may not like this album. I grew up with this music, so there is a nostalgic aspect for me.

Basically the tracks cover twenty years of Nat between 1943 to 1963. Most is mid 1950s and beyond, and the track selection seems to be focused on songs from his earlier years that would be a permanent part of his repertoire. Obviously these songs have been rearranged and lushly backed. Personally I think they are as valid as his trio work because the updated arrangements reflect his shift in focus from virtuoso pianist to beloved vocalist. If you prefer the trio work, including his vocals, I recommend that you consider [[ASIN:B000BM6AMY Transcriptions]]. On the other hand, if you want some of Nat's most memorable work this compilation is a treasure.

title: Excellent for fans - title is somewhat misleading
text:
This five disc set is more than just Trio recordings. In fact on some the 'trio' is backed by larger ensembles, or they are backing a vocalist (or are actually a quartet). As long as you know up front what this set contains you will not be disappointed.

I will admit that some of the tracks and overall mastering leaves something to be desired. Some tracks are so perfect that you marvel at the clarity of seventy year old recordings. Others are not so spectacular. For die hard fans this is the price we pay to hear some of this early stuff, especially since a good amount was never released on record. This is because much of this material was recorded on V-Discs intended for armed forces radio broadcasts for troops during World War II or for commercial radio broadcasts. Moreover, a lot - but not all - of the tracks are from the 1944-45 period, making this an excellent companion set to a collection titled [[ASIN:B000BM6AMY Transcriptions]] that features the Trio from 1946 to 1950.

Since Roy F. Johnson's very helpful March 23, 2011 review provides a complete track list, I'll cover the highlights of each disc in this set:

DISC ONE: covers 1944-45 with the classic trio (Nat King Cole backed by Johnny Miller on bass and Oscar Moore on guitar) and clocks in at 36:51.
DISC TWO: All of the tracks are from 1945 and clocks in at 42:22.
DISC THREE: Nat King Cole backed by Johnny Miller on bass and Oscar Moore on guitar, and clocks in at 46:32.
DISC FOUR: A treasure for me because I am also a fan of Anita O'Day and the last five tracks feature the Trio backing her vocals. Clocks in at 35:12.
DISC FIVE: This seems to be a catch-all that features 1940-41 performances of the Trio with Wesley Prince on bass and Oscar Moore on guitar, to circa 1949-50 performances as a quartet that included Jack Constanzo on congas and Irving Ashby on guitar, to mid 1950s TV broadcast material.

Overall this is a wonderful find for hard core fans. For casual listeners the sound quality may be a little disappointing, but I awarded it five stars anyway because some of the performances are otherwise hard to find.

title: Some of NKC's best work
text:
I have always treasured Kat King Cole's trios in any incarnation and this is one of the sets that I often have playing in the background. All of the tracks were recorded for Capitol's transcription service between 1946 and 1950. See David Slaughter's helpful May 28, 2006 review that explains what a transcription service was.

The sound quality is as good as can be expected for tracks that were recorded for radio broadcast using the relatively crude equipment and techniques from the period. Do not take that to mean that it's poor or marginal - the discs are both listenable and enjoyable. If you are on the CD version of this album you will note the absence of sound samples (at the time of this review). They can be found on the MP3 album version at [[ASIN:B000T00OS4 The Nat King Cole Trio - The Complete Capitol Transcription Sessions]]. Give those a listen and you will hear what I am trying to describe.

What I love is the music (most of the tracks should be familiar to any fan), and the musicality of the trio. In particular I love the first two discs of this three disc set because they feature Cole's classic line-up with Johnny Miller on bass and Oscar Moore on guitar. The third disc features Irving Ashby on guitar who also crops up on a lot of Jazz at the Philharmonic sessions from the same era (as does Cole!) Those JATP sessions are not in this set. If you have not heard them they are worth tracking down. But I digress.

If you are a musician this music is worth dissecting because the trio (especially the Cole-Miller-Moore incarnation) managed to blend melody and harmony within a solid rhythmic framework that did not require a drummer. As a drummer I found this humbling and enlightening.

As a listener or fan you will probably enjoy this set for the entertainment value alone. The material in this set is what propelled Cole into the mainstream in a time when the airwaves were truly segregated. Again, listen to the sound samples to which I linked above to hear why.

title: Enjoyable, but not an 'essential' for fans of either McRae or Brubeck
text:
It took five sessions and a year to put this album together. Some of the material is from [[ASIN:B0013AZPU6 The Real Ambassadors]] sessions and two of the tracks are live from the Basin Street East in NYC.

I love the way McRae handles Brubeck's material. Her vocals are a perfect match to the Quartet's style of playing, and it's a treat to hear how well they go together. It's a shame that there are no sound samples on this page (although you can listen to some samples on [[ASIN:B00CLRY4QG Carmen Mcrae Sings "Lover Man" And Other Billie Holiday Classics & Dave Brubeck's Compositions]]. The recording quality is top notch to my ears, and most of the songs are studio recordings that have superb mixes. Most importantly, McRae's vocals are clear and you can hear her every nuance as she sings through the track list.

For my fellow jazz geeks I am including the dates for each track. Note that all were recorded for Columbia Records in NYC, and with the exceptions cited below, McRae is backed by the full quartet - Brubeck on piano, Paul Desmond on alto sax, Gene Wright on bass and Joe Morello on drums:

Tracks 1 and 8 were recorded on December 14, 1960.
Tracks 2, 4, 5 and 7 were recorded on September 9, 1960.
Tracks 3, 6 and 9 were recorded on December 15, 196.
Tracks 10 and 11 were recorded live on September 6, 1961 at the Basin Street East in NYC.
Tracks 12 though 14 were recorded in September and December 1961 for the album titled The Real Ambassadors. Paul Desmond is absent from the Quartet for some reason.

The bottom line: while this is not an essential album for McRae or Brubeck fans, it's enjoyable. It provides yet another example of McRae's talent and versatility, and it also gives a rare listen to Brubeck and Quartet backing vocalists. Although this is not the first nor last time the Quartet would back a vocalist, this particular album is my favorite among them.

title: Brimming with energy and has a rich sound
text:
This is a gem of an album and one of my favorites by McRae. It was recorded live for Atlantic Records at Donte's Club in Los Angeles on November 6, 1971 and released the following year.

What I love is not only the choice of songs,, but the sound quality and the performance itself. The set list not only contains established standards by Ellington, Cole Porter and the other greats, but some new (at the time) material. Including Burt Bacharach's 'They Long To Be Close To You' in the set was a wise decision in my opinion. It deserves to be a standard. Of course there is the obligatory Billie Holiday song that McRae would include in all of her performances. On this album it's I Cried for You, which was one of Billie's first recordings in 1936.

For some reason there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review. That is a shame because the sound quality is superb. The engineer managed to capture not only the energy from the live performance, but the richness of the ensemble backing McRae. Indeed, the musicians backing her are perfect for the material: Jimmy Rowles on piano (who wrote the Ballad of Thelonious Monk), Joe Pass on guitar, Chuck Domanico on bass and Chuck Flores on drums. Inexplicably there are fuller orchestrations on some tracks, which is not documented in Atlantic's documentation of the performance.

If you love hearing some of the best songs from the Great American Songbook performed by a master this album will delight you. There is a cohesiveness to the album that earns kudos from the production team as well as the performers. Interestingly McRae and her ensemble perfromed 32 songs the night that this was recorded. One can only speculate as to why a volume 2 wasn't released. Regardless, this is - in my opinion - some of McRae's best live material.

title: Always breathtaking
text:
This album frequently finds its way into my rotation and for good reason: to me the musicianship of Peterson backed by Ray Brown on bass and Ed Thigpen on drums is jaw dropping. No matter how many times I play it, the reaction is the same.

If you are looking at the CD version's product page you will notice that there are no sound samples. You can hear those on the MP3 album's page at [[ASIN:B00397F0WY Night Train]] (that album contains an extra track that is a fragment of Night Train.)

What draws me into this album is Peterson's amazing technique that is matched by Brown and Thigpen. I have followed Peterson's later work after this particular line-up disbanded and have yet to see or hear any other rhythm section keep and significantly contribute to the music the way it's done on this album.

When this album was originally recorded in Los Angeles on December 15 and 16, 1962, the first eleven tracks comprised the original album. The bonus tracks on this release may have come from the same session (for example, Volare was recorded during the December 16 session and went unissued and My Heart Belongs to Daddy was recorded during that session as well.

Discography aside, this is a hard driving and swinging album on which the classic trio (Peterson/Brown/Thigpen) are cooking. The energy never ceases to get me moving as well, which is why I play it often.

title: A lot of fire in the music and an excellent job of mastering these 1953 sessions
text:
All of the tracks on this album were recorded in 1953 for Pacific Jazz and their subsidiary label World Pacific. On the first eleven tracks Baker is credited as the leader and on the remaining ones Russ Freeman is billed as a 'feature'. Listen to the sound samples on this page and you will Baker playing with more fire and agressiviness than he later displayed after his style evolved and matured. I love his early work here and his later, more pensive work equally, so this album is a balance for me.

Each instrument is perfectly placed. Each musician is exercising dynamic control, but whoever engineered this session did a remarkable job, and whoever mixed this release did an equally remarkable one to my ears.

The first eleven tracks were recorded for Pacific Jazz under the auspices of the Chet Baker Quartet in a series of Los Angeles studio sessions in July 1953.

The very first track in the compilation was recorded on July 24, 1953 and features Baker backed by Russ Freeman on piano, Red Mitchell on bass and Bobby White on drums.

Tracks 2 through 4 were recorded on July 27, 1953 with Bob Whitlock replacing Red Mitchell on bass.

Baker and Freeman are backed by Carson Smith on bass and Larry Bunker on drums on tracks 5 through 11 that were recorded on July 29 and 30, 1953.

The remaining tracks in this compilation were recorded at Radio Recorders in Los Angeles during a single October 3, 1953 session. This was recorded under the auspices of the Chet Baker Quartet Featuring Russ Freeman, and features Baker and Freeman once again backed by Carson Smith on bass and Larry Bunker on drums.

title: Beautifully arranged and performed
text:
This album not only showcases Pettiford's genius at performing, but also a touch of genius in arranging. The entire ensemble on this album is in top form.

While this page lacks both a track list and sound samples at the time of this review here are the tracks and links to their sound samples:
01. [[ASIN:B003PRLTZA Jack The Bear]]
02. [[ASIN:B003PRLRIY Tamalpais]]
03. [[ASIN:B003PRNRSM Swingin' Till The Girls Come Home]]
04. [[ASIN:B003PRPULO Mood Indigo]]
05. [[ASIN:B003PRLWDO Chuckles]]
06. [[ASIN:B003PRJOT8 Time On My Hands]]

Listen to the linked sound samples for the music itself, but this CD and its mastering are reasons to purchase this particular release. Bethlehem Japan has done an excellent job in that respect. As for the music my favorite track is Jack The Bear, but that is because I am a fan of Ellington's bassist - Jimmy Blanton - who first performed it before his untimely death. I will be bold enough to assert that the song (and Blanton) changed the was bass was played, so having Pettiford reprise it is a tribute to both Blanton and to Pettiford's own genius.

This album was recorded for Bethlehem Records in NYC on Deceber 17, 1954. The front line was comprised of Clark Terry and Joe Wilder on trumpet, Jimmy Cleveland on trombone, Dave Schildkraut on alto sax, Jimmy Hamilton on clarinet and tenor sax and Danny Bank on baritone sax. The rhythm section consisted of Joe Earl Knight on piano, Pettiford on bass and Osie Johnson on drums.

title: Dr. Billy Taylor's best trio incarnation in my opinion
text:
This is a two-album set, both of which were recorded within weeks of each other in January 1956. While there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review), the source albums to which I have linked below have them on their product page. Listen to those for the style of music in this set.

The actual sound quality is, to my ears, excellent. The discs are flawless and the mastering was done right because each member of the trio can be heard clearly in the mix.

Here are the albums:
[[ASIN:B00480YNYW Evergreens]] takes up the first ten tracks that were recorded in NYC for ABC-Paramount on January 1 and 2, 1956. Each one contains the essence of its song, and how beautifully Dr. Taylor renders it. Of course his solid rhythm section comprised of Earl May on bass and Percy Brice on drums contribute to the music as well.

[[ASIN:B004814UKI Billy Taylor At The London House]] comprises the remaining eight tracks. This album was recorded live at the London House in Chicago for ABC-Paramount on January 22, 1956 - just three weeks after Evergreens. It features the same line-up of Taylor-May-Brice and they are definitely attuned to each other. What I love about this is it has the energy that most live albums exude, but the song selection is better suited to clubs and lounges. The first track, The London House, is almost fiery, while other tracks are more pensive and what one would expect from a jazz piano trio on 1956.

This two-album set has Taylor at his peak in my opinion and is, like all of his trio albums, tight, swinging and musical.

title: One of my favorite Baker albums because of the energy and intensity
text:
This exquisite collection of tracks was recorded in Rome on January 5, 1962. I could rave about the music, but since there are sound samples on this page you will be better served by listening to those instead of my words, which fall short.

I will offer a personal opinion and say that Over The Rainbow, is one of the best renditions by anyone, and reason enough to own the album. If you disagree with that, then fair enough because music is subjective. I think you will agree that energy and playing is reason enough to own the album. I sometimes forget the fire and intensity Chet was capable up - then I put this album on and it's a jarring reminder.

In addition to Baker, Bobby Jaspar is another of my favorite musicians. His flute and tenor saxophone playing greatly enhanced the music on those tracks. A big surprise - to me - is Armadeo Tommasi on piano on those tracks. I fell in love with his sound. Rene Thomas on guitar, with Benoit Quersin on bass and Daniel Humair on drums rounded out what I consider to be a solid ensemble. Every musician Baker rounded up for this album added something to the music.

Bottom line is if you are a Chet Baker fan this is a gem. If you love hard bop you have yet another excuse to grab this album. My copy of this album receives a lot of play time.

title: Bargain priced collection of Raney as leader and sideman
text:
This is a wonderful compilation for Raney fans in particular and circa 1950s jazz fans in general. More importantly this set is a treasure trove for guitarists who want to study Raney's incredible technique.

Fifty tracks from eight different albums and ironically none feature Raney with Woody Herman as the album's subtitle implies. However, the tracks are mainly from albums led by Stan Getz and Red Norvo, as well as by Raney himself.

The sound quality is not spectacular, but it's also not terrible. Surely audiophiles will not like this set, but for folks like myself who rip discs to MP3 files and play from lower end equipment the quality is acceptable.

This set is poorly documented, but I have tracked down the source albums for each track. Clicking those links will take you to the album product pages where in some cases you can listen to sound samples and to also read reviews.

If you are looking at the track list on this page they are distributed among four separate discs. Tracks 1 through 12 are on Disc One, 13 through 25 are on Disc Two, 26 through 37 on Disc Three and 38 through 50 on Disc Four. Below I am grouping the tracks as they are numbered on the individual discs. If you want in-depth background information leave a comment and I will provide the additional details.

Here is what you get:
=========
DISC ONE
=========
Tracks 1 through 4 are from the Stan Getz album titled [[ASIN:B000UAWG98 Prezervation]].
Tracks 5 through 7 are from a live Stan Getz album titled [[ASIN:B000005HG4 At Storyville Vol 1 & 2]].
Tracks 8 through 10 are from yet another Stan Getz album titled [[ASIN:B000UB322M Early Stan]].
Tracks 11 and 12 are from a Red Norvo compilation titled [[ASIN:B000000ZDI Trios]].
=========
DISC TWO
=========
Tracks 1 through 6 are from the same Red Norvo album as the last two tracks on Disc One.
The remaining tracks on this disc are from the album titled [[ASIN:B000002X6W Together!]] featuring Raney as a leader in collaboration with Sonny Clark.
=========
DISC THREE
=========
Tracks 1 and 2 are from the preceding album on Disc Two.
Tracks 3 through 9 are from the Red Norvo album titled [[ASIN:B000000YUD Red Norvo Trio]].
Tracks 10 through 12 are from the Jimmy Raney Quintet compilation titled [[ASIN:B005OIARWE Complete Recordings 1954-1956]].
=========
DISC FOUR
=========
The first two tracks are from the preceding album on Disc Three.
All of the remaining tracks are from the album titled [[ASIN:B001ZNCCG6 A by Jimmy Raney]] featuring Raney as a leader.

This is a great deal for anyone who wants to establish a collection of Raney's albums as both a leader and sideman. You will get some incredible material featuring Stan Getz, Red Norvo and Sonny clark (among others) in the process.

title: Fans of both Sonny Clark and Jimmy Raney should own this album
text:
I love this album for a number of reasons, but the foremost one is this is one of the best collaborations between Jimmy Raney and Sonny Clark.

What makes this especially valuable is it provides an opportunity to compare and contrast Raney with Grant Green who would be a later collaborator with Clark. The similarities and differences between the two are illuminating. For one thing both approach the guitar the same way that Charlie Christian did: like a horn more than a string instrument, and Raney's playing on this album illustrates that very well. However, you can hear Raney's attack dominate his style on this album. Compare hat to Green's playing that uses a lot of sustain and the differences emer\ge.

However, the above mentioned aspect of only one element of this album. Clark's playing is - as always - impeccable, and the other musicians are solid too.

At the time of this review there was no track list on this page, so I am providing one to which I will refer during the rest of this review:
01 Once in a While
02 Pennies from Heaven
03 Yesterdays
04 There Will Never Be Another You
05 Body and Soul
06 Stella By Starlight
07 You Go To My Head
08 Jumping For Jane
09 Invention

Tracks 1 through 7 were recorded in Paris on February 6, 1954. The first six tracks are also on the out-of-print album titled Jimmy Raney - Guitaristic that was recorded for Vogue, while track 7 was specifically recorded - for the Xanadu label - for this album. These tracks feature Raney accompanying Sonny Clark on piano and backed by Red Mitchell on bass and Bobby White on drums.

The last two tracks were recorded almost a month earlier for Metronome on January 13, 1954. They were recorded in Stockholm and feature Raney and Clark accompanying tenor saxophonist Gosta Theselus. Red Mitchell is credited as the bassist with Elaine Leighton on drums. Leighton is special because she was a successful drum kit player during an era when that instrument was dominated by men. She was in Stockholm for these recordings because she was part of a Jazz Club USA tour of Europe.

title: A great way too jump start a Jimmy Raney collection
text:
Although the title implies four albums featuring Raney as leader, it's actually three and one led by Stan Getz. I am not quibbling because this is a wonderful set of Raney's work from 1953 through 1956. And on three of the albums he accompanies instead of backs, so it's a glimpse into his work as part of the front line as well.

This set has four albums, plus a track from a fifth one, contained on two discs. The sound quality is more than acceptable to my ears, even the 1953 tracks which were recorded on relatively crude equipment by today's standards.

What is lacking at the time of this review is a track list. Or documentation for that matter. I have compiled both and have also linked to the source albums of which all but one contain sound samples on their product pages. Here is what this set contains:
========
DISC ONE
========
[[ASIN:B000000Z4Q A by Jimmy Raney]]. It took ten months to complete this album, but to my ears it was worth it. It was recorded in three sessions for Prestige at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio with a solid rhythm section that appears on every track: Hall Overton on piano, Teddy Kotick on bass and Nick Stabulas on drums on all but the first four tracks, which feature Art Mardigan on drums.

The first four tracks were recorded on May 28, 1954 and is essentially a quartet. On the next two sessions John Wilson joins on trumpet. Tracks 5 through 7 were recorded on February 18, 1955, and the remaining tracks on March 8, 1955.

All were recorded for Vogue in Paris during the same February 10, 1954 session and feature Roger Guerin on trumpet accompanying Bobby Jaspar on tenor sax. Raney is a member of the rhythm section that was led by Maurice Vander, with Jean-Marie Ingrand on bass and Jean-Louis Viale on drums.

This is one of two sessions for the album, and the only session featuring Raney. You can hear samples on that albums's product page on its tracks 1 and 2, and 8 and 9.

title: One of the essential Raney albums
text:
Reviewer Alex I. Link is correct: there are echos of Charlie Christian in Raney's playing, both here and on other albums. Specifically, he plays his instrument like a horn. Each note flows as though from a tenor saxophone instead of a guitar. I love how he supports the music in a way that is atypical for a member of the rhythm section into where guitarists were commonly pigeonholed. Raney could work in that capacity - and did for folks like Stan Getz on other albums - but here he is in the front line with Bob Brookmeyer.

This album works, too, because of the rock solid rhythm section. Both Dick Katz and Hank Jones added their magic on piano, but the pairing of Teddy Kotick on bass with Osie Johnson on drums also helped. Johnson is one of the unsung drummers of his era who had a solid reputation among his peers and a very successful career as not only a drummer, but as a composer, arranger and vocalist.

It was recorded for ABC-Paramount in July and August, 1956. The line-up features Bob Brookmeyer on valve trombone accompanying Raney, Dick Katz on piano, Teddy Kotick on bass and Osie Johnson on drums.

The July 23 session recorded tracks 2 and 3, and 5 and 7. On the remaining four tracks, recorded on August 1, Hank Jones replaces Dick Katz on piano.

title: A snapshot of Clark's work in the mid-to-late 1950s
text:
The three albums on this two disc set were all recorded for Blue Note at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio. The period is 1957 through 1959, and the sound quality is very good, but short of spectacular. They are, however, more than adequate for ripping to MP3 files since that format loses some fidelity by its very nature.

There is an incomplete track list and no sound samples on this page at the time of this review, so I am going to provide links to the source albums and some documentation below. Note that the albums in this set are as originally released. That means that there are no bonus tracks or alternate takes that are usually included with reissues and rereleases. However, this set has some excellent music and features some true giants from the era.

Do bear in mind that this is a narrow snapshot of Clark's playing during a specific period. As such these albums augment, but not defined. In my opinion no Sonny Clark library is complete without some of his earlier collaborations with guitarist Jimmy Raney or his later ones with guitarist Grant Green. I can make recommendations for those if you leave a comment or contact me. Here is what you get:
========
DISC ONE
========
[[ASIN:B0048WBKP0 Cool Struttin']] recorded on January 5, 1958. Features Art Farmer on trumpet accompanied by Jackie McLean on alto sax and backed by Clark on piano, Paul Chambers on bass and Philly Joe Jones on drums.

title: Two Jimmy Raney albums on one disc
text:
First I want to address the mastering and sound quality. Fresh Sound Records did a great job on both counts. I have a growing collection of their reissues and have never been disappointed.

Run through the sound samples on this page to get a feel for the music if you are not familiar with Raney. To me he is one of my favorite jazz guitarists and I do not normally listen to guitar-centric music. If you are familiar with him then you are in for a treat.

This is a two album set with the first eight tracks comprising the original album titled [[ASIN:B004810XEU Jimmy Raney - In Three Attitudes]] that was recorded in NYC for ABC-Paramount in three sessions in May and June, 1956. Of the three sessions the first was on May 14 and recorded tracks 1, 4 and 8 with Raney accompanying Bob Brookmeyer on valve trombone, backed by John Williams on piano, Red Mitchell on bass and Osie Johnson on drums.

On the May 23 session that produced tracks 3 and 6 Raney is accompanied by Al Cohn on tenor sax and backed by John Williams on piano, Whitey Mitchell on bass and Jack Edie on drums.

Tracks 2, 5 and 7, were recorded on June 15 and feature Raney backed by Hall Overton on piano, Red Mitchell on bass and Osie Johnson on drums.

The remaining tracks comprise the album titled [[ASIN:B001NZ4Z02 Jimmy Raney Featuring Bob Brookmeyer]] that was recorded for ABC-Paramount in 1956 and features the following line-up: Bob Brookmeyer on valve trombone accompanying Raney, Dick Katz on piano, Teddy Kotick on bass and Osie Johnson on drums. The July 23 session recorded tracks 10 and 11, and 13 and 15. On the remaining four tracks, recorded on August 1, Hank Jones replaces Dick Katz on piano.

This is a great combo set in my opinion and essential for jazz guitarists. What I love most is the cross section of ensembles in which Raney displays his chops and musical ideas.

title: One of the essential Raney albums
text:
Of course I am being subjective when I claim that this is essential, but even the most objective person can make the case that this album has a lot going for it if you are a fan. Or a guitarist for that matter.

The sound samples will tell you whether or not this is essential, and also will provide a good indication of the sound quality. It's all about the music, though, so essential or not this album is plain enjoyable. Do be aware that this is NOT bebop - you can hear a lot of Miles Davis' 'cool' influence in the music, and it's obvious that there is also a West Coast influence. Of course there is an echo of Charlie Christian in the playing because Raney has a tendency to play the instrument like a horn the way Christian did. What binds this together is Raney's fluid playing and his penchant for picking instead of chords. In many ways his style also reminds me a lot of Herb Ellis - not the same, but there are common elements to the way each approach guitar. Make no mistake, Raney had his own sound and it shows through this album.

It took ten months to complete this album, but to my ears it was worth it. It was recorded in three sessions for Prestige at Rudy van Gelder's Hackensack, NJ studio with a solid rhythm section that appears on every track: Hall Overton on piano, Teddy Kotick on bass and Nick Stabulas on drums on all but the first four tracks, which feature Art Mardigan on drums.

The first four tracks were recorded on May 28, 1954 and is essentially a quartet. On the next two sessions John Wilson joins on trumpet. Tracks 5 through 7 were recorded on February 18, 1955, and the remaining tracks on March 8, 1955.

title: Mann oh Mann!
text:
This set contains some choice work by Mann in 1957 and '58. In fact, some of this work ranks up there with my all time favorites and I am a big fan. What is missing from this page at the time of this review are track lists and sound samples. Plus Real Gone Jazz is good about putting bargain sets together and not so good about documentation. I will rectify that below.

First, the sound quality is pretty good. There are no needle-drop transfers and the tracks sound as though they have been remastered. This is not stuff that a true audiophile will enjoy, but for casual listening or ripping to MP3 files the sound is good enough.

I am linking to the source albums so you can go to their product pages and listen to sound samples and read individual reviews. While you are at it check the total price if you purchased the albums separately. Physically the four albums are on two discs. Here is what the set contains:
========
DISC ONE
========
[[ASIN:B002G6ESH2 Yardbird Suite]]. Herbie is on flute for all but two tracks on which he switches to tenor sax. He is accompanied by Phil Woods on alto, nicely contrasting with both the flute and tenor sax. The rhythm section is comprised of Eddie Costa on piano and vibraphones, Joe Puma on guitar, Wendell Marshall on bass and Bobby Donaldson on drums. Such a large rhythm section provides a full sound and solid foundation for Herbie and Woods. The session itself took place on May 14, 1957, and from the energetic yet 'cool' sound it's as though Spring was in the air. Tracks are:

Honestly, it's difficult for me to tell who is playing what on the tracks, so I've managed to track down that information for each track. title: Double album with comingled tracks
text:
This is a five star album for the music, but I subtracted a star because the two albums that comprise the sixteen tracks are interleaved. If you own one or both of the source albums the sequence (or lack thereof) is disconcerting.

Listen to the sound samples to hear why I claim the music is five stars. What I love is this collection has Raney in a number of ensemble configurations and he shines in all of them. He never overpowers the other musicians, always playing tastefully and supporting the music. But he is also not subsumed - you can hear his contributions to each track. If I had to describe his playing it would be that he is a quiet force to be reckoned with.

Here is what is on this album and as you see the way the tracks of each album are interleaved I hope you understand why I subtracted a star:

Tracks 1, 2, 4, 5, 9, 11, 12, 14 are the album titled [[ASIN:B004810XEU Jimmy Raney - In Three Attitudes]] that was recorded in NYC for ABC-Paramount in three sessions in May and June, 1956.

The first session was on May 14 and recorded tracks 9, 11 and 14 with Raney accompanying Bob Brookmeyer on valve trombone, backed by John Williams on piano, Red Mitchell on bass and Osie Johnson on drums.

On the May 23 session that produced tracks 4 and 5 Raney is accompanied by Al Cohn on tenor sax and backed by John Williams on piano, Whitey Mitchell on bass and Jack Edie on drums.

The remaining tracks, 1, 2 and 12, were recorded on June 15 and feature Raney backed by Hal Overton on piano, Red mtchell on bass and Osie Johnson on drums.

Tracks 3, 6 through 8, 10, 13 and 15 through 16 are the album titled [[ASIN:B001NZ4Z02 Jimmy Raney Featuring Bob Brookmeyer]]. This was also recorded for ABC-Paramount in 1956 and features the following line-up: Bob Brookmeyer on valve trombone accompanying Raney, Dick Katz on piano, Teddy Kotic on bass and Osie Johnson on drums. The July 23 session recorded tracks 8, 10, 13 and 15. On the remaining four tracks, recorded on August 1, Hank Jones replaces Dick Katz on piano.

title: Two of Mann's gems from early '62
text:
By the time Mann recorded these two albums he was in continual transformational mode and was shifting towards Brazilian music. The two albums in this set - and especially Right Now - retain a flavor of Afro-Cuban rhythms and also foreshadow his move towards 'world music'.

However, the dominant theme is Brazilian. Cycle through the sound samples on this page to hear not only the unifying theme of these two albums, but also hints of departures from that theme. There are markers and nuances throughout that require many listens to entire tracks to absorb. This is a set that you are likely to play often if you are a Mann fan.

Brazil, Bossa Nova & Blues is on the first six tracks. It was recorded for United Artists in NYC in early 1962. Personnel are Mann on flute accompanied by both Haygood Hardy on vibraphone and Dave Pike on marimba, and backed by Billy Bean on guitar, Bill Salter on bass and Willie Bobo on drum kit. This ensemble is augmented by Carlos "Patato" Valdés on congas Jose De Paula on tambourine and Carmen Costa on maracas.

The remaining tracks are the album titled Right Now and were recorded in NYC for Atlantic on March 12 and April 19, 1962. This album features Mann on flute accompanied by Haygood Hardy on vibraphone and backed by Billy Bean on guitar, Don Payne and Billy Salter on bass (depending on track) Willie Bobo on drum kit, and a percussion section comprised of Carlos 'Patato' Valdes, Johnny Pacheco and Willie Rodriguez.

title: Three excellent albums from 58-59
text:
At the time of this review this set is cross linked with another set of Chet Baker albums, so if the review makes no sense I am reviewing this three album set: [[ASIN:B003BWQF4Y Three Classic Albums]]. Another identically named set titled [[ASIN:B004BO8GKM Three Classic Albums]] is comprised of three different albums. I apologize for any confusion, but Amazon slips sometimes when it comes to managing their catalog.

This set contains some of Baker's better recordings from 1958-59. While his own playing is excellent the value of these albums lie as much in his sidemen as it does in Baker himself.

The sound quality of the discs are top notch to my ears. They are not audiophile quality, but the mix is right and each note by each musician is clear.

What is lacking on this page at the time of this review are sound samples and background information on each album. I have linked to the source albums below. Each link will lead you to a page that does have sound samples so you can get an idea of the music. Let those guide you with respect to the music itself, which I am betting that you will find to be gems on every track. I have also provided background info on each so you can see who accompanied Chet - and there are some genuine stars.

Here is what you get:
=========
DISC ONE
=========
Tracks 1 through 9 are the album titled [[ASIN:B000UBK0D6 Chet]] that was recorded in NYC for Riverside on December 30, 1958 and January 19, 1959. The December 1958 session produced the first seven tracks and features Baker accompanied by Herbie Mann on flute and Pepper Adams on baritone sax. They are backed by Bill Evans on piano, Kenny Burrel on guitar, Paul Chambers on bass and Connie Kay on drums.

The last two tracks were recorded during the January 1059 session and feature the same line up except Philly Joe Jones replaces Kay on drums.

Tracks 11 through 13 are the album titled [[ASIN:B000UBPTNC Chet Baker In Milan]] that was recorded for the Jazzland label in Milan, Italy on September 25 and 26, and October 6, 1959. The first session produced track 10 and the September 26 session recorded tracks 11 through 14.

=========

Bill Evans on piano led a rhythm section comprised of Earl May on bass and Clifford Jarvis on drums. On the July 22 session that produced the remainder of the tracks Bob Corwin replaced Evans on piano.

title: Definitely essential for fans
text:
One of the most represented artists in my jazz library is Mann. He is somewhat controversial for evolving his music into something more commercial, but to me he is an innovator and he definitely thinks, composes and plays outside of any rigid box purists would like to see him constrained by. I will admit that I tempted at times to join the purists, but I keep purchasing his albums and this set is a treasure for me.

The sound quality is top notch. As always audiophiles will find something to lament, but I do not have megabucks invested in high-end gear so I cannot tell the difference. If you are picky about sound approach this with some caution. If you intend to rip the tracks to MP3 files then I think you will love this set. Note: lately Real Gone Jazz - this label - has been issuing these albums in MP3 format only. I think it's a step forward, but apparently this one has not made it to that format at the time of this review.

Documentation is so scant that it's a joke so I tracked down the source albums and background information on them. On the source albums linked below most have product pages with sound samples. This was recorded live at the Storyville Club in Boston on October 28, 1951.
