Indeed, on a few tracks he played his tenor like an alto with blazing speed. However, there is nothing I can put into words that could convey as much as the sound samples of the tracks. While they are missing from this page at the time of this review you can listen to them on the first twelve tracks of this set: [[ASIN:B009LRQ8U4 Stan Getz: Eight Classic Albums]].

The line-up backing Getz includes a stellar rhythm section led by Al Haig on piano, with Jimmy Raney on guitar, Teddy Kotick on bass and Tiny Kahn on drums.

Haig's playing in particular is interesting if you are a fan because you can hear subtle changes here from his earlier playing. He still had the pyrotechnics when needed, but is more under the music supporting Getz. Ramey on guitar was highly regarded by his peers, but sadly never received the recognition he so richly deserved. Listen for him on the sound samples to hear what I mean. Kotick and Hahn are rock solid and provide the perfect foundation for the melody and harmony.

title: Early 1950s recordings featuring Getz backed by some greats
text:
At the time of this review this page had neither a track list nor sound samples. You can find not only the track titles, but listen to sound samples by going to the album titled [[ASIN:B00EAUX93Q The Jazz Collection Volume One]] and listening to the samples of tracks 13 through 20. The samples will tell you everything you need to know about the music. Plus the sound quality of this CD is well above average. The label, Fresh Sound Records, has done an excellent job of remastering it.

While the music brushes against the emerging subgenre that would be called hard bop, the ballad numbers are exquisite and you can clearly hear Lester Young's influence on Getz on those.

This album was recorded for Roost in three NYC sessions: The first session on January 23, 1951 recorded Penny and features Getz backed by Horace Silver on piano, Joe Calloway on bass and Walter Bolden on drums.

On the second session - August 15, 1951 - the following tracks were recorded: Yvette, Potters Luck, Wildwood and Melody Express. They feature Getz backed by Horace Silver on piano, Jimmy Raney on guitar, Tommy Potter and Leonard Gaskin on bass (depending on track) and Roy Haynes on drums.

The final session was on December 19, 1952 that recorded Autumn Leaves, Fools Rush In and Lullaby Of Birdland. Getz is backed by Duke Jordan on piano, Jimmy Raney on guitar, Bill Crow on bass and Frank Isola on drums.

title: A hidden gem
text:
How this escaped me I do not know, but I recently discovered this on a Stan Getz set called [[ASIN:B009LRQ8U4 Stan Getz: Eight Classic Albums]] and was blown away by both the line-up and the music itself.

Music first: listen to the sound samples on this page for that. To my ears it's incredible. I own a few Tjader albums and have been a fan from the first time I heard him on some early Brubeck albums. Getz is also one of my favorites. But to be honest, the cherry on top for me is Scott LaFaro. My treasured Bill Evans recordings are the ones that feature him and Paul Motian backing Evans. Put together with Vince Guaraldi on piano, Eddie Duran on guitar and Billy Higgins on drums and you have an all star ensemble playing incredible music.

This album was recorded for Fantasy in San Francisco on February 8, 1958. For me personally this one has moved up to my short list of favorite albums by either Getz or Tjader, and it gets frequent play time - especially when I am driving.

title: Decent pressing and totally true to the original 1959 release
text:
Before proceeding I want to disclose that I play this on a relatively cheap turntable connected to a computer via USB. That means that the signal I hear is digital even though it's coming from a vinyl platter. Still the sound quality is excellent and I can only imagine how it would sound on a proper, analog system.

Since there is no track list nor sound samples on this page at the time of this review I will provide them. Here are the tracks:
SIDE A
A1 Nina Simone: He's Got The Whole World In His Hands
A2 Chris Connor: Cottage For Sale
A3 Carmen McRae: Old Devil Moon
A4 Nina Simone: I Loves You, Porgy
A5 Chris Connor: Try A Little Tendernes
A6 Carmen McRae: You Made Me Care
SIDE B
B1 Nina Simone: For All We Know
B2 Chris Connor: What Is There To Say
B3 Carmen McRae: Too Much In Love To Care
B4 Nina Simone: African Mailman
B5 Chris Connor: Good Bye
B6 Carmen McRae: Last Time For Love
You can listen to most (but not all) of the sound samples on this page: [[ASIN:B00AMCUTRU Nina Simone and Her Friends]].

The music on this album speaks for itself and I personally am happy to have what amounts to a compilation of three great vocalists. Nina's piano work is an added bonus. Listen to the sound samples and decide for yourself.

All of Nina's tracks were from the December 1957 session that produced her debut album titled [[ASIN:B00E7NIT5O Little Girl Blue (Remastered)]]. In fact some tracks from that album are repeated on this one. She is backed on the tracks on this album by Jimmy Bond on bass and Al 'Tootie' Heath on drums.

Carmen McRae's tracks were all recorded in NYC on October 6, 1954. She is backed by an ensemble comprised of Herbie Mann on flute and tenor sax, Mat Mathews on accordion, Mundell Lowe on guitar, Wendell Marshall on bass and Kenny Clarke on drums.

For Chris Connor the tracks were recorded in separate sessions in August 1954. Try a little tenderness and What is There to Say were recorded in NYC on August 9 and 11, 1954 featuring Connor backed by a drummerless trio comprised of Ellis Larkins on piano, Everett Barksdale on guitar and Beverly Peer on bass. The other two tracks by Connor were recorded in NYC on August 21, 1954 and feature Connor backed by Ronnie Odrich on flute and clarinet, Don Burns on accordion, Joe Cinderella on guitar, Vinnie Burke on bass and Art Mardigan on drums.

I think the highlight is Nina Simone, but I also love Carmen Mcrae's tracks. In fact I love all three. this is more of a compilation of Bethlehem's top female vocal talent in the 1950s, although it was released after Nina had left the label on not so good terms. But that is another story and has nothing to do with the wonderful music on this album.

title: Beautiful remastering of Nina's debut album
text:
The remastering on this disc is superb to my ears and you can get a taste of not only the music but the sound quality by listening to the samples on this page. Those should guide you more than anything I can possibly write. Let your ears be the judge.

I have always loved this album because many of my favorite Nina Simone recordings are contained on it. While we all have different tastes I will reveal that my favorite track is My Baby Just Cares for Me. That was the song that hooked me on Nina in the first place and is one I often play. It's been covered well by others, but the way Nina sings (and plays) it makes it her song. I believe the rendition on this album is the definitive one. Of course that is me revealing my personal tastes and if you disagree I am sure your favorites are equally as valid. Frankly there is not a single dud on this album. At least to my ears.

For background information Nina recorded this album in December 1957 for the Bethlehem label in NYC. This CD contains all of the tracks that were released on the original album in 1958. Since it was originally released in mono the remastering to update the sound on this release is remarkable in that it does not have that unnatural sound of early stereo circa 1958 (subsequent releases after the first pressing by Bethlehem were in stereo - or what passed for it back then.)

Nina is backed by Jimmy Bond on bass and Al 'Tootie' Heath on drums. Her virtuoso piano playing on this album is reason enough to grab it. Her vocals are as impressive as her command of the piano. If you are just discovering Nina I recommend that you also check out this compilation, which contains most of this album: [[ASIN:B0052Q2QG8 Nina Simone Her Greatest Hits]].

title: A lucky accident
text:
By any measure a lucky accident is called a serendipity and my finding this album fits the definition. I was searching for Charles Mingus' tune of the same name and came across this album. After one listen I was sold.

Marsalis, like his brother Wynton, composes and performs with more than a little homage to earlier musicians who defined and refined jazz. That is plainly evident on the title track, Scenes in the City, that is true to the version Charles Mingus composed and released on his 1957 album titled [[ASIN:B009D0N370 A Modern Jazz Symposium of Music and Poetry]]. In fact, each track on this album is an homage to Marsalis' influences or even his contemporaries whom he admired. More importantly he composed three of the six tracks on this album (tracks 1, 3 and 4).

I could babble on, but the best way to get a sense of this album is to listen to the sound samples. You will certainly hear Marsalis' hard bop influence from his short stint with the Jazz Messengers. That he can perform a ballad with beauty is evidenced by his playing on Parable. Overall you can hear echoes of Sonny Rollins and John Coltrane - among others - in Marsalis as well as his own playing. Even the short snippets from the sound samples will bear me out on that point.

If you love hard bop with a more modern flavor this is a great album.

title: One of my favorite Mingus albums
text:
Take my claim in the title with a grain of salt because I never heard a Charles Mingus album that I didn't love. However, the track titled Scenes in the City is reason enough for me to love this album. The words were penned by Loone Elder and Langston Hughes and spoken by Melvin Stewart. While to many this track may be obscure Branford Marsalis actually covered it in the early 1980s ([[ASIN:B0000025WX Scenes in the City]]).

While there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review you can listen to snippets from each track on the MP3 version of this album's page at [[ASIN:B009D0N370 A Modern Jazz Symposium of Music and Poetry]]. Let those guide you.

Do not let this album title fool you. There is no other poetry or vocals on it. Personally I was a little disappointed because the few songs that Mingus composed with words - like Scenes in the City and The Clown - are among my favorites and show another dimension to his genius.

Another reason I love this album is the obvious tribute to Duke Ellington in the other compositions on the album. And the music is along the same lines as the bluesy, gospel-tinged songs on Ah Um and Oh Yeah (both of which are why I am a Mingus junkie in the first place.)

This was recorded for the Bethlehem label in NYC in October 1957 and released the same year. The line up consisted of Clarence Shaw on trumpet, Jimmy Knepper on trombone, Curtis Porter (who would later be known as Shafi Hadi) on tenor and alto sax, Bob Hammer and Horace Parlan on piano, Charles Mingus on bass and Dannie Richmond on drums. Melvin Stewart is on vocals on Scenes in the City.

title: Even if you have one of these album this is a great find
text:
Fresh Sound Records is quickly becoming one of my favorite labels for combining hard to find albums into sets priced reasonably. Moreover, I love their sound quality and this album is no exception.

It's hard enough to find decent recordings of Lem WInchester, so even if you own one of the two albums on this disc it's priced to still be a bargain. While there are no sound samples on this page (at the time of this review) the pages of the two source albums do have them and I encourage you to give them a listen.

Here is what is on this album: tracks 1 through 6 comprise [[ASIN:B001ZNC61W Winchester Special]]. This album was recorded for Prestige at Rudy van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs, NJ studio on September 25, 1959 and features Winchester and Benny Golson on tenor sax backed by Tommy Flanagan on piano, Wendell Marshall on bass and Art Taylor on drums.

The remaining tracks are the album titled [[ASIN:B007ZB87KM Another Opus]] that was recorded on June 4, 1960 at Rudy van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs, NJ studio. This album features Frank Wess on flute and tenor sax and a rhythm section comprised of Hank Jones on piano, Eddie Jones on bass and Gus Johnson on drums. It also features three of Winchester's own compositions.

title: A hidden gem with one of my favorite Jazz Messengers line-ups
text:
If you will pardon the pun this album is off the beaten path of Jazz Messenger albums. I do not know how it managed to slip past me for years, but it's quickly become one of my favorites.

While I can cite the line-up or the fact that all but two tracks are Jazz Messenger alumni compositions, the essence is in the music itself. If you are looking at the CD version's page there are, sadly, no sound samples at the time of this review. There are samples on the MP3 album's page at [[ASIN:B000TRS6IM The Big Beat (The Rudy Van Gelder Edition)]]. Give those a listen to get an idea of the music.

While the samples are short, if you are familiar with this edition of the Jazz Messengers with Lee Morgan on trumpet and Wayne Shorter on tenor sax you will find the compositions to be familiar sounding. Not repetitive, but familiar because three of the tracks (1, 2 and 5) are Wayne Shorter compositions and one (Dat Dere) was penned by Bobby Timmons who is on piano on this album. Alumni Bill Hardman wrote a song as well (Politely).

The album was recorded at Rudy van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs studio for Blue Note on March 6, 1960. Morgan, Shorter and Timmons are backed by bassist Jymie Merritt and, of course, Blakely on drums. This is hard bop at its best, albeit with a mellower edge that characterized the group with Morgan and Shorter in front. It's still hot and it's still driving, but is more complex and cerebral to my ears.

title: Late Lem Winchester albums that are essential for fams
text:
This set contains two complete Winchester albums plus tracks from two others led by Etta Jones on which Winchester was a sideman. I love this one because it shows the contrast between Winchester's percussive style of playing the vibraphone on instrumental albums and his ability to support a vocalist on Jones' albums.

Sadly there are no sound samples on this page at the time of this review. However, on the Nelson/Winchester co-led album and the Etta Jones albums in which Winchester is featured the source albums do have sound samples. Allow those to convey the essence of the music.

All of these tracks were recorded in 1960. The following provides the background information for each:

The first eight tracks on Disc One are the out-of-print album titled 'With Feeling' that was recorded for Prestige/Moodsville. The recordings were made at Rudy van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs, NJ studio on October 7, 1960 with Winchester as session leader backed by Richard Wyands on piano, George Duvivier on bass and Roy Haynes on drums.

All of the remaining tracks on that disc, and the first three on Disc Two are a collaboration between Oliver Nelson and Winchester titled [[ASIN:B000000Z86 Nocturne]]. This album was recorded just prior to the above on August 23, 1960. It was also recorded for Prestige/Moodsville made at Rudy van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs, NJ studio. The line-up features the same line-up with the addition of Oliver Nelson on both alto and tenor saxophones.

On the remaining tracks Winchester is a sideman on albums led my Etta Jones. Tracks 4, 7 and 9 are from the album titled [[ASIN:B000UBRR9G Hollar! (Remastered)]] that was recorded at Rudy van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs studio on September 16, 1960. Jones is backed by Oliver Nelson on tenor saxophone,, Lem Winchester on vibes, Richard Wyands on piano, George Duvivier on bass and Roy Haynes on drums. The remaining tracks are from the same session with the same personnel, but were released on the album titled [[ASIN:B000UBJACS Something Nice]].

title: Where it all started
text:
This is the Messenger's debut album - the one that launched a band that would come to be known as a veritable incubator of talent. I could wax both poetic and enthusiastic about this album, but there is nothing I can possibly say that will convey more about the music than the sound samples. If you are in the CD version of this album's product page (at the time of this review) there are no samples, but there are on the MP3 album's page at [[ASIN:B00138J8O2 The Jazz Messengers]]. Give those a listen because each musician's playing can be heard at least a few tracks, and the overall performance of each song is captured.

The first seven tracks on this album are those that comprised the original release in 1956. The bonus tracks here are from the same session - they just were not packaged into the original US version of the album. Interestingly most of the tracks on this album are Hank Mobley compositions (1, 5, 7, 8 and 10 through 12), which showcase his creative genius since he was just 26 when this album was recorded. Horace Silver also contributed two compositions (tracks 2 and 4), so for a debut album the producer took a risk not often taken back then by allowing an album of predominately original material to be recorded.

All of the tracks were recorded at Columbia's 30th Street Studios in NYC on April 5 and May 4, 1956 with Donald Byrd on trumpet accompanied by Hank Mobley on tenor sax, and backed by Horace Silver on piano, Doug Watkins on bass and Art Blakey on drums. For an inaugural album this one is special for both the fact that some young musicians were allowed to contribute their own compositions and the way the ensemble played them: with fire and passion.

title: Jones' first three albums as a leader
text:
This is a three album set that features Jones' first three albums as a leader. Not only do they showcase his abilities on both bass and cello, but his ability to lead large ensembles. These albums were all recorded while he was a member of Cannonball Adderley's quintets and sextets, and a large number of sidemen in this set are from those groups.

Although there are no sound samples on the CD version at the time of this review there are on the MP3 album's page at [[ASIN:B00FMVUJEO Sam Jones Cello & Bass. The Soul Society + the Chant + Down Home]]. Let those guide you. The music is definitely hard bop and has some all star musicians on each track. If you are familiar with Adderley's work you will be right at home with these albums, and the cello (and on some tracks flute) add a wonderful dimension to the hard bop genre that this set represents.

Here are the albums and who performed on them:

The first eight tracks is Jones' debut album titled [[ASIN:B000000Z80 Soul Society]] that was recorded for Riverside in two March 1960 sessions in NYC. On the March 8 session the line-up consisted of Nat Adderley on cornet, Jimmy heath on tenor sax, Charles Davis on baritone sax and Jones on cello. The rhythm section was comprised of Bobby Tommons on piano, Keter Betts on bass and Louis Hayes on drums. This session produced tracks 1 through 4. The remaining four tracks were cut during the March 10 session with Blue Mitchell on trumpet, Jimmy heath on tenor sax and Charles Davis on baritone sax. The rhythm section was comprised of Bobby Tommons on piano, Jones on bass and Louis Hayes on drums.

Next eight tracks are the album titled [[ASIN:B000000Z9D Chant]] that was recorded for Riverside at the Plaza Sound Studios in NYC on January 13 & 26, 1961. Track 12 on Disc One and tracks 1 through 3 on Disc Two were recorded during the January 13 session that featured a large ensemble comprised of Nat Adderley on cornet, Blue Mitchell on trumpet, Melba Liston on trombone, Cannonball Adderley on alto sax, Jimmy Heath on tenor sax and Tate Houston on baritone. The rhythm section was equally large with Victor Feldman on piano, Les Spann on guitar, Jones on bass and Louis Hayes on drums.

Tracks 9 through 11 on Disc One and track 4 on Disc Two were recorded during the January 26 session. Personnel were the same brass and reed members as the first session accompanying Jones on cello. The change up was in the rhythm section, comprised of Victor Feldman on vibraphone, Wynton Kelly on piano, Keter Betts on bass and Louis Hayes on drums.

The remaining eight tracks are the album titled [[ASIN:B000000ZA2 Down Home]] that was recorded in NYC for Riverside on June 25, and August 15 and 16, 1962. For 'Round Midnight, Falling in Love with Love and O.P. the line-up is Les Spann on flute, Jones on cello and a rhythm section comprised of Joe Zawinul on piano, Israel Crosby on bass and Vernel Fournier on drums (the latter two of Ahmed Jamal Trio fame.) Those tracks were recorded during the June 25, 1962 session.

All of the remaining tracks are from the August 15, 1962 session and feature Snooky Young, Blue Mitchell and Clark Terry on trumper, Jimmy Cleveland on trombone, Frank Strozier on flute and alto saxophone, Jimmy Heath on tenor sax, Pat Patrick on baritone sax and flute. Depending on the track Joe Zawinul and Wynton Kelly were on piano, Jones on cello and bass depending on the track (when he is on cello Ron Carter takes over on bass) and Ben Riley on drums.

title: A tribute from one great to another
text:
Peterson perfectly captured Sinatra's innate sense of swing in each track. More impressive is how he nailed Sinatra's phrasing. I am not surprised that he had the chops to pull it off - of that I would never have any doubt. I was pleasantly surprised, though, that Oscar would alter his signature style to ensure that you could hear Sinatra in every note. That is what a tribute should be, and this album sets the standard.

Listen to the sound samples for a taste of what I am trying to convey about the music. As for the musicians, Peterson, Ray Brown on bass and new (at the time of this recording) member Ed Thigpen on drums are simply superb. Even in the few seconds per sample you can hear a seamless ensemble that is playing with taste. I am sure Sinatra was more than a little pleased when this was released in 1959.

In addition to the music the tracks selected for this album could not be more perfect. Some songs with which Sinatra would be later associated - Strangers in the Night and My Way - has yet to be written, although Come Fly With Me is conspicuously missing from the set list. But I am not quibbling. I am so pleased with what is on this album and how it's played that I feel fortunate to own it.

This is one more example of Peterson's versatility as a musician, and one of many amazing albums he, Brown and Thigpen recorded in 1959. In less than three months after the May 1959 session that produced this album the trio would go to Chicago and produce ten classic albums in the short span of July 14 to August 9. I sometimes consider this album as a warm up for that marathon series of sessions.

title: Beautifully shot and great music
text:
I've always loved this particular line-up of Cannonball's various quintets and sextets. This sextet has the versatile Yusef Lateef on not only tenor sax and flute, but oboe. There is a Chico Hamilton quality to both performances on this DVD. My only lament is that bassist Sam Jones was not given the opportunity to display his talents in cello when Lateef was on oboe.

I also love the beautiful contrast of black and white video that adds a wonderful visual effect to the music itself.

This DVD totals nearly an hour and forty minutes that captures two European performances. The first performance is from March 24, 1963 in Lugano, Switzerland amd features performances of the following songs:
Jessica's Day
Angel Eyes
Jive Samba
Bohemia After Dark
Dizzy's Business
Trouble in Mind
Work Song
Unit 7

The second clip is from a broadcast two days earlier on March 22, 1963 from Baden-Baden, Germany. The songs played during this much shorter set are:
Jessica's Day
Brother John
Jive Samba

The full sextet in both sets are Cannonball on alto accompanied by brother Nat on cornet and Yusef Lateef on tenor sax, flute and oboe. The rhythm section is comprised of Joe Zawinul on piano, Sam Jones on bass and Louis Hayes on drums.

If you are a fan this ranks up there with some of Cannonball's other video performances including the May 12, 1964 BBC broadcast of Jazz 625 featuring Adderley's sextet and Ralph Gleason's October 24, 1961 broadcast of Jazz casual (to name two of my favorites among more than a few videos of Adderley.)

title: Early quartets from 1951-52
text:
This album is a collection of Brubeck's earlier quartets with all of the tracks recorded for Fantasy Records. These are interesting because he and Paul Desmond on alto sax had established the basic sound long before bassist Gene Wright and drummer Joe Morello would join them for the 'classic quartet' era.

One other thing that is interesting is even though recording technology was relatively crude in the very early 1950s the sound quality on this album is more than acceptable. I have noticed that about a number of albums I own that were released by Fantasy during that era.

Listen to the sound samples to ensure this is what you are looking for. The reason I mention this is because many folks are so imprinted with the classic quartet that they are put off by the prior line-ups. Also the samples will give you a sense of the sound quality.

For me this album contains some of Paul Desmond's better work. Yes, he improved with age, but there is a quality to his alto sound here that draws me in.

Here is the background information for the tracks:

Tracks 1, 3 through 5 and 12 were recorded in Sam Francisco in November 1951. Dave and Paul are backed by Wyatt Ruther on bass and Herb Barman on drums.

Tracks 6 through 9 were recorded in San Francisco in August 1951. Dave and Paul are backed by Fred Dutton on bass and Herb Barman on drums.

Tracks 2, 11 and 13 through 17 were recorded live at the Surf Club in Los Angeles in September 1952 with the same line-up except Lloyd Davis replaces Herb Barman as the drummer.

This is truly a peek into the past with respect to Brubeck's quartets. If you are a fan the tracks on this album are well worth exploring. If you happen to play alto sax I would strongly recommend this as a near essential album. Desmond = to me - is the centerpiece.

title: Beautiful arrangements beautifully played
text:
This is one of a handful of albums I turn to after particularly stressful days. It's soothing, but I marvel at the arrangements and the deep feeling each musician contributed. Don't take my word for it - listen to the sound samples. Each short snippet is truly indicative of the mood of the entire track. No long prelude or intro followed by faster tempos. Pure chill music that is played from the heart.

One thing that is great - to me anyway - is there are three of Nelson's own compositions on this album (tracks 1, 2 and 4.) It's a testimony to Prestige's Moodsville producer's foresight to take a risk and allow that. Most labels played it safe back in that era. Of course having Ellington's In a Sentimental Mood in the list is a cherry on top. Again, for me since I am an Ellington fan. The final thing about this album that I love is the fact that Lem Winchester is a member of the ensemble. I have every album he ever recorded that features him, which is what led me to this one in the first place. That's not to diminish the contributions of the other members of the ensemble: Nelson's command of both alto and tenor saxophones on this album is impressive, as are Richard Wyands' piano work, and the outstanding contributions made by George Duvivier on bass and Roy Haynes on drums.

This album was recorded at Rudy van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs, NJ studio on August 23, 1960 and released the next year. Wichester would lead the same rhythm section two months later to record the album titled [[ASIN:B009V8T0CQ Lem Winchester With Feeling]].

title: Parlan's first six albums as a leader plus one with Dexter Gordon
text:
This set comprises Parlan's first six albums as a leader - all for Blue Note - plus one led by Dexter Gordon. This incredibly prolific output was accomplished between 1960 and 61, and does not account for all of the recorded work Parlan did during that period.

I especially love the way this set and the first six albums in particular allow a glimpse into Parlan's professional growth. And it is evident even though some of the albums in this set were recorded almost back-to-back. Part of Parlan's success can be attributed to bassist George Tucker and drummer Al Harewood. They are on every album and grew with Parlan. Another thing I love is the collaborations with Stanley and Tommy Turrentine who are on two of these albums, as well as the final album featuring both Freddie Hubbard and Dexter Gordon on the only album in this set not led by Parlan. Lest I forget, the album featuring Booker Ervin and Grant Green is also priceless.

Instead of babbling on I will answer the two burning questions you may have. First, how is the sound? To my ears it is not only excellent, but I did not experience the media flaws that another reviewer reported. Second, what is in this set? I have taken the time to track down the background information of every album in this set, as well as to link to individual albums. Unfortunately almost no albums linked contain sound samples, but there are sound samples for every track on this page: [[ASIN:B00ESXJX26 The Jazz Collection]]. Let those be your true guides.

Note: Each of the seven albums in this set were recorded for Blue Note at Rudy van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs, NJ studio. Here is what this set contains:
==========
DISC ONE
==========
[[ASIN:B004C6QET4 Movin & Groovin]]: Parlan's debut album as a leader that was recorded on February 29, 1960. He is backed by Sam Jones on bass and Al Harewood on drums. Tracks are:
01. C Jam Blues
02. On Green Dolphin Street
03. Up in Cynthia's Room
04. Lady Bird
05. Bag's Groove
06. Stella by Starlight
07. There Is No Greater Love
08. It Could Happen to You

[[ASIN:B000005H93 Us Three]]: Recorded April 20, 1960. Bassist George Tucker joins the trio, giving Parlan a solid, long term rhythm section of Tucker and Harewood. Tracks are:
09. Us Three
10. I Want to Be Loved
11. Come Rain or Come Shine
12. Wadin'
13. The Lady Is a Tramp
==========
DISC TWO
==========
The first two tracks are Us Three continued from the previous disc.
01. Walkin'
02. Return Engagement

[[ASIN:B002WY66I2 Speakin' My Piece (XRCD24 Master)]]: Recorded on July 14, 1960. The Parlan-Tucker-Harewood trio joined by Tommy Turrentine on trumpet and Stanley Turrentine on tenor sax. Tracks are:
03. Wadin'
04. Up in Cynthias Room
05. Borderline
06. Rastus
07. Oh So Blue
08. Speakin' My Piece

[[ASIN:B001CRGTLO Headin' South]]: Recorded on December 6, 1960 with Parlan on piano backed by Tucker and Harewood, plus Ray Barretto on congas. Tracks are:
09. Headin' South
10. The Song Is Ended
11. Summertime
12. Low Down
13. Congalegre
==========
DISC THREE
==========
The first three tracks are Headin' South continued from the previous disc.
01. Prelude to a Kiss
02. Jim Loves Sue
03. My Mother's Eyes

[[ASIN:B003ZXOETC On The Spur Of The Moment (XRCD24 Master)]]: Recorded on March 18, 1961 and is another collaboration between the Parlan-Tucker-Harewood trio and brothers Tommy Turrentine on trumpet and Stanley Turrentine on tenor sax. Tracks are:
04. On the Spur of the Moment
05. Skoo Chee
06. And That I Am So in Love
07. Al's Tune
08. Ray C
09. Pyramid

[[ASIN:B001O12TIU Up & Down]]: Recorded on June 18, 1961. Parlan, Tucker and Harewood are joined by Grant Green on guitar and Booker Ervin on tenor sax. Tracks are:
10. Books Beat
11. Up and Down
==========
DISC FOUR
==========
The first four tracks are Up and Down continued from the previous disc.
01. Fugee
02. The Other Part of Town
03. Lonely One
04. Light Blue

[[ASIN:B0002IQ9RI Doin Allright]]: This album was recorded on May 6, 1961 and is led by Dexter Gordon. Gordon's tenor sax is accompanied by Freddie Hubbard on trumpet with Parlan, Tucker and Harewood holding down the rhythm section.
05. I Was Doing All Right
06. You've Changed

title: Solid three album set from Wes' later Riverside era
text:
This is a three disc set that contains an album on each disc. There are no sound samples on this page so I am going to link to the original album product pages which contain sound samples. The sound quality on the three discs in this set is uniformly excellent and beautifully mastered (to my ears).

DISC ONE contains the album titled [[ASIN:B00004UEIC Incredible Jazz Guitar (20 Bit Remaster)]] that was recorded for Riverside at the Reeves Sound Studios in NYC on January 26 and 27, 1960. Wes is backed by a strong rhythm section comprised of Tommy Flanagan on piano, Percy Heath on bass and Al Heath on drums. You can listen to sound samples on tracks 17 through 24 of a compilation titled [[ASIN:B00EI17QMM The Jazz Collection]].

DISC TWO contains the album titled [[ASIN:B000000Y5C Movin Along]] that was recorded for Riverside at the United Recording Studios in Los Angeles on October 12, 1960. Wes is accompanied by James Clay on tenor sax and flute, and backed by Victor Feldman on piano, Sam Jones on bass and Louis Hayes on drums. According to one discography Wes also played bass guitar on some tracks. Click on the link to the album linked to listen to sound samples.

DISC THREE contains the album titled [[ASIN:B00CTCI568 So Much Guitar! (Original Jazz Classics Remasters)]] that was recorded for Riverside at the Plaza Sound Studios in NYC on August 4, 1961. Wes is backed by a solid rhythm section comprised of Hank Jones on piano, Ron Carter on bass, Lex Humpheries on drums and Ray Barretto on congas. Sound samples for this album can be heard on tracks 45 through 52 of a compilation titled [[ASIN:B00EI17QMM The Jazz Collection]].

As you can see (and hear if you checked out the sound samples) this is a excellent selection of Wes' work for Riverside in the 60-61 time frame. He is still playing pure jazz and had yet to add a more commercial flavor. To my ears this is a golden era in his too-short career.

title: Album + bonus soundtrack
text:
This outstanding album is really the entire title album that was recorded in Los Angeles for Verve on October 11, 1957 (tracks 1 through 8) plus bonus tracks from a 1958 French movie titled Les Tricheurs. The sound samples on this page will tell you more about this album than I can possibly describe in words, so let those and your ears guide you.

Tracks 1 through 8 feature an all-star line up with Ellis accompanied by accompanied by Stan Getz on tenor sax, Roy Eldridge on trumpet, Ray Brown on bass and Stan Levey on drums. The music is every bit as energetic as the short sound samples hint at. And even with Getz and Eldridge dominating the melody line Ellis has ample space to solo.

The final four tracks were recorded in Paris, France on May 1, 1958 and have an even heavier star studded line up. Like the forst eight tracks this was also recorded for Verve and feature power pairings of Dizzy Gillespie and Roy Eldridge on trumpet, Coleman Hawkins and Stan Getz on tenor sax and a dynamite rhythm section comprised of Oscar Peterson on piano, Ellis on guitar, Ray Brown on bass and Gus Johnson on drums.

While Ellis was always amazing in smaller trio and quartet settings, he absolutely shines in these larger ensembles - and commands the same attention as some of the big dogs from that era.

title: Ahmed's third album - a little more conventional
text:
This is Ahmed's third album as a leader and is most straight jazz than the preceding two or the one that would come after it. There is still a fusion of East African indigenous and US jazz music, but in a less pronounced way. That said, the music is still exotic while more accessible to 1961 listeners whose tastes - for the most part - were rooted in more conventional styles.

I tested this LP on a low-end USB turntable and it sounds excellent. Unfortunately the gear I used will mask lower fidelity that better equipment would reveal so please factor that into your purchase decision.

At the time of this review there are no sound samples or a track listing. For the sound samples please do to this compilation album titled [[ASIN:B0053ZG86M The Essential Collection]]. The corresponding tracks are 1, 5, 7 through 9, and 15. The track list is:

SIDE A
A1 Nights On Saturn
A2 The Hustlers
A3 Oud Blues
SIDE B
B1 La Ibkey
B2 Don't Blame Me
B3 Hannibal's Carnivals

This was was recorded on May 23, 1961 at Rudy van Gelder's Englewood Cliffs, NJ studio. Personnel include Tommy Turrentine on trumpet accompanied by Eric Dixon on tenor sax, Bilal Abdurrahman on clarinet and percussion, Ahmed on bass, Calo Scott on cello and Andrew Cyrille on drum kit.

title: A rhythmic feast
text:
Before I jump into my boring details give the sound samples a run through. This is not the thunderous Art Blakey driving the Jazz Messengers. It is the synthesis of Blakey's influences when he spent time in Africa during 1948-49. While those influences cropped up in his playing this album is the music itself. Pure West African versus the more East African influenced jazz that Ahmed Abdul-Malik would record a year later in [[ASIN:B000UBMXGI Jazz Sahara]].

Note the subtle rhythms from the sound samples. The full tracks are actually mesmerizing, and the arrangements are way off the beaten path in one respect, but a direct connection to the roots of American music in another.

Not only is the music unique, but so is the line up. Blakey enlisted some top drum kit players to assist, including Papa Jo Jones, Art Taylor and Charles 'Specs' Wright. He also had a large percussion ensemble comprised of Sabu Martinez, Ubaldo Nieto, Evilio Quintero and Carlos "Patato" Valdes. The rest of the ensemble included Herbie Mann on flute, Ray Bryant on piano and Wendell Marshall on bass.

This album was recorded at the Manhattan Towers in NYC on March 7, 1957 for Blue Note. It's remarkable that all eight tracks here were recorded in a single session because there was a blending of musicians from multiple backgrounds. If you want music that is off the beaten path this is an album to consider. Let the sound samples on this page guide you.

title: Sketchy sound quality, but a gem for fans of Bird or Chet
text:
This is an informally taped jam session at the Trade Winds in Inglewood (a Los Angeles suburb). It was recorded by an avid music enthusiast named Bob Andrews of nearby Orange County. Andrews made the tape at the behest of the bassist in this session, Harry Babasin, in June 1952.

What impresses me most about this album is the pure white hot energy by the ensemble. This isn't the Chet Baker of ballads, but a man possessed and spurred on by the rest of the band. Sonny Criss holds his own with Bird, but there is no mistaking who the master of alto is when Parker does come in on his horn.

The line-up is Charlie Parker and Sonny Criss (alto saxophone), Chet Baker (trumpet), Al Haig (piano), Harry Babasin (double bass) and Larance Marable (drums). This album captured the second set (Bird was late arriving), and probably would have been forever lost to history had it not surfaced in San Diego in 1990. The sound is surprisingly good for an amateur recording, and the music, as I stated above, is full of energy. For me stumbling across this record is serendipitous and I do not take it for granted - it gets a lot of play time, especially when I am in my car.

title: Close your eyes and you'd swear it is Lester Young
text:
This is a compilation of sessions that was recorded in 1949 and 1950, but not released until 1967. The sound samples on this page not only convey the essence of thie album, but you would swear that Getz is channeling Lester Young. It's uncanny. Young - Pres - is one of my musical inspirations and this album had me fooled.

Note that Getz is only on tracks 1 through 8. The final four tracks are performed as a piano trio.

Track 1 was recorded in NYC on June 21, 1949 and features Stan Getz on tenor sax, Haig on piano, Gene Ramey on bass and bebop pioneer Stan Levey on drums. Of the five tracks recorded during that session as the Stan Getz Bop Stars only this one made it to this album.

Tracks 2 through 5 were recorded in NYC on July 28, 1949 as the Al Haig Sextet. These tracks feature Getz on tenor sax, Kai Winding on trombone, and Blossom Dearie's vocals on tracks 4 and 5. Haig leads a rhythm section comprised of Jimmy Raney on guitar, Tommy Potter on bass and Roy Haynes on drums.

Tracks 6 through 8 were recorded in NYC on January 6, 1950 and feature Getz on tenor sax, Junior Parker on vocals and Haig and his trio as the rhythm section (Tommy Potter on bass and Roy Haynes on drums.)

The final tracks were recorded in NYC on February 27, 1950 and feature Haig and his trio (Potter and Haynes).

title: THE Tjader album to own!
text:
Normally I refrain from caps and exclamation points to emphasize, but in the case of this album I lost control of myself. There is nothing I can write to describe the music on this album better than the sound samples on this page can convey. I need to add that while the sound samples should hook you they pale in comparison to the foll tracks.

The line-up alone will give a hint of the quality of the music. Cal is on vibes and is accompanied by Paul Horn on flute. Horn honed his skills with Chico Hamilton's Quintet and he brings some of that magic to this performance. The rhythm section is comprised of Lonnie Hewitt on piano, Al McKibbon on bass, Willie Bobo on drums and timbales, and Mongo Santamaria on additional percussion. Bobo and Santamaria are practically household names in Afro-Cuban music to this day. Less known is Al McKibbon - a wonderful bassist in any jazz subgenre - is the man responsible for Cal espousing Afro-Cuban music. All together this ensemble is on fire on this album and is why I am gushing bordering on hyperbole.

There tracks were recorded at the second Monterrey Jazz Festival in the Sunset Auditorium in Carmel, CA on April 20, 1959. The tracks here were originally released as Cal Tjader's Concert By The Sea, Volume 1 and Volume 2 by Fantasy records. Personally I believe that this album represents Tjader's finest recorded work - studio or live - and having both original albums combined here is wonderful.

title: A tjader gem from 1958
text:
This album was recorded in San Francisco for Fantasy Records in 1958. The music is the epitome of West Coast jazz and this album for unknown reasons is not as well known as it deserves to be. It's certainly a treasured part of my Cal Tjader library.

Unfortunately this page is missing a track listing and sound samples at the time of this review. I'll list the tracks below, but more importantly I recommend that you go to this page and listen to track 20 through 29, which is most of this album: [[ASIN:B00EHAJ1PO The Jazz Collection Volume One]]:

The tracks are interesting in that they are thematic. Each title has something to do with the city of San Francisco, and the music seems to perfectly capture the essence of the title subjects:

A SIDE
A1 Running Out 3:19
A2 Raccoon Straits 2:24
A3 The Last Luff 3:39
A4 Sigmund Stern Groove 4:37
A5 Coit Tower 1:35
A6 Triple T Blues 6:01

B SIDE
B1 Union Square 4:20
B2 Skyline Waltz 3:43
B3 Viva Cepeda 3:40
B4 Grant Ave. Suite 7:20

Personnel on the album are Cal on vibes backed by Manuel Duran on piano, Eddie Duran on guitar, John Mosher and Jack Weeks on bass (depending on track) and John Markham on drums.

This is some of the finest, most laid back jazz I have heard and it is a tribute to The City and the jazz scene there in the 50s and 60s. If you are a Tjader fan this is one that I consider to be essential (or at least strongly recommended.)

title: Early Tjader as a leader
text:
My first encounter with Tjader was when he was the drummer for early Dave Brubeck trio recordings. Fast forward to 1954 and he had developed his distinctive style on vibes as heard on this album (he also plays timbales on some tracks here.)

Listen to the sound samples on this page and you will hear how amazingly well Cal assimilated Afro-Cuban rhythms. Indeed, he had mastered a number of genres, but the flavor on these tracks echo George Shearing's influence on him, as well as other sources. For example his friend, bassist Al McKibbon, exerted a great deal of influence on Cal to immerse himself in this genre, which opened doors to other like minded musicians. McKibbon is not on this album, but the line-up clearly shows why the music on this album is true to form: Manuel Duran on piano, Carlos Duran on bass and dditional percussion by Edgard Rosales, Bayardo Velarde and Luis Miranda.

This album is This is credited as Cal Tjader's Modern Mambo Quintet. It was recorded in San Francisco in September 1954 for Fantasy Records. For me this stands as one of the better examples of Cal's professional evolution because the arrangements and the performances on this album foreshadow some of his best later work.

title: Essential Mingus for fans and fun for everyone else
text:
As of this review there are no sound samples on this page. You can listen to samples on tracks 14 through 17 on an eight album compilation titled [[ASIN:B00E63A5H0 The Jazz Collection Volume One]]. While the full tracks are works of genius (to me anyway) the samples are sufficient to convey the essence of this album.

In Mingus' own words he set out to create an album that had a strong swing. In that he succeeded. He also claimed to have created his first blues record. That, to me, is a stretch with the exception of Blue Cee. However, those are my opinions and you should depend on the sound samples to guide you and make up your own mind. Or just enjoy the music without over analyzing it. The bane of my being a musician is that I sometimes forget to just enjoy it and this is an album that begs for just that.

I will confess that my favorite track is "The Clown", which is narrated by Jean Shepherd of A Christmas Story fame. The other track that I consider to be a highlight is "Haitian Fight Song" in which Mingus takes a solo that shows his mastery of his instrument (I tend to forget what a virtuoso bassist he was because his antics and his compositional genius sometimes eclipsed his skill on bass.)

The album was recorded at the Atlantic Record Studios in NYC on February 12, 1957 (The Clown and Reincarnation of a Lovebird) and the remaining two tracks on March 13, 1957. Personnel are (besides Mingus and Shepherd): Shafi Hadi (who is credited as his birth name of Curtis Porter) on alto and tenor Saxophones, Jimmy Knepper on trombone, Wade Legge on piano and Dannie Richmond on drums.

title: A treasure from 1954
text:
Believe it or not but I have two different copies of this album (forgot I had it and purchased another). One could make a case that I am merely senile, but it can also be explained by the fact that this is a glimpse into Mingus' genius early on.

What I love about this album is that it is early Mingus establishing his own vision and path. In fact, this was his second album (the first was [[ASIN:B003ENX0QG Jazz Composers Workshop]].) You can already hear how he was to develop and evolve if you listen carefully and critically. His innovative use of non-traditional jazz instruments, such as Jackson Wiley on cello on What is This Thing Called Love, Minor Intrusion and Stormy Weather.

If you are a Mingus fan this is an insightful examination of his early work as a leader and one that I recommend. The album was recorded in December 1954 and released in 1955 by Bethlehem. It features Thad Jones on trumpet, John LaPorta on clarinet and alto sax, Teo Macero on tenor sax, Jackson Wiley on cello, Mingus on bass and Clem DeRosa on drums. Note: this album is also included on an eight track compilation titled [[ASIN:B00E63A5H0 The Jazz Collection Volume One]] (see tracks 34 through 37 on that page.)

title: Dynamic with the Trio & Pres, plus
text:
I am not going to dissect the music or give a dissertation on Pres or any of the other members of this session. Instead I am going to let the sound samples on this page convey the essence of this album and you can let your ears and personal tastes decide. I will say that this is one of my favorite albums and I will admit to being biased. Lester is my most significant musical inspiration. Not something you would expect from a drummer, but it's true.

Back to the album: this contains every track that was recorded on August 4, 1952 in NYC. Oscar's trio comprised of bassist Ray Brown and guitarist Barney Kessel was augmented by J. C. Heard on drums to 'fatten' the sound. Frankly I think Oscar, Ray and Barney would have done just fine on their own. A drummerless trio was a proven formula for them and would continue to be for another seven years. I do think that Heard does add something special though.

What makes this work so well is - to my biased ears - Lester's tone and phrasing foremost. But to be objective I also think that some of the magic is from Ray Brown's keen understanding of melody (something that is not often found in a bassist), and the rich harmonic support Kessel adds.

According to a discography I checked this album represents every track, including a fragment of I Can't Get Started on track 14 that was recorded during the session. As a parting note I will reiterate that I am very biased towards Lester, so take some of that I have written with a grain of salt. Let the sound samples guide you.

title: Two perfect backing groups for Anita
text:
First I would like to thank the reviewer of the very helpful February 18, 2013 review for including a track list, which was unfortunately not included on the product page. Since there are no sound samples on this page either I will provide links to the individual albums that comprise this set. If you follow those links you will be taken to product pages that do contain sound samples.

The first ten tracks is the album titled [[ASIN:B000V697T8 Anita O'Day And The Three Sounds]] that was recorded for Verve in 1963. Anita is on six of the tracks backed by the Three sounds, with the remaining four as instrumental performances by the Three Sounds. Gene Harris on piano brings a definite blues feel to each song, with a top notch rhythm section comprised of Andrew Simpkins on bass and Bill Dowdy on drums. They provide the perfect backing for Anita at this stage of her career because there is an edge to Simpkins and Dowdy that matches her own persona.

Different and a little more exotic are the remaining tracks, which are from the album titled [[ASIN:B000VRH2IU Time For Two]]. This collaboration with Cal Tjader is as well done as the pairing with the Three Sounds. Tjader brought to this album a strong sense of Afro-Cuban rhythms, as well as the ability to play laid back, straight-ahead jazz. The former played directly into Anita's percussive singing style, while the latter was a major comfort zone for Anita. There are two examples of music that showcase both the Latin and the straight-ahead pieces on this album: An Occasional Man for the former and I'm Not Supposed to Be Blue Blues for the latter. The chasm between those two styles showcases Anita's versatility.

If you are an Anita O'Day fan these two albums are a refreshing change from her more standard trio backing. Not that there is anything wrong with those, but these are like adding an exotic spice.

title: Interesting smaller group recordings by Norvo
text:
This is a wonderful cross section of some of Norvo's circa 1940s recordings. The best starting point to get a feel for the music is to listen to the sound samples on this page. Those will not only convey the sound quality and the music from this point in Norvo's career, but also showcases his versatility.

The first seven tracks are from an out-of-print album titled Improvisations. 1 through 4 were recorded in NYC on July 27, 1944 with Norvo on vibes accompanied by Aaron Sachs on clarinet and Teddy Wilson on piano, backed by Slam Stewart on bass and Eddie Dell on drums. Tracks 5 through 7 were recorded in NYC on NYC, October 10, 1944. These tracks are performed by a larger ensemble featuring Joe Thomas on trumpet, Vic Dickenson on trombone and Hank D'Amico on clarinet. The rhythm section has Norvo on vibes and xylophone, Teddy Wilson on piano, Slam Stewart on bass and Specs Powell on drums.

Tracks 8 and through 11 are from an album titled Red Norvo's Nine, and were recorded in Los Angeles. 8 and 9 were recorded on October 14, 1947 and feature a session with Norvo on vibes and an ensemble comprised of Bobby Sherwood on cornet, Benny Carter on alto sax, Dave Cavanaugh and Eddie Miller on tenor sax and a rhythm section featuring Arnold Ross on piano, Dave Barbour on guitar, Billy Hadnott on bass and Jesse Price on drums. Tracks 10 and 11 were recorded on November 28, 1947 with an all-star ensemble featuring Ray Linn on trumpet, Dexter Gordon and Jimmy Giuffee on tenor sax (with Giuffree doubling on alto sax), and a rhythm section comprised of Norvo on vibes, Dodo Marmarosa on piano, Barney Kessel on guitar, Red Callender on bass and Jackie Mills on drums.

The next five tracks are backing Kay Starr and were recorded in Los Angeles on December 1, 1947. Starr's vocals are backed by Dick Anderson on clarinet, Dave Cavanaugh on tenor sax, Norvo on vibes and a rhythm section comprised of Arnold Ross on piano, Jack Marshall on guitar, Red Callender on bass and Jack Turner on drums.

Remaining tracks are from an out-of-print album titled Red Norvo at the Xylophone that was recorded in 1947 and released in 1949. As the title implies these tracks feature Norvo on the xylophone and that alone has value to anyone who plays mallet instruments and wishes to study his technique on that particular instrument.

The book is lovely, but my continued pet peeve with books like this is the manufacturer’s insistence of printing on both sides of the damned pages. So you can’t frame one picture without losing the image on the other side. It’s annoying.  I’d gladly pay more for a book with printed images on only one side & on watercolor grade papers.  So instead I guess I will be yanking these out, scanning them, & printing them on my own watercolor papers so that I can use the images on both sides.  The paper just does not hold up to a lot of media of you choose to use both sides in my experience. Ever.  I believe I now own all, but one of JD books & I will be buying it for myself for Mother’s Day. Lol. I love her art. I love her stamps. I love this book, but I’m knocking a star bc printing on both sides is stupid imo when the book is meant to be used to create more art.  Why limit the artists by making us choose which side to use for framing or which side to use if we choose to cut one side up & decoupage it onto something. We are then paying double for half a book! title: Aweeeeesome.
text:
If you're looking for a comprehensive resource for NCLEX prep, look no further...this book is fantastic. Extensive topic coverage complete with rationales for every response. Prefer going online to take quizzes? No problem this book's got that, too. (Although the content online is a tad bit confusing to navigate, once you figure out how to get to the quizzes section, you won't forget.) I have several books for review and this one is my personal favorite. Some of my professors loan this text out to students, but I prefer 24/7 availability in my own home! :-) Happy studying, future nurses!

UPDATE: I saw sooo many reviewers having trouble getting to the online content to take system-specific quizzes that I decided to post instructions here on how to get to the right place.

1) Go to the Pearson Pegasus log-in page once you've set up online access, and log in.
2) Click on the book title on the left side of the website.
3) On the next page, on the left side near the top, you will see a menu bar that has the following options: "Today's View, Course Content, Grades, Communicate". Look just BELOW this menu bar and you will see the following options: "View All Content, Course Calendar, Learning Objectives."
4) Click on Learning Objectives.
5) On the left side, you will see the following options: "Client Need, Topics Areas, Integrated Process."
6) To take quizzes related to your system or topic of choice, click the plus sign for "Topics Areas".
7) Click on your system of choice.
8) On the right side, there are several options for that topic of study. Scroll down to the bottom-ish. You will see a heading called "Self Study" for that topic of study. Click on it.
9) A separate pop-up window will appear so that you may begin your quiz.

I hope this is helpful. If you have any problems or questions, feel free to comment below. Note that the online quiz portion only works with Internet Explorer and certain versions of Firefox, but not with Chrome.

title: Great Story!
text:
Cool Wind's Gate by Wayne Bernard Sr.

Many books and stories written about the antebellum south and Louisiana in particular, usually tell one of two tales... a life of ease and prosperity on a grand plantation or the atrocities committed against those same men and women in bondage whose slave labor enabled the life of ease and prosperity. Cool Wind's Gate though, while still set in pre-civil war Louisiana, gives a different accounting, a better way that could have been, one that I wished as I was reading it were true.
The story of Cool Wind's Gate grew out of the belief that slavery was wrong. Mr. Clem Collins of Wisteria plantation knew that to simply liberate his slaves wasn't enough. Without a means to care for their families and lacking protection from the prejudices and cruelty of the outside world it would do little good to set them free to starve or worse. He had a plan though, a broader vision of how a good life could be had by everyone. A life filled with well-earned respect, dignity and love. And Clem had Will Trahan, who would see to it that the vision of self-sufficiency and autonomy would become the reality.
Cool Wind's Gate is written simply in a straightforward way. I would have liked more descriptive features of the book's characters, but at almost 900 pages, the author gives us a very authentic story.

Howe and his army defeated the Birtish generals in their endeavor to take control Albany, New York City and the Hudson River. Nice large sized print (great for those of us over age 50) and an easy read which made it such I didn't want to put it down. This book would make a great present for the history buff in your life, especially if they are from the NY area.

title: Great full picture book, just love, love, love!
text: Absolutely amazing book. It is jammed with pictures and history and is truly impressive. This matches up to the standards of the Life series of picture book, with incredible never seen before photography and facts. This would make a terrific holiday present, especially for the WWII veterans in your life. But honestly, I have a son in the military who is in his early 30's who would love this just as much or even a younger child to show them the horrors of war. It makes a great coffee table/conversation piece book. I definitely recommend this for yourself or for someone you love.

title: Great book, lots of historical rarities, easy to read!
text: Excellent read by one of my favorite authors of all time Winston Groom (author of Forest Gump and the Aviator). I love reading history books, particularly American, and figured with the title of this book and with the author who wrote it, I could not go wrong. Nice size book, larger type (for my middle aged eyes) and once I started, I could not put it down. I read each General on individual days and I learned more about them then I ever knew from anything school books (or television) had ever taught me. I was particularly enamored by the colorful piece on General Patton. This would make a great gift for someone or just buy it for yourself.

title: A wonderful read. Great for the history lover in your life!!!
text: Absolutely wonderful book of two treasure hunters who set off to investigate and discover a pirate ship. Easy read, I found it next to impossible to put down. Robert Kurson tells a little known tale of intrigue and you almost feel like you are reading a fictional account with the way the wonderful story telling proceeds. I am now hooked on Kurson's writing style and intend to pick up Shadow Divers on Amazon as well. I could go on more, but in reading the other reviews on here, there is really little new to add. Great read, entertaining, will keep you mesmerized from start to finish.

title: Amazing recipes, beautiful book!
text: Of course, I found out about this cookbook as a result of being a huge fan of the television show. I immediately preordered and waited patiently for the book to arrive. I could not be more delighted! A great book chock full of delicious recipes for all courses and put together in an easy to follow format. I made the beef stew first and it was a tremendous hit with my family. Bravo Gabriele! You outdid yourself with this cookbook and I can't wait until the next one comes out!!!!

title: Another winner from National Geo!
text: I travel a lot. Have been to Rome three times and I am always looking for new places to explore. This National Geographic Traveler guide to Rome is incredible. I love these guides better than any other (think Rick Steves). They are comprehensive, colorful and all inclusive with a variety of maps and places to visit off the beaten track. I am returning to Rome again in November of this year and this guide will be with me all the way. Kudos to National Geographic, best tourist guide on the market today!

title: Amazing fictional book that reads like non-fiction
text: Trieste is one of the most amazing books I have read in ages. Normally, I do not like fictional accounts of historical events (given that the lines are usually blurred between reality and the author's spin on the truth). But Trieste is different. It is well written and the reader feels like they are in Italy during World War II and searching for Haya Tedeschi's son she had with a Nazi SS officer. Truly an emotional account, the reader is thrust back in history to one of the most horrific times one can imagine to be living in Italy. I would love to find the time to read this again as I think the read will be even better the second time around. I truly recommend Trieste to anyone who loves non-fiction and love/family stories. Kudos to Dasa Drndic

title: Simply Wonderful! Simply Italian
text: This is one of the nicest books/cookbooks I have ever owned. Illustrated beautifully, the insight to the world inside Harry's Bar (and kitchen) is well worth any price. I ordered this book as I am planning a trip to Venice at the beginning of April (fifth time to Italy, first time to Venice) and I was curious as to what the foods would be like (and to try some recipes for myself in advance). This book does not fail to deliver both. It also comes beautifully packaged in a sleeve and makes for perfect gift giving. I can't want to seek out and find Harry's when I go there next year and, if I am lucky enough to meet the owner, will thank them profusely for putting this together. Bravo!

title: Great pocket travel guide
text: I have been traveling to Italy at least once or twice a year for the last 5 years and I am hooked on the language, culture and people. This travel guide is great. Having visited most of the main cities several times (Rome, Florence, Venice), I was looking for a guide to assist me in looking for off-the-beaten path sites. I love this Lonely Planet guide. It is informative, beautifully illustrated and has many maps to help me get around as a single traveler. I have owned several Lonely Planet guides and I am never disappointed with the up to date and comprehensive information you get from them. It is convenient enough for me to carry in my purse, yet with enough information to be the only guide I will need. Kudos to Lonely Planet for another great travel guide! I highly recommend it for anyone looking to rent a car and travel into some of the lesser known areas of Italy.

title: Heart warming story
text: Loved this book. Don't pay attention to what the others have written about it being boring. I enjoyed every page and cried like a baby several times throughout. If you are an animal lover and love true stories, go for this book. I can honestly say I liked it double that of Marley and Me and would highly recommend this to everyone. Great read, won't want to put it down once you start.

title: Great read, especially for young people
text: I love the outdoors, animals, nature and true stories. This book encompasses the best of all of them. I found it to be truly inspiring and well written (to the point I couldn't put the book down and read it cover to cover). I highly recommend it to anyone who loves survival stories, true life experiences and animals (especially the glorious wolves). Great read for everyone, truly inspirational.

title: Just in time for my trip!
text: Going to Rome later this month and needed a guide book for my visit. I had signed up for several tours which were meeting at obscure tourist points. I had googled the internet to try to find where these places were and was only able to find one of them. I had figured that I would need to get to Rome and ask someone in the hotel (in my very broken Italian) where it was that I needed to go. In comes the Lonely Planet guide to Rome. First thing I did was go to find the locations I couldn't find anywhere else. As it turns out, the meet-up places I had been looking for were actual 'local aliases' that if you were a Rome resident you would know. The Lonely Planet guide had these listed both ways and I was not only able to read about the locales, but also locate them on the enclosed street maps. Kudos to Lonely Planet and their terrific tourist guides. I had used them before in Paris and Ireland, but never had needed them like I did this time. And forgetting all this personal information I needed, rest assured there is plenty of other tourist info like entry times and fees for tourist sites and reviews on restaurants as well. If you are going to Rome,  you need to bring this with  you!

title: Excellent traveler's resource!
text: I have been to the Tuscany/Florence region twice in the last year and have another trip planned for this October. I originally wasn't going to select this book, thinking I already knew everything I needed to about this most beautiful area of Italy. But I received this Frommer's book and I am finding it a tremendous read! I am finding information on little known towns (for example Livorno) which I had never heard about in my travels (it's called the Venice of Tuscany). The book is a perfect size for travelers, recommending some wonderful restaurants in the cities (some of which I will also be trying in October)and many little known towns and tourist attractions (in addition to the more well known Florence/Pisa/Lucca/Sienna attractions. The pictures are beautiful, maps are all inclusive and the guide is written in clear English (to assist when in the areas where some may not speak the language). Hours of operation of tourist attractions as well as entrance fees are all in there was well. If anyone is traveling to Italy and plans to spend any time in the Tuscany region, this is a must read and take along. I highly recommend for all!

title: Most wonderful book about Israel I have read
text: I actually made a pilgrimage to Israel in 2011 and used this book as a sort of a guide to the history and the legacy of the country and its people. I highly recommend this as a personal story which is relatable to anyone who wants to know more about their heritage and family. I learned a lot about this magnificent country and it was a very enjoyable read.

title: Disappointing at best
text: Buyer beware. I guess I thought at $15 this would be a regular size book. Of course, shame on me for not looking at the dimensions. This is a small almost pocket sized book with limited information in it pages are small with large type most with black and white pics). I never would have purchased this had I paid attention to the specifications. I would return it, but I used it in my 4 for 3 package and if I returned it, I would lose out. Disappointing, terrible purchase.

title: Excellent - Comprehensive guide
text: Used this Lonely Planet guide on two trips this year: Once to Rome and Umbria and the other time in Lucca/Pisa (Tuscany). It was informative and the maps and pictures were wonderful. With my limited knowledge of the Italian language, it was nice to have a guide, in English, which explained details of things (i.e. pubic transportation, hours of operation for museums and sightseeing, fees, etc). As a matter of fact, I used the bus almost exclusively when I was in Lucca to get to the airport and the city of Pisa and the Lonely Planet guide helped me with everything I needed to know. I used to be a Fodor's fan for travels in the past. However, I will now be purchasing the Discover series for whenever I go abroad (in fact, Discover France is next on my list for 2012). Highly recommend!!!

title: Informative book - not so easy to use
text: Got this book as part of the Vine program. I work a lot in excel with basic formulas and formats. My son in college learned a lot with excel that blew my mind. When I saw this book, I jumped on it thinking it would help enhance my knowledge of the application and allow me to accomplish some of the things I saw my son capable of doing. To be honest, I hate manuals and instructions. I was hoping this would have been more of a tutorial (like excel for dummies), but I found it somewhat complicated. I guess if I was looking to do a particular feature, I could look for it in the index and follow the instructions. But, I really was looking for more a tutorial that could step me through how to make more robust spreadsheets. If you are more technology savy than I am, this book may work for you. I just found it kind of cumbersome and complicated. I will keep it as a desk top reference in case I need specific help.

title: Standard Fodors
text: Great travel book on France. I have been there twice already and got this book for next summer's trip to Toulouse. Not rating it as a 5 star as I don't see any out of the way places or exotic finds for the experienced traveler. This book is great, though, with pictures and maps and is great for a first time visitor to France. As expected, a lot of the book is dedicated to the Paris area. If you are planning a trip to Paris in the near future, this book is a must have for any tourist new to the area.

title: Great book to travel with
text: I just returned from a week in Ireland and used the Lonely Planet Discover Ireland while traveling. I found it concise, colorful, chock full of information and containing loads of maps and visitor site information. I typically use Frommer's guides when I have gone to Europe in the past, so this was my first use of the Lonely Planet series. I would highly recommend the book for anyone traveling to the Emerald Isle as an alternative to what I feel can sometimes be the complexity of Frommers. I have also obtained the Lonely Planet guide to Italy which I have not, as of yet, been able to use. Hope to travel there in the late Fall time frame and will be reviewing that one as well upon my return. However, I am fully confident that the book will serve me as this one on Ireland did.

That being said, I was looking for more knowledge of all the contraversies that followed them throughout their career and loved it when I was offered this book. I devoured every page and found something to learn and gain insight on in every chapter. This book makes for a wonderful read or even a great present to make to someone who was a child of the 60-70's. It was an incredible eye opener for me. I highly recommend!!

title: Exactly what I needed

title: Tragic yet well written
text: I am having a difficult time deciding how to review Ablutions: Notes for a Novel. Although I must admit it was one of the most well written, interesting books I have ever read, I also found the stories to be tragic and depressing. I guess that's just how life is some times. I am rating it as a three star in the hopes that some readers will see it as the classic novel it has potential to be. But I am unable to move the rating to a 4-5 star as I think the author could have done better than some of the grotesque tragedies he was portraying in the second person story characters.

Perhaps it's because of the book claiming to be more family oriented, it may a more simplified version of cooking 101. I would highly recommend it for families with children in the the tween years where you are looking for things to do on a rainy/snowy day. I should have read the description a little more careful when ordering. It's a story filled with facts, legends, lore, science and history. A really wonderful read and makes an enlightened gift to give to your self or someone you love.

I will also say that the edition I had came with a sample audio CD as well, and I will be ordering the full version. There were moments I laughed and moments I cried, but most of all there were moments that brought me back almost 30 years to my childhood growing up in New York. title: Beginner to Mid-level Moodle User - Worth its value.
text:
Overall a good book to help Instructors, Faculty and new Instructional Technologist with limited to mid-level Moodle Knowledge.
Pictures are represent what you expect to see in Moodle from a faculty member's perspective to allow you to build your course and get it up online ready to go.
Chapter 1 - Developing an effective Online Course
-- Provides some reasoning on why and how regarding Moodle and teaching. It could provide Instructional Designers a reference to provide faculty who are questioning the process and over all course design.

The book covers a wide variety of areas to assist the course development process and more importantly how you will then use the course to teach effectively to students. It doesn't get to far into the weeds so if you need that level of fidelity then this isn't the best book for you (Experienced Moodle users moving from 2.x to 3.x version). Additionally, if you're experienced the beginning of each chapter on a bit of instructional design/pedagogy might put you off. I personally like the reminders as an Faculty Developer and Educational Technologist. Sometimes you just need to review the how and why to get better.

I like how the author has gotten into Workshops and Portfolios, two the least used modules I've seen implemented by faculty at 3 decent sized institutions. She provides explanations on why and how to use these sections to get most every one started and follow ups with examples on how to use them to further the learner's engagement

It's a good starter book for Moodle course design and implementation. Don't count on reading cover to cover in a day or so. But each chapter allows the reader the ability to jump to an area you need assistance with.

title: Up to date - good reference book
text:
Returning to academia after a few years of being out of the game for a few years.
I needed a book to update my educational technology and e-learning knowledge without proclaiming technology is the answer to elearning vs solid instructional design principles.

The book adheres sound instructional technology and design while providing the reader with updated information on Web 2.0 as it relates to elearning. The book was a good read, the references back and forth on how to use, design and facilitate elearning was very useful.
I was able to quickly bring my knowledge back into the current decade/year and make good use of the information as I designed faculty development modules for our professors as we expand our online, social media and blackboard integration into the classroom and across the learning spectrum.

text: First let me say that I am new to the vegan diet, so I have collected a handful of books I thought would help me... having said that - this cookbook has NO photos.  :(  But... it still has a long list of useful recipes.  Most are listed gluten free and soy free - if that matters to you.  At the top of each page and under the recipe name it tells you this info...  I haven't found any strange ingredients (meaning you can't find what you need at the local grocery store - as we live in a small rural town) and no super special pieces of kitchen equipment... so I consider that a bonus.  I am not a trained culinary chef and I manage to understand the process of these recipes... I am a fan of one pot cooking (in all fairness some of the recipes use more than one pot - but served in one bowl..), so this book appealed to me.  I like the Red Bean Gumbo (however I replace the green bell pepper with a red bell pepper as I am not a fan of green bell pepper and I omit the okra - not a fan of that either)...  very satisfying. In the book it mentions that "gumbo" is the African word for okra!  Hmm... I like gumbo... but sans the okra. haha.  In any case, I purchased this cookbook and a handful of others to help inspire me to try to eat vegan.  Now... if we could get them to add photos and a spiral back (to help keep the book open while you are using it in the kitchen) it would be a 6 star.  :)

text: My husband is a type 2 diabetic and we wanted to explore the vegan diet option to help... First I will say that this cookbook has NO photos.  I am always a little disappointed by this, but seems like more and more cookbooks these days are photo-less.  :(  On the upside, there is a very good informational (in my opinion as a vegan newbee) forward in this book with useful info about substitutes and options... The recipes seem to be fairly straightforward (no culinary degree needed or super special equipment) and tasty.  I really love the chilled watermelon soup - it's more delicious than one might think. Wish the book had photos and a spiral back to help keep it open while in use, but even without that I think this cookbook is worth owning if you are interested in trying the vegan lifestyle.

title: Easy Vegan Breakfasts and lunches
text: I am a Vegan beginner... so I was looking for cookbooks that were not too hard to follow and would offer some inspiration... this cookbook is great on all accounts.  So far, I haven't found anything too difficult or needing odd tools or ingredients so weird you can't find them...... so that's all a plus. It does say "Easy Vegan"... but just to be fair, I have found that vegan cooking can take a little more time for me as I am not accustom to it... yet...  I'm working on it.  One the best features in this cookbook are the photos!  So many cookbooks these days are without photos - which is not very inspiring - I mean - I get that the photos are expensive to add, but they make - or break a cookbook in my opinion.  One of our favorites is the peanut butter banana pancakes...  There are a lot of recipes using what you would expect... black beans, quinoa, lentils and the usual veggies and some nuts.  Honestly, if you're looking to venture into the possibility of a vegan diet, out of the 4 books I ordered, this one is the one I usually reach for.  Book and movie reviews are very subjective, and I get that.  I try to be as helpful as I can when reviewing such items.
