This is a very well written novel. The characters were very realistic, and it is easy to see that the author has first-hand experience in a hospital. If I could, I would give this novel ten stars.

title: Fascinating book for Everyone
text:
I have been a huge fan of Lonely Planet guidebooks ever since I first ordered one on Rome with kids as the target audience. I like the adult Lonely Planet guides, too, but when it comes to children, no one does it better than Lonely Planet. So when I had the chance to review this book, I jumped at it, and I was not disappointed.

"Lonely Planet Not for Parents Real Wonders of the World" has as its subtitle "Amazing Stuff to Know about the Coolest Places on Earth," and that just about sums up this book. The book is divided into eight major sections, each having seven to nine topics. Some of the major sections are Stupendous Structures; High Tech; Cultural Wonders; Hidden Places; Thrills, Spills, and Games; and Fright Night. Each sub-topic is composed of two pages loaded with a collage of photos and graphics, and while there is some text, it is not overwhelming. The topics are wide-ranging, from Barrow, Alaska, to Pompeii, to the catacombs, to outer space. While the guide is aimed at children (about age 8 and up, I would say), I am convinced that most adults would learn a thing or two from this book.

The book is oversize, so it is not a conventional travel book. Rather, it is a great "Let's find something interesting to read" book, one that I can see kids returning to again and again. It is well made with heavy paper and a sturdy hard cover, so it should last through several children. I give this book my highest recommendation.

title: Excellent guidebook
text:
I ordered this guidebook, Lonely Planet Hawaii, because my husband and I took an all-too-short trip to Hawaii earlier this year, and we are both eager to go back and experience our 50th state in a little more depth than we did the first time around. I was hoping that this guidebook would help, and I was not disappointed.

Hawaii is a beautiful and complex state, and this guide covers just about every aspect of it: people, culture, history, natural resources, ecology, and cuisine, to name just a few. The book helps the reader plan a trip based on his or her individual interests, whether they are artistic, historical, or nature-oriented. There are the usual "Where to Stay" and "Where to Eat" features, as well as some "Don't Miss This" features as well. If you are traveling with children, this book includes several child-friendly attractions to help you plan a trip that the entire family can enjoy. The book includes an up-to-date driving map that includes each island, helping in the planning of an itinerary. It should be noted that the maps are not street maps; rather, they give an overview of each island. If you want a street map, you will need to go elsewhere. (I suggest the Auto Club, which has superb maps that alone are worth the price of membership if you travel a great deal.)

In our previous travels, we have relied on Eyewitness Travel Guides, and if I were forced to select only one guide, I would prefer Eyewitness. I do not know if they have one on Hawaii, but I suspect they do. The advantage of the Eyewitness guides is the superb photography that accompanies many of the cultural and geographic entries. Eyewitness claims to be "The Guides That Show You What Others Only Tell You," and we have found this to be true.

However, this is not to denigrate the Lonely Planet Guide. It too has photographs, though far fewer than an Eyewitness Guide. It includes a wealth of information about Hawaii, so much so that I am convinced that even a native Hawaiian would learn a great deal about his state by surveying this guide. A tourist will find it extremely helpful and informative. Highly recommended.

title: Superb supplement to your new Apple laptop
text:
Like the many other "Teach Yourself Visually" books, "MacBook Pro" is an excellent book for anyone who has or is planning to get an Apple laptop but may want some help finding out about and navigating all that it has to offer.

"MacBook Pro" is set up logically, and the reader can easily find the area he or she wants to learn about and simply go through the step-by-step instructions. The photos are excellent, and they are photos, not diagrams or sketches. The index is easy to use as well, and you will definitely learn a great deal about your new Mac by using this handbook.

Highly recommended, especially for the technologically challenged.

title: Simply fantastic
text:
This is the latest of several "Teach Yourself Visually" books that my husband and I have ordered to help us use our electronic devices more fully. Like the others, "iPhoto for iPad" does not disappoint. In my opinion, these books are all you will ever need to help you use your devices more effectively.

First of all, the book assumes nothing more than that you have an iPad and the you want to work with your photos on it. The chapters are made to order for those of us for whom technology is decidedly not "second nature." They begin at the most elementary level imaginable--looking at your photos and experimenting with different ways of viewing them. From there, you learn how to import your photos and use the Cloud. There is a great chapter on organizing your pictures into albums and editing your photos with special effects. You learn to "photoshop" your pictures and use color and filters. There is a chapter on creating advanced photo effects that I am not ready for just yet, but I look forward to learning about sharing photos and making journals of our travels. We do not have an iPhone, but if you do, you will enjoy the chapter on iPhoto and the iPhone. It is important to note that you do not have to cover all these areas if you are not interested. The book is set up in such as way that browsing and selective learning are easy.

Second, I love that this book has photographs of exactly what you see on your own screen. Not diagrams or sketches, but real photographs. These photos accompany easy-to-follow, step-by-step instructions. They take nothing for granted, which I appreciate a great deal.

Third, I like the use of white space. The pages of this book are not cluttered up with "stuff" on every inch of space.

Finally, I really enjoy the sidebar "Question and Answer" sections that accompany almost every step, and I found the index complete and easy to use.

In short, if you are mystified about how to integrate your photos with your iPad (or even your laptop computer), this is the book for you. I cannot imagine that it would not be helpful to just about everyone. It has my highest recommendation.

title: Heartwarming tales for dog lovers
text:
Anyone who loves dogs will love and appreciate this book. "Devoted" tells the brief stories of 38 dogs and their human companions, and each one celebrates the bond that we humans have with our dogs.

I enjoyed all the stories, but I was especially touched by the story of Schoep (which I think is pronounced "Shep") and his owner, John Unger. Schoep was adopted by Unger from a shelter in Wisconsin, and he was probably the dog most in need and least likely to be adopted. Nonetheless, Unger wanted to adopt a dog that had been abused and help him realize his full potential. Unger worked tirelessly with Schoep and eventually transformed the dog into a wonderful pet. The best part of the story, though, is that, just as Unger had saved Schoep, Schoep eventually returned the favor, as only the thought of leaving Schoep alone saved Unger from killing himself at an incredibly low period in his life. Readers will love the photograph of Unger floating in the water with Schoep lying on his chest, asleep and perfectly content.

This is only one of the many stories of the fantastic intelligence, loyalty, inventiveness, and amusement that dogs offer in return for our custody of them. I was impressed by the variety of dog breeds that were represented in these stories, especially by the number of "pit bulls" that appeared. This breed has an unjustified reputation for vicious behavior, and this little book will do much to help readers overcome any prejudices they have. There were a few greyhounds as well, and as I have a cousin who works with greyhound rescue, I know firsthand how wonderful this breed is as a pet.

The book is replete with beautiful photographs as well: the reader sees each dog profiled and usually his or her owner as well. Each story is short enough to be read in only a few minutes, and each dog has something to offer that will just make you smile. I can see this little book as the perfect holiday gift for a "dog person."

It is hard to imagine that anyone would not enjoy this book. I highly recommend it.

title: Inspiring story of a gifted teacher
text:
Let me say at the outset that I am a retired English teacher, and I love books about school and inspiring teachers. When the opportunity to read an advance copy of this book was offered, I accepted with enthusiasm, and I was not disappointed.

"Drama High" is the story of the kind of teacher any parent wishes their child would have, Lou Volpe, who taught at Harry S Truman High School in Levittown, PA, for over 30 years. It traces his evolution as a teacher and as a person. Volpe's first attempts at theater were not successful, but in theater he had found his life's work, and he never stopped challenging himself or his students with ever more demanding and out of the mainstream drama.

"Drama High" is written by Michael Sokolove, a former student of Volpe, and although the respect and affection he has for Volpe are evident, they do not prevent him from giving a clear-eyed account of a year in the life of this remarkable teacher. In addition, we see the many challenges faced by urban teachers and students today, primarily through the lives of Volpe's cast members. In presenting "Good Boys and True," a play that pushes the envelope in several respects, Volpe knows that he is taking a risk, but that fact does not prevent him from going forward and entering the performance in the International Thespian Festival in Nebraska, the Cannes Film Festival of high school drama. Competition is fierce, and Volpe is facing schools with state of the art facilities and nearly unlimited resources. The story of his journey is one the reader will not soon forget.

One thing I loved about this book is its unabashed assertion that the arts matter. Today's emphasis on testing in schools has all but eliminated many arts programs, sapping the life of the school experience. Drama, music, dance, visual arts, all must take a back seat (if not be thrown out of the bus entirely) to test preparation. This is a terrible loss both for individual students and for society.

If you are interested in reading an excerpt from this book before you buy it, go to the New York Times website and find the Sunday magazine for September 15, 2013. There you will find an extended summation of "Drama High" entitled, "If All We Had Was a Bare Stage with One Light Bulb, We Could Still Do Theater." That title just about sums up Volpe's philosophy: Drama is so important, so central to life, we will do it any way we can.

One more thing: As I read this book, I was constantly reminded of a documentary film I saw a few years ago. "The Hobart Shakespearians" is about another inspiring teacher, this one in elementary school, who brings Shakespeare into his fifth or sixth grade classroom. He, too, was the sort of teacher you hope your child encounters at least once in his or her school career. You can get this film from Netflix, and I hope you do.

title: A valuable tool
text:
I ordered this book because my husband and I are thinking about setting up a living trust, and I was interested in seeing whether or not we could do this without a lawyer. This book is extremely clear and well-written; it does not assume any legal knowledge other than general information, so it is easily accessible to the lay person. It seems to me that this book covers every conceivable question one could have about trusts, from basic questions like why a trust is a good idea and why people set them up, to complicated questions about selling property that is in a trust, revoking a trust, or leaving property to minor children. Each chapter has many concrete real-life examples of each major point the author is making. I especially liked this aspect of the book as it broke up the expository parts with clarifying examples. I was also impressed that with the purchase of this book, you can go online and download, free, any legal documents you may need in order to set up your trust. You also have access to the NOLO website, where you can find out about any changes in the laws regarding trusts.

Now, the ultimate question: Would I set up my own trust after reading this book? To be honest, I am not sure that I would, but that is more about the sort of cautious person I am than about the quality of this book. In my opinion, even if you do end up going to a lawyer to set up your trust, if you read this book you will be far more informed that you would be without having read it. You will be a better consumer, and you will understand far more of what your lawyer is telling you. I have learned so much about trusts from this book, even though I have not read every single chapter. I do recommend this book to any lay person who is interested in setting up a trust. I do not think you will ever regret your purchase.

title: A cookbook just for fun
text:
I have never, even in my wildest dreams, imagined myself a member of the preppy group. So you can imagine my surprise to find that I was already familiar with many of the recipes in "The Preppy Cookbook," and that a few of them were identical to those my mother used to make when we were kids. I ordered this cookbook for review because I am a "reader" of cookbooks, not one who consults them only for recipes, and I knew that this one would fit that category. I was not disappointed. The interesting and occasionally tongue-in-cheek commentary that accompanies each recipe is fun to read.

"The Preppy Cookbook" is divided into several sections: The Formative Years (comfort food you will likely recall from childhood); Summer & the Living is Easy, The Sporting Life (snacks and drinks for after golf, etc.), The Grand Tour (recipes from other countries), Brunch as a Verb, The Cocktail Party (appetizers and more drinks), Luncheons and Showers, and Home for the Holidays. Each section has a lighthearted introduction to the sort of recipes you will find within, and the photos are good, though they are not in color, and not every recipe is photographed. The cookbook ends with a section devoted to stocking your kitchen and pantry with staples that will be useful in creating these recipes.

I liked this cookbook more than I thought I would. The recipes are, for the most part, very easy to put together and do not use exotic ingredients. I do question some of the directions; for example, for the recipe for flank steak, I recommend marinating your steak for at least eight hours before you grill it. And some recipes are simply traditional favorites given new names--for example, the ubiquitous cheesy potato casserole is called "Hangover Hash Browns." There is something for everyone in this cookbook. Even people who like to can and preserve food will find the "Branston Pickle" recipe intriguing. And for you traditionalists from the mid 20th century, the recipe for creamed chipped beef is identical to my mom's, though she often served it on English muffins or toast.

This is not an all-purpose cookbook like Mark Bittman's "How to Cook Anything," but it has its place. A college student or young person just starting to cook could do much worse than this book; its simple and easy-to-follow recipes would be a godsend to a new cook or frazzled mom. I enjoyed it a great deal, and am happy to recommend it.

title: Keep reading!
text:
"Unseen" by Karin Slaughter is only the second novel I have read by this author. The first (sorry, I cannot recall the title) was great--fast-paced, intriguing, and not a Will Trent book. Like that book, however, "Unseen" takes place in Macon, Georgia, and has many good, bad and truly evil cops in it. It was a slow read at first, because most of the characters are cops, and there is just not enough variety, at least for me, to make it interesting.

The exception to this is Dr. Sara Linton, who is in love with Will Trent, an undercover agent in this book who is likewise in love with her. Unfortunately, he is still married to Angie, who is said to be mentally ill, so he is not free to pursue a relationship. Another character, Lena, is a police officer who is hated by the reader but loved by her fellow police officers. This disparity is incomprehensible. Lena was Sara's deceased husband's partner on the police force, and Sara blames Lena for her husband's death. Although she is not at all likable, she adds a great deal to the novel.

In this novel, Sara thinks Lena is trying to kill her own husband, Jared, who is Sara's stepson. This four-star novel has many twists and turns as the other police officers think Lena can do no wrong. A reviewer in our local newspaper recommended this book, but commented that it is very helpful to have read the previous Will Trent books. I completely agree with this. You will be much happier with this book if you have read the other books in the series.

title: Moving but frustrating memoir
text:
"Blue Plate Special," a memoir by writer Kate Christensen, begins when she is about two years old with a memory that will haunt her for the rest of her life. If anyone doubts the tremendous influence of parents on their children, both for good and ill, you have only to read this searing and effective memoir. At two, Kate sees her adored but remote father beat her overwhelmed mother at the breakfast table and then leave for work as if it were an ordinary day. This event, and others like it, forever affects the way Kate responds to men and influences nearly every choice of man that she makes throughout her life. Choosing unsuitable men is one major motif of this book, and the reader suffers along with Kate as she struggles with each one. Not until she is in her forties does she resolve parental issues and make a superb choice in a partner.

This book is very well written, and, as the summary notes, each event in Kate's life is described at least partly in terms of food or the absence of food. For me, this was some of her best writing. No matter what she is describing, whether it is a simple soft cooked egg or a more complex chicken tagine, she makes the food sound great. Her writing here reminded me of Ernest Hemingway (though I suspect she would abhor this comparison)--but Hemingway could describe food so that you wanted to go fishing, catch a trout, and cook it over an open fire on the side of the stream. These food descriptions are like that, and Christensen includes one or two recipes at the end of every section of the book.

Kate's mother eventually leaves her father, taking Kate and her two younger sisters with her. Though this is Kate's story. I felt great empathy for her creative but depressive mother, who truly gave each of her children as many opportunities as she could with her limited means. Each of her three daughters is affected by parental dysfunction, and each responds differently. For many years, Kate identifies with her "strong" father, choosing men essentially like him, and blaming her mother for her weakness. Each daughter is estranged from the mother at some point, and I was frustrated with all of them for the judgment they brought to their mother, who definitely had her limitations but who was creative and artistic and encouraged artistic expression in each of her daughters. Especially annoying (but utterly believable) was how quickly each daughter would respond to very infrequent contact from their father, as if he were a great dad rather than a deadbeat loser.

Another aspect I liked was the unstinting honesty with which Kate recounts each event in her life. She does not make excuses for her behavior, and this is a rarity in memoir. With the help of therapy, she has excellent psychological insight into her own choices. In my opinion, quite a number of her problems would have been mitigated if she had consumed less alcohol, but that is not a choice she made. The reader suffers with Kate through each failed romance, rejected manuscript, and hung-over morning after.

I definitely recommend "Blue Plate Special" for anyone who enjoys good writing and in interested in the formation of a writer. Though I have not read any of the author's other books, I was interested in how she took incidents from her life and reworked them in her fiction. I hope to read more of Kate Christensen's work, and I wish her well.

title: Good for tweens and early teens
text: I did not read these books myself; they were a birthday gift for my 15-year-old niece.  She was absolutely delighted, so on that basis, I recommend them.  I was also impressed that the language is appropriate and that sexual content is virtually nonexistent, based on the observations of other reviewers.

title: Great crime novel
text:
I write here as one who has never read a book by Allison Leotta, but "Speak of the Devil" has made me want to read everything she has written. The main character in "Speak of the Devil" is Anna Curtis, a sex crimes prosecutor in Washington DC, who has just become engaged to Jack Bailey, chief of the DC homicide unit. Jack has a six-year-old daughter, Olivia, and his late wife, Nina Flores, had been killed four years earlier by one of the street gangs of Washington DC. Most investigators believe that that the crime was committed by MS-13, a notoriously violent and ruthless DC gang. The leader of this gang is Diablo, accurately named "the Devil." Diablo's skin is completely covered in tattooed hieroglyphs. His nose is two sunken holes; he has long black hair and two fleshy horns protruding from his forehead. Indeed, he is aptly named.

Diablo and his gang appear throughout the book as Anna Curtis and Jack Flores attempt to solve various gruesome crimes occurring in the DC area. There are many twists and turns, and a huge red herring that comes as a total surprise to the reader in the last third of the book. I really enjoyed this book and recommend it to anyone who likes true-life crime fiction. The author's experience as a sex-crimes prosecutor for 12 years in Washington DC is evident on every page, and she is a superb writer. If I could give the book more than five stars, I would. Highly recommended.

title: Excellent, but for very young children
text: This is one of the best books in the "Dummies" series.  Unlike many of them, it is beautifully illustrated and colorful.  It gives wonderful descriptions of Apps the are appropriate for young children.  I was hoping to find apps that were suited to older tweens and teens, but this book is really for young children and early elementary age kids.  However, if this is the age group you are searching for. I recommend this book highly.

title: Fast-paced and absorbing
text:
This is another excellent novel from L. J. Sellers. He has once again shown how great a writer can be.

Detective Jackson's ex-wife has disappeared; he learns of this while on vacation in Hawaii with his girlfriend. His daughter Katie calls to tell him she needs him to cut his vacation short in order to help locate the ex-wife.

Back in Eugene, Oregon, Jackson is sure that his ex has been kidnapped, and he fears for her life (for his daughter's sake, not so much for his own). A ransom note is received, but a rescue attempt ends in total failure. Sure that his ex wife is dead, he nevertheless continues the search because of his daughter.

The ending is a complete surprise and will make many readers say "What???" If you like detective fiction, you will love this novel. I certainly did--four stars.

title: Very difficult
text:
This is an excellent geometry text for honors and advanced placement students. It is extremely challenging and provides in-depth learning for students who enjoy the challenge of math or who have access to a teacher or tutor on a regular basis. It is far too difficult, however, for the typical high school geometry student. It is very proof-oriented, and the difficulty may discourage the student who may like math but does not want a career that is dependent on it. For the budding engineer or scientist, this book is a great choice, but it is not for everyone.

That said, I want to point out one aspect of the book that is great. Each chapter has three levels of practice problems, labeled A, B, and C. The A problem set is for everyone, and B and C levels are for those who want a greater challenge. I wanted this book to use for a geometry course for home schooled students, who meet with me only once a week. This is not nearly often enough, given the difficulty of this book. However, in a school, where students and teacher meet five days a week, the levels of problems provide the teacher with great flexibility. I could see the book being used at several levels.

In short, this is a great book, but it is not the best choice for me. However, if may be a good choice for you. I suggest that you buy a used copy so that you can judge for yourself before you invest in the entire course.

title: Good for light reading, but shallow
text:
"Chocolate for Two" is the fourth book in the Waverly Bryson series by Maria Mumane. I have read only this one, so take that into consideration when assessing my review.

As tis book opens, our heroine, Waverly, Is recovering from having been almost literally left at the altar by a cad who appeared on her doorstep two weeks before the wedding and proclaimed he did not love her. A popular young woman with many love interests, Waverly is a well regarded talk show host who also owns her own very successful business, Waverly's Honey Shop. Despite all this, her self esteem is shaky until she meets Jake McIntyre, a wealthy scion of an upper class family.

Naturally, they fall in love. We seem to be headed for a story book ending, but wait--we need some drama. Enter Jake's parents, specifically his mother, who is controlling and insufferable, in the nicest possible way (ahem). She hopes to take control of the wedding and make it a huge expensive affair in Florida. Waverly and Jake, meanwhile, want a small intimate wedding in New York. Jake is besotted with Waverly and pretty much defers to her on every issue, but at the same time he does not help much in dealing with his overbearing mother.

The novel is a fun beach read, good for a rainy day on the porch. There is humor and emotion, as well as many sidebars with Waverly's career and business. Eventually, Waverly finds a retailer who somehow makes her see everything, both professional and personal, in perspective, and the ending is light and satisfying. You probably will not remember this book too long after you read it, but you will be entertained as you read, especially if you are a fan.

title: An absorbing and quick read
text:
Set in the fictional town of Red Paint Bay, a typical small town where everyone knows everyone else and nothing is kept secret for long, this book deals with a long-buried secret that is about to re-emerge and haunt many, especially one family.

This family is headed by Simon Howe, who was born and raised in Red Paint and is now the editor of the town paper. He is married to Amy, a psychotherapist, who runs the family with an iron hand. Their son, Davey, is a more or less typical teen, but he gets into trouble and is grounded regularly for some pretty bizarre behavior, such as throwing knives at his best friend. Simon and his staff are always trying to think of events to fill their small-town paper. It has been said that when the gods wish to punish us, they answer our prayers, and this is true in spades with Simon. His 25th high school reunion is approaching, and in this town, that qualifies as front page news. It is here that the excitement and horror begin.

Simon has been getting a number of unsigned postcards, the content of which ranges from mundane (Will you meet me for dinner?) to threatening. He decides to meet with the postcard-sender, and though he is instructed to come alone, Amy insists on coming with him. Davey is left alone with strict orders to stay in the house. (Never a good idea in a mystery book.) The mysterious writer is a no-show, and when Simon and Amy return home, they find that Davey has disappeared. The police are called, and Davey is found safe in a treehouse. But how did he get there? There is, of course, a connection with the mysterious postcard-writer.

The story gets better with every page--I challenge you not to finish this book. Many interesting and typical small town characters have their roles to play, and the mystery deepens with each chapter. If you enjoy mysteries with a small town flavor and fast pace, you will like this book. Highly recommended.

title: Great for a select audience
text:
Let me say at the outset that I am a great fan of Cook's Magazine, the magazine whose compiled articles compose this superb cookbook. For those unfamiliar with it, each issue of Cook's Magazine takes a few dishes and explores in excruciating detail how to make each one. For example, take beef stew. The magazine would examine every aspect of several recipes, from cuts of beef to cooking time and temperature, to when to add the vegetables, to how and why to brown the beef, and on and on. After experimenting with several, or even dozens of recipes, the magazine gives the "ultimate" beef stew recipe, one that will produce perfect results if followed exactly, even for the novice cook. Along the way, you get a lesson (or several) in the science of food, why some things work and others do not.

This massive cookbook (486 pages) is excellent, but it was a little overwhelming, even for me. I love reading about food and learning what works and why. And I have never tried a Cook's recipe that failed. However, I can see that this cookbook is not for everyone. If you are looking for recipes with 5 ingredients or less, or that use a lot of processed foods, you will be disappointed.

So why five stars? Because this cookbook does a superb job of what it sets out to do. The reader learns the techniques of food preparation, the science (with accompanying diagrams) of why some things work and others do not, and in the end gets a great recipe for whatever it is he or she wants to make. The book covers all sorts of food, from bread and muffins, to meats and poultry, to vegetables, to eggs and cheese, to desserts--be sure to try the recipe for Perfect New York Cheesecake--the ultimate best.

I recommend this book for people who enjoy the "why" of food preparation, not merely the "how." It will take time to go through the article on even one recipe, but you will be rewarded with not only a great recipe, but with greater confidence in your cooking skills.

title: Good, but read the first novel first
text:
"Stranger in the Room" is the second in a mystery series by Amanda Kyle Williams. I would have enjoyed this novel much more if I had read the first, as I am sure it gives much-needed background information. There are numerous characters to follow, and the story lines gan get confusing.

The setting of this book is Atlanta, Georgia. Keye Street is a Chinese orphan who was adopted by an American couple and who grew up to become a profiler for the FBI. She has a mentally ill cousin, Miki, whom she wants to protect, but Miki is highly unreliable, always in trouble or about to be victimized. Keye has problems of her own: she is a recovering alcoholic who has been sober for four years but has neglected attending her meetings, and the stress she is enduring make her more vulnerable to a relapse with every chapter.

Keye's work as a profiler makes her a natural help for her boyfriend, who is on the Atlanta Police Force. She also has a detective agency that she runs with her friend, Neil. All of these story lines come together as numerous people are murdered along the way, and we are led into a story of sexual obsession and anger. A bizarre and disturbing subplot deals with a mother and son team who are supposed to be cremating bodies but who instead throw them away.

I would like to read the previous book in this series. This one is well written, but it moves a bit slowly until about two-thirds of the way through.

title: Another hit for fans of Roy Grace
text:
This is the second book I have read in the Roy Grace series, and I honestly wish I has begun at the beginning. So many of the characters have histories in previous books of the series, and knowing about each one would make reading this one a richer experience. Still, I enjoyed this book very much and will gladly read more.

In the current book, Roy Grace is given the duty of protecting a superstar singer and actress named Gaia in the usual locale, Brighton. Gaia is in Brighton to shoot a movie in which she plays the mistress of King George IV, and she has been getting death threats. In one attempt on her life, her assistant was murdered. In an apparently unrelated event, a murder is committed at a chicken farm, and only the torso of the victim is found. Are these related? This is a mystery, so of course they are, though the reader is not let in on the secret for a long time.

Meanwhile, on a personal level, Roy's fiancee Cleo is pregnant, so he is trying to get his long-missing wife, Sandy, declared legally dead so he can marry Cleo. Another woman comes to Brighton to look at the home Roy and Sandy shared. She, too, has a child--is it Sandy's child with Roy?

This book has a lot of twists and turns, and some questions are left unanswered. It makes me want to read the next book, but in the meantime, I will read the previous ones in the series. I enjoy Peter James as a writer and give this book four stars.

title: A "fix" for Randy Cohen fans
text:
I must confess at the outset that I am a big fan of Randy Cohen, and I looked forward to his "Ethicist" columns each Sunday in the New York Times Magazine. When he left a couple of years ago, I missed him, even though I thought his successors did a good job. And I like the current Ethicist, Chuck Klosterman, very much. Still, I was happy to see a book of Cohen's columns compiled and categorized.

The columns are loosely grouped into one of several categories. Some of these are Family, Home, Money, Civic Life, Animals, Sports, Work, School, Arts, Love and Sex, Religion, and Community. What I like especially about these ethical dilemmas, and Cohen's comments on them, is that they make the reader think, and in some cases, vehemently disagree. Most of them would make interesting (if not always convivial) dinner conversation. I almost never go away from a response thinking, "Well, obviously!" So much of what we deal with in modern life is not obvious, and the columns Cohen has selected for this book reflect that in spades.

This book goes beyond a simple compilation of columns, however. First, each section is prefaced by a short essay on the topic in general, highlighting both the topic itself and the author's views in general. Second, a few of Cohen's columns generated much response, for example, a column about whether an IT worker is ethically required to report the presence of child pornography on his boss's computer. In these cases, Cohen describes and quotes extensively from the response(s), which are usually objections to what he has written. He evaluates the writer's point of view, sometimes agreeing at least in part, but more often clarifying his own thinking. In reading these, the reader gets a short course, not just in ethics, but in critical thinking.

I enjoyed this book a great deal, and I recommend it to anyone interested in thinking about everyday ethics in today's world.

title: Tween Horror
text:
"The Cavendish Home for Boys and Girls" is aimed at the 10 to 14 age group, but my guess is that older teens and even adults may enjoy it as well, though not for the same reasons. First, the target audience. This is a horror fantasy, plain and simple. A children's home staffed by monsters masquerading as kindly caregivers, a house that changes shape and comes to life, children trapped with no hope for escape--all of these elements are well integrated in this excellent book. I will not review the plot, as other reviewers have done so quite well, but I think most tweens will be hooked by the strange Harry Potter-esque events that occur within the house, as well as by the efforts of the heroine to save the day.

Now the older readers. When I began this book, I immediately thought it was a sort of Stepford Wives for kids. Children, especially strange or odd children, or those who are for any reason outside the norm, are kidnapped, or disappear, only to (sometimes) turn up weeks or months later, transformed. They suddenly fit in; their odd individuality has been excised. As I read on, however, I began to think of this book as a cautionary tale against conformity, perfectionism, and intolerance. For me, the most insightful lines in the book occur when Miss Cavendish, the villain, says to Victoria, the heroine, "You and I are just alike." And the truth is, they are. As Victoria experiences the house in all its horrors, she realizes her own tendencies toward judgmental condemnation of others and love of doing things "just so," attitudes that can lead, in adulthood, to intolerance and bigotry. In addition, Miss Cavendish cannot enact her villainy without the consent and collusion of nearly all the townspeople. This idea is given expression in a metaphor, that of puppets; each citizen of the town is no more than a marionette. This part is horrifying to any reader.

This is not a light and sunny book. Victoria wins, but only just, and her victory is not a lasting one, as the epilogue of the book suggests. Perhaps we are being set up for a sequel? In any event, readers young and old will appreciate the powerful descriptive passages and superb writing. Five stars.

title: Gripping psychological thriller
text:
I am one of those readers who is new to the novels of Karin Slaughter and her dyslexic hero, Will Trent. Head of the Georgia Bureau of Investigation, Will is a hero with a lot of baggage. He has found love in the beautiful pediatrician Sara Linton, but Sara is justifiably cautious about involvement with a man so damaged as Will. All this is background: readers of Slaughter's other books will already be familiar with it, but I was not.

In "Criminal," the time shifts from the early-to-mid seventies to the present day. Georgia in the seventies was a place teeming with racism and sexism, and the police department was not immune to either. The subject is prostitution, and the story centers on Lucy Bennett, who was unlucky enough to be led into prostitution to feed her increasing drug addiction. Lucy's pimp is the stereotypical bad guy, taken to an extreme. When Lucy decides to run away, she meets up with an even more evil, almost Satanic figure. The reader should be warned that these passages are not for the faint of heart. Slaughter does not mince words or pretty up what she is describing. You will see in detail the sordid side of life.

The conflict is of course between the criminals and the police. The title is ironic in that the police are in many ways criminals themselves. The reader may become frustrated at all the plot twists and seemingly unrelated digressions, but don't worry--everything is tied together in the end, as it should be in a good police procedural.

"Criminal" is so well written that I am determined to get Slaughter's other books and read them in the order she wrote them. If you are already a fan, buy this book with confidence--you will not be disappointed. Highly recommended.

title: Superb help for iPad users of any age
text:
My husband and I purchased an iPad about a year ago, and it has become one of our favorite electronics ever. To help us become acquainted with all that it had to offer, we bought iPad for Dummies for Seniors, which was very helpful. When iPad for Older and Wiser became available through Amazon Vine, I decided to order it to compare its helpfulness with the Dummies book.

iPad for Older and Wiser is excellent, even better than the Dummies manual. It has extremely clear, step-by-step instructions and numerous helpful illustrations. The summaries and quizzes at the end of each chapter were a good way for the reader to see if he or she had gotten the main points, and if you did not, you could go back to review. It is also an excellent reference for each chapter; a sort of mini-index. The format is appealing, with a lot of subtle color and well-designed paragraphs and bullet points. It is wonderful to have this reference handy when I use my iPad and explore all its capabilities.

I recommend this manual to everyone, not just seniors. Unless you are supremely computer-literate, it will help you with your iPad more than any other reference I have found. I am looking forward to reading other books in this series. Five stars and more!

title: A bit slow at first, but ultimately rewarding
text:
I selected "The Unlikely Pilgrimage of Harold Fry" to read and review because I loved "Major Pettigrew's Last Stand," a book to which it was compared in the publisher's preview. And while I prefer "Major Pettigrew" for its pacing and multicultural appeal, I wholeheartedly recommend "Harold Fry." It has charms of its own.

Henry David Thoreau observed, "The mass of men live lives of quiet desperation," and I could not help but recall this quotation as I began Rachel Joyce's lovely debut novel. As the novel begins, Harold is merely existing. The reader is not given many details, but it is clear that Harold's marriage to Maureen is an empty shell, and that there are problems in his relationship with his adult son, David. Then Harold gets a farewell letter of sorts from a friend, Queenie Hennessy, and his carefully orchestrated charade of a life begins to come apart. Queenie had "done something nice" for Harold twenty years previous, and he always regretted not thanking her. Whatever this is is shrouded in mystery, and many readers will suspect a long-past affair. All these questions are a bit disconcerting, but if the reader is patient, all will be resolved.

Harold writes a "pro forma" response to Queenie's note, but as he goes out to mail it, something prevents him from putting it in the first mailbox he comes to. He passes postbox after postbox, and eventually makes an impulsive decision to walk from his hometown to Queenie's hospice, about 600 miles. Thus begins his transformation from a kind of living death to fullness of life.

Readers who are familiar with Joseph Campbell's "The Hero's Journey" will immediately recognize the motif: the hero leaves the world he knows to embark on a quest. Along the way he meets both helpers and tempters, and he eventually returns to the known world with a fullness of knowledge or with something to enrich his community and himself.

Harold Fry fits this motif to a tee. He meets many people and even animals along the way, and he gains something of value from each of them, even those who would deter him from his quest. Meanwhile, back at home, Maureen is undergoing her own transformation as she worries and responds to Harold's calls, postcards, and gifts. Nothing is as Harold or Maureen expect it to be. And the end of the quest is rewarding, but not in the way Harold imagines.

One final observation: This is a beautifully written novel. Most readers will love the use of language, especially in descriptions of the natural world. I am stunned that this is the author's first novel, though she has written many screenplays for the BBC. I hope to read much more of her work.

Most readers will like and appreciate "Harold Fry" if they persevere through the ambiguity at the beginning. Everything falls together eventually, I promise! Highly recommended.

title: Girl, Interrupted
text:
"The Mirrored World" by Debra Dean is a good introduction to the culture of upper class and royal life in the Russia of the 1700s. Born into a minor titled family, Xenia is only about six when we first meet her. She lives a conventional upper class life, doing essentially what is expected of her throughout her adolescence and in the early days of her marriage. Unlike many women of her time, she marries for love, and she is blissfully happy at first. The first half of the book covers this part of her life.

Xenia's happiness does not last long; two unexpected tragedies occur, throwing her first into deep mourning and then into a complete breakdown. The second half of the book traces Xenia's transformation into a "holy fool" or a "fool for Christ." She sees the emptiness and transitory nature of earthly possessions and joys and relationships, and dedicates herself to service of the poorest of the poor. While many saintly men and women have had just that sort of insight and made exactly that same service to the poor their life's work, Xenia goes to an extreme, to put it mildly. We see Xenia's family try to help her, to no avail.

As I read this book, I could not help but think that one age's sanctity is another age's madness. To me, Xenia seems truly to have lost contact with reality. A religious person may say that she simply made contact with a greater reality, but I am not so sure. I feel certain that if a person acted this way today, he or she would surely be institutionalized or at least treated with medication.

Xenia is a saint in the Russian Orthodox Church, and the book purports to show her path to sainthood. It does this in lovely and often poetic language. The descriptions of the Russian landscape and way of life among the upper classes were excellent, and I kept reading the book largely for the superb use of language. But I doubt that Xenia is a saint for our times. For that, check out Dorothy Day or Maximilian Kolbe.

title: Great short stories
text:
I loved "Shout Her Lovely Name," a superb short story collection by Natalie Serber. Each of the eleven stories in this collection explores some aspect of the mother/daughter bond. While other emotional entanglements occur, this bond predominates.

The first story was my favorite. Told in second person, it captures well the utter frustration of a mother whose daughter is struggling with an eating disorder. Neither mother nor daughter is named, and this adds to the universality of the story. The emotions depicted run the gamut from exaltation to utter despair and everything in between. While I am not a parent myself, it was easy for me to believe and relate to each and every line.

The next nine stories are loosely linked. They center around the relationship between Ruby Goddard and her mother, Sally, and eventually to Ruby's daughter, Nora. We first meet Ruby as she is coming home from college for a visit with her dysfunctional parents. From there, the stories explore Ruby as she tries to find herself in several ways: through travel, through study, in various relationships with men, and finally through motherhood. I found each story compelling and interesting, psychologically true and extremely well written.

The final story was, in my opinion, the least successful of the eleven, and I am eager to know what other readers thought of it as well. Longest of all the stories, it introduced new characters and simply did not work well for me, which was surprising as I loved the other stories. Despite this, however, I gladly give this collection five stars, and I eagerly await more writing by Natalie Serber.

title: Ambivalent feeling toward this one
text:
The premise of "Afterwards" by Rosamund Lupton is similar to that of "The Lovely Bones": a dead (or nearly dead) person communicates with others in an attempt to uncover a crime. In the case of "Afterwards," the crime is arson, and the beginning of the book is well done--fast-paced, interesting, and engaging. The main character rushes into a burning school to save her teenaged daughter. Both mother and daughter are severely injured in the fire, and their spirits communicate with one another as they lie in comas in the local hospital. Then minor characters (father, son) become involved as Mom tries to discover who set the fire and why.

After this superb beginning, this novel simply bogs down. It is too long in the middle, and there is far too much psychological analysis for my taste. Of course the reader wants to know underlying complexity of motivation, but too much is too much. Mother and daughter communicate, and parts of this section are confusing. It is occasionally difficult to know who is speaking. Mom finds out things she never knew about her family--surprise, surprise--and the incredible and undying love of a mother for her child is repeatedly reinforced.

In the end, the reader discovers who set the fire, and the answer is very unexpected. There are any number of likely suspects, and the motivations of each are explored, but most readers will not guess the identity of the arsonist.

To sum up, this was a good story, but not great. I notice that many other reviewers have mentioned Lupton's other book, "Sister." I plan to read this book to see if I can get a better handle on her storytelling. For now, count me in the ambivalent category.

title: Some satisfaction; some mystery
text:
"The Cottage at Glass Beach" by Heather Barbieri is set on the coast of Maine, an inviting setting if ever there was one. The back story is fairly straightforward: Nora goes with her two young daughters to the cottage on the beach to escape the incessant pressure of the press resulting from a scandal involving her husband and his mistress. In addition to this major conflict, issues arise as the older daughter blames Nora for her father's infidelity and Nora herself has to resolve issues with her own mother.

So far, a pretty typical summer read, right? Now comes the mysterious part: A stranger appears seemingly out of nowhere to entwine himself into Nora's affairs. This touch of magical realism surrounds the story of the selkie, seals who shed their skins on land and become human. Unfortunately, this aspect of Irish folklore is never fully explained, and the mysterious stranger seems jarring to the plot.

Despite this, however, I suspect that this book will find a wide readership. It is a satisfying beach/summer read, but I urge readers to familiarize themselves with the selkie myth before beginning the book. You will appreciate the story far more if you do.

title: Caution:  Not for Everyone
text:
I selected "Cloudland" by Joseph Olshan to review because I enjoyed "Clara's Heart," one of his previous books. I looked forward to a coherent and literate mystery. Unfortunately, "Cloudland" is neither.

At the center of this book is a college writing teacher, Catherine Winslow, who has been fired from her job for an affair with a graduate student. Catherine is a fan of Wilkie Collins, a writer best known for "The Moonstone," whose final unfinished work, "The Widower's Branch," is rare and obscure. In fact, Catherine has one copy; only four copies exist in libraries in the United States. This unfinished work describes a series of murders.

Catherine becomes involved when several women are strangled in her small Vermont town. Because some of the details of the murders mirror those in "The Widower's Branch," suspicion begins to fall on persons who knew the book or who had access to it. Catherine is not suspected in the crimes, but she is asked to help evaluate the evidence because of her specialized knowledge.

The actions of several characters are inexplicable. Why does Catherine continue to see her much-younger lover, despite a truly frightening event that is told in flashback? How is it that a police detective is familiar enough with obscure works of literature to frame a series of people for the crime? At every turn, characters act in bizarre and irrational ways.

The end of the novel is especially strange. Catherine links the death of one of the victims to her own difficulty believing in love. Yes, that's right--it is all about her. I found this ending clunky, egocentric, and unsatisfying. I must say, however, that I was grateful that the book finally came to an end.

I hope that anyone thinking about purchasing this book will read the review of another Vine member, Robin Wolfson. She has written an incisive, humorous, and compelling review of this mostly incomprehensible book. Do yourself a favor and read before you buy.

title: Engaging book for Disney enthusiasts
text: My niece had this book (and all its companions in the series) on her birthday list.  She absolutely loves the books (I purchased the first three in the series) and stays up late at night to read them.  Her brother enjoys them as well, and he is not the most enthusiastic reader in the world.  I recommend these books for kids about 10 and up who love Disney and would enjoy an adventure set in one of the theme parks.  The books are easy to read but not short, ranging from about 300 to over 500 pages.  Despite their length, however, they are very popular with our family.

title: Excellent Coming-of-Age-Novel
text:
"Mister Death's Blue-eyed Girls" by Mary Downing Hahn is the somewhat-fictionalized story of a true event, the murder of two teen-aged girls on the last day of school in 1956. In an afterword, the author tells of her distant relationship with these girls and the impact their deaths had on her, her friends, and the entire community. She says that she has been trying to write this book for fifty years, and in my opinion, the resulting novel was well worth the wait.

The story is told from the points of view of various narrators, the main one being Nora, alter-ego of the author. Other narrators include Nora's best friend, Ellie; the boyfriend of one of the victims, Buddy; the murderer himself, Mister Death; and Mister Death's younger brother. There are also diary entries of several of the teenagers, which serve to fill in important background details. This multiple narrator device is useful for a crime novel in which only the murderer knows "who done it"; the terror and confusion experienced by the victims' friends result from the killer never being identified.

The novel is set in the fifties in Edgewood, Maryland, a suburb of Baltimore. The cultural references are perfect: the music, the clothing, the hairstyles, the drinking and smoking in the park, the pre-Vatican II atmosphere in the Catholic Church, the suffocating small-town ambiance, the rigid class divisions among the townspeople and the teenagers as well--all pitch perfect. The murders happen on the last day of school, and they abruptly force Nora and Ellie to realize that bad things can happen to your friends, not just to people on the news that you don't know. One major result of the crime is a crisis of faith in Nora. As she tries to understand how God could let such a thing happen to innocent girls, she is offered only platitudes by the priests of her church. She decides that she cannot believe in a God who can stand by and allow evil to happen.

At the same time, she is exploring her own literary interests, and this adds an important dimension to the book. She begins to read real literature, not the True Confession magazines she passed time reading before the tragedy. Poetry by Wordsworth, Walt Whitman, and T. S. Eliot; French novels, and modern American classics are all referenced, and they reinforce Nora's growing conclusion that the God she was taught about in church does not exist; that when we die, we become part of the earth forever. At one point, she describes herself as a pantheist. I found this part of the book very affecting; most people go through a crisis of faith at one point or another, and this one is well handled.

One other aspect of the book that will resonate with readers is the reaction of the townspeople to the murders and their desire to find and punish the killer. When Buddy is arrested, he is manhandled by the police, who release him after 48 hours because there is no evidence that he committed the crime. But none (or almost none) of the townspeople let a lack of evidence stand in the way of their judgment: they "know" that he did it, no matter what the police say. Buddy's life is made a living hell, and only Nora and one other minor character take his part. Of course, there are no Miranda warnings, and the rush to judgment prevents the police from finding the true killer. Readers may recall Columbine or other school-related shooting of recent years. This aspect is a good cautionary tale about how wrong we can be, even when we are sure we are right.

I give this book my highest recommendation. It is aimed at a teen audience, but I think adults will appreciate it as well, especially those of us who recall the fifties and are happy we have moved on as a society in so many ways. Readers will like Nora, an imperfect but appealing heroine, as she struggles with the unthinkable. Five stars.

title: Simply bizarre
text:
When I ordered this book to review, I was not aware that it was the latest in a series of books, the Lake Loon Mystery series, all mysteries dealing with the residents of Lake Loon, a small town in Wisconsin. Perhaps if I had read the previous books and come to know the characters and environs better, my opinion of this book would be different. However, to a reader just picking up the book and expecting a good mystery, "Dead Tease" is a great disappointment.

First of all, the characters in this book are a mish-mash of strange and weird personalities: a crazy doctor, her evil mother, the odd police chief, her sometimes lover, an unbalanced wife, and at the center of it all, the main character--is it Jim or John?--a philandering Don Juan who is the CEO of a small clinic at Lake Loon. To have a good reading experience, the reader has to care about at least some of the characters, but these were too strange to elicit empathy.

Second, the plot is weak. The "dead tease" could be any one of them, not that the reader cares much who it is by the end of the book. A reader should be able to look back after the mystery is revealed and see how it unfolded, but this reveal is just confusing.

Finally, the number of grammatical errors in this book was distracting. I realize that the advance copies we get in the Vine Program are uncorrected proofs, and I expect to see some errors, but I have never seen so much that needs to be corrected--spelling, punctuation, usage, even names of characters. When a previously unmentioned name was introduced, I hunted through the book for who he was--to no avail. The book does not have to be grammatically perfect, but it should be able to be read without annoyance.

The only virtue of this book is its brevity. At 170 pages or so, at first I thought I had inadvertently ordered a children's book. The subject matter, however, is definitely adult. To repeat, maybe if you are a fan of this series, you will enjoy this book. But I strongly caution anyone who just picks up this book in search of a good, well-plotted mystery: You may be disappointed.

title: Challenging and slow to start
text:
"An Uncommon Education" by Elizabeth Percer traces the life of Naomi Feinstein from early childhood through her college years at Wellesley and, briefly, beyond. Though there were moments of lovely writing and insight, I found much of this book a tough go.

The reader can look at other reviews for a summary. I will try here to describe the strengths and weaknesses of the book. First, some of the writing is excellent. The book is slow-moving, especially in the first half, and much of the writing describes the thoughts of a sensitive, intelligent child dealing with a loving but depressed home life and the pain of being the odd man out at school. Naomi's insights are beyond her years, and her struggle to make even one friend is well-documented. The pace of the book picks up when Naomi finally goes to Wellesley, fulfilling her father's dream for her (and, she thinks, her own dream). At Wellesley, surrounded by other highly intelligent and driven women, she begins to find her true path. The second half of the book is much more satisfying than the first, much better paced and far less ruminative. Naomi's friendship with a Japanese economics student, Jun Oko, is central to her becoming the person she is meant to be.

But there are other aspects that are problematic, at least for me. First, the book begins with a long treatise on Naomi's father's near obsession with Rose Kennedy (and Naomi's fascination with Rose's daughter Rosemary, who was lobotomized in her early 20s and never recovered). It is Rose, however, who is the father's real obsession, especially with respect to her frustrated desire to attend Wellesley, which was sacrificed to her father's political ambitions. He thinks of all Rose could have been with a Wellesley education, and Naomi is encouraged even at age six to aim for Wellesley. The first scene in the book has Naomi as a child getting sick at the Kennedy house in Brookline, Massachusetts. This entire theme recurs again and again, and I found it annoying, repetitive, and pointless.

I expected to love this book. I enjoy coming-of-age stories, and I loved Curtis Sittenfeld's "Prep" and the film version of "Dead Poets Society," and when I read the advance information that this book would appeal to fans of these works, I enthusiastically ordered it. I have to say, however, that it was a disappointment. I wondered at times if it were more memoir than novel, and I think it would have worked better as memoir. Most readers will be put off, I think, by long passages describing every thought and every nuance of every thought.

I hate to be so critical of a author's work, especially a first novel. I know how hard it is to write, and I think this author has great promise. I wonder if, years from now, this book will be re-issued as a "first novel" by a great writer whose later work is far superior. I can see that happening, and I hope it does.

title: Fast-paced crime/suspense novel
text:
"The Professionals" by Owen Laukkanan will appeal to many who enjoy the suspense and crime genres. The novel is almost exclusively plot-driven, with little or no atmosphere, characterization, or psychological insight. However, plot drives many novels of this kind, and they are wildly popular. I predict that this novel will find a wide audience, too.

The story begins as four college friends, unable to find well-paying jobs, turn to low-payout, high volume kidnappings of wealthy businessmen. The kidnappings are solely about money; no violence is ever involved. For two years, they move from "job" to "job' until one day they kidnap a repellent man with mob connections through his wife. For the first time, their carefully planned routine goes awry. At the same time, the law, represented by State Investigator Kirk Stevens and FBI Agent Carla Windermere, is taking an interest in this kidnapping and others that are at first seemingly unrelated. The bulk of the book concerns the efforts of the four young people to evade both the law and the mob.

This novel is easy to read and moves along quickly. At 370 pages, it has 93 chapters, many only two or three pages long. I would classify this book as escapist reading. There are many implausible situations that will leave readers wondering how this or anything even remotely like it could have happened in the real world. The book will not satisfy fans of authors like P. D. James, but James Patterson fans will be happy for another writer to fill their bookshelves. The author's note suggests that the he plans more books featuring Stevens and Windermere, so perhaps their characters will be more developed in later books. They are likable people--maybe a made-for-TV movie is in the offing?

title: Great for the middle school crowd
text: This book was a gift to my 13-year-old nephew, who loved it.  He told me he read it in one sitting--and he is a reluctant reader.  I wish there were more books like this to engage boys for whom reading is a chore.  No inappropriate material at all--just a fun, engaging story.  Highly recommended.

title: A supberb aid for math-o-phobes!
text:
As a fan of Kevin, Winnie, and the gang in "The Wonder Years," I knew that Danica McKellar had majored in math at UCLA and graduated summa cum laude. I did not know, however, that she had written a series of books aimed at helping girls get over math phobia and excel in a subject that is necessary for almost every high-powered career. I looked into this book when my niece was struggling with pre-algebra, and bought all thee books in the series.

Before I gave "Kiss My Math" to my niece, I went through it very carefully, working out all the problems. Danica's approach is chatty and very "girl-friendly"--she includes testimonials from girls and young women who struggled with math, questioned its usefulness, and eventually overcame its difficulties. She also writes encouraging little pep talks, and urges girls not to dumb themselves down in the hope of attracting a boy. Any boy worthy of you, her message goes, wants a smart, secure, confident girl. These are even quizzes of the type found in teen magazines, such as "What kind of test taker are you?"

The math is explained in a very down to earth way. This book is 180 degrees from dull and boring--my niece loved it when I finally gave it to her. I wish more problems were included, but anyone wanting more problems can go to Danica McKellar's website. Still, a hands-on accompanying workbook would be nice.

I wish math were taught this way to girls everywhere. I am now tutoring my niece (and her brother, who does not like these books so much!) in pre-algebra, and I intend to help them through algebra next year. I hear that McKellar in planning a geometry book, and I certainly hope she publishes it in the next year or so. Congratulations, Danica, on a wonderful series of books, and on helping girls everywhere really understand math for the first time.

title: Fast-paced and exciting
text:
"The Innocent," with its super-heroine Vanessa Michael Moore, is hard to put down. Vanessa, or Michael/Miki as she prefers, is the protector we all wish for, a Superwoman of sorts who fights for the underdog and especially for victims of abuse. She will bring to mind both a female version of James Bond and on the darker side, the heroine of Stieg Larsson's wildly popular "Girl" series, but she is really her own person.

Michael is asked by a good friend to rescue a teenager, Hannah, who was taken from him as a very young child and is being raised by a cult, The Chosen, based in Argentina. This cult has all the negatives we associate with false religion, including brainwashing, mistrust of outsiders and the early sexualization of the girls, who are then used as sex slaves. All of this is done in the name of religion, which does nothing to protect its members, but rather exploits them in every way imaginable. The plot of the book involves Michael's attempt to rescue this child.

The reader should be warned that the book is quite graphic and brutal in some scenes. These are the parts that will remind readers of the "Girl" series. In addition, Michael is not a perfect heroine--she has many demons of her own, which she deals with through drugs, insomnia, and nightmares when she eventually can sleep. Her own childhood comes into play, through both memories and nightmares. Michael's efforts on behalf of the abused reflect her own determination never again to be a victim.

I have not read the first book in this series, "The Informationist," but I certainly plan to do so. And I am looking forward to what I hope will be a long and thrilling series of exciting and intriguing books.

All in all, a great and fast read, fully deserving five stars!

title: Excellent and fast-paced
text:
Unlike many other reviewers of "Dead Man's Grip," I was completely unfamiliar with the Roy Grace detective series. An avid reader of mysteries and detective fiction, I selected this book based on the brief description on the Amazon Vine newsletter, and I am thrilled that I did.

The book begins with a multi-vehicle auto accident in which a young student at Brighton University is killed. This student is the scion of an American Mafia family, which explains much of what happens throughout the book. Carly Chase, a young single mother to a four-year-old, is charged with manslaughter. Carly is clearly innocent to the reader from the beginning, but she is in the wrong place at the wrong time. DS Roy Grace is the lead investigator on this case, and he is determined to discover the truth. As the book proceeds, everyone else involved in this accident meets an untimely end.

The book is very readable and fast-paced; in fact, it was hard to put down. There are some scenes of terrible brutality, so the reader should be prepared. They are crucial to the discovery of what actually happened. An unsavory character, Tooth, will also disturb some readers.

I loved this book and am going to read all of Peter James's Roy Grace mysteries in order. I am sure that there are aspects of Roy Grace's background that will be filled in by the previous books. I cannot believe that I have never heard of them before, as I read a great deal of detective fiction. I did not want this book to end, but the ending was great. I highly recommend this book to anyone who likes mystery/detective fiction.

title: Interesting but bleak
text:
"The Sisters" by Nancy Jensen will likely have wide appeal and readership. A multi-generational family saga, it begins in 1927 and ends 80 years later. The two main characters at the beginning of the novel are sisters, loving and close at first but separated because of misunderstanding, miscommunication, and mistrust. Each sister's life is then followed through the Depression, Word War ii and the Vietnam War, and into the 21st century through her descendants.

The structure of the book is chronological, but the point of view shifts between each sister and her descendants, both children and grandchildren. Time shifts of anywhere from a few months to several years divide the chapters. There is a genealogy in the front of the book, and it is a good thing, too--I referred to it several times as I was reading. I found it a bit confusing to remember whose daughter was whose, and I liked it that I was able to figure out how old each narrator was in each chapter.

Though I did like this book, and I understand why it is titled "THe Sisters," I felt it could be titled "The Mothers and the Daughters" with equal justification. Certainly the women in this novel are fully realized characters, each with her own personality and strengths and weaknesses. The men, on the other hand, range from brutal and monstrous to cold and calculating to dishonest and unethical to ineffectual and weak to stolid and dependable. Not one is more than a caricature. Each woman, however, is both a mother and daughter, by birth, adoption, or informal but strong familial or emotional ties. Each of the original two sisters suffers as a result of the decision made early on to escape an absolutely intolerable situation, and the capacity of each woman for meaningful relationships with men is totally compromised by these events.

Readers should be warned that this is not a happy read. While there is a hint of contentment and resolution at the end, it comes at the cost of much suffering through years of misunderstanding and failure to relate. if you want happy talk, go elsewhere. This book is not for you. It is, however, very well written, interesting, and engaging, and many women will enjoy it. (Men, not so much!)

Book clubs will enjoy discussing this book. I hope the publisher includes a reading guide in the final publication copy.

title: Warm and compelling
text:
"Emory's Gift" is the story of a 13-year-old boy, Charlie Hall, whose much beloved mother has recently died and who is trying to cope with all the trials of early adolescence, and then some. His father is well-meaning but emotionally absent. His friends desert him when he needs them most, at the start of junior high school. He is small for his age, ungifted athletically, very bright, and awkward with girls--a perfect storm of teenage angst.

Into all this comes Emory, a huge grizzly bear, who is more than he seems to be at first glance. To tell more would be to give away important parts of the story; suffice it to say that Emory becomes a touchstone for Charlie and a litmus test for every human character in the book. If Charlie is the "hero" who must endure trials to find his destiny, Emory is the "animal/helper" whose guidance is essential. Charlie endures all tests and emerges having found a path through junior high school and into adult life.

While the target audience for this book is probably young adult, any animal lover will appreciate it. Well-written and insightful about human nature, it contains some spectacular descriptions of nature, but not so much that a reader would become bored. The author captures perfectly the emotions of a young teenage boy, and teens of either sex will be able to relate to Charlie. Adults will appreciate all over again that they got through this time of life, and will, it is hoped, look upon young teens with more empathy.

title: Excellent account of a family in crisis
text:
I am positively blown away by "The Grief of Others" by Leah Hager Cohen. It has a depth rarely seen in "family in crisis" fiction, and I was impressed from the first page.

The book tells of a year in the life of the Ryrie family, with one extended flashback to eight years previous. The point of view alternates among the family members: Ricky, the mom; John, the dad; Jess, John's young adult daughter by a brief encounter in his college years; Paul, the adolescent son; and Elizabeth (Biscuit), the 11-year-old daughter. Another important character is Gordie, a young man whose father has just died and who is involved at the periphery of the family.

Although many strains are present in this family, the precipitating crisis is Ricky's third pregnancy. In her fifth month, she discovers that she is carrying an anencephalic child who, though he may be born alive, has no chance of survival. Told that most women in her situation choose abortion, and afraid that John will pressure her to do just that, Ricky tells no one about the baby's prognosis, even after he is born and dies 57 hours later. This deception is not revealed for a year, and its consequences form the substance of the book. Each family member suffers in his or her own way as a result, and each expresses grief and anger in different ways. Even before the truth comes out, each family member knows that something is wrong, but no one, even Ricky, knows exactly what.

Two aspects of this book are especially worthy of note. First, the novel is psychologically astute. Each character is fully developed and believable. Thoughts, attitudes, actions--all are authentic. The book has a psychological depth that makes most other characters seem flat. The reader sees each one, even the children, as whole and hurting human beings.

Second, the writing is simply wonderful. I was especially taken with the author's use of metaphor. Each figure of speech was fresh and arresting in its impact. There was not a hackneyed phrase in the entire book.

If you enjoy fiction dealing with families in crisis, you will love and appreciate this book. It is head and shoulders (now THAT is a hackneyed metaphor!) above most other fiction of its type. I recommend this book without reservation.

title: Difficult to like
text:
I hate to give books I review three stars--it seems so wishy-washy. But "This Beautiful Life" by Helen Schulman has forced me to do just that. The cover art for the book is inspired--the "beautiful life" that the Bergamots have worked so hard for is a house of cards, one that comes tumbling down at the first storm.

I will begin with the positives. Schulman has written a devastatingly accurate portrayal of the nouveau riche of New York City. Their obsession with money and status is well drawn, from the boss who deserts Richard Bergamot at the first sign of trouble, to the shallow and gossipy "friends" who do the same to his wife, Lizzy. The reader cannot but despise these people, and one would think that he or she would find him or herself automatically in sympathy with Richard, Lizzy, and their teenaged son, Jake.

However, one would be wrong. Though I wanted to like these characters, I could not. The parents leave a perfectly wonderful upper middle class life in Ithaca, New York, where each has a satisfying career at Cornell University, for the seductive bright lights of New York City, where Richard has been offered a dream job at a university that sounds a lot like Columbia. Lizzy gives up her career to manage her children's lives, "the deal," as Richard characterizes it, which ultimately leads her to frustration and substance abuse. The son, Jake, is typical of his age (15), but not all that likable either. Five-year-old Coco Bergamot, adopted from China, is by far the most attractive member of the family, but the reader wonders how long her irrepressible spirit can last in this land of spiritually dead or dying people.

The book is a fast read, and I think it will find a wide readership, since the central incident, sexting, is much in the news today. There are glimmers of excellent writing, but the overall impression is just appalling. I found the book's end ambiguous, filled with regret over opportunities lost. The book is a cautionary tale of what happens to people who make money their god. They are sorry in the end, but it is too late.

title: Interesting and Provocative
text:
I selected "Light from a Distant Star" because I had previously read some of the author's work and enjoyed it, especially "Songs in Ordinary Time." Mary McGarry Morris's latest effort is not quite up to "Songs," but it is worth a read nonetheless.

"Light" is a coming of age story that will appeal to both adults and adolescents, though I suspect some of the nuances of the book will be lost on teens. The central character, 13-year-old Nellie Peck, is beautifully drawn, with all the innocence and confusion of her age. She prides herself on having what Holden Caulfield called "an excellent BS detector," and she struggles to remain true to herself, even when family, peer, and other pressures mount.

Each character in the book is facing some sort of crisis. The parents are facing imminent financial collapse, and each deals with it in diametrically opposite ways; the older sister is trying to re-connect with her birth father; the younger brother is trying to overcome shyness and insecurity. A wider circle of friends, relatives, and neighbors each has his or her own eccentricities. In the midst of all this, a murder occurs, and Nellie finds herself the star witness. Ultimately she has to decide not just whether or not to do the right thing, but what the right thing is in the first place.

This novel has been compared with Harper Lee's "To Kill a Mockingbird," but I think the comparison is not merited. Whatever the chaos in Lee's book, it had a moral center, Atticus Finch, that was solid and true, around which the entire narrative circled. There is no real moral center in Morris's book, which makes the confusion of the central character very understandable.
