title: Twenty dollars for this vinyl edition seems reasonable.
text:
I have this album, purchased for six dollars heaven knows when, and probably decades ago. There are many interpretations of Kreisleriana; I have two: this one and Cynthia Raim's performance for Connoisseur. Arrau's performance sounds a bit deliberate, especially the first track: Ausserst bewegt. Ausserst bewegt is half-etude and half caprice. It plays with meter much in the same way that Schumann did for quartet 2, opus 41. The phrases overlap each measure by one triplet sixteenth note, except when they seem to catch their footing, except that they don't. Great fun. I prefer Raim's interpretation, because it seems more fluent and sustains clash of lopsided phrasing and the seeming regularity of triplets. And her interpretation seems to capture the drama. Arrau does much better with "Sehr innig und nicht zu rasch." He takes his time and makes this rather long movement serenely beautiful. Where he lacks the aggressive energy of Raim's performance on side one, he pulls more emotion out of the music. On track seven, Sehr rasch, he shows his ability to match anyone's tempo and dynamics. Amazing.

And while this isn't an audiophile-quality performance, and it is close-mic'd, there is plenty of detail in the sustains and mechanics of the piano. If you like vinyl, this is a pretty decent deal. But you may find it for a lot less at a local used records store.

title: Brass Quintet...where's the tape?
text:
This LP was purchased in 2011 as new old stock: a sealed lp from 1972. I remember hearing this LP at the local public library as a junior high student and wanting to buy it. 30 years later I have it and it's not all that great. The LP pressing is noisy and the levels exceed the dynamic range of the LP, so the sound is distorted. Furthermore, the Partita for Brass Quintet and Tape is all brass and no tape... they actually didn't perform it with the tape accompaniment (unless Lazarof recorded other brass players for playback). I don't think that it is his best work, either. In summary, I recommend avoiding this LP, which turns up online from time to time as an overpriced item. Instead...

Readers of this review should sample the amazing Naxos CD of Tableaux/Symphony #2/Violin concerto. Lazarof writes great music. The quality of the recording is top-notch, too. For that reason, if his music is to your tastes, I would forgo the MP3 format and buy the CD.

text: I really do like the Hypnosis Network Series but I think they are too expensive compared to other cd's readily available. But if you have the money to spend, these cd's are worth the price.  This series, Core Inner Strength, is focused on working on your self-esteem and and self-confidence.  These sessions reminded me very much of the type of session you would undergo if you went to see a psychiatrist that utilized hypnosis in their practice.  There is no background music and no wave sounds. All you hear is Dr. McNeal's calm soothing voice.  She first puts you into hypnosis and then once you are "under" and in a safe place she talks to you about trusting and finding your inner voice, self-confidence, self-esteem, and feeling safe in your life.  Again, no bells and whistles or new age stuff but just the type of session that you might get if you went to seek help from professional western doctor to help you regain your self-esteem after some sort of emotional trauma from childhood, a divorce, or mild depression. It's somehow powerful, and mellow at the same time, exciting and full of passion. I would not normally think a cd was worth this price, but I do with this one. I wish I knew more about it's origin, where the music comes from, what it's all about, etc. I do think it has a spiritual quality, and don't know if they are singing about their relationship with God, or a person, or both?
I say it is worth it because I would pay that to see them one time, and with the cd, I can hear it over and over again. Also, because it's unusual, it has grown on me. At first, the verdict was out. I was not unimpressed, but it did not knock my socks off. As each song played, I began to say wow, pretty impressive, and then listening to it again, it was a lovely experience. Worth a try.
It looks, from the cover, like your typical "new agey" cd, but it's way beyond that.
Also, there is some "techno" like sound in there in certain songs, and usually that turns me off, but it's good music.I mean I do like techno to an extent, but often I find it cheapens music, lowers the class of a piece, but that doesn't seem to happen here. Hope that helps.

title: Title is ONCE You Move
text: This is one of the early CDs from the ORIGINAL Eden Regained Christian rock band, based in Newark, Ohio, and formed in 1995 with a group of Newark High School students. The band's skilled instrumentations, heavy guitar sound (formed by three guitars plus bass) and beautiful vocal harmonies, along with their good looks, stage presence and message, made them a very popular band in the MIdwest in the mid- to late 1990s. There is another Christian rock band floating around YouTube who has stolen this band's name, but this CD, Once You Move, belongs to the original Eden Regained, who also crafted The Clean EP and Ascension before the band's breakup in 2000. title: Fairly Typical for it's Time
text: The singers & orchestra do a good job. The audience is quiet except for some applause and there's very little stage noise. The booklet, in Italian and English includes the complete libretto and has a good ammount of information about the composer, the libretto, the original cast & performance history. It does not have any information about the current cast nor does it have a synopsis of the plot & I was not ready to read the 47 page libretto to learn the plot. Also, there are only 8 tracks per CD which means some of the tracks combine a scene, aria, duet and or chorus all together instead of breaking them up into separate tracks.  Even worse, there are no timings on the tracks. Each CD is approx 64 min and after doing some searching I found the track timings at Presto Music. CD 1 track 1 - 8:12; 2 -2:45; 3 - 1:51; 4 - 5:59; 5 - 11:49; 6 - 12:46; 7 - 4:09; 8 - 17:06. CD 2 track 1 - 12:46; 2 - 6:36; 3 - 6:20; 4 - 7:21; 5 - 4:09; 6 - 9:30; 7 - 10:00; 8 - 6:38. As for Persiani's music it's pleasant with some interesting arias & duets. If you've heard any of the music of his contemporaries such as Morcacchi, Vaccaj, Ricci or Mercadante or one of Donizetti's lesser more slap dash operas you'll have a pretty good idea of what this opera sounds like. If you're looking for something really great from this era & you're tired of the same old Bellini & Donizetti try Meyerbeer's Italian opera & even better the operas of Giovanni Pacini.

title: Franck's Top Three

The Symphony, performed by the Philharmonic Orchestra and Constantin Silvestri is a bit slow and lackluster. The 1st & 2nd movements are both about one minuet each slower than another recording I have. That may not sound like much but it does make a difference. If you're going to own only one recording of this symphony, this is not the one to have. I checked & my other, more recent recording is also by the Philharmonic orchestra, but a different conductor (Francesco D'Avalos).  It's much livelier and more satisfying.

title: Very Attractive Piano Sonatas
text: Pinto (1785-1806) died at age 20 of TB. These teenage works are so attractive that one wonders what he might have  achieved had he lived a full life. title: Dull Performance
text: I owned this recording and having listened to it a couple of times I was always left with the question, why was this opera so famous? It was dull & plodding. Then I bought the 1954 performance by Callas & Corelli and I had an ah ha moment. Listening to that '54 performance compared to this modern performance made me realize what a difference great singers can make. The '54 performance was so great that I now understood why this opera was so famous & highly thought of in it's day. The quality of the recording here is obviously better than the '54 recording, but that's the only good thing I can say about this recording when comparing the two.

title: Worth Buying Just to Hear Corelli
text: A recording of a 1960 performance from La Scala. While not as good as a modern studio recording, the sound is perfectly acceptable. No noise from the stage or audience except very enthusiastic applause. The chorus, orchestra and singers are excellent. Callas is Callas whether you love her voice or hate it (this audience loved her). Corelli, at the height of his career, is the stand out. Incredible, voice, high notes & emotion. I've read that someone thought this opera contained some of Donizetti's best music. I'm not too sure of that. I'm not a big fan of Donizetti though I've heard most of the recordings of his operas. To me, this one falls somewhere in the middle, not the worst, but not up there with his hand full of best operas. There are some pretty exciting arias and duets for Callas & Corelli and some good choruses & act finales. With lesser soloists this opera probably wouldn't sound as good as it does here.

title: A Pleasant Salieri Opera.
text: A live recording from Verona, Italy. Very little stage noise & the audience is quiet except for applause after nearly every number. The sound quality is good. The singers, chorus & orchestra all do a fine job. As for the music, while there's nothing here that will keep you "humming a tune" ever after, there are many very melodic, pleasant & quite pretty arias & duets to enjoy. This opera wasn't one of Salieri's succeses. Apparently it wasn't the music that was to blame but the story which was about women characters taking on male roles & vice versa & even a gay character. The 1795 audience was not ready & rejected to opera.  If you're a Salieri fan like me this is a must have, if you're just looking to sample one Salieri opera, then the "Grotto of Trifonio" or the "Falstaff" might be a better choice.

title: Good addition to my Spohr music collection
text: These overtures are better than I thought they'd be. They've inspired me to explore some on Spohr's dramatic work, not just his orchestral & chamber music.

title: The Least Interesting of Spontini's Big Four Operas
text: Spontini's fame & reputation rested on his last four operas (La Vestale, Fernan Cortez, Olympie & Agnes de Hohenstaufen). Today only La Vestale keeps his name alive, if just barely. In my opinion, Olympie is the least interesting of the four. Originally written in 1819 for Paris it was a modest success. It was then rewritten in a new German edition for Berlin in 1822 & was much more successful. Then in 1826 the German edition was translated back into French & given in Paris quite successfully. It's the 1826 edition that's recorded here. The singing & orchestra are fine & the music is OK but nowhere as interesting as the music in Fernan Cortez or Agnes de Hohenstaufen. These last two operas however do not exist in modern recordings which is a great pity because in my opinion both are much better than either Vestale or Olympie.

title: Good Premier recordings
text: These are the first recordings of these two works. Steinberg (1883-1946) was the son in law of Rimsky Korsikov, the teacher of Shostakovich, & a fellow student with Stravinsky (who he beat out in a competition much to Stravinsky's chagrin over many decades). While Stravinsky went to the West, Steinberg stayed in Russia & remained very little known outside Russia, The two earlier symphonies recorded by Neemi Jarvi are very good in the style of Tchaikovsky & Glauzunov.. These are two later pieces. The symphony is a piece of Soviet ear music commemorating the opening of a railway. Programatic music with folk melodies. Well orchestrated. Worth a listen but not going to be a piece I'll listen to again for a long while. The violin concerto (from 1946) is much better, Very mush in the Romantic idiom, it's a very appealing work.

title: Outstanding example of French Grand Opera
text: A live recording from Turin, Italy in 1974. Audience was very quite. Sung in Italian rather than the original French. Based on the 1817 revision rather than the 1809 original. Sound quality is very good (vastly better than the 1951 Naples recording). Bruno Pevedi (a world class tenor in his day), singing the role of Cortez is outstanding. Chorus & orchestra are also very good, the soprano is the real weak spot for me (especially compared with Renata Tebaldi in the 1951 recording). The opera is wonderful. Some very fine arias & duets & especially outstanding & dramatic writing for the chorus. Why this opera has not had a really good, modern, studio recording is a mystery to me. So many much poorer opera have been recorded over & over I wonder why this very exciting opera has been ignored. To my ear, this opera is much more entertaining than Spontini's vastly better known opera "La Vestale". What may have held this opera back is that it has an all male cast except for one soprano & the lead character (Cortez) does not make an appearance until the second act. Highly recommended to anyone who enjoys French Grand Opera, Meyerbeer, Halevy's La Juive, etc.

title: The book is better the more I think about it
text: Kind of a young adult version of "Oryx & Crake" where teens navigate what they think is an awesome world but is really a dystopian future dominated by corporate advertising and the protection of Americans from knowing about the damage caused elsewhere in the world by their habits. People have chat feeds and shopping recommendations plugged directly into their bodies from birth. It took a bit to get used to the language because nearly every sentence is in teenspeak but you soon realize the entire society is this way — even the parents are, like, "Dude" and "Whatev." Their limited vocabulary weakens their ability to express their emotions when things start to go wrong. title: A personal gift from Kleiber to us all
text:
Thanks to this recording, we finally get to know how a Kleiber's Mahler would sound like. Unless you are paying some offshore sellers near $100 for this CD ... the experience alone is well worth the price (near double of other classical music CDs in Amazon)

Like one of the reviewers has mentioned, the tempo for 'Abschied' is indeed curiously on the fast side. The pace is more curious than the fact why Kleiber choose to conduct a Mahler piece at all. Perhaps the Mahler revival in the 60's had motivated him enough? But why the fast tempo?

Nevertheless, IMHO, Das Lied is Mahler's farewell piece, not a death bed piece like the 9th or the 10th. It is like how we get used to numerous versions of comatose Faun (Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune) or Mahler 9th. Kleiber's choice of tempo seems right to me.

I am so very grateful to own this CD

title: Local California talent that needed a manager to take them National
text:
Rick Glenn and the Texas Aliens were a phenominal California house band for a small night club just East of Los Angeles. When the club owner realized he was turning away more people nightly than what his club could hold, he began looking for a larger facility. He credited the band for bringing in the crowd and therefore built a new bar around the band and their unique abilities.

They found the location in an abandoned FRY'S grocery store shopping center in Colton just next to San Bernardino and north of Riverside. The band and the bar staff built the entire new bar by hand. The story was that the stage alone took enough lumber to build a 3 bedroom house with a 2 car garage. All of the tables and bar stools were also built by hand and all were at standing height so that if there were more in your party than the number of stools available you could still gather round. Each table also had special hooks underneath so that ladies had a place to hang their purses.

Originally the new club in Colton could handle up to 2000 per the fire marshall and it wasn't long before the word spread and once again the club was standing room only and people were made to wait in line outside in case someone would leave (One out = One in). On Friday nights it was quite common for people from San Diego and as far as San Francisco to charter a bus and bring their party to Colton to the Mulelip for a weekend of dancing.

It wasn't long before the crowd had outgrown the bar and within the first year, Rick, the band and the club owner began negotiations to buy out the rest of the shopping center and enlarge the club. It was closed for about a month while they did the renovations, moved the stage back to accomodate a much larger dance floor. They also at this time increased their service to include a full-service Steak-House restaurant (The Upper Lip) inside the club. One of the draw backs to the new larger club was that there were no cables long enough anywhere in the world to reach from the new stage location all the way back to the sound booth at the back wall. And the sound engineer would have needed binoculars to see the stage. So the sound booth was moved to the middle of the dance floor, which created a small island for dancers to dance around. (Country music dancers dance around the floor as opposed to Rock & Roll dancers who dance ALL OVER THE FLOOR).

When they re-opened the Mulelip could boast the largest country dance floor in the U.S. - even larger than Mickey Gilley's in Pasadena, TX. Although Gilley's was a larger club in square footage, the Mulelip had a much larger dance floor.

The secret to the whole adventure was the genius of Rick Glenn and his uncanny ability to read a crowd and know what song to call next in order to keep them dancing. They used to joke that they really didn't need as many tables and stools because people were never at the table but on the dance floor instead.

Rick's vocal abilities were so good that when he sang a Johnny Cash song, you'd have thought that Cash, himself was on stage. Rick could do that with Merle Haggard songs, Charlie Pride songs and just about any other male country singer. The beauty of it was that he wasn't trying to do impressions of those artists but rather paying homage to them and to the song and his voice had the special qualities necessary. Each artist also had their own unique timing and phrasing and Rick could duplicate that like no other.

The problem came to be that although Rick could give such special treatment to the male songs, he didn't have the vocal qualities to duplicate those songs sung by female artists....and so a lovely young ladie named Stephanie with a voice from Heaven would come out and sing two or three songs per set.

Besides Rick's talent, he was backed by one of the most talented bands of the day that included a drummer who could match riffs with Buddy Rich when called upon to do so but who also knew how important his steady back-beat was to keep the dancers on the floor. He had to have the most boring job in the club just hitting the bass drum with his foot on the down beat and slapping his stick on the snare on the off beat. ( there isn't much more to country drumming than that). But he was right there - solid as a rock - every night, every beat and every off-beat. The mark of a very good drummer.

If Rick Glenn and the Texas Aliens had had the talents of a Colonel Tom Parker to manage them who know where they would have gone in the music business.

title: Be sure to find a digital theatre with THX. It's worth it.
text:
Episode 2 is everything I hoped it would be and more. The story shows us the turmoil in the senate, the believable relationship between Anakin and Padme, Anakin's conflict with the Jedi and it also has many subtle and prominent connections to episodes 4-6.
This episode also has a lot of treats for fans. Namely Jedi and Bounty Hunting action. We see more of the Jedi temple, we see a spectacular battle involving more than a dozen Jedi in a small area (something we've never seen until now) and the pinnacle of it all is of course, Yoda. Yoda looks great. His character is very well done in this outing. Plus, we get to see him fight, which is a real treat and great fun to watch. Seeing Jango Fett in action is like fulfilling every Star Wars fan's fantasies about what Boba would've/should've been doing in 4-6. We never really saw Boba do much. But Jango goes all out. We see him fly, shoot and use all kinds of gadgets. His space battle with Obi-Wan in the debris ring is spectacular (this is where THX sound really pays off) Episode 2 leaves Star Wars fans satisfied in many areas.
I was lucky enough to be able to see Episode 2 the way it's meant to be seen, on a digital screen. Digital projection is absolutely wonderful. The picture is crisp, no scratches, dots or dust. It's like watching a DVD on a huge screen only 10 times better. Digital projection combined with THX sound makes for the ultimate experience. It is my advice that you make the extra effort/time to find and get to a digital theatre near you. If you really care about seeing this movie in the best way possible, it's certainly worth the trouble.

title: A Delightfully Quaint Postcard of an Album!
text:
I developed an appreciation of this 1961 compilation of Perry Como's Christmas songs as a child.His Christmas specials were still being aired, and I have memories of a younger sibling struggling to repeat the line from Frosty the Snowman, "Frosty clumsy as he can be....", and being unable to say the word, "clumsy" as a toddler.
Robert Prestergaard's commentary on the back of the jacket of the vinyl record painted a cozy, sentimental picture of Christmastime, its tradition, the carols, and of the well-liked Mr.Como himself.
The album begins with a lightherted, well-orchestrated version of T'was the Night Before Christmas, followed by The Twelve Days of Christmas,then we hear God Rest Ye Merry Gentlemen, followed by C-H-R-I-S-T-M-A-S(which I performed as part of a Sunday School choir one year ),then Joy to the World, then a kazoo-laden version of Rudolph, the Red-Nosed Reindeer, then the aforementioned Frosty the Snowman, The Christmas Song, a rare carol called That Christmas Feeling, then I'll Be Home for Christmas, then Silent Night, O Come All Ye Faithful, then Jingle Bells, a sweet, reverent version of White Christmas,and finally, a swing-era version of Winter Wonderland.
Admittedly, other Christmas albums have captured my fancy and invoked my passions since this one did.But I now listen to it with the sentimentality one might have for an old Christmas greeting card from years past, and when listening, I enjoy once again the warmth and amiability that has become the hallmark of a great artist's legacy.

title: In a Word, Superb!
text: 25 years ago this  week, shortly after purchasing this album, I taped the beauteous and reverent promotional special for it.The banter of the TV program could be a little hokey, but like the album itself, it was very well put together, although Natalie Cole and Tammy Wynette, who performed the songs, Grown-Up Christmas List,  and Away in a Manger respectively, were absent from that special, as they are now, sadly absent from our world.  Foster initiates  with his rendering of  Carol of the Bells,  Wynnona follows with a warm and hearty version of Blue Christmas, BeBe and CeCe Winans perform The First Noel, followed by Johnny Mathis' classic version of The Most Wonderful Time of the Year.After Natalie Cole's aforementioned offering, we hear Michael Crawford's O Holy Night( as a huge fan of his, this was the piece de resistance that led to my purchase of the album).  Vanessa  Williams' Go Tell it on the Mountain/ Mary Had a Baby is next, followed by Peabo Bryson and Roberta Flack's I'll Be Home for Christmas, Celine Dion performs The Christmas Song, and after Tammy Wynette's performance, the ensemble give us White Christmas in the finale.  A quarter of a century after its release, this is still a great Christmas album, and the videos from the promotional television program, which may now be viewed on You Tube only serve to enhance its greatness.

title: First in a Series of Entertaining and Educational Albums
text:
This was the initial album of a three-album ( the last part being a 2 in 1 deal) set to which I was introduced as a child because my parents ordered the set from TV Guide. Listening to its contents as a 10 1/2-year-old in the early '80s familiarized me with the main events of that decade due to the chronicle of notable historic events on the back jacket. It was from this album I learned of such events as the disappearance of justice Joseph F. Crater, and the Lindberg Baby's kidnapping. The music teacher I had the previous year made me fully aware of the Great Depression of the '30s, which hadn't happened for me despite frequent viewings of "The Waltons" from pretty early on, when she played the original Broadway cast album of "Annie". But the noted events on the album's jacket and the songs featured gave me more of a feel for what that time was like.
Interestingly, this album features many artists who were still alive when it introduced me to their work, such as Woody Herman, whose "Blues in the Night" is featured, and I still get a kick out of Artie Shaw's instrumental rendering of Cole Porter's "I Get a Kick Out of You"( I recall first hearing the lyrics in the 1946 film, "Night and Day" some years later).
But the album begins with the Andrews Sister's 1937 classic, "Bei Mir Bist Du Schoen", followed by Eddie Cantor's "Makin' Whoopie", then we hear Judy Garland's tribute to Clark Gable, "You Made Me Love You".
Louis Armstrong's "A Kiss to Build A Dream On" purportedly came from a later era, as perhaps did Tommy Dorsey's "Tenderly".
Tony Martin presents his tart and mellow rendering of "All the Things You Are", we hear Bing Crosby's 1936 offering, "Pennies From Heaven" from his movie of the same name, the King Cole Trio, with an early vocal by Nat perform "Sweet Lorraine", Guy Lombardo gives us the comically wistful, "Boo Hoo", and Ella Fitzgerald scats along with "Lady Be Good".
I belong to that odd but phenominal tribe that develops more of an affiliation to music decades older than we are than with contemporary sounds. I make no apologies for it. It caused me to develop a certain reverence for the endurance of the Greatest Generation as they weathered the first half of a catachlysmic two-decade ordeal of economic hardship and extreme global conflict and the songs that helped lighten their burdens through it all.

title: My Love of the Music of This Era Officially Began With This!
text:
My parents purchased this album, along with its '30s and '50s &'60s counterparts sometime back in the 1970s, and from my preteens onward, it provided me with countless hours of entertainment and information. I developed a weekly ritual of just listening to all three of them (favorite songs only) on the living room record player--rather unusual for a Generation Xer.
But, of course these songs have a beauty that the often synthesized music my contemporaries listened to in the 1980s lacked, and in addition to familiarizing myself with the major events of the decade, as chronicled on the back of the album's jacket (which proved to be very helpful with my knowledge of history).
Our musical journey begins with the stately somberness of Jimmy Dorsey's 1941 winningly formulaic hit, "Amapola", which starts out as a solemn tango accompanied by Bob Eberle's beautiful vocalization, becomes jazzier in the middle, and is capped of by Helen O' Connell's bouncy finale.
We then go to a number that was my initial favorite on this album( which I'd initially heard on a Bing Crosby album my Dad purchased shortly after Bing Crosby's passing, and had recently been recited by my current English teacher), 1944's "Swinging on a Star" by Bing Crosby, initially performed with a Boys' Choir in the film "Going My Way", but which is performed here with the Williams Brothers, including an up-and-coming Andy Williams. We then hear the Ink Spots' "If I Didn't Care", then a slow version of "Tea for Two" by Eydie Gorme that seems out of place and from a later era.
Then there is crooner Dick Haymes' (and the Song Spinners') 1943 rendering of "You'll Never Know"--the beautiful result of a contentious musician's union strike that led to a slew full of a cappella hits at that time. In the emotional depths of this performance, the backup group warble traces of what would evolve into the doo-wop sould of the following decade.
Freddie Martin's 1945 instrumental rendition of "Symphony" is next. He also had a rendition with vocal accompaniment.
Side 1 ends with Judy Garland's rendering of "The Trolley Song", from her 1944 film, "Meet Me in St.Louis".
Satchmo's original 1940 rendition of "Blueberry Hill" begins side 2. The chorus on this one is lovely, but it always did sound as though Louis Armstrong needed to clear his throat before beginning his vocal on this one.
Sammy Kaye's emotional "Harbor Lights", also from 1940, was performed with a tropical flare.
Then we have The Mills Brothers' "Paper Doll" from 1943, the sassy swing number which these "Four Guys and a Guitar" ( which was their group's earlier name) turned into the biggest hit of the decade.
The lovely feminine harmonizing of the decades three top "canaries" ( the popular name for female singers of the time) the Andrews Sisters imbues the cheerfully sung, but wistful, "I Can Dream, Can't I?", then their pal and frequent collaborator Bing goes solo on "I'll Be Seeing You", and we end with Judy Garland and Gene Kelly's "For Me and My Gal" from the 1942 movie of the same name.
While I find intriguing that Glenn Miller, the decade's most popular band leader was excluded from this roster, I feel this is a great mixture of samples of the popular music of the decade, depicting feelings of values, a sense of fun, mixed with emotion-laden piety( as is expressed in "If I Didn't Care" and "You'll Never Know" in lines about speaking their loved one's names in prayer), longing, and hopefulness largely against the backdrop of Mankind's deadliest conflict.
Subsequent generations who listen to these songs may feel that in a small way, they have lived at least a little of the journey of the Greatest Generation along with them.

title: Part of the  Album Trilogy Largely Responsible for My Love of Oldies
text:
I'm a Generation Xer who came in at the tail end of the '60s and learned to enjoy many of the hits featured on this two record album, as well as its two predecessors of the '30s and '40s when I was a pre-teen in the early '80s.
I enjoyed the uniqueness of the arrangements, including Teresa Brewer's bouncy "Music, Music, Music", which I saw her perform on "The Muppets" some years earlier. A revived , "I'm Gonna Sit Right Down and Write Myself A Letter" by Billy Williams is given an early Rock 'n' Roll era twist, The Four Aces' "Love is a Many Splendored Thing" is presented with grand Oriental Splendor... Sammy Davis' Vegasy styled "That Old Black Magic" begins the '50s album with vigor and swing, Don Cornell's "I'll Walk Alone" is a 50s styling of a World War II era favorite, The Ames Brothers revamp the song, "Undecided", Peggy Lee gives her cafe styling of "Mr. Wonderful", The Lennon Sisters' sweet harmony infuses their 1956 rendering of "Tonight You Belong to Me", Al Hibbler's "He" is appropriately reverent , "Blue Tango" by Leroy Anderson (which I recall hearing in "La Bamba") reflects the popularity of the Tango in the early '50s, Earl Grant's "Ebb Tide" is serene, and in recent days, with the passing of Debbie Reynolds, I've thought of how my mom once told me stories of having elegant dress parties with friends as a teenager with songs like "Tammy" playing on the record player.
Selections from the 1960s include Len Barry's "One, Two, Three", Brenda Lee's "I'm Sorry", Bert Kaempfert's "Wonderland by Night"and Spanish Eyes", Louis Armstrong's "Hello Dolly", and a few more that represent the era quite magnificently.
On the back of the jacket, there is a chronicle of the major events of both decades, including the Korean War, Queen Elizabeth II's coronation, the implementation of television in daily American life, The debut of Elvis Presley and Rock' n 'Roll, Princess Grace's wedding, the ascension of Sputnik, Alaskan and Hawaiian Statehood, the U2 Scandal, the election and assassination of John F. Kennedy, the debut of the Beatles, the assassinations of Martin Luther King and Robert Kennedy, Man's arrival on the moon, and finally Woodstock.Much of my familiarity with this era stemmed from this album and its predecessors, and all three were instrumental in my doing well in history classes.
Like its predecessors that chronicle the music and history of the 1930s and 1940s, this album is a rare find that any collector should be proud to have.

title: Christmas in the '60s...
text:
I grew up listening to the vinyl version of this 1964 album, whose roster is filled with an exotic array of neo-classical carols, often heavily laden with emotion.
The soft, hazy, heartwarming photo of a stylishly beehived young mother with an ethereal looking infant, purportedly, an updated take on the Madonna and Child, is the cover for Harry Simeone's excellent presentations, including his signature version of "The Little Drummer Boy", a powerful, intense, and sparkling version of "Hallelujah", an updated version of " 'Twas the Night Before Christmas" with orchestration more than highly reminiscent of an earlier one by Simeone's one-time associate, Fred Waring, a light and abbreviated version of "What Child is This?", and Side One ends with a distinct version of "Carol of the Bells".
Side 2 begins with Simeone's take on the Italian carol, "O Bambino", and then we hear, "The First Christmas Carol", followed by the calypso carol, "Mary's Little Boy Chile", a wistfully reverent and reminiscent, "Every Christmas is a Birthday", then a bouncy and delightful, contemporary orchestrated "Christmas Tree", complete with a base guitar, and a delightful chorus of children in tow, and finally, "Sing a Song of Christmas".
50 years later, this reverent gem still holds its magic, still typifying the musical stylings of its era retains a high level of appeal , and will continue to do so as years go by.

title: The Hybrid Theory EP
text:
I'll avoid talking about sellers and just tell you about the EP itself:

There once was a little bad called Xero created by some southern California natives looking for a break. Lineup changes (particularly the introduction of a new lead singer/screamer from Arizona) and a name change later and they released a self titled EP called The Hybrid Theory EP. The name change reflected their intention to create music that fused together elements of hard rock, hip hop, pop, industrial, and techno into one hybrid of style. One more name change later they released a full length album called Hybrid Theory under the name Linkin Park and became one of the biggest bands on the planet.

The tracks on The Hybrid Theory EP have popped up here and there on future Linkin Park albums and EP's, but it's only found a fully remastered release as a benefit of joining Linkin Park's fan club LPUnderground. That's really not a good thing for LP fans who might have felt a little put out by the band's movement away from their roots, abandoning a lot of the hard rock that drove their early mainstream releases.

On this particularly EP, it's easy to see what's going to drive LP to become so big. The pop sensibility that allows them to create songs that will stick with you, but not grate on your senses is there. The crisp lyrical flow of Shinoda's raps is ever present. The driving guitars, the beats, the turntables; all there. If anything, some of the tracks in this EP are better than some of the tracks that appeared on their first two albums. If anything, though, moving to a major label helped them hone in their influences allowing them to work as more of a cohesive unit then they sound like here.

Lyrically, I would say there are some tracks on here that definitely trump the material of their debut album. "High Voltage" is one of the best raps about the form ever written, and the re-envisioning that appears on the Reanimation album doesn't quite do it justice. It appears as though they maybe they didn't think their audience was quite ready for a complete hip hop track on their debut, but I think it would have been highly beneficial considering the albums and tracks that came after. Also, where Hybrid Theory was very "me-centric", it could have used a dose of the song "Carousel" which is an interesting look at addiction without directly blatantly stating exactly what the song is about.

If you can get a hold of it, and you're a Linkin Park fan, I highly recommend that you take a listen to The Hybrid Theory EP. You'll easily get a base for where this band has come from, and if you prefer old school LP and haven't heard it then it will help tide you over for a while. This EP will definitely give you a sense of how the band has progressed from the times before they were signed to a major label.

4.5/5

text:
I suspect that the people who will read this review have already played the game. So I won't take up too much space in describing the music. The sound quality is superb. Also, the packaging is very attractive.

As most Xenosaga fans are aware, Mr. Mitsuda created the soundtrack for Episode I, using the great Royal Philharmonic Orchestra. And that soundtrack received a lot of well-deserved praise and recognition. When it was announced that Ms. Kajiura would compose the music for Episode II, some of the fans where doubtful. After the release of Episode II, it became clear that although the soundtrack was very good, fans did not like it as much as they did the first game's music. During the short wait for Episode III, there were endless discussions on the many forums dedicated to Xenosaga as to who the fans would like to compose the music for the third episode. Let me just say that I am glad Ms. Kajiura had decided to stay with the project and compose the music for Xenosaga Episode III: Also Sprach Zarathustra. Her composition, in my humble opinion, is even better than the one that Mr. Mitsuda created for the first game. With this soundtrack, Ms. Kajiura has firmly established herself as the equal of Mr. Mitsuda. I highly recommend this CD set to fans of the game. Listening to these tracks will bring back the thrill and exhilaration that you experienced while playing the game.

title: Hidden Gems Await
text:
Franz Liszt was the showman (some would say rock star) of his generation and that tends to muddy his modern day reputation. One thing that often gets overlooked, along with all the piano playing and scandalous behavior, Liszt not only managed to invent the symphonic poem (from the concert overture), he also wrote a dozen intriguing examples.

Today, Les Preludes is the only truly familiar tone poem - the music used in countless cartoons when I was growing up - but even that piece is heard less frequently these days. This first volume (of two) of all 12 tone poems by Kurt Masur and the Leipzig Orchestra is a true eye opener, giving us several rarely head pieces.

Along with Les Preludes we get the rousing and relentless Mazeppa, and then the lyrical Orpheus, and the unjustly neglected Tasso. In all of these works Liszt builds an entire piece based on a few small motives and then rings surprising variations on them. In Tasso, the somber opening theme becomes a waltz and then a victory ode. This idea of "thematic transformation" would influence many later composers.

Masur and his team has a fine understanding of this repertoire and gives these works the poetry and vitality they need, and the sound is still quite good. To be honest, Liszt can fall into bombast at times - Festklange is a good example here. But there is a lot more in these seven pieces than just bombast and this is a great way to explore an important corner of classical music that is almost forgotten these days

title: Minnesota blues
text:
Pat Donohue continues to disprove the notion that northern boys can't pick and can't play the blues. This album is so skillfully crafted that he makes it sound easy. Put it on, and it feels like an old friend just stopped by with his guitar to play you a few tunes and share a couple of beers.

For those that have already heard him play, then all I need to tell you is that this album is up to the same high standards as his others. You won't be disappointed.

For any that have never heard Pat Donohue, you're in for a treat. The only way it could get better is to be able to hear him live.

Some of the tunes are so much fun, it's easy to forget that you're listening to one of the world's best finger-picking guitar players, others are so good that it seems incredible that this isn't a New Orleans bluesman, but a northern boy from the great state of Minnesota.

The album is well balanced between blues, jazz, bluegrass and a few bits that defy classification. If artists that play around with some of the traditional forms bother you, then this album probably isn't for you, but if you simply want to listen to an incredible guitar player, you couldn't find a better choice.

title: Simply the best!
text:
Lil Darlin' is a tune very few people identify by name, but almost everyone recognizes when they hear it. Probably because the tune is one of the most recorded pop tunes writer Neal Hefti can claim. Hefti, himself, recorded it on numerous sessions and compilations, but the version Count Basie's band performed, using Hefti, and later Quincy Jones, as arranger is the real "hit." Usually upbeat in tempo, this lp presents a softness of sound and harmony that is just beautiful.

Sadly, there is no perception of how wonderful Neil Hefti's music is, not is there many attempts to revive his wonderful library. If you find this LP grab it, if you see a cd by Hefti jump on it, but listen to some of the best big band, full orchestra, music you will hear. Remember Henry Mancini, Count Basie and Duke Ellington usurped Hefti's catalog more than once!

title: One of the Rarest HS!
text:
Sadly, Stu Phillips is almost a forgotten arranger of a non-descript studio string orchestra. He told me that it was fun, but he had to move on to other projects. The HS stayed alive though, under other directors. However this single LP has been tragicly overlooked by the cd re-issue powers that be. Yet this one LP has some of the best arrangements, and the best selections of the whole HS catalog, excluding the Christmas treat CD. I cannot figure it out, but one listen to songs like "Blue Velvet" and "Our Day Will Come" and you'll be as puzzled as I am as to why no one has re-issued this gem.

I first heard this LP played over a late night easy listening program in Harrisburg, PA. The station, or the on-air DJ chose to play it in its entirety. I was hooked. You might hear selections from this one on satellite, but it deserved to be taken as a whole, it's that good.

The truely best selction is the marvelous classic by the Everly Brothers, "Let It Be Me" but at a close second is Ketty Lester's hit "Love Letters." Phillips' arrangement is "straight from the heart! This is a "must own" disc for the serious EL lover! Worth every buck.

title: Mystery Clue
text:
Whenever I see a cd, lp, et al selling for like $30-hundreds of dollars, I assume there is one mystery involved. Why so much? There generally, for us audiophiles two possibilities; 1: It stinks, but is the only copy on this planet, or the likely 2: It is awesome, and there are like a half dozen on this planet!

On "Dreams and Themes" let me answer the dicotomy for you...It is the latter! #2 and the fact that it so powerful, one asks why has no one re-issued it to make a sure income, easily putting them into the 1% bracket? Take one selection, the "Theme from M-A-S-H" and you'd know why this is a gem. I have the original soundtrack, I have probably a dozen discs listing that as being included, but no where, repeat NO WHERE, can you find a version to match this one. "Agave" is somewhere between Esquivel and Cal Tjader and will leave you wanting to play it again and again. I tear my heart out I loaned the cd copy I had to some friend because like a thought, it was gone. I have hired detectives to hunt whoever it was down. sadly,no source on the internet offers the whole D&T playlist.

Patrick Williams is had disappeared from the recording scene, but with his recent release, his music, surely, will be sought out. Get your copy of "Dreams and Themes" while they are out there...then ask for, like, a gazillion dollars when they disappear again. Truely one of Patrick Williams' best, ever! Mystery solv ed!

title: no, not that Steve Miller
text: More of an engineer and producer than performer, he did write, produce and perform upon a couple of his own titles. 'Singing Whale Songs In A Low Voice' is listed as avant-garde jazz, but it isn't really that adventurous, more like '70s fusion and contemporary jazz. Here, Miller performs on several different instruments including keyboards and guitar as well as composing - very well I might add. It has its moments of intricate fusion, such as Dreams Passed By Pts 1&2 as well as Forgotten Parkland and Truffles In Transit, all of which could have fit nicely on a Weather Report or Return To Forever album. By the same token, the beautiful, minimalist Simple Song could rival Bob James or Dave Gruisin's best efforts and Little Bird (passarihno) is as catchy and ebulant as anything Spyro Gyra ever did. A very engaging album. Sadly, this being a sort of personal project, it never really received much of a push, being on Miller's own small Hip Pocket label. Thus it was never released on CD, which is ironic given that Miller was one of the industry's earliest champions of digital recording technology and served as a board member to the RIAA for its Compact Disc division. Very well recorded as one might expect, it did embrace the technology of the day (1883) so the sound is a tad dated at times. Still, this is one of the '80s better jazz releases and just begs to be released on CD. One can only hope that if Mr. Miller is still with us, he might get around to doing just that.

title: Very strong release by John
text:
I won't hide the fact that I'm a huge Digweed fan, having followed him for about 10 years and always go to his shows whenever he's in town, which is usually once a year, twice if we're lucky. Over the last 10 years, I've seen him go from bangy progressive house/progressive trance to dark progressive, to experimenting with electro/prog rock which gave way to minimal, then coming back full swing to the recent version of progressive house.

Another reviewer labeled this album as "too spacey". Electronic dance music (EDM) comes in all forms and shapes and it's very hard to please all as each of us has individual tastes so I will not refute the other reviews. Usually it just comes down to, "did the DJ play the type of sound that I like?" So I'll just say that this album sounded like John. The sound is full, intense, and edgy. It reminded of the vibe I got from listening to his 2007 Essential Mix Warehouse Project set. It's also nice to see a double CD release again since it allows for better pacing and buildup. With single CD releases, too often, just when you think the album's picking up, it's over - this was true with his previous Transitions CDs. CD1 is noticeably more tame than CD2 which starts off with a bang and doesn't quit. I found myself smiling throughout the entire CD2 since the vibe was closer to his live sets.

If you're just starting out in progressive house or EDM for that matter, I'd highly recommend GU013 Ibiza by Sasha which IMO is the best EDM album released. If you'd like to get more of John, you can download his live sets that were broadcast over his Kiss FM shows over the last 10 years (get the live sets, not the studio mixed ones) or Essential Mix sets throughout the years. If you go to johndigweed.com, you can listen to his current Transitions radio show for that week. The best thing however is to catch him live and make sure you stay til the end b/c when he shifts into his "peak time mode" (aka "vortex") late into the set, it's game over! He will literally tear you into shreds. He's a different man in his lives. This album is not quite "peak time" material but it does have quite an edge.

These pioneering DJs like Digweed are all over the age of 40 now and (sadly) the day might come sooner than later that even John will be hanging up his headphones so catch him while you can!

title: Perfection Personified
text:
'Bruno Walter is the gold standard of Schubert, i.e., perfection personified.

Franz Schubert's symphonies are by turn, lyrical, sensitive, lively, passionate and powerful. And in this remastered 1962 recording, so is Bruno Walter. The composer and conductor fully complement each other, and the result is wonderful.

I recently bought a CD set of von Karajan conducting Schubert's 5th, 6th, 8th and 9th symphonies. They were so bad, I spent the greater part of the day debating with myself whether to let my dog play Frisbee with them or donate them to the city/county library. The library won out, but just barely.

If you're new to Schubert, give this recording a try. And if you love Schubert as he was meant to be performed, you will love this CD. I've heard many different interpretations by many different conductors. This is by far the best.

title: Muy Bueno!
text:
In the summer of 2007, I walked the 500-mile Camino Frances pilgrimage trail in northern Spain. Before I left home I began brushing up on my Spanish, which had deteriorated since I studied it in high-school during the 80s. One of the products I used was Elisabeth Smith's One-Day Spanish, and I found it to be quite helpful while on the Way.

The package contains one CD and a language cheat-sheet. Every morning during my commute to work, I went through a couple of Ms. Smith's lessons. Her instructional format is clever: she plays a seasoned expat air traveler who winds up sitting next to Andy, a linguistically-challenged English bloke heading to Spain on holiday. To pass the time she promises to teach him fifty Spanish words and some helpful phrases. There are ten tracks of lessons on the CD, nine of them on different topics such as Getting About, Shopping, and At a Restaurant. The final track is a comprehensive quiz to test your retention.

Since I was traveling in Spain, I found it helpful that Ms. Smith focused on European Spanish vs. the Latin American variety found on most Spanish language programs. Of course, both types of Spanish are quite similar, but there are some minute differences, such as how the Spanish pronounce gracias as "grathias." I also liked hearing Andy, a non-native, pronounce Spanish in a way that an English speaker like me could understand and relate to. In addition, the fifty words and smattering of helpful phrases is a realistic amount for the average traveler to master. And the travel-based dramatic format is relevant and entertaining. A big plus is the ability to burn the CD into iTunes and transfer the lessons to an iPod (although the track titles did not automatically download). It was nice being able to revisit a topic and fortify myself for the next day's linguistic adventures.

However, I had a couple of pedagogical barriers to overcome. Although I felt comfortable learning with Elisabeth and Andy, it's still ideal to hear a native speaker to get the correct nuances of pronunciation. That's why I supplemented this program with Pimsleur's Quick and Simple Spanish. Second, One-Day Spanish is somewhat rapid-fire due to the dramatic episode format, and at first I felt a bit put-off because I was used to the standard audio learning methodology. Andy learns the words and phrases in about seventy-five minutes, but it took me a lot longer via repetition (and I still needed a refresher here and there).

Therefore, I recommend that you begin using One-Day Spanish a couple of months in advance of your trip, and also supplement it with another travel-oriented Spanish language program featuring native speakers. The Spanish I managed to learn came in handy during my trek on the Camino, especially in the smaller towns where English was barely spoken - if at all. It certainly made ordering important pilgrim staples like red wine and coffee with milk that much easier.

Most people can't or won't pull out all of the stops to learn a language for a two-week vacation. But it really helps to have some working knowledge of the local lingo, and Elisabeth Smith's One-Day Spanish has the words and phrases needed to separate the travelers from the tourists. Recommended - and don't leave the cheat-sheet at home! NOTE: For other iPod-friendly Spanish language programs, check out the free Coffee Break Spanish Podcasts on iTunes, and iVideo Spanish by Penton Overseas.

title: Raw Talent!
text:
There is an earnest innocence in this collection of live cuts from 1967. The pure talent and raw energy that the Bee Gees exuded in the sixties is startling evident here. Most of the songs are from Bee Gees 1st, except for ‘World” and ‘Mrs. Gillespie’s Refrigerator’. A sparse band with no help from conductor Bill Sheperd (a true genius), these songs display five teenagers with the world in front of them.

It is bewildering how these live cuts got released on a label that’s virtually unknown (Vogon) when Capitol Records owns the song rights. The CD contains some generic liner notes, but does list that the album hit #7 in the USA and #8 in the UK. It also states that all songs were recorded in 1967. These songs achieve a nice elegance but ‘To Love Somebody’ truly stands out as a phenomenal piece. I think anyone could enjoy this album.

title: Historic Recording - Poor Quality
text:
This collection has some big issues. First, it is the only decent recording before the 1976 double-album, “Live…Here at Last”. It was also a true turning point for the Bee Gees having released “Main Course”, one of the few albums that Rolling Stone magazine gave great kudos to. However, Bee Gee fans are lacking in good quality recordings before 1976 and unfortunately this falls into that category.

The sound is not well mixed. The bass is very low and the middle sections and vocals are television quality. It does however show off Blue Weavers keyboard contributions both on synthesizer and piano. The Bonaroo Horns are truly appreciated here in the recording. I don’t think you could get a better recording on YOUTUBE. Even the sections between songs are poorly connected with audience clapping getting cut short and, in some cases, the first second or two of the songs missing.

The presence of Yvonne Elliman is fantastic. She helped introduce the Bee Gees slow soulful version of “To Love Somebody”. It also doesn’t hurt that she was contracted to RSO records and and backup on Eric Clapton’s albums at that time. Great song.

But if you can forgive some of these misfortunes, you’ll enjoy the time period. Its hard to believe at the time that this was the first big comeback. The addition of eight other songs from 1974 Melbourne help round out the collection. It would have been nice to see a photo or two of the brothers with guitars on stage instead of the standard sit and pose photographs that you would see in an average publication. The minor liner notes could have been better.

title: The First Three Albums Plus More!
text:
This first reissue of the Bee Gees classic albums by Rhino Records proves to be a collectors dream. Not only are "Bee Gees 1st", "Horizontal" and "Idea" Remastered, but each album's song is repeated in Mono and Stereo making for unique sound differences. Each album is suited with an additional CD of outtakes, alternate versions and unreleased material.

The first album contains all three versions of the Bee Gees first international hit, "New York Mining Disaster 1941" as well as alternates of key album cuts. There is also plenty of extra material such as the sixties rocking "Gilbert Green" and the vaudeville-like "Mr. Wallor's Wailing Wall" with Robin going at it with warbling intensity. Robin's lead on "One Minute Woman" proves that it must have been a tough choice of which brother's lead vocal to use on the original album. "House of Lords" contains some nice original storybook lyrics while "I've Got To Learn" brings out the rock and roll the Bee Gees can so deftly handle.

"Horizontals" supplement disc contains the rare "Barker Of The UFO" and other B-Sides such as the whimsical "Sir Geoffrey Save The World" and "Sinking Ships". There's the brilliant Beatles-esque "Out Of Line" and the "Kinks" influenced "Ring My Bell". This disc also showcases original curiosities such as the Middle-Eastern themed, "Deeply, Deeply Me" and the psychedelic "Mrs. Gillespie's Refrigerator". The three Christmas songs are rare and unusual additions, especially for a box set such as this.

The "Idea" second disc contains some alternate songs, along with rare B-Sides, such as "The Singer Sang his Song" (originally optioned for an A-Side release) and the rare A-Side, "Jumbo". Barry belts out the blues on "Chocolate Symphony" and "Bridges Crossing Rivers" proves the Bee Gees were an original band with more than clever hooks and lyrics. Maurice's keyboards and mellotron use is consistently ear-opening. Following in the Christmas foot-steps of novelty songs, the Bee Gees give us two versions of "Coke commercials" released in their sixties heyday.

The liner notes are some of the most comprehensive since "The Authorized Biography Of The Bee Gees", containing detailed month by month history of those first two years, original album artwork and rare photos. In addition, every song is listed with writer credits, place of recording and date of recording. Even the albums label name and copyright number is posted. Can you get more detailed?

Considering that this entire set is completely Remastered and there is ample new material along with alternate versions and outtakes, this is a Bee Gees fan dream come true. It is hard to believe that there is still more unreleased material, but this should satisfy the public as to what actually happened with the Bee Gees those first two classic years. It's a true gift of music.

The set is marketed in digi-paks (half cardboard and plastic), which has proven to be arguably less durable than simple jewel case, but that's a minor concern, all things considering. Excellent liner notes by Andrew Sandoval - a veteran of pop music history.

title: The Album That Topped The Charts!
text: In 1978 all four Gibb Brothers wrote, produced and released the Top Song of the year, "Shadow Dancing".  It settled Andy Gibb into mainstream conciousness as a rock star and teen idol not to be dismissed.  It garnered more hits like, "Why" (released overseas), "Everlasting Love" and the #2 unbelievably beautiful ballad, "(Our Love)Don't Throw It All Away".  The other six songs are strong as well, but don't reach the level of intensity, save for "I Go For You", which was donated to UNICEF.  This album reached number one and the reasons are all in the ear.

title: Pinnacle Of Their Career!
text:
1974-1979 was the pinnacle of the Bee Gees career and creativity. They were the top band in the seventies. So, this collection is a wonderful set with some important items missing. This is the holy grail of seventies music by the biggest band at the time. Never mind whatever is happening with Barry Gibb, Rhino and Warners. This set has its triumphs and miss-steps.

“Mr. Natural” was the first change from the ballad-stuck Bee Gees where producers Arif Mardin and Robert Stigwood heavily pushed the Gibbs into recording something different than the usual ballad and dip more readily into their R&B. Soul music was already in their blood but it was stuck. With Mr. Natural they released three singles, all seemingly odd choices from an album that has great songs. From, “Heaving Breathing” and “I Can’t Let You Go” to the powerful “Dogs” and “Down The Road”, it is a great collection. All their harmonies, songwriting skills are heavily pronounced. Only “Mr. Natural” had the funk that was the turning point but it was a good funk.
*In the UK the album did not chart nor did the three singles, “Mr. Natural”, “Throw A Penny” and “Charade”.
On the next album, “Main Course”, Arif Mardin pushed them harder and they went to Eric Clapton’s Miami recording house, 461 Ocean Boulevard. It was there that they produced some more of the classic ballads, “Country Lanes”, Songbird” and “Edge Of The Universe”, but the R&B and funk got so good it sky-rocketed them up the charts. Sure the country flavored, “Come On Over” was a hit for Olivia Newton-John, but “Jive Talkin”, Nights On Broadway” and “Fanny (Be Tender With My Love” were huge hits. The rise was starting fast. Barry’s newly discovered falsetto started a new qualified sound that helped enormously.
*In the UK the album did not chart. “Jive Talkin” charted #5 and “Nights On Broadway and “Fanny…” did not chart.
The subsequent album was solely produced by the Bee gees with Arif Mardin out of the picture, so the pressure was high. The Gibbs set forth and produced an even more consistently R&B/black sounding ‘white-eyed soul’ album than before. Nearly every song was soulfully arranged with the black Philadelphia sound and it was a huge hit. “You Stepped Into My Life”, “”Lovers”, “Children Of the World” and “Subway” were strong album cuts, but the singles were stronger than ever.
*In the UK, the album did not chart. “You Should Be Dancing charted #5, Love So Right” charted #41 and “Boogie child” did not chart.
“The Miami Years” is an interesting collection from the “Saturday Night Fever” album and other album cuts and singles from that period. This is a controversial album. The songs include the four new SNF from that album along with a Samantha Song hit, “Emotion” (#4 in the UK) - two Andy Gibb cuts, “Warm Ride” and the single “(Our Love) Don’t Throw It All Away” - the B-Side to “Stayin Alive”, “If I Can’t Have You” (a #4 hit for Yvonne Elliman in the UK) - another Bee Gees country chart, “Rest Your Love On Me” (also an Andy Gibb album cut) and an odd B-Side from “Mr. Natural”, “It Doesn’t Matter Much To Me” (a song that has three different versions) and is a typical Bee gees pop ballad. Since “Stayin Alive” was so huge, the 12” version is also included with a strong horn section. All these songs have been released digitally before.

After “Saturday Night Fever” (charting #1) and numerous singles written and recorded by others, The Bee Gees were beyond touchable as the kings of pop radio. “Spirits Having Flown” was a Barry falsetto dominated album with him taking the lead on every song. The dance numbers and disco were gone, but the R&B and funk remained on great songs like, “Search, Find”, “Living Together” and “I’m Satisfied”.
*In the UK, the album charted #1. The single, “Tragedy” charted at #1, "Too Much Heaven charted at #3 and “Love You Inside Out” charted at #13. The song, “Spirits Having Flown” was a hit at #16. Andy Gibb’s version of “(Our Love) Don’t Throw It All Away” went to #32. This is amazing as are the songs.
The disappointing part of this collection is the lack of lyrics, photos or notes. There is NO booklet. The Bee Gees considered themselves songwriters first above everything. And no notes demarking the historic rise of this period is perplexing. This is such an amazing story of pop history the note and photos that could have been included boggles the mind. Who made these decisions? The clam box is typical for reissues now and the five albums are faithfully reproduced front and back, but in cheap cardboard sleeves and not plastic CD’s. The songs that were not previously remastered are done well now. “Mr. Natural” shows new life as do the others.
It’s an historic release of a fantastic period of music and the music makes up for most omissions, but there is still hope that a better collection might come in the future. If not for being five amazing albums, I would never buy this ‘box set’.
*Album and single charts information taken from, “The Authorized Biography” by Barry, Robin and Maurice Gibb as told to David Leaf and Wikipedia.

title: Short, Sweet & An Overlooked Gem
text: Even though this CD barely garnered a hit, "Saw A New Morning" and was poorly received by the public, the concerts were still going strong during this period (1973). Hedging more towards country, The Bee Gees crafted some fine acoustic work here with, "South Dakota Morning, "Living In Chicago" and the upbeat rocker, "Come Home Johnny Bridie". "I Don't Wanna Be The One" and "My Life Has Been A Song" are a tad bit of the old cornball ballads. However, "While I Play" is a Barry Gibb standout cut. Recorded with such celebrated studio musicians as, Jim Keltner on drums, pianist Jane Getz, 'Sneaky Pete' on steel guitar and the Bee Gees own, Alan Kendall, this album is first rate. It is a shame it only clocks in at less than 33 minutes.

title: The Official Poppy Appeal Single!
text: Robin Gibb's last single is an official British release through the Poppy Appeal to raise funds for The Royal British Legion. This revamped version of the Bee Gees 1968 #1 has a slower less urgent feel, but sounds just as emphatic in its appeal. Robin shares lead with the famous "The Soldiers" (Sergeant Major Gary Chilton, Staff Sergeant Richie Maddocks and Lance Corporal Ryan Idzi). Their vocals are just as appealing as any artist covering any Bee Gees song. The B-Side is the instrumental version and showcases the simple yet powerful arrangement of this classic song.

title: Collector's Item!
text: Originally released as an album and cassette in 1976, this collection and a one LP version of 'Odessa' were released to remind people that before "Jive Talkin'" and "Night On Broadway", there was anothor style the Bee Gees were famous for. This album contained the biggest hits from the sixties period ("Massachusetts", "I've Gotta Get A Message To You") through their early seventies period ("Lonely Days", "How Can You Mend A Broken Heart"). All Top Twenty hits with a few #1 hits thrown in made for a nice reminder compilation. Never in anyone's wildest dreams did they think that within one year they would hit their peak (1977) and surpass that in 1978-1979. This is a great set - too bad it isn't available on compact disc, but it is available on this very rare 8-Track tape. Who cares about the audio quality. This is a real keeper!

title: Extensive Collection Of Dance Songs!
text: This is one of the lengthier and more extensive extended CD-singles the Bee Gees have ever done. Only the "ESP" remixes from 1987 are better and that is very hard to find. However, other than the single mix that did poorly on the charts, the rest of the "Paying The Price Of Love" remixes are high-tech synthesized drums and jazzy piano inventions. Its good if you are into that kind of interpretation.

title: Substance & Style!
text: This CD contains four hit singles, although the only one to chart in the USA was "Paying The Price Of Love", a fair, but unsuccessful attempt at 'hip-hop'. No matter. The rest of the album is wonderful. "Kiss Of Life" has an upbeat tempo with a killer chorus, while "How To Fall In Love, Part I" contains some of Barry's most soulful singing. Robin matches this soulfulness with his own on "Heart Like Mine". "Blue Island", a beautifully harmonized ballad dedicated to the children of Bosnia, has an amazing harmonica solo; unusual for the Gibbs. The remaining songs are all high tempo, especially "Above And Beyond" and "Fallen Angel", the latter being one of the Gibbs most danceable songs to date. The big sleeper here is, "For Whom The Bell Tolls", a romantic power ballad that should have been a big hit.
